I didn't have high hopes for Waking Mars going in. I didn't read too much about it, but from what I gathered it looked like your dime a dozen side scrolling platformer. After starting it initially, the game crashed. That was a bummer. Restarting it worked though. Initially the voices did not work, so I thought I was going to be reading the whole game. Another restart fixed that as well. I was happy to hear that the voice acting is this game was well done and not cheesy. I then realized that there is no combat in this game. I assumed all the creepy plants in the screenshots were enemies. The entire gameplay of Waking Mars consists of literally waking mars. You are planting seeds everywhere and starting life on the planet. Some of the plants hurt you though, and there are a few hazards to avoid. I found the simplistic gameplay fun and the biomass tasks rewarding. Character movement felt a little awkward at first, but I quickly adapted to it. Most of the areas you travel in look the same, but I appreciated the environments and ecology in game. The story is engaging as well. It isn't revolutionary by any means, but it kept my interest. The "I'm a funny robot" cliche is kind of tired. I completed all the endings (I think). I finished in about 9 hours, and I was surprised it lasted that long. I appreciate length in games like this.
I highly recommend if you enjoy a chill, not difficult game. The crashing and other bugs were annoying, but restarting seemed to fix them so I didn't mind it as much. There are no jump scares!

First impressions:
When I saw the title "Never Alone" and a girl with a fox on it, I was instantly interested in this. I read up on some reviews and saw some game play on Youtube. When I saw that I could get the main game and its DLC, Fox Tales add on for about $5, I decided to finally pick it up.
I guess I was a little leery about the "documentary" aspect of it, not quite knowing how it was going to work, but, once playing through the game and watching these very short segments of cultural information and footage (they are not boring at all!), I realized to what purpose it all truly was. They set the mood instantly as it thrusts you onto the frozen tundra, surrounded by cold, snow, and vicous predators. You can watch the short cultural segments all at once but I much enjoy them as I'm playing the game. With each new segment that's unlocked, I get more information about the world that I'm in. I view them as cut scenes for the game and helps to set the mood for the next league of the journey.
The game itself is a side-scrolling platformer. I enjoy it very much, and I enjoy the graphics as well. The game is beautiful for what it offers. So far, the controls are nicely responsive. Playing on a keyboard, switching between the characters is efforless and I can pretty much control both characters with ease with only one hand. I just got to the village and I look very forward to more of what this game has to offer.

Steamworld Dig 2 is all about progression. You start the game with a pickaxe and walljumps but by the end you have a jetpack, triple grenade launcher, flaming pickaxe, and all manner of life preserving upgrades.
Movement feels good after you get a few upgrades, there are a few quirks to mining that may tick people off (you can't hit blocks while you are jumping) but taking some time to learn the game if you weren't already a fan of Steamworld Dig 1 will help. Tip: Stand on the edge of a block to hit a block that is one further away than where you can normally hit.
Backtracking to complete earlier caves isn't a pain thanks to the transit system or the constant need for more money to spend on upgrades.
You are heavily rewarded for being on the lookout for hidden passages and secrets. There are caves (puzzle rooms) towards the end of the game which will test your agility, timing, and sometimes patience, yet you always complete one feeling just a little proud.
The visual style is charming and the music is adequate. There is a large variety in visual design for the places you explore, to name a few: nuclear-irradiated underground forest, apocalypse god worshipping temple, and a very cyberpunk-inspired robot graveyard.
I highly recommend Steamworld Dig 2 and also 1 if you haven't already played it, it's considerably shorter than 2.

Some will be confused as to why I recommended this, I will explain why.
Short answer: it is enjoyable to play, but probably wait till more patches come out. A good time to check back on it would be with the next season release happening this summer.
When I bought this game, I was excited for the concept and the game looked graphically decent.
I still like the concept and the game still looks decent. However, the lack of support from the devs is concerning. There are some very severe issues with the game and they aren't being addressed in a timely manner that is comforting to us the players.
One of them (and this is one of the biggest ones) is the game having a sh**ty peer 2 peer system for matchmaking. You are not put into a match based on your skill, and with a competitive game like this it needs to be, instead it prioritizes connection rather than skill. At the same time, having a match being dropped due to one of the players having a bad connection is very common. Sometimes you get connected to a match after a lengthy wait in the que, just to have an error message come up saying that the connection was lost.
A common scenario to see during gameplay is this:
You are in the middle of fighting an opponent. You land a hit that kills your opponent. However, either his connection or someone else’s connection goes bad and the server attempts to reconnect you to the match. It may succeed, but it also brings back to life the opponent you just killed, you are unprepared for him and he ends up killing you instead. It's very frustrating cause you worked for that kill, only to have the game go "Nah, he's back".
A second issue the game is more monetary.
There is an in-game currency known a steel. You collect it whenever you play a match or complete what the game calls orders. You then can use the steel you collected to buy many things for your character. (emotes, skins, effects, ect). However, you can also buy, with real world money, gear that your character can use that helps their stats. Whether its more attack damage or taking advantage of a game mechanic called "revenge" (another issue with the game and how it is implemented) that is supposed to give you an edge if you get gained up on.
The main monetary issue comes with micro transactions.
Micro transactions are the bane of many players existence. For the sole reason that it is a pay to win mentality. You pay for extra steel, so you can then use it to buy better gear. With that better gear, you don't need to be as skilled as other players and it provides an unfair advantage over those who went through the game the normal way.
That being said, as of April 2017 there have been some changes towards these issues. They are slow in coming out, but they are fixing these issues. The issue with steel has been mostly fixed. However, we are still stuck with terrible peer 2 peer and micro transactions.
And yet I still recommend this game, it is immensely enjoyable to play (when it works correctly) and the potential this game has is plain to see if you get past the issues.
Rainbow Six Siege, a very popular game that I also enjoy, also had its share of issues. However, these issues were eventually dealt with and the game is steadily growing in popularity.
For honor has the same potential RB6 has. Just give it time.

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to take control of a cool looking dinosaur and wander around aimlessly while you slowly starve to death? Well, wonder no more, because that is exactly the experience that this game provides!
All joking aside, let me say that I tried very hard to enjoy The Isle. It is a really cool concept, but suffers from terrible execution. I mean, taking on the role of a dino in a prehistoric world and hunting or foraging to survive while fending off other dinos sounds really cool. Except in this case, it really isn't.
Playing the game as a carnivore means you start out as a lowly velociraptor, too weak to kill anything except other velociraptors or the lowest tier herbivores. Okay, sounds a little challenging but that's the fun, right? Well, yes, until you factor in that there are no NPC dinos of any kind. You need to kill other dinos for food, so being able to survive and progress in the game means actually being able to track down one of the few other players on the map, which can be quite difficult as the maps are so large. Even on full servers I frequently starve to death without seeing another living soul or a corpse to scavenge for sustenance. Herbivores don't fare much better either. You start out pretty much defenseless, and despite the lush, beatiful plants growing literally everywhere, you can only eat a very limited variety of plants that can be very difficult to track down. For either type of dino, there are very few ways of tracking down food. I've seen mentions of a scent mechanic, but I have yet to actually see it implmented in-game.
The one thing this game has going for it, and the thing that reeled me in, is that it is quite visually appealing. The environments look and feel like a prehistoric world. The dinos are very well designed and the skins, sounds, and animations look great. The concept and visual design aspects of this title really are good! I have to give the devs credit for that.
Maybe I'm missing something, maybe I'm looking at The Isle the wrong way, or maybe I've just missed the point, but The Isle just doesn't feel like a "game" to me. The progression system feels pointless and arbitrary. It's meant to be challenging but in it's current state it feels broken and dependent on a player base that is just not there. Aside from fending off starvation and dehydration, there isn't anything else to do. The speed at which hunger/thirst meters drop means you are constantly running between sources of food and water, if you can actually manage to find either, which means there isn't even much of an opportunity to explore the environment.
I realize this is still an Early Access title, but it has a long way to go before I would recommend it to anyone. I will gladly give it another shot if there are updates that address the sort of issues I mention above, because as I stated it really is a good looking game with a cool concept that has a lot of potential. It seems like it should be a really fun take on the survival game genre, but in it's current state it is just really unsatisfying.

Gameplay-wise, this is a not too difficult platformer. You have different blocks with different abilities, and you make your way through different obstacle courses with them. At points it can feel tedious, but overall it's solid.
However, this game is really a proof of just how important a strong narrative is. Your block-moving is narrated by a rather charming British fellow; said British dude delivers the narrative in what I felt was a real Hitchhiker's Guide style. The story isn't shoved down your throat, and somehow manages to impart a sense of personality to a game who's characters would otherwise just be "Red Block, Orange Block That Sucks at Jumping, and Blue Block that Floats." You'll care about your little colored squares, and this makes the game's short length even more disappointing.
Overall, I dig it. Solid, if at times tedious, platforming game with a charming story and excellent delivery.

FOR HONOR REVIEW
For Honor is a midieval themed melee combat game with playable charaters from various countries/cultures during the late Medieval period.The three factions in the game are The Knights,The Vikings,and The Samurai.You must join either of these three factions when you start multiplayer,but dont worry the faction just symbolizes what "country" you fight for so you can play as any charater you please.The game has a pleathora of features such as detailed customization with almost all the characters(Except for the assassin and other charaters,they are stuck as female,thats elgaliarian amirite?) various maps with complex twist and turns leading to intriguing encounters on the map(The game also runs like butter which is great).FOR HONOR also has same of the best combat in a melee combat game i have ever seen(im talking better than mount and blade).The combat works to have a counter for any attack or any defense meaning that people who spam attacks can get utterly destroyed in this game giving you know how to parry or guard to counter them.A player who goes for a extreamely defenseive playstyle will also be wreched by unavoidable attacks and timed guard breaks.With all this in mind,the game forces the player to adapt to whatever situation they find themselfves in.The game tries to nerf people who double team poor players by adding the revenge mechanic.If you block enough attacks or attacked frequently several times the player goes into revenge mode which gives them huge bounuses to their health and stamina for a short time.You would think i would recommend this game to everyone right? absolutely not,this game has microtransactions that would enable someone to get gear and level up very fast which creates the one but fatal inbalence in the game.The gameis also is impossible to play at times because the servers are not dedicated,which for a big budget company such as Ubisoft,is disgraceful and spits on the consumers face.The game does have a main camapain and you can play agaist bots with friends which is more stable,but the campain is not memorable in the least and playing with the AI becomes very redundant at times.in short FOR HONOR is a great game smuthered in garbage and human waste...and you'd probably not want to get a bacterial infection.

A game which is beautiful in its simplicity, managing to tell a charming story which is able to make the player feel for the main protagonist and all other characters, although they are just coloured quadrilaterals. It is fascinating how this little red rectangle and its companions feel more human to me than most characters in video games I have played. To further enhance the effect of the writing - through the use of a narrator who lends his voice to express each of the characters thoughts and doing his task superbly - and the clear, simple visuals of the game, there is a wonderful ambient soundtrack, fitting perfectly. Most importantly the platforming and puzzle solving elements never get in the way of the story telling; instead it is used a way of connecting the characters by having them to work together, thus making this game all in all a short, but beautiful and lovely experience.

Stories Untold is a mix of puzzle game and walking simulator and is more of an experience than a game. It is split into 4 episodes and even has a retro Stranger Things-style opening to reinforce the sensation of watching an old TV series. Graphics are intentionally grainy and things clearly take place in the 80s, from the references to the technology. The first three episodes seem completely disconnected at first (in atmosphere, location and even gameplay), but the fourth episode ties everything up.
If you like puzzle games and walking simulators, play this game. It will be right up your alley (though beware that it might feel a tad short for its full price tag, so maybe wait for a sale). Even if you could not care less about the 80s (the story told here is universal enough).
If you only or chiefly care about gameplay in a game, you should stay away from this experience (and many others).

Gun Wings is a shmup/danmaku (bullet hell) game released in 2015 by DEZ Studio. For a cheap price, this game is quite a steal as it offers a challenging gameplay with a unique mechanic for both beginners and veterans alike. Sadly, it has a low replay value due to the low amount of content in this game. Despite being overshadowed by more well-known danmaku games, Gun Wings is still an enjoyable game.
Gun Wings sets itself apart from other danmaku games by featuring a bullet-absorbing mechanic. In short, you are able to absorb bullets with the same color as your character to fill your Charge Gauge. While full, you're able to use a Charge Shot to convert bullets with different colors into points. This seems to be the only real way to score, as there are no advantages of grazing in this game.
Other than those unique gimmicks, everything is commonly found in danmaku games. You're able to choose to control one of the 3 girls available. There are also two types of weapons to choose. Generally, Weapon 1 is the Spread type, while Weapon 2 is the Forward type. Holding the shot button while using Weapon 1 charges your weapon gauge, and releasing it while the bar is full will make you perform a powerful shot. Choosing Weapon 2 will grant you extra homing/spread bullets instead, helping you to cover more enemies whilist dodging. As such, both weapon types are properly balanced to handle the enemies in the game. In the end though, there are not much variations as neither your Charge shot nor Bomb type will change.
While not featuring fantastic compositions, Gun Wings still has several good BGM and SFX in its own right. It might be offputting at first, but it certainly fits the gameplay in many situations.
Gun Wings has good enemies and characters designs. The bullets are easily differentiated from the backgrounds, too. However, the enemies' planes might be hard to see while facing an onslaught of bullets, potentially causing derp deaths. Main menu UI is fairly generic though. As a side note, it is quite common to control girls in Japanese danmaku games. Controlling girls as the ships rather than planes commonly found in conventional danmaku seems to be a hit-and-miss for some people. Though in the end, it's only a matter of personal preference.
+ Cheap Price
+ Accompanied with Steam Trading Cards, beautiful Profile Backgrounds and Achievements
+ Unique bullet-absorbing mechanic
+ Steam Cloud support
+ As a niche little feature, you're able to shoot enemy planes on the main menu.
+ Generous in allowing you to use many continues
+ You're able to continue playing at the stage where you've quitted the game.
-
Bullets travel quite fast in this game, especially during boss fights. While justified by the fact that the density of bullet is lessened, it is still hard to attempt to dodge the bullets.
-
Later levels feel like they belong in the difficulty above them. Even on Normal, beginners will certainly start having difficulty to keep up with the game starting from the second part of stage 4,
- Unlocking Training mode is pointless, as the player who actually need to use it is required to complete the game on Hard first.
- The enemies' planes might be hard to see while facing onslaught of bullets, which might cause several derp deaths.
- Lack of content
- High Score is not differentiated (e.g. by difficulty, girls and weapon types)

First off, I just want to say how awesome that the capability of playing the Half-Life 2 series with my best friend is indeed impressive on it's own. The way it's working now is definitely good. However, I didn't say perfect.
Now, forcing a single-player game to be co-op can be done, but playing the whole way through, bugs and glitches are bound to be present, so be wary! Some examples are both of you spawning without Gravity Guns, sometimes a neccessity for certain parts of the game, cutscenes sometimes having distorted and hilarious model glitches, some lag spikes, one specific level that you actually can't progress through so you have to load it individually, and other small things. That being said, this game still runs rather smoothly.
Another thing we found later in the game is the difficulty. With 2 people, it's understandable that the enemies would pose a bigger challenge than with one. That being said, although a challenge is welcomed, sometimes even Easy difficulty can't save you from the swarms of almost endless Combine waves and their auto-locking high-damaged weaponry. Some experiences will cause some foul language to emit, truthfully.
Regardless of these small drawbacks, I didn't pour 22+ hours into this along with my best friend with a terrible experience. Quite the contrary, actually. I loved taking on the world of City 17 and all it's secrets by my own wits, but to take it all on with one of my best pals was an even more enjoyable time to be had. This mod is created very well for two players, such as respawns, battle sequences, and just general gameplay works very well. It's clever, works well, and challenging.

If you find the game too hard or too easy, you can adjust the difficulty by changing some server variables in skill_mod.cfg. For example, if you set sk_dmg_take_scale3 to 2.5 and sk_dmg_inflict_scale3 to 1, the enemies will be very dangerous, but at the same time not spongy.

Wow...I was not expecting this... It's dark, it's creepy, it's depressing, it IS a psychological horror...but it's worth it.  Without spoiling it, here is my review of
.
In an unknown limbo-like world, you awaken.  Strange figures, stranger people with even stranger minds, and a single question...to dig or to not dig?  The choice is yours...or are there other choices with other consequences?
The music is beautifully composed by Edwin Montomgery, who crafts music that fits the eerie mood within this short work (which should take you about 30 minutes, give or take a few).  The most beautiful and captivating is the main theme, simply labeled
...haunting, yet beautiful.
The art-style to this game is very simplistic, though it feels amateurly done...but to fit the eerie mood of this title, it works.  It's supposed to feel wrong, because the world is wrong...or is it right?
This whole game is a short experience that makes you think.  In the end, you realize how much a choice that belongs to you truly matters.  It's free, it's short, it has achievements.  You can't go wrong here.  My only complaints are that the text auto-scrolls a little too quickly for me and the text can be hard to read (White on white.  Dark grey on grey/black...)
8/10 I chose to dig.  It was my choice.

The depths of ships, weapons, armor, etc is staggering.
The only thing I don't like about this game is that it takes forever to do things when you get to the upper levels.  Can only upgrade 1 building at a time, can only equip items on one building at a time, ships can take over a week to construct, etc.  It makes the game drag on at the upper levels.  But getting to those upper levels is a lot of fun.
I've also seen a lot of Negative reviews saying you have to Pay To Win.  This is a bunch of BS.  I haven't paid real money for anything and have had no problems.  Sure, I can't complete with the people way above me but I'm not supposed to.  Farm resources, upgrade, buildings, repeat.  I've never had to sit and wait because I didn't have enough resources.  Rather I wait because I'm waiting for a building to get done upgrading.  Sure, you can pay lots of money to make things finish faster but that's true for any game of this stye (e.g. Clash of Clans, Game of War, etc).  Or, you can level up more slowing and learn as you go and not have to spend a dime.
Try it out.  You'll probably get hooked.

is a FPS horror game, coming from the indie developer, Microblast Games. It was the first of Microblast titles that I've tried and I'm more than positive that it's gonna be the last of their titles that I'll ever be playing. At this point, we are used to indie horror games with poor environment design, broken or nonexistent stories and grindy rendering but this game takes the badly done horror game concept to a new level.
From the tedious scraps of unhinged narrative, I'll try to present a baseline for the story. In a somewhat western setting, we have an old and bitter hunter called Walden living alone near the Ravin Town. Supposedly, he's been to a shooting years ago and lost so much blood, that it was a miracle for him to be alive to begin with. After the incident, Walden locks himself into his cabin, never to interact with the people of Ravin Town for years. On a fateful day, he leaves the cabin and notices an unholy darkness covering the area. He takes his gun and decides to investigate, only to discover the townsfolk to be butchered and the town itself in ruins. Thus, his journey to take revenge for people he has never interacted with begins.
Graphics give you the feeling that this game should be hailing from 90s, not only 2 years ago. Objects are riddled with odd texture bugs and the environment design is tediously repetitive. Camera view is either too dark to see anything or all infested by blasting neon colors of blurry visuals as if Walden is in a bad LSD trip. There are no character animations in the cinematics; only close up recordings of character models in obscure positions, standing solid in really weird poses. They are quite spastic. I think the developer had no idea how to animate to begin with, so tried to sell this piece as an artistic choice.
There is no voice acting at all. You are presented bits of narrative in between chapters, and the narrative is not only riddled with grammatical errors: it is horridly bad and meaningless. No definitive storytelling, no cause-consequence relation, no logical dramatic arrangement. Only over dramatic statements with absurdly empty undertone thrown around.  The setting itself isn't consistently logical to begin with. You'll go through your village, a mountain highway, an abandoned ship (?), a dungeon (wtf???) and a cemetery without meaningful story arrangement for any of these places. And that ending... well, you gotta love last minute enforced plot hooks and this one takes the cake with those! I literally fell out of my chair laughing the minute I heard the name of the main villain.
Game dynamic itself is so badly broken, with no tension build up necessary for proper horror at all. You stumble upon jump scares every 3 minutes - consisting of either obscurely rendered close ups of monsters or some graphic images in negatives. All of those jump scares come up with ear♥♥♥♥♥♥caliber sound effects though, which is straight annoying. You run around with a mini-map directing you towards the next mission and either grab keys or shoot at some nugatory monsters. Walden's gun is probably the most useless weapon in video game history, by the way. It is a rifle - which Walden carries like a pistol - that takes 8 seconds to load. This is somewhat alright if you are facing a single monster but it becomes hellishly useless when hordes of monsters are running after you in the following chapters. Considering you have no sprint option; you run around, fire and run around some more while you wait for the gun to reload and repeat. That is all you can actually do in this game.
Is it scary? Nah, it's so bad that it kinda ends up being good. That's why I completed the game to begin with. I was amazed at every little thing that I've stumbled upon, getting curious how worse it could become by the end. Atmosphere-wise, the soundtrack is the only good thing about this game. Consider yourself buying a music CD for a dollar. So it's good purchase in the end.

Secrets of Grindea.....how do I say this in a way that people will think, "Wow, this games sounds good, I should play this?" Well I don't know honestly. But I'll try my best!
Okay so here we go! Secrets of Grindea, first look before buying it I though to myself, "Eh, this games doesn't look too bad. I hope it's not like every other rpg I've played." So I bought this game knowing that it was still early access. What a gamble!
Okay now lets talk about my first reaction.I booted up the game, (do people even say that anymore?) and was welcomed by a nice and catchy theme song, one I still cannot get out of my head. I proceeded to select stroymode, singlplayer and boom I was in the game! I played through the intro, the first boss, the second boss, and the first two areas. I fell in love with the game because it was really unique and interesting, let's not forget about fun!
Fighting! The combat is smooth and not boring, plus the cartoonish style makes it enjoyable. Two handed swords are slow, one handed swords are fast like they should be and wands make magic dealy but don't hurt much. The skills they have add a sort of customization to the game that can make a player speicalize in what they want wether its a tank role,  supportrole, or somwhere in between. Magic in the game is fun though some of the schools of magic,which are ground, wind, ice, and fire, are better than the other this can lead to a broken system where one school of magic in the game is never used making it pointless.
Another great feature of the game is the pets! You got to love the pets they're soo CUTE!!! *cough* *cough* On a professional note pets are a fun feature that really adds to the game. The best part of the pets is  that you can feed them certain items that boost your overall stats. This is great like I said previously but broken becuase the game itself has no protection against hacking. You could hack in a billion speed potions if you wanted to and feed them to your pet which makes you OP as heck and can ruin the gaming experience.
Lets talk about the gameplay, so far in the game at the date this is written you can only play the game up to Mt.Bloom, which is okay because the game is still in EARLY ACCESS. The monsters can be challenging at times and make you upset. I don't know how many I died by a monster and said," I am going to destroy your face!" I am looking at you Halloweed. The leveling system is pretty fair with a great exp rate through out the story. The bosses are nice with a unique challenge for all of them, you have to create tactics and learn the bosses attack patterns before you can triumph over them. WARNING: Prepare to get creamed by some bosses!! The level spikes in each area you go to are mostly appropriate besides the third area which can get a tad tough becuase of certain enemies. ( I swear the Yeti species hate me >.> )
What is an RPG without multiplayer, am I right? Secrets of Grindea goes about there Co-op experience just fine. You can play story mode with friends or play Arcade mode with friends. There is no match making feature currently in the game so you have to go make some friends to play multiplayer. During the story mode when you play multi player whoever is the host of the game it's their story, so don't expect to pick up where you left off in the story mode with your friends if you try to play solo. When you play solo it is your own story on the specific character. The Arcade mode is where you traverse through floors trying to make it to the end, if you die you start all over and loose your gear. There is a warning though, this mode could potentially ruin the story line.
Overall this game is really fun and I reccommend that eveyone gives it a try. I rate this game, IN ITS CURRENT STATE AS OF 6/26/2016,  8.5/10 Paws

For Honor is a midieval themed melee combat game with playable charaters from various countries/cultures during the late Medieval period.The three factions in the game are The Knights,The Vikings,and The Samurai.You must join either of these three factions when you start multiplayer,but dont worry the faction just symbolizes what "country" you fight for so you can play as any charater you please.The game has a pleathora of features such as detailed customization with almost all the characters(Except for the assassin and other charaters,they are stuck as female,thats elgaliarian amirite?) various maps with complex twist and turns leading to intriguing encounters on the map(The game also runs like butter which is great).FOR HONOR also has same of the best combat in a melee combat game i have ever seen(im talking better than mount and blade).The combat works to have a counter for any attack or any defense meaning that people who spam attacks can get utterly destroyed in this game giving you know how to parry or guard to counter them.A player who goes for a extreamely defenseive playstyle will also be wreched by unavoidable attacks and timed guard breaks.With all this in mind,the game forces the player to adapt to whatever situation they find themselfves in.The game tries to nerf people who double team poor players by adding the revenge mechanic.If you block enough attacks or attacked frequently several times the player goes into revenge mode which gives them huge bounuses to their health and stamina for a short time.You would think i would recommend this game to everyone right? absolutely not,this game has microtransactions that would enable someone to get gear and level up very fast which creates the one but fatal inbalence in the game.The gameis also is impossible to play at times because the servers are not dedicated,which for a big budget company such as Ubisoft,is disgraceful and spits on the consumers face.The game does have a main camapain and you can play agaist bots with friends which is more stable,but the campain is not memorable in the least and playing with the AI becomes very redundant at times.in short FOR HONOR is a great game smuthered in garbage and human waste...and you'd probably not want to get a bacterial infection.

Personally I have tried many metroidvania games and I don't really like them. They're neat and kind of clever but not really that much fun to play. The only metroid games that I do like are the original ones.
Steamworld dig 2 is a game that I do like. Not because I'm a metroidvania fan or I like the steam world games per se. I like Steamworld dig 2 because it's so well made. It's made by people who loved it. It's a child that grew up in a happy family.
Exploring is fun. Upgrades feel meaningful and let me explore new places and reach spots I couldn't before. There is some sense of excitement when I get a new toy. For me this is the meat with metroidvanias. Exploring and feeling good about upgrades.
The game is fairly easy, at start at least, but it's challenging enough that I can't just play without thinking. Which is a very good thing. But it's easy enough that I don't have to restart from the starting area every 5 minutes because I died.
I would warmly recommend this game to people who enjoy metroidvanias and like the steam world game series.

One of the most well-known point ‘n’ click adventures games from the end of the 90s, Broken Sword is still an enjoyable story almost twenty years later. It may suffer from blocky animation and dreadful voice quality, but the thrilling plot and the quality of the puzzles will always make it a true classic.
Broken Sword: Shadow of the Templars is Revolution Software’s best-known and probably most successful game, known for its sheer length (easily over 12 hours for a first-timer) and good puzzle balance.
The story can be described as a modern conspiracy theory thriller featuring an everyday man getting drawn deeper and deeper into the Templar myth, while trying to solve an ancient riddle and staying ahead of his murderous pursuers. To do his he travels all over the world from Ireland to the Middle East, aided by a sassy photojournalist and a bunch of stereotypical, yet cartoonishly entertaining supporting cast.
The puzzles are what you expect from a classic adventure game. They are complicated, sometimes convoluted, not too often logical, but if you get yourself in the typical adventure game mind-set, most of them can be passed with little difficulties. (Except the goat. *censored* that goat.)
Although Broken Sword features some exceptional backgrounds and decent animation, it is not without technical difficulties. Especially when it comes to audio: most of the dialogue sounds as if it was recorded in an underground chamber, and none of the actors do a particularly good job. Also, in the Remastered Edition there is an additional prologue segment that just does not fit into the game at all.
But these are really minor complaints compared to the sheer amount of fun one can have with this classic adventure title that is still one of the best of its kind even to this day.

I can't quite blame you if you have not played Waking Mars. With the sheer number of 'Metroidvania' titles out there anymore, this one does not immediately stand out with its somewhat drab visuals.. However, even an hour with the game will expose it to be something different and, perhaps, deeper than your standard game of this genre.
Perhaps the biggest difference here is the means of progression. Most science fiction games are incredibly light on science with the setting being a pretense for futuristic gunfights with monsters. Waking Mars on the other hand feels more authentic, placing you in the role of a scientist who peacefully navigates the planet of Mars. Instead of fighting the inhabitants of the planet, you are rebuilding a dead ecosystem through careful management of the organisms in a manner that vaguely recalls Pikmin. The mixture of these lite strategy elements with Metroid-like exploration delivers a game that is honestly like nothing else on the market at present. Despite the non-violent premise, the action never feels boring with a complex world, interesting puzzles, and solid platforming.
We likewise get a thoughtful story that avoid most of the common video game cliches. Instead of an evil mastermind or mindless monsters driving the conflict, the struggle of the characters is one against the harsh environment of this alien world and is, to a lesser extent, questions of ethics. There is a surprising amount of drama here, and it makes you wonder why more games can't try this sort of man vs nature type of approach. This is hard sci-fi for fans of authors like Isaac Asimov and Arthur C. Clarke, and as someone within that camp, it's incredibly satisfying. Waking Mars also gets points for its diverse cast that lacks even a single white male character and stars a British-accented Asian man and an African-American woman. The characters in this game could have come from basically any demographic, but developer Tiger Style went out of their way to represent groups usually not seen in games. The dialogue is smart, furthering the credibility of the science in the game, and the voice actors fit the parts they were cast very well, sounding comfortable and intelligent.
All in all, Waking Mars is a refreshing game in just about every way, and while it's not an entirely obscure game, due to it appearing in a number bundles, it deserves to be mentioned much more frequently than it is. With this game now being five years old, it does not seem that Waking Mars had the influence on game design and storytelling that it should have, but it stands as a shining example of how science fiction video games can be every bit as insightful and thoughtful as other media. The fact that it is an entertaining game to play, as well, is the icing on the cake. I can't recommend this game enough to anyone looking for something different.

Waking Mars is a fun puzzle game.  The description tries to sell it as a platform game, but I would not call it a platformer.  You have a jetpack with infinite fuel.  So you fly around, with no real danger to yourself.
The goal is to grow the ecosystem in each area of a cave.  As the ecosystem grows, you unlock more rooms.  Some rooms have new types of plants or creatures, so as you move forward in the game, the ecosystem changes slightly, but with the same goal.  Grow Plants, and Unlock More Caves.
With basic gameplay, the story is actually what pushes this game over the edge.  As you move forward into the cave you learn more and more about the cave itself, and it runs into a great Sci-Fi story.  Nothing groundbreaking, but just a nice story.
Achievement Quest - This is an easy 100%.  Most achievements are based upon learning about the different plants in the game.  If you can't seem to find research about a plant, a quick google search will find what you are missing.   Also, getting the largest ecosystem in each are is important, as it will unlock other achievements later.

Another pleasant surprise from my backlog. Despite how it looks and what the Steam tags say, this is neither an adventure game nor a platformer, but more of an exploration puzzle game. You are exploring a cave system on Mars, gradually discovering various interacting lifeforms of a once-thriving ecosystem. It's up to you to restore some of this ecosystem by gathering seeds, and planting them in places where they're most useful. For instance, by providing food for some critter, which you need to multiply so you can feed them to another critter, producing fertilizer so you can grow bigger plants.
The ecosystems are not particularly deep (which is good, since otherwise they'd get overwhelming), but deep enough that it's a joy to see a restored one at work, with plants waving around, and critters going about their business, eating and getting eaten.
You move around with a jetpack with unlimited fuel, which is fun. The objectives never felt overwhelming or unfair. There are no time constraints, and you don't need great reflexes. The story is entertaining, and the characters have a lot of personality.
All in all, I had a lot of fun with Waking Mars. If you want a game that is both relaxing and engaging, this would be a great choice.

So, having just played through the game with two friends,my immediate impressions are kind of mixed. I absolutely love what the developers set out to do, the game succeeds in its goals of educating players about a unique culture and way of life, and I think that the way in which the game was developed in collaboration with an alaskan native people is a beautiful approach, that will perhaps inspire other developers to do similar things.
Younger generations are becoming increasingly native to digital media and environments, so it makes sense to adapt and preserve as much human culture as possible in a format that will appeal to a modern and future audience. So, for that reason alone I would reccomend this game.
On the other hand, I found the game itself uninspiring. The controls were unreliable, the puzzles and traps were irritating, rather than providing the player with a satisfying sense of accomplishment, there were physics glitches, and although the interaction between the girl and fox was novel at first, it was not enough to set it apart.
Ultimately the game itself undermined the story and atmosphere, and I couldn't help wondering if the overall experience would be better if it was stripped bare of the cumbersome mechanics, a thought echoed by the friends I was playing with.

Steam world dig 2 is a metroidvania and nothing more. If you're familiar with this genre you know exactly what to expect.
Personally I have tried many metroidvania games and I don't really like them. They're neat and kind of clever but not really that much fun to play. The only metroid games that I do like are the original ones.
Steamworld dig 2 is a game that I do like. Not because I'm a metroidvania fan or I like the steam world games per se. I like Steamworld dig 2 because it's so well made. It's made by people who loved it. It's a child that grew up in a happy family.
Exploring is fun. Upgrades feel meaningful and let me explore new places and reach spots I couldn't before. There is some sense of excitement when I get a new toy. For me this is the meat with metroidvanias. Exploring and feeling good about upgrades.
The game is fairly easy, at start at least, but it's challenging enough that I can't just play without thinking. Which is a very good thing. But it's easy enough that I don't have to restart from the starting area every 5 minutes because I died.
I would warmly recommend this game to people who enjoy metroidvanias and like the steam world game series.
*disclaimer* metroidvania is a game where you explore a non-random world (often in 2D) and gradually upgrade your character's abilities and gain access to new areas and secrets *disclaimer*

An FPS with an original spin--guns and magic.
Engaging story with original and unique combat. Guns and shadowy demons? That sounds awesome, and it was.
The Darkness 2 is a hallway shooter but with a twist--you've got the power of Hell on your side! And the story keeps you interested the whole way through--especially the characters. The voice acting and writing is on point. From the first cutscene, I was hooked. From the first firefight, I was having fun and enjoying this game.
You shoot guns--quite a few, actually. You use demony magic to fight bad guys. You upgrade your weapons and powers which is fun and satisfying when you learn a new ability and become more effective at killing.
The boss fights are fun, the combat is solid, the story is great. If you love to shoot guns, want a solid story, and like to just see chaos and gore, The Darkness is for you.
The game is a bit short, and it ends on a cliff-hanger, and there are a few "Oh this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" moments in the game, and maybe the combat gets a little repetitive, but overall, it was a great experience and I was able to enjoy the game as a whole.

This game it is not a complete disaster, even though I do not personally recommend it.
It's not recommended only if you've played the original The Darkness on console.
In any case: this is what I call a missed opportunity. The Darkness II tries to continue the adventures of the unlucky Jackie Estacado, tormented by the death of his girlfriend Jenny, with The Darkness itself to spice the things up.
As written in the comic books, Jackie is the carrier of an antique evil force that humans passed on from generations to generations constantly fighting its counterpart, the Light. In this chapter we'll se a mysterious cult who is pursuing him to steal his mystical power. Unfortunately, the plot is the weakest part of the experience, and it is a shame, because the gameplay is satisfying. Being the Darkness is a good experience, you can feel like an overpowered creature who can slaughter and kill everything it breathes. Although there are few powers that  you can play with, they're fun to use. Also the environment interaction is pretty good, in fact you can take various object with your demonic limb and throw them to your foes with enjoyable and squishy results. The game encourages you to do so in many different ways, as you can earn Dark Essence (XP) to unlock powers and abilities.
The gunplay instead, it's sufficient: no recoil, the weapons sound and feel all over the same. The only difference you can tell about them is the fire ratio. It suffers from the modern FPS syndrome: high difficulty = enemies have lots of health points, so going further with the game usually is just trying and failing with a poor challenge. At least there's not regenerating health because you have to eat hearts from dead enemies in order to replenish it.
There is also a limited multiplayer coop mode with 4 characters to choose from with different skills and abilities, but it adds nothing to the experience, it's just another excuse to shoot everything. Maybe this mode was built in order to extend the game length, because the singleplayer campaign is very short (about 6 hours).

A lot of people would apparently disagree with me but I feel like there must be a nostalgia factor that I'm missing out on. Objectively speaking, this game would have been fantastic to experience in 1996. Plenty of witty banter and dialogue, and fluidly animated cutscenes. It's damn impressive how much animation is provided for random interactions that don't even advance the story in any way.
But that's sort of the problem. At first it's not a big deal- there are a few characters to interact with, and a few items in your inventory. It's neat to experience the combination of interactions. Until both categories grow larger and you suddently have to start asking every single person about every single item. Some interactions are over quickly, some take minutes to complete as the NPC tells you something inane. Speeding through interactions can become clunky as you watch your character stumble around the screen with their pathfinding alorithm only to show up at their destination and shrug their shoulders, a way of telling the player 'nope, that won't work.' Fine, but you could have just said that to begin with.
I was absolutely shocked to find out that apparently this Director's cut had substantial sections of dialogue missing. With each syllable of spoken dialogue I pray that the game takes mercy on me and makes it the last. And you guys wanted MORE?
You might argue that the superfluous dialogue is optional. You don't have to ask everyone about everything. Well, sometimes you do. Sometimes when the puzzle solutions are completely arbitrary you'll wander around for ages in hopes of obtaining a relevant clue, only to find that you forgot to use that one item on that one thing that gives you that one other thing. Of course you need to take a tissue full of facepaint all the way to syria, to polish a statue, to sell to a tourist, to get fifty dollars, to buy a cab ride. You might also argue that I have a short attention span. I want to know which one of you enjoyed pounding through minutes of dialogue with the shrill-voiced woman in the hotel just to get that room key.
The dialogue is not really witty. I laughed a few times because of how stupid it was.
The story is arbitrary and convoluted.

Gameplay: The story telling ability of this game is fantastic. You become easily connected to these blocks imply by the narrative. The story it tells is not a complex one, but is certainly engrossing. With a new mechanic/character being introduced very frequently, the game doesn't get repetitive before it ends.
Visuals: The minimalist style of this game is well executed. The basic shapes of the characters match the basic shapes of the level, while the colors of the character pop with brightness. It's very easy on the eyes, and is generally fun to look at.
Audio: The narrator takes the spotlight as the only medium of storytelling. His voice is comforting and certainly easy to listen to for the entirety of the game. The game has few sound-effects, but this works in its favor as it stays consistent with the minimalist theme. The soundtrack is really decent and well composed, but can get repetitive after a while.
Replayability*: This is where the game really lacks for me. I could beat the game within 4 hours, and that was not even speed running. I found myself getting bored of the game when trying to play it a second time. Although the minimalism adds a flavor not seen a lot today, it leaves for the player to miss the first time. Also all the puzzles can be solved in a very finite amount of ways.
Point where I'd say you have to buy it: $1.50
*This varies A LOT from person to person, so only rely on this category from me if you've agreed with my other reviews' replayability sections.

I deeply regret discovering the Broken Sword series as late as I have. I am a huge fan of the classic adventure game genre - always have been thanks in no small part to my father, who has fond memories even of the original Zork. Broken Sword should have been a huge part of my life years ago, and while it wasn't, I couldn't be happier that it is now. Amazing 2D art style, fantastic writing and voice acting, some of the best puzzles the genre has to offer - all of it is just... breathtaking. I finished the game in one long, sleepess night full of clicking and thinking, fully immersed in this world presented to me. The story is wholly unique and spectacular and the characters are beautifully constructed. At this point, I'm gushing, but really, this game really shocked me at just how well put together it is. I highly reccommend it, both to fans of the genre and fans of a good old fashioned story. (My one complaint is that, for the Director's Cut version, they recorded new dialogue for Nico. However, the rest of the game uses the old dialogue from the original game, and the transition between the two qualities of sound can be rather jarring.)

(*sigh*) Another experimental game I really wanted to like, but let me down by the end.  It starts off really strong, but the last chapter is frankly trite and anti-climactic.  What's worse is, the "twist" -such as it is- gets revealed very early on in the final episode, and then it spends the next hour of gameplay beating the player over the head with it.  It goes on for so long that I started expecting a twist on the twist, but nope.  Then on top of that, the generally pretty good text segments devolved into games of "guess the exact phrasing the designer wanted you to use," to the point I had to look up a walkthrough a couple times only to confirm I was doing the right thing but with the wrong verb.   Also, compounding my irritation with the last chapter are some severe framerate problems that (due to all the lighting/lens effects) made it extremely unpleasant to play and very nearly caused me to just shut it off.
Fixing the technical issues and improving the text segments' parser would help the game from a playability standpoint, but nothing will solve my irritation with the direction the story took and how hamfisted the delivery became.

Very simple, yet beautiful game. The narrative is simply perfect and even though the game takes only 4 hours to complete, there is more story and emotion to it than you would expect. The authors managed to give soul to colored rectangles. You cannot even compete with that.

As it stands right now, I am recommending this game based on what it is in it's current state.  Be aware that it's an early access title, so it will (hopefully) continue to change and improve in a lot of ways.
That said, I'm really impressed with the game for what it is.  So what I'll do is just list the pros and cons here and I'll update my review with each patch to see if they address some of these things that could be universal issues.
PROS:
- A ton of fun
- Easy to pick up the controls and get used to gameplay
- Leveling system encourages you to keep playing more matches
- Different maps that are immersive and a blast to creep through and hunt down your enemy
- Awesome artifact system
- Plenty of weapons and equipment
- Not necessarily Pay 2 Win despite what people think.  Yes, you can hurry up the progression of leveling and getting gold, but you can't really purchase OP weapons with it that you can't get without playing some matches and leveling up, etc.
CONS:
- No option for friendly fire off (aka, you can damage your team mates even by accident) * THIS NEEDS TO BE FIXED, it ruins the experience when someone decides they want to be a funny guy and start team killing.
- Match making is a bore, it can take anywhere from 1 minute up to 20 minutes depending on how picky you are.  It's also somewhat unbalanced.  You can be paired with people who are clearly higher levels than you.
- Shotguns need nerfed big time.  You can practically use it as a sniper rifle to an extent.  At least add some sort of spread on the shots.  Right now it's too OP.
- Some of the features such as leveling up and skills aren't explained as well as they could be.
- Poor chat interface, ie; you can't even really chat with team mates before the match starts to organize strategies (if you wanted)
- Some stuttering issues and frame drops at the start of maps (sometimes) - but it's early access and it's still being optimized.
- No Free play (so it's not like an open world STALKER game, but I don't even want to compare to it STALKER games aside from that it has anomalies and it's gameplay mechanics feel similar) * This is alright honestly, it's not a big deal to me.
SUGGESTIONS:
- It would make the game so much more difficult if you forced everybody to turn off the crosshair.  Some people might disagree with this - but I LOVE a first person shooter that actually kills the crosshair option completely.
Anyways, it's free to play.  So the least you can do is give it a shot.
I plan to continue playing regularly and I'm excited to see what other features they come out with and what they fix / change.
As a whole, I feel like the game needs balanced a fair bit.  But it's free to play, so you might as well give it a shot.
EDIT:  To the people who's comments I've deleted because they say I can't make a reivew for the game based on my low play time: it's a free to play game.  If you need to read a ton of reviews to make the call on playing something that costs you nothing (except time), then maybe you shouldn't be considering the game in the first place.

You will have to use your brain, but will also have a lot of fun doing so, and there is always a feeling of satisfacion when you hear the audio cue indicating that you solved the puzzle.
The strongest thing about this game is it's story and everything related to it. You play as George Stobbart, a young American lawyer, and Nicole Collard, a French journalist, who get involved in a murder investigation that ends up leading them on  a quest to find an ancient Templar treasure. The story is pretty interesting and it did keep me hooked to the screen despite not having a shocking twist or big reveal. A nice take on the Temlpars before the Den Brown era and the time when Templars have become,in my opinion, so overused that they have become annoying. It is a simple story of mistery and adventure, but quite an enjoyable one. Mostly thanks to fantastic writing and voice acting. It is a joy to listen to all the characters and their conversations, and the game is filled with entertaining side characters.It is truely amazing how much work was put into every character that comes in contact with the protagonists, to the point that you remember each and every one of them and some of their lines. The game has a serious tone most of the time, but just enough humor to keep a smile on your face. Conversation that include both George and Nicole are especially fun, since their common dialogue is some of the best in the game, and they have quickly become one of my favourite game couples.
An excellent story, great writing, awesome and fun puzzles. What more do you need for an excellent p'n'c adventure?

Warning: Long!!!! TL;DR at bottom!
At first begins a normal text adventure, which I was expecting. I love text adventures. But this came with a twist. They put time designing visuals and audio cues. Which really amps up the production quality. Even the slightest door creak, can make it that much more immersive. Whoever did the sound design, well done. SPOILERS AHEAD - It is not all that it seems, later on, as you progress. It gets a bit more challenging.  Towards mid/late game you find out more of the story and without saying too much about it - I want to say that I am absolutely mind♥♥♥♥ed. And I love it. How common it is to say it was a "such a twist" moment. But regardless of that common phrase, it's something unexpected, and absolutely taking it to the next level in terms of quality. What began as a normal text based adventure, turned into an intelligent immersive text based game with an outstanding story behind it. Some might realize it sooner, some later, like myself (for story elements) which is totally fine. The game's pacing is good as well. Minor spoilers: What I find ingenious is that what I felt like "Oh god I have to do *that* again?!" or "Ugh i have to go back around... look at that thing over there..." or "what did that say again?" -- Later on, you'll realize all of those tedious moments, mattered. Things changed. Recalling those previous events showed a level of understanding for the player. I felt scared, sad, hopeful, and intrigued, to list a few emotions during the playthrough. Again, I want to point out how well the sound is. Recordings, transmissions, etc, the quality was amazing (of course, in my respective opinion).
MY ONLY ISSUE - Is the length. I finished in approx. 2 hours. With only using help for the morse code bit. I did stumble here and there on a few parts, which is fine. Challenge is welcomed. I am only wishing I had more. More logs, more chapters, more information. If not on the same story arc, a new one should be created by  the developer, because they have made something outstanding in a market for text adventure lovers.
Would I reccomend this game? I would DEFINITELY reccomend this to anyone who likes text based adventures! I read occasionally and enjoy "choose your own text adventures" and found this absolutely thrilling.
Final thoughts / TL:DR = Fantastic quality all around, only complaint: Want. More.
Would I buy from this developer again? Yes! From someone who hasnt' heard of them at all. They have exceeded and went above and beyond my expectations (in terms of a "text adventure") - They showed that they can make something. And that something is of great quality. I hope there is more to come. I've said this already but seriously, the sound is phenominal, really made it immersive for me.
edit: other thoughts from other reviews: add tweaking settings such as optional fps cap - add optional text speed adjustment - press space bar to show all text (rather than waiting, some were impatient, i thought it was OK) - Add in "help" text to those who don't understand commands /// seems like it would fix a lot of your negative reviews.

Pros:

-Real time fleet battle
-Rotating events on a regular basis
-Many sectors you can jump too

Conclusion:
It is fun as long as you manage to fight alliances on similar or slighty better tech level but the latest emergence of mega alliances like UA, IVC and others make it very hard to fight a single alliance.
This game could be a lot of fun but it is on a downward spiral of becoming unpleasant to play for players who do NOT want to spend real money into this game.

I find this to be a very enjoyable game overall and I would recommend it.  I was big fan of RTS games before becoming a predominantly console gamer.  I tried a few mobile games (Boom Beach, Clash of Clans, etc) but found there was nothing "Real-time" about it.  Enter Vega Conflict, a game which I originally found on my phone.  I took a liking to this game due to the fact that the combat was in actual real-time, not like other games where you can only choose where to attack (and possibly redirect them slightly).  There is a lot of depth to the combat in this game, with many different ship classes, weapons, shields, and upgrades to choose from to customize your fleet.  Fleet size is limited, which I feel helps with fleet diversity and forces players to fly their ships with some skill, rather than the smash my army against your army mechanics that many RTS devolve into.  The game features monthly events that provide new technology and ship types if you are able to kill a large number of computer enemy fleets.  This game is also a social experience, as I'm sure most MMO-esque are. With all of that said, no game is perfect, and this one has some flaws.
This is a free-to-play game that leans on timers; that is, you can either use your purchased "coins" to speed up processes (building ships, repairing ships, building your base, etc) or wait out those processess out for free.  This can create some instances where you are facing an opponent who will spend his real-world money to continually repair his ships to attack and defeat you, regardless of your respective skill levels.  The monthly events are geared toward high-end players who have been playing the game for a long time; as a newer to mid-level player, there isn't very much for you to do during these.
Overall, my experience with this game has been more good than bad and I recommend RTS fans give it a try.

Essentially from the get-go this game is broken down to it's core principles, it is ment and designed to be a skill based medieval battle game and so far it is a "choose the most OP character to win game". To start off the battle system involves a three-way directional attack/defend control system, you simply point your mouse to your desired direction and either wait untill an attack lands or you can attack by using your LMB/MMB/RMB for different attacks. Unless it's just me, this system either seems to be bugged or sometimes it seems to simply just not block the incoming attacks, I have played with friends and they say they should have hit me and I even notice my character not being hit, when it looks like I should be. Secondly the major flaw in this game is the character choice, all of the three factions (Samurai, Viking and Knight) all have four character choices of which are the same type of unit just in a different faction. So essentially there are only four character choices which is not many for a game that costs £40. The problem with the characters is not the limited choice it is the fact of how unbalanced they are, the Viking Beserker type unit does not rely on skill, if you were to play this character then you would simply look for any kind of ledge/cliff and consistantly push your opponent towards it using a "shield bash" move which btw is difficult to block or dodge and then use your charging move to launch them off of the cliff killing them instantly. Well you might ask, "Why can't we just attack the Viking while he shield bashes?", well my friends this is no easy task as any character can anti-shield bash which essentially returns the shield bash back to the original "Shield basher" and then the process repeats of shield bashing to a cliff. Then finally you might ask "Why don't we just anti-shield bash him?" well children, the problem is, is that the Viking just as so many other characters has unblockable attacks which also btw take half your health off in one fell swoop, literally. So to summarise you cannot kill this character or any alike (every character) untill he messes up by not pressing a key. So much for a skill based combat system.

I've played over 100 hours on the xbox one and just recently bought the game again on PC to participate in more tournaments.
Conclusion:
Its a great game but not for everyone. If you are willing to put in a lot of time to be competitive this game is definitly worth the money it is alot of fun has a VERY high skill cap and an active community with regular tournaments, however if you are looking for a game to play more casualy you probably wont get any fun out of it as you will be stomped by people who understand the meta which is not tought well in any of the in game tutorials if you are not willing to put in the time to learn these things or dont have a friend who can walk you through it, it can be frustrating to get past the steep learnign curve. Also, since there is no split screen you can't slowly learn the meta with local friends before going online like you can in most fighting games.
There are only 2 or 3 game modes that have lasting appeal, if you are more interested in the 1v1 2v2 or 4v4 elemination style game modes you can get a lot of time and fun out of this game, however, if you were drawn in by the massive moba esque control point capturing game mode you might be disappointed to find it lacking depth and getting old pretty fast, thought that is far more subjective than the rest of my review.
ADDRESSING SOME COMPLAINTS
The game is a great non conventional fighting game with a strong meta and playerbase. People who complain about balance are generally being a little picky, while no game will ever be perfectly balanced and there are certainly charcter tiers in this game aside from one or two character who are just bad most characters are balanced very well you just need to know how to play against specific playstyles. As for the complaints about microtransactions I dont really understand what people are complaining for. I got the game at launch and at this point I've already goten everything for every I want for every character that I play without spending any money or even specificly farming money in game, i was able to unlock all of it by just passivly playing the game.
People also complain a lot about the connection issues and this is a real problem though not as big a problem as some make it out to be. I personly dont have much issues with disconnections but the P2P servers can cause some frustrating moments in a game that relys heavily on reaction. That being said while this is the area that needs the most improvement I dont think it is game ruining. If i had to estimate I would say 1 out of 10 games you play you may experience a moment or two of lag that gets you a bit tilted, then 1 out of maybe 15 or 20 game you play you might experience a dc, though most disconnects arnt from server side but from rage quiters. (I have 300mbs down internet for reference)
OTHER COMPLAINTS,
this game has a VERY steep learning curve its easy to think you have a handle on what you are doing since it offers mulitple tutorials however there are absolutly essitial points of meta that are left out of all in game training that can leave you at a massive disadvantage without you even knowing you are missing something.

Now I completely missed the first game, I still haven't watched any gameplay but after seeing SteamWorld Dig 2 in the new releases section on Steam memories flooded back of those old mining/exploration games. That, I feel, is the main book of this game. Even with the amazing visual fidelity,  animation quality and quality platforming gameplay the exploration and mining genre is perfected here.
Controls are tight, well you would expect this I would even make the claim they surpass even Spelunky's controls by comparison. Primarily it really is strictly a gamepad game however it can be played on keyboard and have key binding options.  If you try using a switch controller it even shows the visual buttons on the HUD which is something rare to see in a game.
Visually at first glance it might fool some people due to its layout, but it is some of the best visuals I have seen in an indie game in many months. Performance is smooth, if you meet spec requirements you have nothing to worry about, 60fps, with some minor support for 21:9 (cannot test properly only by stretching window mode).
Sound design is great,  there is no spoken dialogue apart from gibberish designed for each character but it suits the style the developers were going for. Sound is dynamic in various parts of the game, when you run out of fuel for your lamp you will hear the general ambiance soundtrack die out also leaving you will a reminder that you have to upgrade your fuel consumption.
Estimations for gameplay time are likely 12-14 hours for one playthrough,  however for me I would estimate over 55 hours. I guess I'll find out exactly how many hours when I do complete the game and achievements.
10/10

Ah, Broken Sword. I have heard a lot about this series as the years passed and now I had the opportunity to play it myself. Normally not a fan of point and click adventures I have to say that given the age and history of the game I really like it. Some cliché story elements to be sure but what really struck me was how incredibly witty this game can be. I have too many scenes to quote that if I would merely start I would quickly fill several pages worth.
The puzzles also stood out for me. Decoding messages and moving puzzles around in a fashion that I have, to my great disappointed realization, never encountered in any form in any modern game. The puzzles are simplistic in nature but brilliant in execution and are genuinely tricky even for a puzzle veteran like myself.
The hints system is a gem for people prone to getting stuck. It levels small suggestions to more direct hints to giving you the solution outright if you as for enough hints.

I hated having to slowly struggle through this interface in order to march along the rails towards a telegraphed, downer ending.

This is a fantastic gateway drug into gaming. It's intellectually stimulating, nonlinear, nonviolent, and rewarding.
The game has you traveling between chambers and establishing interactive ecosystems while negotiating emergent behaviours. Trying to raise the combined biomass of all your creatures is a delicate balancing act that has you weigh the utility of a given plant against its adverse or beneficial effects on the microcosmic chamber ecosystem. The challenges can be tackled nonlinearly, and while they can be cheesed—by taking resources from other chambers—the satisfaction of establishing a self-sustaining and propagating food web and growth pattern is pretty damn great.
The visuals are bright and fantastic, with it's parallax-heavy and vaguely paper-like aesthetic giving the whole experience a much cheerier tone than you'd expect from 'trapped underground on mars by yourself.'
The story is inspiring, if a bit slow. The AI companion is absolutely hilarious. It's a good way to spend an afternoon (or more, if you're interested in getting the special ending).

I came to this game with negative expectations and it won me over.
I bought this severeal years ago and assumed it would be just a reflection of that time's 2D indie boom. I was wrong though. The gameplay is easy to understand and the game is sincere in it's core. It wants the player to have a sense of discovery and exploration of an alien world in a different planet. And it works.
The game is mostly simulation mixed with platforming. You investigate elements/creatures and their behaviors. Then you manipulate them to serve you and make the environment thriwe by making the elements relate with each other.
The game has metroidvania type elements where you are granted new tools to fix old areas and you are required to do purposeful work with the tools. You get to know the areas well. You are having some part in creating your own experience in the game and the game not forcing you to progress linearly.
There are certain parts though where the next steps aren't obvious and can cause some frustration. These were relatively short lived though and not really a big thing. I actually enjoyed it because it made me more attached to the puzzles the game had to offer and got to know the mechanics better.
Only negative parts for me were:
* Collision detection
--> Got stuck in ground once but just once
* Too much effort into making your robot companion ART funny
--> The game is self aware of it being tedious though
* Visuals look like cut & pasted jpegs
--> However the use of assets were good and created memorable events and rooms with the assets even though the style wasn't really up there with the rest of the game
* Achievement unlocking
--> I had troubles getting 0CT0 achievement even though I had gotten the upgrade from it
Overall I enjoyed what the game had to offer and was impressed how the game used it's mechanics and visual design. I didn't feel I wasted time while playing this game.

Warning, possible spoilers below.
I'll start with the good things about this game, as I can tell the developer put some sort of effort into it. The music was really nice, it actually helped provide a creepy atmosphere for at least the first 3 or 4 levels, I don't know if it continued as I gave up upon seeing the werewolf for the first time and realizing that the gameplay doesn't improve in the slightest.
Now for the bad. First point: Gameplay. I like a good story, but even more important is the gameplay, how you interact with the world and it's creatures. The gameplay here consists of move objects, fire one shot every ten seconds or so if you're in combat, strafe at a ridiculously slow pace against enemies that move slightly faster than you, and walk along a very linear path while enjoying acid flashbacks that will hurt your eyes.
Second point: The story. It's not that bad honestly, but it doesn't really make up for the terrible gameplay which is what I was hoping for. I can pull through a rubbish game if I enjoy the story it's telling me, or vice versa but here I got nothing. No voice acting, which was fine as it's clearly low budget and bad voice acting ruins games for me nearly every time. So you learn the story from the little subtitled bits that appear in between chapters. Not a problem here, I love subtitles as I often miss things without them. However, I do like it when things are spelled correctly and the overall story makes sense. The biggest sin is that it tells you things that just happened, or puts you in danger then solves the problem for you in the next sentence. Perhaps it improves as you go along.
Third point: The visuals. No, I don't mean the graphics. I've been gaming since the late 90's, graphics are not what I look for in a game and here they're servicable. When you can see anything, that is. The game is so bloody dark I couldn't see more than 4 feet in front of me. This actually added a bit to the atmosphere, but at the cost of frustrating me to the point where I very nearly gave up on the prologue. Also, the acid flashbacks I mentioned earlier. They were just unpleasant, broke immersion, hurt my eyes, and actually made some of the jumpscares less effective.
Fourth point: Jumpscares. I'm a naturally nervous guy, I startle very easily. Thankfully the jumpscares here were weak enough to provide just the right amount of tension for the first few chapters. They come very often though, so it gets a bit repetitive. Nearly♥♥♥♥♥♥myself at the start of whatever chapter it is when you see the werewolf for the first time though.
Overall, I bought it for 54 cents Canadian and got roughly half an hour of semi-enjoyment out of it. Not bad really, but I could've put the money to better use. If it's dirt cheap because it's on sale or you've got a coupon and some money to burn, go for it. Otherwise, just watch The Fragnostic's video for it. I got more entertainment from 5 minutes of his video than from playing this game.

Secrets of Grindea is an amazing experience single player, and even more fun with a friend... or 3!
With a playstyle similar to The Legend of Zelda: A link to the Past for SNES, the game is familliar to old school gamers. The aestetic appeals to a wide variety of gamers young and old. The gameplay is fun, very addicting, and will have you trying different character builds, and *Grindeaing* for every item, card, and achievment in the game!
Story mode is fun and with amusing and quirky dialog at times.
The highlight of this game, and the greatest challenge, is the Arcade mode - where you try and compete for the top single run score in the world by adventuring through room after room, floor after floor where the environment, monsters, and bosses reflect the story mode progression. This is no easy task, and will have you coming back run after run to upgrade your camp and gain more perks to give you the edge you will need to reach #1!!
All in all, if you like simplistic action rpgs with puzzles and rewarding combat prowess, then just BUY this game.
The best part is that at the time of this review - the game is still in beta and is not even fully complete - but still worth every single penny, and then some!
