Used to play this game long before it came to Steam.
As for a browser game (and it's a browser game after all) it's very solid and packed with stuff.
You have construction, research, combat.
Can't call it a budget 4x game, for there is no exploration element.
You have ship editor, which, to some extent, allows you to customize your fleet. Various equipment, both researched and acquired through blueprints will help with that.
And you have real fleet PvP, although only in 6vs6 max format. But it's very real and feeling cool. Seeing a couple of frigs destroy a full fleet of battleships for the first time would make you **** bricks.
Also base assaults are interesting. There is no impenetratable defence, but if you lack in skill, you'll have unpleasant moments assaulting clever enemies.
And couple of words about the community. It's nice if you don't behave like a **** in your own sector. Don't attack, don't steal cargo unless it's marked "free" in chat.
So, to summarise.
Pros:
1. Base construction and planning
2. Ship customization
3. Nice graphics and art
4. Cool PvP
5. Microtransactions are really not necessary to play
6. If you are nice to community it'll be nice to you.
Cons
1. All the features of a F2P browser strategy game are present (long building time, microtransactions make life easy etc)
The game is definitely worth trying.
Oh, and not to forget the possibility to play on Android and IOS.

Let me qualify here, I like this game quite a bit and I think it does deserve all the praise it recieved. So why the negative review? Well for one, Steam doesn't give me the option to have a neutral review, and two I want to give potential buyers some reasons as to why they wouldn't want to buy in. Most of the negative reviews don't really do that, at least not in detail.
I've been following this game for a long time, a lot of love has gone in to its development, and it really shows through the quirky spritework. The problem with the development is that it's just been so painfully slow that I can't recommend spending $15 on it at this point, because the desire to check back in after a few months when nearly nothing new has been added fades away after over two years; and that's how long I've had this game. It was first released for beta purchase around April 1, 2014.
Over the course of two years, the story has essentially gained one new dungeon (of which there was only one before) along with a marginal amount of content that shows this game is going to be in development for many more years. The content that's there is good, sure, but it's not so stellar as to justify playing through the story more than once or twice.
The real mode that seems to add playtime to this game is its arcade mode, which is roguelike in nature, and requires a good understanding of enemy/boss patterns to do well in. Players play through two floors representing each area in the story mode, complete with enemies from said area, and have no chances to heal except at the end of each floor. Despite having numerous floors and all of the enemies from the story mode, it's pretty light on content in terms of roguelikes. There are unlockables and such, but they only give minor advantages, and as a result adding more floors to the mode seems kind of pointless in its current state. Even after over two years of going back to this game I struggle to reach the 7th floor of what must be over 14 at this point. There isn't much incentive to bother trying to reach those floors either.
So should you buy this game? Well that depends on how patient you are. After two years I'm pretty burned out and don't see myself playing this game for a long, long time. If you think you can wait for what could be 5 years to play a finished product and want to support the developers, then by all means get this game. If not, keep an eye on it and pick it up a few years down the road when it has a more justifiable amount of content to offer.
Edit: Thanks for all the support guys, since this review got so much attention I want to add a little more.
If you're worried about spending $15 on a game that won't be finished, don't be. This game is a safe buy in my opinion. Even though the development has been very slow, it has been extremely consistent and the team behind this game definitely has what it takes to finish the job. Secrets of Grindea has been in the works since 2011, and the quality of the content in it has only improved since. Their
has a weekly recap that is posted nearly every week without missing a beat. So if you're interested, definitely keep an eye on this game, because it is one of the better early access titles out there, despite the slow development speed.

A solid point and click adventure, and a very famous one as well.
First of all: If you are into the genre, I recommend the game, but there are certainly points of critisim to make.
There are some really stupid plot holes, as well as unbelievable character developments. Fe.: Certain drawings are wrong or differentiate from the dialouge popup to the actual character model. A window had a hole cut into it from the outside on a lower part of it then from the inside. Some solutions to puzzles wouldnt be solveable in reallife.
. The characters mostly act on pure coincidence rather then on common sense, making it hard to sometimes solve puzzles for no reason other then "because". One puzzle from the directors cut to mention here, you gotta solve chivered letter and one letter only accurs ones at in the entire letter, as a signitur, on its own. If you place all other characters correctly, the last one remaining is the signature which is: "X."..... but you have many letters from the alphabet left that are not used, so really the signiture could be any of 5 or 6 different letters.... Yet your character only accepts "the one true solution".
As in other p&c adventures your  main characters show no hesitation of just stealing useless crap (and holding on to it) for no reason at all (fe. tools from toolboxes, random cloth pieces, a toilet chain, plaster, and a towel), while being the good guys (in deponia fe you are at least a "i dont give a ♥♥♥♥" kinda person, while you are playing good people in this one). Of course most of theses items are magicly important 20% later into the story, but there is no way the character could have ever know that days beforehand.
Simply put, the motivation of the characters is basicly non-existing. The entire premise of the main plot is based on the main character being near a crime when it happend. His thinking: I gonna solve this murder..... BECAUSE! THATS WHY! Justice... and stuff.... i guess?
Finally: The new story elements are hidden from niko from the actual main character, for no apparent reason, just so they developers woulndt have to rewrite parts of the original game. Its rather clumsely pasted inbetween the first half of the base game.
Aside of this story flaws. The drawings are acceptable, yet you can clearly recognize the new content of the directors cut due to its higher resolution and as mentioned above, does sometimes display slightly different clothing etc.
The higher resolution options sadly dont include a 16:9, the game is locked to 4:3. But thats to excuse due to a original release date of 1996 (afaik).
Now to the actual gameplay:
The puzzles are nice, not repetetive and sometimes very challanging. Yet some parts are just not correctly explained or hinted during the storyline. One part especially points you towards a ceratin location (both in dialouge and the diary) but actually wants you to go somewhere else entierly, without the directors cuts addition of the hint system this wouldnt be solveable at all. This situation happens about 2 or 3 times during the game, but only onces its a clear mistake of the devs (or translators maybe?).
Other then that the directors cut adds new puzzles and doesnt just rehash older ones, as well as adding new setpieces and animations.
Despite my review sounding rather negative the overall experience of the game is very good. I recommend this game, for genre lovers that is. If you dont like point and click adventures, what are you even doing here?
If you like them, nothing tooooooo wrong with this. Flaws? Yes. But have you played monkey island 2? Same flaws.

I think people are majorly overreacting. After about 100 hours, I have had a positive experience with the game. Connection issues are annoying, yes, but they're not as bad as people make them sound. With my high quality internet, I have yet to disconnect from a game myself. A lot of what people think are disconnects are actually just people rage-quitting because there is no penalty for leaving a game early. When the host is the one who rage-quits, that's when the problems occur. The game has trouble resynchronizing under a new host. I'm sure this will be worked out over time.
The game is highly skill based. Possibly the most skill intensive PvP game I've ever played. As you level up through the multiplayer, you acquire new gear with different stats. You CAN purchase the in-game currency, steel, to get this gear early, but does so is just a time saver. Anything you can buy, you can earn through play. Even the cosmetics that people cry are too expensive aren't that bad. If you doing all the daily orders (which are typically easy to complete), you can earn around 1500 steel every day. Having played only 100 hours (not that long for a game like this), I have competitive gear and have a few cosmetics I like. I have NOT spent any money on steel. You also get steel for completing the campaign and training modes.
I think most of the people who are leaving negative reviews on this game are just upset because they're bad at this skill oriented game. Some stuff is out of balance, yes, but the developer has recently stated that they'll but putting out changes WEEKLY. That's impressive enough for me. And if the multiplayer is as bad as people say it is, I'd still recommend the game for its well thought out story mode.

Broken Sword is a fantastic game, and the director's cut edition certainly attempts to improve upon it, but some of the attempts come over as rather half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and not well thought of.
The game plays like a typical point & click adventure game. You search for objects and interaction points in the environment that the objects can interact with. Unfortunately, the object interaction is rather two-dimensional. Where monkey island used verbs (e.g., 'use X on Y', 'look at X', 'push X', 'pull X', 'talk to X', 'open X', 'close X', 'talk to X'), the interface of Broken Sword is very much simplified.
A left click performs the main action on a target, while a right click inspects the target. The main interaction is whatever the game deems you should do to the target. A door gets opened, a person gets spoken to, a button gets pushed. This removes a bunch of interactions, while streamlining the gaming process. Furthermore, it makes it very easy to just try out every object on every target if you are stuck. Five objects on 1 target result in 5 actions, yet 9 verbs for 5 objects on 1 target results in 45 actions, forcing you to think rather than just to try.
The gameplay in the DC edition has been further simplified. For instance, actions cannot lead to player death anymore. Instead, the character will inform you that what you're about to do is definitely not a good idea. Objects are highlighted on the screen, so they're very easy to find. While carefully examining the screen makes you think about what objects would be interesting to inspect, highlighting the objects removes this entirely. While it can be cumbersome, I personally feel it is part of the game and do not consider this an improvement. At the very least, this should have been an optional setting we could enable or disable.
Hints are certainly a good addition to the game. Nowadays with the easy access to walkthroughs, the temptation is too large to just ruin the game for yourself if you really get stuck (it keeps getting easier and easier to resort to a walkthrough). Hints will help you out, but still make you think. This is an excellent solution to the widespread availability of walkthroughs.
Talking to NPCs in the game is done by using avatars/player faces (or however you want to call it). I'm not a big fan of those, as I prefer the old method where text was displayed above the character in a distinct color. This is probably just nostalgia speaking, though, so I can hardly blame the devs for making this alteration.
The DC edition has more scenes than the original, and that's fantastic. Unfortunately, it seems not all of those scenes are voiced by the same characters and at the same audio quality. In some cases this is really noticable, even without a good set of headphones. The extra scenes are very welcome, though, especially if you are a big fan of the series. It just feels like the developer either did not know how to prevent inconsistencies with the content (e.g., different graphical styles that clash, and audio quality and voice differences) or approached it in a very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥way.
While the game is worth the asking price, I'm drawn on whether I would recommend the director's cut edition or the original. The DC edition has the advantage of being on the steam platform and having extra content, but it also adds some aspects you simply cannot disable that diminish the gaming experience.
As a result I will recommend this game only because the original is not steam. It is a shame, though, that they did not allow you to switch between the original and the DC edition in the settings. In that case, the game would have gotten a more certain recommendation from me, and most of the criticism would be trivial.

All the negativity for this game is astonishing. I think it all stems from the fact people enjoy this game, so much so that the bugs are more noticeable. If I don't like a game, I move on. If I love a game like this one, then yes I want all the kinks to be ironed out. The state of the game bug wise has vastly improved since launch.
Pros:
- Gameplay: It's unique and brings in aspects of multiple genres (fast paced like an fps, strategic like a moba, and in depth combat like a fighting game), and does it well.
- Graphics: it's beautiful, especially if you can manage to run it on ultra
- Customization: out of the box there's quite a few different characters with a healthy amount of unlocks to make your hero unique. There's room for more in depth customization but then again when isn't there?
Cons:
- bugs: or "tech" needs to CONTINUE to be addressed and fixed
- network: disconnects, although not very prevalent for me now, still exist and are annoying
- Steel: in game currency is slow gaining, and the prices  of skins are quite high, which promotes buying (with IRL money) steel packs.
Conclusion:
Awesome game. I'm hooked. As long as Ubisoft continues to communicate the issues they are working on and follows through on them, I'll keep playing. Make it less of a cash grab and that will promote long term play as well. Can't wait for competitive.

Waking Mars is a fantastic puzzle platformer, but it's entirely story-driven, and is more reliant on its narrative than its gameplay. While the gameplay is rewarding and engaging, it's not particularly difficult. The game is extremely forgiving. There is quick-travel to any discovered location, deaths are meaningless, and every decision you make can be reverted. Even if you missed the special ending, you can simply load your file from the final location and try again.
The plot is compelling, and the art is beautiful. The entire story is fully voice-acted, and while that feature alone has merit, the quality of the acting is the game's biggest letdown.
The entire game can be completed in a single setting, and there's no replay value. But for what it is, it's worth recommending.

Having just finished my second playthrough (this time with the Hard Mode mod) I feel informed enough to write an accurate review of this game.
For me, Frictional Games have been the shining example of how to realise video games as a legitimate and effective form of story telling, this is why when I think of Frictional the first thing that comes to mind is 'Story' not 'horror.' The horror genre to me is associated with pure shock-value rather than story or atmosphere, and in this sense SOMA (along with FGs other games), is not horror. If you want horror I suggest the Outlast series or something because this game is not that.
For me, SOMA is a dark sci-fi which plays on the deep philisophical classics of conciousness, identity and what it means to be human in order to craft its narative. Is it our physical composition that makes us human? Or is it our conciouss mind? This is the question that I was continually asking myself when for days after I had finished the game.
The level design is masterful as always with FG capturing the claustrophobic WAU-infested corridors of the underwater deep sea reseach station just as well as the musty dungeons of Brennenberg or the cold mysterious rooms of The Shelter. SOMA does away with the health system of previous games; if a monster catches you'll first be knocked out and if it gets you again then game over. This is definatly an excelent feature as the game can loose alot of tension if the player is forces to repeat a sequence.
One of the two major critisisms I've seen of the game is that although the player is forced to make choices at certain points, these choices do not have any real long term consequences. I however believe this is niether a flaw nor a missed opportunity. It forces the player to really think "What would I do in this situation" rather than "how can I get the best (or worst) possible ending.
The second major critisism is that the enemies, although terrifying in appearence, become tedious obsticles as they can be effectivly avoided rather easily. This has been a problem for all Frictionals games but SOMA does take it a step in the right direction by fielding a very diverse range of enemies each requiring different tactics to avoid. The devs manage tension very well in SOMA with periods of terrifying danger been broken up with spates of almost peaceful exploration meaning there's no 'desensitization' to the atmosphere which was a problem for me in the Penumbra and Amnesia series.
To wrap it up SOMA is an amazing narative that relies on a chilling atmosphere and disturbing plot rather than cheap scare tactics and is absolutely worth the buy for anyone who enjoys story more than actual gameplay.

Waking Mars is a unique take on the Metroidvania concept.  You play a trapped scientist exploring an subterranean Martian ecosystem, and the only way to survive is to learn how the mysterious organisms coexist and manipulate those relationships to progress through the cave.
You have no weapons, tools, or keys, except for the seeds of the creatures that surround you, and each room requires a different combination of organisms, planted in fertile soil, to survive the unique conditions there and open the way deeper into Mars' crust.  It is not a fast-paced experience, but it is rewarding.
It is easy to recommend this game, but it is harder to decide to whom the game is best recommended.  It's nominally an action platformer, but both the action and the platforms are in short supply.  I think it's a management game more than anything else.  You have a supply of seeds, and a series of challenges to overcome with that inventory.  Some rooms will produce surplus seeds for you; others will require seeds from elsewhere to be completed.
Then you get your hands on the self-propagating pH-altering spores and things get a little frantic while you try to meet your goals without your carefully balanced rooms disintegrating.
The story is well written and the voice acting is excellent.  The characters are skillfully realized.  The graphics are pretty, for sprites, and the music is good.  The gameplay has some rough edges, but nothing worth a thumbs down.  Mostly you will get information about new species that you don't think you've earned, and whenever a cutscene gets triggered you lose control of your character.  I never got dumped into magma or similar danger, but I think it could happen.  Fortunately the penalty for death is essentially nonexistent thanks to a robust autosave system.
If you're into management and puzzles, this one is worth checking out.  It's not really for action platformer fans, though, unless you are interested in seeing the concept dramatically deconstructed.

Let me sum up The Darkness (1) for you(Just in case you didn't play the first one): The player takes the role of Jackie Estacado (voiced by Kirk Acevedo), with the story presented as a future-narrative on the present events observed by the player. On the eve of his 21st birthday, Jackie is targeted for assassination by "Uncle" Paulie Franchetti (voiced by Dwight Schultz), a New York Mafia boss, following a failed task to retrieve money for the latter. While hiding in a cemetery bathroom, the Darkness (voiced by Mike Patton), an ancient demonic force that has inhabited his family for several generations, awakens within Jackie and slaughters the remaining mobsters, with the benefit of Jackie becoming the possessor of seemingly unholy demonic abilities that work only in the dark. Using these powers, Jackie proceeds to destroy Paulie's business by killing his biggest drug peddler, Dutch Oven Harry (voiced by Richard Leighton), and burning down the slaughterhouse where he stores his money. In retribution, Paulie and his main enforcer, Captain Eddie Shrote (voiced by Jim Mathers) of the New York City Police Department, kidnap Jackie's girlfriend Jenny Romano (voiced by Lauren Ambrose). They take her to the orphanage where Jackie and Jenny grew up and murder her in front of a powerless Jackie, who is unable to save Jenny due to the Darkness deliberately restraining him.
Jackie then commits suicide out of sheer emotional stress, finding himself in the Otherworld, the realm of the Darkness, which is home to patchwork undead beings in World War I outfits fighting each other and physical manifestations of the Four Horsemen. He meets his great-great-grandfather Anthony Estacado (voiced by Kirk Baltz), who reveals that it was he that brought the Darkness into the family and tells Jackie how to free himself of the Darkness by invading the castle in the Otherworld and facing the Darkness there. Jackie is interrupted in his journey through the Otherworld and brought back to the living.
Once he recovers, Jackie determines that he must dispose of Captain Shrote before he can face Paulie. After failing to kill Shrote at his apartment, Jackie steals a briefcase containing illicit goods in Shrote's ownership from a Turkish bath that is used as a front by his corrupt police officers. Jackie rigs the briefcase with an explosive and sets up a meeting with Shrote at Trinity Church. Jackie heads to the meeting to kill Shrote, but he is instead captured by his men following a shootout. After overhearing about a shipment of drugs that a Chicago mob is entrusting to Paulie to handle from one of Shrote's officers, Jackie triggers the explosive, killing Shrote and his men along with himself. Jackie re-awakes in the Otherworld and lays siege to the Darkness's castle with Anthony's help. Anthony is mortally wounded in the attack, but before he can tell Jackie the last steps needed to free himself from the Darkness, the spirit pulls him away.
Jackie faces the Darkness and surprises it by willingly being taken by the Darkness's power, allowing him to fully control the spirit back in the real world. However, the Darkness tells him that while he has control now, each time Jackie takes a life, he will become more consumed by the Darkness. He lays an assault on the drug shipment, causing Paulie to flee to the safety of a lighthouse mansion for fear of retribution from the Chicago mob. Jackie takes advantage of a solar eclipse to raid the mansion and finally kill Paulie. The Darkness revels in Jackie's murderous spree, and fully envelops Jackie.
In the epilogue, Jackie finds himself in a dream, lying on a park bench in Jenny's arms. Jenny explains that they are only allowed a few minutes to be together one last time to say goodbye. Jackie tries to ask how, but Jenny just quiets him, allowing them to enjoy the last moments together before Jackie wakes back up with the screen fading to black.

Picking up not long after the first game, Image and Form's SteamWorld Dig 2 sees you playing as Dorothy, who appeared in the original as a merchant.
On the trail of Rusty, the original game's protagonist, Dorothy ends up falling into an ancient mine, where she finds mysterious technology that upgrades her and ultimately defeats the first boss, Fen, who ends up joining you in your quest, albeit somewhat reluctantly and sarcastically.
A metroidvania game set in a steampunk world mixed with the Wild West, the game blends these three genres perfectly, the music and world design in particular standing out.
The main map, which is an enormous cave set below the city of El Machino, is packed with loot to smash your way to, varying from simple gems, junk, and rare loot. But keep in mind that the rarer loot, while much more valuable than the generic loot, takes up significantly more space. You'll also find yet more upgrade stations, giving you various abilites, including the ability to run and shoot explosive blobs fueled by water.
Inside the main cave are even more caves that are optional for you to explore, the end result usually being finding one of the many secret room or the rarer loot, vital if you are aiming for 100% and to have every single upgrade unlocked.
Being a metroidvania game, SteamWorld Dig 2 has a huge map that will have you backtracking fairly often upon acquiring the necessary upgrades. Like in Hollow Knight, it updates as you progress through the game but unlike that game, you don't have to track down the mapmaster to fully unlock the map for that particular area, instead it is unlocked from the start, making traversing throughout the game simple. It also shows you exactly how much of the map has been unlocked, incredibly useful if you are intent on fully exploring.
Combat is rather simple, which is just fine. You can't jump on enemies as that hurts you (even cacti hurt you, despite being a robot), but you can use the basic attack or if you want to be more tactical, lure them under a heavy block, weaken the dirt under it and watch as they get crushed. Or you can go for a more ranged strategy: drop down so they are at the same level, hit them with an explosive blob and let them die a fiery death, or... you can just run them past them if you really don't want to fight.
In summary, SteamWorld Dig 2 is a better version of the original, while being its own game at the same time. If you love your metroidvania games and don't mind doing a hefty amount of digging, then I highly recommend this game.

Having played the original SteamWorld Dig in ~5 hours, SteamWorld Dig 2 is a welcome sequel with more of the same gameplay you know and love.  Amazing atmospheres, simple to follow storyline, superb soundtrack and ultimately easy to grasp gameplay (controller recommended!).
I completed SteamWorld Dig 2 in 7 hours, having "silver star" all categories save Wealth, which was Gold.  64% of secrets discovered.  This should kind of elude to how compact the game is and how there is not much replayability once you've completed it - similar to its predecessor.  I also felt the game was much simplier than the first; the puzzles were not very difficult and the combat was easy.  These are not meant to sound negative - just know this going in!
As a major highlight, the game possesses a new upgrade system focused on "tool mods."  Throughout the game you will buy or find Upgrade Gears to be used on your tools, which give specific perks - with better perks costing more gears.  What makes the system great is that these gear's being spent are never permanent and can be swapped between other mods any time you are in town.  It makes for great change in strategy and play styles.  There are also some interesting secret tool mods to be found, such as one that causes your enemies to explode when they die, increasing the overall game challenge.
A great platformer and "mining" game with a storyline to boot; though truly, I had hoped this sequel would carry along with it a non-storyline mode that just involved mining infinitely for profit, but alas, will need to fulfil this desire elsewhere.
Pick it up!  If you enjoyed SteamWorld Dig, you're guaranteed to love this second instalment.

Just went through my first playthrough. (Knight difficulty)
Wow. Holy poop. What a game.
First, there is no shortage of shmups in indie gaming. From your arcade classic Raiden clones, to your side-scrollers that are influenced by Steel Empire - you can't type the word "indie shooter" in the search bar on Steam and not find at least a few dozen decent games that can satisfy that itch for a few bucks and a few hours. It takes something special for a game to stand out on it's own in that genre.
Enter: Gryphon Knight Epic.
If you've been gaming for a long time, right off the bat you'll recognize SNES-style 16-bit graphics. Not some cheaply-made pixel art to rush out an idea and sell it. The game's art is freaking gorgeous. Serious love went into this by some very talented artists.
I highly recommend an XBox360 controller for this game. The full support is super fluid and very responsive. Usually I favor KB&M over controller, but certain genres make the exception.
The lore of the game is really well done. Simple, to the point, and doesn't try to take you on some fanciful journey or make you read boring texts. There's just enough there to keep you interested and then get back into the action. That balance is a very overlooked aspect of retro-influenced games but can be a make-or-break for players.
The challenge isn't complicated - scroll to the left or the right at your leisure and take out enemies without losing too much health or dying. The checkpoint system isn't unfair at all if you die, either. I should mention that when you die, you definitely feel like it was your fault - not the game's (usually, but I'll note that below*). It's up to you to dodge and maneuver just like any shmup at then time your shots. There are three different difficulties - Squire (Easy), Knight (Normal), and Epic (Hard). For achievement hunters, you can't get most achievs unless you're playing on Knight or Epic - so get those thumbs ready!
*NOTE: I wish there were some way to turn off the Dash rune. Double-tapping a direction to try and fine-tune my position has made me take damage I wouldn't have otherwise taken and lead to a death or two. That's my only gripe.
The weapon variety is awesome, but honestly I didn't really feel any need to use anything but the starting crossbow maxed out and firing charged shots (on Knight difficulty - could be more of a factor on Epic, but I don't know). I think there are about 10 different weapons total? But along with that, you have potions, runes to discover and level up, and squires (little dudes that help you out) to tailor to your play style.
There is so much to explore in this game that I fell I've only scratched the surface. You're pretty much guaranteed to like this game if you like shmups. I'm in love with Gryphon Knight, one of the most satisfying indie 2D arcade-style shooters I've ever played.

I have always wanted to own a proper F1 game. The only ones I owed were F1 2001 for the Xbox (don't get it, it sucks), and F1 2011 for the 3DS. I never got a real good one until now.
F1 2014 is my first real Codies F1 game. 2011 for the 3DS was just an expirament. And it seemed to have failed, because we don't see anymore 3DS F1 games. Coming from that game, the handling of the cars were different.
2014 in my opinion is my favorite F1 game, with 2013 coming right behind. Lots of people who want to get on the yearly Madden boat with F1 games decided to put a lot of similarities between '13 and '14. Yeah, they are similar, but vastly different. Codies said that '14 didn't have a lot of effort put into it because of their focusing efforts on making F1 2015. Apperently not enough effort. '14 is the best F1 game for PC, and so far, '15 is your only choice on new-gen consoles.
So what changed? Well, several new tracks come in, both brand new and returning to the '14 season. Sochi, in Russia, Bahrain, under the night lights, and Austria's Red Bull Ring (formerly A1 Ring) and Germany's Hockenheimring come back. These tracks fun to drive. Also, the physics have changed due to engine and body changes, which will stir up some changes. The Young Driver Test has been removed in favor of an Evaluation Test that is 1 lap around Monza, which can be skipped. I would've liked the YDT to come back though due to potiential newbies to F1 racing, but to make it skippable.
Except for the tracks and handling changes, your standard features are still here. You have your standard Grand Prix mode to run single races or full race weekends. You then have your Career mode, that has been changed to allow you to join your team of choice right away instead of working from the bottom. You can choose to run a 7 race, 12 race, or 19 (full) race championship. Then you have your multiplayer options to play online, split-screen, or LAN play. I couldn't say anything about multiplayer because I play alone at home, and plus the online is a ghost town. I really want Codemasters to use their RaceNet hub system to allow for cross-platform play, but maybe that's out of their reach. Then you have Proving Ground, which is your challenge mode. Then finally you have My F1, which is just fancy for saying 'Settings'.
All in all, 2014 is the greatest so far in the form of PC F1 games, since '15 is very buggy, has broken wheel support, and special for PC, game crashes. At least '14 can run a wheel well. I haven't tried it with the G27, but I'd assume it would work.
9/10 Same as '13 in a lot of areas, but why fix what isn't broken. Put on some different toppings and you get F1 2014.

I went in thinking it'd be a fun little text-adventure game with a neat overaching story. While that impression wasn't exactly wrong, the game definitely blew my expectations away in terms of how it'd go about that.
The production quality is amazing, from the sound and music design to the art/graphics. Each episode felt very authentic for the genre it was trying to nail, and it made for a super immersive experience. The story-telling and writing were also spot on, which I wasn't expecting, but was very, very happy to have experience. That, combined with the game's meta, made for a very interesting time that I had a lot of fun with.
Each episode felt unique, and the game eases you into more puzzling situations that use new mechanics, which was nice. The episodes were all a blast to play, too! The whole time, I was muttering to myself like a madman as I tried to walk myself through puzzles, or cope with what the game was throwing at me. Easily 40% of what I was muttering was, "What the ♥♥♥♥?", and I mean that in the most endeering way possible.
Overall, game is a blast. It constantly sent chills down my spine and had me on the edge of my seat as I got closer and closer to the end of each episode.
I did have a couple of gripes though. There were a few typos I noticed throughout the game. Nothing major, but it was there--some missing words or mispellings around; nothing that prevented me from figuring out puzzles. Second thing, is the game didn't lock my mouse in, so I would occasionally tab out when I clicked after my mouse drifted over to the second monitor. I'm not sure if this is an issue unique to me, since I've seen no threads on it, but it'd be nice to see a fix for it if it's a game issue.

A fun game with many technical problems that unfortunately makes it unplayable in my opinion.
Had I bought this at the full price of 19.99 euros I would have been more dissapointed, but I didn't expect much as I launched it as the first game also had problems similar to this one.  (recieved this as part of the autumn star wars bundle) Having originally played this at release on the 360, I was cautiously looking forward to playing this at a higher resolution and framerate.
After cranking up the graphics and setting the resolution I launched the game, being greeted by a, what seemed like black screen with the classic Star Wars music playing extremely choppily. Fraps reported 2000+fps in the cutscene, but the screen was black. After a few seconds, the classic Star Wars text intro played, equally choppy. It went from being 2 fps to a freeze frame before jumping to another freeze frame. Deciding to save myself a headache, I skipped the intro, being greeted by another slap in the face. The game is locked to 30fps. After playing for a couple of minutes, another cutscene played, as broken as the intro. It played fine for the first few seconds before the audio imploded and the screen froze again. After waiting a couple of seconds, it put me back in the game, this time at 5-10 fps which lasted for about 20 seconds before struggling its way back to 30. After it reached 30, it was as steady as a rock though, which is a plus I guess.
After playing through the first level and skipping yet broken cutscene I looked online for solutions to my problems. I downloaded a 60fps exe from the pc gaming wiki (awesome site, check it out) and it played fine until the next cutscene, which instantly crashed my game. After that, the game refused to start, so I removed the modified .exe and repaired my game, switching my resolution temporarily to 1680x1050 just to get the game to start again. Switching back to my normal resolution and getting to the same spot as before instantly crashed the game. I gave up at this point. I'm not going to play a game on the pc at unsteady 30 fps without functioning cutscenes and intermittent crashes. I don't enjoy playing a ticking time bomb, where every second the game might crash.
It's a shame because this game would be a blast to play at 60+ fps @1080+ resolutions. The gameplay is a faster, more fluid and fun version of the first and it really makes you feel powerful.
Save yourself a headache and don't get this game if you can't live with the aforementioned problems. The cutscenes give the levels context and without them you're just running around killing stuff, which is fine for some people, but not for me as a Star Wars fan and someone who cares about the story, no matter how bare bones.

The Darkness II is emblematic of so many of the worst narrative and design concepts of gaming as a medium.
It’s a game so obsessed with its own mythos, so completely devoid of self-awareness, and so appallingly misogynistic that it is often actively painful to witness. The entirety of The Darkness II seems designed around alliterative bullet points: “guns, girls, and gore.” In many ways then this isn’t terribly different from so many shooters, but where The Darkness II sets itself apart is in how much it revels in its own stupidity and filth.
It’s going to be important later on in this review, so just so we’re all caught up let’s quickly run through the basic premise behind The Darkness II: brooding protagonist has nothing to live for; girlfriend gives him purpose; girlfriend is killed to get back at protagonist; protagonist has nothing to live for and decides to kill everyone. Somewhere in there is also the fact that our protagonist, mafia kingpin Jackie Estacado, has a demon (the eponymous Darkness) living inside him which gives him superpowers and mostly makes him invincible. From here on events unfold as they typically do, with the introduction of a cult hell-bent on taking Jackie’s darkness (because that’s what cults do) causing all sorts of chaos, as Jackie all the while holds up inside his head lamenting the loss of his girlfriend and showing emotions™.
Though its stereotypical setup might lead you to believe otherwise, The Darkness II’s biggest problem isn’t in its rudimentary plot (though that’s definitely one of them) but in how its only means of creating conflict and motivation for its characters is through violence toward women. Jackie’s girlfriend, Jenny, is fridged before the prologue is finished (a carryover from the last game) and from that point on The Darkness II kills literally every single female character in the game for the sake of motivating Jackie, all while neglecting to give them even the smallest bit of personality, as ultimately their only reason for inclusion (beyond to be fridged) is to be objectified and tortured.
What’s possibly even worse than the way The Darkness II treats women is in how it attempts to mask its misogyny under faux-emotional maturity and narrative sophistication. Developer Digital Extremes dedicates a not-insignificant amount of time to attempting to humanize the relationship between Jackie and Jenny, but because Jenny exists merely as a narrative prop with all the personality of a perverted body pillow these segments feel like little more than gross reminders of how one sided and shallow their relationship actually is. It doesn’t help that Jackie is something beyond unlikable with a penchant for juvenile philosophy, as he sits in the dark gun in hand and recites odes to his own amorality. The Darkness II was never a game with a penchant for subtlety, but its writing is so horrendous and convenient that it can’t even scrape by as merely clichéd, but instead doubles down on its tropes, on its misogyny, on its pornographic love of meaningless violence, and then tries to sell it to you as mature storytelling.
Some might say this is just staying true to The Darkness’ comic book roots, but justifying The Darkness II’s narrative disaster through its mirroring of another work does little but damn them both. And to that point there is little about The Darkness II that speaks to its awareness of the tropes it’s employing, as it is so abundantly self-serious that it is impossible to enjoy it as knowingly dumb or comically grotesque the way one might enjoy a B-movie. In the few cases where The Darkness II tries to introduce some levity to its proceedings it predictably punches down, with sexist and ableist jabs that are neither clever nor shocking, but just as cheap and untasteful as the rest of the game.
And low and behold if this isn’t as exceedingly routine a shooter as its narrative deserves. The Darkness II’s main mechanical hook is using your two demon arms in conjunction with more ordinary guns to create a sort of synergistic ultraviolence, but in application your demonic appendages are little more than glorified swords and grappling hooks. There was a lot of room for The Darkness II to create interesting encounters focused around forcing you to think creatively with the one thing that sets this apart from any other shooter, but The Darkness II is wholly and unapologetically married to its power fantasy mundanity, and so you are left with room after room of decidedly uninteresting grunts to tear your way through as if the thrill of watching your demon arms rip a man in half is enough to make combat interesting.
The Darkness II’s demon arms reminded me a lot of Bioshock’s plasmids, but where Bioshock used its plasmids to setup interesting dynamics between you and your enemies, The Darkness II is focused on nothing but accommodating as aggressive a playing style as possible. And that’s not inherently bad, but there is nothing about how The Darkness II plays that makes that aggression satisfying. The shooting is loose, your arms are overpowered, the enemies are tedious and ordinary, and you’re constantly being funneled down the tightest of corridors. The Darkness II tries to counteract this by implementing a kill based scoring system reminiscent of Bulletstorm, but it lacks the depth and creativity that made kills in that game so entertaining, settling here for a narrow range of possibilities which mostly serve to distinguish between gun and darkness kills.
The Darkness II’s mechanics would feel like a missed opportunity if the entirety of the framework surrounding them wasn’t so unsalvageable. The Darkness II is a game reeking of the worst sorts of narrative based sexism, marrying its violent tendencies with misogynistic conveniences, and the sort of discriminating carelessness that video games so often try to pass off as a sign of their maturity. To the contrary The Darkness II is one of the least innovative and sophisticated games I have played in a very long time, seeming to exist for the very sake of regressing videogames back to a time when nobody questioned why every female character has enormous breasts or why they are constantly getting kidnapped.

I was torn down the middle the entire time I was playing SOMA but ultimately I have to give it a recommendation and here's why.
On the one hand you have the game itself: how it plays, how it looks, how it sounds. On the other hand you have the philosophical discussion to the question "what makes us human?"
The game plays like any other Frictional Studios title of recent years: You explore a degrading environment of a specfic thematic design (in this case an under water research complex) looking for notes to put together the story and items necessary for progression. Along the way you'll encounter enemies which you cannot fight so instead you must run and hide and as has become the norm with Frictional's games, looking at the enemies directly will ♥♥♥♥ with your screen.
All in all, actually playing SOMA can feel a little bored and repetitive when played in large chunks at a time so I recommend to take it as one level per sitting to avoid the annoyance.
The visuals and sound design are what this game does much better then the gameplay as the grotesque and macabe distortions of organic/metal abominations are some of the most disgusting and skin-crawling I think I have ever seen and they are accompanied but the most well recorded and synthesized sounds that I cannot begin to describe them adequently.
But the reason I really have ended up recommending SOMA is for the discussion it breds into a very pertinent philosophical debate. "What makes us human?" is  avery important question to ask. We live in a time where technology is becoming more and more a part of everyone's everyday life to the point where we can ask the question if we would still be considered human.
SOMA delves into that very idea and while it takes a rather fantastical and far fetched interpretation of their answer, it still is enough to warrant discussion and be thought provoking enough to get my recommendation as a must play.

is a very cute game that offers a lot of story and history. It explores the culture of the Iñupiat people (Alaskan Natives) and, specifically, the story of nature and its massive influence upon the world. As you explore the amazing landscape that has been laid out before you, you will begin to appreciate the intensity and dedication to quality in which the Iñupiat have presented this game. Not only does it offer stunning graphics, but it provides such a storytelling that you may sometimes question whether it even is a game at all. Please do not, however, let that deter you from purchasing this. This can easily be classified as a documentary within a game, and I believe that a lot more 'games' like this should be created. Not only does it let you explore a culture, it also educates you on the beauty of the world and what it truly has to offer.

tl;dr: Great game, but a few details are lacking. I don't really get disconnected a lot, but I do sometimes. Don't really get it why people hating on the game as much though.
Now in-depth:
Combat
For Honor boasts a really good combat system, which, apart from a bit of cheese, works very well and is rather enjoyable. During a fight you have a very tasty mix of predicting enemy actions (rock-paper-scissors kind of system, but usually you get more than just one option to counter enemy) and having good reflexes during the fight. Combined with a very original approach to "1 versus many" situations (Revenge system), executions, effects, customisation gives you a very satisfactory feeling when fighting and some sense of progress, and with that all your skill matters the most. Within some match modes (i.e. Dominion) it is also crucial to take down crowds of AI soldiers, and de-stressing yourself by ravaging a bunch of them also can feel very good. Where combat falls off tho, is the said cheese. Some classes and some aspects of the game make people become frustrated (for example, a character with maxed out "Revenge gain" gear stat becomes incredibly strong and at times almost unkillable when ganked with several people). Even though those situations are still doable (many characters can disable an enemy when he's rampaging during "Revenge mode", and a well-coordinated gank can take even those guys down eventually), I can understand why people don't really want to look further into the game, because solution is rather unobvious.
Out of combat
Outside of matches there's a "world map" on which there are territories to get from a faction to a faction. After each match, you get those "war assets", which you can deploy on the map for your faction. At the end of each turn, your faction wins all the territories on the frontline on which it got the most war assets, and your faction loses territories if amount of war assets is lacking. It gives some sense of progression as well, as the tide of war swaying back and forth. At the end of the round (several turns), faction with the most territories controlled wins it and members of all factions recieve corresponding rewards (obviously the winners of the round get the most). Now where this is not good, is that it gets boring eventually and you stop caring. Since people play all over the world, you may find yourself going into a well-deserved sleep in the evening after your knights captured almost the entire samurai territory, just to come back into the game tomorrow and find out that when you've been away, samurai captured the entirety of *your* territory. And it gets like that almost everyday.
Customisation in the game is very unique, too. Your gear can have a few variations in looks, and it also has stats which are applied in some gamemodes. You can't max out selected stats, every piece of gear has 3 stats, and the more you increase one - the more you lose in the other. You lose out much less than you gain though, so in the end you really do become stronger, but you'll have to sacrifice some drawbacks for it. Now it sounds great and in practice it is, but some gear combinations are pretty tough to deal with. So, if you want to neither learn how to play against them nor be attentive to who you're fighting, then it's probably a bad idea to play some fun gamemodes like said Dominion or Skirmish. As of non-gear imrpovement, you get to choose your "feats" (active or passive abilities unlocked during a match), colors, engravings, symbols etched onto your armor, executions and emotes your character can perform... And also make your very own emblem! It allows you to get some really cool combinations (and look of the gear can help as well), so visual customisation is 100% "a go".
Community events liven things up a bit, and give very generous rewards, but this doesn't give much motivation to play yourself (logic "let them do it and all of us get the rewards"). Apart from them, you always get your daily "orders" which give (especially since recently) a generous amount of steel (in-game currency), and also you can get additional orders, if you like, from a good selection of them.
Matchmaking is also kinda good, but it's also very weird. It matches usually similar parties, even if they got much better gear or total level, but it doesn't encourage you to play as different characters and explore the roster. It seems like matchmaking operates at least partially relying on a "total reputation", which is basically amount of levels you "clocked" on your characters. That means, if you, say, play a lot on one character and then, after a lot of time try something new, you'll have to play just as effeciently on the other character or matchmaking will be unbalanced. It seems like it doesn't operate on total reputation alone, but it definetely affects it, so it's possible to start out a new main, but it is not quite encouraged (which I dislike).

This is a visual novel, but it doesn't offer the variety I'm used to in such games. The option to choose your own name doesn't exist, the characters are very one-dimensional with only one graphic for each, the mini-game is completely and totally pointless, and the length of time this game encompasses does not allow for any real feeling of connection with either the story or the characters. On the plus side, the art style is good and the soundtrack is soothing. This is one of the most fun schmups I have ever had the pleasure of playing.  As you can tell by the trailer, this is a schmup where you play as a knight, riding on a gryphon and shooting everything that moves.
What you might not see is all the cool adventure/rpg mechanics that are built into it.  Each level has branching paths, hidden items, and upgradeaple weapons/runes.  As you kill enemies you collect gold and you can use this gold in the shops to buy potions, sidekicks that help in combat, and upgrade your items.  It is a really cool feature and is not something I have ever seen implemented into a game like this before.
The graphics in this game are wonderful, beautiful sprite work that cover a variety of historical/fictional settings.  There is also a story in this game that is far more enjoyable than your average schmup.
I am a casual schmup fan, if you are into hardcore bullet hell shooters than this probably is not the game for you, but for anyone who enjoys classic sidescrolling shooting gameplay but is turned off by the hardcore bullet hell genre than give this game a shot.  I loved it and can't think of a single negative thing to say about it.
Beautiful game lots of potential. can't wait to see what they do with it in the future.

TL;DR
Short but interesting mystery/puzzle game with some text based problem solving.
If you are, like me, a child of the 80's and grew up with Commodore 64 you'll probably like this games atmosphere. However I don't think it's accurate to call it a text adventure even though some episodes contains text based problem solving. Compared to the text adventures of old, like Infocom's, it's really much more simple and straight forward, so don't but the game expecting a new Castle of Terror or Leather Goddesses of Phobos.
I must say that, even though the game is short, I very much recommend it. The creepy feeling of not knowing what comes next, or even why you're doing the things someone tells you to do, is seldom seen in games nowadays. Instead of focusing heavily on graphical quality and/or action, like many games today, this one focuses on the story and puzzlesolving. Some puzzles are quite tough, often because it's hard to see or hear and sometimes because they simply are hard. A word of warning though, if you don't like blinking lights you might want to skip this game because one puzzle requires you to look into a strobelike light to solve it.
The audio is excellent and the use of it caused a few jump scares.
The video quality is good but not like many other games today, although that might be the developers intention to get that 80's VHS look. It is surprisingly demanding on the computers hardware as I noticed considerable frame drops in some segments, and I have a GTX 980Ti which should run this without any problems. Poor optimisation I guess.
The only thing I didn't like was actually the ending. The game mechanics felt original but the story turned out to be quite common in the end.

A simply fan/tastic/ puzzle platformer. I love that you can use keyboard or controller, something I switch between, because I can't decide which I like best, though I believe I got used to controller a bit quicker and it was easier to switch between characters.
The story is really, really good. I found myself easily attached to the characters. Must play if you like puzzle games and/or platformers. The ending is really great as well.
I played this with an Afterglow Ps3 controller, using Xpadder.

I got this from a bundle and I have to say I've read longer and better free-to-play otome visual novels than this. I don't mind that the art is lacking but the writing...isn't good. It's not the worst I'd ever read but I expect better from paid content. For example, it makes no sense for these guys to go from 0-100 in love already. They don't know anything about the main character (MC)—the reader barely knows anything about the MC. You could pop the love interests and MC in a saltshaker and I wouldn't be able to tell them apart because that's the same level of depth and personality they were all given.
It's really sad because South Korean culture was watered down to make it more palatable for a non-Korean audience, especially from a westerner's perspective. It throws American stuff in your face wherever possible. In fact, there's a random clubbing montage with real life people that was really out of place. The clubgoers consisted of way more white people than Korean people—there was like 1 Asian guy in the crowd. Then there's another scene where they were having breakfast and they're like, "Yeah, America does breakfast the best!" I don't know if the writers didn't care enough to do research on Korea's breakfast foods—or research on anything—but that's just lazy. The speech style ("Dam [sic] girl you really got moves!), the setting, the characters—everything was Americanized.
Nothing about this game was Korean and I expected as much, especially considering the title. If you're looking for a cheap otome title, I suggest looking in the Free section. You'll find more fulfilling content there.

While not exactly classic side-scrolling shmup gaming, if leisurely adventure style shooters with cognizantly melodramatic, cliched storylines and decent attempts at psuedo-historic humor are your thing, then maybe so is Gryphon Knight Epic.
Pros:
-Sound, Movement and firing controls are adequate.
-There are multiple branching paths in each stage, secrets to uncover & many items, weapons and spells/potions to find.
-The hitbox seems fair, as are the enemy layouts on medium difficulty.
-You can change firing direction at almost any time, which allows added flexibility,
-The world map and market/enhancement systems add potential for depth and substance.
Cons:
-Because this is not a bullet-hell style shooter, it sometimes seemed difficult to maintain any rythm during the more intense/clustered sequences.
-I found some dialogue to drag a bit, which does slow the game down.
-Sprite animations are sometimes choppy at best. This may be an artistic choice by the developer, but it could affect gameplay immersion.
-Sometimes the branching paths and backtracking can be boring, and seem like a sluggish mechanic; Otherwise, this idea works well in areas where puzzle-solving, secret areas etc. add variety to the formula.
If you enjoy finding everything and forming strategies to defeat enemies, then this game should be enjoyable.

Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars is one of the most popular point-and-click adventure games made in the 1990's.  Originally released in 1996, the 2009 Director's Cut is an update that adds additional content as well as change some parts of the game, the latter which will be described later.
As a note, while Nico Collard appears in most of the screenshots and in the banner on Steam, the vast majority of the game is centered around George Stobbart.  This is a heads up to those who were looking forward to playing as a female protagonist.  Having never played the original, I can only accurately comment on the Director's Cut version.  It's pretty apparent while playing where the new audio is used due to the difference in audio quality.  The newer audio sounds fuller with less static while the older ones sound a bit quieter.  Fortunately, despite the differences there's no noticeable variations between the voice acting of the same characters, which would've been jarring if there were.  Because this is not a modern remake, the artwork, while beautiful, is noticeably lower resolution, so I preferred to play it in windowed mode.  As another note, playing fullscreen on a 16:9 ratio monitor will leave the game in its original 4:3 ratio with blackbars on either side, which I prefer to a stretched image.  Also for some reason it looks like Nico Collard wasn't completely animated by hand as certain actions will replace her sprite with a 3D model.
Overall the game has solid puzzles and a good comedy vibe to a rather serious plot.   There are many locations to visit and a soundtrack to match, and there is plenty of dialogue and banter between characters.  There is a hint system if you get stuck, but I highly recommend to try your hardest to solve the puzzles yourself otherwise you may spoil your enjoyment of the game.  Despite its age, the game is not dated and is recommended to all those who enjoy point-and-click adventure games.
My wish for improvements in the game would be for more consistency between the newer assets and the game.  Also having read about the differences between the original version and the Director's Cut, I wish that this version would have all of the content available in the original and any differences between the two would've been toggable in the options.  I think these changes would've satisfied those new and old to the game.
________________________
Now onto the differences between the original and Director's Cut.  Because I haven't played the original, I can only comment on the more obvious changes that I've read about.
- It's possible to die in the original game.
- Removal of interactions with many objects in the game. This change is probably due to the nature of the times where people have more games to play and are less likely to continue if they get stuck.  The downside is less dialogue.
There are no CGs, and the game is extremely short. Doesn't really go into Korean culture.

Waking Mars is a very interesting game. I've always been on the lookout for games about ecology, and to my surprise Waking Mars turns out to be a really good example of this. As you explore a Martian cavern system you'll discover a variety of "Zoa" lifeforms that have different characteristics, behaviors, and interactions. It then becomes your job to manage the varied species carefully in order to maximize the living biomass in all parts of the cave. It's tricky, though - I've had at least two species near extinction before I realized what was going on, and I had to frantically protect and cultivate the few remaining specimens back to a safe population level.
It's a compelling game that doesn't have many issues. The only problems I've noticed with it, besides somewhat sluggish and finnicky controls, are a bug with one of the achievements and an issue where on newer versions of Windows you need to go to the executable and disable display scaling on high DPI settings (under compatibility settings) or else the mouse becomes useless.
Besides that, though, it's a game with interesting ecological mechanics that's well worth playing!

Thomas Was Alone is a very interesting game from the well known indie developer Mike Bithell. In it, you control many different personalities that take up the body of coloured polygons. Each of the different characters have their own abilities, Chris being a red cube that can hardly jump and John being a slender yellow rectangle that can leap a mile. There are dozens more to be played with.
All this in a platformer with solid level design, but not at quite the fluidity of Super Meat Boy. Whilst on your adventure through the eerie but relaxing world of Thomas Was Alone, you can also indulge in the very superb narration by Danny Wallace.
All of these factors make for a very enjoyable experience, and I heartily recommend Thomas Was Alone. If $10 is too much, do not worry as it frequently goes on sale and has been featured in a number of bundles thus far.
On the more technical side of things, I experienced no issues whatsoever, and you should have a consequently bug-free experience. There is unfortunately no Steam Cloud support, but the game isn't the longest and so this won't pose much of a problem for the travelling gamer.
For the achievement hunters, all 35 achievements within Thomas Was Alone are extremely easy to achieve, and should not take more than 200-250 minutes to complete. The game itself lasts about that length, too.

Right off the bat, I want to give a big thank you to Ubisoft for the free weekend, because I now finally had the chance to play Rainbow Six Siege. A game that was met with mixed reviews at launch, rightfully so, since there were so many problems with the game, and unfortunately it turned away a lot of potential players away, like me. Jump forward to 2017 - the game is not only polished now, but the amount of content it has is just amazing! Huge props to the developers for continually adding new stuff to the game, because I strongly believe that R6S is one of the best tactical shooters I have ever played!
With the little time I have spent playing the game, I found myself blown away at how atmospheric both the combat and the strategy aspect of Rainbow Six Siege really are. I mean this is coming from someone who is not the least bit interested in Counter Strike. In fact, R6S only solidifies how much of a mindless and inferior product CS:GO is. The amount of fun I've had so far surpasses any other tactical shooter on the market that I've come across.
Expect to die a lot. This is a pretty realistic game and very much requires you to plan out your attack, or, in others cases, defense against the enemy team. In that sense, it can become quite the competitive game, where each squad is trying to outsmart the other and it becomes this tense and surreal moment when you get pined down, leaving you to adapt and figure out a way to counter back.
The destructible environments are a key aspect of the game since they pretty much allow you to turn the tide of a situation and overcome it. Granted not everything can be destroyed, in fact, it feels archaic by it's design, but it is also understandable since there needs to be some balance in order to have a healthy competition. I have to admit, breaching through a wall with an explosive, followed by a flash bang is so satisfying and is probably the most awesome parts of the game.
Now, I have to address the multiplayer since this is what most people want out of the game. So far it has been a mixed bag, granted this is during a free weekend, I found most players to be competent, but also slightly toxic in their approach. I guess it's unavoidable at this point. There will be people who are more casual and others who will be aggressively competitive. However, if you have friends or manage to find friendly players in-game, make sure you play with them, allowing for a vastly superior experience. I honestly think that is how the game is meant to be played.
One last thing. There is a lot of debate on what version of the game you should purchase. I could write a short book about this topic, but the easy answer lies with you. Are you the type of person to grind for their loot? (in this case we are talking about characters and cosmetics) Or are you the type of person that wants most, if not all, of the loot at once? Whatever version you choose know that you are getting all the content either way.
Overall, I believe Rainbow Six Siege to be one of the better Ubisoft games out there. If you love tactical action, if you love strategy, if you love shooters, if you love having fun with friends then by all means give this game a chance. Thank you!

This game has a cool premise, but in my opinion it has some serious flaws.  You can read the other reviews for what people like about the game, and I agree with some of that.  It is really neat to see the different ecosystems in each room grow and flourish.  My review will just detail the reason I quit playing.
My big problem with the game, and the reason I quit playing after enjoying it for a few hours, is that simple mistakes can be too catastrophic.  It's fine to have a way for players to screw up.  A "fail state" is healthy for most games.  But usually that means just trying again, resetting the level.  The basic premise of this game is that you must create enough plants/creatures that are worth life points, and upon reaching a certain amount of life points in that room, you can move on to the next area.  I went ahead and threw some plants down in one room, not really thinking much of it.  Before I knew it, one particular plant (spores) had overrun the entire room, killing off everything else.  These plants are worth very few life points, so I needed to replace them with something more impressive.  I then realized that these spores had also ruined all of the fertile patches of ground, so that I could not plant the good things that would actually help me.  To undo this plague, I needed another plant (lava plant) that I didn't have the seeds for.  To get those seeds, I had to wander all over the map just hoping to encounter a lava plant.  There's no indication on the map of where you can get particular seeds, you just have to memorize where you might have left one of those plants.  It took me a while, but I eventually found ONE of the seeds that I needed, that I had apparently missed when collecting them before.  I think if I hadn't left that one seed behind before, I may have soft-locked the game.  Anyway, with this one lava seed I was able to destroy all the spores, as the lava overtook the room in a similar fashion to how the spores had.  The lava plants were still not worth enough life points, though, and I would have to go through another couple layers of destroying and replanting everything through various methods if I wanted to finally get things running.  Upon realizing how long this would take, I just gave up.  Trying to fix this mistake had become far too monotonous, and AFAIK there is no way to reset the level to just try again.  You're stuck spending forever cleaning it all up.
This wasn't even the first time that placing an incorrect plant had awful consequences-- earlier I came across a tunnel with a couple of acidic fertile patches.  I had encountered only one type of plant that could be placed on these so far, so I went ahead and planted them there.  As it turns out, the only way to beat this level was to let loads of creatures march back and forth through this tunnel so that they can bring seeds back to their hive and reproduce.  If I had not placed my carnivorous plants, this would be very easy.  It would be an automatic win.  Since I did place the plants, though, these creatures I was supposed to breed were constantly being killed.  There was no way to remove the carnivorous plants-- I just had to sit and wait for good RNG to get the creatures through the tunnel safely.
TL;DR -- This is a cool game until you make a mistake, and then it is an absolutely miserable experience.  I can not think of another game that has such incredibly time-consuming and unfun results when you do something wrong.

Already from the first minute or two of playing this game, there have been a couple of jumpscares. These jumpscares are quite cheap - not screamers, fortunately - but in a sense, these scares are pretty effective for an early development game designer.
The graphics of the game are not very appealing, they are very... well just not very good. I have a strong feeling that this game was made using the Unity 3D Engine, due to the scenery. The scenery is also very cheap, but once again - this is a good start for a beginning game designer.
I have noticed from the beginning cutscene, there is text dialogue to read at the bottom of the screen. In order to make the game better, I believe that if the creator was to get some voice actors to simply read that dialogue and put it into the game, it would already be so much more effective and intriguing. Perhaps a scratchy voice, considering the character is a hunter.
In addition, the cutscene doesn't contain any motion. It contains camera movement, but the characters in the cutscene are standing still and are not moving. Perhaps some rigging and animation could fix this and, once again, effectively make the game better.
The game reminds me a little of the Amnesia style. You can pick up and throw (kind of) objects around such as chairs and tables. A hand is shown in the center of the camera view when you look at an object that can be grabbed.
The title screen is simply a rifle spinning around in circles, however it still seems pretty effective. There is motion, at least, unlike other indie games' title screens.
The jumpscares mainly consist of visual effects and really loud, strange volume. This is quite effective - I almost headbutted my desk.
There are notes that can be picked up and read in the game. These are of good style and contain some good information to set the horrific scene of the game. Also, there is lots of blood and gore in this game, but the models used for the humans and the horse are not too exciting. They look like mannequins.
There is a map that shows you where to go, which is a decent addition to the game because you have something to show you what you are supposed to do and where you are supposed to go. The jumpscares still happen through the entire game and do make me jump out of my seat.
The creator has successfully used the right music to create tension and drama. Music is a very important thing in videogames, for without music there really is no build up in tension.
Enemies in the game consist of very basic coding: they follow you and you die if they touch you. This makes the game incredibly easy as far as shooting the enemies, however extremely hard when enemies spawn in opposite locations around you, meaning that if you try to dodge one, another one will be near you and could possibly almost touch you. I actually found the last mission so hard that I was unable to complete it - it just seemed impossible to me. Of course it's not impossible, but after many tries, I had enough.

I first heard about this game (or rather read about it) when I saw an article saying that this game was "an interesting spin on old text adventure games". This was back when it was only known as "The House Abandon" which was a demo at the time to show off the game.
And boy, am I happy I picked this up when it got out.
This game breaths in new life into the text-based adventure genre that has, more or less, become a niche genre. "Stories Untold" is a 4-part text-adventure game (sort of), with each episode having its own story and plot. The game puts you in the shoes of the episode's protagonist, as you try to fulfill the objective of the episode, by using computers or other text-based interfaces.
If you're really giddy to try this game out before buying, you should download and play The House Abandon.
Much like old text-adventure games, the length depends on how long it takes you to complete a puzzle or trial-and-error your way through the game. In my case, I was mostly stumped around Episode 3 and early in Episode 4, due to a puzzle element introduced in Episode 3 that was somewhat hard to decipher (mainly due to audio issues I had on my end). Otherwise, the game (I found) was pretty straight forward. The game has a lot of neat mechanics and switches them up. I won't exactly spoil them, but it's some neat ways to play around with the text-adventure medium.
Now, let me put down the positives, neutrals and negatives I've had with this game:
Positive
- Music and sound design is head-on! Going through certain episodes had me at the edge of my seat in fear.
- Masterfully crafted plot.
- Each episode keeps you coming back for more, to unearth the plot.
- Well done mechanics that toy with the text-based medium.
Neutral
- True to the text-adventure medium, you'll hit either a lot or no "sorry, you need to be more clear"-messages. I got a little bothered when I kept trying to observe certain things, but the game would just go "sorry, no can do", even though I was sure I was clear enough.
- The puzzles in Episode 3 are nice, but I had heavy issues during a puzzle that heavily relied on sound cues
amongst other codes later on.
- Graphics settings are really lackluster, but I somewhat didn't mind. Mainly cause the game looked and ran relatively nice. Emphasis on "relatively".
- Can't save during episodes. If you wanna save progress, YOU WILL HAVE to beat the episode you're at. I found this somewhat tiring during Episode 3, which I found to be (by far) the longest one.
Negative
- Once you've played through it once, there's really no point in replaying it. A one and done kind of game.
- Framedrops during certain segments of the game. I usually didn't mind it, but when the requirements on the page don't seem to reflect what's needed to run this game in those segments, you'll either crash on a low-tier computer, or have odd and awful framedrops.
- Not a lot of graphical options to allievate any issues related to the above issue.
- Awful mouse sensitivity and somewhat buggy cursor. There's no options for the former, which made my experience during certain segments rather unpleasant.
- A minor one: some achievements seem to be bugged (as of writing, Episode 3's completion achievement is bugged and unachievable).
Overall, my total experience has been rather pleasant with some bumps here and there. With some additional polish (and a hopeful sequel), I could see this game become a nice return to text-based adventure games, potentially reviving the genre. I highly and proudly recommend this game, however do be aware that you should probably have a beefy system for the more intense segments of the game!

Overall, pretty interesting and somewhat unique game!
The 'genre' of this game can be described as 'adventure': It's a mix of exploration, research and some sort of 'puzzle solving', which is mostly about building up an ecosystem using different seeds from different species on Mars. This all is guided by the overall story of the scientists on Mars and their research work.
The ending was interesting, but overall, the story lacked a 'punch' and was not that interesting. The 'research' element (and the 'mystery' on Mars) in the game is quite motivating though and can and will kindle the scientific curiosity in you (if you have that). Also, in general, sci-fi and space fans interested in (good) fictional stories about extra-terrestrial life should have fun with the story-line. Other than the story, the characters were well done with their dialogues and personalities.
Gameplay-wise, the ecosystem-building is fun, but sometimes, progress depends too heavily on specific seeds, which usually have a carry-limit, thus forcing the player to 'grind' a bit to reach the required levels. Also, there was one point in the game where I was kinda stuck and the game didn't offer any good clues, which was annoying.
Still, overall, it was a cool and unique game which turned out to be more interesting than I thought. It's not perfect, but definitely worth playing.
