Overcast - Walden and the Werewolf is an Indie horror game where the player takes the role of the titular Walden, who is a reclusive hunter, living near a small village. One day he finds all the inhabitants brutally murdered and vows to hunt down the beast, responsible for this. Known as being a man without fear his courage is put to the test in this adventure.
The story ties in neatly with the gameplay as Walden is not defenseless on his journey. He can fight back the monsters he encounters by using his rifle. While this might seem to take away the tension at first, this is not the case. The monsters can kill Walden with only one hit, this paired with the comparatively long time it takes to reload, missing a shot can be a grave mistake.
Unsurprisingly for this genre the locations which are featured in this game are grim and dark. This however is bypassed by the use of a lantern which always illuminates the immediate surroundings, so that the player can actually inspect the area instead of just stumbling in the dark. Furthermore there is a handy minimap which can be toggled on to help the player not to get lost.
The atmosphere of the game is mostly conveyed through visual filters. They help to showcase certain things that are affecting Walden and help to create some sense of immersion. Unfortunately the opposite is achieved by the rest of the visual design. While the environments all look okay, some of the models are just off and don't look too scary as a result. The flames of the lantern among other things are especially irritating, as they appear to be all just the same sprite and they always move in sync, which is off putting. Lastly the shadows which are cast by the lantern’s light have a slight delay to them and keep moving after the source of light is already at a standstill. While these things could be accepted in another kind of game, this genre relies highly on immersion, which can easily be broken by menial details like this and thus affects the gameplay.
The sound design is competent. The sound effects for moving objects and characters are both fitting and unsettling and therefore add to the creepy atmosphere. The music cues in and out at appropriate moments and fits the game well.

+ Fitting sound effects
+ Nice atmosphere
+ Visual effects
+ stable gameplay without glitches

- Some unrealistic physics
- Some graphics distract from the atmosphere
- Not very scary for experienced players
The game tells a classic monster story and sticks well to this premise. Unfortunately the creepy atmosphere is not preserved constantly as it is sometimes broken by unfortunate design choices. Nevertheless it manages to deliver some scares, but maybe not enough for horror game veterans. Thus I would recommend this game to people who are new to the genre as it helps them to find out whether they might like the genre by being relatively short and inexpensive and not too creepy to scare them away from the genre from the very start.
5.8 /10

I will preface this by saying I JUST started playing the game to determine my first impressions about the gameplay.  I did this on purpose so that I wouldn't be distracted by all the fluff in this game.  There is, as you can already see, a very pleasant and deliberate art style.  It's inspired, of course, by the tested and established Zelda franchise.  The gameplay also feels a lot like Zelda.  There are other inspirations from SNES-era RPGs, of course, but this is the most salient to talk about - and I'll explain why.
When I say that this game feels like Zelda, I mean that in that it's both limiting and pleasant.  The walking speed is just about the perfect speed to be neither too fast or too slow - it's just pleasant.  The attack length is neither too much or too little - it's just pleasant.  At the same time, Grindea suffers from the same sort of creative stagnation that Zelda's combat had.  There's about 8 types of swords, 8 types of 2-handed swords, 1 bow to my knowledge (really, devs?).  To be fair, this is about the same level of variance that Link To The Past had in it's weapon variety.  But, if you're expecting a modern pc merging of Zelda swordplay and Diablo lootgrabbing, you will not find it here.  There's plenty of the former, none of the latter.  Even Secret of Mana - which you're undoubtedly going to compare this game to - had a more robust combat system where you had to time weapon swings and charge attacks... AND YOU HAD DIFFERENT WEAPONS BESIDES SWORDS!!
I want to be clear, though:  I am enjoying this game.  I'm going to be playing it.  It's too early to tell how good the skill tree is - but I can already tell that levelling up is EXTREMELY satisfying and rewarding.  There is huge potential in this game.  I just really hope that the devs can stop being held behind by LoZ:LTTP and just let their imaginations go - or that the fluff and story make this game worth it.

If you can live with occasional bugginess, this is a pretty and pleasantly otherworldy game which manages to impart its culture to you without forcing it upon you. Given that puzzles are quite often non-intuitive on the first try (some visual cues are obvious, others less so), it's a good thing the auto-save keeps up with you - this is also helpful when the bugs that other people have mentioned occasionally make you die for no reason. Switching between Nuna and Fox is mostly an excellent thing simply because of how they play differently, although there are a few time-critical things where the fiddle of changing between them plus the slight unresponsiveness of Fox makes for frustration.
Generally, though, I'm very glad I've played this: it's a nice world to sink into. I should also say that while I was playing I didn't want to watch any of the 'cultural insights,' feeling that if I'd wanted a documentary I'd have watched one, but having now looked at them after playing the game they're actually well tied in so you feel you're learning something more about the world you were exploring.

"For Honor"
This game is a perfect showcase for everything that's wrong with Ubisoft and Uplay.
At the core, For Honor is a solid, fairly unique combat system with good variation and plenty of depth. There's a number of balancing issues, but on the whole the core gameplay is robust, challenging, and rewarding.
Such a damn shame they wrapped it in♥♥♥♥♥♥
They've started with the usual triple-A practice where they wrap everything in overly shiny graphics and high-quality cinematics to create the illusion of a whole and worthwhile game. They succeeded very well at this. A lot of the graphics are shiny and detailled, the story is grand and cinematic and well-voiced, and the overall aesthetics are very pleasing.
But they ♥♥♥♥ed up the optimisation to such a degree that the stability and performance of the game are in serious jeopardy.
The multiplayer framework was a brave and commendable experiment with subtle loadout differences, P2P hosting, and skipping any sort of balancing and connection stability tests. In the rare event that a match is found without people leaving or being kicked, there is a strong likelihood that your opponents will have a subtle but unfair advantage in their loadout, regardless of whether they play honourably or not.
Additionally, for some reason the Ubiboys saw fit to incorporate a F2P unlock model *within* a full-priced game. You *will* be required to unlock items and heroes with in-game currency after paying full price, and you *will* be confronted with offers to speed up this process with additional purchases. Absolutely disgusting.
The game overall plays with a lot of intriguing ideas and on paper is incredibly appealing, but in practice the effort in creating it has been extremely poorly distributed, leaving the result a horrible glitchy disconnective yet graphically appealing mess. Assuming you have the latest high-end consumer-slave hardware. If your machine is average at best, the game loses its only defence and becomes worthless.
Would not buy again.

SOMA is a narrativefirst-person horror game developed by Frictional Games, who are known primarily for the creation of Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
First and foremost, I think I need to make it clear that i'm not usually a fan of the Horror genre. In fact, until recently, I wouldn't even look at a scary game. But, after much contemplation and mental psyching up, I eventually decided to wean myself into the genre. First, with a non-horror game; I chose Bioshock. A depressing and foreboding atmosphere, but one that fits somewhere into the "Narrative Shooter" area and doesn't feature massive horror elements. Then, I played through the first two Dead Space games. It should mean a lot when I say I absolutely love those two games. I'll rant about those in their respective reviews.
Now, in my latest spooky-games outing, I think it's appropriate that I go back to what brought me in:
THE OCEAN
SOMA takes place in a large series of undersea compounds in the far future that the protagonist must traverse in sequence. The game is a narrative experience, and that's made clear right from the tutorial, where your character is explained to be dying of brain hemorrhaging, and is about to undergo a series of experimental brain scans to try and cure himself. This propels the incredibly strong story forward as you attempt to discover the secrets of Pathos-II and learn about the people who lived, worked, and died there. Honestly, to say too much more would do a disservice to the reader and the game itself, but I will say that I felt incredibly engrossed in the two main characters, due primarily to extremely good writing and voice acting.
The gameplay itself will be familiar to anyone who has played Amnesia. Lots of physics elements, scarce but terrifyingly powerful monsters, and logic puzzles are scattered throughout the game in abundance, and each feels like it spends just enough time with you before disappearing into the ether. That is, except for the Proxies. While I love the terror caused by having to sneak around tight corridors while watching out for how much sound I make, I would prefer if I didn't have to do it three times, with one section being a linear series of corridors where the proxy is directly ahead of me at almost all times. It's frustrating and somewhat tedious, but admittedly still fitting the game's dark atmosphere, so I'll give it a pass.
I only ever got stuck on, maybe, two puzzles, both of which I was able to work through in ten or fifteen minutes. The puzzles themselves range wildly in both difficulty and variation, to the point where they are somewhat jarring. Several felt shoehorned, or had particularly obtuse solutions, but I enjoyed a few that where sprinkled in. Overall, I think it kind of took away from the overall atmosphere having to stop and play some pipe dream or a reflex test every twenty-five minutes. Although I enjoyed the hacking game in Bioshock, so maybe i'm just going a little wonky.
Overall, SOMA is a rich narrative experience with some amazing horror themes and competent gameplay, that's only let down with some strange design choices in places. I highly reccomend.

What turned me off from this game? It's a bit of a story, I think.
Originally I was all praise for this game. I wanted it to succeed and I wanted to see it become something wonderful. I joined the discord not long after, praising the Development Team for their efforts and using my time in the game to feel sort of like a "Dinosaur Adventurer". I would sit and watch players do their things for HOURS on end, enjoying each and every surprise that came my way. It didn't matter to me that I never achieved much in the game - the Developers were adament on ensuring players not progressing much. What mattered was the labor of absolute love and beauty that was displayed.
The Isle isn't a game for the lighthearted. It's brutal, takes no prisoners and if you're incapable of surviving or going along with the intended style of play - survival, in its truest form - then you will fail. You will fail a lot, until you either learn from failure or rage quit. Myself? I loved the failure, it added spice to my adventures and I was absolutely stunned by how the players interacted with the game-world through their dinosaurian characters. It was like me being on some sort of ancient safari, relaxing and wonderfully peaceful, all up until someone spotted me and I had fun trying to get away; running away never helps anyway, but you can try!
No, the game itself is not the problem, neither the intended updates to correct progression and survival issues stated by the community. The game is absolutely innocent of any charges in my review. In fact, I would highly recommend you spend the twenty dollars for under two hours to experience the game. I encourage you to go onto official servers only (probably NY2!) and watch and learn. I encourage you to see for yourself what a glorious game and labor of love this absolute gem is. This, and all with the game, I encourage you to see!

If you're a fan of the original Broken Sword, then, as you can probably tell from the other reviews... This is, by and large, a safe bet for a great game
As a newcomer though... I'm not entirely bowled over
Done right, point-and-click can be brilliant. Certainly, the start of the game is very engaging. You're exploring places for useful / hidden items and trying to work out how to piece them all together. It's not long before you're given some challenging but great puzzles to solve too (the door lock and the decryption of the letter) - The characters are also quickly likeable, and George's charm in fumbling around Paris is certainly endearing. The game also packs a lot more humour than you'd expect - And I confess I garnered probably too much amusement from showing people soiled tissues, drain-openers and desperately trying to make them shake my hand
So why the thumbs down?
After the quick-draw of puzzles at the start, they almost seemed to dry up. The 'thinking' puzzles largely became talking to people in the correct order or showing them a certain item to trigger an event... which then required you to talk to yet more people. Whilst the reactions were fresh and entertaining to begin with, I admit I started getting impatient half way through the game and sometimes skipped through the unimportant dialogue or George telling me the item was not suitable - my heart sank a bit when I walked into a pub of about 5-6 characters... all to talk to, all with around 6-8 potential dialgues (based upon the item I show them). It started becoming a lot of sitting around and wasn't massaging my cerebral matter very much
Your actions also don't really seem to amount to much. You have a few 'options' in dialogue, but where they seem to garner the same results, it felt a bit pointless. You can't exactly seem to do things "wrong", and it's sometimes just trial and error (and clicking) until you find the right one. In effect, you find you're not quite exploring the game, but just fumbling around until you can find the plot trail it ultimately had prepared for you. It basically started feeling like less of a game and more that I was slowly clicking my way through a film
It was engaging enough to see me through to the end, for sure - though a tad anti-climactic. The graphics were delightful (nicely remastered without too many elements where the old pixellated style was evident) and voice acting great... but it just didn't do it for me

I'd gotten this in a Humble Bundle several months back and never played it. It was surprisingly engrossing, and the puzzles were just about the right difficultly for me to have to think about them without pulling up a solutions page out of frustration.
What's actually one of the best things about this game is that in the director's cut there's an in game hint feature for when you get completely stuck! That to me is the reason this game is a recommend. It doesn't matter if you're good and point and click adventures or not. The in game help guide doesn't spoil the solution at first but simply gives prompts to show you where you may have gone wrong.
In my play through I missed one clue and couldn't figure out why I couldn't move on, having the in game hint system helped me to realize what I had missed without spoiling the rest of the puzzle. I love that! Sometimes I miss really obvious things and with other puzzlers can end up stuck unless I want to cheat.
The story line is sincerely good. I liked the amount of real historical research I felt went into it. Everything felt to me like it was actually plausible seeming. The Knights Templar is a super interesting historical subject to begin with, and this game sets up a continuing story line about it in a very sincere and realistic way.
Also there are journalism jokes. That alone makes this game worth getting.
Pros
- great voice acting
- clever story
- solutions to puzzles in game if you get stuck
Cons
- only about 4 hours long
- disjointed animation
- needs more Nico

The "hook" of "Waking Mars", a Metroidvania-style platformer, is that it is almost completely non-violent. While similar games might have progress by running around and shooting the monsters, "Waking Mars" instead has you bring the monster to life. The various chambers have to be filled with sufficient biomass for you to progress, which you do by "planting" seeds (or more precisely, throwing them at various patches of fertile ground) within the caverns.
Calm and relaxing, the danger - and difficulty - level is minimal and the game approaches a serene calmness that is nice change of pace. But while its non-violent take on the genre is unique, it isn't by itself enough to make an entertaining game. As I mentioned, the difficulty level is almost non-existent; despite its pretense, the Martian ecology it presents is extremely superficial and you can spam seeds to achieve victory. Or you could if you had sufficient numbers of seeds; you can only carry a handful of each and too often I had to scurry between caves looking for a specific plant to re-supply my stocks. This made the latter half of the game rather more of a grind than anything else. The lack of variety in levels is also a sore spot, and I quickly got tired of seeing the same red walls. Too frequent cut-scenes interrupted the game-flow as well. Nor were the endings - there are three of them - sufficient reward for all the effort. Kudos to the developers for trying something new, but all in all I found it a flawed game that wasn't much fun to play.

This is a very cool little game.  I recommend it for people who are looking for a non-violent exploration sci-fi experience.  The thing that makes this game unique is the core gameplay element of building ecosystems.  It basically consists of exploring cave systems and finding new forms of life.  These lifeforms are plant-like creature called Zoa which can be planted in different kinds of soil, and you acquire different seeds to do this.  Your goal is usually to raise biomass in any given area.
I loved the rewarding sense of accomplishment when you've built an ecosystem that sustains itself.  Some of the areas are fairly small but there are large open cave sections where you end up building a huge, prosperous system that just keeps getting more and more dense as the different creatures within it interact with one another.  You can also encounter areas which are fairly hard to achieve a desirable sustainability.  Of course, sustainability isn't necessarily your goal in this game, but it is very satisfying when you achieve it.  There is a strong element of scientific discovery in the game but also perhaps a lesson about ecology and how our choices affect outcome.
Aside from the fun of interacting with the various lifeforms, the storyline, while simple, is also very nice.  The two main characters are likeable and the resolution to the plot is pleasing.  Definitely try this out if you are looking for a different twist to the classic sidescroller.

Gryphon Knight Epic is a combination of a Horizontal Shmup and an Action game featuring multiple sub weapons, potions and the ability to head multiple directions in order to discover secrets. We play as Sir Oliver and his fantastic mustache on a journey to save his friends that have fallen to corruption. Always on his trusty Griffin and armed with a crossbow the gameplay will instantly be familiar to anyone that's ever played a shmup. Upon completing the tutorial you will be introduced to the Hubworld where you can choose which level to tackle on next as well as buy items and weapon upgrades with your spoils of war.
Before heading out to a level you can also read about the lore of the person you are about to face to add some back-story to your next opponent instead of them being one of bosses. From the lands, to the enemies and even the weapons there is a surprising amount of lore to everything if you care to read about it but they are in no way necessary if you just want to play the game. Once you select your level you are given the choice of one of three difficulty modes. This is not the type of game where you get much stronger than you were at the beginning so any of the three are viable options from the start. As the games progresses you get more and more weapons but they are just different ways to fight your foes & not straight upgrades.
To obtain new weapons you must trek through the two levels that each stage contains and defeat the boss holding said weapon. Merely rushing through the stages will likely cause you to miss some very handy but well-hidden secrets that every level has in them. From a safe full of treasure to multiple magical stones that grant you permanent abilities like breathing underwater or sand there are a lot of goodies to be found for the sharp eyed player. What is really unique about this is that along with being able to take multiple paths to reach the end of a level you can also turn tail and go back to the beginning of the level scouring for secrets if you so wish. Enemies do respawn so you will be met with resistance however.
The most unique thing about this title is also its biggest flaw however. You will be attacked from both side of the screens but unfortunately turning to attack those on your rear also causes your gryphon to fly that direction making it likely you will crash right into an enemy if it's too close and makes it all too easy to get devastated when there are environmental hazards along with enemies on your tail. To make matters worse turning around to face them even where there are no deadly hazards causes more enemies to spawn in from that side making the situation potentially worse and if you waste your time fighting them you will have flown back in the level quite a bit which in turn causes the enemies ahead of you respawn too. All of that ultimately makes attacking the foes behind you a bad idea and makes the controls feel extremely awkward.
It's not enough to flat out ruin the game but simply adding a stop animation to hold your ground instead of instantly flying directly back into the hazards you just avoided. You have a life bar and can take quite a few hits as well as refill your health as long as you have potions so it is more bearable than it would have been if it was a one shot and you’re dead type of shmup. Putting that issue aside combat is a lot of fun and every stage has completely new and unique enemies for you to face so you'll always be wanting to see what’s next. The promise of a new sub-weapon to mess around with if you can beat that stage's boss is strong enough that I didn't want to put the game down. From bows, slings and firework shooting cannons there is a lot of fun to be had experimenting with your arsenal.
Using a sub weapon drains your energy meter so you can't spam their powers and makes you use it more wisely. All weapons share the same energy pool so there is no real point in switching if you ran out and are waiting for it to recharge. Accessing weapons is done via a weapon wheel that slows down time whenever you bring it up. Potions and squires are also brought up in the same menu. The problem with potions is that you won't know what they do unless you paid attention to its exact shape and color when purchasing it. A minor issue that is easily solved after a bit of playing but having the name of the potion pop up when selected would have been a far better way to handle them.
Squires are basically a tiny ally that is always by your side with a wide variety of effects depending on which one you have equipped. One may revive you when you die, others simply increase the amount of gold you get and others will help you destroy enemies. As you can tell there is a lot of options available to combat that really sets it apart from any other shmup. One thing that takes some time to get used to is how large your hit box is. You will only take damage if a projectile hits Sir Oliver himself but since he is sitting up vertically he is a much larger target than what we are typically used to. Imagine controlling a paddle from Pong instead your typical ship.
Story is told via the lore and dialogue between your character and bosses as well as a few comic like cutscenes. It's nothing that you will remember after turning off the game but it does the job and you can skip all dialogue at the press of a button if you wish. Music is catchy and the graphics are really well done. They are full of a ton of detail and the cutesy look of everything gives it a charming appeal. A single playthrough should be around 3 hours but with higher difficulties and tons of weapons at your disposal there is reason to replay it a few times. Not the longest of titles but every level is very unique and feels like the classic case of quality over quantity. While it may have some issues that are unlikely to be resolved after so long since its original release I'd still suggest it to anyone looking for a title that tries something different with the shmup genre.

Secrets of Grindea is an RPG with real time combat like Zelda,and is fun to play with or without a friend,which is really rare on RPG with MP games.
Pros:
*No class restrictions (you can be a fire mage with a cloud and a ice friend protecting you,i'm serious)
*Puzzles,LOADS of puzzles,and you will need some time to think about some.
*Character creation,not much to talk about here,move along.
*Regions. They can vary from a city to a spoopy forest,and they are all fun!
*Combat,mixing skills,making awesome combos,and crafting another weapon to be stronger,REPEAT!
*Pixel art is great!
*The Story. The characters are lovable,and with time you will change your opinion about some,also,there's some plot twists here,funny jokes there,and TONS of sarcasm.
*Cards,or Monster Cards if you like,are rare drops from enemies,if you got a card from a enemy,it will give you a random bonus and a cute artwork from the enemy you killed,which is ALWAYS a plus in my book.
*Soundtrack is good
*Balanced (at least on normal mode),like the Yetis are MADE to tank your attacks,and some other enemies are made to be annoying.
*Easy to connect to MP through Steam and AWSOME controller support.
*THE EASTER EGGS!!!!!! I managed to find a Triforce near the pile of gold in the flashback sequence!!!! :D
*You can replay bosses to get more loot from them,well,everyone but...
Cons:
*You can't replay Winter's or the Mt. Bloom boss fights,I mean,the Winter boss was one of the most fun boss battles I ever saw,even if it didn't drop ANY loot,I would be playing it for ages,not for the Mt. Bloom boss fights,but they could have some extra loot and the replay feature anyway :|
*GRINDING,and i'm not a fan of it.It's not just walking in circles to begin a battle,you have to kill ALL enemies in the room to spawn another wave of enemies,although this sistem is great,it's boring to get the action going.
*The crafting system could be improved,like seeing the item kinda faded away,because my friend thought the ''red emmiter matrix'' was a calendar,that's right A CALENDAR. And there's not enough recipies...
*Not even at level 10 (max level of skills) my Frosty Friend could kill a Rabby in 1 hit,and a Rabby is the second enemy in the game,and it has ≅ 120 HP.
*The cards are just TOO rare to make it fun to grind,and it's based around luck too,so just to get a Jumpkin card,I had to stop my playthrough over how boring it was to get a 0,5% of card drop,to try again the other day :|
*The ''character portraits'' (the picture that appears when you talk to a character) are bad,they aren't pixelated,witch isn't that bad for itself,but they look more like a photo that has been glued there,the quality is horrible too.
Final Veredict:
9/10

Disclaimer: I've played through this game years ago, and loved it. This review is based on my feelings upon playing it just now on Steam.
The sniping sections? Great, mostly! Pulling off crazy, difficult shots, wiping out entire armies before any of them know what hit 'em, and seeing your plan come to fruition feel brilliant. If it was just for those sections, I'd absolutely recommend this game.
Unfortunately, this game, which has SNIPER right there in the name I'll remind you, has only a handful of actual sniping. Most of the single player campaign is spent with stealhy 3rd person action sequences. Levels usually start off with you just behind enemy lines, armed with a sniper rifle, SMG with barely any ammunation, and a sidearm; the only remotely useful of which is the silenced pistol. You have a few grenades, some mines/traps and binoculars, the usefulness of which I cannot fathom, seeing as how your main weapon has a freakin' scope.
From there you're expected to make your way through hordes of enemies to an arbitrarily chosen sniping spot, snipe out a few waves of enemies, and make your escape. In theory, you can stay far away from your enemies and use your sniper effectively all through the levels. In reality, you're constantly forced into tight corridors and indoors areas, where the game devolves into a run-and-gun action game, and a very mediocre action game at that.
You cannot climb anything(aside from the pre-determined sniping sections), so you can't use verticality to your advantage. This means you often have to walk into large outdoors areas trying to look at every direction and every height at once. There are far too many ledges, windows and rooftops for you to clear, while also keeping an eye on the ground. And even if you do clear them all, the enemies move from one place to another, so a window being empty right now might not be empty in ten seconds.
Oh, yeah, and enemy snipers sometimes spawn seemingly out of thin air. There's a mission towards the end where you're forced to make your way through a narrow road, when suddenly enemies spawn both behind you and in front of you. So while you're trying to fight off the enemies coming from both sides, you'll notice a sniper has spawned on a rooftop to the side of you -- a rooftop you'll likely have cleared by that point.
And if that's not enough to get the salt flowing, the enemies also blatantly cheat, the snipers being the worst offenders. Not only do they have the high ground, having just spawned there (in locations you simply cannot reach), they also have perfect aim and perfect reflexes. Once the enemies know your location, you can't peek your head out without getting shot. It is literally impossible to shoot and enemy before they shoot you, if they know your location. And changing locations doesn't make much of a difference, since the enemy snipers often see you instantly, even if you're in a spot that should in theory be outside of their field of view -- or at least unfavorable for them. They also don't care about minor things like smoke, fire or trees, and they'll see you through all of those obstacles, even if you have no chance of seeing them.
The game is honestly not about planning, scouting, using the terrain to your advantage, aim, reflexes or smarts. It's about trial and error. There is simply no way for you to avoid getting shot at the first time you're playing the maps. You'll have to learn the enemy locations by heart and abuse the game mechanics (using the 3rd person view to look around corners for example) to stand a chance against the masses of enemies and superhuman counter snipers; and even then, you'll often get swamped by hordes of enemies coming from every angle and height, so the game devolves into you camping behind a corner with a SMG, shooting moronic enemies who run into your sights.
So it's not a sniping game, which is a same, since the sniping sections are really enjoyable; just too few and too far apart for me to recommend this game. You simply don't have the tools or means to make stealth viable, and I don't buy games with SNIPER in the name for half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥run-and-gun action gameplay.

Why am I not surprised? An enjoyable game brought down by its horrible netcode/network stability, minimal content, and a feeling of guilt as I spent way more than I should on this game. This is not a $60 game. In terms of core gameplay, it's perfectly solid, but everything around it simply... isn't. While the campaign mode had a surprising amount of production value, it had just as much effort put into the actual story, character development, and careful writing, which was none. It's not absolutely abysmal, but just not worth the time. Nothing matters and it just feels like it's checking off a box on the list of video game requirements. The visuals are quite marvelous and the stages are lively, so when I'm playing multiplayer, it keeps me more engaged in that regard, which I like. I never had any control issues, and the combat was fun. It's much more methodical and patient when dealing with singular opponents and it keeps you on your toes. Battles can be fun... when they're fought somewhat honorably, which is weird considering this game's namesake. Most of the time, battles will just dissolve into a gangbang on one person while their teammates are on the other side of the map trying to take over the territories. Of course, that's only Dominion, which is one of 2 multiplayer modes, not counting skirmish which is just a ♥♥♥♥ around fest. The other is Elimination, which is entirely based on 1v1s. Since everyone is spread out across the map, it's much less likely for people to gang up on you. It's certainly not impossible, but it's less likely in comparison. Overall, the multiplayer content, can be very enjoyable when it works. I repeat, WHEN IT WORKS. Because of how terrible the servers are, it is highly unlikely for someone with a certain connection to experience any match beyond the class selection screen. It is easily the most infuriating thing about this game, bar none, especially when trying to play with friends. There are ways to circumvent the issue, yes, but it shouldn't be an issue in the first place. Ah, to go back to class selection for a sec, I do enjoy the variation among the classes, though some are clearly better than others, and the amount of times you'll see those better classes is obnoxious. The options are there, but all it does is create the illusion of variety rather than allowing it to flourish. Aside from that, the different factions are kinda neat, but don't really add much to the game other than a sense of competition, the music I could barely remember, and microtransactions are a thing. Not much else to say. It's a fine game mechanically, but it leaves a lot to be desired in terms of content and network stability. I'll only recommend this game on the basis that you know you'll be laying a lot of multiplayer and have very good internet. Other than that, wait for a price drop.

This is my second experience with a Sapphire Dragon Productions game, with the first being Love in the Glen. I'm sorry to leave another negative review, but I hope it's constructive. I really don't intend to be mean.
Heart and Seoul (great name, BTW) is an otome (G x B romance) visual novel. Players experience the story through the eyes of Kim Yoon-Ji, who's spending her spring break in Seoul- the capital city of South Korea- after moving from Daegu. Kim agreed to housesit her rich uncle's apartment while he's away in New York on business. Shortly after arriving, Kim meets Park Hyun-Woo (the dark-haired guy), who works as an architect's assistant for her uncle's architecture firm. When he learns Kim is jobless, he introduces her to his best friend, Lee Seok-Jin. Lee is a rising star DJ currently working at one of the most elite clubs in Gangnam (an upper-class district in Seoul). This club is looking for a new bartender and quickly, Kim is hired. Kim spends the rest of her spring break working at the club and hangin' with Park and Lee... Perhaps falling for one of them by the end of the story.
I don't think Heart and Seoul is "terrible". However, almost every aspect of the writing is undeniably subpar, even for a short title. Including other shortcomings that I've detailed below, I wouldn't recommend it in most instances... Especially if story quality is very important to you. In my opinion, the cons outweighed the pros. On the other hand, it's extremely cheap and short, so it's not a huge investment of money or time- however your experience turns out.

I like romance visual novels that aren't wholly dependent on protagonist x love interest romantic interactions, but the non-romantic interactions shouldn't eclipse the romantic ones. The balance is hard to strike, yes, but in Heart and Seoul's case- being advertised as a rom-com visual novel- 95% light-hearted slice-of-life with moments of comedy and 5% romance stuffed in at the eleventh hour is just

The text skipping was finnicky- in order for the Ctrl key skip function to work, you had to press it down before a line of text ends, but thankfully, the alternate skip function works fine (the "Skip" button in the textbox menu). You can't save your game when you arrive at a set choices- this is where you want to be able to do so the most, so it was slightly annoying. In terms of aesthetics, it's on the uglier side... but the text is still readable, which is what will ultimately matter more to me than bells and whistles.
Their expressions never change (not even once, unless I missed them for some reason) and they only move when the locations/scenes shift. Also, Lee's sprite is noticeably larger than Park's, giving the impression that Lee is standing closer to Kim although both guys should be the same distance away.

Just kidding. Ok now on to the meat and potatoes of my review….
Setting
“Heart and Seoul” is a short otome Visual Novel set in Seoul but the core of the story is pretty universal so it’s not like it’s un-relatable on any level. The characters could be called Jim, Samantha and Steve and be New Yorkers and I don’t think the plot would change that much. The whole “Seoul” thing is pretty much a backdrop that provides interesting cultural learnings (yup took that from Borat) and almost serves as a guide from the Korean Board of Tourism.
Story
It’s short, about an hour for a single story track if you’re a fast reader, maybe hour and a half if you read it at the prompter speed. But I don’t feel short is a bad thing, I’m a pretty busy person and I don’t like having to slog through a storyline that is heavily buffered with fluff just to give it extra length. This one gets to the point and there are rarely any dull moments, the characters are always doing something or talking about something that is pertinent to either the characterization of the characters or the plotline. Could it be more romantic and passionate? Yes, this certainly isn’t a Danielle Steele nor is it Twilight or Fifty shades of Grey. On the bright side, if you happen to not like Twilight or Fifty Shades of Grey then you might like this. But yeah, not really that romantic till the end but I don’t really mind it that much as it’s “realistic” as the characters take time to become friends first.
Audio
Catchy pop-y and techno tunes. I liked it, kept the feeling of the game very light. Some nice sound effects too like the phone buzzed when it rang and stuff, could have had more though in my opinion.
Minigame
Match-3! Always fun, especially when you don’t have to pay to use a lollipop hammer.
Art
Character sprites are ok, could be a lot better and maybe some costume and expression changes could be in order. Probably the weakest part of the visual novel in my opinion. I liked the impressionist style backgrounds though made me feel like I was in a Degas painting.
Conclusion
All in all I liked it, it certainly has its faults and it definitely is not the most exciting VN out there. In many ways I feel that in the attempt to be “realistic” and “slice of life” a lot of excitement and passion got left on the cutting table. Though within that I did enjoy a lot of the conversations between the characters and there were a lot of funny moments in the game, which is rare in videogames, and for that alone I feel that one should get this game, even for the few chuckles it will give you along the way!

I just finished this game tonight after owning it for quite some time. It's been around for a long time and there are plenty of reviews already, but I'll go ahead and share my thoughts.
The story is straight to the point and gives you enough information between missions to understand the goal. It's up to you to navigate each area, dispatching enemies while trying not to get spotted or die. If you get spotted, the difficulty increases. The enemies will use cover, suppressive fire, and grenades on your last known location, forcing you to relocate. However, you can always use getting spotted to your advantage by placing traps or flanking.
Luring enemies into traps you can set with tripwires, mines, and dynamite, as well as using ambient noises from bombs and thunder to mask the sound of shots is clever.
The levels are small enough to funnel you toward the objective but large enough to give you a feeling of freedom to maneuver and perform kills how you want.
Later on, toward the end, I felt like getting spotted was almost unavoidable. The enemy snipers will normally spot you first, unless you take things slow and are very patient. Taking time to scout those windows and rooftops is a must if you want to go unseen.
The X-Ray bullet camera is awesome to see, but toward the end of the game, I started to feel like it displayed too often. However, there is an option to turn it's frequency down, or turn it off. I may change these settings if/when I do my second playthrough to speed things up.
There are plenty of weapons to use, and you are able to pick your loadout between missions. You can always improvise by using weapons and equipment from dead soldiers. Unfortunately, you'll only find submachineguns, ammo, grenades, and traps. Sniper rifles are awarded as special items which are collected at the end of missions.
Mosin FTW
If you love anything that has to do with snipers or WW2, then I can recommend it, along with all of it's sequels.

Heart and Seoul is an otome visual novel about a girl that goes to Seoul (the capital of South Korea) on vacation and has a great time there and even has a chance to fall in love. Sounds pretty standard right? Well, it is in many ways and there is no doubt that the plot is very strictly “slice of life” but within it there is something utterly charming and magical about the writing. The dialogue is often funny, sweet and heartwarming and the characters feel very real and well rounded.
I’m not sure if the developers were aiming for this, but the game really feels a lot like a Korean Drama (and if it was what they were aiming for then they achieved this perfectly). The game embodies the sweetness and fun behind Korean dramas really well and as someone who has been to Seoul and Korea I must say that they got the feel down really well.
Now the game certainly isn’t without faults; it is often cheezy, corny and hammy… but so are Korean dramas so can we really blame them? Besides cheese, corn and ham are some of my favorite foods! My other big criticism is that the expressions of the characters never change, that does take away from things quite a bit.
All in all a pleasant VN and in my opinion, the game on steam that best represents Korea and probably the best Korean game out there!

The graphics are top-notch and look like a true labor of love. The animations are crisp and smooth, sprites are very detailed and there's a huge amount of things going on the screen, which actually never distracts and you it's up to you to focus just on the battle or you have the time to look at the background. I think most people won't even notice all objects / details / events on their 1st walkthrough, probably not even on the second.
A story itself is very typical, in the beginning it even takes fun of itself and all the cliches.
The knight saves the princess from the dragon, life goes on, he becomes a fat and lazy husband. But then years later he and his allies find out that the treasures they took from the dragon's vault are not that good for them, after all. The knight meets his doppelganger, which tries to kill him, his friend becomes a villain being under influence of the sword she took, etc.
But that “making fun of cliches” part quickly drops right after the first boss and the rest is just all kinds of variations of “I was evil because of this item, thank you for saving me, now I'm very good”. Overall the story is OK to read and I never had the urge to skip dialogues and cut scenes.
At first I thought that the sounds were weak and the music too ambientish, it surely doesn't have that  energy from combination of sounds and music in classic arcade games (Metal Slug and such). But right after the first level that feeling disappeared completely. It's a different approach, a little bit  more “meditative”, definitely not pumping-adrenaline-action-like.
Overall, sound and music do their job and work for the atmosphere. But can't say I remember any music track after playing the game or have the wish to download the soundtrack.
Gryphon Knight is a medium-paced shoot'em'up. You can fly in both left and right directions on your own, proceeding further or returning back (which makes some enemies spawn). The game also offers you a choice to choose a different path from time to time, combined with ability to always go back it adds a different feel to all maps, not just makes them non-linear, but also somewhat open (you'd need to find secrets and gold).
You have a standard shooting weapon (crossbow) and an alternate one, which is always more powerful, but requires a special regenerating energy to use (acts as a cooldown). You get these alternate weapons from bosses you beat and can upgrade them for money.
The first two levels are pretty easy and follow each other, but then the game drops 4 levels after them and you can choose in what order to play them. Their difficulty varies a lot and many enemy attacks start to feel cheap (take too much HP on Normal). Checkpoints help A LOT here, you can be defeated by the boss, but then go to the map, buy some things and return back to the latest checkpoint. Each death takes some of your gold, but you still earn a lot playing the levels. Still, it's not necessary to grind at all.
The only huge downside was that in the end you're forced to beat all previous bosses AGAIN and then two forms of a final boss. No checkpoints between. It's a typical cheapest trick from some 90s games, which meant “MOOORE COINS, we are not done here”. It's not really a problem and these bosses leave a bit HP after their death, but it kinda made me to drop the game. Well, at least it didn't have an elevator level.
The game has some bugs, the ones which may force you to restart the level.
For example, there was an enemy which had a shield, it had other flying enemies which acted like an energy for that shield and you need to kill them all. But when I did, the shield didn't disappear and the game became an endless loop. It worked only after I replayed the level.
I had also encountered a sound bug (before Jinn boss) which made some “splash” sound to repeat over and over again until I beat the level (almost made me press the Mute button).
Other were rather minor, like sign “Go ->” not disappearing even after you defeat the boss.
A shoot'em'up of a different kind. Beautifully drawn and animated, fun to play. But not really polished and uses some dirty game design tricks (still being player-friendly at the same time).

For me, this game is the epitome of what a good indie game constitutes.  It takes such a simple concept-- that of basic 2D, side-scrolling platformer-- and makes it into something extraordinary.  And that's what Thomas Was Alone is: extraordinary!  Through the skillful use of atmosphere and narration, the player grows to sympathise and even become emotionally tied to the characters in the game, despite the fact that they are, at least in appearance, only a bunch of slightly differently-shaped rectangles!  The gameplay itself is intuitive and smooth, with a strongly implemented sense of co-operation involved, using each of the "characters" to overcome often challenging puzzles and make it to the end.  It is surprising how much depth this game possesses, despite how simplitic it appears.  I definitely recommend this game for anyone who enjoys platformers, puzzle games, a good story, or just indie games in general.  It is a gem.

I've tested this game since it was available as a closed beta in NA. Firstly: I miss the charm it had when it was just released. I'm not sure what's been lost in the time between then and now, but it doesn't seem to be nearly as fun. As you can see, I've played for quite a few hours. You can probably add another 100 hours for the pre-Steam days.
- Plenty of weapon and kit options, with the ability to customize (a little bit) your gear with the promise to be able to customize weapons in the future.
- Lots of different ways to play, granted the only real way to progress is to run-and-gun.
- Free-to-play. Yes, the option to spend real money is there, and it definitely helps to spend money to reduce the "grindey-ness", but it's not completely necessary. Of course the devs want you to spend money... they need as much money as they can get. Capitalism FTW. But seriously, they need to feed themselves and their families, and their investors need to see some sort of monetary gain to keep their interest in the project.
- Squads. One of the ways to avoid being disappointed by the shortfalls of the game. You need one or two friends that can help watch your back, since this game lends itself to multiple paths of attack. Bring your own voice chat client: there's been greyed out options for it in the game engine since at least the closed-beta days, but they're still not active now.
- Easy to fall into the "just one more match" trap. The game is strangely fun, mostly because you think the next match might be more balanced. (See below)
- No way to scout maps before you play, making it necessary to learn them while you avoid getting killed. I'm still learning helpful details 2 years later.
- Wallhacks. ESP. No real anti-cheat, it seems. There's a report option in-match and at the end of the match, but every report needs to be checked by a real human, so you'll find reporting minimally helpful. But you still should. Hackers aren't always on, but you'll run into one or two every hour or so.
- Combine the hackers in the game with poorly-optimized servers and you'll find yourself frustrated about half the time: if it's not the hackers, it's the hit-reg (and netcode) that makes it sometimes frustrating to play.
- Sniping is difficult to do due to the lack of effective hiding spots, if that's your bag. The maps have been designed to discourage sniping and encourage medium to close combat. You can't effectively guard your camping spot since you can only take one (or two) mine/trap options with you in each loadout and there are always multiple paths to your camping spot. Always.
- Ladders... they're just for decoration. Seriously.
- PvE is always coming "later this year". Granted it was supposed to be here 2 years ago, so we'll see how that works out.
- Low player numbers. This creates a few problems with the game, mostly balance issues.
- Tiered matchmaking is broken and has been so for a long time, mostly because the lack of players forces the MM engine to create teams from a wide range of +-3 tiers (out of 10). Playing with more than a  tier 6 loadout during the evening in NA will pretty much guarantee you a slaughter-fest due to the tier 10 pros camping the s*** out of your team.
- Which brings me to game balance: you're lucky if you get a decently balanced match. Often the MM engine will put a bunch of tier 10 players on one team and the rest of the players on the other. Guaranteed stomp-fest every 2 out of 3 matches. It's unacceptable and unnecessary and has been an issue for as long as I've played.
- Spawn protection is a
work-in-progress. It's easily exploited during battery collection matches and is ineffective to help protect your spawn during a raid by the other team. So it's not really spawn protection at all. There ought to be a combination of "you shoot, you lose your protection" and a fenced area that you are invulnerable in for a specified amount of time (so that we don't get snipers camping in a protected base for an entire match). It's not uncommon to find players still being spawn-protected halfway across a map.

Okay, in my view, which isn't always holistic and complete...to the point of 'never'!...up until this week I was looking forward to F1 2015, I watched all the E3 footage, analysed every reveal trailer including the 'features' trailer that had no features! and no career mode, no co-op mode and no extras!
Codemasters reminded me of EA Sports when they released a 'bare-bones' version of FIFA onto the newly released Xbox 360 and got hammered for it! Well it looks like Codies have followed suit! The game does look beautiful, there is no denying that! But the 'new and shiny' label will soon wear off once people realise the ommissions!
F1 2014 has no ommissions and it is a solid F1 racer. It does what it says on the tin! It doesn't make extravagant boasts or melodramatic claims of greatness...it sits you down, slaps you in the face and tells you how it is!
I like that, no bells or whistles, and it's a great racing game! Graphics are still impressive on PC, framerate is solid at 60fps on my computer ( FX-9590, R9 290X, 16GB RAM)...AI is still a bit dodgy at times...the tyre wear bug is still rearing it's ugly head, but generally, this game is extremely enjoyable!
I get tired and bored of the people who moan and ♥♥♥♥♥ about how unrealistic the game is...Codemasters are in a no win situation so they go with the common ground...a game that appeals to a wide variety of gamers! If you want nerdy, anally retentive realism then IRacing has you covered...to me games are an escape from reality, I certainly don't want them to simulate reality in any way!

I don't believe for a moment that this game is ready to come out of Early Access, and it's not because of the graphics. I don't mind Low-Poly games as long as they play well and have an enjoyable enough concept, but unfortunately Park Bound does not play well. Controls are solid enough, but the levels are where it falls apart, and it didn't take long for me to realize that I felt gypped.
Levels are empty, and have very minimal goals and missions; some of them only have one, and those are usually the bigger than average maps. It's difficult for me to understand why the levels are even this big if there's barely anything to do? I've seen some others commonly compare this to an MMO Mario 64, but I honestly can't see it, especially if there are not enough missions to complete for each level. Some missions just have an arrow that points you in a random direction miles away from the start and you have to assume you know wherever it is that it's pointing to. I thought it was just pointing to the very end of the level, but there's no where near enough time to get that far in the arbitrary time limit it imposes on you. Some big parts of levels disable your ability to jump, the only amount of basic platforming this game has given you, and pretty much makes those sections miserable to complete.
Overall not worth the purchase.

This is one of my favourite games, I played the Demo back on PS3 and then bought the game back when it came out. I played the Nazi Zombie Army games then a few years later and I really enjoyed them too. Playing through V2 again, this christmas has been great and it has reminded me how much fun this game is to play.
This is the definitive sniper game, in my opinion and the addition of the surreal anatomical, slow motion, skeletal, destruction just makes it even cooler. In fact, Rebellion has made a great impression on me as an awesome developer with both this game and their spin-off zombie mode. The Nazi Zombie Army trilogy are also really well designed, original and super fun.
The sniping gameplay in Sniper Elite V2 is really enjoyable and the developers do a great job mixing things up and keeping it interesting. There are stealth sections too and the automatic weapons have a nice punch to them. Some people complain online about the close range weapons being too underpowered. I think these weapons feel great, your character can’t take too much damage but neither can your enemies. So these encounters are very satisfying because a well placed headshot from a weaker gun will do the job. While some of the more powerful variants will destroy an enemy at close range.
In regards to the guns, they have included a well designed and cleverly presented selection of weapons. With each weapon feeling like it has its own unique characteristics and authentic details. Varied gameplay elements can force you to change up your approach to sniping and there is nice selection of guns to choose from to get you through.
The DLC is really worth getting too as it differentiates itself from the main campaign with it’s new locations. Each of these DLC missions take place in gorgeous environments that are really fun to play through. The developers also continue there surreal brilliance with the assassinate the Fuhrer mission. This is so cool and I noticed that it’s become a repeated theme throughout the series.
I just replayed this game after buying it in the christmas sale and I also bought the rest of the series. I’m excited to try Sniper Elite 3 and 4 to see how the series has progressed and especially to see how Rebellion have developed their slow motion skeletons.

I never write reviews, but I don't want misinformed people to miss out on this game due to just looking at the current "mostly negative" status. If anything most of the negative reviews are just people circlejerking in their hivemind against Ubisoft.
Here are some of the "big" reasons why people are giving the game low reviews:
1:   There are definitely problems with connectivity, no one can debate that (most online games do, but this is a pretty bad case).
2:   There is some degree of class imbalance, which should be pretty obvious since its a fighting game with different classes, but like all games like these, a skilled player will overcome such circumstances.
3:   A big controversy about the game was that the microtransactions made the game completely pay to win, this is not true at all. Everything except for some cosmetics can be purchased with easily obtained in game currency. You can buy this in game currency, but it doesn't put you at much of an advantage if you haven't levelled your character up much. The whole microtransaction thing is blown out of proportion
The game itself is great, it has unique gameplay, combat that isn't too deep and not too shallow, nice graphics and it is well optimized. The only real problem worth bringing up is the netcode used with the peer to peer networking. This very well could be fixed due to the mass complaints. Don't just look at all the ignorant <2 hour reviews calling it bad. If the idea of the game appeals to you and you can get past a disconnect every now and again, you will probably find yourself sinking many hours into this underrated title.

You play as both George Stobbart and Nico Collard, a tourist and journalist that end up interwined in a thick plot of conspiracy and adventure dealing with the rebirth of the Knights' Templar. The quest for the Broken Sword of Baphomet takes you from the calm and romantic Parisian streets to the most perilous of Syrian deserts as you trek the globe in search of clues and answers to the game's many innovative and ingenius puzzles. Each and every one of these locations are brilliantly animated, resulting in what's simply one of the most beautiful adventure games of recent memory. Broken Sword: Shadow Of the Templars is not to be missed by anyone, whether you are a veteran point and click gamer, or just looking for a thrilling experience with a great plot, fantastic graphics and a somewhat 'Indiana Jones' feel that you won't soon forget!

If you've not heard about it or played it, Thomas was alone, is a top notch puzzler worth the few hours in total it will take you to play it through.
It's the story of a band of self aware AI, the architects, and their quest to the core of their programming to change the system so that all other AI would be empowered to free themselves of a malicious program.
As Thomas and his fellow AI, work your way through levels using each characters innate strengths to help each other through to the portals that effectively end each level.
Based on simple graphics that look appropriate in the setting and add to the atmosphere of the game.
A puzzle element is fun, never repetitive nor ever impossible that you might ragequit, relaxing and quite easily addictive in that you can easily keep playing level after level.

Stories Untold is not your typical Mystery-textadventure. It is better. The game contains four episodes that are unlocked after completing the previous one. They are different and have varying storylines that the player explores in various ways. Stories Untold is the horror game I needed in my life. Although it features minor jump scares and can be scary from time to time, its unique atmosphere kept me intrigued. While the episodes address different instincts and stages of fear, the complete game is full of metaphors and things that will make sense in the end. The game shows how blinking lights, few dialogues and strange noises can influence your reception of a text.
The House Abandon starts as a nostalgic textadventure. The soundtrack in the beginning and the minimalistic setting would have taken me back to the 80s, if I had been alive back then. Instead, I was reminded of TV shows and films. The game certainly did a good job painting a picture in my head that was soon to be destroyed and replaced by a nightmare. As I proceeded the situation seemed to become more hostile and I was eager to receive an explanation. I was waiting for a sign – another noise, a number, a picture of Jesus. Anything. However, the game surprised me an we, the game and I, were playing with each other in a manner that I have encountered seldom.
The Lab Conduct made me a lab assistant – or so I thought. The Sci-Fi setting reminded me of The X Files. Pressing buttons, adjusting settings and being unaware of the consequences of my experiments, things happened and I may or may not have been in Area 51. Up to this point, everything is unclear. All I know is this: Something is happening and I am not the one to give in. Stories Untold shows what text, blinking red lights and an alarm can do.
The Station Process takes place somewhere in Greenland. I am in a remote weather station. I can hear the other stations, but cannot respond. We receive suspicious data and I have to decode whatever it is that we hear. Morse Code, NATO alphabet and a few tedious other riddles make this episode the most enigmatic. You can feel the 80s here. The tension is rising, reports are coming in that lead to more questions than answers. Honestly, I have no idea what I am doing until I leave the cabin and head out into the snowstorm. In first person perspective I need to find generators. Some time later I find myself in front of my computer, amazed.
The Last Session is the final chapter that combines and concludes all previous episodes. Needless to say that this is all you need to know for now.
Stories Untold evoked almost every emotion that I am capable of feeling. It is a little masterpiece that frightened, entertained, and stunned me. It combines text with cinematic and gameplay elements that amplify the experience and create something, for me, extraordinary. In case it has not become clear yet: You should probably invest 9,99 Euro and 2-4 hours and play Stories Untold.
Retrospectively, the game offers you plenty of hints and by the time you finish the third episode, you should have a vague idea of what it is all about. That is to say the game wants you to pay attention to details while deliberately suggesting something completely different.

I honestly thought this game was going to be slightly different. A text adventure game wrapped in a neat 3D environment shell. However, while that is true for certain segments, it soon becomes a very perplexing and thought-provoking puzzle game.
The story isn't a happy one, and it's one that, towards the end, felt a bit ham-fisted. Whenever I see something like that coming, a part of me tries to do everything to avoid it (and the game even mocks you somewhat for doing so; a nice touch). In the end, however, it was well worth the price I paid. A well-crafted interactive story,
Pros
+The atmosphere is amazing in Chapter 1, and was probably my favorite chapter
+The puzzles weren't too dfficult to figure out once you 'got it' but they weren't too easy either
+Not so unique story told in a very unique manner
+The presentation is like Stranger Things meets Myst. Amazingly done.
Neutral
=The price is probably high for some, but I found it fair for what you get, and the quality of the story and how it was presented.
=Some achievements are broken as of my writing this; a patch is coming.
Cons
-The walking segments felt clunky, and there were a few places I got 'stuck' against the environment.
-Some music is too quiet, and other parts are too loud
-The microfiche in Chapter 3 was hard to read. While I understand the controls were there for a reason, I still found it difficult to read some bits that were 'degraded' looking.
-Also in Chapter 3, the morse code segement flew by, and I got it wrong a few times simply because I heard wrong.
TLDR: Stranger Things of video games. Buy if you love good stories that are delivered in unique and interesting ways, and love figuring out things on your own.

The Epic Journey of Sir Oliver and his Gryphon Aquila
In Gryphon Knight Epic, a band of warriors has joined together in order to save a princess and slay a dragon. The warriors are successful in defeating their dragon nemesis and find a treasure horde in the process. Each warrior claims a piece of the treasure for their very own. The protagonist of the story, a knight named Oliver, claims an amulet. Little did these battle-hardened veterans know that the treasure was cursed. The curse allows the warrior to succumb to their inner evil, with only one thing being able to lift this dreadful curse: The amulet that Oliver now possesses.
Okay, so the story in Gryphon Knight Epic is a bit generic. However, I think we can all overlook this. The game is a 2D side-scrolling Shoot ‘Em Up, a genre that’s not exactly known for having detailed and rich storylines. To be honest, this game probably has a bit more story than most that have been created in this genre. Yet, there is one interesting thing that I learned once I reached the end of the story. It is set up for a possible sequel, which I find very surprising. Developer Cyber Rhino Studios must really love and enjoy creating Shoot ‘Em Ups.

This is an... okay game. It starts out pretty strong, there's a solid story throughout, the visuals are decent, the planting mechanics seem pretty interesting. For the first three chapters the game is quite linear, and the fourth (and longest chapter) opens up a little though I would never say it's that exploration-heavy, or much of a metroidvania.
But the game really starts to drag around chapter 4, with increasingly tedious work needing to be done to hit 4 and 5 level biomasses for the rooms. Thankfully there's an event that doubles the effectiveness of these right near the end, so if you hit 30 you're basically done. But it still takes a lot of work and some of the rooms can be really tedious and frustrating, the AI on the moving lifeforms is not very good.
There's also a number of glitches, stuff getting stuck in walls etc. but also game-breaking bugs that can ruin your file; thankfully I did not encounter this but I did get a kind of buggy ending the first time via skipping a large chunk of the endgame sequence by having enough core power to trigger the normal ending. But yeah, this game is... solid. I've wrung about as much enjoyment out of it as I think I'll ever get though and I doubt I'll ever go back and replay it. Get it on sale, not full price.

One of my favorites of the year so far.
An excellent blend of styles make this quite a unique experience. Part point and click, part text adventure, Stories Untold is a compilation of 4 short stories with puzzle elements.
Being that the majority of the game features your characters using a computer of some sort, you'll primarily be using a keyboard to get through each story. This is done either by entering menu hotkeys, inputting data, or by a simulation of text adventure games, which may give some of you a little nostalgia.
As far as the text adventure stuff goes, unfortunately it seems you can't get incredibly creative with what commands you enter. Sometimes certain phrases you try will not be understood correctly and often you can't delve quite as deeply into the information as you might like. All that said, the text adventures can be very immersive, largely due to the way they are presented to you.
As displayed in the screenshots, the in-game text adventures are often not the only thing to focus on. You can essentially leave the game and interact with whatever might be surrounding you by using the mouse. This is a joy to do as it's all very intuitive with simple point and click controls. Often your surroundings will help you with whatever is happening on screen, and discovering what can be manipulated and how you can use that to your advantage is something the game does very well.
Horror-wise, it can be surprisingly creepy. Whether it be an eerie noise in the background, performing strange tasks or an unexpected response from a computer system, you'll have your fair share of tense moments.
The game will likely take you around 2-3 hours to complete and isn't incredibly challenging, but for me, the unique way the game presents itself, the intriguingk, memorable stories and varied gameplay make it worth a purchase.

I don't know what there is to say about this game that hasn't already been said. Despite its early access status, there is so much polish and attention to detail that, at a glance, it could pass as the finished product. I can tell the devs have put their hearts and souls into this game, and I'll be damned if it isn't paying off.
If I had to give praise to anything, it would be the skills and perks available. Players aren't locked into classes, so they have complete control over how their character develops and the niche they fill in battle. For instance, one-handed melee skills that deal multiple hits in one use benefit greatly from perks that improve critital hits. Then, tack on a movement speed bonus for charging skills or blocking with your shield, and you've built an acrobat that hits fast and hits hard.
Of course, there are so many other praises I could sing -- the cheeky jabs at RPG tropes, the deliciously roguelike arcade mode, the atmospheric and memorable soundtrack, -- but words can only do it so much justice. If you're on the fence about this game, do yourself a favor and try the demo. Pixel Ferrets, have yourselves a cup of coffee, on me.

What an incredible game!
Secrets of Grindea is a story-driven game (With phenomenal RPG elements!) where you can customize your character's appearance, skills, and talents. While the mechanics are simple to grasp, there are many unique bosses and mobs that require certain nuances to accomplish.
The leveling system works out relatively well. It never feels like an over the top grind (hah) until about halfway through, where it suddenly starts to feel like it takes longer to level based upon the monster EXP.
Perhaps my only real complaint about the game lies in the skill system. They've set it up so that you get silver and gold spell points, where you spend so many silver points before you may only place gold points to further level up a skill. After spending 17 hours in the game, I've only been able to get one skill all the way up with gold points, as you only receive one point every few levels.
Still, you can completely customize your hotkeys, and they made it quite easy and intuitive. Though it is early access, they've already thought of many convenience things that other games miss: equipping cosmetic items for free, pets that increase stats, NPCs that have witty responses, etc.
It's rare you find an unfinished game that leaves you thinking about it even while you're in the middle of working, exercising, and trying to sleep. I'm only sad it isn't finished! 9.5/10
TL;DR - Buy this game. I'd regret not trying it. Smooth graphics, intuitive gameplay, conveniency in the game, and some light humor! Totally worth the price.

The Darkness 2 is, as the name implies, pretty ♥♥♥♥ing dark.
You play as Jackie Estacado, a mobster whose special skills have allowed him to rise to the very top of the New York underworld. And by 'special skills,' I am of course referring to the ancient demonic entity that lives within his body.
But when a bunch of cultists show up and try to steal the power away from him (because if an ordinary guy can use it to become king of the Mafia, imagine what someone with actual ambition could do with it), Jackie must use his eldritch abilities, and a veritable ♥♥♥♥load of increasingly large guns, to defend himself and prevent the power from falling into the wrong hands.
I'll be honest, I was surprised by how much I liked this game. I picked it up expecting a standard shooter with a vaguely gothic design aesthetic. What I wasn't expecting was a genuinely inventive and unique game with solid gameplay and some smart ideas bubbling under the surface. There are some very creative moments throughout the campaign, first as Jackie explores some strange locations, and then later when the demonic presence starts to drive him insane. The ending also qualifies for the 'Holy ♥♥♥♥ing Christ' award of totally unexpected story turns.
The gameplay is the standard gory shooter, but with the twist of dark and brutal abilities. You have two demonic tentacles which can pick up and throw things independant of your two gun-hands, which led to several situations where I was fighting two battles at once- a mid-range skirmish with a pair of SMGs, and also a long-range stand-off in which I was lobbing sharp objects and spikes at snipers.
You also get health by eating hearts that you tear out of dead bodies, which means the only way to get your way out of a tight spot is to use progressively riskier tactics to kill enemies and regain the upper hand.
Overall, it's a surprisingly enjoyable game with some creative uses of mechanics to craft a campaign that is not only fun to play, but fun as an experience.
Final score: 8/10.

To my surprise I discovered that Survarium installs its own "Survarium Steam Update Service" !!!
This Windows System Service operates outside Steam, so anything could be monitored and/or installed through this service. I wonder why they thought this was needed, why can they not use the normal update process via the Steam client app LIKE ALL OTHER GAMES DO?!?!?
It is NOT okay for any game to install its own system update service! What if all my other games would start doing this as well? It would become a huge mess on my PC with the 100s of games in my Steam library.
Check for yourself: goto Control Panel | System and Security | Administrative Tools | Services
There you will find this new Windows Service: "Survarium Steam Update Service"
Description: "Enables the detection, download and installation of updates for Survarium-Steam Update Service."
Until they remove this game specific update service and start using the normal Steam update service via the Steam client app this game will NOT be installed again on my system!
UNINSTALLED.

I played through the game with my wife in around 7 or 8 hours. The most compelling part of the game is the cultural narrative, which was well presented by short documentary videos and the organic incorporation of Inuit cultural elements. We were both impressed by the artistic representation; visually, it's a pure beauty. By watching how the fox cutely jiggles his body inside the whale's gigantic torso, or the fantastic visual and aural details of the blizzards roaring from the beginning to the end, you cannot fail to feel the creators' love and devotion for the game.
But I still have to point out the major con: The maneuvering of character movements is somehow laggy, to the point that at certain scenes, we had to try devastatingly for more than a dozen times to go through. I first suspected that our computer or the wireless xbox controllers were to blame; but then I saw similar comments from other players though.
Anyway, great gaming and LEARNING experience for a couple who virtually knew nothing about life and culture in the Arctic circle.
9/10 would recommend.
