When I first got this game, I was a bit unsure about it. My boyfriend wanted to play it and insisted that I would find it enjoyable, so I tried it out since you can't knock it until you try it.
(TL;DR - The game is amazing for an early access game, the developers actually update the game almost every 1-2 days. You can end up meeting a lot of nice people in the game as well. The Isle is pretty intense and realistic to the point where you can only talk to your type of dinosaur, which helps in finding food/water if you're looking. Once you understand the different types of calls for dinosaurs, you can tell who's friendly and who isn't. Carnivore or not.)
I had just logged into the game, and it asked me if I wanted to be an herbivore, or a carnivore. So since I don't think I'm good at hunting, I went with herbivore. At first it was tricky. I didn't know what roars were friendly or mean, I didn't know if they were carnivores or herbivores like myself. So I went out and started exploring, I had to eat a lot when playing as an herbivore. First few times, I'd just kill myself repeatedly or get eaten since I wanted to try and get a layout of the land. Then I started learning the map a little more which I was on isle region 2, so I started figuring out where plants were to eat and where water was to drink, and it was troubling since I would never get really lucky and end up near both food and water. There was a time when I thought I was in the clear from predators, and something runs out of the water and kills me instantly or when my heart would stop because there's a giant dinosaur stand right above me. So then I decided to try it out as a carnivore instead, and there was a big difference at least for me. It's easier when you're playing with someone, rather than alone, but it's not impossible to play alone which is nice. The map is huge so when starting the game, you're alone since you and your friends spawn in different places on the map. I made it all the way to allosaurus, and they are my new favorite. Puertasaurus is also a favorite, but getting to that progression point will take a long time. For now, I'm pretty happy with being an allosaurus.
Let me tell you about my first experience being a dryosaurus, I was alone in the night time trying to find my way, find food and water as well. Someone invited me to a party, and they were a bigger herbivore, and lead me to water where there was a herd of herbivores. Herbivores are actually really protective of other dinosaurs who are also herbivores, and as a group we walked from the water, to another area where there was water and food for us. Unfortunately, just as we got there, a utahraptor ran up and bit me, which then I had to rest or I'd bleed out. Its got a great premise: get into some real tests of accuracy and marksmanship and see how well you can do under pressure. Even more frustrating, the cover mechanics, its an afterthought, that unfortunately is a focal point of your survival. A piece of debris or a broken car becomes a life saver, but you can't peek over it unless your cameras facing the right way and in the mean time the AI is shooting you through the tiniest windows and inching closer with their infantry. Typically, when we think of 2D shooters, it's either the old-school games like Life Force, modern-era bullet-hells such as Dodonpachi SaiDaiOuJou, or Ikaruga (because everyone knows Ikaruga). If nothing else, this is a genre open to interpretation. Not every shmup needs to have hundreds of millions of bullets on-screen, nor do they require deep and somewhat obtuse scoring systems. Sometimes it's a good idea to take the basic concept and move it in a different direction. When this classic genre is thoroughly explored, it can result in games like Gryphon Knight Epic. GKE is far from the complexity and challenge of a designed-for-arcades masterpiece, but it is a thoroughly entertaining shooter all the same.
Gryphon Knight Epic is best described as a throwback game. It wouldn't look too out of place if it was released in the late 80s/early 90s. The graphics are appropriate for the time, with a lot of attention paid to background details, which gives every location a high degree of personality. Furthermore, each area of the game includes adversaries that fit the theme. Altogether this makes for visuals that are fun and interesting, but never distracting. After all, you're supposed to be saving the world. It wouldn't look good to take repeated throwing knives in the face, just because you thought a lizard running through the hot sun was your enemy.
As Sir Oliver, your task is to rescue your six comrades from an evil curse. These fallen* heroes have carved away a portion of the world for themselves, and raised an army to deal with anyone who opposes their rule. If you're successful in breaking through their forces and defeating them in a duel, they will surrender their weapon. The parallels to the Megaman series are pretty obvious. In fact, your main weapon is called a "crossbuster" and can be charged up to fire more powerful shots.
Coupling elements of an action-platformer with a 2D shooter doesn't always work. To counter this issue, GKE employs some different ideas. Each of the twelve stages can scroll horizontally, vertically, and even diagonally. There are also alternate routes, a handful of secret areas, and some truly powerful artifacts hidden away. Also, if you think you've missed something, you can turn around to scout a previous section. These slight elements of exploration are well-balanced. They lend the game a bit of an identity, and don't take too much away from the core action. In-between stages you can visit shops to upgrade your weapons, buy potions, and acquire familiars. You're free to take advantage of these luxuries, but they aren't really necessary. If you wanted to, you could complete the entire game with the crossbuster alone. In order to accomplish this feat, you'll have to approach situations with extra care, taking full advantage of your maneuverability.
While there's only so much that can be said about "shoot enemies while dodging stuff", GKE goes the extra mile with its fully realized enemy-design. This probably says more about the games I play than anything, but I've grown accustomed to everything firing an array of colorful non-descript bullets. It doesn't matter if I'm dealing with futuristic battleships, soldiers in ancient Japan, or venomous plants. If they're dangerous, that's because they're spewing pink bullets everywhere. This game is almost novel in its approach. The only bullets you'll be seeing is when they're fired from a pirate's gun. Many of the projectiles in this game are thrown, and fit the location's theme. While it could be considered a minor detail, this level of attention is worth noting. It's also nice that scale is appropriately handled. The action feels really personable when you and your foes are only a few meters away from each other. This slight element of close-quarters chaos gives the game a nice feeling of intensity, without surrounding the player in pink bullets.
Depending on how you approach GKE, it can either be an easy yet enjoyable romp, or tough enough to push your gaming skills. There are multiple difficulty settings, and you can make things easier or harder depending on how many upgrades you pursue. Overall the level of challenge could be considered low, but you can always push yourself to completing stages on the highest difficulty, without taking damage, using only the crossbuster. If that isn't enough, I suppose you could always use a less versatile weapon. As with any good throwback game, there's enough freedom to create your own challenges.
All in all, Gryphon Knight Epic is a worthwhile addition to any gamer's library. It reminds me of those days where I'd visit rental stores, hoping to find some unknown classic, or grabbing whatever had the coolest box-art. Unfortunately, this meant that I played a lot of crap, but I did stumble upon some really good titles. Not every game is going to be as well-known and memorable as Ninja Gaiden, but that doesn't make stuff like Vice: Project Doom any less entertaining. Personally, that's how I'd describe GKE. Even if you played through it, and eventually forgot it ever existed, you won't regret having given it a shot.
*By "fallen" I mean that they've fallen from grace. They're not dead or undead or anything.

I did this review in two ways. Here's a link to the video review, followed by the text if you prefer reading it.
Gryphon Knight Epic is a side scrolling shoot-em up with a medieval fantasy theme.  You play as Sir Oliver riding atop your faithful gryphon Aquila who is not just fierce, but also immune to all damage.  The story premise is that Oliver and his companions have come back from defeating a dragon and plundering its’ treasure hoard.  But that treasure isn’t all that it seems.
Sir Oliver wields a crossbow and the game is done in a 2D retro style.  It released on Steam for $13.99 on August 20th.
This title has both keyboard and controller support.  Both are playable, but as with most games of this style, the gamepad is preferable.  I’m not a fan of how the button remapping was done.  You can fully remap buttons but rather than the traditional Xbox controller representations, or perhaps something that let’s you choose the controller you’re using, you get these number remaps.  Things like the D-pad being referenced by 7+ makes it a pain to remap and remember what button relates to which action.
Sir Oliver controls just fine, with a reasonable variety of extras, including potions, swappable weapons and being able to switch the direction of flight, which is a fairly unique feature to games that scroll automatically.
As far as performance is concerned, the title runs at a standard 60FPS, has windowed mode options and resolution options, but little else due to the retro art style.  It also has independent music and sound effect volume controls.
I really like the variety in combat that the player has control over.  Throughout the game, you will acquire weapons that each have some kind of unique attack in addition to your basic auto-shot crossbow.  This could be things like a vertical column of damaging light, a spread out frost shot, a charge.  And you can swap these out on the fly, as well as upgrade the attacks and their damage.  You also get a squire which is a little floating buff bot, in essence that can be swapped out for various effects.  These are all very nice and I quite enjoyed experimenting with different combinations.
However, the combat and gameplay contains my biggest gripe which is a huge issue in my view for a game in this genre.  It is slow.  When you’re playing a shoot-em-up, especially one with automatic scrolling, in my view it has to be faster than Gryphon Knight.  I was constantly feeling as though I wanted the game to be 30-50% faster in scroll speed and Gryphon movement speed.  There is a speed buff for your own movement speed, but it’s not very much, and the screen speed never changes.  And as a result, the game is actually a lot longer than it needed to be for how much level content it has.
The plot starts off unique, with the adventure essentially taking place after and as a result of another huge adventure.  Without stepping into spoiler territory, the tutorial of the game explains that the weapons you took from the dragons hoard are corrupting their users and it’s up to Sir Oliver to save them.  I liked that part.  I also want to give some mad props to the developers for their extensive compendium that has text descriptions for weapons, enemies, area, items, and all kinds of other stuff including being able to watch cutscenes again.  This was a completely unnecessary feature that was very very well done.
The game advertises localization in English, Portuguese, Spanish and Russian.  I can’t speak to the other languages, but the text is very awkward in English.  Nothing is spelled wrong, but you can tell that the writing was done by someone who’s first language is not English.
I can’t say that I’m impressed by the graphical style.  Retro games are a dime a dozen these days.  Visually, it reminds me of games like Ghosts and Goblins, albeit not as dark.  The characters are unique and recognizable, with areas that are equally unique from one another in their design.
The music is pretty good, with that retro midi style sound you’d expect on something like the Super Nintendo.  Sound effects are varied but sound a bit awkward, especially with multiple death or hit effects occurring at the same time.  The effects just don’t sound amazing
The game is solid and the developer is responsive to fixing problems.  There was a blocking bug that I encountered early on that the dev had fixed within a couple of days, and since that bug, I have not run into any quality assurance issues.  It feels as though the game plays precisely as intended without any deviations.
I enjoyed Gryphon Knight Epic.  I was also frustrated by it on a number of occasions.  For a shoot-em-up it is really slow which actually makes the game take longer than it needs to with how much level content there is.  The title performs well, but that is par for the course with the Unity engine running retro graphics.  The sound design is varied, but isn’t smack you in the face awesome.  It’s a fun title, but a $14 price tag is way too high.

One of rare 2D Medieval Action-Shooter games mixed with elements of exploration and duel-like boss battles.
Being a huge fan of old Genesis/NES games along with Contra, Megaman, Aladdin and Metal Slug this brings back nostalgy so hard that keeps me playing continuously. Lately very often we get release which is supposed to get those effects on players with retro-arcade style and Gryphon Knight Epic is definitely one of them with a bit more of something.
You are taking role of Sir Oliver who retired from his adventures after slaying dragons and winning heart of princess. He is forced into adventures again with his loyal gryphon Aquila once when his “bad side” presented as spirit separate from Sir Oliver and confront him in battle where he win but with luck and brave soldiers our beloved knight get saved along with new chance to make things right. All allies and friends are now enemies, creatures, plants, bird even people will stay in front of your way but you need to fight and get answers on easier or harder way since before every mission you will be able to pick difficulty which will suit your abilities and skills in these kind of games.
Unlike many other retro games you have ability to shift forward or backwards along with moving and collecting or killing what you missed which makes you feel a bit more exploratory oriented. Sure with that being said you do have freedom of shooting but not being able to do actions diagonal or use analog feature fully makes this adventure a bit harder and sometimes unfair.
Along with simple 2D Shoot-everything element style there are slight RPG roots. Through levels you can find variety of gems for healing, buffing shield or ability to destroy everything on screen including small menu to switch weapons, shields or potions which will greatly help you on harder difficulty. In between levels you have a map where you make progress through, along with Market where you can buy potions and many other features including Magic Shop for some abilities as mentioned before and weapon upgrades which cost is increasing with further progress. You are getting coins for every kill or extra moves which you do through level so eventually getting upgrades is possible without harder effort. For fans and players who like more info about enemies, locations, characters and cutscenes there is Compendium aswel which will provide more details about this adventure.

Do you enjoy challenging-but-innovative shooters?  Do you enjoy classic Mega Man gameplay?  Do you like medieval settings?  Congrats, you found it: the only title I've ever seen that combines all three into one fantastic and utterly unique slice of bossome pizza.
The presentation is what you'd expect from an indie game.  The visuals are simple and cute, the sound effects are corny but enjoyable, and the story is interesting but more or less what you'd expect.  The lore is a bit interesting if you put in the time to read it.
That's all fine, but I play games for the gameplay -- and that's where this one shines.  Discover secrets, vanquish badass bosses, and up the challenge until you've mastered the most difficult of quests.  Although there's only a handful of levels, they are wildly diverse and unique.  Every time you fly over a viking-guarded mountain, or soar through a madwoman's castle, you're met with something new which keeps the world around you deliciously fresh.
My only real complaint is the game's brevity.  After a mere sixteen hours, I've managed about four playthroughs, and got every achievement the game could offer.  (It wasn't easy, either.)  Don't get me wrong, though: those sixteen hours were a blast, and profoundly satisfying.
In short: play this if you want something fun, unique, and a little on the harder side, but don't mind simple presentation and under 20 hours of game time.

Secrets of Grindea is a story-driven game (With phenomenal RPG elements!) where you can customize your character's appearance, skills, and talents. While the mechanics are simple to grasp, there are many unique bosses and mobs that require certain nuances to accomplish.
The leveling system works out relatively well. It never feels like an over the top grind (hah) until about halfway through, where it suddenly starts to feel like it takes longer to level based upon the monster EXP.
Perhaps my only real complaint about the game lies in the skill system. They've set it up so that you get silver and gold spell points, where you spend so many silver points before you may only place gold points to further level up a skill. After spending 17 hours in the game, I've only been able to get one skill all the way up with gold points, as you only receive one point every few levels.
Still, you can completely customize your hotkeys, and they made it quite easy and intuitive. Though it is early access, they've already thought of many convenience things that other games miss: equipping cosmetic items for free, pets that increase stats, NPCs that have witty responses, etc.
It's rare you find an unfinished game that leaves you thinking about it even while you're in the middle of working, exercising, and trying to sleep. I'm only sad it isn't finished! 9.5/10

Stories Untold puts the player through four scenarios which all eventually connect to make for a fairly unoriginal but well delivered overarching plot.
The game's biggest draw is its atmosphere and environment interaction. Whether you're playing an old text based computer game (which is fantastically written) in your old bedroom or operating various complicated machines, everything feels intuitive and the immersion can reach incredible highs.
For most of the game you'll be stuck in a static position, unable to move your character freely, sort of like in Please, Don’t Touch Anything or Five Nights at Freddy's. Some parts of the game let you move around like you would in a generic first person game, however these sections of the game are absolutely AWFUL:
-Mouse sensitivy is comically high, making your character do a 360 if you only slightly touch your mouse.
-FOV is weirdly zoomed in and makes navigating the environment feel clumsy and unpleasant.
-Performance drops drastically, taking a perfectly smooth and stable fps count down to 10-15.
-Crosshair disappears, which can make clicking on some objects a bit of a challenge.
My final gripe is that the game is riddled with typos, which only get more numerous as the game goes on
Despite all of this, i still enjoyed my time with Stories Untold immensely, and if the awful walking segments get a bit of polish and the typos get corrected i would recommend this game to absolutely anyone.

Excellent trading game. Get this if you liked the Port Royale (PR) and/or Patrician (PAT) series.
The game is very similar to PR and PAT and some parts are ripped from these games (some sounds and trading goods). The 1st mayor difference you will notice is that there is only 1 screen in which you can do everything. You no longer can go into cities and see how cities look and you can no longer place buildings in places you want. This greatly speeds up the game, because there are no more loading screens. I didnt like the citybuilding aspect of PAT4, because placing buildings was wonky, but I liked the grid system of PR3.
Another mayor difference are the families. Getting married in PR and PAT always felt useless and did not give real benefits. In Rise of Venice (RoV) family members can actually be send on missions. E.g. in the campaign one of my brothers was a doctor and could  cure disease in cities, others were captains and had increased stats, etc.
Ranking up has been changed. You now need to have a certain amount of convoys, sailors/workers, etc AND you need to get permission of the council of Venice. So no more automatic rank up when you have reached the prerequisites. This means that you have to keep the council happy, which means doing missions. Missions are similar to previous games, although the 'search and rescue' missions can be a bit annoying, because ships have a very small line of sight.
Naval battles have been improved. The AI now actually uses chainshot to bring down your sails. I honestly can't say if I can recommend this game or not, so imagine that this review is Neutral.
Story:
The story is kind of all over the place, as if they wanted to throw in as many concepts and characters as possible, which, can, with enough time, work, however, in a 4 and a half hour game, there just is not enough time. Because of this, nothing feels fleshed out, everything is just a kinda' cameo, with little to no-reason-given. This is extremely saddening,
because I love Star Wars for the storys, everything has meaning and a reason for it's existence...
[SPOILER BELOW]
For Example:
[NO SPOILERS]
On the plus side, the story captures your emotion, you feel for the main character and want his journey to come with success, you feel his pain and his reasoning behind all of his actions.
Gameplay:
The game plays pretty much exactly like the first, just with two Lightsabers... The same powers, the same combat and the same enemies, it gets dull very quickly. I mean, yeah, slicing StormTrooper's limbs off is fun and all, but after around 30 minutes, you've seen everything that the game has to offer. If you played the first game, then you know of the Rancor missions, in which you pretty much have to spam lightning until you can activate a quicktime event. This game also has these events, however, you will experience it behind every second door instead of it being 30 minutes apart as it was in TFU I.
Graphics/Port Info:
Graphically, the game doesn't hold up by todays standards, but, that's OK, because what it loses in texture quality, it makes up in Architecture... Every environment is beautiful, with awe-inspiring backdrops and planet design that just makes me want to slow pan and take hundreds of screen-captures. In contrast to the textures within the game, however, the cinematics are stunningly realistic, with faces that just look real and action that just bursts with excitement.
But, as always, there are some drawbacks, the game is capped at 30fps, which just doesn't give it justice, so I would 100% recommend downloading the FPS unlocker online, it just makes the experience tenfold better. To add to that, the PC controls work horrendously, much as TFU did, so, I would recommend you play with a controller.
Conclusion:
The Force Unleashed II is a short, flawwed title that is repetative and suffers from too many Quick Time Events, however, underneath is a reasonably solid story with much power and emotion that is able to drive the player to continue to the end. The game didn't add much over it's predeccessor, however, my fondness for it enabled me to see through it's cons and focus on what is in the game, rather than what is not.
6/10.

This game, wow this game. Don't let the screenshots fool you, this is as amateur as you can get. While it was only made by two guys, Unturned was made by a teenager still in school, his game is a far better game just overall and it's free. The character is using both hands while still somehow picking up boxes and items. I first read about this game in an issue of Game Informer and decided immediately I wanted to play it. A friend of mine is an Alaskan Native and I'd always been interested in the culture since I met her, and this game certainly does not dissapoint on that.
I had issues when first trying to start the game, but after updating my graphics drivers I was good to go - though I had to play in low quality. This is apprently a common issue with anyone playing with Windows - even windows 8.1 like myself - so keep that in mind if you're purchasing without a high level graphics card.
Anyhow far as gameplay goes, I haven't had nearly as many issues as everyone else. I've found the jumping responsive, the borra pretty easy to manage, and the other keyboard controls work fine. I haven't used a controller, so I can't speak for anyone who plans on that, but keyboard is just fine.
The only issues I've had is when you have to make the fox fly and press shift to move the spirits. That can get a bit tedious and annoying, but I also have very short fingers so it's quite a reach for me to keep pressing the shift while guiding with the other fingers. (I know this won't make much sense, but it's due to the fact I dont wish to reveal part of the story).
As for the enviroment, it's lovely. Even on low the graphics are quite nice, and the variety they can create with a rather limited setting is admirable. The ice caves - especially inside the whale - are very pretty. Playing the game kind of made me wanna drink hot chocolate.
I find the story great. It is a classic Native Alaskan tale (I say Native Alaskan because I can't spell the word for the life of me) about a girl, a blizzard, and a special little fox. There are subtitles to read while the storyteller tells the story in the native language. Very enjoyable to listen too. The lack of highly descriptive words makes it all feel more ...true, persay.
As for Nuna (the girl) and the fox, I love them. Neither ever says a word, but through playing them both on singleplayer I kind of get the feel of the connection they have. Nuna needs the fox, and the fox needs Nuna. Neither can survive without the other, each stage requiring them to help one another in many ways. This will especially be enjoyable if you have the ability to play co-op.
And the historical videos that you unlock on the way are maybe a minute long and all very, very interesting. It details how the natives lived, what they ate, how they dressed, played, their beliefs and spirits and everything else, all from various generations of Native Alaskans.
All in all I highly reccomend this game, especially for the sale price. Some people say it's a bit short, but I'm not finding it that way.

I was hoping for something similar to amnesia, but it was a huge step up. Really fantastic game if you are into horror and sci-fi. Especially if you like Frictional's other work, check this game out, it's really fantastic. The atmosphere in this game is top notch, as well as the story, enemy design, locations, music.
I don't know what else to say It's a very solid game, I can't think of anything I didn't like about it other than the story being pretty depressing.
To go into a bit more detail for those unaware exactly what style of game Soma is, you mostly walk around and explore in First Person. Soma is not to be confused with a walking simulator, it has a lot of puzzles and heavy focus on horror like many of frictional's other work.
It has enemies, but no combat. You deal with oppenents by running and hiding rather then fighting. This has a very strong effect on most players, as being defenseless really does makes monsters more frightening. As a long time player of horror games I'm pretty desensitized to most of the tropes, but this game really had me on edge and genuinely unnerved me at times.
tl:dr : A truly fantastic sci-fi horror game, and an enormous step forward from Frictional's previous titles.

The documentary portion of the game is nicely woven into the story and gameplay; informational clips of Alaska and the Iñupiaq people are unlocked by reaching certain points (some obvious, some hidden) of the game. These clips can be reached and watched with a simple tab-key. Once you're done, you can then quickly return to your explorations with another single press of the button. The game's atmosphere is exquisite, sometimes breathtaking and sometimes haunting, and always constantly evoking the harsh beauty of Alaska and its cold winds.
On the other hand, the game itself is linear and short (roughly 3 hours). There is only one major path through the game, and any detours you can take will barely last half a minute and are only there for hidden documentary clips. Further, the controls can be awkward and imprecise, and glitches can sometimes frustratingly send you slipping into a bottomless pit. On that note, the game fortunately frequently auto-saves after every platformer puzzle, so that glitches and your own slips won't set you too far back.
Ultimately, Never Alone is an educational tale, an interactive story. The story it tells and the experience it delivers is well-worth the time and the purchase. Plus, I heartily recommend any game that delivers a positive message like this:

For example - some triceratops protecting a baby rex or a dinosaur of the same species being friendly to you, only to kill you.

I'm writing this review for people who, like me, might look into this game hoping for an adventure game with a decent female lead, or at least co-lead. Spoilers: you're not going to find it in this game.
Gameplay-wise: Speaking as a person who only encountered Broken Sword recently and thus in its newest version only, I found the game passably engaging. The puzzles do make you think and offer a large range of potential combinations, although there are places where it drags because the game expects you to do something completely counter-intuitive and gives no feedback on whether you're doing it right, so you go through every single item and combination thereof, then dialogue choices, and finally click everything before you hit it. The hint system might as well not have existed, since it didn't help me and apparently annoyed previous lovers of the game. The graphics are what you might expect from a decade old game, not really updated but not too terrible.
[Some spoilers] As for the characters, you play as Nico Marlet, who is a fairly decent character, drawn into the murder of her newest interviewee and subsequent meddling into her life, for about 30 minutes out of a 7 hour playthrough. The rest of the time you play as George Stubbart, whose only connection to the whole affair was he happened to be at a cafe when it blew up to kill the man inside, and decided he had to solve the crime for great justice or something. He takes center stage and then keeps it for the rest of the game while Nico sits at her apartment and waits, or seduces someone over the phone, or talks to an archaelogist friend to create a really gross doubly-oneside love triangle centered around her. Also there is a very dubious (consent-wise) scene later in the game between George and Nico, whose romance doesn't really have any substance beyond George thinking she's pretty a few times? So many things seem shoehorned in without proper support. It's both baffling and irritating.
If you want a decent head-scratcher and don't mind a host of gender issues, then pick this up. If you wanted a game which treats its women respectfully, don't do what I did. Buy another game.

Wicked Witches, developed by Ectoplasm Studios, is a third-person shooter in which players take on the role of a witch (obviously). After being falsely accused of witchcraft, our heroine is banished from her village. In retaliation, she decides to become a REAL witch, heart-set on stealing the lives from those who stole hers. On paper, this sounds like a promising concept.  It isn’t often we get to rewrite some of history’s oldest fairy tales. Only this time, you’re the villain.
However, despite the appealing premise, I had built up some general expectations. It’s clearly intended for younger audiences, but that doesn’t give ANY game the excuse for poor quality. For example, look at the first LEGO games. Whether you’re ten or thirty-two, it can be enjoyed by anyone. So, pandering to a demographic that isn’t my own doesn’t give this game the benefit of the doubt, at least not in this case.
We’ll start with graphics. I’d call them mediocre at best. It’s got this odd design I can only compare to papier-mâché.  Thankfully, this game is flushed with colors (for the most part), which makes up for the… uncomfortable character models. They aren’t bad, just… uncomfortable. It’s really the best way I can describe it. Looking at them for too long makes me fidget in my seat.
But, as you probably know, video games aren’t worth a bucket of warm spit without proper gameplay, and my first impressions of Wicked Witches weren’t half bad. You’re primary goal is to kill as many villagers as possible as you complete your various objectives. It plays like a horde shoot em’ up, and it’s a pretty satisfying experience… at first.
There's are multiple spells to unlock, different abilities to master, and to top it off, you can even fly about on your broomstick! Raining fiery meteors of destruction down on fleeing villagers really instills a feeling of power. You’re also capable of “enchanting” certain objects throughout each level. These vary from trees to graveyards to unicorns. Whatever the player enchants will help them on the battlefield. Building up an army of monstrous trees and undead skeletons is pretty cool.
So, after all this praise, you might be wondering why I’m giving this game and thumbs down. Well, here’s why. Despite its achievements, Wicked Witches is tremendously flawed. All the gameplay mechanics mentioned previously are repeated throughout the entirety of this game. You’ll be spamming the left mouse button for the duration of each level, wiping out mindless waves of enemies in a cycle that has no end. Spells hardly vary from one another, as they all work identically; whether it’s exploding pumpkins, cauldrons or meteors, they all provide the same damage and outcome.
Clipping is a serious issue. Enemy projectiles will soar directly through structures, and same goes for your own projectiles. Hell, if you really want to, hop on your broomstick and faze through just about anything! It’s INCREDIBLY lazy game design.
Lastly, I want to talk about the writing, and oh my god, you will cringe like you’ve never cringed before. It’s one of those things you’ll have to see to believe. I’ll spare you the details, but the term “LOL” is used quite often. Yeah, it’s THAT bad.
If you’re over the age of twelve and plan on buying Wicked Witches for your own amusement, I say pass. There are a lot more enjoyable things you can do with your time. If you’re looking for a game to give your kid, this isn’t the worst choice, but trust me, you’re kid deserves better.

Gryphon Knight Epic is a shoot-em-up that was kickstarted back in 2014; combining the genre with metroidvania like design. With the game out now, the merging of the two genres worked pretty well, but there were a few conflicts here and there.
Gryphon Knight Epic follows the exploits of Sir Oliver, after slaying the evil dragon with his friends and winning the heart of the princess, he retired from a life of adventuring until an evil ghost that looks like him begins terrorizing the land. It's up to Oliver and his gryphon Aquila to stop the ghost and save the land from a variety of enemies.
Gryphon Knight Epic is different by the fact that the developers have combined the genres of shoot-em-up with the exploration you would see in a 2d action adventure game. How it works is that each level is played as a shoot-em-up with enemies of varying sizes and damage spread attacking you from all sides.
Unlike other shoot-em-ups, you can shift yourself to either be auto moving left or right at any time. At certain points the level will branch in different directions, allowing you to explore different parts of the level for additional treasure and runes that act as upgrades. Each level features two bosses, one mini and a stage boss, and to the game's credit, the bosses are varied and require different strategies to take down. Before and after each stage, you can buy items to help you and upgrade your weapons.
Exploring the levels will reveal hidden paths and upgrades to help you out.
The game is aimed at beginner to average shoot-em-up fans with three difficulty levels that affect checkpoints, health drops and your gold reward at the end.
With that said, even on the "expert" difficulty, Gryphon Knight Epic doesn't come anywhere near the bullet hell-ness of other shoot-em-ups like Sine Mora. The game does a good job of mixing these genres to create something unique, but the shoot-em-up design and aesthetics do clash with the exploration side.
The first problem I have with Gryphon Knight Epic is how there is a clash between the shoot-em-up elements and the overall aesthetics of the game. The game features a pixel style aesthetic with enemies and environmental obstacles befitting each stage. The problem is that because things blend in together due to the unified aesthetic, it makes the shoot-em-up elements harder than they should be.
The issue is that in most shoot-em-ups, the bullets or projectiles are always completely opposite of the aesthetic of the game, so that they are easily spotted and avoided. But here, because everything blends in, it's very easy for shots and projectiles to blend into the background and make them hard to spot until it’s too late. In one level, you have to dodge attacks from the background environment and it was very hard to spot the safe zones due to how the attacks were animated.
Another part of this is that the game features a character model where only certain parts are vulnerable to damage: Sir Oliver himself. When you're busying flying around trying to take out enemies, it's sometimes easy to forget where you should be positioned to let bullets hit the invincible part which is your gryphon.
The boss fights are all unique and interesting to fight, but I just wish that the entire gameplay was as engaging
Finally, the game is on the short side with only 8 levels. The developers did plan to make more via stretch goals, but they weren't met. The exploration side of the design does feel a little downplayed as each level has only a few alternate paths that warrant exploring.
It feels like the developers were hoping for something greater than the sum of its parts, but ended up with less; the exploration side is limited to a few slight paths per level without any of the deeper mechanics in other games of the genre, and the shoot-em-up aspect doesn't evolve or grow beyond the first level.
Gryphon Knight Epic may not be the most complicated or challenging shoot-em-up out there, but combining exploration does help keep things interesting. Despite my issues with the game, there's nothing here that I would point out as bad or poor game design, I just wish that there was more content on the exploration side and growth on the shoot-em-up mechanics. Hopefully the game will do well enough for the developers to continue working on the series or add more to the game. First, let me just say that I generally prefer supporting smaller devs & businesses where I can. Besides the fact that this game has a lot of ideas that appeal to me, I wanted to support a game that is so clearly an underdog.
This game has some terrific concepts, fun ideas, and charm. Except there's one issue with it: it's not finished.
I think the devs have some great ideas and a solid foundation to build something extraodinary on. "flawed but fun" is a very very generous way to describe this game. It's easy. There's no challenge. Spells have no cooldowns, enemies have no weaknesses/strengths to adapt to - so just pick wichever spell you want to, and spam it until everything's dead. Chances are, you won't die in the process.
Bugs. Bugs galore. Enemies getting stuck in things. Floating enemies running on the spot continuously. flying and randomly getting stick in a tree that visually wasn't there a second ago. scream points that won't collect (spoiler: they need to be collected) movement and jump animations look broken. Granted, the controls are pretty tight, but everything still looks disjointed.
That this game has so few reviews but most of them are positive, is highly suspect.
One look at the forum, and seeing the complete lack of response from the devs from questions tells me one thing: this game is as it is and won't be any more than that. Which is a SHAME because with a bit more polish, balance, and detail, this could have been great.
But I honestly don't feel it's fair to sell this as a completed game when it so clearly isn't. There are good ideas here, and while the execution isn't poor, it's not finished. And honestly, who wants to play a game where your dominant thought is "what could have been..." instead of enjoying the actual game you're playing. I pay for a product, not potential. And I write this with the consumer in mind.
I will be refunding this. in a few months or so, if they've updated and fixed this game at all, I'd consider purchasing it again. But something tells me this game will stay as it is. I hope I'm proven wrong.

I'm not a great shoot'em up fan nor a good player of the genre, but it's graphics and proposal got my attention and, well, got some of my time 'till I've finished it.
Gryphon Knight Epic delivers perfectly what it says it is: a classical game with some HARD challenges. But beatable ones and I need to say I was very surprised I've managed to finish it without a thousand retries. :) Populating all that, it got some half a dozen different scenarios with very unique enemies and bosses, making it a very positive thing about the title, since, even for a relatively short game, it delivers the feeling it is something much larger (of course repeating some scenarios to beat the damn bosses helps with that as well...).
The game story is clichè (most probably in an intentional way) with lots of fun wanna be elements on it. Although I particularly don't get into that style of mood most of the times, I have to say I've laughed on some ocasions... (*maybe some spoiler ahead*) but, despite all my attempt to find it clichè and not that funny, the end of the arc made me respect more the story design and I do congrat the designer for that!
And finally we've got the art... man, the game graphics are wonderfully crafted and detailed. Every single pixel appears to count and I've lost myself wondering around the graphic art much more than once during my play hours. Great job! And trying not to be unfair, many people were complaining about the sound design and music, but although the sound effects are not that great, I do not found it bad, and the music is well constructed in most of the stages!
GKE is a fair priced game (and for it's content amount, maybe a cheap one!) and it will give you some couple of hours of fun, rage and satisfaction!

Years before Dan Brown's Da Vinci's Code made headlines for its religious subject, there was another story that had a similar setting even starting in Paris and ending in Scotland.This gem was Broken Sword: The shadow of the templars a point and click adventure game released 1996 and re-released in 2010 for the PC with more content as Director's Cut.
First I'll talk about the main game and after I will talk about the director's cut.The game begins in Paris where our main character George Stobbart is enjoying his vacations.Just as he drinks his coffee and enjoying the Parisian autumn two people enter the Caffe: a man with a briefcase who stops to order a coffee and after a short time a clown with a musical instrument.The clown takes the mans briefcase and leaves his instrument which is revealed to be a bomb which goes off and that's how the game begins.The whole story is about George's quest to find the costume killer, and as the plot advances we find out the whole story arc is about the conflict between Templars and Assassins and the templars called here Neo-Templars are the bad guys(sounds familiar? :) ).Besides Paris, other places you get to visit are Scotland(twice), Spain and Siria, each with its own feel and colorful characters which make this a game a joy to play even after you finished it once.The game has hand-drawn animations which look gorgeous, the voice acting is solid and the music works very well with the whole game.
The original game has from me a 10/10 rating, I find no issue with it, its a great adventure game with great characters and a good story.
Now about the director's cut, after the success of the first game the game got 4 more sequels: Broken Sword The Smoking Mirror, Broken Sword The Sleeping Dragon, Broken Sword The Angel of Death and recently Broken Sword The Serpents Curse.Between Broken Sword 4 and 5, the first 2 games The Shadow of the Templars and The Smoking Mirror where re-released with more content and improvements.The director's cut of Broken Sword starts with Nicole Collard, not with George a day before the bombing of the caffe and is essentially a prologue setting up the main story.The new content is some levels with Nico where we find more about her past.As the main game starts the first problem appears:the sound quality,the new recordings really stand out against the old ones from the main game,and also some of the character designs look worse than the main game which is weird one good example is when the character visits a hotel in Paris and there is one character reading a newspaper in a armchair, for some reason his outline was removed he looks like a black mass of animation.Also, they changed the interface and added dialogue pics at the top corner of the screen with the faces of the characters with which you hold a conversation.
rating for the director's cut: 8/10 the new content is good, but the technical problems really drag down the score, they could have remastered it better, luckily they remastered the second game perfectly and the problems here are not present.

Who knew that a mobile game could be so rich in content and so well made?  Massive kudos to Tiger Style on this gem.  No other game has been able to accurately portray the profound sense of exploration and discovery in an alien world like this game, except for metroid, and that's saying something.  Speaking of metroid, this game KIND OF has a metroidvania formula, albeit in a very basic way.  It does have labyrinthine maps with some necessary backtracking at times, but no upgrades to speak of.  The story is a very welcome foray into realistic science fiction.  A science team and their AI companion (which sounds excactly like claptrap, not sure if intentional or not) studying and exploring mars in the hopes of finding life.  The game was obviously designed with "diversity" in mind, no caucasian characters exist in this game, just an asian scientist and a black scientist.  The diversity aided nothing in the game and to that effect the black character is fairly annoying with her constant lack of understanding of basic concepts of how ecosystems work and her hyper fascination with acquiring more data regardless of what it means in the grand scheme of things.
Pros
-excellent sense of adventure, exploration and discovery set in an alien world, evokes the same feeling from playing Metroid for the first time
-very unique gameplay, you have no weapons and use plant growth to affect the world around you
-interesting story that any true science fiction enthusiast can appreciate
-"diversity"
Cons
-Can become a bit repetitive after a while, sometimes you need to wait for certain plants to multiply enough to unlock the next room
-Supporting characters are fairly annoying
-"diversity"
Not sure if I would pay $10 as this is the full price of the game, but I picked it up whilst on sale for $2 and would recommend it at that price without hesitation.

Full disclosure: I am a friend of the developers and a backer of this project on KS. That said, my opinion of the game would have been the same regardless.
GKE stands alongside the best shmups I have played. I am a fan of the genre from the days of 1942, R-Type, Raiden and, more recently, the excellent Ikaruga. GKE's medieval setting is a welcome detour from the typical themes of the genre, and fits the game extremely well.
Gameplay is everything you would expect from a modern shmup with a classic feel. Controls are tight - I have used a DS4 with the DS4Windows app and it works great, Frame rate is solid. The large number of items and sidekicks gives the gameplay variety and a helping hand when you need it. Hunting for runes is a lot of fun.
The amount of content in this game is tremendous for its price tag. Environments are very beautifully crafted and full of detail. Each stage is very unique and makes the game feel fresh even after several hours. Enemy sprites are generally good if sometimes too detached from the environment, and some of the animations might have been more polished.
There are many little easter eggs and references to games and pop culture in this game, making it fun to hunt for them in the text and scenery.
Overall a very highly recommended game for shmup fans. On Knight difficulty it should be pretty welcoming even for more casual fans, if you use items and sidekicks intelligently. Veteran shmup fans have only one option: EPIC difficulty!

Despite some minor issues I really like this game. let me start this review by pointing out what I feel Ectoplasm studio got right with this game.
The Pros
-Price
-The characters are fun, cute, and memorable
-The gameplay is smooth and easy to understand
-Terrifying and slaying droves of humans is fun
-Destroying Fairytales is funner
-Powering up the Witch is done in a very traditional way, but someone it feels fresh.
-The odd combination of Cute and Creepy and bright colors contrasted by dark shadows is really nice to look at.
-Great Art work
-The flight system is another really smooth part of the game.
-Cool Music, makes you think of the Tower of Terror ride
-it's one of those games that is hard to classify ( in a good way )
-what is not awesome about making plants do your bidding, or enchanting a graveyard to summon undead minions for you, or turning Rainbow Shooting unicorns into Fire stomping horses to slay your enemies?
BONUS POINTS FOR!
-The little things... The way the characters follow  your cursor with their heads and eyes,  I had them  nodding in time to the music for a few minutes  before I realized I was actually not playing the  game.
The Cons
~Still Some glitches with basic things, no sound effects in the opening parts of the game just music... Maybe there is not supposed to be?
~Unclear on what awards 1,2,or 3 pumpkin completion.
~I had a major issue with Jumping.  The main one being when you jump right before you decent from the apex of the jump, you just instantly end up on the ground, it makes jumping something you really do not want to do.
~Developer assumes people have a brain and do not need more instruction.  For those of us that are Undead or simply don't have a brain, or forgot to put it in our heads when we woke up, some simple instructions on how to change spells, etc would be nice.  Although it is pretty easy to figure out Mouse Wheel up or Down or just use the numbers on your keyboard.
~Would also be nice to have a legend that you can look at to see what keys do what.
~It is a little unclear on how you get new spells, they just seem to appear.  It would be nice to have to work for them, or to have to achieve certain sub objectives to unlock them, and perhaps there is,  but if so, that is also unclear.
~To much up time on Broom flying makes it easy to exploit what is mainly ground enemies.
~All spells are unlimted and do not have a CD. Unlimited ammo would be fine, so would no CD on spells, but when you combine those 2  the game becomes a little easy not having to manage your resources you can just spam everything.

Overall
Wicked Witches is a really fun and refreshing title, It's not to hard, even the hard missions, but it does get challenging.  I really like it when a developer makes something that is "their" game, and they do not try and make it compete with an already over saturated market.   This game definitely feels like something personal to someone, and that alone makes it a great experience.  Who ever came up with the Consept is probably someone I would like to go to a Halloween party , or just hang out in a graveyard with.
This game is well worth the 10 dollars, If you are not hooked by the time you get to the Salem Mission you'll be hooked once you become notorious and have to defend your own home.
Looking forward to seeing more from Ectoplasm Studio.
~Undead Aaron

It's a very good game. It's immersive, atmosperic and interesting.
1) Art. While the animations are pretty simple, the drawings of plants, animals and environment are very rich.
2) Music. It's a well-fitting calm and non-distracting background music.
3) Characters. Each character has its own memorable personality. I especially liked robotic and formal language of ART, and how even characters are making fun of some of his replics. But he still feels like a character with soul, rather than just robot.
4) Story. The story is very interesting and keeping intrigue to the end. The dialogues are very rich and are one of the reasons why the game is so atmosperic and fascinating.
5) Gameplay. It's quite unique and awesome. You gradually learn about different parts of the ecosystem, interaction of them with each other and how to use that knowledge to your advantage. Each chamber is different and some of them pose pretty difficult challenges. I also liked how the map allows you to travel to previously visited locations instantly, thus saving lots of time when you need to get some specific seeds. One thing that can use some improvements is scripting. Sometimes you have to go to a specific place to trigger some dialogue important for completing some game parts. In some cases (pretty rarely though), it's not clear what exactly to do.

This is a game that provides an original experience - it's about growing and sustaining an ecosystem (I don't know why it's tagged as a platformer. You can fly, so there's no platforming element whatsoever). As you explore you'll encounter a number of different plant-like creatures, each with its own behaviors and method of reproduction. You have to figure out how each plant works on your own; there's not a lot of direct explanation, and this discovery aspect is the main draw of the game. Once you've got an idea of how things work, you can decide which plants to grow where in order to revive each area of the cave.
The downside is that it's not all that well designed. The interactions between the lifeforms aren't very complicated, and growing the plants requires too much manual interaction, rather than organizing the environment so that it works on its own, like an ecosystem should. Still, it's worth checking out if you're interested in an experience that you haven't had before.

Edit: I'm going to clarify my previously totally useless review.
You play as an explorer on Mars who becomes trapped in a complex cave system. In the caves, you discover Martian life, which is mostly in plant form. Secrets of Grindea is a top down adventure game that immediately reminds me of the Legend of Zelda series in it's blend of combat and puzzles. While still an early access game at the time of writing, there is more than enough content to justify the fifteen dollar price tag. With an easy to learn combat system and the lack of distinct classes, combat feels smooth and genuinely fun, as one would hope a game with the term "grind" in the title would boast. Likewise, the characters are for the most part interesting, if perhaps not always particularly memorable.
The characters of Grindea tend to alternate between totally forgettable and completely memorable. Your talking loot bag, appropriately named Bag, your close friend Luke, and your somewhat obnoxious rival Marino all manage to establish themselves with completely memorable characteristics - Bag is very cynical and sarcastic, with what appears to be an mix of disinterest and dislike for all things not labeled Very Rare Loot. Luke, meanwhile, is a hardworking powerhouse of a boy, but isn't particularly bright. Marino is a rich, bratty noble, and while that's not particularly deep as a character, he does a good job of making it memorable. On the other hand, quest giver Quinton, a couple of clearly reoccuring, almost Team Rocket - esque thugs, and even the player character's own father all seem to have virtually no personality. In the interest of fairness, these characters haven't recieved nearly as much screentime as Bag, but the problem is that the charcters I found memorable made themselves memorable from the first meeting, whereas all of these less memorable characters have appeared at least twice and still have yet to make any sort of impact on me.
Combat in Grindea, as I mentioned above, is a very easy concept to grasp, if a little hectic in practice. The Z key is your basic melee attack with whatever is equiped to your weapon slot, X raises your shield, and the A,S,D,F,C, and V keys all bind to the various special attacks and spells you pick up over the course of the game. This means that a solid blend of melee and magical combat is more than plausible, although the effort to make that blend work is probably more than a strictly melee or magical style. That being said, the only character I've made so far is very focused to the ice branch of magic, and so I am unable to comment on how balanced the various skills are as of now. Despite this, it's worth repeating that the combat system itself is very enjoyable, and the more polished parts of the game are an immense pleasure to play.
However, it's also worth repeating that this is an early access game, and it began to become extraordinarily obvious when I was coming close to the end of the story mode content simply because the majority of the major fights became seriously unbalanced towards solo players. Perhaps it becomes less of a headache with coplayers in the mix, but one particularly noteworthy boss fight required me to keep putting damage on the boss while at the same time destroying remarkably resilient minions that were spewing poisonous gas across the battlefield. Forget to put enough pressure on the boss, and he will fully heal his minions and render them invulnerable until you go back to putting damage on the boss himself. As a solo player, the task was almost too much for me to handle, and I was only able to scrape by thanks to the points I'd put into my summonable snow golem. I don't take issue with the idea behind the boss fight, but it's more than evident that the devs have yet to find an appropriate balance that challenges a group of playeres and still remains manageable for solo players.
That fight notwithstanding, coming closer to the end of story mode also saw a lot of interesting puzzles and challenges spring forth. There's a dungeon in which the changing of the seasons is required to open up different paths to progress, and there's a sequence closer to the end of the existing content in which a teleportation power from earlier is used to cross elaborate labrynths of cannons, using mirrors and timed launches to get across. While difficult, I found myself enjoying the sequence, and look forward to seeing how the puzzles might further develop with the release of future content.
All in all, Grindea is a fun game that is definitely worth the price, despite it's glaring flaws, and it shows a lot of potential in where it can go from here. While not yet finished, it's a very enjoyable product and looks to be a fantastic game in the making.

This isn't so much a bad game as it is the complete stagnation of two different good series.  As someone who loved Patrician III, I can say that this game basically just copy-pastes most of the good ideas from that game, dumbed some of them down or made you arbitrarily incapable of trading trading certain goods until you unlocked them, and went piddling on ahead with them.
Like Patrician, you basically just get a boat to buy low and sell high repeatedly until you can afford to buy more boats or build a business that lets you make things directly for less price than buying them, then turning around and selling them for even more money you can use to buy more stuff to make MORE money...  Like Patrician, if you're the sort of person who likes managing an empire, and seeing your assets grow and grow while you build up towards even larger steps of growth, this can be fun.  This system is dumbed down compared to Patrician, however, with less interconnected supply lines and with prices much more strictly tied to an "average" price to the point where you don't need to do anything but look for whether something has two or more green bars before you buy it and only sell when it has no green bars.
To this, it adds Port Royale mechanics that make no sense in a game supposedly about the RISE of Venice.  Venice rose in the 9th Century, due to its heavy trading with the Byzantine Empire, but the game starts during the period of the fall of Venice after Constantinople was conquered.  Why focus a game on the "rise of Venice" on a period where they were actually declining?
Because that's when cannons were brought to Europe, and Kalypso didn't want to have to rethink their pirate combat system to work with ballistas...
Additionally, enjoy such traditional Venetian activities as collecting pirate maps to search for buried treasure that totally aren't just ripped straight out of their pirate-themed Port Royale.
Combat is poor, but this is pretty par for the course for naval combat.  There is almost no strategy in a battle with few units on a featureless plane and only a few attacks to choose from.  Add to this, however, that any ship you aren't manually controlling (one at a time) will flagrantly disobey your wishes, and charge headlong at the wrong enemy (no control on who it attacks) even when you want them to retreat. You can, however, tell your other ships you want to fight solo, and it's bizarrely much easier to win fights unscathed when outnumbered 5-to-1 than even odds.  Further, the fire arcs are TINY, (and slightly behind your ship, so you often have to be sailing slightly away from the enemy to hit them), so you have to get EXTREMELY precise with aiming, but the only way to steer is to right click somewhere on the ocean you want the ship to go, and hope your ship interprets that as going the same angle you wanted it to go.  The game doesn't tell you this, but merely left clicking fires cannons (instead of having to click a ship, which meant juggling two places your mouse needed to be at the same time), but you still may want to just repeatedly pause and unpause until you're sure you're near the "green ring" before firing.  Don't think that combat is difficult because of this, however, because it's most certainly not.  The AI is blindingly stupid, and will follow a predictable pattern of sailing directly at you until they get within a certain distance before turning to broadside to actually fire. You can simply sail away until it triggers this charge at you, turn broadside at them, fire when they get within range, and turn away to create more distance before they can manage to get to broadside and fire back, forcing them to chase you again.  There is no limit to the size of the battlefield (no shore in spite of it being painted on the skybox), so you can kite enemies forever.  Fire chain shot until they have no sails and are helpless.  When no enemy has sails, canister shot them to tiny crews and then board to ensure you capture basically every ship that ever fights you (besides maybe galleys, where it doesn't matter if you shred sails) and sell them for massive profits.  It's the most tedious, but most profitable part of the game.  You CAN auto-resolve battle, but that just gets your ships sunk, and auto-resolve never captures ships, so it's a choice between either your patience or your profits.  Also, because of the fact that combat is best performed out-maneuvering your opponents, the giant carracks that are presented as the "best ships" are actually some of the worst, while tiny but maneuverable barks that are the third ship you get in the game are the best combatants.
The game also completely lacks even the stakes that even Patrician managed to have.  You have "rivals" in Rise of Venice, but they don't rival you in any meaningful way.  This isn't a 4X where territory they take is territory you are shut out of, the "rivals" are just other random ships with colored flags that trade and build things, occasionally getting to a good deal before you did.  Since the Patrician-style mechanics where all developments help improve economic development and "rising tides lift all boats" are in play, however, the existence of your rivals actually helps you, instead of hurting you.  When you can't afford to keep pumping money into expanding housing, the rivals occasionally will, and that just creates a larger market for your trading empire to profit off of.  Likewise, this isn't even a race to be doge first, those other guys are just THERE.  They hypothetically can sabotage you, but only do so if you drop relations with them, and that only happens if you sabotage them, first.   They have no personality, and there's not even any clear reason WHY these three other random yahoos are your rivals rather than any other random trader.  Well, no, it IS clear - because "rivals" are just slots for multiplayer players, so in singleplayer, the bots replacing rivals are there, but they have essentially no relevance to the game outside being somewhat more likely to build housing and industry.
Add to this lovely quest-breaking bugs, where you can complete a quest, but still fail it because the game doesn't recognize your success until time runs out, and you've got a very frustrating experience.
This is a game that should have taken tried-and-true mechanics into a new setting to make something new and interesting, but instead, it's just a Frankenstein's monster with no identity of its own since these pieces of existing games were cobbled together with no rhyme or reason.  It certainly can be fun, as I wouldn't have played it this long if I didn't still love the basic premise behind the series, but it's fun because of what was done better in other games. The city building and trade route management was better in the now MUCH cheaper Patrician III.  If you like the piracy and combat, you should be playing Port Royale, because your opportunities for piracy are severely limited.

Never Alone is an absolute gem among games, no matter the genre or generation. You play as both Nuna, a young girl trying to save her village, and Fox, Nuna's furry animal companion (who, yes, is a fox), to advance through the side-scrolling platformer stages. The player alternates control between Nuna and Fox to use their abilities to help each other surpass obstacles and continue on their quest. I've seen some complaints about the gameplay, but I really have none (rare!). I used a controller and I thought the game was extremely responsive and tight. Nuna kept up when I was controlling Fox and Fox trotted along when I was controlling Nuna. Anytime I died I felt the brunt of the blame was on me because I was rushing through, not paying attention to things like the wind direction, wind speed, icy water, frozen spikes, or any other perils that awaited me. In general, Never Alone rewards patience and pattern recognition, except when platforms are collapsing under you or threats are chasing behind you. There
a slight learning curve, though: throwing the bola (your only weapon/tool), even when using the thumb stick on my controller, was tricky, and there's no guidance at all when it comes to the few combat situations in the game (Do I shoot the polar bear? Do I shoot the Terrible Man?), so I died many, many times, but the checkpoint system and respawning system work well and caused very little frustration. I found Never Alone adequately challenging and forgiving simultaneously. Watching a polar bear maul me to death
disturbing, though.
The story is based on a culture rarely examined in gaming and, honestly, that's the big reason to play this title. Don't misunderstand me: the gameplay here is solid. But it's the story, the characters, and the Alaska Native lore that really captivated me and made me play this game. Furthermore, I cannot stress enough how absolutely
this game is. The graphics and atmosphere, while respectively simple and sparse by some standards, are truly a joy to behold. Narration is unique, genuine, and subtitled. There are even some tears to shed. You'll know it when it happens.
As you play, you unlock documentary-style video "insights" that shed more light on the Alaska Native culture on which the game is based. I completed the game in roughly 2.5 hours (I have not yet purchased or played the DLC, Foxtales). Now I need to unlock the few videos I missed during my first playthrough and give them all the viewing they deserve. The interviews are very interesting and educational and the production value is high. Some people have been describing this as an "educational game." I disagree; "educational game" has the connotations of tedium and boredom. The adventure of Nuna and Fox is
a chore. This game was created to be a game, and it's such a
game that it makes you want to learn more about the source material. If you enjoyed Valiant Hearts (another wonderful experience and one of the best games of the past few years), you'll most likely want to play this game. Never Alone shines like an ice shelf in the sunlight.

SO.. Where do I start?  I had to make a transaction to sell some uneeded stuff over the steam marketplace so I literally looked for the cheapest game that I thought I may could put up with one day and found Overcast - Walden and the werewolf for $0.14..
Overcast - Walden and the werewolf is a physiological horror game that eats at you with the erie atmosphere not knowing when, where, or what may pop out.  In between every chapter you get cinematic cutscenes that fill in the story piece by piece.  The cutscenes have heroic music behind them and subtitles telling the story.  You have 9 chapters of story to complete which can be completely within a couple of hours at most.
This is a FPS.  In the left hand you have a lantern, the right you have your handy rifle.  You only get one gun.  One bullet and then you have to reload everytime.  Only a couple of keys to control the whole game while having the "hand" cursor the same as Penumbra or Amnesia games to grab and move objects around.
While being a huge horror movie and game fan I adore this game for what it tries to do.  The graphics are dated and are not pretty as the games today but Overcast proves you can still scare the sh*t out of people without modern graphics.  Now for graphics this games graphics are pretty plain.  Very grainy style graphics that makes it hard to see anywhere far from you.  BUT.  I've seen people get scared and jump at a lot less than this.  But there are a couple of times in the game that I can imagine some people may get freaked out or even jump at.
Gameplay was pretty smooth for me but I did encounter a bug two times during the final boss fight that I guess kept the fight going and somehow I randomly died both times?  After one final attempt before shutting the game off for the night, randomly with me expecting more fight the game ended!

I can understand that this machinism is designed to implant fear or panic but in my case it just annoyed me to no end making things feel very drawn out.
I was not a big fan of the story, but to me it was more of a game with a "base" story that thrown me in the game to play.  The heroic music in each cinematic cutscene made me feel like a badass and even in some combat the music gave me hope!
Bottom line:  For under a dollar if you are a horror fan looking for something to occupy your time for a couple hours, maybe give you a couple jump scares than pick this up.  I do recommend this game because besides the final fight I had no problems running or playing this game.  It has a story, it was in 3d, and could get a couple good jumps out of some people. Tradition and culture play an important role in rural or non-urban regions of human civilization. The Arctic and Antarctic regions are among the coldest places in the world -where survival and community building goes hand in hand. This game is based on the folklore of the Alaskan people - passed down through generations - explaining the harmony of nature with the people and the origination of a blizzard. And if I were to describe it one word - I'd say it was- Beautifully Magical. (I know that's two but I hope you get the point.)
I'm in awe of everything from the unbelievably good level designs - to the traditional style of narration in the native tongue - to the simple idea of having actual real life interviews of people currently living there explaining the background and their way of life. It was a journey that I will cherish right up there with games like "To the Moon" and "Limbo".
The soundtracks lend it a surreal feel and completes the whole childrens tale - fantasy like setting. The levels are not too difficult overall, but there are a few parts I had to repeat a couple of times. Like I said above, the game was a magical experience as a whole and hesitating to give it a shot would be travesty of blasphemous proportions.

This game is a masterwork of how to make an adventure game and one of the very few adventure games that can live up to any classic Lucasarts titles. Top-notch voice acting doing justice to a script filled with laughs, sly wit, and over the top spoofs and in its own way is every bit as good of a narrative as the Dreamfall series.
Once you move away from the story elements Broken Sword shows itself in every way to be a superior game. The inventory system is better, the graphics have been updated, the puzzles mesh with the story, and the in-game hint system both manages to keep immersion intact while allowing the player to set their own level of difficulty, in saying that, it’s still the original content that steals the show.
It's impossible to objectively criticize the first instalment of the Broken Sword series without nit-picking. Perhaps the only fair criticism is that the puzzles are not super demanding even without the hints. However, the sad truth is the most of the challenge to the puzzles in other games comes from bad design, not intellectual sophistication. When all and said and done Broken Sword: TDC is the best adventure game because everything in it just works synergistically to keep the player to keep on playing.

Credit where credit is due, when the game works it's a fun game and the P2P works surprisingly well compared to most other games but in the long run you might get frustrated becasue of a player exploiting unbalanced characters or connection issues that will boot you from a game and give you no credit for your accomplishments.
