Every now and then a game comes along that tugs at your retro-gaming bones with simple sprites, easy controls and basic mechanics. Gryphon Knight Epic is one of those games, but do not let that be a disservice because at its heart the game is pure and enjoyable and priced perfectly.
You play the role of the Knight and his trusty steed, the Gryphon who for all intents and purpose are one in the same as you venture forth together on your epic tale of good deeds and adventure all wrapped up in a simple yet at times devious, shoot-em-up. Yes indeed, Gryphon Knight Epic is a side scrolling, 2D, flying fest with large sprites, retro looking graphics and a distinct Aladdin feel to it though not as good looking as the wonderful Disney game of times long past.
At first you may feel that this is a child's game, and it can indeed be played by children without much upset or hardship but as you progress the games difficulty rises and whilst always being a simple shoot-em-up compared to some of the bullet hell games out there, it does get decidedly tricky at times and offers up a decent challenge to your average fan of the genre.
Progression in the linear levels offers up bosses to fight and a story to play along with that whilst nothing more than the standard fantasy fare we would expect from such a themed game it is as interesting as any other game of its ilk out there and is better than many due to its easy controls and colourful looks. The actual gameplay consists of scrolling one way or the other, and you can change direction on the fly, pardon the pun, whenever you so desire so as to get the dragons, birds or bandits you missed on the way over and when the boss fights come you are often forced to change direction to get the best hits in. This offers a variety over the standard left to right games but does not add any real depth other than the aforementioned boss fights.
The sound effects and music are of a decent level and fit the games look and feel and more importantly do not annoy as many others do. I played Gryphon Knight Epic solidly for two hours and not once did I wish to rip my headset off and curse the audio, and this is rare for me. Graphics options are basic but you can jump the resolution to the current console standard of 1080p and let’s be honest, this game does not need a 4k screen to be enjoyable. Do not expect any fancy shaders or AA in the game, again that retro gaming look just does not require them.
Now I must admit to not being the greatest shoot-em-up fan in the world. To me they are the kind of game I will play for twenty minutes before getting bored and changing up to something with a little more adventure and story however I do still play them on occasion when in the mood for mindless finger tapping. Gryphon Knight Epic fits that perfectly and does not suffer from it despite my own personal feelings of it being slightly dull and boring compared to other games from different genres, again though this is not my kind of game so for it to even keep me occupied for those twenty minutes says a lot.
If you are a shoot-em-up fan you will most likely enjoy retro games too and this may well serve both of your needs in one. Its a perfect price for what you get and I would be surprised if you came away feeling let down. It’s on Steam right now so do yourself a favour if you enjoy these kinds of games and go pick it up, you really have nothing to lose.

There was a popular article by Old Man Murray which used Gabriel Knight 3 as an example for the kind of nonsensical, ridiculously contrived puzzles that killed adventure games. This point & click classic is an excellent counterargument. With its high production values, interesting - if slightly cliched - story, fun characters and good puzzles, it's a reminder of why many of us enjoy adventure games.
The puzzles only get frustratingly difficult in one or two places, but the solutions are always logical and with not an onerous amount of try-everything-with-everything-else tedium. Sometimes solutions to later problems are hinted at elsewhere, so it really helps to pay attention. The voice acting is great for such an old game, though recorded a little unevenly. Play with subtitles so you don't miss anything.
There are a few bugs in the Linux/Steam version I played - mostly to do with skipping during cutscenes. Having now finished the game I don't feel I missed anything though.
Looking forward to getting to the rest of the series.

Thomas Was Alone is a charming little platformer indie game. I don't think I've ever felt so many feels for a group of rectangles, before. Thomas is a small, red rectangle AI, and at the beginning of his journey he is, indeed, alone. This soon changes, and his posse grows more and more over the course of the game.
All details of the characters and plot are told by a relaxing British narrator, the kind you may have already encountered in LittleBigPlanet, or The Stanley Parable. Not only is he a good storyteller and pleasant to listen to, he's funny on occasion, as well.
The characterization given to these rectangles is varied, well-defined, and quite interesting. Their story, though not overly complicated at first, really draws you in by the end, with some good twists and turns. For a bunch of colored quadrilaterals, these guys have quite a journey. The best part is that the gameplay always reflects these shifts in plot (and vice versa) in fitting ways. In this way, the puzzles and platforming stay as fresh and compelling as the plot to the very end.
Thomas Was Alone does a lot with a little, and I have to respect it for that.

This is just lovely. Yes, it's another indie puzzle platformer, but that's almost incidental. The puzzles are decent (not too easy, but they shouldn't give most people much trouble if they're used to this sort of thing), and the platforming is good, but it's the characters and narration that really bring everything together. The narrator is just as important in this game as Bastion's was, although he functions in a more traditional way. He (and the excellent writing) will make you actually care about featureless rectangles and believe they have feelings and unique personalities, even though they never say or do anything themselves. As you move them around the levels solving puzzles, he describes their thoughs, hopes, and dreams, and you become invested in them. It's definitely pretty high up there on my list of games I've played recently.

Taking place in a submerged and desolate research facility, a place where robots think they’re human and biomechanical constructs stalk decrepit, rusted hallways,
‘s story is a surprisingly thoughtful and philosophical one. While there are monsters to evade and puzzles to solve, the story is what really makes
’s latest endeavor stand out.
The attempt is a rousing success, so much so that the horror elements actually feel tacked on.
is at its best when the player isn’t required to creep around, hiding from screaming mutants in ways evocative of
. If you’ve played one of the hundreds of horror games available since
first caught the world’s eye, you’ll know what to expect. A lot of crouching and avoiding, tossing debris to mislead creatures and sneaking past them, or running for your life when caught.
Visual design deserves a lot of praise. From the desolate feel of the underwater station to the quasi-organic growths bursting from the walls,
has created a game that looks as beautiful as it does disgusting.
A competent vocal cast keeps the story believable, while background noises and monstrous screams are suitably intimidating. Music is very rarely used, but perfect every time it occurs. The voice of the main antagonist is a little flat, but he mostly does a decent job, with the support character of Catherine providing the real meat of the tale.
is a survival horror game that is undoubtedly one of the best of the genre. While the monster encounters feel forced and are a weak point of the game, it does little to lessen the experience.
- Great story
- Smart, intellectually coherent storyline
- Impressive and believable environment
- Some frustrating puzzles
- Not as scary as some survival horror games

How Do I start with this review...
Same way I start with the game. Confusion.
You start off with a knife, and a level 0 character. You kill some creature things and they give you some exp. You gain a level. Kill some more, gain another level. Die, lose all your levels. That's about all I can do.
The graphics seem odd, I'm playing on max graphics, and they are very pixelated. Flat flowers, plants, trees, etc. I saw Plants and grass floating in the air, Trees with no detail at all, just a brown tube stuck in the ground with limbs, and it gets worse. Looking out in the distance you see buildings, all lined with pixels. I found the only place where graphics seem to be reasonable is by standing a few steps away from the object. Up close it's clearly bad, and far it's bad, but a bit away, and it looks okay, just okay. In the 20 mins I played, I died 4 times. Losing all I had, and starting fresh in a different area.
The enemies, are flesh colored humanoid creatures, and they appear to have 100 different light sources pointed directly at them. They are hard to look at with the shininess. Against the plain drab pixelated background, an overly shiny enemy stands out, and blinds you. The enemies feel like they should be taken on in a group, as more than 2 of them together, become a serious problem for you. Unfortunatly, No other player, in the most populated server, was anywhere near me.
To worsen the enemies, only about half of your attacks actually connect with the baddies, the other half, even if you're right next to them, apparently go off into space. As you run away from large groups of baddies, you'll find yourself running into invisible walls, everywhere. In ponds, open streets, open fields and wherever they can place one, you'll find one. I even get hurt randomly sometimes as well. Which does not bode well for me, in a game where your life is so important that it means starting completly over when ended.
Overall, i'm sure there's things i'm missing in this game. Features that solve some of the problems I was coming across, but unfortunatly, they did not present themselves in the time I was still interested in the game.

I bought this game quite a while ago, but put it aside, as at the time I was still having too much fun with Port Royale 3. As both games share the same main gameplay principle, playing both simultanously didn't work for me. I recently started thinking about going back to Port Royale 3, but then I remembered I haven't given Rise Of Venice its rightful chance yet, so I started playing this instead. As evident by my play-time counter (almost 30 hours, as of writing this review), I got hooked very quickly, just like with Port Royale 3.
Simply put, Rise Of Venice is a trading simulator with some strategy and political elements. The idea is to build your business empire by building businesses in cities, and trading the goods between them by your naval fleet. Just like in the real world, there are politics involved, as your competitors have their own agendas and interests, which hardly ever align with yours.
Just like with Port Royale 3, there's a story-driven campaign, which I believe is the best way to start the game. Except in Rise Of Venice, the campaign feels much more than a mere tutorial. I've actually found myself enjoying the plot and the missions presented to me, and was disappointed to finish it. I really wanted it to go on. :)
After the campaign, the game turns into a "Free Play", where you continue to build and maintain your empire. You still get missions, but there's no deep or interesting story behind them, as there was in the campaign.
All in all, I really love this game, and I strongly recommend it to anyone who likes this type of games.

BRIEF OVERVIEW:
35MM is a Russian post-apocalyptic story following two survivors as they make their way through the desolate land, finding remnants of what was and is. The game displays a very grim and enticing atmosphere, drawing you into it's bleak setting. Despite the linear path it takes, it gives a sense of scale in many of the levels, allowing you to easily get lost within the Russian wilderness. It's quite fun for a screenarcher, as there are plenty of opportunities for captivating screenshots. However, outside of some exploration, the game doesn't offer much in the ways of actual gameplay, and without a lot of patience, you may find yourself quickly bored of it's lack of interaction.
STORY:
The story in 35MM, despite being a focal point of the game, is rather mediocre. The characters aren't particularly interesting, and it's not as if we haven't seen virus' wiping out humanity in fiction before. However, the silence of the game and the visual storytelling can be quite intriguing, and the lack of character gives a much larger sense of two normal men surviving in the apocalypse. The ending is rather meh, mainly for trying to tie the two character's stories together, which really comes across as incredibly coincidental, effectively killing the atmosphere quite a bit, rather than tugging at your heartstrings like it evidently intended to.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay in 35MM is a mixed bag. The bulk of it is exploring the abandoned ruins of post-apocalyptic Russia, bringing a lot of fond memories of STALKER and Metro, although perhaps borrowing too much from those two in its design. There are quite a few minigames that are only ever used once, which is a rare sight these days, and reminds me somewhat of old point and click adventure games. There is combat, and it is pretty dull, which is fine given that it is sparse. Outside of that, the game doesn't offer much. One of the main issues with the game is the lack of direction in achieving the good ending, as you are really left up to a guide to figure that out. Achievements as well are very hard to find without a guide.
VERDICT
35MM is an interesting game. It's well made for an indie game, and despite the dullness of some parts, it manages to remain mostly engaging throughout it's relatively short run time. It took me about 4 and a half hours to beat this without ever having to restart, and at $9.00, you could do worse, however I would wait until it's on sale, as you'll be less likely to be disappointed. I'd only recommend it if you enjoy atmospheric and exploration games, and even then take it with a grain of salt, especially if you have to start over.
Cheers,
John

I absolutely hate this game in its current state. I am quite disappointed with all the lost potential. But that does NOT mean it's a bad game. I've had so much fun playing this game, and I can't recall if I've had this much fun in any kind of multiplayer game in the past few months.
This game is super, super fun. But it has way too many issues for me to keep playing it on a long term basis. I really want to like this game, but there are a lot of balance issues that need to be addressed.
The developers definitely seem passionate about it and I hope their passion does not run out. I hope the game improves in the coming months and I'd love to offer suggestions and advice for an improved experience.
The game's menu UI seems a bit lazy. They could have definitely made it more 80s-style aesthetic, like how Alien: Isolation captured the retro-sci fi style in every aspect of their game. I think the game's intro movies with all the logos etc are beautifully done. But that aesthetic and feeling comes to an abrupt halt with a generic looking menu with basic fonts and text. It's too simple and it doesn't fit. I wish the menu and UI would receive the same treatment as the into movies for the Gun Media logo and so on. It would help with immersion and also make the production value seem higher.
To be brief, the animations, look and feel of the game seem a bit cheap. The models for the characters are ok, with the exception of all Jasons who are wonderfully done. The voice acting is acceptable. Pamela Vorhees on the other hand is quite well done and I always love listening to her.
The game needs severe optimisation, because it runs poorly and looks poor too, even on Ultra settings. The game can benefit from community feedback regarding the balance issues. Jason is overpowered in all the right ways and should remain the same. BUT, the few ways the counsellors can escape him feel insufficient. Only a massively coordinated team can take on Jason, which means Jason would be cheesed throughout the match and would struggle with keeping up. Jason's traps are not enough and cannot be used again once set or triggered. I've only given some examples out of many. There is a lot of work left in the game and it feels incomplete.
But if you get the right kind of players, you can definitely have a lot of fun in the game. I would still recommend it because of the fun factor. The only issue being, that fun factor quickly runs out and you don't feel like playing the game again, because it's repititive and the few options you have have not been tested properly at all. If the developers maintain  healthy communication with the community, we will have a fantastic game soon.

I give it a thumbs up but play this game at your own risk...
As many have pointed out this game involves a lot of AFK due to the fact that progression on the servers is time based.
Meaning 1 hour for your first carnivore evolution and from there another 5 hours to evolve again (into a a utah raptor) and so on and so forth until you finally become a Rex or something similar
This game is similar to gambling  except you only get to place one bet and the odds are stacked against you, let me explain.
For starters you are tossed onto a map (Currently the Region 2 one) and until you learn the map you'll get lost often and likely starve or die of thirst unless you randomly run into a lake that has a dead carcass nearby to eat  (if you're lucky)
You'll spend the majority of time hiding in bushes and scavenging while praying a bigger dino doesn't see and eat you.
Personally i've already died more times than i can count and most deaths came from being killed by a bigger dino or breaking a leg from a small fall and then getting killed--oh and btw prepare to break your dinos legs often even the slightest fall can break a leg on the bigger dinos.
Now i hate to use this word but "Toxic" seems to accurately describe most players on the official servers.
Consider this, if you have food that will last you a few hours and a smaller dinosaur wanders by will you kill him and ruin his 6 hrs of progression or spare him and continue to eat the meat you already have?
Unfortuneately most players seem to "kill for the thrill" so if you think you'll be shown any mercy around bigger dinos think again.
But wait there's more---If you die in any way whatsoever you have to start completely over---To hell with going down a notch or 2 they start you back at square one
After you die (and you will) and start over you'll likely lack the motivation to progress again for a few days or weeks even until the day comes that you're bored and want to give the game another shot
In the end the game will give you mixed feelings. Distrust is common on official servers, nobody wants to group since the person could get them killed and then they'll lose the hours and hours of progress they have.
I'm still giving this a thumbs up because 20 bucks is worth it but only if you can accept the fact that you're going to die and lose everything you worked for.
If you can get past that fact then the game can be quite fun. Fear of death is an excellent fun factor to keep you motivated to play your Dino but once death occurs the motivation is gone obviously---i mean unless you get off to being a useless tiny beginner raptor that can't kill anything except baby plant eaters.
Should you buy it? I guess

Right off the bat, I want to give a big thank you to Ubisoft for the free weekend, because I now finally had the chance to play Rainbow Six Siege. A game that was met with mixed reviews at launch, rightfully so, since there were so many problems with the game, and unfortunately it turned away a lot of potential players away, like me. Jump forward to 2017 - the game is not only polished now, but the amount of content it has is just amazing! Huge props to the developers for continually adding new stuff to the game, because I strongly believe that R6S is one of the best tactical shooters I have ever played!
With the little time I have spent playing the game, I found myself blown away at how atmospheric both the combat and the strategy aspect of Rainbow Six Siege really are. I mean this is coming from someone who is not the least bit interested in Counter Strike. In fact, R6S only solidifies how much of a mindless and inferior product CS:GO is. The amount of fun I've had so far surpasses any other tactical shooter on the market that I've come across.
Expect to die a lot. This is a pretty realistic game and very much requires you to plan out your attack, or, in others cases, defense against the enemy team. In that sense, it can become quite the competitive game, where each squad is trying to outsmart the other and it becomes this tense and surreal moment when you get pined down, leaving you to adapt and figure out a way to counter back.
The destructible environments are a key aspect of the game since they pretty much allow you to turn the tide of a situation and overcome it. Granted not everything can be destroyed, in fact, it feels archaic by it's design, but it is also understandable since there needs to be some balance in order to have a healthy competition. I have to admit, breaching through a wall with an explosive, followed by a flash bang is so satisfying and is probably the most awesome parts of the game.
Now, I have to address the multiplayer since this is what most people want out of the game. So far it has been a mixed bag, granted this is during a free weekend, I found most players to be competent, but also slightly toxic in their approach. I guess it's unavoidable at this point. There will be people who are more casual and others who will be aggressively competitive. However, if you have friends or manage to find friendly players in-game, make sure you play with them, allowing for a vastly superior experience. I honestly think that is how the game is meant to be played.
One last thing. There is a lot of debate on what version of the game you should purchase. I could write a short book about this topic, but the easy answer lies with you. Are you the type of person to grind for their loot? (in this case we are talking about characters and cosmetics) Or are you the type of person that wants most, if not all, of the loot at once? Whatever version you choose know that you are getting all the content either way.
Overall, I believe Rainbow Six Siege to be one of the better Ubisoft games out there. If you love tactical action, if you love strategy, if you love shooters, if you love having fun with friends then by all means give this game a chance. Thank you!

It was okay but I maintain that the movie would've been better if it didn't fall into the trappings many horror titles do nowadays.
The suspense was often short lived and broken up all too soon by excessively loud noises.
Horror, as an umbrella term, has an expected flow that primarily centres around that release of endorphins.
If the suspense doesn't match the pay off, then it was all for nothing and essentially the viewer blows their load early.
Doing this regularly doesn't make your movie/game scary, in fact it makes it safer.
When you jump because of some loud noise they added in editing they are devaluing the potential for real fear.
Real fear being that which stays with after you're done with the movie/game and makes you think.
Real horror gives you more than a laugh after the blood rush wears off.
It can be that lack of jump or even silence without a pay off that truly throws the viewer's expectation.
Expectation being a big part of horror, you are anticipating fear and preparing yourself when you see the typical ques.
Some of them are so blatant they effectively have a big banner saying "JUMP SCARE IMINENT".
The word jumpscare has become synonymous with the horror genre and thus I don't really consider this a horror game.
It's closer to that of a psychological game, fear is not the main motivator here:  curiosity is.
Imagine a Twilight Zone like puzzle game where each episode you are thrust into some weird and wonderful version of our world.
A lot of people here will liken it to Stranger Things and I see exactly where they are coming from.
However I think it's more of a throwback to how older movies focused on making the viewer scare themselves.
Just remember that nothing is scarier than your own imagination.
This game is a fear enabler, there is nothing inherently scary in the game, it's all you baby.
So why hasn't this review talked about the mechanics or the story at all?
Honestly, I think it's something best left experienced.
I would gladly pay for more and I hope they keep them as original and interesting as they did here.
One last word of advice if you do consider giving Stories Untold a go:
make sure you're alone, it's dark and you got some comfortable headphones on.
That is if you want to be scared, I dunno, I don't wanna be responsible for any heart failures or nothing.

To begin, I am a major Formula 1 fan and usually pick up the game every other year to see all of the major changes for the games. I started with F1 2010 on the xbox 360 and then F1 2012 on the 360 before finally making it to F1 2014 on the PC.
Pros:
- Runs at a solid 60+ fps 1080p while recording
- Graphics appear to have become better since 2012 (although i was on console for that)
- Learning curve is reasonable. You can pick up the game fairly easy and every couple of races you can turn up the difficulty a little bit or turn off some assists to get better.
- You get to experience the new turbo F1 cars.
Cons:
- One major graphical error that bothers me to no end is that fact that when you are in the "TV Pod" camera mode as well as the driver's camera mode, the mirrors provide you with absolutely no information. The mirrors look like they came straight out of pole position. Legitemately, the reflection of cars in the side mirrors give you no benefit because pole position had better graphics detail and animation.
- Home menu and submenus not necessarily the most intuitive
- After exiting fullscreen through an Alt+Tab, the game cannot be put into fullscreen mode again without exiting game and launching game again (this may only be a problem for me but, I have to launch it using Nvidia Geforce Experience or it won't be fullscreen at all)
- It's the same game as years prior (Coming from 2012 to 2014 and from console to PC, the only difference I notice is the graphics, the cars are supposed to feel completely different and be harder to drive with the new regulation changes, but I feel as though I'm still driving the 8 cylinder naturally aspirated F1 car with blown diffusers from 2010 and 2012.)
Overall: If this is you first game in the F1 series, get it. If you already have a game but are looking for an updated version with an all new feel, don't. The game is a Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V of previous years. Unfortunately this is the Madden of racing games and I don't see the game changing this pattern in the near future.

TL;DR Think God of War Lite. Not deep; simple and fun. Buy it if it's on sale.
Having never played the first Force Unleashed I can't, of course, compare the two, which has its advantages and disadvantages. I think the biggest problem I ran into having missed the first installment was being thrust into the middle of a plot that desperately requires context. Playing all the way through allowed me to put together many of (what I presume to be) major plot points from the first game, but the lack of background for every character except Vader made the plot feel pretty shallow. At first I thought the two main characters promised to be pretty likeable throughout, the banter between Starkiller and the General being playful and enjoyable at least initially. I sort of expected a character like starkiller to fulfill a stereotype that would suit any 19 year old darksider of that name; gutteral voice, brooding angst, and a hood worn far too low over the face. I was pleasantly surprised to find starkiller's demeanor to be far more relateable and altogether human. A little over halfway through the game, after listening to the old Jedi and the young Jedi bicker like a married couple, each pouting and throwing fits at various intervals, their personalities began to grate on me. I found the most overall pleasant character to be the love interest and she was offscreen roughly 90% of the game. To be honest, though, our two protagonists were still much less flat and unlikeable than I expected so I can't be too harsh.
As far as gameplay is concerned it wasn't anything particularly unique. It felt like a hack n' slash with superpowers (think God of War but less interesting). I think all of your force powers are unlocked within the first quarter of the game which meant that you had plenty of time to master and upgrade the ones you wanted and ignore the ones you didn't but unfortunately there wasn't really enough of a selection to make combat really feel like your own. You are given virtually no variability as far as melee combos which is a little disappointing since I occasionally like to feel like I'm doing more than just mashing the attack button until a finishing move happens. The game tries to present the player with some customization with the unlockable saber crystals but honestly once I locked in the ones that gave me more force points I didn't even bother anymore. I will readily acknowledge the pleasure in using force powers to mow down scores of Stormtroopers, turn lightsaber wielding baddies against their friends, and redirect projectiles at whatever other enemy the arbitrary targeting system for force throw decides go for (which is another gripe I have). The inclusion of quicktime events as all but mandatory is frustrating. Getting to watch our hero dismember robots in spectacular ways is very, very cool; I found my mouth slightly agape the first time I watched Starkiller detonate the hulking fire droid. Watching our hero do the same exact thing dozens of times because it is the quickest way to finish off those enemies, however, turns into a chore pretty quickly. The length of the game (for me) was about 6 hours which felt brief given the lack of replayability in the design, but I do think the game knew when to quit since the gameplay hadn't gotten the chance to become intolerably stale before I hit the ending sequence. The game did not know, however, how to challenge the player once a grasp has been gotten on how to use the OP Jedi. I never really felt more than marginally challenged by the game and the platforming section near the end of the game posed more difficulty than the actual final faceoff (which was a joke of a fight), and that's funny given how admittedly bad I am at video games. The ease of play mixed with some of the semi-interactive non-combat sequences of force feats manage to really make the player feel the power of the force that is dwelling within Starkiller, and it's always fun to feel like a superhero, but those looking for a challenge will find themselves crawling back to Dark Souls so they can feel human (or hollow) again.
All in all I had a very good time playing the game. I never really felt bored, though I never felt very challenged either. The game feels like it was built for youngsters that are a fan of the series rather than seasoned gamers that are looking for something deep or immersive. If you are a fan of Star Wars or a fan of hack and slash gameplay with a throw-away plot then I would recommend you buy it, just not for full price.

Stories Untold is an experimental game that mostly succeeds.
Focusing on atmospheric horror, you'll find yourself genuinely unnerved as the mystery unfolds around you. Jump scares are used very sparingly, and always subtly and respectfully. Locking your perspective to a limited view in front of you forces the game to focus on audio and lighting cues to unsettle you, so I heavily recommend playing with headphones in a dark room. Hearing things happen around me and being unable to look around was a great move. I often felt the need to look behind me in real life to calm those nerves. Without spoiling, these kind of scares can only be executed in a video game. To me, this is horror done right.
The gameplay can be frustrating at first, especially if you're new to text-based adventure games. The only tutorial offered at the start is a line of text in the loading screen that can be easily missed. Acceptable text responses themselves are fairly limited, and the game sometimes completely misunderstood my inputs to do the opposite of what I wanted. Once you get a hang on the game's internal logic, though, gameplay flows at a nice pace.
Puzzles between each of the stories are varied. You'll interact with hospital/scientific equipment, radios and occasionally walk around (though this comes with frame rate issues), keeping the text-based gameplay from feeling stale. Puzzles themselves mostly involve following instructions. While not being challenging, they do force you to consider your actions and take in the horror.
At some point, the horror gave way to the intrigue of the story. You can figure 90% of it out by the second story if you're paying attention, but the game continues to drip feed interesting revelations up to the 4th story, where everything ties together in a satisfying way. While short (~4 hours), it's complete and doesn't overstay its welcome. I'd recommend setting aside an evening to play it through in one sitting for the best experience.
The game is priced fairly. If you're interested enough to read this, you should have a good time. If you have reservations, there's no harm in waiting for a 50% sale when its flaws will be much more forgivable.

Star Wars: The Force Unleashed II is the second instalment in the series. Being developed by Aspyr Media and published by Lucas Arts, taking place between the 3rd and 4th episodes of Star Wars. The game was released in October 2010 on PC, Xbox 360, PS3, Nintendo DS and the Wii.
The game continues the story of you playing Starkiller, a student of Darth Vadar. The gameplay is very much the same as the first game, but we have some new additions to his force abilities, such as Mind Tricks, allowing you to mind control enemies to either fleeing the fight or fighting on your side. The second new element is the ability to use Force Fury; which is basically you enraged form that allows you to go crazy with lighting fast light sabre hits, fancy flips and electric force shots and all sorts of craziness.  The overall gameplay is essentially the same as the first game, though. Enemy fights throughout the level are very samey throughout your play through; with a few new enemies being added in which require a “rock paper scissors” way of thinking so only one of your abilities beat them, whilst the rest of virtually no damage. The boss fights in Unleashed II are a bit of a let down apart from the final scenes. Quick time events play a prominent part in any boss fight which is something I absolutely detest most of the time. It felt very cheap and showed a lack of innovation to force a key boss fight to be resolved by simply using quick time events. The only boss fight throughout the game that was anything at all compelling is the final fight with Darth Vader which is rather memorable in my opinion of being one of the better boss fights from the series so far.
The graphics are sadly very drab too; the low-quality textures and poor quality models ruin the game’s aesthetic. The game does have a few redeeming factors in that the special effects from lightning and the light sabres do look really good, though. The voice acting from the main characters just feel a little bit off; I couldn’t quite put my finger on what was different but it just felt very poorly executed in the final cut. Darth Vadar and Yoda have the best voice acting throughout but the main character, Starkiller just sounds so monotone that you’d find it a challenge to stay awake listening to him for any extended amount of time.
Difficulty wise, Unleashed II is easier than the first game; there are no challenging fights or platforming scenes, you can ramp up the difficulty at the start of the play through but the lack of being able to change this on the fly once you have started is disappointing. Like I said, boss fights usually conclude in quick time events and regular enemy fights are nothing other than a time filler as they offer no challenge what-so-ever.  I finished the game in just under four hours; which is similar to the time it took me to finish the first game, so there has been no improvement made on the amount of content on offer. This was another huge disappointment for me as the story really could be explained and drawn out a little longer for the benefit of the player. You may be able to squeeze a second play throughout of this game but only if you didn’t finish the game the first time round on hard mode. There is a selection of collectables to find throughout the story mode which allows you to customize your light sabres colours but there isn’t really anything else other than that available.
The game is also riddled with technical problems. The main one being the frame rate is capped at 30. This is an absolute disgrace even though it was six years ago – don’t cap frame rates.  Secondly is the huge amount of graphically tearing and no options are available for v-sync to fix it. I also had a number of crashes to desktop during my time playing too; these come just before you reach a save point on a level too which leaves you with the annoyance of having to replay the last checkpoint of the previous stage too. It’s also worth mentioning that I played the game completely using my 360 controllers, the mouse, and keyboard support is lacking so I wouldn’t even suggest trying them.
Sadly Star Wars: The Force Unleashed II is a poor excuse for the second instalment in this series. The first game is a country mile better and being a fan of Star Wars I was hugely disappointed with the overall production values on offer here as well as an extremely short experience.  The technical problems and repetitive nature of the gameplay does the game no favours either. This game is nowhere near worth the price of £14.99 and it should not be recommended for anyone but hardcore fans of Star Wars, and even then it is with a huge caution.

Just got done playing. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ Where do I begin?
This game ♥♥♥♥ed with me. Like, really hard. Not only did Frictional Games make SOMA scarier than Amnesia, but it got scarier the more I progressed through the game. I didn't even think that was possible, and what I think helped that greatly was the world building.
SOMA does a wonderful job conveying a sense of helplessness and confusion when you start out. You wake up in this alien environment and you have absolutely no idea where you are, what's going on, how anything works, and you end up having thoughts like "What's this? What's that? What does this button do? Should I press that? Where the heck am I going?"
Another thing that contributes to how SOMA does a great job at making you feel like you're in the future is it's sound design. Now, I'm an absolute nerd when it comes to attention to detail and BOY does SOMA's sound design have plenty of it. Have you ever thrown a power drill or a wrench in real life? It doesn't just make a single sound, it makes a new sound every time part of it hits the ground. SOMA's sound design pretty much nails it to a T, and I've yet to see a game go to such great lengths to replicate that kind of realism.
When you're not throwing power wrenches around, the environment you're in is always bustling with noise. There's never a true moment of silence in SOMA. The place you're walking through could be old and you'll constantly hear the building settling. Sometimes you might hear a loud noise and you'll get startled, or footsteps that are not your own, meaning that a monster might be following. Speaking of monsters...
I feel like the monsters are easily one of the scariest parts of the game. But of course they're supposed to be scary! They're monsters! They chase you all over the place and want to kill you!
NO.
These monsters are legitimately ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying. To bring up sound design again, the gargles, moans and groans these monsters emanate make them sound truly horrific. I'm never gonna forget the first time I encountered The Construct and tried to hide from it as it wandered around my area, stuttering, buzzing and making all sorts of malfunctioning noises while doing so.
Each of these monsters seem to have a specific mechanic tailored to them, and while I'm not going to spoil anything about them, I will say that I felt something along the lines of unsettling accomplishment when I figured out how they work. But believe me, they managed to induce all sorts of feelings for me. Fear, panic, anxiety, worry, stress and... Admittedly frustration at a few points. While I love this game, the monster encounters do tend to get a little irritating. Especially if you wanna get on with the story.
I won't say anything about the story. I feel like you need to experience the game itself to truly understand what it's about. Just prepare to be mind♥♥♥♥ed several times throughout.
All in All, SOMA is a fantastic game and definitely Frictional Games' best game to date. I can't wait to see what they put out next.

I am not sure what i think about this game. I am not all that familiar with this genre but i have played Patrician IV and this game is extremely similiar to that game in almost everything except the setting. The game is certainly prettier and die hard fans could probably name thousands of ways that the games are different but i found the games to be so similiar that i would have been really disappointed if i had paid a whole lot of money for it.
Luckily i did not and if you have not played Patrician IV then there is no reason for you to care. But people who have should know about this.
Now concerning the game itself. I really enjoyed my time with the game at first. The game should should be pretty easy to get into both for newcomers and old fans and it is really fun at first to travel the Mediterranean Sea buying low and selling high. Setting up trade routes, building industry and expanding your trade empire is really fun and relaxing but the game is just way too easy.
You really have to try to fail at making money and after a couple of hours you should have been able to set up some trade routes which basically makes you a bunch of money without you having to do anything. There is a bunch of stuff to do in the game but it all comes down to making more money and it is often more time consuming than it is challening.
Sure you can produce your own wares to increase your profit margin which means that you have to make sure that your factories have the required raw material and so on. But why would you do this more than once only to increase the profic margins that are already good enough.
Sure you can try to make some more money to buy some new ships and create an extra trade convoy but you have already done this a bunch of times and the endless loop of making more money so that you can make more money gets old.
I found the game lacking in having interesting stuff to spend your money on. Some people might be satisfied with simply making money so that you can make more money but i found that really boring after a while and there really was not anything there to keep my interest after that.
Oh and the naval combat is crap. It controls really odd and for some strange reason the devs decided to take away the slowed down speed modes in the combat. So the combat is really fast and i thought that it turned into a hectic mess. You can also only control one ship at a time and the ai takes control of the rest. This is functional for normal sea battles but it turns into a mess when you have to sail around and try to catch a ship so that you can board it.
I have probably sounded quite negative about the game but i absolutely do not dislike it. It is a charming and simple game about trade and i would recommend it to people who is looking to spend some hours doing just that. But i did not find the depth in the game to keep me interested after a couple of hours and you should probably take that into consideration when thinking about the price.

An outstanding story-based game with horror and puzzle elements. This is not an out-of-this-world experience with impact on future generations, but this is a damn good title with little to no impact on future generations. It's kind of short and simple; it took me 5 hours to complete it and the puzzles were a piece of cake. Sounds kind of negative, doesn't it? Don't let that fool you, because what you're looking at is an extremely well made game – made by only one man. The game works on the Unity Engine, but the graphics don't make this game beautiful – the landscape does. And, oh boy, it's a beautiful one. Those undead trees, eletric poles and cities have some feel to them. I have about 10 screenshots from the first chapter alone! Really, a beautiful game. Apart from that, this game does a pretty good job at scaring the player, although you won't find many jumpscares here. I think that's cool because I hate jumpscares. A piercing atmosphere does one hell of a job. Closer to the ending, the game becomes scarier. But enough for that, I'm an inexperienced horror player and I don't want to fall into disfavor with some veterans. The ending is surprising, but it didn't leave crying in the corner rethinking all my life choices.

For Honor had quite a rough start and there have been close to no efforts to fix them yet. Connectivity seems to be terrible for quite alot of people and there are certain abusive combat-combos on multiple classes which are getting abused - At the moment it's best to wait and see if the core issues are getting fixed, making For Honor a great game...
The 41 hours I played were quite enjoyable, especially considering this is an online game with team driven co-op and thus potentially toxicity - The players I met where to 95% friendly, even willing to teach me if I fcked up!
I guess I just got extremely lucky but I got close to no connectivity errors (in my entire playtime around 8 DCs).
Gameplay itself is fun, learning new moves and playing new classes is rewarding and there are multiple fighting techniques and chars to master. The story can be finished in a few hours and is sorta clichée and dull - but playable non the less.
Graphics are fairly beautiful and the game preformed quite well on my PC ( /w 16GB RAM & Nvidia GTX 960 Card)
The major issues are laggy peer2peer connections and abusive combat mechanics plus an unfair matchmaking (especially in 4v4 matches - you can potentially have a team of new players fighting against hardcore veterans) - there are also some abusive move-combos going on which sadly haven't been fixed as of now. The seasonpass plus the in-game microtransactions are bad jokes of Ubisoft as well - and are absolutely unneccesary!
Overall the positive aspects outweighted the negative ones for me - probably due to me playing 2v2 or 1v1 and thus (mostly) not having issues like fighting /w toxic teammates in laggy matches vs high rank players - it's been a good game while it lasted!
I really would recommend the game - even if it's only for the story and 1v1/2v2 combat,

So, what can you say about a game that is widely regarded as one of the great classics of adventure games? A game that is often among the top five of various best-of-lists? A game that is held dear by many a gamer around the world? A game that already has been drowned in gallons of words over the decades?
Well, I can say I finished it, I guess... And I can say that I'm having a hard time understanding why Broken Sword is so highly regarded by so many people nowadays. Let me clarify my history with this game though because maybe that'll illuminate my lack of enthusiasm. I did not play it back in 1996 when it was released, nor did I play it in 2009 when the Director's Cut was released for Nintendo consoles or in 2010 when it was released for PC/Mac. No, I played it in September 2013 without any prior knowledge. Now, I'm an old man and I enjoy a Werther's Original as much as the next old geezer, so I generally don't have problems with older games for pure technical or gameplay reasons, as they're the games I grew up playing. And yeah, the graphics are fine, the music is fine, the animations are fine, the sound quality is mostly decent, the controls are fine and whatever else is fine. The puzzles are mostly above average, the voice acting is quite alright and the UI doesn't make me want to vomit.
The problems, for me, are the dialogs, the story and the characters. The dialogs are just not funny. Not at all. But they're clearly meant to be funny, which makes it cringeworthy. George is amassing all his wit in every interaction and let's lose some quip that is just so out of place. It's not only not funny, it's also not tied into the conversation, so he comes across like some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who constantly interrupts the people he starts to talk to with random and oftentimes even mean sentences. It's really enervating and you start to ask yourself why do these people keep talking to him...
The story on the other hand is kinda meandering from some place to the next and then in the end George literally tells us out of nowhere what it is all about and I wondered how the ♥♥♥♥ he knew that... It's really badly written, which is surprising considering that Broken Sword was always lauded for the writing.
And lastly, at least to me, the George and Nico dynamic just isn't there yet. It gets way better in Broken Sword 2 and especially 3 but in this game they just don't really click, imho. Again, it's really weird since the characters were highly praised back in the day. According to Wikipedia and Mobygames.
So apparently the Director's Cut cuts a lot of content in dialogs, puzzles and areas that was originally in the game. I don't know, maybe the game is really, really cool with intact dialogs and story and the original version deserves its place among the greats but this here does not. Or maybe it is just one of the games that has sooooo horribly aged that nothing of its former glory is left. Like GoldenEye 007 for the N64 or WarCraft 2...
It's worth to buy in a 75% sale just to play one of the classics but you're probably better of buying it from GoG where you get the Director's Cut and the original Version together.

As  the title suggests, there is more content then the original game. Not much more, save for an intro sequence where you play as Nico, that has been added for a bit of extra gameplay, This isn’t bad as it sets the scene well.
There are however, some seriously lazy things to behold here, Perhaps the most in your face of these is the voice quality. As far as I can tell, the sound files have been ported from the original game, and are very low quality in places.
The Voice acting is a bit hit and miss I have to say. Some of them forget which accent they are supposed to be using for their assigned character, which is actually at times more accidentally comical than anything else.
The game has quite a few places to go, and things to see, and all are very well realized. The game will take you from France to South America, to The Middle East, to the UK. You will also encounter quite a large number of interesting people along the way, with some truly memorable dialogue.
For the bulk of the game you play as George, who is very well voice acted whereas Nico unfortunately has a voice actress who falls into the inconsistent accent category. This however is not enough to take away from how cool the character is.
There is one major fall that the game takes. and that is in some of its overly elaborate puzzles. Some of which are too abstract, and as a result can make the game become rather boring. I reached a point where I simply couldn’t be bothered any more.
Over all, the game is good, well written and it has a nice colorful art direction, but should you wish to try this one, be ready for frustration and a degree of boredom

There's a surprising amount of modern sensibility to this remake of the original Broken Sword.  There's a helpful hint system, interactive objects flash with a small icon, and there are the usual visual and audio upgrades you'd expect.  You'll still run into some infuriating moments of classic adventure game puzzledom, but the hint system is fairly clear and the pixel hunting is, thankfully, kept to a minimum.  The hand-drawn graphics look sharp, but sometimes the speech seems slightly off, as though some dialogue was spliced in using different equipment.  It can be a bit jarring.  For the most part, though, this is a serviceable remake of a classic adventure game, and the story is still a fun little mystery romp.

I really, really want to like this game, and in some respects, I do. Overall the game is pretty fun, but that fun takes a huge hit from two main points. First, the trial and error type gameplay really plagues this one; you will find yourself replaying a section of a mission a dozen times, each time figuring out another little trick, and each time getting a little farther. It is nearly impossible to play through this game in one go; thjere are too many sneaky enemy snipers, to many times when enemies randomly spawn in behind you, and too many areas that have too mnay men for you to know who to kill first. The second issue, which somewhat stems off my last comment, is that this game can't tell if it wants to be a stealth game or an action game, and that really shows during some of the missions. You will go through an entire area being perfectly stealthy, complete an objective, then suddenly it is swarming with enemies. The game will force the player into intense combat whether they played 'well' or not. The game does not handle these intense sections well, and you will, as before, find yourself trying over and over and over until you are lucky enough to make it through. These two things really killed this game for me, and made it unenjoyable and just too much of a hassle to get through. Side note: I waws playing on the hardest difficulty, but that's really no excuse.

Summary: 80's horror, Great Atmosphere, and pretty great story with a realistic and creepy setting and situation. I am going to be asking for a refund for this game for three simple reasons:
First, a little bit of context: I played ALL of the Infocom games at release way back in the day, and loved them; I'm an old gamer. This is a good representation of those arts. (Yes, you had to fight the 'parser' to phrase your commands just so back then just like this!)
But I think that the dev's missed the boat on these three things...
1) You want me to play a text-based game yet in the first game there is so much of my real-world monitor space that is wasted! All of the 'action' happens on the little in-game monitor to the left. I get that other things will happen later on, but this is just wasteful.
2) That in-game monitor... wow. Any monitor we had back in the day that flickered and bounced like that would have ended up on the trash heap. You always had the option of hooking up your C64 or Apple IIe to your TV set, so there were better ways to game. Seriously, that isn't what I remember it being like.
3) The sequencing of the internal games. I *HAVE* to complete the first before I can play the second, third or fourth? Design a better meta-game, please. I don't mean that sarcastically. There are several reviews that say people are stuck here or there... give us a little more freedom to choose our path through your story. Both text-based adventures, and certainly the over-all artform is centered on user choice. Give us a little more room. By forcing the sequence you are betting the success of your last three games on me being able to complete or even like the first.
There ya go!
Thanks dev's for the effort, but this isn't my cup of tea at all.

This game has driven me to make my first serious review about a game, ever.
This game is one of the most satisfying RPG experiences I have ever had, ranking above many AAA games.
Everything about this game brings about an intense craving to
in the best possible way.
Pros:
-Large skill tree filled with unique and interesting abilities.
-If you like an ability you can level it up over time to make that ability do more awesome stuff
-The freedom to mix melee / ranged spells to create a unique playstyle
-Epic and highly original bosses that are frequent and challenging
-Colorful and vibrant art style with very well done sound effects
-Likeable characters and lighthearted approach make for an enjoyable story with a mysterious undertone
-Main quests take you to several areas that are have their own unique themes and enemies
-Regions are fairly large with explorable secrets and puzzles containing hidden loot
-The everpresent chance of obtaining "cards" is one that creates the urge to grind each area's different enemies
-Not only do enemies drop cards they drop crafting materials as well as rare and unique equipable gear to further create incentive to grind
-The trio over at Pixel Ferrets are incredibly talented and hard working
-Weekly dev blog updates along with frequent patches add tons of content at a high rate
-Buy them coffee to add hyperspeed perk to your favorite dev team
Other Pros:
-Easy to connect multiplayer supporting up to 4 people
-Well done controller support
-A talking bag that roasts people
Cons:
-Smallish amount of craftable material (But of course more will be added over time)
-Some bosses are way harder than others on the hard difficulty (perhaps need more difficulty settings?)
As an early access review the full potential of this game has yet to be realized however; this game has so much personality, tied with a fun combat system and an enjoyable playthrough experience making for a game that has a lot to give.
This game is growing fast so you'll always be able to come back and enjoy more of the world of Grindea!
I would highly reccommend that you purchase this game if you love RPG's because this RPG is every gamers wet dream.

Fantastic potential!  Above average story, fun, engaging script, and likable character tropes.  The visual style lends itself well to all aspects of the game.
However, this is a game where combat is the bulk of play; in its current state combat is just a little too clunky for my liking to give this game a solid recommendation.  That being said, much of player control is surprisingly tight and responsive.  The problem is that there are too many zerg-rush rooms to let skillful control shine.  Anemic character reach is punctuated by punishing post-swing recovery, and the mobs of enemies ensure that, whether you hit your target or not, another enemy will likely be shooting you in the back during your recovery frames.  Shield-block input seems sluggish deciding between whether you told the character to strafe with the shield up or to change direction to block the sword about to slash your back open.  Perfect Guarding is just an absolute mess when 4+ enemies are wailing on you.
I'm hopeful this will end up a gem of a game, but right now stay away unless you're interested in playtesting to contribute to its growth.

This game ♥♥♥♥ed with me. Like, really hard. Not only did Frictional Games make SOMA scarier than Amnesia, but it got scarier the more I progressed through the game. I didn't even think that was possible, and what I think helped that greatly was the world building.
SOMA does a wonderful job conveying a sense of helplessness and confusion when you start out. You wake up in this alien environment and you have absolutely no idea where you are, what's going on, how anything works, and you end up having thoughts like "What's this? What's that? What does this button do? Should I press that? Where the heck am I going?"
Another thing that contributes to how SOMA does a great job at making you feel like you're in the future is it's sound design. Now, I'm an absolute nerd when it comes to attention to detail and BOY does SOMA's sound design have plenty of it. Have you ever thrown a power drill or a wrench in real life? It doesn't just make a single sound, it makes a new sound every time part of it hits the ground. SOMA's sound design pretty much nails it to a T, and I've yet to see a game go to such great lengths to replicate that kind of realism.
When you're not throwing power wrenches around, the environment you're in is always bustling with noise. There's never a true moment of silence in SOMA. The place you're walking through could be old and you'll constantly hear the building settling. Sometimes you might hear a loud noise and you'll get startled, or footsteps that are not your own, meaning that a monster might be following. Speaking of monsters...
I feel like the monsters are easily one of the scariest parts of the game. But of course they're supposed to be scary! They're monsters! They chase you all over the place and want to kill you!
NO.
These monsters are legitimately ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying. To bring up sound design again, the gargles, moans and groans these monsters emanate make them sound truly horrific. I'm never gonna forget the first time I encountered The Construct and tried to hide from it as it wandered around my area, stuttering, buzzing and making all sorts of malfunctioning noises while doing so.
Each of these monsters seem to have a specific mechanic tailored to them, and while I'm not going to spoil anything about them, I will say that I felt something along the lines of unsettling accomplishment when I figured out how they work. But believe me, they managed to induce all sorts of feelings for me. Fear, panic, anxiety, worry, stress and... Admittedly frustration at a few points. While I love this game, the monster encounters do tend to get a little irritating. Especially if you wanna get on with the story.
I won't say anything about the story. I feel like you need to experience the game itself to truly understand what it's about. Just prepare to be mind♥♥♥♥ed several times throughout.
All in All, SOMA is a fantastic game and definitely Frictional Games' best game to date. I can't wait to see what they put out next.

I think I'll recommend this game, even though I have several issues with it.
The two that has the biggest impact on how much I enjoy playing 35MM are the english translation and the implementation of the subtitles. Sometimes I find it difficult to even understand what any given line of dialogue should mean and it's not helping that the subtitle is showing for a shorter time than needed to actually read it. The game needs an english translator. That alone would make playing it a much better experience.
The other thing I found to be a drag at times is the save system. You can't make your own save, the game does it for you at certain checkpoints. A single save. As in one save throughout the whole game. This way of doing this has two consequences for me: one, if I die because of a, say, missed trap in a doorway, I have to restart the 'level', which could mean replaying something that I already spent 20-30 minutes on; and two, it strips me of the choice of redoing an earlier level or restart the current one on my own for whatever reason, for example achievements. If you want to do all the achievements in the game, I'm fairly certain that you will have to start at least one new game after you finished your playthrough, unless you are following a guide.
35MM is a slow game. The definition of a walking simulator, I think. Resources are few and far inbetween, the atmosphere is depressing enough due to a worldwide epidemic and the gameplay involves very little action. I came across only three moments where I needed to run or fight. Granted, I'm only halfway through the game.
The pacing has trouble maintaining an even interest, at times. Some scenes are unnecessarily dragged out, so is the dialogue and the animations are slow and very minimalistic. Also, you don't always know what you need or can do in any given situation, which is bad writing, I guess.
I attribute all the issues I mentioned in this review to the fact that the whole game was developed by a very small group, probably only one person doing the bulk of the work.
And that is why I can't be angry at this game. The world has enough to offer that might keep you exploring while you follow along the otherwise simple story. I recommend this game, if for nothing else than the effort put into it.

Never Alone is, at heart, a documentary - but it's an interactive documentary. It's fun to watch a video about living at nature's mercy and having to pay attention to the weather, and then having to pay attention to the sound of the wind and movement of snowflakes to know when to duck from a sudden wind change. It's a great way to listen to a story and to get a feel for a cultural context.
As a side-scroller, the controls are a little sticky. There were times when I was frustrated, not because of my own lack of ability, but because my character wasn't grabbing on to the ledge I was hurling them toward. It didn't happen enough to make the game unenjoyable, and the frequent checkpoints reduced my level of frustration, but it would have been nice for the game to have been a bit more tightly coded.
The style is beautiful. I loved the scrimshaw style of the cutscenes, and I enjoyed the detail put into the gameplay graphics - such as Nuna's change in pace when she walks through deeper snow, or the way she digs her hands through the snow to get a grip when the wind is blowing her away.
The gameplay isn't too difficult - well within the abilities of a casual gamer (especially with, as I said, the frequent checkpoints). This would be a great game to share with kids while learning about First Nations communities.

Let's pave out the shortcomings before arriving at the scores of strengths this game offers.
Never Alone is a short experience, clocking in at 2-3 hours (played locally on my wife's account), perhaps a bit more. You will have likely read this in the reviews, and I concur that it is a brief game. It could be said that it never outstays its welcome, and that the continuous new challenges introduced with an applaudable learning curve offset its short lifespan, but the fact of its brevity remains nonetheless true.
In addition, we played co-op and found it sometimes difficult to determine exactly where we were going; it was much more of a freeform, faster-paced Limbo experience than, say, a Portal type of deal where the objective is clear from the word "Start" in every room. Again, what offsets this is the impressive checkpointing that never fails to pick up and keep the pace good and strong throughout.
Now, for what makes this game excellent is that it is, to be blunt, a cultural triumph. It makes me proud that this game even exists. It could have had far more flaws, it could have not been beautiful from start to finish, and it would have still been something tremendous. This is all without considering the fact that Never Alone was a joy from start to finish, on the eyes, the adrenaline and the mind.
Never Alone is the modern-day, digital version of a scrimshaw; a carving and capture of a fiction deserving of preservation. It presents this as something skipped for the uninterested and something relevant for the curious - each Insight into Iñupiaq history becomes all too relevant once playing through the part after its found. As a capsule of cultural heritage it doesn't come across as a history book with a platformer attached; rather, the entire experience is one seamless package. The puzzles are of Trine descent, as are the visuals, but with two characters comes a sense of focus and flow that keeps the pace at a strong level throughout. No section drags on for too long, no mechanic is repeated too soon, but the difficulty curves upwards at a respectable pace.
For co-op, Never Alone has the applaudable quality of never making it feel as if I was stepping on my partner's toes. In fact the flow of the thing was almost enhanced, with two pairs of hands at the helm - a feeling that could have all too easily become frustration or annoyance but instead veered well away from them.
Overall Never Alone is something that needed only the time it took to become something memorable both as an experience and as the story of a people's way of life. Whether or not you're interested in the latter, the game stands strong for any fans of puzzle platformers, but for those who might be touched by the tales the narrators have to tell the experience will be unforgettable.

Deep down, For Honor is a nuanced and unique fighting game. The characters have interesting and diverse playstyles, and the controls are very good. This game had potential.
Unfortunately, the good game within For Honor is overshadowed by mind boggling design decisions and lazy, greedy corporate influence.
There are 4 different types of games you can play in For Honor. Either 4v4 Control Point, 4v4 or 2v2 Elimination, or Dueling. (There is another gamemode called "Skirmish" but Ubisoft put it in the same queue as elimination so good luck finding a game where people don't instantly all quit out). This is a ♥♥♥♥ing $60 game, remember. For some perspective, 10 years ago Call of Duty 4 was released for $60 with
This highlights the main problem I have with For Honor: it's value. This is a $30 game at most, and even then, the amount of micro transactions present would still be insulting. Good luck customizing your character: stat bonus gear is based on RNG loot boxes, and cosmetic gear will cost you 10+ hours of grinding.
The balance of the game rewards defensive strategy and punishes aggressiveness, turning any evenly skilled fight into a staring match, waiting for the other to swing so you can parry, or waiting for a chance to guard break. The warden has an unblockable shoulder bash that can be chained infinitely. The peacekeeper is so poorly designed and balanced she has been completely banned in tournament play.
Another annoyance is the matchmaking, in that there is none. The game just seems to throw everyone and anyone together in a game, so you'll commonly be going up against players 10x your level with gear stats to match. Maybe this is just from a lack of playerbase, but the skill based aspect of this game no longer matters when you're going up against players that can kill you in 2 hits because their gear level is 70 levels higher than yours.
To sum it all up, For Honor has great ideas that are overshadowed by poor balance, a strict and boring meta, and Ubisoft's grubby corporate hands. I can't recommend spending $60 on this game, and yet I also don’t know if I can recommend waiting for the price to drop, as the playerbase has dropped by 87% since launch, and by that time there may not be anyone left to play with.
I think 2017 is truly the year of the indie game. There are so many better designed, better supported games out there with devs that actually give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don’t support Ubisoft’s asinine business practices. Skip this one.

There's a lot of give and take with this game, but for most people I wouldn't recommend it.
If you like games that are slow-paced, atmospheric and involve a lot of exploration you will like this. Think of it like a point-and-click adventure with some minor FPS elements.
If you want some action, it's there but it is far too spread out and most of the game moves at a sluggish pace.
If you want some story, again, it's there and it's presented competently but it's pretty simplicstic and overall too short.
If you want to free-roam, there is a bit of off-the-path exploration and some secrets/bonuses to find but for the most part the game railroads you down the plot and most of your decisions don't matter.
If you want horror, there are a few spooky sequences and diseased dead people but the assets get recycled so much you get over it pretty quickly.
If you want a survival experience there are supplies to scavenge and manage, but in the middle of the game you're practically tripping over food/aid/batteries/ammo and the game is too short for them to become scarce or critical.
It is certainly an interesting game and it definitely has some strong moments, as well as a few intereting and unique puzzles to solve but it can't seem to commit to any particular direction. I was expecting something a bit more like S.T.A.L.K.E.R., but I got something closer to Dear Esther. I still enjoyed it, but see little reason to go back.

I will try to keep this review short, but no promises.
I've loved every second i have spent on this game. There is a wide variety of in-game servers with different rules, communities, and playstyles required for each of them. Like to prowl forests at night as a sneaky predator? Check. Love teaming up with other players in order to survive? Check. This game has a lot to offer, and to think it is still only early acess! It has a lot of potential and I cannot wait to see what it becomes in the future.
Now, that was the extremely short version of my review above this message. Like all games, there are ups and downs, pros and cons, goods and bads, whatever you would like to call them. Right now as I post this review there is a system in the game, which is called Progression. You start as a small, low-tier dinosaur and slowly work your way up to the food chain, until you can play the stronger, more commonly known dinosaurs; Triceratops, Stegosaurus, Tyrannosaurus Rex, Spinosaurus, ect. This system is getting the boot later on, so it is not sticking around too long, but for now it is extremely grindy. The costs to progress to higher dinos are really high- getting past the first tier requieres sixty points in some cases, and you only get one point a minute. So that's a straight hour of gameplay to get to the second tier dinosaur.
So, this system takes a long time, and is very difficult. Con. Thankfully it is going to be replaced by a better system pretty soon. Pro.
Moving on, the graphics in this game are too excellent for words to describe. Pro? Kind of. The graphics are so outstandingly great that you may not be able to run this game at more than a few frames per second, even on the lowest settings. So that is a middle ground point of sorts between Pro and Con.
There is a wide variety of in-game servers for you to choose from and play on. Some are called Realism servers, and try their best to make rules that would make the game as realistic as possible; making specific profiles on dinosaurs to follow and simply put, trying to replicate the way animals behave today and put them into their server.
Another type of server if Realism servers are not for you is a No Rules server. It is exactly what it sounds like. On these servers it is extremely difficult but at the same time very rewarding to get to the highest tier dinosaur. Other players/dinosaurs may kill you for no reason at all, herbivore dinosaurs may team up with carnivore dinosaurs, gigantic "mega packs" of top-tier dinosaurs may roam the map, and many other things.
There are also the more casual servers, with only a handful of rules and leaving many things up to the players' choice. I mainly play on only one of these servers so i cannot list the most common rules of these types of servers, but a pro about them (or the one that i play on at least) is that the communities are very relaxed and very close.
Anyway, that is all I believe I have to say on The Isle. I hope this review helped you decide if you want to buy the game or not and I hope it answered any questions you had on the topics I covered! Best of luck surviving in the game of The Isle! ;)
