Unfortunately this isn't a game I would want to play again anytime soon. As I have understood, a lot of original content was cut from the game and replaced to make the game more storydriven as well as helping you along the way to solve things a.k.a handholding.
~ Good ~
Graphics:
I think they are beautiful for its time. The animation is extremely smooth, the characters move realistic and at times it's hard to think they are built out of simple pixels. The backgrounds are all well detailed and even the background characters have solid animation.
Voice acting:
It's quite obvious some of the voices were re-recorded and others are still old. Sometimes it will sound like someone is sitting in an empty room, with a slight echoing sound to it. Other times you hear that the sounds are clearer. The english voiceacting is fine. Nicole has a lovely voice, but I honestly can't understand a thing she says without subtitles. She has a very thick french accent, so it isn't the fault of the game.
Characters:
I found that the background characters bring most of the fun to the game. Some of them are very weird in a quirky way (the kebab seller) and they are the ones responsible for the funny dialogue. Between the boring story, it was fun to hang around and talk to these characters. I wish there had been more of this and less about the Templars.
~ Bad ~
Story:
I honestly found this one boring, hence why I am reluctant to play it again. I think it was a bad thing to give the story so much focus. As you are mostly trying to find information about it, all you do is listen to people talk, talk, talk, talk, talk... ugh. The ending was also grossly dissapointing. Imagine spending hours upon hours trying to find this one final part and it's not even half of what it was hyped up to be.
Dialogue heavy:
This game relies heavily on you listening to conversations and if you don't snap up the important parts, you are going to have hell trying to solve some of the puzzles. A lot of the dialogue feels repeatetive as you are asking about the very same thing. The “oh so myserious” Templars and everyones opinion on it.
Soundtrack:
I found all the music out of place and some of the special effect sounds got on my nerve. Whenever the characters are experiencing a happy moment, the cheesiest of tunes plays in the background. The music also seems extremely loud compared to the voice acting. I keep the music at 20% and the voices at 100%, yet I still find that cheesy tune overpowering some of the conversations.
Whenever you try to use an object on an area which you'll be able to use an item at some point, a glittering sound is played. I am guessing to help the player find clues, but it becomes extremely distracting and tedious, especially when you have 10 items to try. There's also short tunes playing anytime the characters make a conclusion to something, which also gets quite cheesy after a while. Despite these obvious hints, I found the game wasn't clear at all as to what it wanted you to do. Your only kind of help is a question mark that pretty much repeats the very same question you have, without giving any hints at how to solve the problem.
Lack of interactions:
There really doesn't happen much in the game besides dialogue. Most of the puzzles are solved by listening to dialogue or showing the right item for more dialogue. Sometimes the only way to advance the story is talking to everyone in a different order to get the information you need. And the sad things is, the dialogue about the story is the most boring part of the game. I only had fun when I was allowed to use items in the environment to solve things, or try to figure out how to get past guards without them taking an item from me. Dialogue is 90% of the game and the rest is some puzzle solving.
Awful minigames:
The first minigame involves solving a cypted message, which contains at least 2 names which you have heard maybe once or twice throughout the gameplay. Another terrible minigames involves you having to put roman numbers in order of a message, then click a button, then order them correctly again. All in a specific order. And what happens if you mess up 7/8? The whole puzzle resets and you have to do it all over again! Ugh! And the numbers move slow.
Removed content:
This game has obviously been censured by removing the death scenarios. There was supposed to be a timed action scene with a deadly outcome, but instead George will automatically solve the problem for you. So much for suspense?
It's also dissapointing that once you solve one of the bigger mysteries, the screen just cuts and all you get is George words about what it was. Appearently he picks up an item from a room, but seeing him do so is completely removed, as is everything he does and sees in the room. And this is after solving the tedious roman puzzle! Way to go rewarding the player by removing one of the most important scenes after forcing them through the worst minigame.

A valiant attempt at updating a classic, but sadly problematic. I loved this game back in the mid-90s, and couldn't wait to play the new, updated version. But, while they flesh out the character of Nico and expand on her background and personal stake in the investigation (an unnecessary change, but fun), they also seem to have...er...forgotten scenes from the original game. Important scenes. Scenes that move the plot along, explain details of the narrative, etc. Were they omitted? Cut for time? Bugged?
EG: In the original, George steps into a hidden alcove in Ireland, and discovers an important clue -- a portrait with an image and a name. But in the Director's Cut George steps into the alcove and then it suddenly cuts back to Nico in Paris; she engages in her own new bit of investigation for a while (completely tangential to the main narrative), and George reappears in Paris not 5 minutes later with only a note in his journal about what he found in the alcove. Why was this changed? What is the purpose of it? They removed a scene CRUCIAL to the main narrative just so they could shoehorn in a mildly interesting superfluous side-story. That could have made a certain narrative sense, it's true, but they didn't alter anything George says or thinks after the scene was cut; he then refers to what he apparently saw as though the player/audience should already have seen it for themselves. Problems like this abound, as do audio hiccoughs -- like when one character is supposed to be speaking, but for no reason the voice-actor of the person they're speaking to is reading their dialogue, complete with the wrong accent and gender! It's bizarre! Did I get some sort of April Fool's Day edition of the game?!?
In fact, the more I look at the art and advertising for this updated version, you'd think George was the shoehorned in side-character! All the focus is on Nico, she begins the game, her personal side-narrative takes precedence over the main investigation, and George just comes across as a bumblin' sidekick. It's surreal -- like an alternate universe version of the game I loved. Why not release a separate game or expansion featuring all this new Nico-centric material? It would have saved them the effort of cutting out the old scenes and bugging the audio and video of the game...
In any event, i cannot in good conscience recommend the Director's Cut. The Nico side-stories help pad out the game, but come at too high a cost.
PS: This game also perpetuates the myth that the Templars were idol-worshipping pagans devoted to Baphomet, a legend which (like "Baphomet") was created during the waves of persecution & torture instituted by the French with papal approval in the 14th century C.E. / A.D. This detail will drive historians and even casual enthusiasts crazy, and miseducate those ignorant of the Templars' history and the Crusades, but it doesn't ruin the game itself. Just be forewarned!

Text adventure! Psychological horror! Losing your mind! Untold Stories brings 4 related stories to you that peel back the onion of the main character's mind in interesting and strange ways. You find yourself having to discover what happened to you. You are seeing nightmares at times where you can't tell if it is reality, or a subconscious nightmare. Is this really happening? Is this some sort of experiment on you? Have you discovered sci-fi beings that are there to help, or hurt you? Your mind goes through many scenarios in the four tales trying to figure out just what happened to you, and why your mind is doing this to you.
Stories untold is predominantly a text adventure game where you enter commands to tell the game what your intentions are. There are parts of the 4 stories, however where you do interact with the mouse, and even sections where you walk in first person for most of the episode. This doens't mean that you do very little other than type. A couple of the stories contain some pretty interesting puzzles in them. Working in a lab using equipment to study something. Another has you working with a radio and deciphering codes with a manual. They are all logical and can be figured out, but they do make you think a little bit about how to finish the tasks, especially when you work with the radio. I found these puzzles fun to work with.
I played this straight through in one sitting. It took me about 4 hours I would guess. I found the atmosphere to be excellent, with the music and sounds bringing a feeling of dread and fear at many points during the episodes. The episodes all work together in some way to tell one story about the main character. You puzzle it together fairly easily, and the ending isn't left open for interpretation. While I am not sure I am fond of the ending that much, the journey was good enough to make me think there was more at play than what the end result would come to.
It is a bit of an experimental game, but it has no bugs I found, and everything is professionally done. Having much of the story told as text actually increased the tension for me rather than being able to see everything in front of me. So in that sense I liked the format quite a lot and would play more games like this. If you like to play weird adventure games, and especially things that try to play with your mind a little then I would definitely give it a go. I bought it at full price and am not disappointed with it so I would recommend it to most who are intrigued by the concept at that price point. If not...just wait for a sale and buy it at half off. ;)

Short version:  8 out of 10 if you're a fan, 7 out of 10 if you're not, and maybe 6 out of 10 if you don't like action games.
Why? [SPOILERS AHEAD]
First of all, it's STAR WARS, so that has that going for it.  Even with the whole "Legends"/"Canon" thing, the story is enjoyable and engaging.  The final sequence before facing Vader in the end is incredibly well done:
- cramped camera (normally a bad thing, but here it really highlights the stress and pressure that Starkiller feels, an outstanding cinematic technique)
- the lighting (stark, clinical white in places, but it still manages to look dark and insidious; the blood-red lights at each of the abberant clone-tanks really accent the sinister operations there)
- the Force energy (Starkiller's surroundings crumple and disintegrate, which provides a VERY visual metaphor at how he's struggling to keep from losing his mind.)
While you need to have played the first one to really understand all the nuances of this game, the cinematics and dialogue fill in the blanks enough for brand new players to grasp the events and goings-on.
The ability to customize not one but TWO lightsabers not only provides gameplay bonuses but can also serve as roleplaying tools if you so desire.  You start with red crystals but can find others as you play...
RED: no bonus
BLUE: lightsaber strikes replenish Force meter
GREEN: more health pickups from defeated enemies
YELLOW: lightsaber strikes deal additonal lightning damage
CHARTREUSE: lightsaber attacks deal additonal corrosive damage
ORANGE: lightsaber strikes deal additional fire damage
PURPLE: take less damage from attacks
PINK: Force Fury meter recharges faster from attacking
LIGHT BLUE: Force powers use less energy
LIGHT GREEN: health regenerates faster
LIGHT ORANGE: more experience points for collateral/environmental damage
BLACK: lightsaber attacks have a chance to disintegrate enemies
WHITE: more experience points for defeating enemies
Force powers make a comeback, and are more streamlined.  Plus a new one, MIND-TRICK, where you can make enemies flee the battle (often by jumping of a ledge to their demise) or even fight for you.
The voice acting is well done.  You hear the unbridled power when Starkiller taps into Force Fury and the despair when Vader outmaneuvers him.  Rahm Kota speaks with authority on the starship Salvation and speaks out of weariness when he knows that Starkiller is the only one who can turn the tide.
~~~~~
The reason for the multiple scores is relatively simple.  Most people know that the game was rushed due to the Lucasfilm/Disney merger; and with this game being the second in a trilogy, the fact that the trilogy has been shelved indefinitely... that can put a downer on somebody.
If you are a STAR WARS fan who enjoyed the films, the TV shows, and what else, then you'll enjoy this game.
Put it on your wishlist, watch for a sale if you're worried, there's a decent amount of replayability and the difficulty can be whatever you make of it.
If you want something that you can just button-mash through, then play on easy.  You'll still be able to enjoy the story.
If you want to feel like every battle is like when Luke faces Vader in the second Death Star, then play on the hardest difficulty setting.
Unfortunately, and as much as it pains me to say it... if you're not a fan of action games or combo systems you may not have as much fun with this.  If you're not a STAR WARS fan, then why are you even reading this?
It's not a BAD game by any means, but as I said before, it's clear that there was more to be had but real-life events forced their hand.
~~~~~
SYNOPSIS:  At once engaging, enthralling, and haunting; the continuation of Starkiller's journey is made even more poignant by the fact that it is *not* canon.  You see the formation of a Rebellion that now never was against the machinations of an Empire that now never were.
It's a bit like the work of an artist.  Once they're gone what they've made is now priceless.
Even though Starkiller is no longer "real", his struggle is, and that's the soul of this game.

This review is available as a video and written transcript.
Video Link:
Transcript:
Performance
While I do commend Stories untold for supporting 144hz monitors, it’s a big shame that the game isn’t optimized to maintain that high framerate in its walking segments. In the limited times you get to explore your surroundings, the game’s fps maintains at about the mid 40s to 60s which is an unacceptable count for a game like this on a gtx 980ti. Also as a side note, can we please stop labelling graphical presets as beautiful and fantastic. There’s no sense of scale there or description of what each preset entails and I think a simple, low medium high and ultra will suffice.
Story and Characters
Stories untold tells its tale in 4 segments that last about 30-40 minutes each. It’s first story begins with a young man returning to his family’s house and what seems like a normal text based adventure starts to rear its horror filled head when the boy discovers an old computer.
As he begins to play a game on this computer, strange things start to happen and a much more gruesome and chilling depiction of the game’s recent events are laid out. By the end, we have more questions than answers but at that point, it’s time to move on to the next segment. Now each story puts us into an entirely new setting and we rarely get the time to connect the dots before we’re sucked into whatever objective we have at the time but the game’s overall plot relies on the underlying mystery that links these 4 stories into one nightmare.
Sure, there are a few nuggets of information that hint at this link but it’s not really till the last third of the game when it’s explicitly pieced together. While overall, the story isn’t anything spectacular, I think this is a game to be played for that experience of not knowing all the answers just yet and just kinda letting your mind think of all the possible explanations. The game certainly gives you plenty of them with the expansion of the narrative’s overall scope and it did an excellent job in managing that scope to its relative play time. By the end of it all, the plot points were covered in a satisfying manner that gave previous actions new meaning and it was definitely a story I looked back on fondly. Definitely one worth playing in a single sitting.
Gameplay
Each segment of the game uses classic text-based gameplay mechanics where a monitor tells you the scene and you in turn, type out actions your character to take and it’s good to know that none of them play out in an overly obtuse manner. So long as you stick to common actions like “go to”, “read”, “open”, and “look around” you shouldn’t really have any problems figuring out what to do next. It’s unfortunate that the game doesn’t incorporate more modern terms like the phrase “flip switch” to do the same thing as “use switch” but that’s a minor complaint at best.
With that said, some segments also feature other types of puzzle solving that fit into its setting, so things like deciphering morse code or conducting experiments are also on the table. Again, none of these feel unfair EXCEPT in the last segment where they come back without their instruction manuals meaning there’s a chance you’ll fumble around trying to remember how to solve a particular issue. Otherwise, gameplay for the most part is a simple yet effective channel of progressing the narrative.
Presentation
Visually the game is mostly great with one or two hiccups. I absolutely love the way the background changes as you discover new things in some of your text adventures and the game varies the overall setting of the different segments enough to keep things from getting stale. It uses the text well to set up a word picture through its description of not only where you can move but also the sounds and smells that assault your senses as you navigate your way through the rooms.  All of this amounts to a pretty good horror atmosphere that will keep you on your toes without relying on the tired out tropes like jumpscares right up in your face. On the other hand, texture quality could be improved upon and the game could really use better antialiasing but that’s mostly only a problem when you have the ability to freely walk around the map.
Now alongside these scenes is ambient background music in the form of synthwave that’s present just enough to fill the silence but also soft enough to leave room for the real atmosphere changer that are the sound effects. These effects really are the main reason you’ll play the game with the lights on, from the startling crackle of a lamp to the abrupt ringing of a phone. They do well to keep you on your toes while letting your imagination be your own worst enemy here and when working together with the visual changes you experience throughout your playthrough, they do a great job in immersing you into the horror experience.
Conclusion
Stories untold will likely be complained about for its short play time in relation to its 10 dollar price point and while I think there’s a discussion to be had there, most of them neglect to mention what the game actually accomplishes in its 3 or so hour time frame. To me, this game provides an unoriginal but ultimately interesting story with a satisfying end, alongside classic yet simple gameplay mechancis. Mix all of that into an amazing horror experience that keeps you fearful at the idea of a threat instead of a tangible one, and I think it makes for 10 dollars well spent. This is a game that does not overstay its welcome as so many other horrors do, instead understanding its limits and playing to that limit.

SERIOUS REVIEW
This game is...amazing. As in, so amazing, that I have to write a review. Anyway, this review will have minor spoilers. I try to avoid them as much as I can, but there will still be spoilers.
YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED
Also, this review will only talk about story mode, not arcade. There's a TL;DR at the bottom.
So, the game starts out with you waking up for your Collector's Exam. You are then explained to by your father that you have to get ready to be a Collector, as they are the defenders of humankind and collectors of loot.
Oh by the way, you are given a sarcastic talking bag who is going to be your companion for the whole game.
So, I'm going to try and avoid spoilers as much as possible, so I won't go into the story much further.
The story is really good. It's not a game where you just decide to become an adventurer and drop everything, but there are actually a group of adventurers called Collectors, and you're training to become one.
You then go through a bunch of challenges (after running into a boss I won't spoil) that teach you the basic mechanics of the game.
You are then faced with a GIGA SLIME, which is basically just a giant slime. After defeating it, it explodes and dies, but summons one last slime. You run up to it and kill it, and then BOOM! YOU GOT A TRADING CARD! I'll explain what those do later in the guide, but they're basically just powerful buffs. The announcer gets a hilarious expression and goes crazy saying 'They got a card! That hasn't happened in XXX years!' I don't know exactly what they said, but it was somewhere along those lines.
If you haven't already figured it out from the title, this game has grinding. And I'll be the first to say, I
grinding. I've dropped tons of games just because you have to grind. But this game does it

You feel like you are all powerful when you're grinding. You kill and kill and kill hoping to get that one drop you need, or a card. 'What's a card?', you ask again. Well, I guess I'll go into cards now.
Cards are an extremely rare drop from almost every enemy in the game, that gives you a permenant buff. The Frostling Rogue lets you have a chance to steal gold when you hit enemies, the boar gives you an attack speed boost, and so on. That's really the main focus of grinding, as you'll probably get enough items to craft that sword/armor you really want along the way.
Also, there's no healing items. This might seem bad, but it's actually really good. The game would be way too easy with them, and it adds a whole new level of strategy. You don't realize it, but in most games we're a bit careless because we can heal. I didn't even realize until I died about twenty times trying to defeat a boss.
It's beautiful. The music goes so well with wherever you are. I'm speechless.
The 8-bit graphics are amazing too. Somehow, the devs made every motion in the game extremely smooth.
I'm just starting my hard run, so I can't say muchy about that, but on Normal it has a very good difficulty curve. If you don't grind too heavily, then you'll be just powerful enough to beat all the bosses.
It also does a very good job of surprising you with the difficulty of the bosses. You could be plowing through enemies, thinking that the boss would be super easy, seeing as the enemies for that zone are. You walk into the room and BOOM! You just died 20 seconds in! Remember that talking bag I mentioned earlier? He gives you tips on how to do better. Some of them are just crappy ones like 'Watch for a pattern!' but others are really good.
TL;DR GO BUY IT ALREADY!

A beautiful piece of entertainment combining the classic platformer game with some amazing storytelling. The fact that this game's collectibles teach you about the Iñupiat people and their way of life is a wonderful bonus. No longer do you have to worry about gathering collectibles for little to no reward other than an achievement or some gimmicky in-game costume piece. You actually feel like your efforts are being justly rewarded. The game mechanics are a little tricky at times and the AI got difficult to work with towards the end, but that didn't stop me from enjoying the game.
The simplicity in the art style and overall story helps sell this game as a must have. This game shows that there is no need for complex stories of betrayal and revenge. All you need to tell a good story is the combination of a believeable world and believeable characters. Never Alone exhibits these exceptionally with a warm and caring approach with the narration tracking the player's progress throughout the game. The stylistic approach is beautiful and the transitional sections provide a wonderful view into how stories are actually presented by the Iñupiat.
I bought this game purely out of fascination for the Inuit people in general. I was curious to know more. This game did not dissapoint. If you want to know more about these amazing people as they etch out a living on the ice, be sure to get this game. You will find yourself falling in love with how beautiful their holistic way of life is. This game is a truly amazing experience and is worth every cent.

Rise of Venice fits into a weird sub-genre of sail based economy simulator.  Rise of Venice is almost an identical clone to Partician and Port Royale.  The major difference comes down to the maps.  Rise of Venice original covers the area of the world Genoa and east while the Gold version extends to the Portuguese coast of the Mediterannian.
The game is broken down into ships (convoys), businesses (production buildings), and warehouses (where you manage resources).  The game can overly overwhelm new players to the sub-genre but it comes with an excellent single player that breaks down the game.  The single player campaign can take up to 20 hours to complete while the free play will be worth another 100 hours.  Add in the Challenge Mode and you are looking at a grand total of 160 hours of gameplay in this game.
Unlike previous titles the game has improved ship combat.  However, all ship combat is mouse based.
For what you're paying the game is well worth your time.  It's not going to be your most favorite game in your library, but it will be one you will find yourself unable to simply quit.

Let's start off by saying not all survival games are for everyone and survival games are not for everyone.
If you are a survival game fanatic and you like fast paced PVE and of course PVP than this game is for you.
This game resembles the following games the most: STALKER, The Division (not released yet), a bit of Metro and some crumbs of Infestation and Rust.
This is one of those games that brings a fresh view upon the open world survival mmo type of games. I say this because the game includes:
-Missions: Courier missions, Special Escort Package missions, Fallen Safezone missions and more
-Crafting: You can craft makeshift weapons and military grade weapons from parts and household items scattered across the map
-Character customization: Although you pretty much need to pay micropayments for most of these, it's really worth it. The prices are really low and you really feel like you are getting value for your money. For example I charged my account with 165 Gold Coins (for 6.99) and bought a hell lot of skins and taunts, also Golden Keys for Golden Crates and I'm happy as a clam.
-Exciting PVE and immversive environment: Let's start off by saying: OMG the graphics and the environment guys! :O One of the best looking Survival MMO's out there alongside DayZ. The engine is epic, the optimization is well done. Constant 60 FPS on Ultra for me and even for older PC's of my friends have 60 FPS on Medium and/or LOW and the game still looks stunning.
You constantly s**t your pants in the metros and in tight corners in the street when you hear the screams of the monsters, especially when it's a PVP situation as well. You have to be extra careful.
I could go on and on for hours straight talking about what I like in this game, but to sum up: It's alot of fun with 2 friends beside you.
Well done Phosphore Games!
But please do hear the community out! Bring more servers, do some updates and add new features as the community would like to see this game grow in 2015 and still wants to play it in 2016.

Divine Souls is a decent brawler that can be compared to Dungeon Fighter Online.  The game is old, but still fun to play if you enjoy similar games.  I'd give the game a 6/10 based on gameplay alone.
Overall, it's a decent time waster and has controller support, but it's held back by the  Korean Fatigue Point system, limited inventory space and the almost nonexistent player base.  Three hours are more than enough to burn your daily Fatigue Points and you only get 24 inventory slots of which potions/quest items occupy at least half.
The game is basically on life support since I only saw three people in my entire time playing and two of them didn't speak English.
Divine Souls is worth the download if you're desperate and want to kill half an hour, but I wouldn't recommend it if you're looking for a primary game to play.

Some bugs are still in game, but it's worth buying it.
*Edit: New maps added 2 new characters, i hope they'll add more content in future.

This game is no doubt a good quality game. Though there are a few things I have to say.
If you're going to get this game just for the campaign (which a lot of people do) just know that you MUST be connected to the internet to be able to play anything this game has to offer. Another thing about the campaign is that it's mainly an over glorified tutorial. Throughout its whole few hours of gameplay it keeps teaching you things to do. Now don't get me wrong I loved the campaign and all the little "side missions" you could do it was a nice time.
Onto the multiplayer. Lately there's been a few updates changing a bit but here's the gist of it. Server issues where you get disconnected every now and then aside. When first starting out you will at least once every 3 games get into a match with someone either on your team or the other that has way more experience than you. In my opinion this is sometimes good as you get used to how more "elite" players move and act. But it may be tedious since you may die more often than kill or just even survive.
Also once you get one character to renown which is this games version of prestige that adds up to your profiles overall skill level. So let's say you leveled your warden and Kensei to 4 renown. (Total of 8 renown) and you end up wanting to try out the lawbringer you'll end up with your teammates and other team being around that skill level 3-10 renown. Meaning you'll get screwed over a bunch until you get used to the new class and get new and better gear.
That being said. GEAR.  Gear in this game is a bit broken in the sense that it could get you an advantage in some moments in this game. Some people build their characters around revenge which is a game mechanic that generally gives you extra health and power once you block enough or get hurt enough (without dying) that you can activate it. Which the developers say they'll be nerfing soon since it's too easily gained and a bit too powerful with some classes. So this may change when you read this.
All this in the end I want to say that it's a pretty epic game. It has its downsides but the overall quality is great.

The fantastic concept and gameplay are severely held back by poor execution of the meta-game.

Early Access Review of 11/1/2017
I really loved this game around a year ago, it was honestly a lot more fun then, but now not so much. I used to get home every day log in to my favorite large public server and have a blast playing with friends. Now the community and game has changed as a whole.
Pros:
Good graphics: game can look amazing if the map makers (dev or community) uses the right assets, but the maps do look gorgeous at times. Sometimes the lighting goes bad, but the developers are rather fast when it comes to fixing those issues. The new map they are revamping now looks amazing and photorealistic with it's new weather mechanics.
Dinosaurs: the models are pretty spectacular in this game, they also have some nice animations and sounds. Best dinosaur depictions you can currently find.
constantly updated game: the game gets updated one to three times a week, it changes so rapidly it's nice pacing because new things are always coming out.
Cons:
Toxic community, the community is so toxic and blindly follows the developers no matter what happens. You also need discord to play this game, a large amount of servers require you to be in their discord. This wasn't as bad a year ago, but now discord nessisary if you play this game. Also there are known predators in this games community, not the dev or games fault, just watch out if you do get the game there are a couple. If you're lucky you might find people commenting on my review bashing it or me, just read any other negative review.
Developers: Some of the developers are out of touch with the game, the devs are at times as toxic as the community. Something they will log onto offical servers and kill players with overpowered borderline unkillable dinosaurs and ruin hundreds of hours of progression. Also, edit forgot to mention this before. The lead developer, Dondi, said he would refund any negative reviews around a year and a half ago, and they also pull up bad reviews on his twitch stream and the offical Isle Discord and bash them publically.
Boring gameplay: You have sandbox, which is a content dump of playing as any dinosaur you want and try and make your own fun, and there's progression which is just wait x amount of minutes to unlock a new dinosaur, hopefully better than your last. The big difference between the two is progression is horrendeously boring now with offical servers taking hundreds of minutes to unlock dinosaurs. In theory it wouldn't be so bad, but currently it just isnt fun unless you have friends. Also there is a new gamemode called survival coming out, but i cannot speak on that given it's still work in progress and does not seem to be close to done, at least publically. But the premise for both these gamemodes is sit, walk/run, eat/drink basically make your own fun, it's a glorified walking basic hunger/thirst simulator as a dinosaur, if you can find food or water that is.
Balancing: Dinosaurs balance is terrible. There are a couple key gameplay aspects, bleed and bonebreak. Bleed is when you get bitten by a dinosaur that does bleed, and if you don't rest to heal it off you will eventually die from blood loss. The more bleed you have the more health you loose. Some top teir dinosaurs can easily shrug off high amounts of bleed and the balance between carnivores and herbivores is nonexistant in mid to low teir. Most of the mid to low teir herbivores are 1-2 shot by their carnivore counterparts, some herbivores don't even have ways to defend themselves, aside from hiding and hoping someone hasnt turned down their render, or sees your dinosaur load before the bushes do. High teir is not balanced either, Tyrannosaurus rex is the king of the game, being able to easily dismantly almost any other animal in a 1v1 senario. Being faster and hitting harder than every other high teir, except acrocanothosaurus (but he doesn't no enough damage or bleed to do much to rex), and T rex has an insane heal rate. But high teir dinosaurs did get a stamina and speed nerf (in terms of trot speed) so now you can escape them. Unless you're a low teir herbivore, if you are they'll probably still catch you.
Maps: Small gripe but especially on region 2 and v4 the maps have so many cliffs and terrible spawns. Some of the community maps are horribly optimized and at times the offical maps are too. But there are often times broken spawns with dinosaurs spawning above the ground and breaking their legs, and also the amount of cliffs is unbearable. On the v4 map carnivores had two spawns, above a group of canyons or by a lake. Unless you knew how to navigate the maze of canyons good luck trying to survive and find your way to water. Not to mention region 2 has so many mountains to make it feel articially bigger navigation is tedious and annoying. Also my biggest gripe with offical maps is that herbivore food is at times extremely scarce, recently it's gotten better, but one of the devs has said multiple times herbivores should end up fighting for food. The irony is that herbivores are more plentiful than carnivores (in reality of course) is because usually they don't fight directly for food. Their food is so plentiful competition over food is rare, discounting hippos, rhinos and elephants killing other animals over territory or other reasons. Herbivores simply don't starve unless their's an overpopulation, and in the isle over 70% of the playerbase is carnivore on any given server without special rules or limits.
Developer priorities, the developers, mainly the lead, have constantly changed their priorities and left multiple game mechanics simply broken or abandoned. Some things like, Camarasaurus still not having an attack, were said to would only take minutes by another dev, but over four months later it still is defenseless. Mutiple times in game development they've broken key mechanics and left them, unless they were still working on fixes and it simply takes multiple months to fix an issue. Including but not limited to, herbivores not being able to eat, progression plants being bugged, plants not despawning on v3 after being eaten, crashlogging, leaving hypoendocrine T rex in the game for three months, even though it was suppose to be removed in a month or so, puertosaurus not taking damage, camarasaurus not having an attack, v3 lakes being unswimable until just a couple weeks ago, multiple dinosaurs spawning with 1/10 of food, mutiple maps being abandoned and remade.
Dinosaurs: The last con is that even though these are the best depicitions of dinosaurs in any game by far, there are a few issues. At times dinosaur skins are just nonscensical copies of mammals mashed together in hopes of it looking good, and this point is highly subjective so keep that in mind. Some dinosaurs designs or animations just look down right dumb, weird or just bad. For example, new allosaurus model, it has a sawblade on the back of it's head, the new stegosaurus model has not been reanimated so it looks like a sickly hunchback with a glasgow smile, T rexes new run looks like a confused fish bird, pssitacosaurus is so extremely slow if anything finds you good luck and camarasaurus looks like it's a bag of bones in its rear quarters. Their sounds are often times horrible and robotic, some dinosaurs have amazing nice sounds, but others were not blessed with good sounds, full sized juvi rexes, acrocanothosaurus, spinosaurus (sounds like a wind tunnel), triceratops sounds like a clogged toilet (except it's friendly call), therizinosaurus (nails on a chalkboard), dilophosaurus and velociraptor (both have good friendly calls but every other sound they make is painfully robotic).
I want to recommend this game, but in this current state it's not fun to me anymore and i don't play it as much as i used to. If the game improves I will surely update my review, but unless you really want to play as a dinosaur i would wait to purchase this game. Also don't let the trailer fool you, every one of those scenes is staged.

Broken Sword: Director’s Cut does a lot of the little things wrong. Back in 1996, the player was thrown out into a graphic noir world very much like our own, one brimming over with unique personalities who don’t think of themselves as cogs in a giant machine, but people getting suitably annoyed at the pushy American who won’t stop showing people the soiled tissue he found in the sewers and asking them if it means anything to them. Now updated, a lot of the dialogue options are cut in an attempt to streamline the adventure, making the Templar mysteries a significantly greater focus point, but in doing so, it robs the title of so much of its former wealth. Interactive hotspots are not only slashed in half, but are made instantly visible, taking away the nagging frustration of room-sweeping with your mouse to find them yourself, but also highlighting just how much the new version wants to hold your hand. Including an in-game hint system is understandable: a stuck player only needs visit numerous online walkthroughs should they decide coping with their frustration early is better than the cerebral rewards of working through a puzzle, but gone also are the numerous instances where George could make a fatal mistake. Leave an exclusive French hotel with an important and newly-discovered clue, and fail to remember the pair of Italian gangsters hanging around the entrance, and the last thing you’ll remember before being gifted a pair of concrete shoes and invited for a swim is an aggressive frisking and an insincere goodbye. Now, try and leave through the same door, and George will warn you that it’s not a good idea. Then tells you exactly why!

Ah, one would agree that Thomas was Alone, is a very simple indie title with a very clear message. It's platforming isn't very challenging, yet engaging; it's graphics are simple colours relating to each character; and it's story with so much more depth than it lets on.
Firstly, the gameplay mechanics.
When stripped back to the mechanics, Thomas was Alone is a platformer. Players control one of 7 blocks which each have a unique ability: Thomas is a red rectangle who can jump fairly high; Chris is a square who can fit into tight spaces; Claire is a box who is resistant to water.
Water is perhaps the only obstacle in this game. The characters are able to fall without fall damage, and   there is no way to accidentally leave the gaming area. As such, you simply have the challenge of climbing up platforms and using characters to get each other character to checkpoints. You can do this by using the characters to build stairs, bridge gaps over water, and allow jumping to get to higher places.
Secondly, the graphics.
Graphics wise, the game is fairly simply and minimilistic. A single colour represents each individual character, and most of the platforms and waters are a bland sort of texture to distinguish their identity. However, what amazed me was the dynamic lighting and shadows that exist with the world. With the rising and falling of platforms, or the jumping of the boxes; lights and shadows dance brilliantly in the background.
Now we get to the biggest draw-point of this game: The Story.
Don't get me wrong, those who enjoy platforming would probably have a good time with this game; but being one who has finished the game, the thing I remember most is the emotion impact of the story. There is no direct 'dialog' or interaction between the characters. What keeps the story running is the amazing narration of Danny Wallace. His words tell us a story and bring the blocks alive with humerous and enganging thoughts and perceptions.
It's amazing how this narration really has changed the game from a simple platformer to an engaging story about the heroics of coloured shapes. Fans of the platforming genre will enjoy this game, but due to the non-challenging puzzles and quick gameplay, it may not be as engaging as some modern platformers.
Yet, deep within the game is a strong and emotional story, and an experience most gamers will not soon forget.

I hate puzzle platformers. I mean, I really ♥♥♥♥ing hate them. They're dull and lazy and completely void of anything I'd consider fun. The typical indie hidden message tends to be stapled to these things each and every time, which doesn't help.
Thomas Was Alone is an indie puzzle platform. Oh, and I absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing love it.
It doesn't have the most challenging puzzles. It doesn't have any difficult platforming sequences. The gameplay is actually fairly average. There are some high points, to be sure, but that's not what will bring you to this game. The thing that will surprise you is the sound, music, story and narration.
In a game whose asthetic is as simple as it gets, the other pieces couldn't be more fulfilling. The music sucked me in immediately, and as the narrarator -- a charming Brit -- told me about the characters, I became attached. The rectangles you play as begin to take on some depth as actual characters in the story. You feel bad when they're by theirselves; their friends not there to help them. You feel good when the least capable shape gathers the courage to go through the level because he's in love.
It sounds awful, I know. But it shouldn't take more than fifteen minutes for the game to, at the very least, pique your interest. It's my favorite game of the first half of 2013. Also, just as a tip for anyone going into the game: pay attention to the quotes all throughout.

First off: I dont think this game deserves such negative reviews.
Survarium is a post-apocalyptic FPS shooter that can go from tactical and methodical to a twitchy run-and-gun in minutes. When compared to other shooters of this nature, Survarium exceeds in both of these categories. In addition, you can, for the most part, decide which playstyle you want by changing the gamemodes. Not that the gamemodes themselves are twitchy/tactical, but most of the fast-paced CoD players will be in Team Deathmatch, and you can find a tactical experience by just searching for a different gamemode.
Moving on.
This game isn't pay-to-win. The weapons you can buy with Gold (What currency do you think this is?) are mostly variants of other weapons, just with skins. And there aren't many of them, a large percentage of the guns in this game can be bought with the earned currency. Armor is likewise limited if you intend on paying Gold. On this note, I've also never (so far) had a death that I found unfair. And I've never found a player who paid to have a serious advantage over me.
Survarium is also, definitely, a grind. Not a wholly boring grind, but still a grind. Not everything will be availiable at first. The main currency, Silver, is gained at a decent rate and the items bought with it (Everything) are priced fairly. All in all the grind is worth it, and levelling up a faction, unlocking new weapons/armor, and just winning a match is rewarding.
Oh yeah, and the gameplay itself.
Like I said, playing Team Deathmatch is a deciding factor in whether you'll get a "twitchy" match or not. But another factor is the map. Maps vary greatly, some being large, open, and with good long-range combat and sightlines, and others being tight corridors with minimal sightlines. Some of these maps are also stunningly well-made, with the cover, paths, sightlines, and everything being very thought out.
TL;DR?
This game is definitely worth it, if you're a tactical or twitchy player. Great maps, great graphics, and a bearable grind. Plus it's free, so what could you loose?

This game is the third consecutive F1 instalment I played and third that’s probably going to get more than 100 hrs of my attention. Even though people bash this game for basically everything from graphics to content-related mistakes to less fun from the gameplay, I found it just as enjoyable as 2012 and 2013.
Why do I like it?
Basically it’s a new formula. New teams, new cars, new steering wheels, new rules. I was actually shocked by how much the car handling has changed. When I stopped playing 2013 game I was ruling the grid in a Lotus (4th best team of the season) with legendary AI setting and all assists off. I got into 2014 Ferrari using the same difficulty settings and in the first race qualified… 18th. The game is still demanding (maybe even more), some new aspects of driving were tweaked (in this one you can see and feel tyres cooling down on long straights, which creates a new set of challenges). And even though Mercedes are quite dominant in the game it is possible to win driving a different car, and some race events (like mid-race rainfall) can shuffle the grid in a way which creates way more interesting result than in real F1 timetables. The game surely isn’t flawless, but its strong roots still make it a solid product.
Why some people have a point bashing this game?
Yes, the new cars don’t have KERS, so there is no “boost” button to press when you feel you’re not fast enough. Presence of the 8th gear isn’t much of addition in terms of gameplay. Yes, Williams definitely has the wrong steering wheel. And yes, some tracks are unchanged, even though some of them were in reality altered for 2014 season. This last one isn’t entirely true. Canadian GP has a modified asphalt run-off area which was covered with grass in 2013, and some new buildings appeared in Monaco (most notably on the left of the famous tunnel exit). Plus two completely new tracks appeared on the calendar. The fact that some tracks were updated, while others were just pasted form the previous game makes me feel that development of the game was cut short at some stage.
I still love the graphics, but what I have a problem with is that the cars somehow got ugly on the details. And I don’t mean generally uglier car designs. In 2013 I loved the front wing camera in the replays, in 2014 it just shows how underdeveloped the car model is in terms of detail. Just closely watch the nose and floor of Ferrari F14T – you’ll notice some very crude edges and weird shapes.
Some people say that this game is just a 2013 mod featuring new cars. Sadly I have to agree. The full price is regrettable. Probably marketing strategy is meant make money of the newcomers. A person who had the previous game and buys this one for a full price may get furious.
Do I recommend it?
Let’s say a conditional “YES”. I marked “recommend” for this review because I have positive feelings about the game. But it clearly does not deserve thumbs up and “hell yeah”. You should definitely buy this game IF you are an F1 fan who wants to experience how formula changed in 2014, or if you like race simulations and haven’t tried F1 yet. And most definitely if you find this game on sale. The 2015 game will hopefully be better and all “next-gen”, but so far this is the only one with turbo engine F1 cars.
PS: Fromula 1 fan ranting (you can stop reading, unless you are an F1 fan too, or a 2015 developer :)
I found that the game was dumbed down a bit in terms of campaign interface, first race and team choosing. It’s nice that you can now select “length” of the season (number of featured races), but if they add an option of shortening a season I’d like to manually discard some of the races from the calendar. Some people liked replacing testing day with a simple racing sequence to evaluate player’s skills, like in GRID series. But I’m afraid it doesn’t work too well. When I tried it I found that it was around 1 lap of the simplest track (Monza) and all the assists were by default on. I almost crashed on the first corner when I started fighting with AUTOMATIC gearbox in an F1 car. Nice for newcomers, but will irritate the hell of the gamers who actually know what they’re doing. Also now you get to choose ANY team at the start of your career. A rookie in Mercedes AMG? Why the hell not. It actually doesn’t bother me since everybody can immediately choose their favourite team, and not struggle with Marussia or Caterham (yuck) for at least half of the season. What bothers me is that the team’s performance is defined at the starting point. Generally the developers decided that the big three is Mercedes, Red Bull, and Ferrari. This hurts Williams which had a terrific 2014 season and their performance in the game is way lower than it should be.

In principle, this Game adds a very nice spin to the well known The Guild/Pirates!/Patrician/High Seas Trader/A.D.1602/Port Royal... settings. It enables you to build up a grand empire from zero up, advance to political honors and get filthy rich.
Graphics: Nicely done, do their job. Nice zoom-in/zoom-out function. 8/10
Sound: Not groundbreaking, but OK. 7/10
Mechanics & Gameplay: One of the strong sides of the game. Nice trading system, OK combat mechanics with some tactical depth. Interface works very well after a brief learning curve. 9/10
Long-term motivation: Here is the point that I found weak. After some hours the game got repetitive. I felt as if I had achieved enough money to get more or less what I wanted. Only I couldn't motivate myself to do it anymore, as it now felt pointless. In contrast to other "endless" building or build/fight/think games, such as the Guild, SimCity 4, X3:AP, I didn't have any goals that I badly wanted to achieve then... 4/10
So, do I recommend this game? Yes, I still do! It's a well balanced, atmospheric sandbox. I would not recommend buying it at the current standard retail price, though. Wait for a sale and then grab it up for 15-30 hours of playing (or maybe more, who knows).

Alright. Take the stage structure of devil may cry 3 and 4, add a delightful combat system that feels like a Chinese combat video with twin swords, add the most cliche get the girl story, impressive graphics, a dumbed down upgrade system, and there's the game.
Gamplay wise, this is leagues better than the first, there is a more realistic idea of what lightsaber sword play should be like, with the same amount of fundamentals seen in normal sword play dealing with the leg work. There are very few bosses here, but unlike the first game, these bosses all are fair to fight. You don't have to fling objects at everything to win. But, there are times when it is almost an implicit need to do so.
The variety has taken a significant plunge, basically to the point where there's gun guys, a few saber guys, and the atat and the mid sized counterpart. So you're basically Chinese dual blade warlord guy running through the game killing like the same 8 guys.
The game is pretty fair on hard mode, enemies who would normally get torn in half, still get torn in half, the guns hurt bad, and the larger enemies serve more as upsets rather than enemies, because just one of them getting their way, or you ignoring them is enough for you to die, a lot. Fortunately by the time you're dying for some balance, you'll be able to throw your saber. So yes.
The layout of the game though, is pure poor, you basically play as a runaway, and after you realize there isn't much to do outside, you go right back home. If the combat elements and graphics didn't take such a fantastic leap, I'd really just consider this dlc. There's nothing really here aside from fancy Polish and a very powerful situation bound by Neanderthal basic instinct.
If I could have a wish, it would be that the two games trade combat systems, because the first one is abysmal when it comes to combat, but the story elements and pacing are pretty normal, and the RPG elements are very nicely done as well. But the poltergeist combat vision is what destroys that game, where here, it's basically everything but the combat, experience system, graphics.
If you're like me, and need a PC 3rd person run around cut stuff find stuff game, but NEED actual combat, get this. It's different, wild fun that will keep you happy for like 4 hours... Just, put it on hard mode.
Honestly, because of how star wars is and how rich it is in potential as well as marketing, I don't know how they haven't even begun to put their foot into the market as some actual scenarios that have Jedi doing things like these that isn't only centralized in the militia vs army type of combat. Especially if they're trying to force their way into (The ending of this game). They need to carry over that combat style, and make money, because PC needs more games with satisfying combat.

Story wise, as many people have mentioned in other reviews, SOMA is filled with philosophical conundrums centering around the concept of what makes us who we are etc. At the beginning it seemed rather hamfisted, annoying and makes the protagonist come off as a whiny b itch at times. It also appeared to be going nowhere, but lo and behold, in the second half all of the discussions the protagonist has with his sidekick actually do find their place. There is a moment in the later parts of game
which is the first truly emotional scene and which gives meaning to the seemingly dull philosophical babble. The subsequent ride
only nails it further. In short, it makes you think.
The ending is a textbook definition of "bittersweet". Some people say it's bad, but honestly I think this would've been the way I ended it too. One could see it coming a mile away after the event
, but it still had an emotional impact. However, it also reveals that the decisions you make throughout the game have literally no impact on anything, including the ending, except a few lines of dialogue.
At this moment I would like to point out my biggest problem with the game. It takes around 8 hours to complete. That is fine by me, horror games are pretty short most of time. Additionally, it's longer than Amnesia by a good margin. Unfortunately, it takes around 4 hours to truly get going. The first half is nothing special, really. It gave the impression of being rather unamazing in story and atmosphere. After the 4 hour mark though, the game finally shows its true colors - the atmosphere goes through the roof, the story becomes engaging, the monsters stop being annoying without losing their scare factor. The ambient tracks become more visceral, the environments are more devastated and coated in organic matter - reminiscent of System Shock 2.
What's better than Amnesia, is that monster encounters are significantly rarer, thus making them more impactful. Nevertheless, they're not scary enough in my opinion, though they do create heart pounding tension, which is a decent substitute. The level design is an upgrade too: the levels flow better, there are subtle hints hidden throughout which do not insult the intelligence of the player, but seem rather clever. Music (aside from ambient tracks) is present - it didn't stand out much, except for one or two tracks.
In conclusion, SOMA is superior to Amnesia in story, gameplay (as in monster encounters and puzzles) and atmosphere. However, I don't think Amnesia is a masterpiece (a good game, but nothing to write home about), so make of that what you will.

Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna in the Iñupiaq language) is an indie platformer that transports you into two legends (as of the expansion) from the indigenous Iñupiaq culture of Cook Inlet, Alaska.  You take on the role of two characters: Nuna, a young Iñupiaq girl, and a white fox named... well, Fox (no relation to a certain Nintendo franchise).  In the core game, the pair go on a quest to find the cause of harsh blizzards that are devastating Nuna's community; while in the expansion, Foxtales, they set out to stop the rampage of a giant mouse destroying the countryside.  They might be regarded as "weird" storylines from the perspectives of a lot of gamers - but then, this doesn't come from the culture of most gamers, does it?
As a platformer, the gameplay is fairly standard.  There are single player and local co-op modes, but I haven't had the chance to do the co-op yet.  In single player mode, you switch back and forth as needed between Nuna and Fox to get through the various stages.  Apart from standard movement, Nuna can climb ladders, lift and throw objects, and throw a bola as a projectile weapon. Fox has a higher jump and can scratch his way some distance up a wall, as well as doing wall-jumps back and forth; he can also squeeze through tight spaces and move the spirits of nature around you to places where they can help you get where you need to go.  You can also crouch down to brace yourself against blizzard winds so you don't get blown back.  The difficulty level starts easy and gradually increases before a spike near the end, but it's nothing that anyone with patience and persistence can't get through.  You'll find yourself increasingly needing to switch back and forth between the two with good timing to get through some of the environmental puzzles, especially near the end.  I found several of these puzzles to provide a satisfying challenge, though it's certainly no Portal or Professor Layton.
The gameplay is, however, not without its flaws.  The responsiveness can be a tad laggy in some cases, which can result in running off a platform or missing the timing to get through a puzzle or boss - NOT a good thing when your characters' lives are on the line.  From time to time a character (usually Fox) would get stuck somewhere.  And sometimes the AI would make one character catch up to the other after you'd specifically put him/her in a particular spot.  I also noticed that in the more graphically demanding areas (particularly in the coastal village with the Northern Lights), there was a bit of slowdown on maximum settings.  This plus the glitches can result in a few moments of banging your head on the keyboard.  However, these are pretty much the only bad points of the game, and they are far from being gamebreakers.
Graphically, it's not as "good" as a triple-A title, but it is still a very beautiful game.  The creators did their best to capture the feel of the remote Alaskan wilderness in platformer form, and for the most part it worked.  From snowy landscapes to riverbanks to the Aurora Borealis, this game delivers some real eye candy.  The core game is also interspersed with cutscenes done in a beautiful scrimshaw art style that really capture the cultural feel of the game.  The soundtrack is also quite good, with many ethereal tracks to complement the game environment.
However, Never Alone shines the most in its other genre: edutainment.  This game was made to give the world a perspective on the Iñupiaq people - a group not often thought about by most - and in that regard it will blow you away.  Apart from the storylines in the core game and expansion, which come from traditional legends passed down through generations, you can unlock over 20 different videos with snippets of interviews with the Iñupiaq people talking about their lives in the Alaskan wilds and about the different cultural practices and perspectives. This was one of my favorite parts of the game as a whole, and as an anthropology major I ate this stuff up.  You can tell the developers did their homework in making the game, as many of the credited people are themselves Iñupiaq, and institutions like the Smithsonian and various Alaskan cultural groups are listed in the Special Thanks section.  And you know they wanted to reach as many people as they could with this game, because it's available in sixteen different languages from almost every continent. In the future I would like to see similar games about the stories and aspects of other indigenous cultures - perhaps the Navajo or Sioux for North America, just to start.
Overall, the game isn't particularly groundbreaking in terms of gameplay, and there are flaws about which you will no doubt complain.  However, the main purpose of the game is to chronicle the culture of the Iñupiaq, and in that regard it gets it very, very right - and beautifully so.  As a platformer it's decent, but as edutainment it is truly a gem.  Even if you only play this one time, it will be a playthrough you will not regret.
RATING: 8/10.  Buy this game, particularly when it's on sale!

This game is a side scrolling platformer where you can switch between two characters (a girl and a fox). It's based on a native Alaskan story and is about a girl who sets off to find the source of the blizzards that are harming her village only to find a magic fox who goes along with her
Good points:
-  The animation in this game is beautiful and really adds to the games charm.
- Incoroporates informative videos that you can unlock and watch to learn more about the native Alaskans and their culture.
- Nice story based on native mythology which is relayed by an Alaskan native narrator as you play giving a more authentic atmosphere.
-Fun gameplay that encourages you to use the fox and girls abilities. Also features co-op where one player controls the girl and the other controls the fox.
- Fox Tales DLC is a nice addition that adds a few chapters where another story is told through the medium of the girl and her fox.
Bad points:
- When playing solo the AI character can be a bit unreliable at times as they sometimes fall or miss a jump which put you back to the checkpoint.
- While i really enjoyed it the game is a bit short.
Overall this is a nice charming platformer whose native Alaskan influence give it a unique autentic atmosphere. If you enjoyed Brothers: A tale of two sons you'll enjoy this.

- The character's walking and running speeds are incredibly slow. The game as a whole is very slow paced.
- Invisible walls are everywhere. The opening scenes are in a flat forest-like area and there are no real-world boundaries preventing you from walking in any particular direction, until you hit an invisible wall. Games like Gone Home and Fire Watch have convincing ways to prevent the player from going away from the goal, with house walls or mountains respectively. This game is set in a place where you could theoretically walk in any direction as far as the eye can see, so the developers had to use clunky invisible walls. It's really frustrating to walk for thirty seconds and be met with an invisible wall, only to have to walk back to where you came from at a snail's pace, all while in a drab, foggy forest.

Nonviolent exploration platform games are a rare breed. Waking Mars doesn't have to do much to stand out from such a thin crowd. And yet Tiger Style went above and beyond to make the game a standard-setting platformer on its own merits.
This is yet another mobile game that doesn't feel at all like a mobile game. The controls are tight and smooth. The art assets are gorgeous, including the face close-ups which accompany all the dialogue. The voice actors are engaged and well-directed.
Much has been made of the Metroid roots of the title. The chatty trio of protagonists somehow feel more alone on Mars than silent Samus did on Zebes. Tasks must be completed and resources collected in order to press forward. Paths branch and reconnect, many of them essentially optional. Still, Waking Mars feels like its own game rather than a derivative. The primary mechanic of the game - using alien seeds to establish life in the depths of a cave slowly waking from centuries of slumber - is novel and intuitively implemented. Waking Mars is no reskinned shooter.
What most impressed me was the way the curtain was lifted on the final element of revelation. To some extent the game suffers from tutorial syndrome as your helpful companions chatter along; they always seem to be one step behind your own grasp of what you need to do. But the understanding of just what might really be going on under the regolith is something the game lets you deliciously realize on your own. This quiet revelation is well-paced with just the right hints along the way. The game is short, but it's full nonetheless and ends exactly where it should. The endings are brief but satisfying.
It's absolutely worth picking up, especially if it's on sale.

This game is a cool throwback to old style text adventures, having a few short text adventures mixed some point and click scenes (which mostly are about solving number puzzles).
Unfortunately, depending on your luck, you may find the game will be way too easy or extremely frustrating. The text adventure segments mimic a 80's Spectrum computer, but the game is very crude compared to actual text adventures from the Spectrum era. It knows nothing at all about synonyms, it understands none of the conventions of the genre (for movement, object inventory, or getting required information from your surroundings), and puzzles are not actual puzzles but a bunch of 'guess the word' block walls that usually rely on you remembering some detail about your surroundings that sometimes you won't be able to get again. Any 1983 text adventure from a real Spectrum completely destroys this game in both a technical and gameplay level, not to mention any of the modern quality interactive fiction you can play today.
The point and click segments are not much better. The puzzles are uninteresting, and rely mostly on you trying to make sense of small, blurry print, or distorted voices saying something that resemble English numbers (there is a subtitles option, but it is useless, as it works only on flavor text). Hopefully you have English as your native language or a very good hearing.
It is also an extremely short game that you'll finish in a single sitting, and a short one.
There are some things the game does right, though. The story is great, and the way the four apparently undisconected stories are tied towards the end is a genius move. The graphics are really great, and the renditions of 80's equipment and computers is very, *very* realistic. I experienced a few graphical glitches, but the game worked fine most of the time.
I find it really disappointing that the amount of love given to the presentation and the original idea didn't follow through to the implementation of the actual game elements. This could have been an amazing experience if the game had a proper text adventure engine and better puzzles. As it is, I can't really recommend it.

This is a brilliant, modern take on classic text adventures.  In the episodes I've played thus far (the first 3), the atmosphere is unsettling and spooky with beautiful graphics helping to set the tone.  Speaking of tone, this game unashamedly mimics the style of Stranger Things, both in terms of visual and audio style, but it works REALLY well.  Playing the game feels a lot like being in an escape room, if you've tried those.
The first episode is close to a classic text adventure, albeit with a more simple vocabulary.  Without revealing too many details, the later episodes have you actually interacting with the environment around you in addition to the terminal.  In the second and third mention for instance, you'll constantly be adjusting dials, pushing buttons, and referring to references, in addition to typing on the terminal.  Compared to the first episode, these later episodes focus less on the old-school text adventure and begin to add in more mixed media content.
The only negative point for me so far was a difficult puzzle in the third episode (if you're getting out a pen & paper, you've probably seen it)  The puzzle itself is very fair, it's just difficult if you don't have the right skill to complete it.  I'll leave it at that.
The atmosphere is spooky and unsettling, but not super scary.  There are a few video/audio flashes but nothing I'd qualify as a jump scare.  There are no graphic depictions of gore in the episodes I've played so far.
I'd highly recommend this game if you like story based games (think Gone Home) that are more about experiencing the content.  I'm not sure if there are multiple endings to the episodes but generally, this is going to be a short, high quality one-time adventure for most people.  If you're on the fence at all, please search for 'House Abandon' on itch.io and you can download the first episode for free.  I wasn't sure if this game would really hook me because I don't love classic text adventures, but this modern spin on a classic formula is dripping with style.

If you've played any of the other offerings in this series then this incarnation will be largely familiar. While the handling is quite different and does reflect some of the changes in the 2014 season you could just be driving the old V8s as the developers haven't bothered to implement the more refined features of the 2014 engines. In fact, there are fewer engine features in this game than in the previous games. Now you've just got the loud pedal, the stop pedal and DRS. There's no implementation of boost or energy recovery, something that seems to be a key factor for the real cars. Whether the developers didn't have access to this sort of information, thought it would be too complex for the average gamer or were just too lazy to put it into the game it does mean that if you're thinking of upgrading to the latest version to get the features of the 2014 spec engines then you're going to be disappointed. If you're happy to carry on with the V8s and an earlier driver line up then hang onto your cash and wait for the new technologies to be properly developed.

If you are a wheel user who is happy to pay for what is essentially the same experience as F1 2013 (and one that has arguably less content) but with the new cars and tracks, then F1 2014 might be for you.
However, if you use a controller then steer clear, do not waste your money! The handling model is ruined in this one. Driver aids are forced upon you and it makes everything drive like junk. This is applicable to you whether you used assists before or not. Though if you didn’t use assists then the difference is even more aggravating. All the nice driving feel is gone. For them to claim this was in the name of accessibility is just baffling. The games have always had options to turn assists on for new players. Why couldn’t these new assists be included in said options? How does it make sense to force them upon people who purposefully turn assists off!?
What is left is a game where driving is a chore not a challenge. The cars feel awful but at the same time you will find it hard to ever spin or lock a tire. Instead you will be stuck throwing yourself into corners like an idiot because the traction control will just do the work for you, otherwise you can’t keep up. Driving fast with a controller in this game feels like cheating and going back to 2013 I was well aware of how much worse of a driver it had made me.
In terms of content the only real addition is a shortened career mode, in which you advance through teams by setting their drivers as rivals and beating them in a best of 3 races. I actually think this is pretty cool and I hope it stays in the series. Apart from that everything is the same but they cut the classic cars and tracks, along with a lot of the new driver testing stuff.
This is what you get when you take a franchise that already struggles for new content because of its annual release schedule, then tell the developers they actually have less time than usual because their 2015 version needs to be next gen and released early than usual. Hopefully it makes up for this mess.

I'm a big fan of the Kalypso titles. I played most of the economics titles with the exception of tropico which i will try someday. As for Port royale and Patrician , RoV follow the logic of the economy of Kalypso titles with enough difference to have its own title, you don't place building or expand your city size like Patrician or Port Royale. Everything takes place in the wolrd map , which is not a bad things as it saves tons of loading screens. RoV requires you not to play in '' God mode '' meaning if you scale back too much the map you will miss everything froms teachers to black market or chests floating around. With the DLC the map get a decent size, still much smaller than Port Royale but bigger than a Patrican map. In short if the others titles i mentioned pleased you in the past, RoV is for you. HOWEVER, and i must warn you all, there is a massive crash bug regarding Nvidia cards which as of July 25 2014 is not yet solver at all. Yes friends almost a year out and there is still a major crash bug unresolved with no news as of we are working on it.... If you are the kind of people getting angry at stupids bugs AVOID this game at all cost. The only thing that keep me going is my addiction to the capitalism system Kalypso titles gives us. Because of this i will not recommend this game to anyone. A TDR bug with one of the most popular 3d cards of the decade means a broken game that should not have been released.

The worst of it all, besides horrible loot grinding and character balancing, is that they'll blame the concept, not the execution. They'll ignore the fact that they KNEW there were half a million people who were ready to buy this game but they ♥♥♥♥ed it up because they didn't want to obligate checks to reliable dedicated servers. They'll pretend that it was this games story, its bold new ideas that failed and not the fact that their bugs made this game unplayable for over half of the people who purchased it.

I almost judged this game by the graphics, and I'm glad I didn't.  The controls work well and the levels are very well designed.  Fast travel seemed like a strange addition at first, but it's almost open-world, with in-game reasons to go back and fix places you've already been.  The dialogue is well-written, all characters are well differentiated, and I'd say the highlight of the game is the story -- which is a lot harder scifi than I expected.  A pleasant surprise.
Gameplay is based off of studying and manipulating an alien ecosystem, with no weapons to speak of.  In particular, figuring out how to make each life form produce its seed pod, which can be used for many different functions, is vital.  It's one of those games that puts you in an unfamiliar situation, where you have to figure out what you can do all by yourself -- and unlike some of them, it pulls it off neatly.
The game IS short though.  It took me a little under 10 hours for a blind 90% complete playthrough.  Since I got it on sale for $2, it blew my socks off.  If I had to pay the full $10, or maybe $5-7 on a cheaper sale...?  It might still be worth it.

Very ambient game, got it on sale for 2$ and it was a very pleasant surprise.
You play as Liang, an astronaut a few centuries in the future sent to explore newly discovered life in a cave on mars after the disappearence of the rover 0ct0 in the aforementioned cave.
what you discover is a curious mechanism of what appears to be a self perserving ecosystem:
each chamber in the cave will not open until there is sufficient biomass in it- ensuring that the inner parts of the cave remain safe from the harsh conditions on the surface until it is ready.
For me the characters (Liang and Amani) were very likeable and creating a self sufficient eco system that would ebb and flow from stage 4 to 5 within a chamber was very satisfying and felt natural.
That being said, the gameplay was got very repeptetive and the scenery was quite monotone at some points (though I suppose being it's placed in mars there's not much to do about that.) and the jetpack was a bit clunky at some points (when you hit a rock with your foot and the game decides you're trying to walk)
OVERALL:
- Very ambient, atmospheric game
- Science is just detailed enough to make you think how accurate it is
- Gameplay-driven story that is very interesting
- Likeable Characters
- Gets a bit tedious sometimes
- Repetetive towards the end
- Whole heartedly recommended!
