This is a fun, classic-feeling ARPG that's just as enjoyable solo as with friends, although I prefer multiplayer.  Difficulty ramps up with friends (up to 4). The game will provide 6-8 hours (curerntly as of this review) of base "Story Mode" content.  The temples ("dungeons") are very well thought-out and provide adequate challenge and they also display innovative mechanics. I played through story mode with 3 players in about 7 hours, and I wish there was more or more replayabilty in story mode.
"Arcade Mode" is a bit slow to get into, especially with friends. The replayability is there, but it's kind of a slog to get started (and re-started).
I bought the 4 pack from their website; would I spend $15/per player again on this game? Probably not. It's unfortunately, at best, a ~$7 game right now. I do however recommend this as an enjoyable game.  The value, however, isn't there just yet.

Stories Untold is a fantastic science fiction / horror adventure heralding the old days of text based adventure games intermixed with fun and sometimes frustrating puzzles.  It riffs hard on the Stranger Things vibe, throwing 80s nostalgia into the mix with a well developed story and gorgeous visuals.  It's an atmosphere that immerses you and gave me a jump or two, despite the fact the game doesn't have actual jumpscares.
I wasn't quite sure what to expect coming in, saw it on Steam and it definitely grabbed my attention.  I was expecting a simple game, but my expectations were greatly exceeded.  Gameplay is short once you're familiar with the gameplay and what it expects from the text based entry.  Definitely keeping my fingers crossed there may be more episodes to come.  I loved every moment of this game from start to finish and do recommend keeping a pencil and paper at hand for Chapter 3.
I was able to play mostly through the game on my junky 2 GB nvidia laptop (frame rates were acceptable-ish for the system), but found myself having to fall back on my 8 GB desktop for the fourth chapter (8-12 fps on the laptop, but not unexpected), the game can be graphically intense on some systems, but I imagine you could manage on 2 GB.
Very refreshing and enjoyable.  Well done.

I liked the first Force Unleashed. I played in on 360 and thought it was fine. I got this on a sale a long time ago and never got around to playing it. Until yesterday.
And then I beat it.
I am not good at video games. But even I thought this game was ridiculously easy. And short. Which is not helped by the game's lack of difficulty. Seriously, I was done in about 4 hours on medium difficutly. And I took my time to try and find some of those dumb holocrons and mess around with the force powers. I have been told the dark ending has some additional stuff to do. But I didn't pick that ending. Given how the game closes with the light side option, there is still more stuff to do anyway. But that's not in this game.
When you play the game, it basically becomes: saber attack with lightning or use lightning. The combat was not interesting. The enemy types were very predictable and were not well placed. The boss fights were not any better. I really only remember two: the giant monster and the last one. I'm not sure if I missed bosses or just misunderstood what parts of the game counted as boss fights. But those fights were just boring.
The story is also pathetically weak. Even by old EU Star Wars standards. To be fair, it's really hard to make a story be relatable when your main character is so stupidly overpowered. I get that the super powers are the point. They enable the "fun" of the game. But it's really not fun. There is nothing to do worth doing. Even if we assume the game was fun to play, that's no excuse to go this lazy with the plot. And to end on that cliffhanger? Why? Just finish the story. Who thought this was enough content? I guess I shouldn't be too upset, I didn't like what they did up to that point.
tl;dr - The game is short, easy, forgettable, and just bad. If you are looking to waste money and are a Star Wars fan/somewhat liked the first game, just buy something else. Seriously. Don't buy this game.

But the CONS
* Biggest one is that your control over auto trading has been DRASTICALLY reduced from Port Royale to the point where autotraders often no longer make a profit (You cant set the game to load from a warehouse and sell down to a specific price anymore. It has to be either warehouse activity only or city activity only. There is a 'captain' option which allows this, but is an AI automanage system resulting in the AI selling down to the price of production... meaning no profits) - only option then is to micromanage...

*The senate system (pleasing each family) is a burden and the sabotage system isnt fun, rather they are frustrating (Senate members are fine with sabotaging and stealing each others goods and cities, but when the player goes privateering, everyone hates you!)
Port Royale was much better and had a MUCH bigger map.
The campaign can be finished in around 8-10 hours
With just a few hours the game can be "completed" (Supplying every city with all the goods they need)

This is a fun game when you play it for what it is. I really enjoyed the time I put into it. The game plays much different than any of the current Motocross racing games and it shouldn't be compared to them because of this reason. You can't play this game expecting it to play like the MX vs ATV series or MXSIMULATOR, this is a racing game on dirt bikes, not a simulator.
The single stick driver controls feel dated when comparing it to MvA Reflex, but the controls work for this game. The scrubing feature feels great, even though the animation does look a little wonky when it comes back. But the way it plays is nice in the game and you'll be spotting your landing on the way back not staring at the animation.
I never got a chance to play online against other players, that would have been very interesting. The AI gives you a good run from time to time, but nothing like another human player would.
If you're looking for a fun, good looking dirt bike racing game I would suggest this game. The Tour mode is like a career mode where you level your rider up, get new gear, better teams, etc... I really enjoyed playing this mode. My only complaint is that you're not able to put your name and rider number on your rider, these are assigned for you.
Overall I would give this game a 7\10 and I suggest that any fan of dirt bike videos games give it a chance.

Quite a bit of negative comments for this game, though I believe largely undeserved. This is a trading/political (lite) simulator. The crux of the game is to further your personal success across a defined region. Many claim the campaign is too simple and after a few trade routes are established This may be accurate, however, the campaign is primarily a long tutorial, not desigend to be crushingly hard. The heart of the game lies in the Free Play mode through setting the world up and stacking the odds against you to begin with which gets increasingly fun, especially if you reach in to the dark corners of your mind and do some backstabbing and pillaging. It is most definitely a title built upon the foundations of the Patrician and Port Royale series, however, the steps taken to create a more fluid engine are very welcome. Seemless transitions into ports provides easier access to the game menus and provides a neat "tilt shift" effect to the world. If you are looking for a good trading simulator focused more on running your businesses than battling pirates Sid Meier's style, then you will fall right Rise of Venice. Highly recommended.

First, I think it is best to start by saying that if you are looking for a good racing sim that covers the F1 2014 season then this is a must have. It gives you the new turbocharged cars, the 2014 track list and the 2014 roster (exempting some mid/late season changes).
There are a lot of reviews that call this a "copy/paste" of F1 2013's gameplay. That is correct but only because F1 as a actual sport is not one that changes it's entire rule structure, driver roster or track schedules in massive ways. it's a sport so any evolution is going to be slow and gradual. Going into F1 2014 with the understanding that it gives you exactly what it's title says (a F1 2014 season game) will probably save you from getting super upset.
I mean, seriously. Are people expecting races on the moon or something? Perhaps Jet powered cars with missile launchers? It's a F1 sim/game so it is going to use the material that the actual sport provides.
The only really significant downer is the lack of 2013's classic mode but considering how limited in scope the classic mode is in 2013, I suppose I can understand why they want to wait until they can really do more with that concept and I don't think F1 2014 was the place for them to do that (though I think expectations are high for F1 2015).
So, with that out of the way, lets talk about specifics.
1.) Graphics. This title is not going to be a massive jump from 2013 but it does the job perfectly. The car models look fantastic. The tracks look good and effects still do the job as well as you would want them to. The real standout however is the rain effects. Codemasters seems to understand the importance of good rain effects and how it effects the gameplay.
2.) Sound. The sound is great. The cars sound correct and reflect the 2014 move to 6cyl turbocharged power units. The rest of the effects do the job just fine and give you plenty of situational awareness.
3.) Physics/handling. This is where I think a lot of people have the wrong attiude in their reviews. They get so used to 2013's handling (with more downforce and less torque) that the 2014 cars can come as a surprise since they feel ENTIRELY different. This can make it difficult for those that mastered F1 2013 and some will get frustrated at having to adapt to a new driving style (just like the real drivers had to deal with). The handling is a real high-point in F1 titles and this is no different.
4.) Gameplay modes. It does not have the classic mode which is fine but the rest of the normal options are still there. The only big change is the switch from a long "young drivers test" to a short evaluation lap which can either be welcome or unwelcome depending on your skill level going in.
Overall. while it lacks the classic cars and tracks of 2013. It still provides a solid F1 2014 season experience that accurately reflects the technical changes in a satisfying way. If you want a sports franchise to change in leaps and bounds then you probably are not being reasonable but I suspect that a lot of the big stuff is being saved for the F1 2015 release.

Full Disclosure: I played this game single player using an x-box one controller.
THE GOOD: Where this game shines is in when you're exploring levels and platforming at your own pace. You have to use both protagonists intelligently in order to reach new areas and progress. Also, during certain sections of the game, huge gusts of wind act as both a mechanic and a hazard. In the former quality you have to time your jumps with when a gust of wind is blowing towards an otherwise impossible to reach platform. In others, you have to press a button to hug the ground and keep from being blown off to your death. Rather than annoying these sections are placed in such a way that they enhance the platforming, immerse you in the Alaskan setting, and are enjoyable. The art style is phenomenal and gives this game a very Miyazaki quality. It's just really beautiful to look at and has echoes of Shadows of the Colossus or Ico underneath. The voice actor chosen for the narrator does a great job of giving this game's story an authentic feel as well. Whenever a cutscene featuring him plays you'll feel like you're being told this story by a village elder. When combined with the art style and music the game becomes something very unique and entertaining. And finally, the movies you can collect through the game do offer an interesting look at Inuit culture and are very enjoyable. Since this game does have many problems it may be worth your while to look these up on youtube as they explore a way of life that is both beautiful and harsh at the same time.
THE BAD: The bosses are by far the most annoying sections. Boss battles usually happen in two ways: one, where you're running away from said boss and two, where you're using environmental puzzles to fight these enemies. Let's start with the former variety. These are chase sequences where you're given a relatively limited amount of time to clear obstacles and progress. Since you can't take your time to figure these sections out they totally kill the feeling of exploration that the game employs brilliantly everywhere else. One particularly frustrating quality to these sections involves the girl's main weapon: the bolo. During the course of the game you'll gain access this throwing weapon which requires the girl to stand still, pull in the opposite direction she's facing with the right analog stick, and then quickly push the stick in the opposite direction to let the weapon fly. The aiming for this weapon is finicky and makes it so that even when you get used to how it works you'll often enough miss your target. Now during the exploration sections this is just a minor inconvenience but having to stop and aim an imprecise weapon during a chase sequence where death happens in a matter of seconds it becomes really frustrating easily. Needless to say you'll die a lot because of this alone.
Now for those segments where you have to fight a boss. These come in the form of timed environmental puzzles where if you take too long to figure out what to do the boss will kill you. Again the feeling of exploration that was such a joy becomes discarded in favor of a typical platforming boss fight. Though these sections happen only a few times since they come after the game has spent much of your playtime teaching you to run away from bosses and to explore environments at your own pace to progress they seem to circumvent the overall feel. If you're like me you'll feel cheated and very annoyed by this. Another issue which will probably be most solo gamer's tipping point is a particular boss. I'll not spoil it's plot details but during it you have to control both the fox and the girl character in order to avoid one-hit, homing missile-like balls of death. All this while using said balls of death to transform parts of the environment into tools you can use to kill said boss. This section was built for co-op and the game's designers didn't afford any changes to make it manageable if you attempt this solo. Now I'll admit, with enough time and effort this section can be overcome but the payoff is just really not worth the struggle to do so. While the latter boss type is rarer the former happens way too often and ultimately I wish the developers had turned these into cutscenes rather than make 'em stuff I could play.
This game does have a lot of really good qualities. The art style will appeal to anyone who's a fan of Miyazaki. Combined with the music and the narrator you get a sense of authenticity that's rare in games. With interesting mechanics the exploration sections are a real joy to play. And the videos you can collect are worth watching, if only to learn about another culture. However the numerous boss sections just drag this whole game down and make it too frustrating to be worth a recommendation.

SOMA is hard to not judge side by side with the Amnesia games, as they are made by the same company, Frictional Games. The similarities are abundant, which may be seen as a negative, however seeing as the original format wasn't anything to complain about, keeping the format the same doesn't strike me as a problem. However, the strong similarities quickly go from welcome to questionable. While SOMA doesn't have a sanity meter, you are still supposed to not look at the baddies, for fear that you'll "Short Circuit". One could even be led to the assumption that SOMA is merely a reskin of Amnesia. Same play style, same pacing, similar enemies, though Soma takes place underwater. It sure as hell won't let you forget it either. The action scenes are broken up by long walking segments from station to station, with very little to do or interact with. If you are considering purchasing Soma for it's horror aspect, this part is important. SOMA is not very scary. I can't think of any jumpscares aside from when the baddies find you. It's more a stealth game, sneaking around enemies. The enemies aren't varied either. The first one you encounter is a rogue robot patrolling a part of the first station. That is the only time the enemy types vary from the normal. To the game's credit, they do get more difficult due to your location. The closer you are to the "ARK", the harder the enemies are because they are closer to the heart of the AI mess that took over the stations. The AI, also known as the WAU (Warden Unit)'s backstory is also hard to follow unless you thoroughly read all of the available dialog in the game. WAU's ending was more or less "Go to a place and interact with a thing" Which solves the entire WAU problem. Not even a fight. Come to think of it, you don't fight a single thing in this game but one robot who doesn't fight back. But maybe that's the psychological part of psychological horror. Overall, the story is definitely the best part of this game, and if you want an arguably easy, arguably not horror, horror game that has a good story, this game is for you.

After having owned this game for about a month, and played it for about 50 hours, I feel I can finally put a serious review out for anyone wanting to buy this game. This game has a lot of pros and cons, and I am gonna difference those in two categories.
Pros :
+ The posibilities this game offers. Friday the 13th is one of those games that give players a good amount of choices to escape from the Killer (Cops, Car/Boat, Running out of time or even killing jason.) It will take some time until all of these options are used, mainly the jason's death option which is the hardest to get in this game. Overall, the possibilites to escape are vast and the environment this game has to offer and sets you in is stunningly beautiful.
+ Improvement. The development teams always try their best to improve the game by posting constant updates regarding content or bug-fixes.
+ The ''Teamwork'. This game is based on Teamwork, and it often pays out and even helps you making new friends. The fact that there is a microphone option for both the Killer and the Counselors gives the two factions a way to communicate and establish plans to escape.
+ The Graphics. Of course, this one was a must. The graphics in this game aren't maybe the ''best'' but they are far better than in other horror games such as Dead by Daylight.
+ The content. This game offers true class-specific content. For example, when playing Chad (Strong with melee/lucky) you will mostly use baseball bats as a gataway option, but if playing the fat guy, you will be carrying the battery/fuel asking for the stronger teammates such as the black guy/chad to cover you, since your domain of expertize is reparation as you are a nerd. The classes are well-balanced, and every counselor has it's pros and cons, making each of them truly unique and offering different type of gameplays for a variety of peoples.
Cons :
- The Price. It simply is too high, altough having good launch content, the maps are overall poorly made, having an amassment of same looking cabins with nothing unique to them. It would've been more wise to price this at $25 and not $40.
- Rulebreakers/teammers. There is countless teammers that ruin this game by either helping out the Killer or simply the Killer helping the Counselor to escape whilst killing everyone else.
- Still a good amount of bugs to fix. Sadly, altough wanting to improve, the team since to sometimes fail to fix some key bugs such as the possibility for a counselor to flip the car if hit. Another example to that is the fact that by fixing some bugs, they brought some new ones which weren't even taken in consideration, and which is a BIG MINUS for the Counselors : The Perks bug.
- Lack of map diversity.
This is all, I will try to add some elements as the game progresses.
I would give this game a rating of 8/10.

Slow and desolate atmosphere overcomes some hiccups.
35MM struggles at times. It drags its feet, it stumbles. A cosmetic bug here or there. Very loose translations/subtitles. A slow story (that was enough for me). And more than a handful of completely unintuitive moments. But this clunky charm somehow ends up just that. Charm. It adds to the slow pace and atmosphere in some weird messed up way. That's the real selling point here; The atmosphere. You feel the desolation and death around you. But the characters have also clearly accepted the situation. Moments of urgency arise for certain but there's a calm acceptance to most of the game emanating from the characters. That could very well turn players off in the form of boredom. Gameplay is mostly within the realm of a slower "walking simulator" but some mini-puzzles, item gathering, and even acceptable gunplay all sneak in.
It is clear the ambition behind this was larger than what was achievable. And I think the creator did a great job reeling that ambition in and applying it within the means possible. I've seen some atrocious Unity games but this one is a looker as far as Unity is concerned. The environments are meticulously detailed and have set pieces placed with care rather than copy and pasted. You travel from countryside villages to big cities. From barns to underground railways. While all draped in a post-apocalyptic smokey gloom, they're all unique and contrasting. A real beauty. It also manages to deliver multiple gameplay ideas without getting carried away. QTE-like moments, gameplay cutscenes, random interactions that even include using a lathe. It all just works together without anything feeling too out of place suddenly. A true effort to make a complete game with unique moments.
Overall the "charm" was something I could work with. While 35MM certainly could use polishing, I like it as is. It made for an interesting experience. Save the polishing for the next project! Tons of potential from the creator. A soft recommendation as it may not hit home with some.

Thomas Was Alone is a simple platformer. You play as blocks, and you need to get the blocks from point A to point B through an obstacle course. There is a twist, though, and that twist is that this game has an amazing story and characters. The game's story rivals most triple-A titles and the characters are extremely likeable - although flawed, which is saying a lot considering they are all different sized and coloured rectangles and squares. The quality of the game writing is absurdly high to achieve this, and the entire story is bundled together with amazing narration featuring the vocal talents of British humorist Danny Wallace (who won the BAFTA Performance award for his part as the narrator) and a harrowing, calm soundtrack by David Housden.
I definetly recommend Thomas Was Alone for anyone who is even remotely interested in totally abstract storytelling, and minimalistic design.

I really want to love this game. The foundation for something really special is there. You can tell that a great deal of talent, passion, and care have gone into the product so far. However, at this juncture in the prerelease, it is still too unfinished to warrant a recommendation. Once the initial novelty of playing as a dinosaur wears off, every couple minutes of excitement or fun you will experience in the game is encumbered by hours of monotony or extreme frustration.
As of now, I have nearly 600 hours into the game, and you might wonder how I can feel justified in NOT recommending a game that has offered 600 hours of play time. That is because a minimum of 95% of the time I have put in to the game is spent AFK or grinding (pressing E to eat or drink.) The carnivore progression system is time based. In order to progress up the food chain to better, stronger dinosaurs, you first have to pay your dues as a small carrion feeder creature. There is next to nothing to do as a tier 1 or 2 dinosaur, but hide in bushes until you get hungry, come out to feed, and then go back to the bushes to pass the time. You are so slow that migrating across the expansive map is basically out of the question, as it is very easy to spend hours without seeing a carcass or another player, and it only takes minutes to starve to death.
The best strategy for progressing is to just have the game up on one monitor and come out to eat and drink as necessary in between doing other tasks IRL. It used to be that you could run the game in the background, switching between other applications as necessary, but now the game must be in focus, otherwise Battle Eye will shut down your client after about a minute. You must constantly ensure that The Isle is in focus after you perform some other task on your pc. This is really irritating. I understand that they don't want everyone to just AFK for hours on end, but why not address this situation by making low tiers FUN to play, rather than attempting to force the player to engage with an extremely unstimulating and pointless experience? Another useful strategy is to write a script that will exit the game after a certain period of time, so you can get up and walk away from the computer while your dinosaur progresses, and it won't starve to death if you can't come back.
There is one another viable strategy for progression, which involves joining a "mega pack," but I'll talk more about that later.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. On the highest settings, it is one of the best looking games I've seen. The animations are stunningly realistic. It looks so good, that you could make mock nature documentaries out of it. In fact, maybe nature documentaries are what they had in mind when they spent the time, effort, and capital making the game look and sound so amazing. Whatever their reasoning, it certainly was not just to have people play the game with pleasing graphics, as that is out of the question. Playing on high graphics settings puts the player at a distinct disadvantage. You will THINK you are hiding in a pitch black night time shadow, invisible to all players, only to be destroyed immediately by a player who has shadow rendering turned all the way down.
I learned this when trying to hide in the shadow of a cloud that was rolling over the scenic, moonlit plains. I thought it was such a cool game mechanic to be able to hide in moving shadows at night, waiting to ambush unsuspecting prey from the cover of darkness. Wrong. If you try this, you will quickly be picked off by a player who can't even see the shadow, as I was.
You also must turn down a draw distance setting, as this will allow you to see dinosaurs that are supposed to be hidden in bushes at a certain distance away. Why do dinosaurs render at greater distances than bushes, if bushes are intended to serve as cover? I don't know, but take advantage of it. Other players certainly do. And once shadows are off, and draw distance is lowered, you are left with a very mediocre looking environment.
But as far as gameplay, what happens when, after 5 or 6 iterations of failing to progress through lower tiers (spending several hours each time), you finally attain a decent dinosaur? Well, at this point, the game has the potential to be extremely fun and rewarding. Typically, at tier 3 you can start migrating across the map, as your hunger and thirst will last for a reasonable amount of time, and you are relatively fast. At tier 4, you even start feeling somewhat comfortable being out in the open for extended periods of time. Hunting, stalking, and tracking prey by their footprints is exhilerating. Defending carcasses from smaller scavengers is a great deal of fun. Assuming that you don't get stuck in or fall through the map, or encounter a "mega pack," you can expect to have a very enjoyable experience at tier 3+.
I mentioned mega packs once before. They are indeed your only salvation if you want to progress through the lower tiers without being AFK, or staring catatonically at an uneventful screen for hours on end. They will also completely ruin the game for you as a higher tier dinosaur if you're not involved in the pack. Honestly, every other issue with the game, including the boredom and complete lack of gameplay for low tiers, could be forgiven if not for the "mega pack" issue.
A mega pack is essentially a large group of many different species, typically including several apex carnivores and large herbivores cooperating with each other, usually while all pack members communicate over Discord or other third party service.
I could be wrong here, but my impression was that the devs intend to build a somewhat realistic dinosaur game, where the incentive structure of the game is meant to provoke reasonably natural behaviors from the players controlling the animals. "Mega packs" prove that this game is no where near that ideal, and for anyone looking for an experience like that, The Isle will seem basically unplayable, at all tiers. You can't hunt members of a mega pack without being killed, and if you just leave to another part of the map, everyone else is AFK waiting to progress. Most active players want to be in the pack, because it virtually guarantees their survival.
There are some private servers that attempt to remedy this situation. "Realism" servers attempt to force players to behave naturally, through an honor/taddle system. In other words, for everything to work properly, each player must memorize a set of rules for every single dinosaur, interpret those often ambiguous rules properly, and then report players who misbehave to the server admins, who will enforce rules arbitrarily. No thanks.
There HAS to be an incentive system that discourages interspecies cooperation which is derived from game mechanics. Maybe a territory system for preds, or a fear system for herbivores. Who cares, anything at all. Until mega packs are destroyed, this game is a mess. It was a mess a year ago because of mega packs, and it still is. Life in a mega pack is like a simulated office party. Everyone just sits around the water hole waiting for food to appear. Not to mention that in order to retain favor in the pack, it is best to interact directly with the target demographic of the game in a Discord server, which I found to be obnoxious and insufferable. It's not at all what I'm looking for in a nature simulation.
It should be a testament to how fun this game CAN be, that I have endured so much monotony and irritation just to progress to high tiers in this game. The Isle sat running idly, eating CPU and GPU cycles on my pc for at least 500 hours in total, all so I could play as an allosaurus or an acrocanthosaurus occasionally. The Isle has huge potential, and if they fix it, I'll change my review to reflect that. But for now, it's broken, and I'm out.

I loved The House Abandon, and Stories Untold completely exceeded my expectations. I thought it was a short and sweet experience, and the production value/bizarre narratives made it worth the price. I played the game from my television, so some of the smaller details were somewhat difficult to make out even with the zoom function, but otherwise I the "Text Adventure within a game" medium was handled visually about as convincingly as it could be. Play this if you like text adventures and puzzle/simulation style games with interesting/creepy narratives.
Pros:
-Nails atmosphere and mystery elements
-Great synth soundtrack
-Distinct styles and settings
-Lovely set design and visual direction
-Puzzles make you feel like you're doing stuff without leaving you totally in the dark
-Refreshing take on the Text Adventure format
Cons:
-Controls feel sensitive and unwieldly at times
-Quite a few instances where actions taken do not reflect correct state change on the environment when the "Look" command is used
-Command parser could be fleshed out a bit
-Some details can be difficult to make out
Overall, a solid experience. I hope to see more in the future!

My first impression of this game was that of a cheap alien shooter with a jetpack. OOooooh how I was wrong. Sure its graphics are far from impressive, but that's not what they were aiming for.
Now I'll start with what I enjoyed the most of this. The soundtrack. The music is so strange and unique, so it fits this alien world perfectly. But, truly, many of the tunes are just great tunes! You can check it out in the DLC, its free!
What I'll remember most profoundly about this game is how unique it was. Its system is unlike any other game out there. Sure, it borrows a few generic concepts from Metroid, so yeah, its a Metroidvania game (but those are awesome!). But it differs in that theres no combat in the usual sense, no weapons, no direct attacking. Rather, you throw seeds around and grow different plants that have unique abilities, to suit your needs. Got hurt from acid or nasty plants? Grow a healing plant. Want to water a dry area to grow more plants? Grow a water plant. Then theres more unusual situations of having to grow predatorial plants to eat the "enemies"... but I digress.
Another unique thing is that there is no enemies, nor antagonist for that matter. Sure, the wildlife you encounter might attack you, but only if you invade their territory or get too close for comfort. They just mind their own business, being generally neutral, like the wild in real life. Its nice not to have stupid cliched "bad guys", and it just works!
Its all about the exploration. This game is surprisingly deep and you'll have much to discover, everytime adding a new entry in a nifty little encyclopedia (like a Pokedex), giving you hints on how to interact with things in interesting ways. The game is very smart in how it always manages to surprise you. It presents you with a new lifeform, and you just gotta... experiment with it. Its really fun and I'm not gonna spoil any details.
If theres one thing that it fails at, sadly, is replayability. Its very long and tedious at times, but it was worth it to see what happens next. If you already know what next, however, theres very little incentive to go through the hoops a second time.  I'd replay it in a heartbeat with a friend though, to showcase it!
All in all, I REALLY recommend this game and strongly encourage game developpers to take a gander at it, this hidden gem of originality.

YES! GIVE ME MORE!
Summary:
Terrifying, interesting, Inception level twists. The individual stories are a bit short but the collection is great. Hopefully the beggining of a comeback for text adventures!
Full Review:
Finally someone has taken the idea first seen in Call of Duty: Black Ops and realised its full potential!!!
Not only does Untold Stories allow text adventure fans the chance to play new and interesting text adventures with the benefit of atmospheric graphics, sounds and music, the game creates a whole new mind-bending genre of text adventure where you are within the world of the story as it unfolds around you.
The realisation that I was in the house in which the first story was happening and the fact that I could hear and see what the character was doing was a big enough surprise, but to then find out that HE could see and hear what I was doing created one of the greatest twists I have ever seen in any game or movie.
Which brings me to my next point; YES, IT'S SCARY! I've played many text adventures and while the horror adventures were fun they were more intresting for their puzzles than their scares. NOT THE CASE HERE. I feel as though the developers were conscious of the fact that many text adventure enthusiasts would be sceptical of a horror text adventure and consequently decided to make it utterly terrifying by making it seem like a normal text adventure at first, then slowly introducing the new, terrifying elements. I'm pretty certain that for this, The House Abandon will probably be thrown amongst the high ranking text adventures for its groundbreaking revitilisation of the genre (hopefully).
The proceeding chapters, however, are no less innovative. I won't give any of it away as I've already somewhat spoiled the first episode, but I'll just say that the twists and turns in the other episodes are just as impressive and shocking.
The art quality equals that of the story telling. The music is extremely effective and the voice acting is also great.
The only issue I feel is present in these adventures is their length. NOW LET ME BE CLEAR; for £6 the four episodes in the game collectively more than make it worth the cost. However, the great fun in a text adventure was being able to come back to it every evening and continue your adventure, sometimes weeks and that's not counting the replays. Unfortunately these stories can be completed in 30 minutes.
I've not replayed any of the episodes yet, so I can't say whether or not there are alternate paths, storylines or endings, but I feel pretty sure than in at least one of them there is more to the story than I experienced. It will be dissappointing if this isn't the case.
Overall, this is perhaps the most exciting game I've played in nearly a year, and has made me so excited to see new text adventures of different genre's and size that could be made this way.
Hopefully, this will be the rebirth of a legendary game genre.

) Either too much is going on for me to register what's happening, I'm unable to get strong enough to properly face this boss/foe, and/or the skills I have are weak than they should be.

See cards as a reward for grinding/farming excessively as they give you benefits whether to your stats or purchases (that I've seen so far). After having this game on my wish-list for over a year, I finally bought it not that long ago. It wasn’t everything that I expected it to be, but it was a new experience that I don’t regret.
If you couldn’t tell by the previews and screenshots, this game is a side scrolling platformer.
The game is around a four hour play if you failed as much and as often as I did. Its price is just about right for a game of this length. The DLC, Fox Tales added about an hour’s worth of play making the whole game around 5 hours long.
It isn’t as punishing as some platformers can be, as if you die you are dropped right back to where the puzzle began most of the time. However it is a game with one-hit kills, so one mess-up and you have to start back at the beginning of the puzzle again. There is a 2-player option but it is local so your friend has to be in the same room. (I don't have a problem with that at all.)
Some parts were frustrating because of controls, specifically towards the end. The spirit moving ability was the most frustrating. It was hard in some areas where speed was necessary and that made it very difficult. I spent much too long on some of these instances. There are times as well where the fox or Nuna would move without my command and end up dying because of it. (I played single player the whole way through.) There were also times that I forgot which character I was and I jumped to my death. The final chase had a lot of frustration for the same reason as before; fox’s spirit ability moved too slowly if you were too close to the intended object. Some of the puzzles got frustrating and took me a while to figure out. Those were rightfully so as they were the climatic “battles” with the antagonists of the story. So difficulty was merited.
Story was good. I wasn’t absolutely enthralled with it, but it was an interesting look into a famous Inuit story.
Art design was interesting and gorgeous. Some of the fur didn’t look very good up close, but overall it was a pretty game and definitely worth a buy. The 2D cut scenes in particular were cool and the spirits were also interesting to look at. The Northern Light children were particularly creepy.
The music didn’t stand out to me too much as it was very slow and atmospheric in most parts. However, I am a fan of powerful sounding music that is fast paced or loud so this may have been lost on me do to my taste. It is still good for setting the lonely mood throughout the game and fit the game perfectly. I do not regret buying the soundtrack.
I enjoyed the insight videos throughout the game and even went back to fetch all the owls that unlocked them. I liked this as I enjoy looking into cultures. (I would not have guessed that the Inuit culture viewed the Northern Lights and a semi-malicious presence.
The DLC, Fox Tales was short like I expected it to be. The Giant Mouse was rather creepy honestly and the first time we saw him it scared the crap out of me. I liked the boat travel and the bloops of the ice chunks when they fell on things made me laugh.
As before, some puzzles were frustrating, especially the last one due to wonky controls and over-all difficulty. Swimming was almost as difficult to control as the spirit moving ability.
Over-all, I recommend this game. It is worth a buy and a play-through. It’s not one my all-time favorite games but it was an experience I enjoyed.

When you are playing solo, occasionally the computer will move the character you are not controlling in a way that causes it to die - forcing you to start over.  That gets annoying after a while.  It happens most when you are controlling the fox, which is too bad because playing as the fox is much more fun than playing as the girl.
All-in-all, I give Never Alone a 3 out of 5.  Nice graphics, excellent animation, and interesting videos, but stale gameplay.

If you're a 2D platform fan and enjoy chilling on the weekend with something cute, with the feeling that mindless shooting isn't just the right thing for now - this is the game for you.
Never Alone is a fun, enjoyable title with very relaxing gameplay, soothing music, adorable companion at your side and a first hand sharing of lifestyle as well as lore of, well.. Eskimos!
The more you play, the more you discover the lore told by younger and older people from Inupiat tribe.
So not only do you enjoy the game itself, you're also expanding your knowledge about something very unique.
The corelations of stories and the game itself makes this title one of a kind and very addictive within first minutes of starting it.
The game gives a child-like feeling, where you're the child and Never Alone is the adult who is telling you an exciting bedtime story right before you'll go to sleep. You're drawn to the main character (Nuna) and letting go of her without knowing how the story ends is very close to impossible. You just have to get to the end and think of '5 more minutes' which turn into hours that seem timeless - exactly the way it used to be as a kid when you closed yourself in your own fantasy world.
Sum it up?
Buy it. Game in it. Remember it.

As you can probably see from above; I do not have much love for this game but hey; if you understand Russian and don't mind walking simulators; this could be the game for you.
Me personally though; would not buy again, or for anyone, or even accept as a free gift.

Broken Sword is a Point and Click adventure game, one of the first 'modern' ones to hit the PC scene back in the 90s. At the time it was hailed as a fantastic game, and even now nearly 15/20 years on, I'd still consider it a game that's worth playing for the experience.
The art work still holds up, where as the animation is basic, and the voice acting has been poorly recorded, but I can forgive that. The voice acting itself is outrageous with some of the most over the top accents you'll ever here - Geordie accent included!
Some of the puzzles are still genuine headscratchers, but the good type - Mav, Priit and Saj attempted to help. Attempted.
The game felt a little long winded by the end, so I'd be interested to know which new scenes were added to the Director's Cut (as I'm not entirely sure they were needed). However, overall I'd recommend this to any PnC fans, but perhaps wait for the Trilogy in the sale if you're a curious bystander.

Ok, ok, so this game has MANY problems, not just in the bugs/glitches but in the playerbase as well. Some problems (not regarding bugs, considering these bugs have been talked over so many times and are being fixed by the devs) include:
•Jason using the same kill that is the first one unlocked and the easiest grab-kill to use (as it doesn't require flat ground like many other kills)
•Jason's that spam the melee attack to kill every counseler
•Lack of text chat in-game for people without mics to communicate while playing.
•Lack of balancing that results in low-level players and high-level players being mixed together
These are just some of the issues the game has, some of these may be opinion based but this is a review with my opinions. Regardless of these issues, this game is absolutely fun, even with randoms. Lobby's become a mixed bag of people, and you'll meet plenty of different people, some fun, some competitive, and some just salty, but it doesn't matter who you are playing with because the matches are usually fun. Yes, sometimes you will get screwed over at the beginning of the game as a counselor by Jason, but you won't get horrible matches every time you play. Playing as Jason is a blast too, since he's the big-bad of the game and has great abilities to use at his fingertips.
With the negative backlash this game is getting, it's been said that the game is buggy and unbalanced, but the game is still great to play, even better with friends. I recommend this game not for the playerbase or the connection it has with the franchise, but for the gameplay that grabs your attention and makes you think on your feet both while playing as a counselor and Jason.

This game poses big philosophical questions. Who are we? What makes us what we are? What does it mean to be human?
STORY:
The story in this game is fantastic; a very well written and captivating experience that is emotionally moving. Not only will the story be emotional, but it will also bring up big philosophical question on existence and reality in which is executed perfectly in the game. A very memorable story that can be appreciated for years
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay keeps you constantly engaged within the world as you explore Pathos-II and its multiple research sites. There are no loading screens in the game which I personally like as it doesn't suddenly break you from the game. It saves at checkpoints and you can return later if you want.
The environments in this game are very detailed and well-designed. The monsters are creepy however after a while they become more of a hassle as avoiding them is tedious. There is a mod however that doesn't necessarily remove the monsters, but rather makes them unable to attack which in its own way adds a whole new eerie setting as the monsters shuffle alone down dark corridors, looking at you strangely.
GRAPHICS:
The graphics in this game are beautiful. I loved taking screenshots throughout the game and looking at the beautiful scenery that was present everywhere in the game. This game has some of the best graphics I have seen in games.
CONTROLS:
The controls are fluid and handle quite well. They don't feel clunky or jagged at all and the controls are very easy to learn.
STABILITY:
The game while it may seem to slow down when saving a checkpoint will run smoothly after a couple seconds and runs very well for a game with such great graphics and no loading screens.
OVERALL (TL;DR):
This game is a gem in which is a great experience. The story is amazing and memorable while asking big philosophical questions. The gameplay is engaging and will keep you captivated in the well-designed environments. Some of the best graphics I have personally seen ever can be found in this game as it is definitely on par with today's standards. The controls are fluid and handle very well; they are quite easy to learn. The stability in this game is overall great and well optimized for a game with amazing graphics and no loading screens. A must-buy personally.

Contrary to popular belief, Thomas was not alone.  He had lots of friends of different dimensions, jumping heights, and special abilities.  These abilities work together to solve various puzzles in order to reach the escape rectangles matching each of the characters at the end of each level.  The puzzles are mostly pretty simple and not at all difficult, but some can be tedious requiring repeated stacking of the different characters in order to climb over obstacles.
The graphical style of the game is deceptively simple.  The game has very good lighting and background effects which lend a nice atmosphere to the levels and provide some contrast to the very simple characters and rooms.  It is a very nice aesthetic and I think most people will enjoy it.
The best part of the game though is the narration.  I don't think they could have picked a better voice for the role and it is very well written as well.  The narration follows the thoughts of each character as you progress through the game and gives life to the colored rectangles morso than many games with human characters.
It really is a fantastic little game, though quite short.  I was able to finish it in 3 hours, but it was a great 3 hours.  Highly recommended.

não é algo fácil de se explicar. Basicamente, ele é uma aventura textual experimental. O que isso quer dizer? Que assim como todos os jogos do estilo, todas suas ações (ou boa parte delas) são realizadas através de texto. Você escreve os comandos. Mas Stories Untold subverte tudo que é esperado do estilo e vira o gênero de pernas pro ar. Com uma história incrível, mecânicas únicas e capricho imenso na parte áudio-visual, Stories Untold é a primeira surpresa de 2017.
Stories Untold é dividido em 4 episódios e cada um segue uma linha narrativa diferente. Vou me manter nisso porque a história do jogo é algo essencial pra experiência e spoilers podem diminuir o impacto dos eventos encontrados aqui.
Eu levei umas 8 horas pra zerar devido a certas circunstâncias mas eu imagino que Stories Untold deve levar de 4 a 6 horas.
Sem dúvidas nenhuma. Stories Untold foi a primeira grande surpresa de 2017 e algo que vou lembrar por um bom tempo. Suas mecânicas são fantásticas e dão uma vida nova a algo que não tinha mais tanto espaço na indústria atualmente, sua parte áudio-visual é polida ao extremo e deixa você imerso em mundo montado com muito carinho e o enredo é bem escrito, repleto de momentos interessantes e com uma conclusão satisfatória. Por 20 reais, Stories Untold é uma compra obrigatória, seja você fã de terror ou não.

This is a pretty dang cool game. The gameplay and visual themes feel similar to Aquaria or Super Metroid. The music is nice and smooth but also catchy. Interacting with the new creatures you discover is interesting and sometimes challenging. You fill research logs by actually discovering what creatures do in different situations.
I was worried from the description that the characters would seem kind of lifeless, but there's actually a lot of dialog that goes on in the game. Some of it is amusing, some is intriguing. You are a scientist on an exploratory mission that suddenly becomes dangerous, but your character has a tendency to see peace and serenity in situations where others might freak out. He seems pretty eloquent too, and gets a bit philosophical at times. Sometimes you wonder if it's a good idea to wake the life on Mars, and if humans are creating a positive or negative impact. Yet if you continue to play, the impact is unavoidable. Haven't finished it yet, but curious to see where it ends up.

Buy low.  Sell high.  But that's all.  Static map.  Static production locations.  Static prices (dynamically computed, but the cricumstances basically never change).  One or two kinds of random events that increase sale prices for a moment.
The most interesting part is when you can program your own trade routes, and there is a lot of configurability in how to you load/off-load to your warehouses and how you buy amd sell, but for reasons that defy the imagination, this is done via an interface that doesn't let you see a) all of your instructions for a city at once (how much was I buying here again?), b) what the other cities on the route produce or demand at the same time, or c) what the going rates are for such goods or how much of each goods are in stock at the time.  Basically, I think a real Venetian trader in 1455 with a few parchement sheets and some chalk and tablets would have had an easier time controlling his fleet.
The game is thus reduced to programming your obvious trade routes "through a straw" and hoping for a mission as exciting as "Rome needs dyes".  Oh, and there are naval battles but you'll want to automate them anyway.  Except the campaign insists that you play some of them.  So there's that.

The game's meta has completed its transformation into the full defensive, turtling state we find it in now. Parrying and countering guard breaks have become comically easy and the former leads to confirmed damage against the opponent. Whiff your parry attempt? That's okay, you can just cancel the heavy attack that presumably was supposed to open you up to some sort of fair punishment. The worst thing you can do in this fighting game is initiate an attack. Need I point out what is wrong with that?
Couple this game's failed meta with a lack of developer support, balance patches, connectivity and d/c issues, and the mountain of content locked behind the in-game currency system (which, of course, is much more ethical to purchase than to grind for) and you have a botched attempt at what had the potential to be an amazing game. If you played the beta, you at least got to try the game before (what remains) of the community discovered as a whole that there is no reason to initiate an attack if you want to win. Now, I'd wait and see if ubisoft cares enough to fix their flawed AAA title before wasting the time and money.

This game poses big philosophical questions. Who are we? What makes us what we are? What does it mean to be human?
STORY:
The story in this game is fantastic; a very well written and captivating experience that is emotionally moving. Not only will the story be emotional, but it will also bring up big philosophical question on existence and reality in which is executed perfectly in the game. A very memorable story that can be appreciated for years
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay keeps you constantly engaged within the world as you explore Pathos-II and its multiple research sites. There are no loading screens in the game which I personally like as it doesn't suddenly break you from the game. It saves at checkpoints and you can return later if you want.
The environments in this game are very detailed and well-designed. The monsters are creepy however after a while they become more of a hassle as avoiding them is tedious. There is a mod however that doesn't necessarily remove the monsters, but rather makes them unable to attack which in its own way adds a whole new eerie setting as the monsters shuffle alone down dark corridors, looking at you strangely.
GRAPHICS:
The graphics in this game are beautiful. I loved taking screenshots throughout the game and looking at the beautiful scenery that was present everywhere in the game. This game has some of the best graphics I have seen in games.
CONTROLS:
The controls are fluid and handle quite well. They don't feel clunky or jagged at all and the controls are very easy to learn.
STABILITY:
The game while it may seem to slow down when saving a checkpoint will run smoothly after a couple seconds and runs very well for a game with such great graphics and no loading screens.
OVERALL (TL;DR):
This game is a gem in which is a great experience. The story is amazing and memorable while asking big philosophical questions. The gameplay is engaging and will keep you captivated in the well-designed environments. Some of the best graphics I have personally seen ever can be found in this game as it is definitely on par with today's standards. The controls are fluid and handle very well; they are quite easy to learn. The stability in this game is overall great and well optimized for a game with amazing graphics and no loading screens. A must-buy personally.

1 word to rule them; Disappointment.
4/10 overall.
Storyline.
I felt as if the people who made this game did put in work for things other than the artwork.
Like the overexplained or verbose introduction.  I appreciate the effort for the storyline, but spending so much time on narration is very distracting and detracts from the experience. There were also a lot of lapses where I either could not pay attention to the story (it actually did get that boring) or there were some things omitted from it.
There was definitely one there, but it was too long.
Female characters. Girls with boobs.
At character creation, I noticed how the four classes given do not have the option of changing gender roles. An odd approach, nothing to really yell for, but it surely has its weaknesses.
They lacked variety. You have the mysterious D-cup, the happy short big-chested girl, the silent one with big boobs... No kinda of variety in chest size or anything.
The boobs were implemented very well, but in shape and volume. They lacked motion.
The motion is did see, during the first cinematic for the Striker class, was slightly interesting at first, but became insanely repetitive. The really flirty motions weren't too bad, but they looped every half minute or so, so then focusing on the dialog becomes boring.
Also the shading of the chest in the character selection screen. Why are their breasts so dark when the light is coming from a high angle? They're not even wearing anything to cover them...
I don't know. Study one of the VAs you guys got to work on the game. I'm sure a high payraise would do the trick.
Combat.
This one's a pretty troublesome part. I got my hopes up for some great 3-Dimensional combo chaining from the tutorial-- that little box of colorful icons looked pretty damn amazing. The stamina part felt pretty well implemented, the controls felt fairly intuitive, it's almost like the developers were real connoisseurs for MMOs and RPGs. And then I went into my first dungeon.
Some pretty bad ♥♥♥♥ing went on in there. Maybe starting the first dungeon on Hard was not the best descision if I weren't experienced at MMOs, but it was completely ok. This pretty broken combo chaining got me through the entire dungeon easy: Clicking my left mouse button. Amazing huh? In terms of raw damage output, it might not have been the strongest, but with the fact that it costs absolutely zero, you heard it, zero stamina, this combo broke the damn game.
But hey, combos are pretty damn hard to code. Not like the ♥♥♥♥ing ranged hitboxes. Literally the only threat for me was the ranged attackers. That tiny♥♥♥♥♥fireball maintained the hitbox of an actual character. Hmm... Sounds like reused code for hostile entities. It really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off so I tried starting as the Mage. Literally broken.
(Also it gets annoying that EVERY. SINGLE. ATTACK. has some knockback except on bosses. That's why M1 works.)
Look into the code some more. Add some tweaks that might make the game challenging.
Art overall.
I mean, I talked about the girls before, but not the rest of the game.
The art style used here is certainly amazing, but attention is drawn away to it by some other parts of the game.
Animation.
From what I watched of the introductory cinematics, someone either didn't know how to animate smoothly and realistically or just got lazy with Ctrl-V. There was literally an image of some demon slowly panning into a screen of an ungodly color. Talk about top-notch animation. So many ways today to do it a lot more smoothly.
Also bringing up my point from the previous animations of the female characters. They lacked any situational animations. The least you could do is make them have a different loop while talking from when they just stand there looking nice.
Controls.
Like combat, I got my hopes up for this too.
It was cool, using Alt to change from mouse controls to non-mouse controls, something I first saw in Smite.
The ideas were indeed there, but the execution failed pitifully.
The default binds are so annoying. I spent a bunch of time reconfiguring the combat binds only to find out that I overwrote some of my Inventory and Skill shortcuts. Not to mention that the Skill keybind has the same ♥♥♥♥ing bind as some of the combat ones. It's bad for people who care what they do ingame.
This post is too long. ♥♥♥♥ me.

The campaign is short, really really short. Beat most of it in 4 hours on sniper elite difficulty. Got tired of slowly slogging through everything and turned it down to easy mode so I could hurry up and beat it. 5-6 hours of gameplay for a 20$ asking price? No thanks.
On sniper elite difficulty stealth is almost impossible unless you enjoy crouching the entire time through every level at the pace of molassas. The enemies detect you through everything and then aimbot strait to your head. Enemy snipers are irritating as hell since they instantly see and fire at you and have just about 100% accuracy. If you get hit by a sniper you have to wait 15 seconds or so for your health to regen so you can peak out, get hit, and try to get a shot at them again.
The game actually became fun once I put it on easy peasy mode and rambo'd across everything. Which would be great but then the game would probably last you 3 hours or less.
No matter what difficulty you play it on there isn't enough here to justify the price. Wait for a sale, and then maybe buy it.

=== TL;DR section ==========================
Scientific imagination and creativity: 10/10
Writing: 9.5/10
Story: 9/10
Graphics 7/10
Overall: 9.5/10
*** best scientific exploration game ***
*** best extra-terrestrial gardening simulation ***
Bottom line: Go get it, and play it.
==========================================
A very good and immersive game based on a very creative ecosystem and xeno-lifeforms, who makes for an absorbing exploration of this alien environment. This is pure sci-fi, with a very good story, well-written and well exposed. You play a scientist and explorer who explores a martian cave with an emphasis on research and scientific facts gathering. After some time, you start to understand how the pseudo-animals and pseudo-plants are working together and you can plant a "seed" here, remove a "plant" there, feed "animals" here, change the type of terrain here to plant another kind of "seed"... and eventually, you get the desired result to continue your progression. Hazards are not so dangerous, and there is no fighting at all (just the avoiding of some lifeforms that may harm you in some places/phases). Your job is just to understand what's happening and what's in front of you, and how it all works together, so you can use it and make progress in the caves.
Admittedly this is a game made for tablets and phones, as a few negative comments are pointing out ; but these people stopped too soon in the game (considering their time recorded in the game). Actually, there is lots of meat to this game, lots of things to discover and understand, lots of different lifeforms -most of them interact with each other- and lots of places to explore. If you like the game you're going to spend at least 12 hours there (this is the time needed for completing the game a first time and get one of the endings). The last remnants of the old martian lifeforms are dwelling in this cave, you're going to explore it, and eventually discover the secrets of Mars. The art is good, I love the style. The graphics are more than adequate (even if that's a mobile port). The music is very good. This is very atmospheric and the game made me completely lost track of time several time.
There is almost no platform gaming in this game. Flying around with a jetpack is fun (you'll be occasionally walking and/or crawling too). But this is never really difficult and the rest is pure exploration, observation of the ecosystem and use of its natural behavior to help your own goals and progress.

I've put in 34 hours at the time of writing this review and I feel like I have gotten an adequate view of the experience so far. So, drawing to the close of 2015 and with the promise of more content coming from the ingame admins every day, I write down my thoughts in an attempt not to sway you, the reader, into playing and/or supporting this game but to give you what I think is a fair assessment of the game so far.
TL;DR in case you don't feel like reading a lot: This game IS worth trying out, since it's free, just to see if it's your cup of tea or not. There is definitely quality work put into it which makes it appeal to some, but to others it may be a let down. It isn't game that one can simply say: "If you like X you will like Survarium." It's a game one needs to try out for a few hours to see if it's what you like in a Pvp-centric FPS.
The basics of the game are as follows:
You start out picking a faction. The faction you choose can be changed at any time, and of course it is possible to gain full reputation with all of them. There's even an achievement for doing so!
The faction you choose is only really important for the type of gear you wish to rush. Some factions have heavier armor and let you stock more explosives; some factions have lighter armor and allow you to carry more medicines. There is a faction that appears to focus on sniping and one that exclusively helps you deal with anomalies that appear during matches. As you gain reputation, you unlock higher level gear, which determines the bracket you are placed in during matches.
In addition to the gear level of your loadout, your character also levels in an independent "character" level. Levels your character earns give you points which you can use to unlock perks, such as better chambering speed, greater defense against becoming wounded when shot, and even the ability to carry a primary weapon in place of your sidearm.
So you choose your faction and you get thrown into a match with a bunch of other people in starting gear, just to get the hang of things. After that match, you are going to be paired with people in a similar gear level bracket as you.
Your gear all has a set level once you buy it, and the highest level gear piece you have on determines the entire level of that loadout - it's not averaged out between pieces, allowing you to mix and match gear that you like without sacrificing a gear level for it. Weapons and armor can be upgraded a totally of 3 times. Each upgrade gives you a somewhat moderate bonus to things like reload time, movement speed, resistance to bleeding and aoe damage, etc. These bonuses can be rerolled at any time for a potential upgrade, but each gear piece can only have one reroll performed once a day without paying gold. So yes, paying players can spend however much money the want in order to get the perfect little bonuses to their gear - but these bonuses only provide a small benefit at best and are not at all gamebreaking enough for it to be a pay to win feature.
As of right now, for example, my gear level is 4 and I get paired with people anywhere from level 1 gear to level 6 gear. Now, some people may see this and think "Wow. That seems really fair, while also providing a challenge." Hold on - here's where my first (and pretty much my only major) issue with the game comes in.
Yes, it is totally possible to "smurf" matches, meaning that you are a high level player (high character level) wearing low level gear. This obviously gives you, the higher leveled player, an advantage over people who have not played enough to unlock the perks you have. Is this necessarily a bad thing? It can be. Generally speaking, in my experience, it does not make a big enough difference to completely destroy the game's balance... however there are some builds with overpowered speed or defensive capabilities that, when played correctly, wipe the floor with people inexperienced in the game. So, take that as you will - yes, there is a potential for people to smurf matches and annhilate the majority of their opponents, HOWEVER I have personally not had any issue with it in my time playing.
The only other issue I think is worth pointing out is that, while there is spawn protection, it wears off almost immediately after you leave whatever building you spawn in. Spawn camping is VERY real and, if you aren't on guard all the time, savvy players may keep your team pinned down with constant spawn killing. Just make sure you're always staying frosty and keeping in mind that there may be someone lurking just outside your spawn waiting to shoot you in the back definitely keeps it from being too much of an issue. I've done my fair share of spawn killing, and been spawn killed plenty. I don't see it as a huge issue, but some people may, so bear that in mind if you decide to play this game.
Anyway. the game consists currently of waiting in a queue to join a match, then playing the match, receiving rewards and leaving the match... rinse, repeat. There are differnet game types to keep things interesting: a straight up TDM, a capture the objective mode, and a sort-of-capture-the-flag where your team must bring batteries back to your base while keeping them from being taken by the enemy team. Apparently there's a free-for-all mode as well, but I have yet to get into one of those lobbies for some reason.
The maps are all very well balanced - open while not being too large, vertical variety as well as horizontal, lots of cover in strategic places, many ways to get to anywhere you would need to go, and no overpowered sniper positions!
That's essentially it. Player progression, gear progression, and killin' people. Pretty standard fare for a PVP lobby-based FPS.
There is an somewhat fresh concept that makes matches interesting, which I touched on earlier: Anomalies. Essentially, anomalies are floating aoe gas-orbs that damage players that don't have resistance to them. They spawn in static places on every map, adding a touch of strategy to matches that I find sometimes refreshing, and sometimes annoying. There are, of course, different ways to gain resistance to anomalies - through gear, medicines, or character level perks. Collecting anomalies gives the player different buffs, which can be extremely helpful in the right situations, but don't do anything so gamebreaking as to make the player invulnerable (at least not that I've encountered so far). As far as I can tell, you lose the artifact you collect from the anomaly upon death and must collect another one if you want the buff again.
Now I think it's important to lay out where I have managed to get as far as progress goes with 30 hours ingame. Note that I have not spent a penny on the game as of right now to get where I'm at. I will touch on what many people consider the "pay to win" aspects of the game at the end of the review. As of right now, my character has no premium status and no premium weapons or armor.
Currently I have tier 4 unlocked in two trees and tier 6 in one. This means I can potentially wear tier 6 gear or use a tier 6 weapon, and have my gear level be 6. However I choose to stay with my tier 4 shotgun, AKM, and autopistol because they feel SO good compared to the higher tier weapons of the same type. My armor is a mix of anywhere from tier 1 through 4 items, all upgraded fully with decent bonuses that I didn't really have to roll too many times to get where I wanted. I have a little over 200k silver, which is the currency used to reroll upgrades and buy new gear, as well as about 1k spare parts, which are used to upgrade gear to its highest bonus tier. So far I haven't really had to "grind" for any currency... just played the game and earned it as I went. As far as the premium gear goes that everyone seems to think is pay2win... they have the same stats as other gear of the same level and the only real difference is their looks and a bonus to silver earned... nothing OP at all.

Waking Mars is an exploration platformer where your primary direct game mechanics are picking up and throwing seeds.  Really.  And it is quite good.
Basically, life has been discovered on Mars.  You are one of the astronauts who has been sent to explore said life on Mars.  You make first contact with them and discover that they are these plant-like lifeforms, that produce seeds, which you can use to plant more of them.  There are also, conveniently, barriers that open when you have enough of them growing.
That last bit might seem like a convenient gameplay mechanic, but it actually ties into the story.  Yes, a surprisingly intriguing story follows from all this.  The whole game took me about 11 hours to complete, and I can vouch that the story is interesting.
The game is an exploration-heavy metroidvania, consisting of interconnected areas to explore and grow things in.  There is a certain depth of strategy to how to grow things, since different things have different biomass values, and you need to exceed a certain biomass value to proceed, or to unlock other features.  Also, you can pick up some seeds, but not others, and not all terrain is suited for planting all things.  And then there are more complex mysteries that lie deeper within...
Your exploration is punctuated by your contact with your fellow crew members -- one person back at base, and one AI who is a little annoying (and the other characters lampshade this).  These characters are okay -- if anything, their voice acting is better than their actual scripts, which are a little redundant.  That said, the characters are (needless to say) part of the plot.  And there are even multiple endings.
In fact, you could actually make this game more like a silent-protagonist Metroid-like game with a strong element of the player learning game mechanics without being told -- I mean, heck, that's basically what happens anyway, except for the "I wonder how you might be able to do such-and-such" that the characters sometimes say.  I strongly recommend this if this game ever gets remade.
Aside from the somewhat chatty NPCs and the occasionally irritating physics (the player-character insists on taking a moment to get his footing very often), this is an excellent game, so I definitely recommend it.
(Disclosure: I acquired this game as part of the Humble Bundle with Android 6.)

I would not recommend buying this game.
In comparison to the first game, the developers have added nothing noteworthy that is new or even slightly different. The combat, skills and even level design is pretty much just more of the same. It would have been nice if (like most hack and slash sequels) they had added one or two new skills to unleash on unsuspecting storm troopers but sadly, even the kill moves (on larger enemies) are pretty much the same as the first game.
The story is passable, but is not written half as well as the first game. (potential spoilers!) The real big dissapointment is that the ending really does not lead into the first movie (episode 4 A New Hope) at all as it does not explain what happens to Starkiller, General Kota, Juno, Proxy or even Darth Vader. There is a very small (even miniscule) implication that Boba Fett reclaims vader, but it is so vague it is unreal.
Secondly, the game itself is tiny. I have completed the game in a matter of hours, even having to replay 3 of the levels twice due to constant crashing and movie skipping (more on that in a moment). If you take into account the level replays and deduct them from my play time, I would say that this game lasted no more than 3-4 hours tops. In comparison to the first game that took approx 9 hours. What is even more annoying is that several of the levels are based in the same areas of previous levels and so the scenery only really has 3 or 4 notable changes. Ultimately it made the content that is there to play feel very lacking too. The gameplay in general is largely generic too and there were several times wher I forgot I could even upgrade my force powers because in honesty, the "upgrades" didn't really feel like they upgraded anything at all. Aside from the colour of my lightening changing from blue to purple, the force moves seemed to be as potent at the end of the game (post upgrade) as they did at the start. In other words, they barely changed.
Finally, the games stability is terrible. Now I played this on Windows 10 Professional, and to begin with I had no issues at all. About 1-2 hours into the game though, I would suddenly get a black screen where nothing happens. I could bring up the in game menu and even go back to the start menu, but the game itself would grind to a halt. If I tried to reload the level, the level would play with no sound. The only way I could fix this was to exit the game completely and restart it, replaying the level from the very beginning (cut scenes and all). This easily added 2 hours (possibly more) onto my overall play time and was extremely frustrating.
Another frutrating thing for me was the camera on the jumping levels. Essentially these levels turn the game into a 3d donkey kongue esque platformer where you have to climb to the top, and more often than not I would find my character missing a ledge by a nat's whisker, either pushed off by an invisible air wall or simply jumping in a different direction to where the camera was facing. Again, multiple deaths here added to the games pathetically short play time and didn't add challenge, just frustration.
I would say if you absolutely need to see what this game has to offer, then buy it on a console., This PC port is buggy as hell and really is not worth the money they want for it. The story is nonsensical and does absolutely nothing for bridging the first game to the original Star Wars Trilogy and so it is easy to just pass this game by and forget it ever existed.
I would say, save your money and replay the first Force Unleashed. It is much better than this one.

Phase two: Who flinches first? it all boils down to who messes up faster
