I bought this game because I liked photography. While I can't say for sure why it was named 35MM, 35mm is popular focal length especially for street photographers. The film camera in game seems to have a 35mm focal length lens, as evident by how wide the pictures are.
Lots of things the game doesn't tell you how to do, such as you're hungry when your screen flashes and that hunger and health is pretty much the same (Because you can use food or a FAK). Also doesn't tell you why your screen flashes and I had to find out by searching.
Quite difficulty without walkthrough, lots of places have objectives that are not very obvious. Maybe this can take your time.
Has trading cards if you like that, and also has achievements which don't seem too hard.
Lots of work has been put into giving a very cinematic feel. It's kind of like Life Is Strange's kind of cutscenes. Lots of selective focus and flare. Graphics otherwise seem good but may look less pleasing up close.
Performance friendly-ish, I did crash a few times and I didn't turn SSAO and motion blur on, but that's about it.
Pretty good story. Not very much re-playability I suppose.
Now, because I like photography, let's review the camera!
Can't use viewfinder.
When you take a picture you cannot preview the composition, your field of view is tighter than the 35mm lens.
No manual focus or even aperture control.
Seemingly 1/infinity shutter speed, but probably because I have motion blur off.
ISO 100 apparently but it's ok, the in-game HDR feature in the options menu makes the picture look very nice anyway.
Not so strong flare resistance, in fact in some shots it's more flare-ish than player view.
When hungry/injured, your pictures get the screen effect too (What the hell?).
And probably the worst issue; THE SHUTTER LAG IS INSANE! The player takes like a second to move his finger to press the shutter release.
Despite being a film camera it has seemingly infinite film though so that's nice.
Edit: Also seems to be f/8 or something, very wide depth of field.
Overall not a very photographer's game as I expected but it's a nice game after all.

This game encapsulates PEREFECTLY how you make sequels: not a mere repetition with new weapons and characters with better graphics, but rather being better in every way than their predecessors. Without spoiling anything, this game takes Amnesia: A Dark Descent's horror formula and style to a new level. Horror that doesn't rely on jump scares, but rather constant discomfort wherever you go, and an horrific terror that follows you whenver you so much as know the monster is nearby.
Not to mention SOMA is truly a worthy descendent of Amnesia in many other ways. The graphics look great, and are well-used with the art style and level design. Voice acting is far more diverse and improved compared to Amnesia. The story is much more in-depth and developed than Amnesia, and the gameplay is certainly far improved.
If you liked Amneisa, you will love SOMA, and if you loved Amnesia, then SOMA will be heaven for you.

I've put in 34 hours at the time of writing this review and I feel like I have gotten an adequate view of the experience so far. So, drawing to the close of 2015 and with the promise of more content coming from the ingame admins every day, I write down my thoughts in an attempt not to sway you, the reader, into playing and/or supporting this game but to give you what I think is a fair assessment of the game so far.
TL;DR in case you don't feel like reading a lot: This game IS worth trying out, since it's free, just to see if it's your cup of tea or not. There is definitely quality work put into it which makes it appeal to some, but to others it may be a let down. It isn't game that one can simply say: "If you like X you will like Survarium." It's a game one needs to try out for a few hours to see if it's what you like in a Pvp-centric FPS.
The basics of the game are as follows:
You start out picking a faction. The faction you choose can be changed at any time, and of course it is possible to gain full reputation with all of them. There's even an achievement for doing so!
The faction you choose is only really important for the type of gear you wish to rush. Some factions have heavier armor and let you stock more explosives; some factions have lighter armor and allow you to carry more medicines. There is a faction that appears to focus on sniping and one that exclusively helps you deal with anomalies that appear during matches. As you gain reputation, you unlock higher level gear, which determines the bracket you are placed in during matches.
In addition to the gear level of your loadout, your character also levels in an independent "character" level. Levels your character earns give you points which you can use to unlock perks, such as better chambering speed, greater defense against becoming wounded when shot, and even the ability to carry a primary weapon in place of your sidearm.
So you choose your faction and you get thrown into a match with a bunch of other people in starting gear, just to get the hang of things. After that match, you are going to be paired with people in a similar gear level bracket as you.
Your gear all has a set level once you buy it, and the highest level gear piece you have on determines the entire level of that loadout - it's not averaged out between pieces, allowing you to mix and match gear that you like without sacrificing a gear level for it. Weapons and armor can be upgraded a totally of 3 times. Each upgrade gives you a somewhat moderate bonus to things like reload time, movement speed, resistance to bleeding and aoe damage, etc. These bonuses can be rerolled at any time for a potential upgrade, but each gear piece can only have one reroll performed once a day without paying gold. So yes, paying players can spend however much money the want in order to get the perfect little bonuses to their gear - but these bonuses only provide a small benefit at best and are not at all gamebreaking enough for it to be a pay to win feature.
As of right now, for example, my gear level is 4 and I get paired with people anywhere from level 1 gear to level 6 gear. Now, some people may see this and think "Wow. That seems really fair, while also providing a challenge." Hold on - here's where my first (and pretty much my only major) issue with the game comes in.
Yes, it is totally possible to "smurf" matches, meaning that you are a high level player (high character level) wearing low level gear. This obviously gives you, the higher leveled player, an advantage over people who have not played enough to unlock the perks you have. Is this necessarily a bad thing? It can be. Generally speaking, in my experience, it does not make a big enough difference to completely destroy the game's balance... however there are some builds with overpowered speed or defensive capabilities that, when played correctly, wipe the floor with people inexperienced in the game. So, take that as you will - yes, there is a potential for people to smurf matches and annhilate the majority of their opponents, HOWEVER I have personally not had any issue with it in my time playing.
The only other issue I think is worth pointing out is that, while there is spawn protection, it wears off almost immediately after you leave whatever building you spawn in. Spawn camping is VERY real and, if you aren't on guard all the time, savvy players may keep your team pinned down with constant spawn killing. Just make sure you're always staying frosty and keeping in mind that there may be someone lurking just outside your spawn waiting to shoot you in the back definitely keeps it from being too much of an issue. I've done my fair share of spawn killing, and been spawn killed plenty. I don't see it as a huge issue, but some people may, so bear that in mind if you decide to play this game.
Anyway. the game consists currently of waiting in a queue to join a match, then playing the match, receiving rewards and leaving the match... rinse, repeat. There are differnet game types to keep things interesting: a straight up TDM, a capture the objective mode, and a sort-of-capture-the-flag where your team must bring batteries back to your base while keeping them from being taken by the enemy team. Apparently there's a free-for-all mode as well, but I have yet to get into one of those lobbies for some reason.
The maps are all very well balanced - open while not being too large, vertical variety as well as horizontal, lots of cover in strategic places, many ways to get to anywhere you would need to go, and no overpowered sniper positions!
That's essentially it. Player progression, gear progression, and killin' people. Pretty standard fare for a PVP lobby-based FPS.
There is an somewhat fresh concept that makes matches interesting, which I touched on earlier: Anomalies. Essentially, anomalies are floating aoe gas-orbs that damage players that don't have resistance to them. They spawn in static places on every map, adding a touch of strategy to matches that I find sometimes refreshing, and sometimes annoying. There are, of course, different ways to gain resistance to anomalies - through gear, medicines, or character level perks. Collecting anomalies gives the player different buffs, which can be extremely helpful in the right situations, but don't do anything so gamebreaking as to make the player invulnerable (at least not that I've encountered so far). As far as I can tell, you lose the artifact you collect from the anomaly upon death and must collect another one if you want the buff again.
Now I think it's important to lay out where I have managed to get as far as progress goes with 30 hours ingame. Note that I have not spent a penny on the game as of right now to get where I'm at. I will touch on what many people consider the "pay to win" aspects of the game at the end of the review. As of right now, my character has no premium status and no premium weapons or armor.
Currently I have tier 4 unlocked in two trees and tier 6 in one. This means I can potentially wear tier 6 gear or use a tier 6 weapon, and have my gear level be 6. However I choose to stay with my tier 4 shotgun, AKM, and autopistol because they feel SO good compared to the higher tier weapons of the same type. My armor is a mix of anywhere from tier 1 through 4 items, all upgraded fully with decent bonuses that I didn't really have to roll too many times to get where I wanted. I have a little over 200k silver, which is the currency used to reroll upgrades and buy new gear, as well as about 1k spare parts, which are used to upgrade gear to its highest bonus tier. So far I haven't really had to "grind" for any currency... just played the game and earned it as I went. As far as the premium gear goes that everyone seems to think is pay2win... they have the same stats as other gear of the same level and the only real difference is their looks and a bonus to silver earned... nothing OP at all.

A classic point-and-click adventure game revisited. Broken sword was, I think, the first game of its kind I ever played.
It's been a long while since I played the original game, but it is obvious that they added in quite a bit with this version. I think there are some new areas and gameplay that wasn't there before, to flesh out the story a bit. They added character portraits and a few scenes. They also modified the user interface.
The game has a good story, and plenty of locations and puzzles to solve. Mostly, the obstacles are easily overcome, but I actually had to use the hint system a couple of times and even a walkthrough to get past some points. There were a few oddities too, but no serious show-stoppers. Some of the improvements are so-so, but all in all, a good experience. I clocked in about 10 hours of play time, exploring most of the dialogs.
If you're into adventure games, or remember playing the original, I have no trouble recommending it, but the original game is probably just as good.

Never Alone além de jogo é um documentário.
Se passa no Alasca e retrata as características culturais dos habitantes do local (antigamente), lendas e acontecimentos climáticos. O jogo é bem fofo e bonito, e à medida que você vai passando pelas "corujinhas" presentes nas fases, você vai desbloqueando um fato cultural sobre aquela fase ou sobre os elementos da mesma, que é um vídeo que você pode assistir naquele momento ou posteriormente através do menu do jogo. O jogo é curtíssimo (você terá no máximo 5h para zerar e para assistir todos os vídeos-documentário presentes).

A história em si não é ruim, só que talvez ela não tenha sido muito bem representada no jogo, o que peca um pouco. Apresenta alguns bugs que não atrapalham tua jogatina mas que perde ponto do mesmo jeito. Controles fáceis, trilha sonora não tão presente porém gostosa, cada elemento, personagem e ação têm seu som característico e fiel.
Eu gostei do jogo mas eu recomendo mais pelos vídeos desbloqueáveis do que o jogo em si. A parte documentário torna mais interessante e reconhece um povo que muitas vezes não ouvimos falar o suficiente mesmo sendo Estadunidense e que possuem amor e orgulho da cultura de onde vêm. As conquistas são fáceis (não sei pela DLC mas deve ser também) e tem a ver somente com o decorrer da história. Não se esqueça de encontrar todas as corujas para ter a oportunidade de ver todos os vídeos.

DOCO: Never Alone isn't just "small girl and her fluffy friend go on an endearing adventure". It's also a documentary short film about traditional Iñupiat culture. Iñupiat folklore has some beautiful (and perhaps wise) concepts concerning harmony with nature, and while, like me, you may not find all the film clips interesting, some definitely are. I enjoyed the anecdotal segments especially. Also, the mythological segments (although I
intended to skip them) do add meaning to the games highly fantastical story.
FEELS: I was surprised how quickly and deeply I engaged with the characters. I think cuteness lead to empathy and empathy lead to tension. Some utterances potentially overheard by my neighbours included "NO....... NO..............", "WHAT THE ACTUAL ♥♥♥♥", and "CLIMB LITTLE FOX, CLIMB!". The swift, brutal deaths, magnified by your companions heartbreaking reaction, are a little disturbing and slightly guilt inducing, for me evoking slight semblance to
, except more family friendly.
GAMEPLAY/PUZZLES: Speaking of LIMBO, Never Alone is
more puzzle-platformer than I was expecting; and I found the specific puzzle design more frustrating than engaging, particularly in the second half as the platforming puzzles became increasingly time limited. I died and retried a lot at some points, often left asking "but where am I supposed to
?". From a design perspective, I like puzzles, and I like intense chase scenes, but I dislike when the two are combined and I'm not given sufficient direction or time to ponder an obstacle. I suspect I could have benefited a lot from the local co-op mode, had I had a foxy friend free for furry frolicing.
Edit: After playing
, the gameplay and controls in Never Alone could only be seen as "average"; not terrible but not mind blowing either. They are tertiary to the games cuteness and mythology, and would not be satisfactory if it were any longer.
PRICE: Another potential neg is $15 USD may be a little high for a 3 hour game, according to Steamland precedent. I personally picked it up on sale and feel I paid an appropriate sum o' dosh.
Above caveats notwithstanding, I'm recommending this because I feel it's one of those
well executed, short & sweet little indies which don't come along too often.

Never Alone is a fairly short (a few hours the most) and small puzzle platformer game that combines an old Alaskan Inuit folktale, puzzle platformer and short documentary in one. By progressing in the game and puzzles one can unlock short (app. 2 min) pieces of documentary, called "Cultural Insight", that explain a little about Inuit life, the people, and the story you are in, following a small girl that decides to investigate the cause of the blizzard that's afflicting her village. On her journey she meets a snow fox she befriends.
Most of the puzzles are fairly straight forward and not too difficult, with an occassional exception maybe. I've played it entirely single player mode on keyboard and mouse, which can be a little tricky sometimes, having to switch between Nuna and the fox, but the controls work fine. There's no combat involved in this game.
You'll be prompted about the Cultural Insights every time you unlock them or when you are on a loading screen, which may be intrusive to gameplay to someone who wants to focus on the game, but I didn't find it all too annoying and interesting to watch. You can watch them at any time (again).
The value of the game in regard to the price may depend on how much value you take out of the story, the documentary and gameplay really.

Horror that doesn't rely on jump scares, but rather constant discomfort wherever you go, and an horrific terror that follows you whenver you so much as know the monster is nearby.
Not to mention SOMA is truly a worthy descendent of Amnesia in many other ways. The graphics look great, and are well-used with the art style and level design. Voice acting is far more diverse and improved compared to Amnesia. The story is much more in-depth and developed than Amnesia, and the gameplay is certainly far improved.
If you liked Amneisa, you will love SOMA, and if you loved Amnesia, then SOMA will be heaven for you.

Dead Noir The Heart is a basic investigation game that left me underwhelmed.
You can find a about 15 minutes of gameplay with commentary here:

Theres not much to be said about this game, mainly due to there not being much to do in it.
You play Jackson Corpse, a retired cop who now does freelance investigations for the police. Your asked to investigate a crime scene, that ends up being a chain of crime scenes.
The investigation part of the game is simplistic, you walk around the room until you get near enough to something of interest then a prompt to investigate comes up. This is repeated multiple times per crime scene until you have found them all. Once all clue are found you can then use "detective vision" to see the flow of what happened.
While the premise is interesting, and I liked how the description of information found is tied into the scene, the implementation is simplistic. Its not hard to find the clues, with most found in a few minutes and I almost felt I could have just watched the game do it for me and got the same experience. That's a shame as I can see what the developer was going for, but it just doesn't hit the mark.
As stated, the game is controller only, but I don't see why there isn't mouse and keyboard support as there is no advantage to using a controller.
The graphics are simple, and I found that sometimes the items are clipping into each other. This is especially obvious with the woman that you speak too, who was always looking in the wrong direction and seemed to be part of the chair she was sitting on. The background music was fine, but the game had no way to turn it down or off if that was your preference.
For me, the game didn't hit the mark. I don't regret buying it, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone I know.

This game offers truly expansive maps with amazing graphics. However, the game is lacking common sense features at the current time which make it incredibly frustrating to play. While I'll still piddle around with it at current development, it wasn't what I was expecting out of a game that was thoughht to be fully released this year, according to the description. I would not reccomend it, and it wasn't worth the $20.
Before a short listing of pros and cons, I'll give you a run down of how your gaming experience will go (for progression mode):
- spawn in a random spot on the map.
- look around to see how large the area is, and have no idea where you are.
- after a few minutes of prodding, you'll realize you have no minimap of any sort, not even coordinates to use with player made maps or guides, and you'll be mad as hell
- start sprinting in one direction, barly make it anywhere before your dino is exausted and either has to rest or trot (which gets you nowhere)
- do this several times over
- staart to realize how expansive the map is, especially in comparison to your nearly micrroscopic starter dino and get REALLY angry that you have no minimap of any kind
- realize that you're going to either starve or thirst to death before you ever find food/water
- keep trying to find food/water
- listen to your dino start screaming occasionally because it's slowly dying
- starve/thirst to death not long after
So you decide "I'LL NOT BE DETERRED! I WILL PROGRESS!" So you start a new session. And again. And again, and again, and again, again again again again again again. You'll probably never progress beyond tier 2 (ps, when you progress it just dumps you in a new location and resets thirst/hunger so you get to aimlessly wander and starve to death all over again :) ). Along with the above experience, you might also get to:
- break a leg for seemingly no friggin reason and have to sit around for several minutes while it heals.
- once in a blue moon, you'll find a lake before you starve. Food will be plentiful! There are dinos around doing stuff to entertain you! You go down to get a drink of water, and even though there is a giant trike or rex carcass some 20 ft away, someone WILL come over and kill you for no reason, leaving your corpse laying around. They won't even eat you
In conclusion, kudos to anyone who gets past tier 2.  Sandbox is some good fun though.

The video preview that is on steam for The Isle doesn't do it justice. It is extremely outdated. To get a better idea of what the current state of the game is like, it is worth looking it up on Youtube.
I've have hundreds of hours of fun with my friends on The Isle. Met a lot of new gaming friends on here as well. It is early access, so yes, you don't have the finished product yet, but the developers are constantly working on the game, coming out with new updates and patches regularly.
One thing I really like about this game is the sense of immersion. I can literally get lost for hours in this game with the ambience of it all. You can really start to feel like you are there, feel like what it may have been like to live as the dinosaur you are playing. Sometimes there are moments of peace and tranquility, and other times I have felt like my heart was going to lurch out of my throat as I realize I am being hunted or stalked. There are a lot of interesting dynamics to the game, one of my favorites being that you can nest other players as your own babies. It adds a lot fo dynamic to a natural survival game when you have small things that need looking after... even better that the babies are actually other players to interact with. The animations and sounds are spot on. I also love that the dinosaurs have different ways to communicate, so even if you are playing with someone who doesn't speak the same language as you, or isn't in your discord, you can still communicate basic things to them, such as alerting them to danger, or communicating friendly or aggressive intentions.
I can't tell you how many dreams I have had about The Isle because it can get so immersive. I've had dreams of being stalked by carnotaurs in forests, and I completely blame this game for it!
Right now the game is very survival/openworld/sandboxy. If you like these features in games, you will probably like this.  There are a lot of major changes coming up in this game, so even if you choose not to buy it, it is worth following to see if it may be your thing in the future. The changes that this game is undergoing are IMMENSE. They are adding entirely new mechanics and play modes. The Developers are pretty open with The Isle gaming community and share their progress and ideas. One thing that I respect about the Devs is that even though I find the game fun, they are always wanting it to be better, and actively working on it constantly. You can tell when you have good developers when they do not become complacent.  I just can't wait to see what this game will become!

Games like this have achievements for profile personalisation reasons - people are buying them to be able to earn all the cheevos and be able to customise their profile. I support this - in the past, doing so would require obtaining cards, emoticons, backgrounds etc etc.

Don't get the starter edition - they give you 2 offensive and 2 defensive Operators out of the box - 2 random and 2 may be purchased with the money that they have afforded you. If you want to unlock another Operator, that will add around 20 hours of grind to your game - 40 if you want to get the DLC Operators. If you just wanted to get all the base game operators then you'll have to grind 320 hours just to unlock all of the base game Operators. Unlocking all DLC operators will take around 560 hours to grind.
Even if you get the Operators, you won't be able to customize your weapons at all - at least not without grinding for the same, if not more so for your options. Grinding for a single skin can add another 20 hours, adding a pin can add 30. If you get the Starter pack, you're going to be playing a lot of the same Operators and be all but completely incapable of getting camos and skins - things that are common if not expected for most games - most games that aren't strictly limited to multiplayer.
If you GET the starter pack, getting all of the Operators will run you back 880 hours of grind. No camo, no skins, no gear. Because a skin can be 20 hours grind, and a pin 30, you won’t be able to get these things for many operators at all. On top of this, a helmet will run you another 20 hours, and a Uniform an additional 20. Outfitting a single Operator with 2 camos (one for the side-arm), a pin, a helmet, and a Uniform will add 110 hours of grind to your game - 130 if you have to unlock them first. If you want to unlock and customize one Offensive and one Defensive Operator, it will take you 260 hours worth of matches. And no - even if you do amazing, you won’t get any more or less renown from performance: Losing will always net you around 100 RN while winning can get you around 250 RN - no breakaways for acing the enemy team to get 400 RN on a clutch. If you win every match for 50 matches, you can claim your prize (Operator or Skin) after only 16 hours. However, if you lose every match, it will take you 125 matches and probably longer than 41 hours.
Ubisoft has gone to painful lengths to mitigate fast-grinding, completely mutilating solo-play RN gain to abysmal levels to keep people from achieving their goals slightly faster. God Forbid they get an Operator and a Skin after grinding Solo for 30 hours. Even on their website, Ubisoft recommends to "Purchase Boosters" to get double RN and dip that Custom Operator job from a 130 hour project into a 65 hour project. But these boosters aren't cheap, on level with free-to-play games such as World Of Tanks or Planetside 2. And on top of that, having to grind 130 hours for 2 operators instead of one might be alluring - but you'll have to pay more for the game that you already purchased for the privilege to GRIND faster.
I know what you're thinking: "Why don't you stop being such a cheapskate and just buy the full game - maybe even the season pass for $80 total?" Well that's a great idea! Instead of having to grind 130 hours to customize a new Operator, I can spend 110 hours! I get to pay $80 for the honor of 20 hours of my life back from that potential grind! All you’re getting out of that base game is the Operator, which is fine, but if you want anything more – you’re only scratching off the surface level grinding and unlocking the ocean of grinding beneath. Instead of having to grind 20 hours for Thatcher and then 110 hours for his skins, you get to bypass the initial 20 hours! Granted, this is better for DLC Operators who have an exorbitant 40 hour grind attached to them, but you’re only bypassing unfair design to get at that juicy 110 hour customization grind that you still have to do regardless. No matter what you do you’ll still have to put in that amount of time for customization options. And buying the custom items on their own is no walk in the park either; every item costs about $5. If you want 2 skins, a pin, a helmet, and a Uniform for an operator - you're going to need to cough up about $25. You want to deck out 2 Operators? You need to cough up $50 on top of the $80 you already paid.
I highly recommend you scroll down through the DLC. That will give you a good concept of the price gauging this game has. It's "Fee-to-Pay", you pay money to buy the game so that you may have the honor of paying more money to get what you want.
To put things in perspective from most grinding to most paying, here's the score.
Unlock and Customize every Operator, Starter Edition: 4,180 hours
Unlock and Customize every Operator, Basic + Season Pass: 3,300 hours
Purchase Customization Options, Basic + Season Pass: $830
Purchase Customization Options, Starter Edition: $900
And remember - these are for basic things that have been in games since mid 2000's - typically in games that are NOT LIMITED TO MULTIPLAYER.
It's a real shame, because the game is good. It's highly polished and well designed - a joy to play. But when you look at how much time you're going to have to sink into the game just to make a dent into things, it all becomes moot in the end.
After getting my second operator, Yäger, I wanted to get him a tank pin - I realized that I'd have to grind the game for over 25 hours just to get it - it broke my spirit. How much more will I have to work for and pay for to have the privilege that other games have so freely afforded me.
Don't give Ubisoft your time or money, skip the game. Do something more productive with your life.

Never Alone is a fairly short (a few hours the most) and small puzzle platformer game that combines an old Alaskan Inuit folktale, puzzle platformer and short documentary in one. By progressing in the game and puzzles one can unlock short (app. 2 min) pieces of documentary, called "Cultural Insight", that explain a little about Inuit life, the people, and the story you are in, following a small girl that decides to investigate the cause of the blizzard that's afflicting her village. On her journey she meets a snow fox she befriends.
Most of the puzzles are fairly straight forward and not too difficult, with an occassional exception maybe. I've played it entirely single player mode on keyboard and mouse, which can be a little tricky sometimes, having to switch between Nuna and the fox, but the controls work fine. There's no combat involved in this game.
You'll be prompted about the Cultural Insights every time you unlock them or when you are on a loading screen, which may be intrusive to gameplay to someone who wants to focus on the game, but I didn't find it all too annoying and interesting to watch. You can watch them at any time (again).
The value of the game in regard to the price may depend on how much value you take out of the story, the documentary and gameplay really.

Right off the bat, I want to give a big thank you to Ubisoft for the free weekend, because I now finally had the chance to play Rainbow Six Siege. A game that was met with mixed reviews at launch, rightfully so, since there were so many problems with the game, and unfortunately it turned away a lot of potential players away, like me. Jump forward to 2017 - the game is not only polished now, but the amount of content it has is just amazing! Huge props to the developers for continually adding new stuff to the game, because I strongly believe that R6S is one of the best tactical shooters I have ever played!
With the little time I have spent playing the game, I found myself blown away at how atmospheric both the combat and the strategy aspect of Rainbow Six Siege really are. I mean this is coming from someone who is not the least bit interested in Counter Strike. In fact, R6S only solidifies how much of a mindless and inferior product CS:GO is. The amount of fun I've had so far surpasses any other tactical shooter on the market that I've come across.
Expect to die a lot. This is a pretty realistic game and very much requires you to plan out your attack, or, in others cases, defense against the enemy team. In that sense, it can become quite the competitive game, where each squad is trying to outsmart the other and it becomes this tense and surreal moment when you get pined down, leaving you to adapt and figure out a way to counter back.
The destructible environments are a key aspect of the game since they pretty much allow you to turn the tide of a situation and overcome it. Granted not everything can be destroyed, in fact, it feels archaic by it's design, but it is also understandable since there needs to be some balance in order to have a healthy competition. I have to admit, breaching through a wall with an explosive, followed by a flash bang is so satisfying and is probably the most awesome parts of the game.
Now, I have to address the multiplayer since this is what most people want out of the game. So far it has been a mixed bag, granted this is during a free weekend, I found most players to be competent, but also slightly toxic in their approach. I guess it's unavoidable at this point. There will be people who are more casual and others who will be aggressively competitive. However, if you have friends or manage to find friendly players in-game, make sure you play with them, allowing for a vastly superior experience. I honestly think that is how the game is meant to be played.
One last thing. There is a lot of debate on what version of the game you should purchase. I could write a short book about this topic, but the easy answer lies with you. Are you the type of person to grind for their loot? (in this case we are talking about characters and cosmetics) Or are you the type of person that wants most, if not all, of the loot at once? Whatever version you choose know that you are getting all the content either way.
Overall, I believe Rainbow Six Siege to be one of the better Ubisoft games out there. If you love tactical action, if you love strategy, if you love shooters, if you love having fun with friends then by all means give this game a chance. Thank you!

What is, by me, the best horror game to date, this game strikes terror to ANYONE who played it.
You play as Simon, who got himself in an accident, causing brain damage to him.
After that, he volunteered for a small project.
During him being brain-scanned, Simon wakes up 100 years later on Upsilon (Really bothers me the name isn't Epsilon. Can't pronounce Upsilon.)

The game has the PERFECT! balance between enviroment, game mechanics and phycological horror.
Frictional Games, the creators of Amnesia, thought to themselves:
''Hmm... what if we add monsters and enemies that move as slow as a snail, but when they detect the player, they run faster than the result of a fivesome between a cheetah, Speedy Gonzales, The Flash, Sonic and Usain Bolt, with a rocket strapped on it's back, while it's on cocaine?''
''YES.''
The game's mechanics make it so that everything you do can alert the monster!
Opening/closing doors? Check.
Moving and sprinting? Check.
The sound of your flashlight when it's turned on/off? Why not?
The enviroment is beatiful as hell, can't get my eyes off of it.
But what makes this game is the story. It's like a modern William ShakeSpeare book about horror, traumas, love and drama, really.
Final verdict: 10/10! Nice job, Frictional Games! Keep. It. Up.

Waking Mars is a fun puzzle-like game where you have a lot more freedom and randomization than in most puzzles, and the storyline is pretty nice, too. It's a good way to waste a few days' time. I was surprised to find out there are basically three endings. The fact I apparently finished it before solving one of the major end puzzles gave the game some measure of replayability as I used my previous end save game to complete the bonus puzzle and unlock the two other endings.
In later gameplay, though, one thing really started to bother me, and that was the fact that biodiversity simply didn't work. Instead of a circle of life, you'd have lifeforms destroying each other, taking over each other's growing spot and actually decreasing the total biomass. And since the only real goal, especially in the game's end-phase, is to maximize biomass, you'll generally end up replacing every single plant-lifeform in the whole cave system with the one that gives the most biomass, is harmless to you and the other lifeforms, and on top of that, acts as food production for all of the mobile lifeforms.
As far as I can see, there is no way to make a self-regulating system which involves all of the life in the ecosystem, so yeah, that is a bit of a failure, in my opinion.
This entire rant, however, just shows how engrossed I became in experimenting with the whole concept. Despite this minor annoyance at the end, it's still a very nice game, which I'll probably replay a few times in the future.

I did not have any expectations for this game.  I am aware it's not technically a brand new game.
It is however a FREE Third Person Action MMORPG with a ton of equippable items and a huge emphasis on combination attacks.  The combinations can get pretty intense but it's all spelled out and even has a UI that displays different buttons you can push to continue a combination.  Anyone who is familiar with combination fighting games should have no trouble understanding the mechanics of Divine Souls.  The mechanics themselves are also pleasantly fluid and it's easy to engage in battles to unleash a punishing flurry of attacks.  The special "charge" attacks are devastating.
The RPG element is very big as well and there are seemingly hundreds of missions (a primary story and tons of side-quests).  The voice acting is humorous but it gets the job done (there are text subtitles).  RPG features include crafting, enchanting, upgrades, an auction house and supports both multi-player and single-player battles.  The graphics are not cutting edge but are still smooth and because of this I can run the game in it's supported 1920x1080 resolution with no frame loss.
Overall the game is easy to pick up and start having fun right away. I am level 27 right now.

I'm not really sure what to say here. If you know anything about this game, you know what it's praised for. In any case, I'm going to say it again. It's a simple plataform puzzler with some very interesting level design. Not much to say here, we've been seeing thousands of those. Why does this one set itself apart? Because what it is can't be defined by that alone. As a matter of fact, I would be inclined to say calling it a "game" wouldn't be doing it justice. Yes, it is an indie game, I know. But it's conflicting, for me at least, to label it that. From the perspective of what it tries to accomplish, it is throughoutly "indie": it's short, it's simple, couple-of-minutes fun with one or two gimmicks. But that's not the end result here. It's just the means. You see, Thomas Was Alone isn't trying to be a game. It's trying to tell you a story. The "game" is just the means, just the cherry on top that allows you to grow even more attached to these characters. Yes, characters. While it's not the BEST story I've seen(To The Moon still holds that distinction)... I gotta give it credit. Because I'm caring about squares and rectangles. I'm overcoming my despise for that little orange square called Chris once I learn that he is insecure about his shortcomings, and I'm happy when someone comes around and appreciates him for himself. I'm cheering for James, who thinks he is weird, being a green rectangle who moves unlike everyone else, when in fact his being "weird" is what allows him and Thomas to overcome many obstacles together. Every time I'd put Thomas in a position to aid Chris to reach a ledge, I could feel his cheerful attitude, how he considered Chris a friend despite the latter not caring for him. When Laura would drag herself to aid everyone, it started as a relation born from her "boyfriend", only for her to find in the others true friends who would come back to help her. These shapes ooze more character, more personality and more development than most games I've played recently!
It's a great experience. I have no other way to put it. It is a good game, but it's altogether an amazing experience. If believe games can be art, you owe it to yourself to accompany Thomas while he finds his meaning in the world.

I've played the isle once with a few friends. Although the game concept is good and the over all aesthetic to the game is great (dinosaurs are high quality, maps look beautiful) the community and developer(s) may have goals that are too ambitious for the team size and current computer specs.
Let's start with some Pro's, then Con's.
Fairly frequent updates (what I've seen) the devs do work hard, especially the head dev, I've watched him work and it appears he's busting his A** off to get this game where he wants it.
Good graphics - the game as I said is aesthetically pleasing (if your computer can handle it) and the art style appears to fit itself well.
Game has a ton of potential. I think if these  big (but not horribly difficult to fix) problems are fixed, and the gameplay of the game is finnished I'd happily change this review to a possitive.
Unfortionately, I don't know what else to say.
No real gameplay (atm). You can only be a dinosaur, 60% of the game is roaming because their doesn't appear to be any real objectives or game play, the other 40% is waiting 30 minutes for your broken leg to heal (litterally appart of the game), which makes you walk slower than what'd be considered "bareable" by most gamers, especially on such huge maps. If you break a leg in an area filled with dead dinos (you'll see why this is bad in a later part of this review). Good luck closing your game if you're on a decent / below average gaming rig.
Toxic community. No game or developer is immune to critisism (most devs I've talked to are fine, evidence of that is commented below this review), I find it hard to even write this review because some of my friends practically worship the "game". Large part of the community comes from a game called Primal Carnage, who's server owners will ban you from server's for simple disagreements such as a review like mine.
Game requires high end graphics as a minimum requirement. It could easily allow more playerbase in if optimizations such as despawning dinos after death were put in.
One of the most optimized maps in the game is a community made map. It's heavily critisized and hated for not achieving the extreme ammount of detail everyone in the community dreams about. This simply put, is not realistic. Every game has flaws, because computers have flaws. This map ironically is played on a lot of servers because the other default one's are incredibly difficult to run on the server's end, and the client's end (aka player). Things like render distance, entity spawning and tons of work in optimization need to be put in place. Last I checked, this game was not optimized in almost any way acceptable. If you do get this game, I do recommened playing on said map. It's playable and still very pleasing to the eye (graphically speaking).
Work flow. The work done in the game feels backwards to me, dinosaurs and maps are created, even released without extremely important things like ensuring corpses delete themselves to preventing lag, or adjustable foilage render distances, minimal graphics settings or simple things to do on the maps. Updates worry me because I feel it's just more things that are going to break my game, or freeze my computer.

Picked this up again after a few months off, and all I can say is : Don't buy yet.  Wait for the Scent mechanic to be fully implemented before you buy.
Hardcore dinosaur simulation is one thing. But real animals/dinosaurs have an ability to FIND food if they're 3m away from it - you won't have this luxury. You could walk past food, starving to death, and never know.
The game is gorgeous, gorgeous enough that you'll play it past the refund point before realising that you'd like to do something other than starving slowly to death amid the pretty.  The New Player experience is a penance; enforced hours of playing the ONLY dinosaur who will be as hard and unenjoyable to play as it is. It doesn't teach you anything about the game -  it just teaches you how to starve to daeth.
I like to play herbivore. If anyone tells you that herbivores have an easy time finding food, I suspect they mostly play carnivore. Playing herbivore means walking endlessly - not neccessarily *toward* food - just in the hopes that you will get lucky and find food before you die.  I'd love to die to a carnivore's fangs, or have a spectacular hide/chase, but what actually happens is you starve to daeth slowly, marching endlessly in the knowledge that you have died 4 times already due to not finding any food after spawning.
I once got lucky and made it up to the higher tiers, and can see exactly what the game has to offer. It has many problems at that level, but would still be an enjoyable Early Access experience except...
You will have to start as a tiny dino. You must survive as this tiny dino for at least an an hour before you can progress to a less tiny dino, and work your way up to a medium dino etc. The tiny dino is an excercise in absolute frustration - it would be fun to get chased and eaten, but that's not how you'll die. You die slowly starving to death, being able to see nothing but bushes (because you're so tiny), unable to find food or water no matter how hard you search.  When you die, you'll have to restart, having to survive another agonising hour hoping to get lucky and fall into some food, then water, then more food etc.
Which, again, could be enjoyable - a sort of 'trial by fire' which populates the map with interesting little dinos. Except, if you EVER die again in the game, even if you die after working your way up to a larger dino, you must play an hour of this penance.  A penance that has NOTHING to do with the way the rest of the game plays.

There is no map function. Experienced players will tell you that you need to "learn the map" - which basically means "sink in enough hours that you get lucky enough times that you get to play a dinosaur who can explore the map."
Seriously, the basic tiny dino can't even survive one night without eating TWICE. Which means finding food in the dark TWICE.  There's no map, no tracker, no ability to find it beyond getting lucky and falling into it, there is no skill in this game.

This game pales a little bit if you've been spoiled by things like
or even
, but has its own charm and somewhat languid pace, as there are very few time-sensitive missions. Only one weapon in the entire game is silent, and if you get into hand-to-hand range of an enemy, you're pretty much screwed—sorry, no instant-kill-from-behind mélée sprees.
The graphics are nice, and can be run on ultra settings with a modest machine. I met only one crash that never repeated itself. The close-up bullet-time results of a successful snipe are very gratifying, and can be as precise as you care to make them. (I even fired between the turret and body of a burning tank for a successful headshot. Most other games I've met would have just treated the entire tank as one impervious object and not bothered about the gap between those two parts.)
Enemy behaviors are very realistic
someone spots you: then you might get a frontal assault, or one guy might come after you while everyone else exchanges hiding spots as they "Look for him!" And I pity you when you come up against the Russian troops: I never saw a more random, twitchy enemy in my life, and I'm pretty sure their accuracy with those carbines is WAY higher than your accuracy with the same weapon.
This game doesn't have a healing system, so you don't need to worry about picking up medical kits: it's just a hide-and-recover system, which I like. There are plenty of other buttons to worry about pressing without having to add in some kind of healing mechanism. I didn't find the grenades or tripwires especially useful, but that might have more to do with my play-style than the failure of the development team. I managed to throw a couple of effective grenades, but mostly, if enemies are close enough to you that they're in range of a throw, they're close enough to kill you before the grenade can take care of them. The first documentary released on film was Robert Flahnook's Nanook of the North, an ethnography filmed more than ninety years ago that shows the struggles of an Inuit family in the Canadian Arctic. It is an odd, but pleasant coincidence that the first video game documentary you get to play through revisits this region, telling a short tale that has its roots in the Alaskan Iñupiat people.
Never Alone is, more than anything else, a documentary - not only in its Cultural Insights segments you can find throughout the game by locating the sometimes hidden owls, which are short, filmed clips of Iñupiat people (with care to interview both old and young people) talking about topics ranging from their customs, nature, family and tradition - but in the way the game's own story is told. Adapted from Robert Nasruk Cleveland's retelling of Kunuuksaayuka, Never Alone's story follows a girl named Nuna and her pet arctic fox on their journey to find out the cause of a never-ending blizzard - a journey where they, and you, will meet creatures of Iñupiat myth and lore, and the events will be described to you by a man in Iñupiat language, as if you were hearing an elder tell you a story of his people.
The bridge that connects the player to the proper documentary Never Alone is is the gameplay. You'll traverse multiple levels, each with their own theme but all in the Alaskan permafrost, alternating between Nuna and her fox. Nuna is capable of dragging and pushing things, as well as using a bola you find early in the game to break things and call spirits. The fox can fit in smaller places and climb vertical walls, as well as jump from one wall to another and bring forth any spirits that might be hidden in the levels. These spirits offer help by means of serving as platforms, dangling ropes and climbing creatures that can bring Nuna to places she alone can't reach.
Sadly, said bridge is closer to a makeshift creation rather than a proper, strong one. The game is easy throughout its entirety, but you'll often find yourself being sent to a previous checkpoint because it failed to register you grabbing a spirit's edge or a jump of yours glitched at a ladder's corner. Playing alone I also couldn't help but feel that certain segments were made for co-op play and poorly optimized for the single-player experience: at one point you'll have to evade ghosts who want to use your head for eskimo football, and having to restart a section will happen often, as the character you don't play as will always follow you and will always lag behind. It's a bridge you'll still be able to cross, but most of my failures would be better defined as the game's failures.
The game's graphics work well to flesh out the frozen beauty of northern Alaska, with a detailed foreground that stands against the looming vastness of its varied background, where you'll see from the frozen wastes of the arctic to its starry nights and northern lights. The game's soundtrack is properly downplayed, enhancing the feeling of solitude in frosty Alaska, but what really adds character to the game is the Iñupiat voiceover telling you the story as you play it.
It took me a bit more than six hours to finish the game, and I felt satisfied with what I played. There's little reason to come back if you've already gathered all the cultural insights, though I say that not as a flaw - the game is about conveying a story and introducing you to the Iñupiat's culture, and to tack anything else on for the sake of replayability or length would feel like unnecessary filler, specially because the gameplay doesn't hold itself as a main reason for playing Never Alone.
Never Alone would be better called an interactive documentary than a game. While the gameplay is a weak foundation and alone would not be able to uphold Never Alone, its narrative and documentary aspects strike out as solid pillars, and made me want to go through the game's middling gameplay just to hear more about the Iñupiat from the Iñupiat, and have their stories told to me as they tell to their own. I left the game knowing a bit more about a different people and its traditions, and plenty of curiosity to learn more about them - and that's what I thought Never Alone was about, something it delivers exceedingly well.

I started playing this game on a whim one day when I was really bored but didn't want to play anything too fast paced or strenuous.  For something that came from a random whim and a Humble Bundle purchase I could not have been more surprised.  The story was deeply moving, I found myself playing until 3 am trying to finish the game in one day.  I ended up giving up and going to bed when I realized there was at least another three hours left but I finished it the next day when I got up.
The characters are perfectly written; just enough dialogue to get you to identify with them as people and understand what is happening to the planet.  All of the conversations are thoughtful and while I was, at first, simply trying to ensure my guy survived to get off planet I later found myself ignoring my (technically) impending doom.  The planet and it's emerging ecosystem was far more interesting.
Considering the simple mechanics and that I even went for 100% completion (with some bad choices that required fixing) it's very surprising that the game took me 8.6 hours.  I wasn't rushing but even if I had I likely would have gotten 7 hours out of it.  I've beaten several AAA games in less time and been far less satisfied.  This game is worth a play, just don't be expecting action or horror.  You will explore not only a planet but why it is that way and how your simple bid to survive will impact that entire world and its inhabitants.

After purchasing this on the steam summer sale for 2.69€, i didnt think much of it. Starting the game for the first time, nothing seems too out of the ordinary. Unlike other games it doesnt tell you what to do at all. This can be a blessing and a curse, and in this case, is most definitely the latter. I never got further than the infamous search of the bucket, and the road there felt like a chore. The game is also plagued by low-quality audio loops (you can hear the seams of where the ambient birdsong clips into the start of the loop). Aside from some good looking foliage, the graphics look like something you'd see on the last-gen consoles (no pun intended), and suffers from this ''flat'' look that is common among walking sims where the textures are built from real images rather than built from the ground up. Faces are pretty nice thoe, all things considered. In game as void of content as this, graphics are a bigger deal than you might think, and the overall experience isnt exactly aided by the excessive head bobble that makes me feel ill. Granted, this can be turned off, but not easily reduced to a more comfortable level. As i refunded the game (presumably) early into the story, i cannot attest to the depth and quality of it. However the ability to tell a story with proper grammar is crucial for your investment in it, and this game is sorely lacking in that department.
The game-breaker: I had a weird issue with this game where it would make my audio loop like a truck engine with no oil upon exiting the game, which was only fixed upon restart of the system. However the problems didn't end here. Even after a restart, it wouldnt stop and continued to slam me with BSOD reading: whea uncorrectable error. This led me to believe my OC was unstable and somehow interfered with system stability (altough still didnt explain my audio issue). After numerous restarts and reconfigurations of bios settings i had no luck, and decided to perform a cmos reset. This magically worked for whatever reason and to isolate the issue i proceeded to fire up 35mm once again, ready for some more bucket hunting. After about 10 more minutes i decided to turn the game off, and got the same sound issue as last time as soon as i exited the game. Once again a cmos reset resolved the issue and i uninstalled the game, and returned to my old bios settings with no problems.
If you are having the same issue as me i hope this helped (altough it makes no sense as to why it did...) and use your chance to refund this game if possible.

Only a few hours in and already it has to be one of the most immersive horror games I've played in years. Being developed by the same team behind Penumbra and Amnesia, I already knew what was going to be in store. That being said, it's not as scary as Amnesia, but it's still scary and extremely tense and sometimes even disturbing. The variation within the enemies you encounter all play different, and so you need a different tactic to get past each one. The story is interesting enough with a few twists, and if you're a big fan of mysteries, this game has it. It also brings in some pretty interesting ideas, it forces you to do certain actions throughout that you may not always agree with, but that you need to make in order to progress. The atmosphere is incredible, even surpassing Amnesia in terms of immersion. It's extremely well optimised as well, running on a game engine that has some of the best physics I've seen since Half Life 2.
I feel like some of the enemies could have been made to be a little more scarier, there are some that are downright terrifying but the first monster you face for example is really just a walking brick, but even so, it never stops the intense rush of running and hiding from threats that you cannot attack.
If you're a fan of horror games, this is a must buy, and at the time this review was written, it's got a 66% discount which is an absolute steal.
There's even Workshop support full of custom campaigns created by other people, and since they're unrestricted and can use the HPL engine to its fullest, they can include their own scripted events, animations, levels, voice acting and even custom enemies...
A fantastic game made by a fantastic developer, and I can't wait to see what their next project will be...

I'll keep this review a lot more concise than my usual ramblings...because hey, this is a straightforward game and deserves a straightforward review.
To wit; ASCII Attack is a simple arcade shooter that really embodies the pick-it-up-and-count-on-your-reactions gameplay of classic 80s games, and I mean that in a good way. In a world where game authors slap "retro" labels on anything they've created that is too hard because they've failed to put in the work to balance the gameplay and controls, ASCII Attack is a refreshing return to form as a game that truly embraces the retro feel. The gameplay is often challenging, but never unfair or overly punishing.
Composing the protagonist (a tank) and enemies out of ASCII characters works well, and the two-color factor-feed paper backgrounds are a nice touch (they're configurable, BTW). Even the explosions are little swirls of ASCII characters.
You steer your tank with the classic "Battlezone" dual joystick controls; a gamepad is highly recommended here for the full effect of what the game has to deliver. Sure, you can use a keyboard, but it's not the same. Drop the $25 on a controller if you don't have one -- you'll get a better experience here and be prepared for all of those other games out there that are designed around a controller.
There are enough levels to keep the game interesting (although I'd gladly welcome more), and you can tweak the difficulty as well as other gameplay settings if you blast through things too quickly in normal mode. There are also lightweight achievements of sorts for each level (find all codes, no deaths on the level, etc.) to encourage you to replay it and perform better the next time.
My one gripe is that if your tank touches so much as a single pixel against the wall, it gets hung up and you have to back away to continue moving. As some of the spaces are kind of narrow, they either need to be widened or the tank's friction against the wall needs to be a little more forgiving.
Other than that one little thing, the game is lot of fun -- a blast, really -- and oozes charm from every retro, tractor-feed pore. You could do far worse things with three bucks and your time, and if you manage to find this game in a bundle, grab it. It's one of the ones you'll want to keep for yourself.

ASCII Attack is an old-school top-down shooter with good difficulty balance, plenty of game modes, and a rarely seen control scheme. Its visuals may not be suited for those prone to nausea, but it is great for capturing the magic of old-old arcade games.
As other reviews already pointed it out, ASCII Attack is pretty much a remake of an old Namco game called Assault. It is a top-down shooter, where you drive a tank in realistic manner, meaning both threads are controlled individually. This present one small problem: the game is borderline unplayable without a controller (although it doesn’t hide this fact).
Since this is a simple shooter, don’t expect complex gameplay. The goal of each level is to collect a set amount of code fragments, while trying to dodge the numerous stationary and moving enemies and their projectiles. Like all good games with a simple concept, it is deceptively challenging though—even for arcade veterans, thanks to its numerous game modes.
The simple mechanics are accompanied by a simple visual style, where everything is ASCII art on an old dot matrix printer paper. This minimalism looks great, but presents a problem with the control scheme: since the tank is in the center with the entire level turning around it, players can get dizzy easily. However, those who can take it are awarded with a cool synthetic soundtrack and plenty of levels.

This one really surprised me. Virtually no one on my friends list has it, and it has simplistic controls due to its mobile roots. It still manages to have interesting gameplay with decent balance with progressively increasing difficulty, but what really shocked me was the storyline. With its limited cast of Liang, Amani, and the A.R.T. emoticon robot who acts and sounds like Borderlands' Claptrap, it's managed to make me care about the two human characters. The dialogue intelligently mixes hard science with the fantasy aspects and sprinkles in just a little bit of technobabble. It's compelling to play and doesn't rely on overused gaming tropes like leveling up or endless gradual equipment power progression.
The gameplay is a mix of puzzle and platformer. It's also pretty original. There are few hazards you need to navigate and lots of places to restore your health. The challenge comes with properly filling each area with a sufficient amount of biomass, using the seeds you collect and the fertile ground around you. Though sometimes you may find yourself brute forcing a couple puzzles by herding Phyta into a corner and regularly throwing seeds at them.

Contrary to popular belief, this is not a walking simulator. Anyone, who wants to turn off their brain, relax and just walk around, will be feeling somewhat stressed out as the game progresses: only the first half an hour could be considered a walking simulator. As it goes on, the possibility of failure is more and more prominent.
But other than that, I very much recommend this game. I was playing it in Russian, so I don't know what's the quality of English translation - this might ruin some of the enjoyment. For me, the voice acting and the dialogue were the weakest parts as they sounded very wooden and unnatural.
On the plus sides, the atmosphere is what makes this game absolutely amazing. We don't get this many games focused on post apocalyptic Russia, so this is something that I really appreciated. As someone who grew up in a post soviet country, a lot of the places ht very close to home and made me feel very lonely. The old soviet touch in everything made it a bit odd (sometimes it felt like the epidemic happened in the 80s, but then you see modern pcs laying around) but the village is the highlight to me: I have been to these villages and dachas and to me the feeling of nostalgia was simply overwhelming.
I am not sure if this will have the same effect on people who did not grow up in the same atmosphere, but if you're interested in exploring a desolated russia from small somewhat cheerful cities to old villages stuck in time - do get this game

Zup! 1: 118 achievements, 17 minutes
Zup! 2: 229 achievements, 26 minutes
Zup! 3: 1708 achievements, 48 minutes
Zup! 4: 555 achievements, 23 minutes
Zup Zero: 1043 achievements, 37 minutes

Review date December 2015
I'm a big fan of this game, I've had access since the earliest closed beta.
It is in essense a continually evolving PvP post-apocalpytic shooter with excellent graphics that costs absolutely nothing.
New game modes are added periodically, with "PvE" and "Co-op" scheduled for release when they are good and ready.
The game has had a rocky path to get where it is now, many of the negative reviews you'll see are either outdated (NA server issues on Steam release = "Omg I can't play bad review :(" ) but visible mostly because they got upvoted because they are funny, or simply not relevant to everyone or outright moronic "Too many Russians" etc.
Pros:
Completely free
Absolutely no Pay2Win elements whatsoever
Outstanding development team who constantly update and improve the game balance and economy (recent improvement in ingame non-premium money gain)
High quality visual style
High quality audio
Large variety of weaponry, equipment
Very tactical game experience due in part to massive amount of equipment configurations
Good, if frequently changing, game balance. All weapons are suited to particular tasks. There is no "autopwnmobile" gear.
Cons :
Occassional server instability, massively improved in even just the last few months.
Diverse user reaction to graphical quality i.e some PC's which are high spec struggle to run it, others don't.
No automated anti-cheat system. Hackers must be reported and then banned (though this is a reliable process).
I'm looking forward to where this goes. I've not yet seen any other dev team push so hard for excellence in an ongoing-release title. Hope to see you on the battlefield :)

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Enjoy~

How I feel about "The Force Unleashed II"? Well...it's more of a "meh" situation. It retains the core concept of being overpowered with the force and now you can wield two lightsabers! Sounds fun and it is fun. On the graphics side of things it has improved quite alot - facial animations and character movement have been made to feel more natural. On the gameplay side it is all there - quick and fast button combinations result in making a badass jedi/sith action that makes your jaw drop. But that is pretty much it. The story is ridiculously convoluted - the whole prequel cloning idea brought in the original trilogy mythos. The story feels unfinished and sometimes forced (no pun intended). Grind your way towards becoming overpowered and while advancing the "plot" of the story, face a God Of War style boss battle. Press the right button prompts and you are done.
The techinical and mechanical aspects of the game have been improved, but there is no narrative to drive the player to finishing the game. In the end I would only recommend the game if you could get it on sale, otherwise buy the original with tons of more content and better story.

Survarium is a match based FPS game currently in beta testing.
The atmosphere of Survairum will be immediately familiar to people who have played the STALKER and metro games, as they share a similar vision and many of the same elements.
The gameplay at the moment is in the form of 5v5 matches based on the tier of your gear, and based on 4 different game modes, most of them are pretty standard like ctf, team deathmatch and conquest, but there is a free for all game mode which is actually pretty interesting. There is a freeplay game mode in the works that was promised for the end of 2015, although no one really knows when it will be released.
Not too many people are playing Survarium right now, and so matches can take a while to find, usually 3 minutes or so. You can speed this up by playing on all of the servers around the world, but if you do latency can become a BIG problem for you.
The quality of the visuals is somewhere between STALKER and Metro 2033, better in some areas than STALKER, worse than metro. Overall I think this game looks pretty good, and many of the maps are beautifully designed.
The game features a gear customization system that is satisfactory, with enough gear slots to make me feel like I have a good degree of control over how my character looks. There are also camos you can put on your clothes and decals you can put anywhere.
Overall, this game is pretty good for a beta, the business model so far has been good, and I dont feel like its really pay to win at all, and its one of the few games out there I know of that really feels like STALKER. Jerky player movement and lag can be a problem, but the next patch is supposed to help with that.

A visual novel that sets up an interesting world and something I want to continue learning about, but as of right, leaves a lot to be desired. The biggest problem being is that the story feels like it's being played with the fast forward button being held down. Character building and in particular relationship building feels rushed here, things happening overnight that just don't seem realistic. It's setting the stage, and I understand that, but a more even approach here would have been appreciated as I think the writing can hold up to interest the user.
See, that's the problem about this game in its episodic format in particular. There's some good art work and some interesting world building that develops here: and if the game follows up with some strong episods after it, this could have a payoff that would be great in the visual novel genre. But judging it for what it is NOW, it feels like it's hamstrung by several factors, and doesn't execute on the themes that it wants to.
This could easily change to a recommendation depending on how they follow it up. But for now, it's a game that while it does have things going for it, I can't say it's going to deliver.

Being from Alaska, this game is highly respective of the source culture and I applaud the developers for working so closely with the Alaska Native community in writing and making the story.  Using the Inupiaq language to narrate the story was also a good choice to help place the story in its proper cultural context.  This one game goes 1,000 points beyond Disney's crazy mashup of cultures in "Brother Bear" that is passed off as being "Alaska Native."  The cultural insight videos were nice for me to watch, even as an Alaskan who did not grow up in the bush.
The other aspect that I highly appreciate from the developers is making the game with a strong, clever female protagonist who is non-sexualized.

F1 2014 is the latest addition to the Codemasters racing game series.
Earlier this year announced Codemasters that they were working on two Formula 1 titles, one for the old consoles and one for the new consoles, and unfortunately this is something you'll quickly notice in F1 2014 for generally there has not been much in compared to the 2013 edition, and it can actually be quite difficult to see why there should be changes if you are not familiar with Formula 1 in advance.
When starting the game will no longer greeted by "young drivers test" but instead you get a single round at Monza where you then get proposed a severity and assists. One should therefore no longer perform a number of tasks that test a racing driver then you will get some offers from different teams depending on how well you have done. Instead, you can now sign a contract with any team so that means you can sit down in a Mercedes racing and start winning all his races immediately. One need no longer run for the slow teams and gradually earn to be a top running, you will be just. It leaves a slightly empty feeling that you are allowed to drive for a team without actually and have done to deserve it.
If you have played games series before, there are no major surprises in the career mode. Once you have selected a team starts the battle to become the team's first drive, here you will be weighed and measured on how to cope in the season according to championship points, qualification and race results. Itself, it is will be the team's first run, which will affect the car's setup and how the further development of it takes place.
As soon as career mode begins, the game shows itself from its best side when one starts his first race, it becomes clear that you are not sitting alone in the car, but that you have a whole team behind him that is ready to help someone. One's engineer is often with radio announcements with information about how you're doing in the race and how you can improve yourself. From the start the team's requirements be somewhat reluctant until that has proven its worth, and then they begin to push for delivering results to the team. You will notice that the team's confidence to a slowly being built and it shows by example. may be prompted to save the tires of qualifications because they expect that you could easily go on. It works pretty convincing for it feels namely that the team pay attention to and that they are giving thought to how to cope in the season.
In addition to the career mode, the game this year at a reunion with the fantastic scenario game mode, here is everything as usual, you have the ability to run different scenarios that are taken out of the real Formula 1 world. Scenarios opens the possibility for players who do not have time to run a full 100% run of still having to get up to handle fuel, safety car and more.
When it comes to gameplay feels the game is somewhat different than in the past, this is due to the new regulations that 2014 season has brought with him. The new hybrid cars have been a bit easier to manage because they have shorter stopping distances which makes it easier to correct the drive error as you do. The old KERS system which saved eletrisk energy which you could then use as a speed boost has been replaced with the new ERS. This means that you no longer even rådder of its electrical energy as the car is available.
Unfortunately, featuring F1 2014 no longer on the classics that had been in F1 in 2013, it is shame because it really was a feature that distinguished themselves and who could easily have imagined had been extended to 00s racing cars. It seems odd that you choose to remove such a good feature when the game does not have much new to offer.

Rating this game is really difficult. On the one hand this game makes really fun, on the other hand you always got to think how much better it could have been with a bit more time and money for the producers.
The greatest strength of the game is its gameplay. Cutting of body parts of the storm troopers and use the force to let them fly through the air let you feel like a true bad♥♥♥♥♥and a powerful Jedi. The Force abilities are nearly the same as in the first game, which is fine, because they were great, but this time starkiller got 2 lightsabers instead of one. There are several types of enemies and boss fights, which all need a little bit different approach.
The Story of the game is ok, but not nearly as good as the great story of the first game. You play as starkiller or one of his clones (This not truly revealed in the game, but I personally believe the evidence pro the clone theory is stronger) and need to escape from the empire and reconnect with your friends from the rebellion. The greatest weakness of the game is the length of the story. You can easily beat this game in around 4 to 5 hours. There are only 4 real missions and a ridiculously short dogobah trip, which only consists of one 5 minutes long cut-scene with master Yoda. This is really sad, because I think with 2 or 3 more missions this game would have felt much more completed.
At least there are 4 different difficulty settings und 2 possible endings, which gives you a bit of replay value and outside of the campaign there is a shortly entertaining challenge mode. In the Playstation and X-BOX Version there is also a DLC-Level on Endor, which is quite enjoyable as well.
The Music of the game is really great. Some of the most typical parts of the soundtrack of the classic star wars trilogy are part of this game and feel really fitting in every scene.
Pro:
-Gameplay is really entertaining
- True Star Wars atmosphere
- Great Sound
Contra:
- Length of the game
- Story is not as good as in the first game
Result: At the end I am in the strange position, that I can neither recommend nor disapprove this game. When I think about FU2 I always feel a bit sad, but when I play it (Beat it now 3 or 4 times), I truly enjoy this game every time despite its flaws and have a great time with it.
