Even at this point during its short life, I feel as though the Zup! series has become a little stale to a certain extent. While still all being perfectly enjoyable, the biggest leap in innovation to the overall mechanic has been in the second game where it made the pivotal change of taking the square target block, and making it a rolling, circular piece instead. It seems like a small change, but that one simple alteration really opened up a lot of possibilites. Well, the very same adjustment has been applied to the rest of the game, too, as a lot of the squares have now been replaced by more rolling circles and opened things up once again.
It's funny how such a minor tweek in concept can make such a big difference in play and really switch things up. There are times when it does still feel like you're going through the same motions, sure, but at least not anywhere close to the degree of deminishing returns that it was. Now, rather than having one moving piece making its way around the screen, there are several to be manipulated into place to open up the way. The other "big" change to the game is the introduction of switches that have to be activated to remove blocks acting as gateways to progress. Aside from that, there's nothing else of note to really report other than an improved quality of stage design with more direct interaction and less sitting back and watching, as the previous game was leaning way too much into. Otherwise, players of past games will be on very familiar ground here.
There are suggestions that this may be the final entry in the series (where do you even go anyway after reseting to 0? Which in itself is an odd decision given the complete lack of narrative to any of the titles), as the developer seems to be exploring other games. And you know what? I'd actually be pretty happy if it was. It had a really good run and seems to have been relatively successful for what it is. But I think the audience's patience is starting to be tried at this point, with the combined saturation of the one series (five games in seven months!) and especially now as the b*stard children "inspired" by it are starting to emerge. This is a pretty good point to end on, too, and leaves on a real high. If more are released, I'm sure I'll take the bait and end up playing them at some point just the same, but if this is the final curtain for Zup!, then it was a fun ride while it lasted. Oh, and thanks for the three-and-a-half thousand achievements you gave me as well. Cheers.

If I had to use one word to describe the experience of Never Alone, it would be beautiful, gorgeous, stunning... Oh wait. Yes Never Alone is both a gorgeous looking game, as well as a beautiful experience. Based around myth and legend of the Iñupiat, a native Alaskan people Never Alone takes us on a wonderful journey. You play as a young Iñupiat girl and her arctic fox after they are thrust on an adventure together when her village is destroyed by a mysterious man. The story that follows is both heartfelt, thoughtful and challenging.
Visualy I can't describe how stunning Never Alone looks. The soft snow effects, and precisely detailed backgrounds come alive with each step, sometimes literally. Snow drifts around you and your parka, and ruffles it's fur. Your characters react to changes in the wind, and lighting. Friendly Iñupiat spirits drift in and out of existence to help you along the way. The expressions on your character's faces easily portray emotion as you struggle on and sometimes die after a misstep. Each environment feels alive, even in what may seem a bleak barren land at times.
Behind all the beautiful visuals, a solid, co-operative side scrolling platformer exists. You and your trustworthy fox must work together to traverse a multitude of different obstacles. While your main character is at first limited to running and jumping, your fox friend has several useful abilities. He can climb walls, or jump between them. He can also influence the various Iñupiat spirits around, which provide new platforms to use to get to different areas. Later as the puzzles become more complex you are gifted with various new abilities. A bola for the young girl, the powers of flight and spirit manipulation for the fox. These new abilities are doled out an even pace and give you new things to play with throughout your play through.
Though there aren't a lot of major new concepts here, what is in play is very solid. Puzzles range from simple to challenging, and new concepts come at you regularly. The environments are imaginative, and their uses surprising. Boss battles can be tough, and you will die often as you figure out their patterns. It is very rare however that these encounters feel long, or get frustrating. Most of these tougher challenges involve you taking advantage of the environment around you. And they all make good use of the co-operative element.
Never Alone is built to be both a cooperative or solo adventure, both are enjoyable. As a solo player, it is easy for you to switch between characters, and the AI controlled character is generally smart enough to go where they need to go. Running solo lets you take your time to soak in the rich environments and beautiful effects. Playing as a duo however requires a decent amount of timing and communication as to not die often.
The story in Never Alone, though starting on a tragic note is wonderful to discover. Each environment you enter into tells a story, and as you explore you are given insights into the Iñupiat culture. These are delivered through both video snipets you can view, as well as behind the scenes documentaries. Between each story break, you are treated to animated versions of traditional Iñupiat drawings. These are presented in storyboard format and connect each story and environment together. Your reward for completing Never Alone, is just as beautiful and tragic. It is truly a rewarding arc to follow.
I can't state enough how beautiful an experience Never Alone is. It's visuals, unique setting, story and characters are all a joy to experience. The focal point on the Iñupiat people is both insightful and rewarding. With gameplay that is solid, though not groundbreaking it's very hard to find anything to critizise here. Never Alone is a game you should take your time to experience, and enjoy.

This is simply a beautifully crafted indie game. It invokes a real sense of exploration, discovery and wonder. I really enjoyed playing this game. If you ever find yourself watching wildlife you will find this game really immersive and enjoyable.
You could call it a 2d puzzle game, but that is just not doing it any justice. It uses simple 2d graphics to portray the martian landscape to really good effect. Before I played the game I thought the graphics were too basic, but somehow when actually playing the game I found the art beautiful.
You land on Mars and have to explore, observe, experiment and learn how the martian ecosystem works. You can then manipulate the ecosystem to progress deeper into the cave system to discover yet more organisms and more complex interactions. It may sound daunting, but it is a very gradual path of discovery that is both addictive and rewarding.
As well as the well designed graphics, physics, organisisms and their interactions, it also has a good story, multiple endings and great voice acting. It is just the right length, not padded or bloated. It is just a really sharp polished product.

I feel as if i have played this game long enough to justify my opinion. For honor is, for the lack of a better word a fighting game that uses a system Ubisoft like to call The Art of Battle in where locking on to opponents allows you to pick 3 different directions of which you chose to attack and block from (Up, Right and Left). The game allows you to choose up to 12 different heroes split evenly into 3 different factions Knights, Viking and Samurai. Each hero has a unique fighting style, combos and traits that are somewhat historically accurate to their respective eras and are leveled individually unlocking new traits and gear that you can use to customise your hero. From their weapons blade, hilt and handle to their helmets arms and torso of which can be further tailored with patterns and war paint. The game currently contains 5 game modes  Duel - 1v1  Brawl - 2v2  Deathmatch - 4v4 and Dominion 4v4 (Where you capture points).
Gear can be bought with the use of a currency called steel which can be obtained via orders (quests) or payed for through microtransactions. But unlike most games featuring microtransactions i feel as if its completely optional and not needed due to the amount of steel given to you via orders. The orders require you to play a certain gamemode a certain amount of times or to get certain types of kills in a specific gamemode or with a specific hero encouraging you to try new things and learn more about other aspects of the game you might of otherwise avoided. Some see this as con because it forces you to play certain gamemodes/heroes that you might not like to earn steel for your main, but i think if you restrict yourself by only playing 1 or 2 heroes you shouldnt be playing the game because learning every heroes is essential for further improving your skill and knowledge of the games mechanics and other heroes traits. Although if that is how you would like to play you can always abandon certain orders and have them be refreshed every 2 days that have the main reward of Xp but less steel and there also being 2 seperate orders that refresh daily that has a main reward of steel but less Xp.
I love the game but it needs polishing and some balance adjustments if it plans to go competitive of which that has already began with there being around 5 community tournaments all with pretty high price pools for a game that was released not too long ago. But this still doesn't mean that the game isn't horrendously unbalanced in the sense that 4 out of the 12 classes exceed the other 8 by miles at a professional stand point. This is shown via 4 out the 5 tournament winners playing the same class (Warlord) and the remaining 3 classes being runner ups or 2nd pick in 2 v 2s. I could go into each class but this review is already going to be long enough so im going to end the point by stating the 4 top classes in the game right now: Warlord, Peacekeeper, Conqueror and Warden.
The other probably more problematic form of imbalance is in the games main game mode Dominion. In this game mode it is 4v4 where to win you must obtain 1000 points and then kill the entire enemy team by capturing points spread out across the map. This has been Ubisofts biggest selling point and where they've focused the most in the game. Which some say due to the game being made around this game mode explains why there is such an imbalance in 1v1 and 2v2. The problem lies within the gear, as in the higher your hero level is the better gear you'll have and the more damage and defense you'll have. This was also used in The Division and in that game it also caused a huge imbalance between high level players and low-level players and sadly its no different in For Honor. This has led to high gearscored players winning 1 v 9 due to a system called revenge which is basically a buff you obtain when attacked by multiple players and its buffs vary based on your gearscore. It gives the player HP more defense and an extremely high damage increase again based on your gearscore. The problem can be easily fixed by reducing the defense and damage increase from high level gear, nerfing the revenge buff or by improving the matchmaking which is currently pretty bad.
I have encountered a few bugs the main one being infinite loading screens that can only be fixed by alt-f4 and i have sometimes joined a game where my camera is stuck in the sky and im playing from a top down view like a moba but these bugs are few and far between. The game is peer-to-peer which has caused many connectivity issues since release and is currently still a problem that has yet to be completely fixed although has been improved. The biggest annoyance for me is whenever I get a slight dip in my ping, instead of the game lagging and there being heavy delays on my part, the game instead decides to kick you completely causing all of efforts in a match to be for nothing, this is really bad for those of you with poor internet connections. I do not fault Ubisoft unlike most for going peer-to-peer because i believe there is no need and rarely has been dedicated servers for fighting games due to extra layer of response time on top of the traffic you are already getting, as in your inputs must go through the server then to the player causing  more lag and less accuracy from attacks for example:
Peer to peer:
You ->> Opponent, Opponent ->> You.
Via Dedicated:
You ->> Server ->> Opponent, Opponent ->>  Server ->> You.
The real problem with peer-to-peer is lag switching and its vulnerability to hackers but i think it's easier to deal with hackers than having combos miss even when you're on an even playing field connection wise causing its competitively to suffer. Throughout my play time I haven't come across a single hacker but there have been multiple reports of there being some.
The game does run pretty well on my Gtx 970 on Extreme but i have noticed there are some dips in frames due to the connection issues and when players disconnect. The game looks great and is pretty well optimized unlike some of Ubisofts other games (Watchdogs) but I haven't come across any important performance issues since beta.
Ubisoft has proven that it can support its games after realise, rainbow 6 siege at release had a small player base that died quickly but after many updates, patches and free DLC the game has now been brought back and is seen as one the most competitive FPS. There is already plans for 6 new heroes, new maps and new game modes all of which will be free. Even with its current flaws they are easily avoidable by playing game modes that don't take gear into effect and are easily fixable. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is even slightly interested and with the amount of content coming you are getting further down the line for free, I think the player base will continue to grow during its life time.  8/10

Game review:
-Although the game only has 4 characters (Fighter, Slasher, Mage, and Priest) Its unique game play and the colorful skills are eye catching.
-Divine Souls seems like it has a lot to offer with the in-game play; Items, rarity, enchanting, dungeons, party system, difficulties, item crafting, item dissembling for the crafting materials and much more! It is definitely an eye catcher and its unique style is worth of giving a shot to. With just over and hour of the game play I can see where the end game content can be fun and rewording, as well as challenging.
-Game graphics are realistic and very sharp, something not many MMOs have going for them.
-Controls are set for an Action RPG as the Divine Soul is, which allows you to actually kite the mobs and not just sit around waiting for the skills casted to end.
-The main city is is vast and quests are everywhere!
-Game tutorial and the beginner quests do an excellent job explaining the game basics allowing you to get to advancing your character almost right after finishing them, which doesn't take long at all.
-The game has virtually no lag or delay which makes the game that that much more enjoyable. Not having to worry about those two little things is every players dream and this game offers both of those small but very important features.
-I'm liking what I'm seeing right now. Its basically not your generic fancy MMO because of its unique combat style.
-Overall I would rate the game ★★★★½☆  just from quick experience in it, I'm sure my opinion will change as I keep playing the game and explore more of its content, both solo and teamed up with other players.
-Also for the final note, I would definitely recommend it and if you're liking my review, give it a shot,you will enjoy it as did I.

This is a really enjoyable game. After beating it, I felt it was too short for a moment, but then I realized that it ended just before the gameplay got stale.
What truly makes this game shine is the narative. I haven't played a game in a while that made me feel so... "attached" to my character(s). I could imagine conversations going on between them, what they might look like if they were drawn in detail and all sorts of things that go beyond the base narrative and simple rectangular designs.
The platforming is standard-fare, with each playable character having a unique attribute which can be used to traverse levels and/or assist your other characters in traversing the level. It's simple, but not tedious.
I'll give it a 6/10 for gameplay. It's another INDIE PLATFORMER but the platforming is neither clunky, tedious and it doesn't try to shoehorn in some weird mechanic to give itself some desperate sense of individuality.
I'll give it a 8/10 for story. It's easy to grasp, and changes in ways that you might not expect.
The soundtrack gets a 7/10. It fits the game quite well. But there were no tracks that really "stuck" with me.
For the characters I'll give it a 10/10. The material presented describes the characters in enough detail so that you have a good idea of who they -are-, and what they're like. But it doesn't drown you in facts.
Overall, I'll give this game a 7/10. A little pricey (unless you got it in the Humbe Indie Bundle 8), but a solid (yet very short) game.

Overall, cool way to interact with streams, still being worked on. (hence early access.)

Being the Dino nerd that I am, I purchased this game as soon as it was released to Steam. I've had many fun times, and met some pretty cool people along the way. That is why it sucks to have to make a review like this after all this time.
The optimization, graphics, dino models, sounds, and animations are all spectacular.
It can be aggravating as far as how other players interact with you, but that's all expected in an online game. Along the way The Isle has gone through an overhaul that I believe to be for the worse.
Life, and other games got in the way so I found myself shelving The Isle for a few months. I played it again just a week or so ago, and the new format is absolutely aggravating, and a total timesink. To "progress" you stay alive for about a minute at a time to collect points. You start as the lowest tiered dinosaur for either the Herbivores, or Carnivores. You're looking at essentially playing 30 mins minimum to rank up to the next tier as a Herbivore, and an hour to rank up to the next tier as a Carnivore. That's just Tier 1 to Tier 2. A lot longer to go up from there, being about 5 or so tiers to max.
Ok, not so bad, right?
Wrong.
Not only must you be alive to collect those points, but if you die just once, you reset back to zero. Even if you rank up to another tier, you reset back to tier 1 starting all over again. There's a thing called nesting which enables you to stay that same species as a "save spot" but finding someone, or even staying alive long enough is a total struggle in itself.
Oh, here's the other thing. You have a health/thirst meter. Not a big deal, it's a survival game after all. The devs tweaked the meter to start you from 75% full, to now starting at 50%. Which falls dramatically quick. You have to essentially kill anything in your path (that you can) and hopefully find water out of the gate after spawning to survive at all. Causing many species to cannibalize themselves just to stop starvation as the map is huge (again not a problem, except for the current state of the game.)
Due to this The Isle is not recommended  by me. If you're somebody like me that has 1-2 hrs tops of free time to spend gaming per day/night this is NOT the game for you. If you don't care about the struggles it takes to actually progress to the point of enjoying all that the game has to offer, than it is.
A little sidenote. One of the main devs is fairly combative/arrogant, and his personality through streaming turned me off a lot early on in The Isles development. That's neither here, nor there, but it has rubbed me the wrong way.

Similar to Choice Chamber, Legend of Dungeon Masters is a Twitch Interaction game where you hurt or help a streamer along their way through a randomly generated dungeon in the full game of Legend of Dungeon. The biggest difference with Masters is that it is a separate client that saves your inventory, experience, and currency. Names, messages, and votes are all done through the client itself, so there is no chat spam required.
The client itself is an overlay on top of the stream. Throughout the player's journey, they find chests that are sent to everyone in the audience, who then get a random item based on the chest's rarity, ranging from a single vote to a bazooka to death itself. If you enjoy messing with your friends or love twitch streams, this client is a really fun and simple way to influence how the game plays out.
Even just watching the developers test the game on their stream has been fun to check out once in a while, but how fun it is would heavily depend on the streamer you're watching. So far this has been way better on lesser known streams than ones that average thousands of viewers, but that could change with updates.
Legend of Dungeon itself is a fun little dungeon crawler, and is often super cheap on sale. Even if only one friend owns the game, anyone can download the Masters client to join in on the fun.

So I have seen a lot of mixed reviews about this game and they almost convinced me not to buy it, so even though I don't usually review games, I will put one on here because I feel like is deserves some positivity.
I will try to make this short and to the point. This game is an extremely fun and simplistic survival game. If you are looking for constant updates, constant action, and an easy start, then this is NOT FOR YOU. This game has an extremely sharp learning curve so expect a couple of hours getting killed and learning the ropes. I highly recommend going on realism servers if you want a friendly community and less trolls, unless you just want to go kill people for a couple hours on deathmatch servers, which I personally don't think is a lot of fun. The graphics are beautiful and the controls are great. I have spend 50 hours on the game at the time that I am writing this, and I highly recommend it. The large amount of time it takes to get to a good dino (about 2/12 hours for the one I like the best) helps give it some worth in my opinion and adds a lot to the game. There are so many different was to play, from scavenger, to herbivore, to apex hunters.
If you are looking for a slower pace, yet still extremely engaging game with a simplistic play style and beautiful graphics, then this is for you. If you are looking for a game with constant action and no buildup, then it is not. Expecgt to do a lot of running, searching, and stalking for your prey. It won't just be running out at you. This game is a fun challenge and I highly recommend it.

In short: a (at present) short, but charmingly endearing VN, with an extremely likable cast.
Let’s just get the negatives out of the way, because there are parts of this leave a little to be desired:
- The pacing is off in places. While not a deal breaker, there are moments where the tone is slightly rushed, making it somewhat confusing to follow. This is thankfully not a persistent problem, but does weaken one or two scenes.
- Music loops are sometimes not really effective. At least one music track for the battle/action sequences actually does have a build up: while hitting the climax of these build ups make sequences with action a lot more impactful, it does feel a bit flaccid when it loops back around to the build up while battle is still on-going.
- The character design is a hate it or love it affair. This is more a subjective concern, and one you can more or less settle by looking at the screenshots. Personally, I find the semi-fan service style isn’t too distracting, but again this is a subjective concern.
All right, with that out of the way, let’s talk about the positives, because this game has a fair number of them:
- The general art style is quite unique. The use of colour in the backgrounds and characters succeeds in making both pop, and shows a good level of variance. This is in addition to every character having a very unique silhouette, which helps differentiate between them.
- The musical theme is well earned. There is a close tie in the story between rock music and demons, and to that end the sound track does earn its wings. I can’t say much beyond that due to my tone-deaf nature, but even a pleb like me can see that the rock in this shows a great level of promise.
- Fairly charming ‘fish out of water’ story. While the world and demons of hell are a core part of the story, Toko adjusting herself to the human world serves as a welcome element. The quirky comedy that comes from Toko trying out various human normalities is nicely offset by the constant background fact that she is slowly becoming something she is not, and the natural emotional stress that would bring.
--- Hugely likable and varied cast. In my personal opinion the visual novel’s greatest strength: the two main characters share the screen with a wide range of colourful characters, all with a variety of characteristics and motivations. This is in addition to a number of characters based on mythological figures, all of which have quite imaginative interpretations. Watching the characters bounce off one another, and seeing the conflict that comes from that, is probably the majority of the reason to buy the VN.
Other facts (fair warning, might be considered SPOILERS):
- It has JoJo worthy Stands. Trust me, it’s pretty cool.
- The chibi art is adorable.
- Ginxhou is the best. Search your feelings; you know it to be true.
As it is right now, the length is around 3-ish hours, and as the title says this is ONLY the prelude. That being said, I would consider it a worthy investment into what promises to be a good series.

I seem to be saying it year after year; F1 2011 is Codemasters finest Formula One game. It's disappointing to say it once more, but it's fact. This 2014 game is a step forward in on track driving but still lacking in immersion off track.
The game is enjoyable on the whole and the price drop is welcome since there is alot of copy paste going on.
The ontrack handling is very enjoyable requiring skill but the cars are more realistic and manageable, the brakes on the other hand seem to have been dumbed down in difficulty. You can really push the brakes now and there is a nice little audible that give you a hint in advance of any lockup. It seems to work well for gameplay.
The lack of traction in general has made racing the cars on the limit a hell of a lot of fun and very satisfying in getting those perfect laps, or if you over cook it a little and go into a drift.
The rules changed and removed KERS making overtaking a little trickier, but that in turn made successful overtaking more satifying.
The AI is still not very bright; at overtaking and can easily be lead into trying it around the outside, where it has to slot back in behind. Also sometimes it get offline and seem to just give up trying to take the corner and lets numerous cars go by before it slots back into the train.
There's no 3D modelled interactive agent, no paddock or motor homes. No interaction with the media and no press interviews for podiums. All hurting the game series since losing it in 2012. The animations are all old, even the HUD graphics are 99% from F1 2013.
I'd recommend it just on the racing, but without the immersion it falls down to it's older brother, F1 2011.
Don't get me wrong it's a step in the right direction, but I wouldn't endorse it as is to friends when F1 2011 exists.
F1 2011 might be outdated, but it holds all the longevity gameplay items the newer F1 games by codemasters can only dream about,

I've had it since release day and currently not sure how I fall on this one.
Essentially F1 2013 updated for the season (same engineer, voice commands etc), Codies have at least incorporated the new rules to a great(ish) extent. You'll now take the tyres you set your fastest lap in Q2 into the race so you can go balls-out (if you make it) in Q3 for pole with a set of the softs.
The sounds in general seem pretty good. The engines of the three maufacturers are represented and could be recognised from the onboard footage I watch week in week out on the BBC, Sky,
, YouTube etc.
In terms of gameplay it appears fairly accurate. The Mercedes disappear up the road and the WIlliams, Red Bulls, Ferraris and to a lesser extent, the McLarens, scrap over the other podium spout and the top 10 order.
The total lack of control of ERS is a significant negative for this game though. In a year where the charging and discharging of the non-combustion engine has become an even more pivotal role Codemasters decides to bottle it and take that away from the driver.
The "classic" content from F1 2013 was a huge plus and one I revelled in personally. To not only not improve on but to remove it from the franchise was a bit of a kick in the teeth. The Scenarios and Season Challenges are welcome continues but it feels somewhat lacking. These new generation turbo cars would be complemented by some 1980s turbo kit.
Multiplayer-wise, to date, I've really struggled with this game personally. I've probably spent more time in lobbies than I have racing. Can't think of a game version I've not tried and a lot of games have just ended up being full of kids with keyboards; no interest in a race. Just a destruction derby a lot of the time. I have no time for people who don't leave you room and would rather turn into an accident, lock wheels, than turn away and maintain momentum.
Right now I don't think I'd recommend it as you can be charged a bit of a silly price for it. With it not being next-gen and most of my friends eing on Xbox One or PS4 I've not had to shell out for a console version as well this year.
Do I recommend this game? As it stands, unlesss you're a big F1 fan - and you don't already own it - I'd say no and I wasn't expecting to say that.

Positives: The final battle is pretty good, although it does get a bit repetitive. There are a few fights near the end where it felt like "man, this game is really testing what I know in a good way."
Negatives:
The controls are pretty bad. Blocking blaster shots isn't as inuitive as in Jedi Academy/Jedi Knight, as it requires a separate key press. If you jump, there's very little control over your momentum. You have to double jump to correct your trajectory or air dash to move forward. Which is okay, but there's so little precision with jumping that it can get pretty frustrating. A lot of special enemies have ways to kill them faster via quick time events (not mandatory)- but a lot of times it locks you into them when you don't anticipate it because it is bound to the jump key- so you'll be in the middle of a jump, and you'll snap like 20-30 feet away into a quick time event without expecting it.
This game throws waves after waves of enemies at you, without much in the way of reprieve. I can count multiple instances where there were literally 100+ enemies over the course of a single battle. Granted these are usually lesser enemies (terror drones, for instance) and are used to help you regain health, but the sheer amount of stuff flying at you starts to feel pretty overwhelming. Especially when you have instances of Force Users, Lightsaber Users, and walkers plus swarms of smaller guys trying to kill you (all of which require different approaches and/or force powers to effectively deal with them). I suppose the developers probably wanted the pace to feel frenetic or like an actual battle, but having a bit of time to regroup would be nice every now and then.
None of the characters are particularly likable. Starkiller is yelling in anger half the time for no apparent reason, and near the end he does his best batman "WHERE IS SHE!?!?" impression several times. General Kota is a complete jerk for no particular reason too, so maybe that's why Starkiller is always angry.
The game is also quite short. Even if you play on the hardest difficulty (that's unlocked at the start), you'll get maybe 8 hours out of it tops. Not much in the way of replayability either.

Reviewing this game purely within the atmospheric genre,
, but in the world of gaming generally I found it a bit lacking.
If you're looking for atmosphere, SOMA has it in spades. If you want the thrill of a creepy journey without having to solve puzzles or make any difficult choices, then you will enjoy SOMA. It does those things with style and grace.
The underwater environment of most of the game is reminiscent of Bioshock, and has similar anxiety-inducing use of environmental sound and shadowy, unreliable lighting. Along with the entities you encounter (no spoilers), the game executes the feel of a survival horror that will leave your palms sweaty. I recommend playing alone in the dark, and use headphones if you don't have a killer sound system.
You will find yourself wanting to explore every nook and cranny of SOMA's world.
However, if you're hoping for meaningful player decisions, a coherent backstory, challenging gameplay, or a dynamic world, you will be disappointed on every point.
Don't get me wrong: SOMA's atmosphere is superb, and the things you will encounter are seriously creepy. But I want more from a game than
atmosphere.
SOMA has the same problem of many atmospheric games. It plays like a slow-motion movie, with the player having to do the grunt work of actually driving the story forward. It's like operating some kind of antique hand-powered film projector. The world is expressed in brilliant detail, but it is static. You leave it like you found it in pretty much every way. The game's railroad is so complete and nearly unbroken that the game virtually plays itself. The hardest thing to learn was that almost none of the objects in the environment are of any use, despite the ability to pick up and examine them closely. Your choices are limited to exploring room A or room B first, with no consequences either way. The things that could be hard decisions for the player are simply forced one way or the other.
There are a few other things I could pick on of lesser consequence. Many of the voices in the game which usually provide crucial backstory or atmosphere are so distorted that my two friends and I couldn't understand the majority of it. Trying to replay the dialogue left us frustrated and disconnected us from the atmosphere and the narrative. There are subtitles that can be enabled to display words as they are spoken, so if having text appear on the screen doesn't affect your immersion, that is an option.
Also, this game fails to reward you in any way with a backstory that makes sense or give you a sense that things are connected through a chain of causation. Without spoiling, it suffices to say that the major events of each segment of the game and backstory are never connected. I don't need a game to tie up every loose end, but that's not what I'm talking about. It's more like the game was a series of several spectulative concepts that didn't match, and they were hastily posed in a line. A treatment. An unrelated catastrophe. An unrelated project. Surprisingly, this is a better game than its predecessor. Although there is only one real moment in the game where you feel you’re unleashing the force, the enemy types are much more varied, and the level design is much better this time around. The CGI scenes are still unskippable, but gone are the countless frustrating moments of plunging to your death. In contrast to part 1, Stormtroopers can now be dismembered, which fits the dark story more.
The story’s quite short (you’ll have finished it within 5 hours), and doesn’t really add much more than a happy ending to part 1. You’re a clone (or are you?) who’s out to find some answers and your long lost love. There is some darker story hidden in the challenge levels, which hints at cut content. The game would have been much more interesting had those cut voice-overs and storyboard art actually been translated into parallel game scenes.
One consistent minor point are the small icons for the quick time events; you will often have to redo them, because you simply didn’t spot the tiny icons hidden over the screen. It’s not a game breaker, but it does get frustrating at times.
Finally, be aware, the PC version is missing the Endor DLC that came out for consoles, which reinforces its short length.
It’s a good game, but it still doesn’t come close to the Jedi Knight series.

Okay, so before I tell you all what I think, I'll let you know I am a HUGE fan of Fricitonal. They are easily one of my favorite game companies. Amnesia was the first Frictional game that I played and I loved it. I now also have the Penumbra trilogy and it is very good as well, although significantly more dated than Amnesia. Now, having played Soma, I have to say it is by far my favorite game Frictional has made. I just think everything about it is incredible. The setting and atmosphere are both so well done. One of the things I loved the most is that, instead of thes story being presented to you, you actually have to figure out what's going on for yourself. If you just do a run-through of the game without reading any notes, computer terminals, or listening to audio logs, you will get the very basic idea of the story, but if you actually search for the information yourself, what you find is incredible. All the details, characters, events lace together the more you read and figure out what was happening. The gameplay is still great. The biggest difference between Soma and Amnesia as far as gameplay is concerned is that Soma  has different types of enemies and they all behave differently. You have to figure out how best to avoid them and sneak around them. The voice acting is also very well done. The main character, Simon, is likeable enough. The game is also very deep (pun definitely intended). Some of the questions it asks or ideas and concepts that it deals with are incredibly complex and interesting. I would also say that, while this game is definitely scary, it is not as scary as Amnesia. To me, it felt like, whereas Amnesia wanted to tell a scary story, Soma is telling a story with scary parts. I could go on and on about how much I love this game (As soon as I finished it, I wanted to play it again. It's easily in my all-time top five games.) but I do not want to spoil this game. If you are a fan of Frictional, scary games, games with really meaningful, deep plots, or just want to try something new, please play this game. You owe it to yourself. It's a masterpiece.

A very atmospheric first person sci-fi horror game.
The story starts with you going for a brain scan. After an accident you've got little time to live so you go for an experimental treatment where they're going to take a full scan of your brain. You sit in a chair and the vision goes black. When you wake up you're somewhere completely different - in a space station looking like environment. And here's where the real game starts - you go on discovering where you exactly are, how you got there and how will you be able to escape.
I'm not a big fan of horror games but I must admit I enjoyed this quite a bit. Probably because of a nice balance between the horror scary parts and the exploration parts. And there is quite a lot of exploration and puzzle solving apart from running scared from the entity hunting the underwater research facility which you get to travel through.
Graphics are really nicely done. It's dark, it's damp - it's very atmospheric. The world design is top notch as well. The facility does feel very alien like sci-fi. There's plenty to discover about the previous inhabitants leaving on the base. A nice touch - you're able to pick up any object even though it serves no purpose - but it's fine to do. Looking at numerous photographs also adds to the back story of the full game.
A bit let off is that it does take place underwater and there are plenty of water levels (ugh!). And while the visuals are really nice I did got lost once or twice in them and did not enjoy them as much as the rest of the games. Though entering the really deep ocean places was impressive and scary.
The game is driven by two mechanics - exploration puzzles and horror survival. The first part was definitely enjoyable - you go around the bases, switch a lever here, push a button there. The exploration feels interesting and the puzzles are not that complicated. The survival horror is similar to Amnesia - you have nothing and IT's coming. Not as scary as Amnesia but still too scary for my personal liking.
The game asks interesting questions about identity, consciousness and what it means to be alive. And answers them almost perfectly as far as I'm concerned. Especially with the epilogue. A really nice food for thought.
Overall a great game with a great atmosphere. Highly recommend.

I've never played anything like Waking Mars.  It's a puzzle game based on manipulating an alien ecosystem.  Sometimes you need to find a way to get the plants to reproduce.  Sometimes you need to plant a particular combination of plants.  Sometimes you need to do something in particular with the plants (e.g. herd a mobile plant into a carnivorous plant).
If you die you will lose your progress since you entered the room.  If you keep at it you will eventually succeed.
The depiction of science is pretty accurate.  You will need to pay attention to what happens around you, read research, and experiment.  You will frequently learn things by accident.
The only complaint I have is the game is mildly grindy in places.  Sometimes raising the biomass in a room sufficiently takes doing something repeatedly, for 10 to 15 minutes, rather than just figuring out what to do.  The key to minimizing the frustration with these rooms is usually feeding seeds to the mobile plants while standing next to a plant that produces seeds.  Each time a seed is eaten the seed-producing plant will release another, so this makes the process pretty fast.

We tried out the pre-release on a Vinesauce stream last night. It didn't work well with ~4,000 players, and apparently there was a serious bug that caused people to receive way more items than intended, so that didn't help either. It looks like it'd be really fun on smaller streams, and maybe on larger streams such as Vinesauce if they can find a way to balance it.
You randomly get chests as the streamer explores the dungeon, which have a chance of containing spawnable items such as monsters and weapons. You can drag an item into the stream to spawn it into the dungeon, along with a name and message of your choice. Unfortunately the ~30 second Twitch delay makes this a bit less enjoyable, as it's hard to spawn exactly what the streamer needs (or doesn't need!) when he needs it.
This looks like a lot of fun, but it doesn't work well for extremely large streams just yet.
Note: The "Name" field when spawning an item is for YOUR name, not the ITEM'S name.

Half-Life 2 is fun itself, and I enjoyed watching people play it and I also enjoyed playing it myself. But something like this mod is what I have always been waiting for because it allows you to play with others. Half-Life 2 always seemed like a game that you never really played alone, you either played with someone watching you, or you watched someone else play. Synergy adds the teamwork Half-Life 2 always seemed to almost need.
Pros
-You can play with other people either locally or internationally
-You can customize your experience with community made mods that replace the weapons and other things in the workshop (I prefer not to, but it is nice  to be able to.)
-Ravenholm is less scary with others.
-Custom maps and built in coop maps.
-Works with Half-Life 2, and it's two following episodes.
-Extra supplies because there are more players. ( only good if there are more players )
-Two seated buggy, and other drivable vehicles with even more seats.
-A few added weapons.
-You can play in a squad fashion without npcs.
-You can heal  others and give others ammo.
-You can drop weapons if someone is lacking.
-Teammate glows behind walls
-Selectable playermodels (You can subscribe to a Gordon Freeman model in the workshop)
Cons
-Sometimes, there are too many enemies, but that is understandable because there are more players.
-Enemies deal way more damage and can take more damage. (Also slightly good, because you have to be a little strategic, but it makes the easy difficulty misleading and there should be an option for classic or synergy enemy quantity, health, and damage.)
-Lower ammo limits.
-Sometimes spawn without a gravity gun.
-Rarely spawn without a suit.
-Not all vehicles have multiple seats (Airboat and Jalopy)
Reccommended features to add:
-If it is detected that you cannot move, you can teleport to a teammate. (I don't know how that would be done)
-Takedowns (Would spice things up a bit especially if you happen to be behind an oblivious combine soldier, or if a fast zombie thought it could charge you and get away with it that easy.)
-Secrets (Would also spice things up. I know there are already secret supplies, but maybe a secret message or secret rooms)
-Incapacitation and revival from others. (Requires health from health pool)
-Rare Combine Shield (Can rarely be found and equipped to use like a riot shield, but is limited to one person which could take on the role of leader.)
It's a mod that let's you play with other people and it's free, I'm not sure if it gets better than that. It has definitely changed my gaming experience.

Despite it's short length I enjoyed playing this game. It has charming retro pixelated graphics, an interesting story and some nice puzzles. Two things bothered me though. First of all the main menu lacks a quit/exit/stop option so I had to use ALT-F4 to exit the game. The other thing is more troubling and it's the rhyme. I bought the game because I liked the art I saw in the screenshots and I have a weakness for science fiction. And ever since I discovered the Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy, also for fjords. But I was wondering whether the rhyme would really add something to the game or if it would be nothing more than a cheap gimmick. Unfortunately it's the latter.
In my opinion the game would have been better if they hadn't tried to make every two sentences rhyme. While the sentences do in fact rhyme (most of the time at least, there is some weak and false rhyme here and there) there is no meter at all. Sentences that rhyme are of different length and have different rhythms. I'll use the rhyme visible in one of the screenshots as an example.
"The trail up here will someday be my death", Erlend said, short of breath.
I'll visualise my problems with this rhyme by using italic text to note unstressed syllables and bold text to note stressed syllables:
"








",

,


.
You can see that the first part of the sentence contains 10 syllables and the second part only 6. Instead of having a steady rythm of stressed/unstressed or unstressed/stressed syllables, there is little to no rythm in the stressed and unstressed syllables especially in the second part of the sentence. If you would have to read all of the text in this game out loud, it would be almost impossible to make it sound natural.
This could have been fixed by slightly changing the text to something like:
"







",

,



.
It's still no prose, but now both parts of the sentence have 8 syllables and there is a more natural sounding rhythm of unstressed and stressed syllables. If the entire game would have used proper meter like this, the sentences would have flowed better and the rhyme would have added something to the game.
Unfortunately this isn't the case and almost all rhyming sentences exhibit the same problem throughout the game. It makes the text hard to read and often it's clear that words were chosen not because they made sense but merely because they happened to rhyme.
It's not bad enough to give this game a thumbs down, because I did like it overall. But the way rhyme is used it's clearly no more than a gimmick.

I love Broken Sword. It's one of my favorite adventure games of all time – I grew up with it. Hearing about an update to one of my favorite games made me weary but I remained optimistic. Naturally, I tried to like it. But I just can't.
This revision completely butchered the original on so many levels; it's an absolute disgrace.
The new story arc doesn't bring anything new or interesting to the table and seems unnecessarily tacked on. It explores a side story that is negligible in the greater context and waters down the impact of the original story's writing and pacing immensely (Never mind the fact that the iconic "Paris in the Fall" intro was cut out of the game for it).
The new environments, icons, dialogue portraits and character models look really out of place when displayed right next to their by now 17 year old assets which negatively impacts the cohesiveness: the clashing art styles and different asset qualities make the game feel terribly stitched together.
The new UI, automatically displayed points of interaction as well as the help system make the game unbearable for players of the original version.
Revolution went to the extremes with the handholding: everything is pointed out to you and instantly made visible. You never feel taken seriously as a player and it's almost as if the game doesn't want or need your skills to be solved.
Sadly, they took the phrase Directors
a bit too literally. Besides the aforementioned intro, Revolution removed details like waving flags, idle and dialogue animations as well as ambient sounds but also integral parts of the game like certain dialogues and
. The cut narrative aspects in particular break the game's story and writing which was already impaired by the new sidestory.
The missing details destroy the charm the original used to have. This content was removed for absolutely no logical reason and is a decision of the developer I can't understand or get behind. Who thought this was a good idea? Cutting parts of your story without replacing them with something more meaningful doesn't do the game's pacing any favors whatsoever.
The most jarring of all the omissions however is that you can't die.
(
). Presumably, this was done in order to save the player from losing too much or all of their progress. Removing this aspect eliminates incredibly much suspense and is a case of game design decisions meant to appeal to a more contemporary audience causing the loss of suspense, gameplay, atmosphere and ultimately enjoyment in the process.
If you are curious about the extent of the changes, you can find some of them here:
Regardless whether you experienced the original or not, use ScummVM to play the original release if you can obtain it (Or purchase it via GOG where you will receive both versions with one purchase) and let this abomination rot in the store. You will get a more polished, detailed and cohesive gameplay experience out of it.
Who knows what Charles Cecil and Revolution were thinking. But it certainly wasn't anything good.

By the point of this fifth install of the Zup series you probably know exactly what to expect - a fairly short (about an hour) physics puzzle game where you click red blocks to make them explode (and in a few cases click whitish blocks to make them disappear, although that is more Oik's territory than Zup's). Using these resources you have to get the blue target block/circle reach the green target area.
A lot of the fun here is how repeatable the physics are - you explode some barrels and several blocks might fly around the screen bouncing off strategically placed objects for all of them to land in exactly the right place they need to be for the level to be completably. There is a reasonable amount of puzzle solving with a decent difficulty curve, but nothing too difficult. Quite a few levels also require you to time an explosion to intercept the target ball as it falls past, but in these cases you often are firing multiple blocks, and there will either be a big run off area or a catcher mitt style structure so you don't have to be too perfect in your timing.
This edition adds a new block type of a trigger which has to be hit by a yellow barrel in order to make another block elsewhere disappear, which allows a whole new set of puzzles to be created. My only complaints here are the colour of these triggers doesn't have a huge contrast compared to the normal blocks, so they aren't easy to spot at a glance when first viewing a puzzle.
While a couple of editions of Zup have had level designs that seem a bit too samey for long sections (especially when a new gimmick for that edition gets used over and over in very similar ways), this time the levels seem fairly varied as you go through. The new trigger mechanic seems to get used a lot, but then there are a lot of past Zup levels from previous editions, so creating new levels that aren't too similar to past ones probably explains this.
Overall then a quick, cheap moderately entertaining physics puzzle game with solid level design that is well worth a look.

Thankfully, "Sniper Elite V2" is a FAR better game than Sniper Elite" (the first game in the series).  The developers fixed all my major complaints with that earlier work.  In fact, the only complaints I've got about this game are:
- Enemies spawn in areas as you cross certain points.  You can spend all the time in the world clearing everything out, take one step, and have a whole new batch of enemies appear in the very same areas you just cleared out.  That's a tad annoying.
- In several cases, the newly spawned enemies will default to having seen you (even if you're totally hidden).
- If you're an Achievement hound, there's an Achievement for finding all the bottles and all the gold bars in the game.  The problem is that the bottles are just plain old brown beer/wine bottles in areas consisting mostly of rubble, and the gold bars are practically identical to all the bricks lying around those rubble-strewn areas (except for the fact that they gleam with light).
Normally, I write these reviews after I complete all the Achievements in a game.  But, since there are a lot of co-op Achievements here, I'm doing it now after having finished the base game and a few Achievements here and there.  It took me 21.3 hours to do that.  You'll see some reviews here where people claim they finished the game in 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, etc. hours (those are ones I found).  I say horse-puckey.  Maybe they grabbed their SMG and ran through the thing like they were playing Doom.  But, this is a sniper game where the whole point is to kill enemies from a distance and not be seen while doing it.  So, don't worry about not getting your money's worth.  The game is very well done and even a single run-through will be worth it even at my miserly dollar per hour metric.
UPDATE:  It took me another 16.7 hours (for a total of 38.0 hours) to finish the base game with all Achievements completed.  Definitely worth the money (though it looks like it goes on sale for 5 or 6 dollars every 3 or 4 months).

I hate grinding. I really do. But not in this game as the grinding is rewarding and the battle system is a lot of fun.
Secrets of Grindea is a 2D Action-RPG with roots in the SNES-era ARPG games such as the Mana-series and Legend of Zelda. The battles are fast and the basics are quite easy to learn. You can't just button smash your way through though. The system is very much reliant on your skills and strategies, despite the fact that you can grind for levels to overpower yourself.
The beauty of the game is that you don't have to grind an excessive amount of time, but often you'll want to. If you just want to enjoy the story and explore the world, you can advance fairly quickly through the story. Boss battles are often very tough if you're underleveled but with a correct strategy, they are very beatable without power grinding. You unlock new areas to explore by advancing the story and you are free to roam the areas you've unlocked. The enemies are visible on the map and they are all avoidable.
For the completionists, there is a ton of optional things to do. There's fishing, potion-making, side-quests, secrets, puzzles, pet catching, pet leveling, arena-battles, crafting and a ton of mob drops that are hard to get. I myself have already spend at least 2 times more than my Steam play-time shows in this game, doing all the optional stuff. That was over a year ago when there wasn't this much new content in it yet.
The leveling system is very nice since you get points to spend on skills as you please. There is a good amount of different skills to choose from and all of them have strategic value. There is also a lot of different equipment which you can buy, craft or get as a drop from the monsters.
The story isn't awful either. It's not the focus of the game nor the main reason to buy the game. It has enough meat in it to keep you motivated to go further and to give some context to your adventure but don't expect it to move you to tears or grab you emotionally. Think Pokemon games and their story and you'll know what level of story-telling to expect.
As a big fan of stories and powerful story-telling in games, I would've wanted a more compelling story-telling personally but because of the strong gameplay, the lack of PSX-era Final Fantasy-esque story telling doesn't bother me much at all.
All in all, this has been my #1 most anticipated indie-game since 2013, when I bought the pre-order beta. SoG is a a good balance of excellent gameplay, exploration and story. While the story is not up to par with the gameplay, the complete package is still excellent and the 3 Swedish Stooges can be proud of what they've been working on for all these years.

Full Review:

Platform games aren't at the top of my list - mainly because of their limited world, low replayability and (many of them) being highly linear - however, Waking Mars is one of the most enjoyable games I've been playing lately, and for me, one of the best platform games to date. Its sci-fi/ Mars setting and artwork caught my attention; but it was the goal of creating and encouraging an ecosystem within the Red Planet that sold me on it.
The story is simple and straightforward, but it is intelligently executed and really intriguing. Character development is little, but just right. There are no enemies, only yourself, the 'flauna' and the environment -  but you might be surprised at just how much of a threat you can pose to yourself. The goals are laid out before you in a no-nonsense manner: you are exploring, searching, gathering, manipulating, creating, and de-constructing to create, in a more favourable way to the environment's (and your) needs. There is something to be said for balance, and you learn by trial and error; but don't worry, there is nothing that you can't undo - though it may require a measure of patience.
The game mechanics are superbly fluid - the game runs without a hitch (it's enough for me to say that if I can run this on my present setup, anyone can - trust me). The time, work and research that went into this game is incredible. Overall gameplay is relaxing with adequate moments of doubt, constant wonder and dashes of uncertainty. It is a wonder to me that I do feel a sense of real isolation while playing - I think this is thanks to the beauty of the graphical style and the great music - but this is exactly what I would expect, it's the lonely and mysterious Red Planet, after all. The time it will take you to complete this game? It depends on you. I completed it (EDITED: start to finish TWICE) at the listed time played.

One of the best features of this game for me was the ability to revisit any area at any time without limit. This alone makes this platformer just so non-linear. As well as being vital - you will have to travel around to resupply your seeds, revisit some areas dependant on other areas' progress, or just to re-balance an area if need be - it is a real treat to be able to return and see how the caverns have been thriving (or not) in your absence.
IMPORTANT: If non-stop action, mayhem and destruction - i.e. death-n-glory - are your bread-and-butter, you will fast become bored with Waking Mars. BUT...
...If you enjoy platform games, I believe this is a must for your collection and many will undoubtedly enjoy it. If you are a wary platformer like me, it may blow you away and you won't regret this purchase (reg. price is reasonable; on sale price, you'd be crazy not to try it).

I like it when a game, apart from delivering a certain amount of fun and challenge or aesthetical sensations, actually offers me something valuable, something that I can use to broaden my horizins a little, to fill certain gaps in knowledge or give insights into topics I would normally never explore.
Kisima Ingitchuna does exactly that. Not only does it look and sound great, but it also brought closer to me a certain culture and places that I may never have a chance to experience in person.
Anyway, the review:
- lovely, lively (despite being mostly deserted) setting. Characters are beautifully designed and animated, especially the fox,,, Plenty of little details which indicate that the developers really put their hearts into making the game, like the way the hood falls from the progatonist's head when the wind blows in ther face... The graphics are simple, yet I never felt they lacked refinement. Additionally, despite the locations being often quite similar, I never got the feeling of monotony.
- rather good, I think. The howling of the wind sounds great and its presence nearly everywhere really seems to be one of the factors that create the atmoshpere of the game. The narrator does an excellent job and the music fits the atmosphere very well. Saldy, none of the musical tracks have had a hjuge effect on me and to be honest, I don;t really remember what the music sounded like. It was there, sure enough, and didn't spoil anything but it just wasn't very memorable.
- nothing groundbraking, really. The game is a rather simple platformer with hardly any puzzles for the player to solve and some co-op content thrown in. Playing solo, like I have, it is no harder to finish the game than if one were to invite a friend to help, which I find a very positive feature. The AI of the companion does what it's supposed to most of the time, albeit the number of places where it is necessary is very limited. The game worked nice with a gamepad, until it decided that both characters should perform exactly the same moves, which inevitably led to one of them falling to their deaths... Still, at least I had the chance to see that mouse + keyboard combo work perfectly fine as well
- This is where the game really comes into its own. The story is based on an actual Inuit tale and is a really nice adaptation of a folk tale. The characters are likeable but given that the game is short, there is not much time to see any of their personalities to develop very far.
Were you to consider just the above, Never Alone would seem as an average, pretty platformer. But it's far from that. All the parts somehow add up to much more than just a sum of the advantages. The game has some sort of magic that kept me wanting to play on. This charm is defenitely not to be found in the gameplay but rather in the story, characters, the music and the visuals.
Apart from the game itself, there are quite a few collectibles, which unlock insights (literally) into the culture and the stories that inspired the game. While in the majority of games I just can't be bothered to look at them, here they felt just as much a vital part of the game as anything else. To be honest, I wish there was more. Much more.
In conclusion, I would give the game itself a score of about 7/10. The tangible mechanics, visuals and audio of the game are nothing groundbreaking, although they leave a positive impression. However, the feel of the game, the story and the 'Insights' lift the grade to a final
.

You go through the process of planting seeds, deciding which plants to grow--which you are scored per area based on your choices--exploring, and collecting seeds. It's slow moving, and collecting seeds can be time consuming--even warping back to old areas, just to collect seeds for new areas, sometimes more than once per area.
Watching plants through their animations can be slow growing. I suppose if you want all the achievements, be careful 5 staring each level, then moving on. You might actually miss something.

What a nice surprise this turned out to be. I was expecting one of those cheapo Unity-made "horror" games, but while there are enough scary-tense moments and the usual amount of jankiness, particularly in the animation and translation department, rest assured that this is not your typical Youtuber fodder.
This is the kind of game that suffers from being tagged with a label. Here you'll find ingredients of several genres -adventure, puzzle, horror, even "walking simulator"-, but each one should be taken with a grain of salt. At its heart, the main goal of the game is to tell a simple story while doing its best to immerse the player in the thick atmosphere of a Russian post-apocalypse.
I love how there's little to no hand-holding to guide the player. The identity and the motivations of the main character(s) remain shrouded in mystery from the start, though certain items and areas both serve to provide color and reveal details about the background of this dying world. Little bits of dialogue, notes and paper clippings scattered here and there, and even optional actions help the player put the pieces together.
Progress is stricly linear, but there's a certain amount of freedom for exploration in each area. Puzzles are light and action is sparse. The opening sequence should make it clear that this is an experience to be savored by the more patient of players, the kind that won't mind stopping every once in a while to take in the sad beauty of the desolate environments and, maybe, capture it with the in-game camera to keep a virtual memento. The game does an stellar job in drenching the player in melancholy (aided by the music, which is fantastic) and the ending packs an emotional punch. Highly recommended after all the mentioned caveats.

I never thought it would be possible for a bunch of faceless rectangles to have so much personality and character, but Thomas Was Alone pulls it off, and quite well for that matter. This is largely in part to Danny Wallace's excellent narration that helps tell a story of sentience, self-purpose, and companionship. Like the game's visual style, gameplay mechanics are very minimalistic which helps create a laid back and relaxing platforming experience. The chiptune soundtrack is beautifully soothing, while the controls are tight and accurate. And although the game is short (~3 hours) and never much of a challenge, that really seems to fit the game's style quite nicely. It never drags on and never frustrates, which goes back to that relaxing experience that the dev seems to strive for.
Overall, Thomas Was Alone was a big surprise and a reminder to never judge a book by its cover. A simplistic-by-design platforming game that is packed with some interesting underlying themes and quality storytelling.

Okay. Let's start from the beginning.
The Isle has one of the worst communities in game history. They are just as toxic as the sonic fanbase. Not to mention that the developers aren't any different, they too are annoying. Every Isle server has a... mix of certain people and their personallities. Straight out of the bat, 55% are pretty much trolls and early-game-players that try their best to make an excuse for why they cannot play this certain rule. 25% are actual people that have brains, and 15% are... Unkown and pretty much never answer any chat. And the remaining 5% report literally everything you do. They try their best to get you and/or everyone else in 'trouble.' Yeah, I know what you're thinking. "This is only from your personal experience!!!!" Well, Surely if this has been going on for awhile, then there's countless more people that have at least thought of this in their minds.
Now that that's out of the way, let's get to the real reason I don't recommend this game.
To be honest, I was actually exited for the game when it was released for early access, And it was fun. Back in the day when v1 and v2 roamed, The Isle was a MUST-GET. But, Once v3 came out, everything just changed. The most change of course, was the community.
Yeah, it is still in Early Access, but I had major expectations for it. I expected that the playstyle would beat most survival games, I expected that it'll take over the competing dinosaur games that are coming out.. I expected that it would be similar to a Stomping Lands 2...
Once again, I shouldn't blame the developers for this since once again, it's in Early Access. But I'm not blaming them. I'm Criticizing them. The phrase "Early Access" isn't a tool that can be used against someone if they were to criticize the game. It's meerly pointing out the mistakes and showing them what they should improve.
Gameplaywise, it honestly isn't the best. There's a whole bunch of connection issues that need to be fixed when in contact of another player. Also the goal: Which to grow, Progress to another dinosaur, or to just chill in sandbox, get's really repetitive after an hour of playing. And I mean REALLY repetitive. Playing in an isle server without friends online is like food without a drink. It's useless.
But anyways, Here's the point. Don't get this game UNTIL it fully releases. Why am I saying "Until it fully releases?" That is because I think the gameplay and the community will change until then. If it doesn't, Then I don't know... Support Saurian or something. But yeah. I recommend playing this when it releases.
Welp, these are my thoughts for the game. They may not be positive, but it sure will bring an intresting comment section.
Also, Please do not attack anyone for liking or supporting this game since this is meerly my opinion.

Cute and interesting, The Reject Demon: Toko Chapter 0 - Prelude is pretty good. It definitely makes me excited for the next chapters

The characters themselves seem defined and individual (No character shares too simular of speech patterns.)

The relationship between Toko and Nadia is cute and their personalities contrast and harmonize just enough to make the relationship feel genuine and sincere.

The only thing I disliked is that Nadia's advances feel too rushed in the beginning, though that is later explained. Even so it made it difficult for me in the beginning before knowing the reasons for Nadia being so forward, it felt out of character for the Nadia that had just been presented. (This may be me looking too deep or just me assuming that Nadia wouldn't be the type to flirt like that in the beginning. I may just be picky.)
I tend to prefer to watch feelings develop over time, but this does make more room for us to see where the relationship goes and how it will change. Too many dating sims/ visual novels stop when the characters come together and you never really see how the relationship grows.
So in summary:
It is worth checking out.
and I'm excited to see how the dynamics of their relationship changes over time and with new challenges.

Revised review, after much completation on my part. (I will take Hollow-Oak's advice and actually say what I do not like).
I bought this "game" on sale because I was curious about visual novels. I had heard about them and of course they are more or less mentioned quite often in anime and manga.  Now I know what a visual novel is, and it is what is says it is - a visual novel.  Basically a picture book that turns its own pages.  OK.  I can live with that.
In researching visuals novels I discovered many are interactive, and are simulation games, which is actually what I thought this was.  Visual novels though they fall in the catergory of simulation games are not since they lack any interaction by the "gamer".  OK.  I can live with that too.
NOW about this story.  I found it VERY bizarre.   Here you go flamers and haters I equate this story to 'Rocky Horror Picture Show'.  Bizarre, off-beat, rather disjointed with at best a weak plot (?), if a musical instrument power up can be called a plot.  The story itself made little sense and I did watch it twice just to really try and give this story a fair chance.
I also tried very hard to watch this supernatural girl-fest fiction with a very, very open mind.  Half of my mind says charming love story between two girls, and the other half screams OMG all the things to do if one wants to end up on a missing person's list and dead.  If the writers had really set up the romance better and laid it on thicker then oh say a gallon of jelly on a thin slice of bread I personally could have engaged in the story.  Love at first sight even, would have been better then this tripe.
In conclusion: I will also say the same thing I said about 'Rocky Horror Picture Show' after the first time I saw it.   Hmmm... well...I liked the music.  (And that was the only thing I liked.)

I remember playing and finishing Sniper Elite 2 years ago on the Xbox 360. Since I got this for free on Steam, I wanted to play a few missions and see how it fares.
It’s still exactly how I remembered it, except with better graphics and framerate.
You play as a WW2 sniper, naturally, and complete various missions while trying to be as stealthy as possible. You can attempt to go through guns blazing, but Sniper Elite isn’t a run and gun type of game. This is pretty evident by scarce secondary weapon ammo, scarce secondary weapon ammo drops from enemies and you take lots of damage quickly. It’s do-able but clearly not what the game wants you to do, in my opinion.
Gameplay is “decent”. The main stealth component can become broken fairly easily. The enemies will immediately know where you are when exposed. Somehow they can hit you repeatedly with submachine guns from insane distances. While, when using my own, can’t hit things 20 feet in from of me. There can be wild swings of very good AI and very poor AI.
However, I enjoyed the ability to focus and slow down time for a perfect shot. The popular bullet cam is neat but can break up gameplay when it keeps activating. You can simply turn this feature off, however. In some levels you are given a chance where a loud noise occurs to fire your shot without alerting others. Another neat feature that adds some strategy.
I’ve seen some complaints about AI spawning when passing a certain point in a level. I would agree with this only when they spawn and come out shooting right away. Otherwise, it’s a fairly realistic way enemies may appear. You thought something was clear but it wasn’t.
Graphics are ok considering it was 2012. Some things can look dated but the overall look is still sharp.
One thing publishers need to stop is advertising that must be clicked off before exiting the game. This game is guilty of that. It’s annoying to have possibly paid full price for this game, only to be advertised to when trying to exit out.
+Great sniping game / mechanics
+Bullet cam
+Music/sounds above average
+Graphics as a whole still stand up today.
+Stable
+Collectibles

+Stealth components broken easily
+Enemies know your location and hit with high accuracy
+A.I. intelligence swings
+Repetitive level design / gameplay
+Ads for new Sniper Elite game when exiting
There is some good and some bad here. I’d still recommend it, but nowhere near the full asking price of $20.

Another Zup! game, another month. Ever since Greenlight has been published, it is no secret that cheaply thrown together games created by people who don't have the dedication to create a completed game get published to greenlight every day. Zup! Zero combines two of the things that I dislike greatly, casual puzzle games where levels can be completed in seconds, and games put together in a premade software without trying to create something interesting.
Created in Clickteam Fusion, Zup! Zero is the fifth zup game in a series of bland puzzle games. This time, Zup! is another physics puzzler that uses explosions to guide a blue ball into a turquoise platform. The main interaction in the puzzle is clicking red objects to create an explosion that sends yellow objects  towards a direction and clicking grey tiles to make objects fall. Being a poorly thought out game would normally turn away people from buying such a game.
However, Zup knows that earning a lot of achievements and earning trading cards is an effective way to convince people to buy the game. To further seal the deal, Zup! makes the price at $1, the lowest base price a game can be on steam without being free. Zup! takes achievements to the extreme by generating an achievement around every second you play the game. When you make achievements earned so easily to the point of not having any special merit, then the word "Achievement" loses it's meaning.
Zup! is a game series that will continue to pop up on the steam front page with such a successful formula to attract casual players into buying it.

I would like to start this review off with a disclaimer, this chapter is AMAZING!
BUT, I am noticing a trend of VNs lately releasing things episodically, and there is nothing wrong with that IF you have an ACTUAL release schedule in place already. Right now this game is nothing but a tease with the promise of a game that will come.....eventually. No set release dates, no real promises, and very little information is given other than, 'we have two games coming out before releasing the other chapters for this.' And, of course, no set release dates on those either. So late leaves me here, buying a TASTE of a wonderful game or at least the idea of one with no view of the main course in sight.
To be fair, while surfing through the discussions I did see a post from the developer that stated that one of the games slated to come out before this one has some projected time periods of 'sometime during the winter, we hope, but not nessicarily this one.' That leaves me even more annoyed,
If they put out some proper dates on the future of this series then I will GLADLY change this review to a recommended because the setting, the characters and the story telling meathod are all so amazing, but until they get their release schedule in order I cant, in good heart, recommend this chapter to anyone.
