Honestly this game has a lot of potential, and that's why I'm sad to give it a negative review.
The core gameplay is really exciting, a lot of interesting combos and mixups makes for an interesting fighting game.
The reason I dislike it though is that it's far too easy to be defensive, watching two good players fight is just watching them stand there pretty much until the other attacks.
Then there's the cheese. Enviromental kills, revenge mode, 2v1s etc. etc. I'm not saying they should be removed, they can make for interesting gameplay, but as it is right now you sometimes spawn on a bridge with no ledges where a single GB can kill you because you get thrown off. A ledge here and there is fine, but ubisoft please limit them.
And the game is greedy. Once you've paid $60 for the game itself it keeps asking you to buy ingame currency to unlock stuff. Yes you can also get the same things by playing, but I really hope we'll get rid of the pay real money for a random chance at loot thing. Too many games do it and it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tbqh.
For the servers, yes they are ♥♥♥♥♥♥. As in good luck finding and completing a match of anything not 1v1, 2v2, or elimination. Queuetimes are awfully long, and the servers die all the time mid game. On skirmish and dominion you spend more time finding a game than playing, and only 1 in 3-4 games even finish due to people leaving and the servers dying. Peer to peer works for 1v1s and 2v2s, but ubisoft please get dedicated servers. This game has so much potential.
Also there's gearscore in most gamemodes and if your gear isn't strong enough (which you upgrade by endless grinding of playing the same hero or just buying them) there's a very little chance you'll win.
TLDR: great game, good with friends, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ servers, greedy, bad balance.

Hey you, yes you. Do you like being shot to death 2 mins after you leave the safe zone by other friendly players? Do you like not free to play, pay to win MMO'ish games (that can only seem to support a fairly low number of players per server) where you can buy fake currency with real currency to buy life saving items like melee weapons, health water, gliders, backpacks,  clothes and character emotes (like dancing, gesturing etc)? Do you like droppimg those things on death for assumedly any one to raid (you get to keep your clothes if you are wearing them and I assume the gestures)? Do you like losing all your levels and recreating your character everytime you die? Do you like delivering boxes through empty desolate (but also very pretty - the graphics in this game are nice) landscapes? Do you like a total lack of worthwhile NPC dialogues or character from you NPC's?  Do you like a minimal variety in your monsters?  Do you like not being over inundated with too many servers to choose from (not many left).  Weird glitches when ever you go through water (being able to live under water, having watery distortion follow me while on land)? Then this is the game for you, otherwise take the above in to consideration.
It's not that Nether is actually bad as such it's just the over combination of factors can leave a bitter taste in a new players mouth.
The landscape looks breathtaking when you first log on to it (although it is difficult at first to determin what you can interact with and at what angle you need to be on in order to get the vehicle or whatever to give you the option to do so) though variation is a lacking.
The people all look a little like characterless mannequins (players and NPC's alike) however what few monster desgns there is do look good on close inspection if a little derivative. The monster noises are also quite good if repetitive. From the trailer and from playing the game  it seems to want to deliver what we love from the Last of us (minus the scripted parts), Borderlands series (minimal RPG elements), DayZ (survival with teleporting fleshy monsters things instead of zombies) and Minecraft (the reliance on item crafting).
It makes for an interesting soup of ideas that sort of works but at the same time sort of feels like it misses the mark.
If you have a crew of players I'm sure you can get more out of this, though I suspect  that most of the fun will be had fighting against other groups of players for dominance of the map (though it has to be said that there are a host of other games that can offer this same experience or better).
If you want to try this solo, this game may try your patience.

This game is marketted as a "dynamic graphic adventure." An adventure game that contains dynamic movement of a platformer. I felt that, in its 8 hours of playtime, it contained too much platforming and too little plot for a graphic adventure... and it had two or three fiddly puzzles involving memorization or careful notes that would be too annoying for platofrmers. I think they're annoying in adventure games... The auto-save checkpoints were sometimes oddly placed and the shortcuts that you could open up to retrace steps (frequently necessary) frequently barely saved any time. Psychonauts,  The Cave, A Story About My Uncle, and Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons I think all did this genre better. All these games I mention are really platformers with little violence and without the kinds of formal puzzles in Candle. If you want a platformer with Myst-like puzzles, then this game is for you. It is beautifully animated, although relatively quick and light on story content. But I think there are plenty of games with better puzzles and plenty of games with better peaceful platforming and more content.

If you're OK climbing a steep learning curve while routinely facing opponents that have mechanical advantages as well as more experience, then this game might hold some promise, but if you don't think getting jumped into a prison gang sounds like a good time then stay away from this.

I bought this game for 20 cents, thinking I couldn't go wrong with buying such a cheap game. I was wrong.
The controls are painfuly simple. WASD for movement, left click to shoot, and right click to pick up items/zoom.
You have one gun the entire game. And if that isn't bad enough, it's a single-shot rifle that takes 7-10 seconds to reload before you can use it again. Seriously. Enemies are fairly scarce in the game, but when they show up, they're unbelievably annoying to deal with. The first enemy in the game I had to fight (a giant snake), took me FIVE well placed shots to kill. Needless to say, I had to walk (I say walk, because YOU CAN'T RUN IN THIS ♥♥♥♥ING GAME) in circles for a couple mins after every shot just to reload. The extremely long reloading time wouldn't be too much of a burden if you didn't die after getting hit once. But of course, that is how this game is unfortunately.
My biggest gripe with this game is the graphics. They're honestly so bad, that it serves as a major inconvience when you're trying to figure out where the ♥♥♥♥ you are (which tends to happen often, even though the game is quite linear). The game's graphics are mostly based around an extremely un-needed film grain, which looks like one of those heavily colored instagram filters. Not joking or exaggerting. You do have a lantern in the game, but  it seriously only illuminates your feet. I can understand what the developers where going for with this game; a mysterious, eerie, middle-of-nowhere-fuzzy type of look. The execution of the idea falls more flat than a pancake. The game just looks terribly blurry all of the time, so your characters peripheral vision ends up being vacant; sort of a tunnel vision kind of view. It doesn't help when you're facing the other enemy in the game, (Werewolf) as 1: you can't kill it during the early course of the game, but only slow it down per every shot you land. And 2: THE GAME BECOMES MORE ♥♥♥♥ING BLURRY, AND ADDS AN OBNOXIOUS RED FILTER (call of duty esque; but a lot poorer) so you can only see the shadow outline of the creature.
The story might actually be the strongest point of the game, but that is not saying much what-so-ever. The game has SEVERAL plot holes, and is more rushed than a man who woke up 2 minutes before he has work. Most of the game is making you look in a house for a key, which is used to unlock another house with another key, which is used to unlock another house.....more likely than not for another ♥♥♥♥ing key. The game isn't really ever clear with what your main objective is other than finding the werewolf and killing him. But of course in your quest of doing so, you're stuck going from point A to point B, collecting generally useless things and moving on to the next area (with barely any context to why you're going to this place).
I really wanted to enjoy this game, (hell, i still might try to for whatever reason) but this game takes one step forward, and 3 steps back. Then shoots itself in the foot, because nothing in this game makes any ♥♥♥♥ing sense at all.
I wish I had more to say, but I've ran out of things to criticize. But to summarize, this game is worth the 20 cents I spent on it, but if it was anything over 99 cents I would recommend buying an Arizona instead, since you'll enjoy it more than this confusing, clunky, poorly crafted "game"

SOMA is quite an excellent horror game. It manages to be subtle both in its mechanics and in its storytelling. When comparing this to Frictional Games' previous title Amnesia, while the latter had a creepy environment, pressuring atmosphere and terrifying chase sequences, SOMA also takes a different, more subtle approach with its horror: The monsters' (and
) mutilated designs are nightmare inducing in of themselves, and each enemy has its own unique mechanics that the player must learn in order to survive. But the game really sells in its psychological horror that haunts those unprepared for it (that is all I dare to say about it, go check it out, I say it's worth it!
I am a person who is usually
at handling horror games, especially chase sequences. However, this title, while making my heart race multiple times, never made me unable to proceed forward for more than 5 minutes at most (as opposed to 10-15 mins normally). Part of the reason is that the monsters follow certain rules, and are more about hide-and-seek than chase-around-narrow-hallways-in-frantic-panic (which too many games have). The game rewards those who are patient and dare to examine their behaviour, which I think this is some excellent design.
Finally, those who just can't handle monsters in horror games can download a mod from workshop that makes the enemies passive in most situations. As the game's horror is also very story oriented, you can still enjoy it even when the constant threat on your life is eliminated... for most of the time.

I wonder who was stupid enough to think that making a game about a bunch of anthromorphic rectangles was possibly a good idea.
Well they ought to be proud of themselves, because they were right.
I played through it in one sitting, and it was penominal. The story did a wonderful job of making its characters endearing. The narration is great, the music is amazing, and there's something beautiful about its minimalist graphical style. So many puzzle-platformers try to be the next Braid, but this one wasn't afraid to try something new, and as a result it was brilliant.
That said, it's not perfect. Just know that in spite of what I'm about to say, it's amazing and you should play it.
A lot of the levels are just busy work - making you do a slow but easy task over and over again. A decent portion of the game felt like padding.
There are also a few ways in which the story left me dissatisfied. Spoilers below. Proceed at your own risk.
I wish that the game had focused more on the original group. It felt like we barely got to meet Sarah before she was gone with the rest. It would have been nice to have more levels with them all together, showing off their interactions and giving them a more satisfactory ending. It made sense for them to do what they did, but it would have been nice to see, say, Chris confess his love for Laura and how their relationship would change as a result.
As for the new rectangles, it felt like we didn't the same emotional investment in them that we did in the others. Their personalities and interactions felt very bland by comparison. The twist that GREY WAS ACTUALLY EVIL came suddenly and seemingly pointlessly, and his defeat was unsatifying. Even though the Pixel Clouds had been introduced much earlier, it still felt like it came out of nowhere. And neither Team Jump nor Paul got resolution of any sort - They just kind of disappeared after the third- and second-to-last levels, respectively.
Still, fantastic game. Play it.

Never Alone (Kisima Inŋitchuŋa) is a short and sweet story that you probably haven't heard before. As far as puzzle platformers go, it's not particularly difficult, but what it lacks in complexity, it makes up for in beautiful graphics, atmosphere, and an endearing story.
There are some downsides, where some of the gameplay elements were made difficult by glitches. Often, Nuna would fail to grab onto a spirit or ledge for no particular reason. Sometimes the Fox would move to try and AI its way to where you were going, and the spirit would disappear. It could also be difficult to figure out where to go next, since doing so was dependent the Fox being close enough to a spirit to make it show up, so you would have to know where to go in order to know where to go. There is not a lot of replay value, and even if you're a completionist, it should be easy to get all the achievements on the first playthrough.
Despite all that, I'd still recommend giving it a play-through. It's a unique game and a good example of what a cultural piece should be. I guarantee that if nothing else, you'll learn something new.

The Darkness 2
Rating 8/10
Overview: Underrated First Person Shooter
The Good:
+ Cell shaded graphics
+ The game has a strong narrative which holds the game together otherwise it would turn into a mindless shooter. Although the plot itself is pretty basic the developers did a great job of presenting the story. The characters may be stereotypical of what you would expect in a mafia however it doesn't take away the fact they are believable and expertly voiced.
+ The game features a variety of guns which is what you would expect from any first person shooter however the twist in this game is that you have two demonic arms, one for picking/throwing objects and the other as a high powered melee weapon. You can also execute enemies in some pretty horrific ways.
+ Speaking of gratuitous violence, it works well in this game. Most games have over the top violence just for the sake of it yet I feel this game really nailed this particular aspect, it really sells the notion that you are possessed by dark forces.
+ Killing enemies and collecting relics in the levels allows you to level up different skills among 4 skill trees.
+ New Game + allows you to replay the game with all your acquired skills
+ Easy Achievements, minimal grinding required.
+ Great voice acting
+ Good soundtrack
The Average:
On the one hand the game is short, roughly 5-7 hours in length. On the other hand the game isn't bogged down with pointless filler either, the game does what it wants to without over extending its welcome.
After you complete the main story, you can try the vendetta campaign, an add on to extend your playtime. You can choose between 4 characters, each with their own weapon, skill trees and powers. You can also play co-op with friends. The problem however is that every level becomes very repetitive of killing wave after wave of enemy. The formula wears itself out very early on. This mode is also very short , roughly 2-3 hours in length.
The Bad:
- Multiplayer is dead

Conclusion
It was a sequel that didn't need to be made but in the end it turned out to be a great game to a very underappreciated game franchise. A fun distraction while it lasts and nothing more. Strongly recommend at a discount price.

This is a great "retro" racing game.  Race up to 8 vehicles on various off-road courses.  From the menu you can select the number of opponents as well as the number of laps.  As of now (1/1/2018) there are six different tracks that you can race in either direction, so twelve variants.  You can race a single track, or multiple tracks (& directions) for a total "season" of twelve races.  Points are totaled for each race and if you finish in the top three you can see your car on the "podium" at the end.
The physics seem pretty good to me.  It is a simple game, so no vehicle damage to simulate.  If you hit another vehicle it will move, likewise if you are hit you will move from the impact.  Graphics are nice, but very basic.  Game music is awesome!  When I saw that Jeroen Tel (1980s video game music genius) was involved with this it brought me from "maybe buy this" to "buy this right now".
In the top-down view it reminds me of the old 1980s Nintendo game RC Pro-Am, but without the various powerups that you would collect.  Also, no upgrades for your vehicle.  Switching to the first-person view and chase cameras the action turns more towards the 1990s Mario Kart without the weapons.
I suggest using the top-down view until you are very familiar with the tracks as it's kind of easy to get lost in first-person view if you don't know where you're going.  Views can be toggled mid-race if you change your mind.  You do get one nitro boost, but I tend not to use it as the AI opponents don't get this perk.
So far I have only played this as single-player using keyboard controls.  I do look forward to getting some controllers and having some folks over for a game party.  In the menu, there's an online play option, but it's grayed out for now.  I found the AI was kind of weak at the default setting, but on the hardest setting I no longer win all the time.

This game is kind of loosely based on a true story... as stated from the outset of the game, in the early 18th-19th century women around the world was once being treated for a condition known as 'Hysteria' of which the only cure known at the time was to have their private anatomy rubbed by doctors. Now a days we laugh at this psuedo science which originated out of all things from a stupid Egyptian belief that a woman's private area can move and cause her many problems from nervousness, to fainting, to being irritable and so on.
Doctors around the world were hopeless, people were dying everywhere from all sorts of diseases, but doctors were apparently brilliant at solving 'hysteria'. Eventually this coined disease turned epidemic as women thronged in droves to the local doctors to have themselves cured from 'hysteria'. The disease became so rampant that doctors began to experience a whole range of problems themselves particularly arthritis and cramping and begged each other to discover a better way of solving this issue. Soon doctors began to experiment with drilling machines, shower heads and ultimately electronic toys. Eventually it was these toys that began to be marketed out to the average woman and with all these women finally cured from their 'hysteria' it was once again safe for man to step outside.
We laugh at the fact that mankind in general was ever so stupid to believe this, in fact we are often shocked to find out that this was still being practiced medically right up into the 1950's and 1980's in several locations. The game touches on this subject rather tastefully (but still offers a full refund for those that find the matter too distressing), the thing is though, in the game we are set for some time in the future where for one reason or another this pseudo-scientific belief is once again hailed as the cure for all things and practiced through the curing of pod chambers.
If this subject itself was not too touchy enough (no pun intended) the matter of mental disability is also majorly explored. You see our main protagonist of the game is 'Clara' who wakes up in a 'Hysteria Clinic' to find out that she is being treated for 'Schizophrenia', a mental illness where she claims that she can hear a voice calling her and manipulating her movements. This brings us to you the gamer. Yes you are her mental illness, her mysterious voice, her religious calling causing her to do things that she may not normally have done.
The game was principally made by this guy
who goes onto explore various questions about mental illness. Can it be solved? Is trying to solve it a good thing? Should we really avoid people with mental issues? Can a good voice in our head eventually turn bad? Really Bad? What effect does out casting have on mental people? Does a Schizophrenic become dependent on their voice? What happens if they were ever to lose it? Would they lose their identity? Their will to live?
The game has quite a few laugh out loud moments and plays out more like a virtual novel rather than a game where your choice maybe really matters. There is a heavy amount of written profanity in it, so the game and it's message will unfortunately be appealing to a limited few because of this. There are 6 hidden sound tapes to find in this town known as Delilah and though you can play these audio tapes  as you travel around town the 'true' significance of these tapes will not be revealed until you have all 6 and can open the 'Secret Room' which reveals some very interesting background information and back story involving the audio tapes which i have never seen in game before until now.
Because of it's original story concept and its novel never done before trick using audio logs I have to reward the game with a thumbs up. However if you are sensitive to coarse language you seriously might want to give this one a miss.

The Norwegian video game industry is in many ways comparable to its film industry, desperately lagging behind the rest of the world and constantly overshadowed by its far more ambitious and prolific neighbor Sweden. But like the film industry we've seen more and more gems pop up on the radar in recent years with games like Through The Woods with its exploration of Norse mythology and the thoroughly impressive art design of Owlboy.
The newest installment in this halfhearted renaissance of Norwegian indie adventure games is the delightfully charming Milkmaid Of The Milky Way where even the recipes for butter and cheese are written down in rhymes. You play as Ruth, a young woman living alone on a farm in a remote fjord in Norway where strange things are happening to her farm at night. It's up to Ruth and her best friend Lykke, a cow she's raised from birth, to unravel a mystery that will change her life forever.
Very early on you start to realize that you're playing the classic hero's journey. Ruth is someone who's down on her luck and in a bad place in her life. Eventually she's confronted with some kind of obstacle or struggle she's got to deal with and the action in the story is her fighting against opposition. Eventually she overcomes her struggle and ends up in a place ahead of where she started off at.
This classic structure is prominently featured throughout the game and it creates a pacing that's close to perfect. Not even during a frustrating pixel hunting section in the beginning was I ever bored playing the game and I was genuinely interested in exploring the world and its characters. In the beginning it might be a little jarring reading the text in the game since it's structured like a poem and you wish there was some voice acting to compensate for it but I got used to it very quickly and eventually I realized that if the game had been filled with voice clips reading out the dialogue it would have taken away from the atmosphere created by the music.
The game starts off in a completely unexpected way where both the music and atmosphere are heavily reminiscent of John Carpenter's The Thing with 80's synth music giving off a deeply unnerving sensation that something really sinister is out to get you. It's absolutely wonderful in the way it can go from an old fashioned mouth harp to 80's synth without it feeling weird or out of place and the reason for that is the context in which it is presented.
The game's difficulty is not something I considered very much playing through it because the puzzles you have to solve are all directly related to the dialogue in the game. If you don't know what to do you can get a vague idea through talking to people and clicking on items and not once is something placed on screen purely for the sake of esthetics. Everything has a purpose, be it for solving the puzzles or world building and character development, and you'll find yourself not really thinking about how to solve the puzzles but more about how to reach your goal with the tools you have at your disposal.
This is something I wish was done more in other genres of gaming where things are put in front of you purely for you to have something to do instead of having a direct impact on the main narrative of the game. I can honestly say I was never bored playing this, not even during my 15 minute pixel hunt in the beginning trying to find way into the spaceship because I desperately wanted to get inside and continue the story.
There are some big twists revealed in the second act of the game that you absolutely need to experience for yourself but I wish I could tell you more about them because they are as unexpected as they are imaginative. As you trek your way through this 1960's sci-fi looking spaceship with your cow buddy and a mind for science, kicking♥♥♥♥♥and taking names you'll find yourself lost in its simple but likable characters, nefarious villain and engrossing atmosphere.

Snagged it during the 2017 Summer sale... didn't expect much because frankly I dislike third person shooters. (Anyone remember when they were referred to as "over the shoulder shooters"?) . I was jones'n for some snipen, so I grabbed this and Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2...
S:GW2 wound up being a generic buffet serving of bland samieness... this thing sucked me right in until it almost hurt.
I generally prefer FPS's because I like guns, and the first person genre smears them all up in your face. Scratched and scarred and warty and smelling (of cordite and machine oil).  Not so here. The Pistols and SMG's are practically vestigial. Mere tools to be applied to certain situations.. the star of this game is the sniping; not the rifles, mind you; the shooting itself. And despite being a gun porn aficianado; (I can't own an arsenal of weapons, so I own an arsenal of gun magazines, and have built a denial wall around what they actually do, instead replacing it with a highly romanticized idea of the honorable defence of family and nation with this really cool piece of equipment, blahdeblahdeblah...yeah, I know it's asinine); this title carries itself just fine without the obsessive focus on the weaponry.
It would initially seem the game's "hook", the bullet time cinematic as a reward for a good shot, the kinda disturbingly satisfying x-ray kill cam for really good shots... would get old, and it still might, I'm just scratching the surface of the campaign, but so far it is just that; highly satisfying. Properly cathartic. I like sniping fools in slow motion with some incongrously cheerful music playing.
This one also handles stealth the best way possible for an action game. The mechanics are there, they're very detailed, and they reward you quite well for succesfully pulling them off... however if you **don't** pull them off it is still Video Gamey enough that you can get out of most scrapes by quickly Sniping All The Things; as opposed to the Entire World Ending because a guard spotted you at a crucial moment.
There is a story....
I'm sure...
All in all, it's far more fun then I had any hopes of expecting it to be, (but then like I said, I generally despise third person shooters anyway and I got this one quite on the cheap; so if my expectations were in the gutter to begin with it's no wonder I was pleasantly surprised.)

Loved the idea of this game ahead of time, bringing native justice issues to the forefront (i.e., climate change) while digging deep into a culture's folklore and storytelling, but it carries a number of gameplay issues that detract from the story and what it's conveying.
It's pretty simple: The platforming feels wonky as heck, with you often clipping through things or refusing to turn around and diving off a cliff with an impossible momentum. The final couple sections of the game can be aggravatingly difficult with these buggy controls, and constantly having to switch back and forth between our two heroes doesn't help when you have to reorient yourself with every switch and a timed event threatening behind ya. (These sections feel built for co-op, so I suspect it's much more fun with an interested partner.)
I hope the developers finetune their future products, as I'm definitely interested in what else they bring out if they continue this trip of mixing games and education and good ol' fashioned stories.
It's worth a look if you're interested in any of those earlier things: First nations culture, climate change impacts, and especially storytelling in video games. (The game features 24 bite-sized documentary clips to collect!) But otherwise, the platforming is bonkers and stay away.

I feel I ought to commend the developers on successfully recreating the arctic environment: the snow and ice are pretty to look at, but death come suddenly and with no warning, and you'll be hoping you're out of it very quickly.
Joking aside, the mechanics of the game are marred by a multitude of clipping errors that make the platforming an exercise in frustration. I did get some nice zoomed out views of a few of the stages when I clipped through them, and there were several times that I had to restart from the last checkpoint because it had become impossible to make progress. Whatever nice things I could say about the art or the story, ultimately don't matter because Never Alone fails as a game. Another, more polished attempt might be welcome, but right now this isn't worth playing.
I've seen several reviews also call out the partner AI as deserving of scorn, with the suggestion that this be played co-op. While I certainly saw my AI partner jump to their death often enough to agree with the first part of that statement, I can't imagine playing this with someone else due to the multitude of bugs already discussed.
As for the cultural notes that make up such a big portion of this game, I think it's worth pointing out that they don't tell the whole story. A great example of this is the short video about King Island, which says that people are just now coming back to the island after a long time, but doesn't mention why. A quick search will give you the answers, but its indicative of the narrative shaping that's going on.

Yet further proof - if any more was required - that you don't need visuals to keep a player entertained. Thomas Was Alone's minimalist style could so easily have led to a pretentious, knobby art-game that only a few people could "get", but it manages to be very accessible and you're never left in any doubt about what's going on. The cast of characters are incredibly well-written, especially considering they're all little more than 4-sided shapes. Their unique abilities form part of their personalities: The tall yellow rectangle, John, loves to show off his jumping abilities to an audience, so he understandably feels a bit put out when the double-jumping Sarah joins the group. Claire, the big blue square, can't move fast or jump far and finds life quite upsetting, but when she realises she's the only one who can float in water, she finds a purpose and decides she's a "superhero", there to save the others. You genuinely feel for these guys and, to be honest, I didn't think it was possible to develop a connection to a motley crew of rectangles.
There is a difficulty curve to the game but it never gets prohibitively tough, and it's certainly not a game you'll struggle to complete. The characters and plot are the stars of the show here, and that's exactly how it should be. You won't get a lot of mileage from Thomas Was Alone, but if you're looking for a lesson in how games ought to tell a story, I can't recommend it enough.

35MM is an atmospheric walking simulator with a shallow story.
I'll start of with the pros:
+ The game looks good in different outdoor environments and in the first few houses that you visit. Especially if you've actually visited houses like this. I'm talking to you, Eastern Europeans and Russians.
+ The premise is extremely interesting.
+ Manages to make moments that shouldn't be scary, scary.
+ The game manages to be scary WITHOUT JUMPSCARES. That's a huge plus for me.
And off to the bigger amount of cons:
- The story never explores the main reason why everything is the way it is.
- Most things that happen are either awfully explained just not explained at all.
- The localization sucks. This is some of the worst translating I've ever seen.
- Audio glitches. When characters speak, then sometimes their mouths move, yet nothing comes out. Subtitles still work, so it's the game's fault, not me being crazy.
- Animations are slow and jerky.
- Small gripe, but the fonts just look so unprofessional. It's like reading a term paper, that's been written in Arial. It just looks ugly.
- Most items aren't interactable even though they should, like drawers. Some can be opened, some cannot.
- Excessant amount of invisible walls.
- And the last, but most definitely not the least... the fetch quests. The game has you walk around, just looking for things ad nauseum. In a few cases it's definitely great. Like when you look for a bucket for water in the middle of the night. It makes no sense, but it worked. Or the next day in the same village when you know someone was there when you were waterhunting and now have to find gasoline in the same village, not knowing whether the person is still there.
So... the cons overtake the pros heavily. But why did I still recommend this?
Well, the reason is the huge amount of *memorable* moments. I can list 4 off the top of my head. That's way better than most games. To compare: a huge game like L.A. Noire only had 2 memorable moments for me. And that game's 3-4 times the length of 35MM at least.
Overall:
6/10 - Barely above average
(All games start at a 5/10 and the grade goes up/down based on the pros/cons)

199x is extremely simple as games go, you basically just move around and interact with a few objects or people to propel the story forward. But the story and narrative more than make up for the barebones gameplay as they're truly good: the plot is slowly revealed as days go by and you find out more about Clara, her past and what's happening to the city. The whole thing seamlessly goes from disturbing to surreal to funny without breaking a sweat and it expertly breaks the 4th wall whenever necessary. Clara is also a very interesting character, has a good depth and is hard not to get attached to her as you play the game.
As good as Clara is it's a shame that the other characters you meet are pretty lacking in depth, even those that are supposed to be important in the story: a bit more interaction would have gone a long way in helping the player get attached to them and care about their fate as much as Clara does. The walking around can also get a bit dull as the few areas you travel through feel a bit too huge and, as far as I know, there's no quick walk button.
If you're ok with a game that is just interested in telling you a story then 199x comes fully recommended: there's something in Clara, her narrative and the subjects the game addresses that can easily leave a mark.

I'm a huge fan of sidescrolling platform puzzlers, so I am sorry to say that Never Alone is one of the more disappointing games I've played in recent memory. First off, the game is short. Really short. As in, it won't take you more than a couple of hours to finish, and there's no replay value to speak of. But maybe this isn't such a bad thing when you consider how lacking the gameplay is in terms of creative, original, well structured challenges and mechanics.
As a platformer, the game falls flat on its face. Many of the platforming sections consist of nothing more than holding right and pressing jump when you get to a ledge. There's no timing, no nuance, no sense of mastery over the game's physics to easily perform a series of complex maneuvers.
The "puzzle" elements of the game are no better. It starts of with simple puzzles involving block pushing and sending the two main characters on separate paths that the other can't go through, and then... totally fails to evolve beyond that level of complexity for the rest of the game. At no point did I ever have to stop and think about what I was doing.
A few chapters in the game introduces a projectile weapon that you use to interact with the environment. This weapon is the most frustrating thing to control in any PC game I've ever played. It seems to totally ignore your mouse input at times and quickly shift the aim all the way across the spectrum at others, with seemingly no change to my input. The controls make it difficult just to hit a large target directly in front of you.  This thing must have been designed for a controller, and it clearly shows. If they had optimized it for mouse controls, many of the puzzles would have been far less tedious.
Later on, the character switching mechanic takes on a new twist as the wolf dies and transforms into a flying spirit. You would think this would be a welcome change, but no. The flying controls are extremely slow and clunky, especially when using the spirit's attract ability which nearly put me to sleep. They could have gotten creative with this mechanic, but instead they implemented the exact same "use spirit to bring platform close to girl, switch to girl and jump on platform, switch to spirit to move platform" puzzle over and over again for the rest of the game.
The game's physics and hit detection are totally unpolished and the characters often fail to grab ledges or other parts of the environment. Some times you will die for no apparent reason, and other times things that are supposed to happen don't happen and will force you to retry. The game does give you a checkpoint after seemingly every single obstacle, which helps alleviate the annoyance factor which comes from this but at the same time makes the game feel cheap and unrewarding.
The game is pretty, but that's all it has going for it. Give this one a miss.

Overall, it'd definitely not worth getting. I would reccommend spending your money on something else to strike up entertainment.

For those who want some variety and maximum enjoyment of the game (or already starting to get tired of quick play), here's a little game mode some friends and I kinda made up.
Step 1) Start a private match, make it a full one.
Step 2) Have a designated Jason, this person will essentially be the coach. It is reccommended you pick part 2 Jason so you can have use of a ton of traps (will be explained later)
step 3) Choose a counselor for everyone to play as (different perks are fine)
step 4) Once you've all spawned in, start grabbing weapons and med spray.
step 5) Pick an area that has some space (example: if in Pakanack, pick the lodge) and drop your wepons and med spray in that area.
step 6) Once enough weapons and sprays are put in pile, have Jason lay traps all around it, radomly is encouraged. This is so the battleground is covered in land mines.
step 7) Pick a medium distance away to have counselors line up, and have Jason count down 3,2,1, GO, counselors will race to weapons.
step 8) COUNSELORS FIGHT EACH OTHER TO THE DEATH!
(I understand  A TON of xp will be lost, but then whoever wins will REALLY want to win)
step 9) last person standing is the winner, and gets to choose how Jason will kill them...toilet, fireplace, tree stump, whatever they want.
step 10) repeat, choose different counselor, and switch the role of Jason to someone else.
I had a blast playing this, I hope others can too. Enjoy.

I Kickstarted this game several years ago.  An unrelated game I Kickstarted turned out to be a dud, so I was preparing myself for another letdown.  Fear not...  After the first play, I was super glad this game came into existence.
Candle has a definite stylistic presence.  Kind of like the games from Amanita Design (Botanicula, Samorost, Machinarium), it breathes creative new life into the "oldie but goodie" puzzle game genre.  Graphics are lush and hand-painted, backgrounds are intricate, and many of the puzzles have an interesting twist.  Several times while playing, I had to take screencaps of cutscenes because the artwork was so lovely.  The storyline has a good balance of seriousness and silliness.
Difficulty is not so high that you'll be reaching for a walkthrough, but some puzzles may have to be left to stew in your brain overnight.  All of the puzzles mesh well with the overall framework of the story; they don't feel like they've been crammed in there awkwardly for the sake of giving you something to do.  The music is upbeat and well-matched to the game play, though not as memorable as in some other games.  I experienced no technical problems, performance for me was smooth and saves/loads are very quick.
I'd call this one a must-buy for puzzle game fans.

A very lovely adventure game with handrawn watercolor art, with an interesting story that deepens as the game progresses. It was inspired by Machinarium, and it shows. It has a dark sense of humor, and a wide array of ways to die in the spirit of old Sierra games.
The devs made the interesting decision to make it a keyboard-controlled platformer, rather than a point-and-click adventure game like I initially expected. I don't think much was gained from that decision, and it adds some frustations in certain puzzles, but it didn't ultimately detract too much from the experience. It did make it hard for my kids to interact with, though. Solutions to some of the puzzles are a little too obscure, got kinda mad, but not too far out of the norm for this kind of game.
Ultimately I really enjoyed it, and its visual beauty (and audio - great music and effects) and story made up for any frustrations I had with the platforming or puzzles.

Objectively, the game is quite nice:
- Story : quite ok, basically, you are a sniper from the OSS trying to stop some nazi scientists to fall into the hands of the reds, while also trying to avoid some mass destruction by the nazi. Standard, you are the one to save the world!
- Sound: some nice atmosphere here and there, but quite repetitive. Nothing epic. Gun sounds are a bit dull though.
- Graphics : quite ok for its age, I would even say that it's pleasant to the eye. Textures are well defined, and the FX are nice.
- Gameplay: basically, you have the option to play like a stealthy sniper (no suppressor on your weapon though except for your gun. It's WW2 afterall...) or you can go all out and use your thompson, but should you choose that way, you won't last to see the end of the war :). Something quite nice here is the killcam when you place a nice shot, following the bullet until the target is completely destroyed.
So for any wargame fan, especially on the WWII era, this game can give you some enjoyable moments.
Now despite all that, I found this game quite boring.
First, the missions are really repetitive. They could have tried to vary a bit the objective. Always the same : Insert, kill some adds that pave the way, position yourself in the sniping nest and shoot the target. That during the 11 missions of this game...
Second, you are actually not that much punished if you lack stealth in your approach. You just have to camp somewhere and shoot all the spawning ennemies one by one. Easy. Even in Sniper elite difficulty. So at the end, considering the above, I just ended up sprinting loud to maeke the ennemies go out, killed them all and then moved on to the end.
Therefore, I would only recommend this game if you get it on sale. Otherwise, try your luck elsewhere. Maybe on the 3rd opus or the 4th one, hoping they fixed these downsides.

Where Sniper Elite leaps forwards in graphical quality from it's predecessor it falls back a long way in so many other ways.
Sniper Elite V2 puts you in the boots of yet another hero sniper back in world war 2. The snipers that you are using are old meaning that you are going to be watching for wind direction and compensating for some extreme bullet drop, this is what Sniper Elite V2 does so well. Once you look past the bullet ballistics and the graphics though, Sniper Elite V2 falls apart.
The AI in the game is both good and bad but for the bad part, it is really bad. The AI will try and flank you or at least it feels like they will try to flank you but with the linear level design, it is hard to be "flanked" through the one entrance into and out of the building. There have been points in the game where I have shot an enemy in the head with a silenced pistol and his friend has seen him drop to the floor, then his friend investigates his body, so I shoot him and he lays on the ground next to the dead body, then the next guy sees this and invesigates. I repeate the process for 5 enemys. I stayed in one place and shot in the exact same spot 5 times and killed all 5 enemys. This gives you a rough idea of the AI in the game. This however can be forgiven as I am not too bothered by bad AI so long as I can look past it.
The one thing that I can not forgive in any game is as if the game is being played out like a scripted movie. On another occasion, I had cleared a room with explosives and loud gun fire once the room was cleared I walked to the next room and out the door of the house to find 4 unsuspecting guards that were not more than 3 meters away from the room with loud gun fire and explosions. They were not alerted and did not even seem to care. Another example of this is enemys that spawn in right before your eyes. I cleared a church floor but as I hit the objective marker I literally watched 3 enemys spawn in befor my very eyes.
Sniper Eliter 1 put you in multiple towns with enemies patrolling, if you were spotter it was your fault if you took damage you couldn't just wait and it would all be better, you would have to use one of the few medkits you had. This game you now have the ability to regenerate health like some kind of super hero. Enemies pop up whenever it is convenient for the game to seem cinimatic and movie like. You can look for snipers all you want but you wont see them until you hit the designated spot where they spawn in.
The gameplay overall is very good, it is fun for the most part but has some heavy drawbacks. After playing the first Sniper Elite, this game was a huge step in the wrong direction and makes me worry for the future titles that I am yet to play. I cannot reccomend Sniper Elite V2 for its painfully scriped gameplay that leaves you less feeling like a sniper and more feeling like a poorly designed movie charecter.
Edit: After watching the enemies spawn before my eyes and observing areas before moving to ensure that there were no enemies before I made a break for it and then all of a sudden I am shot by a sniper in the position that I literally just looked at, I have decided not to complete sniper elite 2 and I am moving on to number 3 in hopes that it has been rolled back to the formula used in the first sniper elite.
Edit 2: I managed to slug my way through the game and completed it. This is by far the worst Sniper Elite. Avoid at all costs and play the first Sniper Elite, it smashes this one out of the park.

I found this to be an enjoyable, relaxing, low-key kind of game.  The basic idea is that plant-like life has been discovered on Mars, and over the course of the game you discover other types of organisms and have to spread them around into small ecosystems in order to progress further.  It's very analagous to tending a garden.  Eventually, the story kicks in and you find that these plants aren't the only secrets buried on Mars.
The story is well-done with enough surprises to keep it interesting, the atmosphere is spot-on, the acting is good, and the puzzles are not frustratingly difficult.  The pacing is also good, and the length is exactly right - not so short that I feel like I wasted my money, but not so long that the game mechanics become stale.  Overall, a definite buy.

An awesome indie game on all points. The graphics are simple but nonetheless nice and colorful, and the environment, though only made of caverns most of the time, is varied enough. The gameplay is as simple as the visuals but original and interesting since it is aimed at creating and controlling a martian environment. I could say the same regarding the story. The voice acting and soundtrack are good. I could add that if you are curious and like to explore, you'll find a few secondary objectives to do, which will tell you more about the story or the characters.
Waking Mars is not really difficult, but plants and wildlife do not remain passive and they can make environment control tricky if you're not careful.
What I find really enjoyable is the whole scientific background, as your character does research on the flora and fauna while making progress, and all the findings are written in some sort of database that you can consult anytime. The theories and explanations regarding the environment are quite interesting.
Needless to say, a game that invites you to create instead of destroying is more than welcome.

I started playing SOMA very apprehensively, thinking it was going to be another horror game like Outlast, and I don't much like horror games. I get scared watching  even the tamest of horror movies. So naturally, when the game started I was being extremely cautious with my every movement, jumping at the slightest noise and cowering in virtual corners for minutes on end.
But the setting, the preamble, it just forced me to continue. And I powered through the various levels, defeating my fears of jumpscares and realising more and more that the game wasn't as scary as I thought to begin with. The deeper I delved into the story, the less frightened I became and my fear was replaced fully with excitement, curiosity and eagerness to find out more.
"Horror" games often seem to lack a good story, instead focusing on gameplay to mortify the players, but the horror aspect of SOMA was rather complimenting the story. And the story is superb. You can go into varying levels of detail, chosing to either just plough through the basic line of events or reading every single file and note along the way, trying to find out all of the backstory. In any case, there are quite a few twists and turns I wasn't expecting.
The end of the game left me thinking about it for quite some time. It was not an ending I anticipated, not an ending I had hoped for, but it was an ending to remember.
Visually this game is beautiful in its own right. It paints a scene of devastation, of struggle, of the end, hopelessness and of futility. Especially the unterwater parts of this world are incredibly immersive and detailled; the atmosphere as a whole is on point. The visuals are complemented by excellent sound effects and a subtle soundtrack that deepens the various feelings of dread, loss and misery to make this whole experience even more enticing.
Overall, this game is a wild ride from start to finish but definitely a ride you should try out.

I beat the game on normal difficulty in 6.5 hours. It's a solid FPS in the same league as Bulletstorm, Shadow Warrior, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger, and the like.
Aiming is precise, enemies don't take entire clips to kill (as long as you have good aim), you're rewarded for more challenging kills with more ugprade points, and it's overall a story that makes you want to keep playing to see what happens.
There's still a few things that might've been better about this game. Towards the end, as you start fighting stronger enemies, they start to feel like bullet sponges unless you are pretty much only shooting for their heads (a practice I highly recommend). Also, I felt like the special powers didn't really work well with the gunplay. For most fights, I just found some cover at a choke point and shot enemies in the head one by one - no need for special powers. If the upgrades integrated more with the shooting and were less strictly melee, I might've enjoyed that aspect of the game more and found it to be less repetitive. They also could've encouraged people to adopt a more run-and-gun style of play by including enemies or mechanics that make it difficult to just camp in one spot for the entire game and providing you with more mobility options. I felt that running around and trying to melee enemies wasn't a very viable tactic compared to camping and shooting because enemies could get so many shots on you before you close the gap.
Other than that, the length is great. I don't feel like sections get too repetitive or feel like they're going on too long.
If you like FPS games, you'll almost certainly like this. I would say it's not quite as good as Bullet Storm, Shadow Warrior, or call of Juarez: Gunslinger, but I definitely liked it more than Wolfenstein: New Order.

Unless you are an uber dino lover and enjoy just standing there as a dino, this game is not for you. There's nothing to do besides be a carnivore and kos. Everyone picks the biggest and baddest dino and either sit around a lake making dino roars, or they simply have a button mashing battle with another big dino till they both die.
Anyways, back to progression. I would say about 80%-90% of your time will be spent sitting in a bush (so you don't get killed), waiting till you can progress. Of course that's only if you have a fresh corpse (most likely a kill you didn't get yourself), and water. If you don't have either of those you'll be stuck searching around the huge map for a random body lying around with some water by it. Did I mention there is absolutely no way of finding this food or water? Yeah, no map, no coordinates (they took that out), and trail or clues as to where it could be. Is it realistic? Yes. Is it fun? Heck to the no. Granted, this game is early access and I get that. But as it stands today it is not a playable or remotely enjoyable experience.

So yeah, as it stands, it sucks. Could it be better in the future? Sure. But don't be looking within this, or even next year for that to happen. Game needs to stay in development and out of the Steam store.

It's been a while since I've played a game for the story alone.
Usually in a game in which the main character isn't a blank slate, you'll run into a disconnect between what the player wants and what the characters want. 199X acknowledges this and takes a unique, very direct approach. It explores how a character would act if they were both the lead and a pawn in their own story.
The game itself is very touching, and is maybe second only to Undertale on the list of games that made me care so much for the character, though in this case it was the player character, not the NPCs. God, I could write a whole thing on that aspect alone, but I know I'll pass Steam's word limit.
The soundtrack isn't the best quality, but it's strangely fitting for the game. Think like a more ambient, experimental version of Heavens to Betsy. Overall it looks cheap and thrown together, but I actually love it for that. My only real gripe is some sloppy dialogue in which characters swear way too much or just have a few lazily written lines. Not a deal breaker by any stretch, as I've played a handful of RPG Maker games now and that seems to be a common issue.
Your interaction with this game feels permanent, like even if you reset and start everything over there's always a little bit left behind. It's weird to think of it like that, but somehow, 199X made me feel that way.

I have to confess that I really like RPGMaker games. You never know what kind of a surprise you can encounter with trying a new one. It might either be some clichéd fun RPG, some curious brain scratcher or a really original scenario that could have been one great game with proper budget and engine.
is neither of them. It's a dystopic parody that centers on a well written female protagonist that challenges the idea of free will and societal convention thoroughly.
In Steam Store, the game is briefly defined with these words: "In 199X, you control Clara. That's the problem." Clara is a young woman who wakes up in a hospital building which she has no memory of getting admitted into, only to be informed that her friends made an "informed decision" about her. That is the point that we are emerged into the storyline as the voice and controlling character of Clara. Needless to say, she gets a bit freaked when she realizes that her body is not hers to control anymore. We are controlling her, and we speak in her mind to establish an odd love/hate relationship with her. After that given point, our primary goal is to find a "cure" for Clara's "condition" about the omnipotent and omnipresent "ghost voice" in her head. Namely, the player.
The game challenges the idea of a conventional video gameplay and its framed characters with predetermined personalities who only exist through one storyline and our choice of controlling them. Clara is so well-written as an original personality, with genuine reactions and a literature of her own, you easily get engulfed into your uneasy relationship with her. Her reality, dystopic and nonsensical at first glimpse reveals to become eerily similar to the collective control mechanics of modern day societies that we know far too well. It's a comment, weaved around psychedelic nuances of an unconventional mind.
I must confess that story mechanics themselves are rather crippled compared to excellently displayed dialogue and concept depth, with lacking environment design and some shallow character designs. The story and gameplay is quite linear, maybe as part of the critique it's trying to accomplish. I particularly enjoyed symbolic dream sequences between different days, and a sit-com version parody of Dungeons and Dragons though. What atmosphere lacks in means of display, it most certainly compensates for dialogues worthy of a Beckett play and soundtrack - an original compilation of Kearney, concerning indie, dark wave and psychedelic rock genres which is distributed free with the game.
A warning is to be added nonetheless, that this game is not for everyone with centering on some historical and societal dysfunctions like female hysteria, and its temporal treatment of hysterical paroxysms in an institutionalized manner. With the warning at mind, I most certainly recommend
as a brief and challenging - yet eventually meaningless experience. The worst case scenario with this kind of somewhat funny price, you are buying 3 hours of gameplay and some funny moments.

my overall score: 6/10
pros:
graphics: the art in this game is simply amazing. everything works together perfectly, from colors to background and character design. in between "chapters" you also get short story cinematics that just charming, and made in the fashion of the local art which all together creates an amazing and authentic feeling which last during all the game.
animation: everything moves beautifully. from the little realistic paw movements of the fox that are simply adorable to the way the characters try to balance themselves on the ice, jump around, and even start crying when their partner dies.
sound effects: accompanying the animation, the sound effects for this game are just as masterfully done. the only thing that could make them little cute fox paws even better is the sound of them scritch - scratching on the ice as it jumps from place to place.
story: the story is delivered in a beautiful authentic fairy tale way that really gets you engaged in what is going one. actually, all this game feels more like an interactive story than a game (which some of you might see as a minus but i fin charming). it is definitely a game you would like to share with a cherished person and share a lovely experience
cultural exposure: the game was essentially made to expose  some of the cloture and the charm of the Inuit people. on that front, the game does a wonderful job. as you go in the game you unlock short videos that you can watch as they come or later at your pleasure, that also have to do with the current action that happens in the game, hence explaining why things are as they are and giving the meaning extra dimension, and you also learn about their cloture in a fun and engaging way.
cons:
short game: the game itself is awfully short. experienced players can probably run through it in 2-3 hours. I am not the best at platformers and while stretching it spent around 6 hours start to end.
gameplay: the gameplay is pretty easy and not that complicated. I have not played a lot of platform games as I am new to this, but even I seen platforms where the puzzles and challenges can take you to far better and more interesting places game wise than never alone. it seems like they found it more important to work on the story than the actual game and level design
multy-single player: imo never alone fails on both fronts in this area. the game is designed for 2 players, but you can go through it yourself by playing and switching in game between the 2 characters. that means that there is no real need for a multilayer mode as it does not add any layer of complexity to the puzzles, just lets in another person on the ride and to enjoy the story. while in single player, the switching between the characters is very cumbersome and actually interferes with the game flow rather than help it. so if you can, play this game with another person. it wont make it more interesting, but the flow will be much better.

all in all, I enjoyed the game and plan to go through it again in the future for the experience values. for you guys out there that looking for a challenging and interesting game, it's not the game for you. for those that like a good story and a cute pass time experience that is shiny to the eye, never alone is one game you would love to try.

Teku Studios set themselves the goal to use handmade paintings for all the backgrounds and sprites. So every single movement in this game has been drawn by hand before being scanned, and the result is magnificent. Not only stunning, but also lively as the levels are oozing with movement. Wildlife, plants, falling leaves and even the sky do not give the impression of a still painting, they are all animated. While this amounts to a huge effort, I assumed that the ending levels would start to wear thin, and I am pleased to report that until the very end everything is amazing.
Enough gushing, let’s talk about the game proper hiding behind those pretty landscapes. Candle is an adventure game, with a lot of puzzle elements and a fair share of platforming. Not the Super Meat Boy kind of platforming, more towards Another World (also known as Out of This World) and Flashback with ledges to grab and a specific sequence of movements to achieve with the right timing to get past a deadly obstacle. Just like in those games, there are plenty of deadly traps and dangers to overcome. But no shooting, here we are closer to Oddworld: Abe’s Oddyssee/Exodus where stealth can be necessary to get past hostile tribes. Finally, from its extensive use of “point and click” style adventure puzzles and gorgeous graphics, Candle is also very close to a game like Machinarium. We are talking about mini-puzzles to solve, as well as items to find and use where necessary.
The controls are thus not point’n’click with a mouse, they are based on the arrow keys. And that’s where my main criticism of the game will be: problems with the controls. For many years now it has become quite common to use WASD courtesy of First Person Shooters. Even on gamepads, the left hand is used to control movements. Arrow keys are an outdated model, and furthermore the Spacebar is a clunky way to jump when W (or UP) could do the same solely with the fingers dedicated to movement. Playing Candle with Spacebar + Arrow keys was tedious to me, and it got worse during some of the mini-puzzles in which Q and R are used to rotate some elements. If it was WASD and QE, I could do it all on one hand rather than painfully struggling with some movements on my right hand and some movements on my left hand. I thought that the game was designed for a controller so I plugged one, and it did not work properly. This all would not have been a problem if I could just rebind the keys, but it is sadly not possible and I do not understand why remapping keys is absent from so many games. Rebinding keys in shooters or platformers is absolutely mandatory, dear developers please stop forgetting that.
While I mentioned before that Candle is inspired by some older games, some of their more frustrating elements can also transpire here. A lot of “trial and error” can be necessary during some sequences and it can put off a number of players. I did not find this a problem, because the checkpoints are very frequent and mostly because it reflects the hostile and brutal nature of this unknown world. And just like in Machinarium, there are puzzles or elements to find that will leave you scratching your head for a while or looking for a walkthrough online. I did find some of these moments quite unnecessarily difficult, such as a hidden ledge that I had to reach even though I thought that there was nothing there. I guess it’s one of the downside of having such gorgeous backgrounds! More worrying, there was a sequence in which I thought I could run for a ladder to escape but the ladder somehow disappeared right during that sequence and magically reappeared after it was over. There were a bit too many moments when I was stuck because I had not seen something, and while I add this to my negative points I do not think that the game suffers from this much more than other similar games in the same genre, although a hint system would have been welcome. And for all of those more troublesome puzzles, there was sometimes a brilliant one to counter-balance (the drumming sequence was genius). A recurring theme element of Candle is to activate things with fire, however rain and pools of water can make it more tricky than just going from A to B while carrying the candle.
I am on a roll with the criticism, so I will add the cut-scenes and bubble speech. They are nice and all, but too slow to unfold. Especially since the narrator basically makes a summary of what a character was saying. And what a narrator - Terry Wilton, that you might know from the Trine series to which he added the magic of his voice. Excellent delivery in Candle as well. The story took time to unravel but then was rather good, especially as we get closer to the end. Overall quite charming but with darker overtones. The music accompanying it all was great. Length wise, it took me a little less than 10 hours so it is really a full adventure and not a quick snippet.
As a conclusion, despite having to constantly fight with the controls, I had an amazing time with Candle. Not just because the watercolor art is absolutely gorgeous and the voice of Terry Wilton is fantastic, but also because Teku Studios crafted a wonderful and dangerous world to explore that is full of character even in the tiniest details. Some occasional platforming requires timing and can be tough for those that hate trial and error, some of the items are really difficult to find, but there is still a good balance between everything so that there is always something new to encounter and replace any frustration with marvel. A real diamond in the rough that I will remember as fondly as its inspirations

Secrets of Grindea is a Zelda style action RPG with levelling.
Edit: Originally I had a paragraph here stating that the game is way too hard, but then I learned that I set the game to "hard" when I started - so to complain about that would be dumb :P. The next paragraph still stands though, regarding some of the hard parts of the game.
I think this could be remedied with a pretty simple fix - another branch of magic that lets you heal/buff. The game has no health potions, so you're at the mercy of health drops from enemies.
Also, it suffers from a lack of content. This isn't a hard negative - it's still in early access! From the looks of things, the developers have a ton of content planned. As far as I've gotten though, there are very few side quests or optional dungeons, and not a lot of equipment variety.
Probably the most disappointing thing is that, after I started a multiplayer playthrough with my friend, we don't both get Monster Cards together. Loot in general is shared evenly (in Round-Robin sharing) but monster cards take so long to get that it is very very disheartening to not get one when it drops and your friend gets it.
My last negative point  - the soundtrack is only mediocre. Lots of games these days have phenomenal soundtracks, so you almost expect it when a game hits "Overwhelmingly Positive". I think this game can get there - but the soundtrack isn't helping. It's not bad, but it's not good enough.
The first thing is the graphics - it's BEAUTIFUL. Some of the best pixel art I've seen in years.  Your avatar can be customized with a ton of different styles and colors, and they all look great. Every enemy and character is gorgeously animated . The environment is amazing. This game is just overflowing with great visuals.
The gameplay is a TON of fun. Combat is great with a few snags in my opinion. The skill system lets you pick whatever skills you want first, with 4 different magic elements and physical skills to choose from. There's a good amount of variety in builds and if you have (quite a lot of) money you can respec all your skills. You can stagger enemies and get bonuses from precise shield blocking. Sometimes if you attack too quickly, it eats your input and you just stand there, so that can be pretty annoying.
You have a bottomless bag (No inventory management! 5 Stars right there). Enemies drop stuff ALL THE TIME and its really satisfying to collect it all. And there's a ton of stuff to collect. It's a grind-lovers dream. You can refight bosses to get their rare drops.  Every enemy in the game has an ULTRA-RARE drop as well, which can be fun to farm for.
There's a crafting system that lets you build new equipment with all the drops you collect. IMO the game needs more mage equipment - I still only have 1 wand, from the beginning of the game.
There are so many
mechanics in this game - collecting things is a blast, refighting bosses is excellent, there is a challenge arena, good variety of enemies. It's a ton of fun to play and I can't wait for the full version to come out.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes RPGs or the Legend Of Zelda series.

Teku Studios is praiseworthy for successfully fulfilled what they had promised few years ago: an adventure puzzle game in an immersive, beautiful world. What is worth noticing is that each of the artworks were traditionally hand painted using water colours- notoriously the most punishing medium in art. The design of the characters are simple, okay, but not great: they're your generic tribal folks. It's a shame that they ditched the idea about making the story dark and gorey, I think even in a colourful world it could work just fine. The musics blend well with each environments. Kudos for the music composer managed to bring up the vibes of The Jungle Book in Act 2. The gameplay requires logical thinking (duh!) but also very specific observations of the environments. It happens that the designers want the player to observe their surroundings really closely, the smallest animation details could be your hint to progress the game. It makes you appreciate the aesthetic side of the game, but it could be frustrating wandering around cluelessly about how to move forward. It's  possibly a personal thing to be oblivious towards subtle, hidden clues. I'm pretty content with the game: well made, full of passion and love. Go give it a try!

The most important things to know are these:
-Gear trumps skill.  Firefights will almost always go to the better geared player, regardless of respective skill levels
-Gear requires grinding.  The higher tier equipment takes tens of thousands of reputation points to unlock, and your match rewards will be anywhere from 100 to 1000, depending on how well you do.
-You can pay real money to take a shortcut around both of those problems.  There are real money versions of most guns and armor, and many of them are lower tiered than their normal counterparts, meaning you can pay to use better weapons and armor in lower level matches.  You can also pay for "premium", which gives you a 50% boost to rep, xp, and silver rubles.  Combine that with some other bonuses, and you can cut the grind time in half, all for a low low fee of $9.95 a month! (Actual amount varies depending on how much gold you buy at a time, and how much premium time you buy with that gold at a time)
Oh yeah, and you can't forget the rampant spawn camping.  Most maps have you spawning in or around a building with maybe two exits, so it's not hard for somebody from the opposing team to sneak over there within a couple of minutes of play, and then totally lay waste to your team.  It happens in almost every round, and if you're not experiencing it, that probably means your team is the one doing it.  But I suppose that is to be expected when the maps are so small, and the spawns are so accessible.  Bad game design, through and through.
The research game mode can be fun, if you like capturing/holding/defending points.  Unfortunately, nobody seems to play it anymore, because I've only been able to find Team Deathmatch games the last few times I've logged on.
Also, anomolies spawn all over the map, all the damn time.  They do a ton of damage, even if you have decently protective gear, so they effectively block off big chunks of the map.  They can be cleared, but you're basically giving up a life(or medkit) to do so.
If all of this sounds like good game design to you, then knock yourself out!
If, however, you think a game that has spent two years in beta should have come a bit farther than this mess, then I advise you to steer clear!  I have been playing since almost the very start of the beta, well before it made it onto steam, and the Dev team has not followed through on any part of their timeline or initial promises.  I am a big fan of the STALKER games, so I wanted to support their devs, but this game is little more than a tedious pay to win grindfest.  This game has soured me on the entire concept of early access, especially where money is involved.  Oh, for those of you that don't know, you either had to win a lottery or pay to get into the early stages of the open beta.  They got 25 of my dollars, and that is exactly as far as the STALKER goodwill will get them in my book.

I started playing SOMA very apprehensively, thinking it was going to be another horror game like Outlast, and I don't much like horror games. I get scared watching  even the tamest of horror movies. So naturally, when the game started I was being extremely cautious with my every movement, jumping at the slightest noise and cowering in virtual corners for minutes on end.
But the setting, the preamble, it just forced me to continue. And I powered through the various levels, defeating my fears of jumpscares and realising more and more that the game wasn't as scary as I thought to begin with. The deeper I delved into the story, the less frightened I became and my fear was replaced fully with excitement, curiosity and eagerness to find out more.
"Horror" games often seem to lack a good story, instead focusing on gameplay to mortify the players, but the horror aspect of SOMA was rather complimenting the story. And the story is superb. You can go into varying levels of detail, chosing to either just plough through the basic line of events or reading every single file and note along the way, trying to find out all of the backstory. In any case, there are quite a few twists and turns I wasn't expecting.
The end of the game left me thinking about it for quite some time. It was not an ending I anticipated, not an ending I had hoped for, but it was an ending to remember.
Visually this game is beautiful in its own right. It paints a scene of devastation, of struggle, of the end, hopelessness and of futility. Especially the unterwater parts of this world are incredibly immersive and detailled; the atmosphere as a whole is on point. The visuals are complemented by excellent sound effects and a subtle soundtrack that deepens the various feelings of dread, loss and misery to make this whole experience even more enticing.
Overall, this game is a wild ride from start to finish but definitely a ride you should try out.

In 35MM, you play as Petrovich, a traveller accompanied by a survivor as you wanderer through the barren suburbs and rurals of post-apocalyptic Russia, trying to find signs of life and hope. While you walk along rudimentary dirt roads, managing through quiet forests, and the haunting cities in Russia, you uncover memories of the old world and how life use to be; before things came to be. The world has been ravaged by a deadly outbreak after some "Genius" in a lab coat discovered a new strain variant to the Ebola virus, and accidentally released it, which spread for miles until eradicating most of the human population across the planet. The only ones who have survived turned for the worst, now roam the wastes as raiders, or have become too ill to live. The world of 35MM is the result of man trying to play God, and man inevitably failed. When mankind failed, nature flourished once again because life finds a way.
Bottom line, 35MM seems like a quiet tour of Russia after a deadly virus outbreak. It's feels more of an exploration-simulator, with a touch of horror. Interesting and informative dialogue about your surroundings and history, but poorly executed translation between Russian and English. Minimal combat and intense situations, simple interactions with the world around you, like take/drop, open/close, use/holster. The game mechanics need a little buffing as there we're some noticable bugs.
35MM may not be as immersive as other open-world games, but it does a great job at keeping you engaged with the story and environmental aspects, giving off a sad and mundane, yet haunting experience of a post-apocalyptic Russia.
