I can see a lot of negative reviews, and most of them are just silly, like "it is not free-to-play" ot "the game is too hard, I couldn't takeoff".
Yes, it is not really free-to-play. But you have access to three planes and full Tutorial campaign without paying anything, isn't it enough? It is a demo-version with possibility to purchase the content you need (and you don't need it all at once).
Yes, it is difficult. It is a hardcore simulation game with all the consequences, what do you expect? RoF has a steep learning curve, requires time and doesn't forgive. If you have never played other flying simulators before, you will have to spend hours to learn how to do it. But this game is a perfect "my first sim" game: planes were simple those days, and fights are slow-paced comparing to other games of the same genre (Il-2, DCS).
Just don't try to play it without joystick. Obviously, I'm not talking about gamepads here. If you don't have one, or not ready to learn while trying again and again, or just want a quick pew-pew, then go play War Thunder. In RoF realism is above all. This game is about details and history. It is about times when word "chivalry" still meant something. It is about stuck machine guns and cranking engines, colored scarfs and wind in your face. In short, this game is awesome.

Sniper Elite V2 did everything it could to make me hate it.   It starts by showing you stealth, and how awesome it's bullet cam is, and teaches you how to play the game.
Then it follows it up with a second mission that is impossible to stealth.  The only thing the game shows you up to that point is stealth so you think "This game is broken."  and honestly, yeah it is.  The stealth in this game is broken, it's not "non existant" it's just not possible to do in the second mission (and other missions).   So I put down the game because screw it.  It's not fun.
About a year later I returned to Sniper Elite V2, and said "Screw it, let's just beat the game, get some achievements and never play it again."   I threw the game on "Cadet" and I decide to give it one last shot.
I'm glad I did.  Sniper Elite V2 is a horrible stealth game.  But it's a fun "sniping" game.  You don't play this game like you would play the epic Call of Duty Modern Warfare Sniping level.   You instead play it like you play the rest of the call of duty levels.  Yes you can stealth many parts of the game, but it takes forever and often one misstep brings everything down on you and you'll restart.   Instead the minute you misstep, say "Screw it" and go out gun blazing.  In fact this game has a REALLY good sniper set up.  The player has quite a few tools at his disposal, the Sniping is challenging but fun, the ai does remember where they saw the player last (Which means you can move and then snipe who ever comes looking) and there is a really good level design work here.
And the kill cam.  Dear god, the kill cams are amazing.  For a five year old game, watching a bullet penetrate an enemy from 100 miles away in a unique way every time is weirdly glorious.  The bullet travels, the air manipulated around it until it penetrates (And yes penetrates is the right word) into a body, moving through vital organs until it exits.  It's a glorious moment and while it's over done a bit, it's exciting at least 75 percent of the time, and probably closer to 100.  It's just an absolute exciting experience especially when you pull off that 400 meter shot, or you successfully nail the perfect shot.
So does it make it a good game.  Well that depends.  It's not a great military shooter, but it is a VERY fun sniping game.  I really prefer it on the easier difficulty, and the game feels broken once in a while, or unfair.  But the game makes up for it in visuals, and that feeling when each mission's plan comes together.  It COULD be better, and it's not perfect, but it's worth a play.  I don't know if I'd pay the full 20 bucks for it, but for 10 bucks or less it's easily worth the money and time to play through it.

In all seriousness, this game is awesome and is easily one of my top favorite games of all time.
-------------------------------------------COMBAT-------------------------------------------
The combat revolves around skills dependent on energy and simple attack and blocking mechanics. However, this combat is a blast to play as there are many different builds and playstyles that you could choose so that every run-through isn't the same as the last one. You could be a fire mage, throwing fireballs or shooting down meteors or a summoner or a savage berserker. So many choices are present! The enemies are also never too bland and the ones that are do it because of a reason, as in the case of the slime being generic simply because it's the first monster you ever encounter. Every enemy attacks in a different way or pattern and with the mechanic of perfect blocking which is blocking almost exactly when the enemy attacks, there's a decent amount of skill involved.
-------------------------------------------STORY-------------------------------------------
NOTE: I am just going to address this because of the countless idiots writing reviews about how the story isn't finished. The game is literally in EARLY ACCESS. Of course the story isn't done, but the dev team is working their hardest to provide some crisp quality content and the content that is currently avaliable is so excessive and polished that I find that hating on the game simply because you did one rushed playthrough of the story is simply sad.
The actual story revolves around your journey across the world accompanied by your stingy companion Bag, who is a magic Bag that gives you hint, throws snide and comical remarks about the world around you, and is an essential story factor as Bag acts as an explanation for your endless inventory. I don't want to give too many spoilers, but each encounter feels unique and like a whole new experience. You'll encounter the likes of sentient artifacts, giant slimes, apocolypse causing people and more and the story that revolves around these people and creatures feel unique and as in the case of the last current story arc (as of writing this review), you feel somewhat emotionally impacted about what happens.
-------------------------------------------GAMEPLAY-------------------------------------------
The game is full of puzzles, some ranging from easy but there are a lot of hard ones that make you boggle your mind. There are also a bunch of side quests which will occupy your time while or after you do the main story.
-------------------------------------------ARCADE MODE-------------------------------------------
This mode is unlocked without anything and is a fun and challenging way for you to have fun while you wait for more content to be unlocked in the story mode. You traverse through several floors and you do not regain hp until each floor completion which makes learning how to dodge and perfect block essential. It's a way to help you get good at the game in a fun manner.
All in all the game is pretty nice and is definite refresher from some of the more mediocre games in it's genre!

Well if you're going to play just one survival horror game this year you should definitely play...Alien Isolation.  SOMA is good, but it's no Alien Isolation.  Alien Isolation does literally everything better then SOMA and I feel it's pretty clear SOMA was heavily inspired by Alien Isolation.  From the way Simon moves to the way he interacts with the environment all try and deliver a very tactile feel.  It's very well done, but not as well done as Alien Isolation.  The monsters that are constantly chasing you have a more Silent Hill feel then anything...sadly the way they move is often times ridiculously unfair.  In Alien you feel like the creature is outsmarting you, in SOMA well...in SOMA you can't do much but run.  You are faster then all the monsters so long as you are constantly moving.  Hiding doesn't work, they tend to directly block exits so you have to join them in basically a game of tag so you can get passed them.  It's by far the worst part of the game.
The story is at least very enjoyable although extremely predictable. You are basically the last man on Earth after a comet wipes out all life on Earth.  You wake up in a research facility under the sea and try and figure out what has happened to the last survivors.  Sadly the story is told through notebooks, computer terminals, and voice recordings.  I think this is a terrible way to tell the story, it's not enjoyable and i wish games would stop doing it.  Eventually you meet Catherine and the two of you go on a quest to try and save the human race from extinction.  Luckily, I loved Catherine, if you don't like her, you really aren't going to like the game as I said the plot is pretty straightforward.
After all my problems with the game and story telling I still enjoyed my time playing it though.  I loved the world it created, exploring all environments were a real treat. I adored the underwater world and the sound design is quite impeccable. It just in no way stacks up to the greatness of Alien Isolation, but if you already played that game and want something extremely similar definitely give SOMA a try.  #WORTH $5.

Story (minor spoilers): You're Simon a pretty average dude, waking up to his somewhat normal life in present day Toronto. This was not the setting I was imagining to start with but it was a very cool intro! These beginning moments do an excellent job setting up Simon's backstory while feeling pretty damn eerie. The whole time I was wondering how the hell this normal guy in a normal-ish world was ending up on the ocean floor. So how Simon gets there is truly a setup for what becomes a big plot point that gets used again and again in several ways. The intro takes you through Simon's apartment, the Toronto subway, and to a doctors office. Here things start to get a little weird before Simon sits into brain scanner. This is Simon's brain scan, it ends the intro and effectively begins the exploration of your new reality. I like how it's not explicitly stated initially that Simon is not the original flesh and bones Simon. It puts the player on their toes when they do realize and sets up many more difficult and existential questions later on. So without retelling the story entirely, I will describe how its told and how awesome it was that Frictional effectively integrated so many damn good questions into this plot. So you find out a lot about what happened on PATHOS-II through Catherine. She is a former worker on the station who's brain-scan is now your companion. And It certainly feels weird (in a is this a normal thing now kind of way) because as you go through the game you bring Catherine in and out of existence essentially as you plug her device into and out of terminals. So as you move through the game you're faced with difficult choices that question the essence of humanity from different angles and Catherine leads you there and sets up for this. Catherine seems throughout more aware of her condition as a copy of the original Catherine and this contrasts really well with Simon who struggles with being a copy but also as the player! My instinct was to believe that me(Simon) is more important or "the right" copy, but what Catherine does is leave you at moments where you must pondering your significance. Its kinda like she knows where she fits into the grand scheme of things but we the players don't and need to think on this for ourselves. So all this is to say the plot is a great vessel for these type of questions and these types are super unique to gaming.
Aside from Catherine, there is a lack of humanity in PATHOS-II (which is what everyone in the game is trying to preserve by their own definitions, interestingly enough), so interactions are limited to copies and creatures... which is rough. The other method of story-telling here is environmental. Since there are no humans to speak to we must look to our surroundings to divulge information about what occurred. Luckily your environment is dense with information. It does two things primarily, subtly direct the player what to do/where to go and tells a story. You don't always pick up on these things but when you do it forwards your progress and understanding of what happened. This stuff is great because it really adds depth to the game.
One last method of story-telling is the standard archives, audio-logs etc. These are well done in general and add to the plot, explaining creatures and different events that occurred to the past crew of PATHOS-II.
Gameplay: So there might not be a whole lot of gameplay here but it fits the game for the most part. The standard interaction with physics objects is present but not quite utilized in the same way as Amnesia where you solved puzzles and blocked creatures. Another aspect missing from SOMA that was present in Amnesia is the inventory system. Now I believe this is a minor mistake as I would have liked to reread documents, take notes, and maybe hold items. However the lack of the subtle crafting system and sanity mechanic of Amnesia is not really missed. So what SOMA did improve on was the creature encounters. While I feel like hiding mechanics in Amnesia (closets and piling things up) could've been utilized to great effect, it might have felt overdone after the recent wave of horror games. Instead SOMA adds significant variety to the creatures you come across, both in visuals and the way you can move past them. This is where Frictional's subtle ways at foreshadowing and out-right telling the player what their coming up against shines. The tension build up and release is fantastic in this game. The pacing is evident as you are slowly starved of positive interactions and the atmosphere cranks up the darkness and moodiness, then it happens you see a creature... Often following these sections you figure more out about the story or find yourself in a new open (nonthreatening) area. So I really appreciate this game for those sequences! So yeah, like I began with the lack of video-gamey gameplay is kinda a plus. You get to focus on the atmosphere, creatures, and story.
Atmosphere: If you haven't heard already, the atmosphere in this game is downright great. This aspect is pretty necessary for a solid horror game and luckily Frictional know what they're doing. Amnesia had the hub areas with a wonderful, relieveing atmosphere, areas with creature encounters had a dreadful atmosphere, and some of the set pieces like with Agrippa had shocking/gut-wrenching atmosphere. SOMA does a lot of the same and excels in similar ways. Visually SOMA is denser, there's more going on with more variety. (This does not detract from Amnesia really, only an improvement for SOMA) The sound design is fantastic and absolutely essential. I don't have to much detailed to say here other than that the game had me sucked in fully and sure as hell scared me, so I'm pretty the sounds were doing there job. Now the setting I am a complete sucker for. I have always been pretty damn scared of the ocean and it depths, but I also like to scuba dive and want to go more. Its kinda a love/scared-of-you relationship. So yeah, the contrast between tight, dark stations and sprawling, well-lit ocean floor did it for me. Overall the atmosphere does a great job adding tensions to the gameplay, immersing you in the world, and furthering plot.
Overall: I recommend this game to anyone who wants a tense, horror game experience that is truly dripping with atmosphere; with the bonus (which probably is its main purpose) that it confronts the player with really unique questions and choices over the meaning of humanity and our existence.

While it doesn't stand up to FFT, this game is a solid and fun entry in an otherwise limited genre. The dice and card building mechanics were refreshing, and it was exciting for me to level up and experience the upgraded versions of the cards. Dice rolling, however, became tedious VERY fast. In the very first mission I changed to auto-roll and it's made the game more enjoyable. The music is also very well done and remains interesting after hours of play.
I'm playing on Hard and it's quite challenging. I've only wiped once or twice, mostly in the Elite Skirmishes. Basically a level you've already played but with no story elements and more abundant and powerful enemies. Strategy really will win the game for you. A lot of people also complain about being outnumbered - that's part of the challenge. A challenge I've quite enjoyed. Regular skirmishes are also available, and allow you to level up characters and earn new dice for crafting/upgrading. All matches and skirmishes are winnable if you ... play your cards right.
I've seen a lot of complaints about the game being child-like with characters that aren't fleshed out really well. Perhaps that's part of the point. The playable characters are basically street kids that do what they can to survive. Sure, the writing might be a little juvenile, but when you look at the characters and the subject matter it fits quite well. Further complaints about how slow the enemy turns are - a recent patch included a 'fast forward' feature to speed up animations and dice rolls.
Now I wasn't a part of the kickstarter, and I knew nothing coming into this except for seeing someone play the first mission, so maybe that's why I'm not disappointed. I had no grand ideas about "the next FFT" or anything like that. I am quite pleased with what's been done here and I'm really enjoying my playthrough.
If you enjoy the Tactics-style turn-based grid system, give this game a shot. It's well worth it for the price tag.
Also, play on Hard and try to win the Arena - lots of fun!

Children of Zodiarcs is an SRPG with gameplay that combines elements of the tactics genre with dice rolling and card deck building. Because of this, the mechanics are truly unique and feature a good amount of depth, making these systems the high point to the game. You'll find yourself experimenting with different abilities and decks, switching strategies depending on the battle and enemies you are facing. The game is challenging and can get overwhelming towards the end, since your measly party of three becomes grossly outnumbered and the battles become longer.
The art and music are always beautiful, evoking the atmosphere of games like Final Fantasy Tactics. However, unlike FFTactics, the story is extremely scarce. I definitely wanted more fleshing out of the game's world and characters, just as other reviewers have noted. I do wish there were more customization options, but that probably would've been outside the scope of this relatively small game. In the end, however, I do think Children of Zodiarcs is worth your time and money. I definitely don't regret supporting it on Kickstarter and look forward to seeing what this team has in store for us in the future.

Full disclosure, I haven't yet finished this game and I did help fund this game during development, though I don't think either really has any meaningful impact on my review.
Children of Zodiarcs is a fun game, I just want to get that out up front. It's a turn-based, tactical game with map mechanics that are reminiscent of other turn-based third-person tactical games. If you like that style of gameplay, generally presented, I think you will like Children of Zodiarcs.
I'm going to continue to be up front and say what Children of Zodiarcs isn't: Final Fantasy Tactics.
I want to repeat that, Children of Zodiarcs isn't Final Fantasy Tactics, a successor to Final Fantasy Tactics, a spiritual child to Final Fantasy Tactics, or even a by-blow of Final Fantasy Tactics that likes to masquerade in its parents' image.
But if I wanted to play Final Fantasy Tactics, I'd... just go play Final Fantasy Tactics, so I'm going to move past that point (which seems to be the focus of a number of reviews) and judge the game on its inherent value.
Gameplay is pretty fun for a fan of this style of game, and I think the additional elements (cards, dice, etc) add some interesting components. I'll admit, the dice aspect can be frustrating sometimes, but RNG presented in a fashion that you can mildly alter is kind of cool.
Story from what little I've played seems okay. Amazing? No, but not that bad. Characters are a bit flat in terms of storyline, but the art is good and writing is fine. Did it have the sweeping complexity of a larger RPG? Well, not that I've seen, but for what the game is I wouldn't expect it to.
Ultimately, if you like third-person, turn-based tactical games with a bit of RNG and a bit of customization, I think you'll like Children of Zodiarcs. Is it a perfect game? Nah, not really, nor is it a sweeping epic, but if you want to spend $60 for the latest "sweeping epic" that EA or SquareEnix squeezed out, go do it. If you want to go play a fun, if somewhat rougher, game by a smaller group, then this is one of those games.
With straightforward solid mechanics, a minimalist art-style, rich narration and a nigh unrivalled soundtrack, altogether it completes an incredible game.

If you're looking for FFT / Tactics Ogre / classical 'tactics rpg', this isn't it. There is little to no squad building, character development is linear, and customization is limited. Your party appears to be limited to 3 characters which is fairly small in srpg terms.
While interesting ideas on paper, I personally am not a fan of the dice or the cards system. Personally I find rolling the dice more of an annoyance than anything else. I am aware there is an auto-roll option, which I have turned on. The main reason I find it annoying is that it slows down the speed of battles in a genre where the speed of battles is already very slow paced. Especially annoying is staring at the enemies dice roll for 5 seconds before they do their ability animation; there should be an option to speed that up or skip it altogether. I don't care what dice the enemy rolls; just let me get on with the battle. When a battle takes 13 turns, and there are 5 enemies, you end up spending 5 * 13 * 5 seconds (6 minutes) staring at enemy dice rolls waiting for them to do their ability. I think the dice are an interesting twist on the RNG formula, but I think the implementation just gets in the way and needs some work. I don't care about the dice at all... get the dice out of my face and let me play the game faster please.
When it comes to the cards system, I'm not a big fan either. The cards system replaces a traditional "mana" or "mp" based resource system, and your cards in your hand dictate which skills are available to use. I have two issues with this system. First of all is that my character has abilities that sometimes I am unable to use. In a strategy rpg, I would prefer to have my skills available to use as long as I have sufficient resources. Pretty much all of the "strategy" in strategy RPGs is making the decision of which ability to use. The second issue is that it slows down the pace of battles, since drawing cards requires a unit's turn. I think you start with 4 cards in your hand, and you draw 2 cards at a time. So basically after 2 or 3 turns you have to spend a turn just to draw 2 more cards.
The cards and dice systems kind of remind me of the "laws" in final fantasy tactics advance. It was an annoying game mechanic that is not enjoyable at all, you just have to put up with it.
I would agree with the sentiment of many other reviewers who have mentioned the pace of battle is way too slow. In my opinion this is a pain point for strategy RPGs in general. I think the card and dice mechanics in this game made the battles even slower.
The game is lacking reward schedules. Usually your core loop in a strategy rpg is battle, gain exp + loot (reward), squad management & character customization (reward), progress through story (reward), rinse and repeat. Since there is no equipment, very little squad management & character customization, and character stats development is linear, the main "rewards" of a typical strategy rpg are nonexistant in this game. Making an addicting / enjoyable game is all about reward schedules, and there's just not much in this game that I find rewarding.
No offense but the writing style / humor in this game doesn't really mesh well with the game. A lot of the dialog sounds very immature and childish to me, its almost never serious, always joking around, like I'm hanging out with a gang of little kids. The main character has this ebonics thing going on, which gives me a headache. There was some other character with a southern sounding accent that didn't work at all either. I'm pretty much skipping the dialog at this point because i know it's not going to get any better.
I will still recommend this game, I kickstarted the game, I understand an indie team of about 6 people made it. I don't think they misrepresented the game they were developing. I knew from the start they were doing the cards/dice systems and I wanted to try it. I totally understand the limitations and constraints when working on a small indie team. So even if my review sounded negative, my intention was for it to be constructive criticism and help other gamers decide whether or not they would like this game.
I think the main reason for mixed reviews is that lots of people just want someone to make a modernized classical strategy rpg. If you come into this expecting a classical strategy rpg like FFT or Tactics Ogre, you'll probably be disappointed. If you market your game and compare it to FFT, i guess prepare to expect lots of disappointed people.

The dark 19th century sky is lit up with red flames beyond the mountains next to your cabin. The flames are coming from the town. Your first objective is to get to your basement, pick up your single rifle, grab some bullets and head across the bridge into town. You don't run or sprint. With your trusty lantern to light the way, you begin to cross the rickety old bridge. Halfway across, it breaks and you fall in the river. Undaunted that your neighbors are on fire, you trudge through the shallow water.
When you get into town, its on fire. White ash flutters through the air. There is no one left alive. Bodies in the church are mutilated and charred. The cross at the end of the chapel is on fire. There is a key on a barrel with only one place that it leads. Trying to exit the front double doors of God's house gets them slammed in your face. After taking some time, you manage to get one of the doors open and head to the stable where you use the key to get inside. It is there that you find more gruesome bodies. Even worse than that, you find a black mare on the ground, severed in two. Its pink innards are still inside and that's when you're punched in the face with a horrifying vision. A shock runs down your spine at the startling jump of the vision. Something is in your head and it won't relent until you've dealt with the werewolf.
You head out of town, where you build a bonfire to make it through the night. That's when you're attacked by a giant snake. After shooting it in the face several times, you find that you've been bitten. The world begins to melt around you. The world gets hazy and you struggle to walk through a canyon guided by your map. At the end of the canyon is an extremely tall watchtower. Even in a daze, you walk up a winding staircase to the top where there is only more horrifying death. You find a hidden key to a gate on the ground. Then without hesitation, you find the quickest way down is to leap from the watchtower. With the snake venom running through your veins, you feel no pain or death. You just get up and head through the gate.
That's when you come face to face with the monstrous beast. Your vision goes red from snake venom. It all becomes so surreal. Everything has a blurry green echo as your vision ripples. You see black blades of grass before you see a towering black shadow looking over you. Its pointed ears and arms indicate that its what is in your head. There is no fur on this wolf, its a slick jet black like the charred bodies you had encountered.
The first reaction in your head as it charges toward you is to quickly put a bullet in it. The bullet barely stuns it. The beast drops to all fours as you slowly reload your gun. It charges at you still and you're lucky enough to put a second bullet into it destroying it in a black puff of smoke. Was it real or is it the venom messing with you? That won't be the last encounter with the werewolf as you stagger through another canyon.
Going over a wavy bridge, you come face to face with the werewolf a fifth time. There is no where to run, its just you and your rifle against an aggressive man beast. The other encounters were easier. Some go away in a puff of smoke after one mere bullet. This one is different. Even after you've taken it down, it remains in your head. When you walk through the puff of smoke you jump at a loud screech as the hazy green fog goes blue and the werewolf rises in your mind. Its only in your mind and it won't ever stop trying to scare you.
I'll end the abridged story there, but in case you couldn't tell, Overcast - Walden and the Werewolf is a first person survival horror game. You won't just be struggling to keep your sanity, but you'll be fighting against tar black werewolves, spiders and the slow reload of your single shot rifle. If that wasn't enough of a struggle, your lantern barely lights up a room. Everything that is lit up has an unnatural plastic shine to it.
There is no run, no rebindable keys, no duck and a laughably pathetic jump. You've only got arrow keys, a reload, a mouse click to fire your gun and a right mouse click to zoom in slightly or to move objects. You can lift fallen logs off bodies, move chairs, read letters, pick up keys and ammo all with the right mouse button. There is no pause screen, but there is a menu with only the most basic of screen and graphical quality options. Sorely missing was a brightness adjustment, but I guess you always have your monitor.
After a chapter is completed, you are sent back to the chapter select screen, which takes me out of the immersion. Another thing that really takes me out of the game are all of the invisible walls that surround areas. First around your cabin, even underneath of the bridge there are invisible walls guiding you. I had to hop over clutter that I felt like I should be able to simply walk over. Things like logs strewn on the floor. Even coming up from the basement forced me to jump out. Ladders force you to jump up rungs one by one.
You won't find much animation if any. Cut scenes are relegated to camera effects and you see your character paralyzed in a default pose. The werewolf spiders and snake are barely animated. Its serviceable, but its also glaring. Even the reload animation is just your gun floating from right to left without a hand on it.
The game has a surrealistic hazy effect throughout most of it. Not just being bit by the snake. There are all sorts of camera effects. Everything from seeing what the snake sees in a fish-eye lens to blurry vision. It really puts a unique twist on things and sets it apart from other first person Unity engine horror games. Because of the surrealistic color pallet and fog, even the simple countryside can become a nightmarish landscape full of dead trees and rigid grass.
You won't just be in the countryside, you'll explore an abandon ship next to an ancient web-filled prison fortress. After that, comes a graveyard full unseen spiders hidden in the tall grass. You'll be tormented mentally with jump scares of enemies falling straight on you. It all keeps you off kilter knowing that any second the game will just screech and throw another mind torturing jump scare at you.
Walden has no health, so getting caught by a werewolf or bit by even the tiniest spider will kill him. Every death restarts you from the beginning of the chapter. There is no save, but the game keeps track of the chapters you've unlocked.
The music is surprisingly good and should be applauded. It feels like a real musician added his talents to this game. It was the only shining point of this game. The sound effects though were deafeningly loud for those jump scare moments that we all know and love. There are plenty of random jump scares when you least expect them because the werewolf has taken control of your mind.
To help guide you on your way there is a map if you hit the tab key. It shows you and your direction, but shows your next objective with a glowing area on the map. The only problem is sometimes I went well off the map.
While I do think this is more of a game than other first person Unity engine horror experiences, I didn't enjoy Overcast - Walden and the Werewolf. Supposedly its an hour long game, that took me three hours to complete and it felt like mental torture every step of the way. With all that said, the surrealism and the awful gameplay make this one unique game among its peers. It has been 14 cents before and in many bundles. It might be worth it.

Friday the 13th: The Game is a must have game for anyone who is a fan of the Slasher film genre and Horror video game genre. Yes, it has had some teething problems and launch difficulties. Yes, it still has some programming issues and glitches. But it is still a solid, worthwhile game. Both for the experience of being chased down and brutally murdered by everyone’s favorite machete wielding killer. And the shear joy of putting on the hockey mask yourself and hunting down those horny, drugged up moron teenage counselors and murdering them in all kinds of fun as hell ways ripped straight out of the movies and a few brand new ones.
Ignore the few minor issues it has now, Gun Media is working their collective tails off to get it all patched and fixed, this is a small developer team that’s making this game. And the fact that such a small team made such a badass game in the first place is a minor miracle. Not to mention the fact that they managed to get the rights to Friday the 13th in the first place. Single player is slated to come out this fall, and I can’t wait for that.
So ignore the bumpy start, enjoy the screams of the condemned counselors and have a bloody good time!

Trolls and Toxic players in public matches now can't kill you, or run off with vital components to escaping Jason's clutches. Car Keys, fuel tanks, batteries and propellers now show up on the map if they are picked up once. Either when a counselor drops them, gets killed or escapes, they now show up on the map.
The addition of another Jason, another map, more counselors, and even more gruesome kills, with more of each to come, is just icing. This game keeps getting better, and in my opinon, is well worth the $40 I paid for it.

TLDR:
Really amazing competitive shooterwith plenty of characters for you to choose from (with more coming). Amazing gameplay, very much worth the money.
Basically...
There are a whole lot of characters to choose from, ones for defense and ones for offense. Offense has better scopes (Acog) for farther ranges (some defense operators have the acog). There are three gamemodes. You get paired with 4 other people (5 in a team), or you can squad up with your friends. You shoot and kill all enemies or play the objective.
Gameplay:
Bomb:
A multiplayer gamemode where defenders protect two bombs. Attackers need to plant a defuser in the same room as one of the bombs. If the defuser defuses the bomb, the attackers win, but if the defuser is disabled, the defenders win. If all attackers die, but the defuser was planted already, the game will still go on until the defenders disable the defuser or, if they run out of time to disable it, the attackers can still win.
Secure Area:
A multiplayer gamemode where defenders protect a room with a biohazard container. Attackers need to stay in the same room as the container for a certain amount of time to win, the defenders can stay in the same room and prevent the attackers from gaining any "time".
Hostage:
A multiplayer gamemode where attackers need to extract a hostage and the defenders need to prevent the attackers from taking back the hostage.
Terroris Hunt:
A solo or Co-op gamemode (up to 5 people). They can play the same gamemodes listed above, but with bots. They can also choose the difficulty- Normal, Hard, Realistic.
Situations:
Singleplayer content. (ish) I would classify it as tutorial gameplay. There are 10 Situations where the game teaches you how to play certain characters. After playing all 10, you will unlock an 11th, a situation that you can play with friends or randoms.
In casual, the objectives and the spawn place or random for all players.
In competitive, players can choose where they spawn (attackers) or where they want the objective (for defense only).
Ranking System:
Personally one of my favorite ranking systems because you retain your rank even when you done play ranked games, unlike other games *cough cough* Overwatch *cough cough*
Bronze4 B3 B2 B1 Silver4 S3 S2 S1 Gold4 G3 G2 G1 Platinum3 P2 P1 Diamond
Lowest ---------------------------------------------------------------> Highest
You play ten placement matches at the beginning of the season and you will be placed based on how well you do, the majority of players are in Silver and Gold.
Community:
I'm not sure about others, but from my experience, competitive has nicer people than casual. When I make a good play in competitive, the enemy players will congratulate me, but when I'm in casual and make a good play, the enemy team will cuss at me. Feels bad man. *keep in mind these are my experiences*
Graphics:
Graphics are great, there are some settings that will DEFINITELY tank your pc, but they might have fixed that by now.
All maps look very beautiful at all ULTRA and you can definitely tell they took their time making it.
Controls:
Basically what you would expect with any shooter, except ctrl is lay down, alt makes your character make less noise, but makes you move slower. You can ping so that your teammates know what you want them to do.
DLC:
For me, since I love shooters with destructible environments, the DLC was very worth it. ALL PLAYERS get all the maps that Ubi comes out with, but they dont get the operators for free.
Season pass holders get more xp, more renown (in game currency), and higher chance of getting loot boxes (called Alpha packs). They also get all of the DLC operators for free, without paying any in game currency. It may feel that getting money in game is hard and takes a lot of grinding, but when you start playing more, you realize that you get a LOT of renown really fast.
Overall...
An amazing game with a lot of content. Well worth the money. Get it with a few friends, your experience will be so much better, whether you play it really competitively or just mess around.
Pros:
- Great graphics
- Great community
- Plenty of content
- A lot of variety
- Not repetitive
- Competitive
Cons:
- Ubi doesnt always keep promises, they ended up not making a map they promised us
- Sometimes it glitches, but Ubi has done a pretty good job at getting rid of the really big bugs

Compared to their previous titles, managing light is no longer a major factor outside of trying to see in a few dark places with an limitless powered flashlight. There's practially no inventory, and the one to three items you will carry at a time will only show up as outlined icons on the bottom of the screen, so gone are the classic adventure game puzzling. Instead, puzzle solving is done primarily through the use of computers, your handheld omni tool and a few inventory items.
SOMA features the best use of enemies from Frictional Games' titles - the different "enemy types" have unique ways of detecting and chasing the player and can cause fear in you since you aren't sure how to deal with them. This is also one of my complaints - you may die to an enemy well before you know how you're supposed to avoid them. Thankfully, I was able to figure it out after one or two deaths (if it took me that much, which didn't always happen). My biggest complaint with some enemies is that their constant interferance (meaning how fast they can get close to you) will require you to stop (to survive) and impede your progress. Yes, I know their whole point is to scare you, to make you think and tread carefully, but some enemies would walk away in a stealth sequence and after about 5 seconds of player movent, you have to stop and wait for them to leave again...and again...and again.
The last thing I'll say is regarding choices in the game. Some players don't like how choices affect the ending. The few moments where the player has a choice, their choice
affects dialogue portions.
SOMA's use of choices may be the smartest handling of player choices because of this.
SOMA is a good horror and puzzle solving experince. I don't think any of Frictional Games' titles are ever truly fun, but are instead engaging in some way, so take that into consideration before buying.

Waking Mars is a port of a tablet game, but unlike the typical tablet port it has excellent mouse & keyboard controls (and also supports game pads, although I didn't use mine). It has the structure of a Metroidvania, but where a Metroidvania has you fighting your way through enemies to acquire new equipment that allows access to new areas, Waking Mars is entirely non-violent (except for the occasional environmental hazard) and has you manipulating the ecosystem in order to open up new paths to explore.
This is both interesting (going against the normal structure of the genre by leaving out enemies entirely) and terrible (it turns out that manipulating the ecosystem by growing and killing plants isn't a great gameplay experience). In fact, I once screwed up the plant life in a room so badly that I resorted to deleting the save file to reset it (fortunately, each room is saved in its own file, so I didn't lose my progress entirely). I suspect that it is actually possible to render the game unwinnable by accidentally eradicating some of the plant species entirely, although I didn't do this. I did kill off enough of some of the more troublesome species that it became difficult to remember where some of their specimens were in the game world in order to collect their seeds on the rare occasions I needed to use them to progress.
Waking Mars is an interesting but not spectacular experience with some nicely drawn 2D art, good voice acting, actual minority characters for a change, and a gameplay mechanic that outlasted its welcome to the point where I took the easiest to obtain ending and didn't bother with the more difficult options. Not terrible, not wonderful, notable because  it is different.

Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is an amazing game which tells a story about Iñupiat, an Alaska Native people's myth legend, called Kunuuksaayuka. You play interchangeably between Nuna and the Fox as you explore and try to save your home village from a terrifying blizzard. The graphics are beautiful and very fluid. It gives you the feeling of a traditional folklore especially when you combine it with the narrations. The story plot is great. The game also features a lot of different puzzles though the game is quite short overall. The cultural insights collectibles are very informative. They tell you more about not just Iñupiat but additional details like polar bears, the tundra and way of life of people who live in Alaska.
Overall, this game is quite an experience. If you're looking for a decent coop puzzle platforming game with a great story then, this is a MUST try for you. The game is quite easier on coop mode but it's also enjoyable in singleplayer mode though a bit challenging.

*EDIT: after having already written the below review: Although I still recommend players experiencing the base game that this title is based off of, it has to be noted that Totally Mayhem and other very similar incarnations of it are all using a Unity asset pack with little distinction between the titles beyond palette swaps or different dialog. I wasn't aware of how similar the titles are until having played most of Totally Mayhem, and seeing another title so similar on Steam tends to cheapen both as a result.*  That being said, on with the original review...
Totally Mayhem is a colorful, loud, in your face arcade-y experience. I imagine the reception to this game may be divisive where some players will enjoy its simplistic, over-the-top approach and others may lament it for being so straightforward and repetitive.
Throughout the course of its very brief playtime (1.5 hrs to go through the base 27 levels)Totally Mayhem is a mostly nonsensical highlight reel of 80s shticky action featuring tons of explosions amidst (intentionally?) bad animations and over-the-top sound effects. The sound effects in the game range from arcade-y blips and "HUH!" jump noises as you annihilate pretty much everyone in your path to loud, blaring music when you complete a level. You can also blow up buildings and vehicles in the game, which make for some large, cool-looking chained explosions as seen here:

While the explosions look nice, other parts of the game seem like they've been made to appear intentionally glitched-out or comical, such as when you kill a ton of enemies at once and their bodies fly toward the sky with the oft-repeated "kill sound" (heard in the trailer as a high-pitched chirping..) This sound effect can become somewhat annoying, and some options to reduce the volume or adjust some of the effects on or off might make the game more accessible.
Speaking of adjusting the game and accessibility issues, myself and another user of the game encountered an error when trying to put the game's visual settings on "high" the game would display the background but not function and was rendered unplayable otherwise. The developers suggested deleting a save file from the computer's registry and not selecting to play on the "high" option as a solution. The game itself looks fine at a lower setting, and I doubt that it would benefit much visually from a boost to its mostly minimalistic graphics, however being told more or less to just not utilize a function still listed as present in the game (and something that seems to still not have been patched out or corrected as of posting this review) is a bit disheartening. This is in addition to losing your game save by being required to delete the game save if trying to access the High graphics option. More info on this glitch can be found at the Discussions post here:
Totally Mayhem seems to be inspired by GTA / State of Emergency's chaos while having more of a neon, Miami Vice aesthetic overall. Some of the enemy designs appear to be somewhat angular and creepy akin to something you may encounter more in Eastern design aesthetics and make for a unique, refreshing look here. The vehicles and turrets you can use feel a bit underwhelming/underdeveloped and I preferred to just be on foot jumping around and throwing grenades or blasting dudes while jumping around like a rabbit to and from. Although you can seemingly hop into any vehicle you want to on the game, beyond doing so to get to a certain area faster before a timer expires or to fulfill a certain mission's requirements (i.e. you're relegated to use a tank at that time..) there is little incentive to do so, as the handling and aiming while in vehicles feels a little rough, and the city has little to discover beyond the occasional hidden powerup box.
The game is very repetitive across its 27 levels for the most part, and many of the levels' objectives are similar, amounting to little more than "blow everything up." You will have to destroy certain trucks, or a certain number of a type of enemy, but the objectives never require much player interaction beyond pointing at, shooting, and making things dead faster than they point, shoot at, and make you dead.
I don't mind the game's repetition and think the trailer for the game does a good job of depicting the simplicity of the game overall. The game runs much smoother than in the trailer and has ~some~ skill required in evading shots or choosing when to grab the various pickups or when to use turrets etc. Totally Mayhem includes some very minimal platforming (in order to get a better vantage point or reach certain enemies you need to defeat) and you have to dodge a fair amount of enemy fire at times, requiring more precision than I thought the game would have while going through its first levels. These sections are more sparse than the aforementioned explosion fest, however, and the game more often amounts to shooting everything in front of you faster than it shoots you.
I was looking for a game to just boot up real quick and enjoy blowing some stuff up, and Totally Mayhem delivered on that mark. It doesn't take itself too seriously, has an enjoyable color palette, and I'm a fan of its shtick of over the top Miami Vice / Hotline Miami / 1980s /  detective on a rampage style.  Although I wish the game made some effort to depict a narrative or storyline inbetween the mostly all menu-driven levels, and I don't see myself playing it much more after having cleared all of its levels, it does include the occassional boss fight to give it more variety to its overall repetitive pace and I did enjoy myself overall.  If you see the trailer and think you may enjoy the game, I think it provides a fun, over the top action experience with a unique minimalistic visual style, just be prepared for the levels to mostly all be the same thing: Blowing stuff up.

Waking Mars has to be the most grounded Science Fiction game I have ever had the pleasure of playing. It feels like something that could actually happen through to the end. All four(?) of them.
The paper cut-out art style makes everything pop in just the right way. It's all very well drawn. Not only is the art good, but the characters are extremely realistic and likeable people that will accompany you via radio on your journey through the vast underground Martian ecosystem.
The best way to describe this game is as a casual 2-D puzzle platformer, gardening/ecosystem creation simulation. It's on the easy side, sure, but you'll definitely get your money's worth out of the story alone. For those asking a little more, you can try and perfect the game. All 110% of it! Personally, I reached 103% and two endings in 7.1 hours playtime, and I was stopping to admire a lot of scenery.
The only cons I can really think of would be after a certain point, things get tedious. If you're looking to squeeze out every last bit of exploration, dialogue, and completion from this game, you're going to be doing a LOT of backtracking to places where you can easily access certain materials. But if you're going that far, you should be ready to deal with such tedium and technically forfeit your right to complain.
All in all, I recommend this game for fans of simple puzzle games, space cadets, and anyone with general interest in good sci-fi. If you really want a deal, wait for it to go on sale or hope it gets thrown into a Humble Bundle again. Maybe even pick it up on Android or IOS if you rather game on-the-go.
Finally, my recommendation for controls is a 360/PS3 gamepad. The keyboard and mouse controls just don't fit very well, but that's my personal opinion.

Hundreds... thousands of hours... over years of play, on Steam, on WeMade, on OGPlanet, ever since the dawn of Lost Saga's age I have been around. Sometimes I quit, but I always come back, this game just... speaks something special to me, no matter how much it changes. It's like turning up the temperature by 1 degree every week, you don't notice the difference unless you compare it a few months later to now. I have to say, do I recommend this game? I wish I could recommend this to anyone, but there are several reasons why I think you should possibly consider thinking about your decision to spend your time attempting to play this game as a new player.
This game is probably the most well optimised game I've ever played on the internet, even against the likes of the classic Valve games. I guarantee you will be able to run this game on max settings with little to no issue. The only problem I have is that the game strangely crashes after a very long session (I'm talking 6-8 hours, give or take, this actually can be seen as a pro to be honest) The game also "Optimises" updates for a long time at the second launch since the update and causes the client to time out requiring a relaunch, but again, very minor.
Lost Saga is a multiplayer online brawler which heavily focuses on Player versus Player gameplay. The most prominent feature is the high variety of classes ("Heroes") and intergangable equipment ("Gears") that can make for a very dynamic, wild and downright unpredictable experience; it would be nearly inhuman to be able to accurately list the number of combinations of equipment and characters possible.
Lost Saga as mentioned is heavily PvP-focused. Although there are numerous PvE experiences, you will find that the PvE will prove to be lackluster and repeatitive after the novelty wears off, though it isn't actually that bad, and functions decently. As of now, there are many, many characters and many many gears, so much so that new players will be overwhealmed and likely not even try to learn what the enemy is using and will be mindflooded. That isn't to say the variety is a bad thing, it's a learning experience, knowing what to expect, and adapting to other players' playstyles. Lost Saga has a very high skill ceiling with most of the characters, though the game can be incredibly frustrating to those who don't know how to exploit the equipment and characters...
I dipped into this slightly in the previous topic, but not enough, as this is a serious issue, and frankly, the only one really turning people off from playing (Or continuing once they are a victim). I'm talking about balance. The game's characters are NOT balanced to each other. Some characters are downright unplayable if you actually want to stand a chance, others are god-tier, having little lag time and incredible strength for their attacks and skills, and with no weakness, encouraging an all-out playstyle that exploits that character's (Or equipment's) power. This is to be expected in a game with this much variety in playstyle: Players will pick and sort out what is, or isn't the strongest, and you will start to see much less variety, and much more frustration if your arsenal cannot compete. What makes it worse is that most of these easily-exploitable mechanics are only achievable in either huge grinds, or through expensive payments. One category of hero (Called Unique) can only be obtained through a luck of the draw, and those who pay can gain a massive boost to their chance in contrast to those who do heavy grinding, no matter how much the grinder works, and these characters are almost always god-tier, and easily exploitable. The community can also be a bit brash and "toxic" at times, though this can be easily ignored, there are blocking features.
In conclusion, is this a bad game? No, it's one of the most underrated gems I think I've ever had the pleasure to stumble across, pure PvP carnage fun. It has seen better days, but I'd say give it a shot, but I warn you, most of the players left are either new players like yourself, or old veteran players that have hundreds if not thousands of hours of playtime on their belts.

This is a Strategy RPG in which their sole focus was the combat system.  Outside of battles, content is as stripped down as can be - you get a world map, you get some random banter between party members, you get to go back and fight "skirmishes" to grind exp, or you get to go to the next story mission.  That's it.
But the combat system....is pretty damn good.  Characters get their own decks of cards with various attacks that you can fully customize in how prevalent each attack is in the deck.  When you attack, a series of dice are thrown, which add (and sometimes detract) effects like increased damage, self healing, special effects unique to each attack, extra turns, extra drawn cards, and so on.  You then get to choose a couple dice to reroll if you want, and the attack hits.  This happens with every attack in the game, even healing and self buffs.  You can customize the dice themselves by tinkering with the symbols on each side out of battle, which lets you customize how often certain effects show up.
It's a wonderfully deep system, and combat is a blast.  For that alone I recommend, but really the game needed more content in general.  There's no equipment on each character outside the dice so there's no treasures to find in map, no optional objective rewards, or anything like that.  Combat is limited to 3 party members so they really amped up the damage....characters can regularly one shot enemies or sometimes even groups of enemies, but enemies are also extremely dangerous (especially Mages, whose damage seems a bit imbalanced, both yours and theirs).

The game is mediocre fun. I guess I'll do a "pros and cons" list like many other reviewers.
Pros:
-Interesting concept. Who doesn't want a game where you take three of history's most respected warriors, and pit them against one another.
-Pretty innovative combat system, I like it quite a bit. Attacking and blocking in certain angles is definitely a feature I'd like to see in other games. It dips a bit into some historical martial arts, but still retains that level of fictitious flair that keeps it flashy and interesting.
-The game looks great, while not being "historically accurate", the costume design is a mix between Hollywood and reality, which is cool.
Cons:
-I feel they could have really taken this concept to a higher degree. It is in a fictitious setting, yet the Samurai are still called Samurai, when they really could have come up with a cooler, unique Japanese sounding name. Same with the Vikings. They could have called them Nords, Northmen, etc. But they just slapped that generic label on them.
-The story was not interesting at all, and did not immerse me whatsoever. The entire time I felt like the story mode was thrown in just to keep people from complaining about there being a lack of one. They really could have amped the game up by taking that extra step to make a unique lore for the world they created, instead of using such generic names and plots.
-A lot of the moves some of the classes have are absolute cheese.
TL;DR in theory the game is interesting, but lacks any sort of substance that keeps me coming back to the game. Lack of story, and lack of any depth whatsoever, makes the entire game feel sort of bland, redundant, and meaningless. Apart from aesthetic preference, there is nothing that draws the player towards a certain faction. What are they about, what is their story, their history, why do they do what they do? None of that plays a factor.

I'm trying to think of positive things to say about this game, but honestly I can't.
First, you can't remap the key bindings, which is a big deal for me as I don't care much for the traditional WASD controls.
Next, the graphics are, to be blunt, bad.  I'm not the kind of guy that needs the latest & greatest graphics --in fact, I still fire up Doom1 & Doom2 from time to time --but in a game like this where there's not much else to do but look at the inexcusably bad graphics as you slowly  plod along, it's inexcusable.  There are much better looking games that are much older, and the animation is some of the most unimpressive I've ever seen --especially the dog you run into early on in the game.
Speaking of slow, your character moves stiffly and slowly --more slowly than I do in real life.  You can sprint, but only for a while before you run out of breath.  So far, this mechanic seems to serve no purpose.
Additionally, nearly all the time I spent in this game was spent basically doing nothing except trying to diving which direction the game wanted me to slowly plod toward, and then waiting for my excruciatingly slow AI companion to shuffle over towards me.  Also, he gives a long and uninteresting speech in a barn which is not skippable, even if you've already heard it before because that's where you left off yesterday.
Did I mention this was yet another "mystery disease wipes out most of mankind" post-apocalyptic game?  Haven't we had enough of those lately?  At least they usually come with some zombies to liven things up...
Really, the rest of my complaints fall under the game basically being inscrutable:
* You can interact with things using the "E" key, but there's little to indicate what you can interact with.  The engine seems picky and inconsistent over whether or not you've got an item centered on your screen to interact with, even when you're butted firmly against it and have it dead center.  Items will apparently highlight a bit to indicate you can hit "E" to do something with them, but even this feature works sometimes and not others.
* There is an inventory system, which also seems to serve no purpose.
* You can pick up food, but it doesn't seem to do anything.  You can also pick up batteries which don't seem to do anything.
* You have a camera that you can take pictures with, but again... this doesn't seem to actually do anything.
* You have a knife that doesn't seem to do anything except cut some threads on door handles, and even then it seems to behave like it passed ponderously through thin air rather than actually striking something.
* Did I mention having to guess where your pokey companion would like to plod along to, and waiting for him there?
* Hey, it's night.  Your vision is darkened and worringly blurry.  Do you need to eat something?  Is your health low?  Do you even have health?  No way to tell.
* Some doors you can open, with some fiddling around with positioning.  Except that one.  Or that.
* Do you need to climb this ladder that obviously leads to a roof?  Can you even climb a ladder?  Just keep fiddling with it and find out! (hint: you can't)
* Go get some water from a well.  We all love fetch quests!  Especially when you're moving like a 90 year old with a glass hip.  You'll eventually find the well through trial and error, but oops!  You need a bucket!  Guess what: it was the bucket you found 30 seconds into this stage and TRIED to pick up, but because the "use" system is buggy, your "E" key didn't do anything with it, and since there's no indication what's something you can "use" and what's just static mesh, you decided it must just be another static decoration like most things in the game.
...and at that point,  I uninstalled.

What is 35mm?
Genre: first person exploration game with fps elements
Setting: traveller trying to find his family in a post-disease Russia
Difficulty: 3/10 --> basically nothing difficult, but shooter passages are a bit clumsy
Length: 3-5 hours for a single playthrough, up to around 15 to get all achievements
Mode: singleplayer campaign
Similar games: Can't name any, sorry ;)
The positive aspects:
- very chastened atmosphere - sets a fitting tone
- landscapes and locations rich in variety
- "side-quests" (achievement stuff) to do along the main path
The negative aspects:
- that game is awfully dark. I had to brighten up my graphics card to see a thing
- needless shooter passages with apparently only a single hitbox
- low walking pace; sometimes you have to wait several minutes before your partner arrives to let the game make progress
- superficial items and inventory management
- story and backgrounds are not fully revealed and explained
Result (and summary for those who have no time reading):
Although 35mm has some downsides, it is worth taking the virtual journey. Being a rather slow, actionless exploration game, the depressing atmosphere and tone of the game make it quite an enjoyable experience.
If you're interested in those kind of games - give it a try!

In this game, however, you have all of your powers from the start, and so if you're on the easiest level or the hardest, you're going to tear every enemy apart with ease. Rarely did I actually use my guns, opting more to rip my enemies to pieces with all of the combo kills. The story is very twisted here, and by the end of the game, you start questioning the game's reality, debating which portion of the game is real and which is the illusion. I highly recommend this, and if you can get a friend or two to play with you, the co-op even continues the story as a side note, letting you see what happens with your crew when you're not around to tie up all the loose ends. It's on sale for 80% off this weekend-- letting a $30 game go when it's $6 would be a shame.
If you want a taste of the awesomeness, try the demo-- it's available for download from this page.

Now that I am capable of taking off, landing and getting the occasional kill, I think that I can say with certainty that this game is quite good.
Is it for everyone? No, it is a flight simulator, as such it requires a joystick, and it has a huge learning curve. But if you can get past those things, you will be rewarded with one of the most satisfying and realistic WW1 experiences currently possible in gaming. Additionally, the community is wonderful, the multiplayer servers  have some very friendly and helpful people who are a pleasure to fly with.
Finally,  this game is not exactly free to play, it is more like free to try. If you install the Free version, you will  have access to 2 planes. To fly other planes, and their respective campaigns you will need to purchase the corresponding dlc package. This does not mean that you cannot enjoy this game, just don't expect to be able to fly every single plane for free.

This game caught my eye during a summer sale. I was browsing through some new releases and decided to purchase it. And as usual, it sat in the back of my steam library until I dusted it off, installed it and started playing.
My first impression of the game was the title screen, with its dark, snowy camp site. And then the title fades in on the screen. Kisima Ingitchuna. I was exited. The actual game begins with a story told through a traditional art form, which is a nice way to start off. In fact, this game itself is basically a story, told through the means of a platformer-style game.
I will not spoil the story here, because it is a good one, and you should hear it for yourself. :)
The game allows you to control two characters. Nuna and the Fox. It can be played with two players (similarly to Brothers), but I was playing it by my self, so I just switched between the two. Nuna can climb ladders and move heavy objects, while The Fox can crawl through tiny spaces and inch up walls. The Fox's biggest feature however, is that he can communicate with spirits. The spirits take form of something in the level and help you traverse the level as Nuna. The contrast of the two make for good gameplay. My only complaint with playing by yourself, is that the AI can be tricky sometimes. The computer-controlled character might jump off and force you to restart the puzzle. While it only happened occasionally, it was still annoying.
The game looks and sounds great. It has a fitting soundtrack that picks up with certain effects, depending on what your doing in the game, which is a nice touch. The graphics have a nice contrast of white and dark, following very closely to Alaska. There are places in the game where colors pop! For example: in one section of the game the Northern lights come down and take the form of little worm-like spirits. They look really cool in the dark of night, and serve the game well.
So, this game has a great soundtrack, nice graphics and solid gameplay... What more could you ask for? Well, the only REAL downside to this game is the amount of bugs. There are some movement bugs and graphical hiccups throughout.
So, to recap:
Pros:
- Good Story
- Enjoyable Gameplay
- Clean Visuals
Cons:
- Minor Bugs
- A bit Short
- $15 Price Tag (I would wait for a sale)

First and Foremost, this game is a REALISTIC WWI flight/combat simulator. Airplanes were only really invented in 1903 and the time frame of WWI the entire technology was only 15 years old, if that. Humans were only learning how to make airplanes that did not kill their pilots, and REALISTICALLY..airplanes at the time killed their pilots A LOT. It is important that your expectations match what this game is, and what it is, is a wonderfully executed realistic simulator of WWI aerial combat. In all questions of gameplay vs. realism, realism has been chosen at every step to the point where the forums have hobbyists who have actually rebuilt full sized replicas of these airplanes comparing the flight charactaristics of the game to the real thing. No small feat for machines which last were militarilly relevant over a century ago. In other words, this is not a casual game by any stretch of the imagination. In fact, I have to say that actually having a pilots licence (and some/lots of hours in real aircraft) is a very large leg up in being successful.
Besides the communications mistep of "I thought I was getting a casual, balanced first person shooter with airplanes, and I keep dying because I am not actually a pilot, have never taken flight ground school, and from no fault of my own don't entirely understand power-on, power-off stalls, never exceed airspeed or spin recovery". The default plane selection in the quick mission is a plane that does not come in the free to play mode. This is possibly the single most head scratching decision in the entire game. Nearly every person who buys this is going to fire up a quick mission and instantly get into the struggle of "what planes am I actually allowed"? The answer is some very good ones...just not default selected for No Good Reason. The Spad 13 is one of the best planes in the game (because it was one of the most technologically advanced airplanes of the actual war, and remember this is a simulator). MORE importantly, unless you actually ARE a pilot, and probably even then, DON'T start like this. Go to the training missions. Finish the first 3. Finishing all of them is a serious, long term project, but the first 3 should enable you to fly without killing yourself, and start to think about how to kill the Bad Guy(s).
So. IF:
1) You understand WHAT this game is and have correct expectations.
2) You avoid a couple of the really dumb UX choices in the initial menu.
3) Do enough training first to not be your own most likely cause of death.
THEN:
This is a 10 out of 10 WWI combat simulator. The UX problems are menu layouts/defaults and not making first things really be first. Once the mission starts, it delivers. It is also 100% possible to play totally Free to Play if you like. The starter planes are really very good, just limited in selection, and not properly set as default.

Never Alone is an atmospheric side scrolling platformer that tells us the touching story of a girl and her companion, a white fox, set out to find the source of the eternal blizzard which is ravaging her community.
The story is based on an old Iñupiaq tale, a symbolic legend of a civilization that has been dealing with nature's hardships for centuries. You guide Nuna and her friend an Arctic Fox in a journey through the Alaskan wilderness.
The art style is so amazing, with beautiful graphics and lovely drawn characters. The stunning environments possibly make Never Alone one of the most beautiful games out there.
In terms of gameplay, Never Alone is a fairly standard platformer. You'll make Nuna and Fox run and jump across icy gaps and snowy platforms, using each one's unique abilities to journey through environmental mazes along the way. Nuna and Fox have complementary skills. Fox jumps higher and, along with wall-climb ability, can summon the ethereal spirits that help them reach trickier spots. Nuna can push or pull objects and use a throwing weapon called Bola, capable of shattering icy obstacles that block your forward progress.
The blizzard at the center of the story plays a role in the mechanics as well. In some levels, strong gusts of icy wind blow across the screen at seemingly random intervals, requiring you to hold a button to brace against the ground and avoid being blown backward. Or in other areas, the wind gives Nuna a speed boost, making her able to reach higher or further away platforms that otherwise are unreachable.
You can choose between playing this alone or with a friend. In single player mode, one player switches between the two. In co-op mode, one player controls Nuna and the other one Fox.
Most of the times the controls are responsive, but there are a few spots in which the collision detection doesn't work as it should, causing Nuna to jump into abyss instead of gripping to the walls. On top of that, the spirit platforms that are activated by the fox only exist when it is close to them; if the fox moves away, the platforms fade out of view and cause characters that were once standing on them to fall.
The game starts at an easy difficulty level - the first few minutes of gameplay are a walk in the snow, or some simple jumps, letting you savour the story. However, the difficulty of the jumps increases as the game progresses. The same goes for the puzzles: some of them require patience, and a lot of trial and error to figure out the correct solution. There's a rough difficulty spike towards the end of the game, where the jumps need to be timed and very precise. However, the game has a lot of checkpoints and in between these checkpoints it autosaves before every jump in order to make it easier for the player to retry them.
The game length is around 4-6 hours, depending on your skills; it has low replay value, but for the 4-6 hours you are playing it, you are transported into the Alaskan way of life with the stunningly beautiful graphics as well as the narrator telling the story in his native tongue.
Throughout the 9 chapters, you will encounter several collectibles. Each of them unlocks a short video - a cultural insight featuring people from the Cook Inlet community talking about what it was like to grow up in the region's unforgiving cold.
Play this masterpiece; it will win your love.

Mars, spacesuits and jetpacks. Don't let the action tag fool you though, there isn't any combat, much less any real action to speak of, just lots of gardening and pseudoscience. Indeed, Waking Mars is a xenoecological adventure to recover a missing exploration probe as you uncover the secrets hidden within the Lethe Cavern.
Start out in a chamber mostly devoid of life, introduce moisture, plant seeds in fertile terrain and watch them spring to life! But as they start to spread out in the area, you might find that it may not be the most efficient ecosystem, or that certain Zoa may threaten to eliminate the rest of it! It's all very simple and there are limited patches for planting, but the number of cross interactions between different species and their environments makes for a surprising level of complexity.
You may have beat a zone by hitting a certain biomass within it and unlocked new areas, but later you might want to revist them to increase the efficiency of the ecosystems in them, improving synergies and generating even more biomass. Or you just want to visit it to pick up some seeds for use in a new area. The game encourages you to build ecosystems that benefit heavily from synergistic interactions but isn't afraid to let you build insane unstable ones that have large amounts of biomass constantly in flux as life is rapidly reproduced as it is destroyed. Sometimes planting a single Zoa (ART, an AI program in your suit will tell you that they aren't plants!) too soon can make it hard to fix as it spreads all around before you can start planting your desired Zoa in other patches. Sometimes the easiest way to stop this happening is to kill it. You may however only carry a certain amount of each seed and that makes you have to think about how you have to go about planting them (though it also means  that it can be tedious if you are trying to populate an area with mainly one sort of Zoa). There is even the potential to wipe out an entire species, though many plants do reappear in later chambers if you accidentally do so in an early one.
While many of the game's quirks make it arguably a better one, it is not without faults. You are almost required to revist some old chambers to do a quick restock of seeds every few chambers and while you can teleport between chambers you have visited I feel it could have been more streamlined.  Speaking of tedium, Ledon Zoa are amazing at providing biomass AND populating entire zones, but can be a nightmare to plant as they float upwards aimlessly, cannot be picked up and crumble with little force. ART is like a less charming Wheatley and can be quite jarring. Fortunately your player character, Liang, is the most likeable character in the game. The signal decoding segments can be a tad confusing and so can most of the endings.
Overall an excellent title, more enjoyable than gardening.
