I still enjoyed this game, just not in the ways I was hoping for. After having played the Penumbra series, and the original Amnesia, I was itching for more. While I found the general 'meat' of those games here, I was let down by the lack of the survival part. It's still good, and if you're happy to focus solely on narrative and atmosphere, this game does both quite well.
Just like Machine for Pigs, gameplay features have been dumbed down or removed entirely. In this case, there was no inventory - and very little reason to explore the world. Plenty of lockers and drawers around PATHOS-II, but very little of use in them. An unlimited flashlight certainly didn't make it any more scary. And my god, that stupid crosshair on the screen is so immersion breaking... I'm glad there's a mod to get rid of it.
Without having to worry about items, or limited light usage, I was able to roam as I pleased and not give a damn about how careless I was. I quickly learned that monsters were a once or twice a segment deal, and was always given ample time to study them and remove any fears I may have had. The atmosphere of horror and suspense, while initially rather strong, grew weaker as the game went on - and I learned the truth behind my character. It left me feeling detached, even moreso with the fact that he was constantly talking (much of the voice acting never had any real tone to it - just mundane chatter, never excited or let down by anything). I could have dealt with the latter if the former had been handled better. There was also a distinct lack of fun running from the majority of the monsters. I couldn't hide in as many places, and the AI generally felt less eager to kill me once I took off running. Double whammy, and a lack of time to bite my nails. Feeling like the monsters only half heartedly wanted to kill me weakened the horror aspect. There were some really cool designs and AI though, and having monsters sporadically move quickly or make extra noise certainly made me jump a few times!
Level design was good, puzzles were good, and the atmosphere went from underwhelming, initially, to downright impressive. The only sections I absolutely hated were any that focused around exploring the ocean floor; they just weren't creepy, nor scenic enough to really warrant the time. This is opinion, of course, but the tight and unpredictable corridors did a better job of conveying the bottom of the ocean science station than the outside did.
I was also a victim of performance troubles. After tweaking settings to get a steady 60 FPS, I still had a number of instances where it dropped for no reason other than lots of lights being rendered. I'm running an i5 2500K @ 4.5GHz, and an unlocked and overclocked RX460. Battlefield 1 runs at over 100 FPS, this game does not.
All in all, this was a good game but not what I was expecting. If you're looking for the survival part, involving searching for crucial items, it's not here. If you're looking for atmosphere, a good story, and introspection based on a few of your choices therein - pick this game up. You won't dislike it either way - and the only reason I'm giving a negative review is because it was radically different from what I'd thought I paid for. I hope the devs take note of my plight, although I'm doubtful when I'm one of very few negative reviews in a sea of positivity.

Waking Mars was a very big surprise for me.  I obtained the game as part of a Humble Bundle.  I'm a fan of Metroidvania games (action/exploration games like Metroid and Castlevania that focus on exploring a large 2D open world for upgrades and other goodies) so this did seem up my alley.
The gameplay of Waking Mars is similar to metroidvanias in its 2D open world and ability to wander, but that's about where the similarities end.  The core gameplay of Waking Mars is flying around with a jetpack through large 2D spaces manipulating each areas's ecosystem in order to unlock more areas and complete main/side objectives.  The ecosystem is a web of plants and a couple of "animals" that depend on each to thrive and reproduce (there's also a research journal that explains each life form's use and abilities as you discover them).  Later in the game you'll find yourself going between several rooms to obtain seeds to enhance other rooms to their maximum biomass level.  Each room has a different ecosystem to work with and different challenges to overcome so the game never feels repetitive or monotonous.  There's no combat here, so you'll purely be picking up and throwing seeds as well as trying to herd around some of the larger seeds you can't carry.  Some plants can hurt and kill you, but the game has a very generous autosave system so death is never more than a minor hindrance as a result of being sloppy (note that I played on normal, the game offers casual and hard settings which I imagine do nothing but change how much damage you receive).
On the technical side I was extremely impressed at the professional quality of this "indie" game.  Graphics are 2D but very detailed and look incredibly sharp and detailed at 1920x1200 screen resolution.  The screenshots on Steam really do not do the look of this game justice.  Voice acting sounds extremely professional and all dialogue in game is fully voiced.  The controls also felt fantastic for a mouse and keyboard user and zooming around on the jetpack and using the mouse to throw seeds felt extremely precise and natural.  The game also ran perfectly without a hitch in Gentoo Linux so clearly the developer has put a lot of effort into proper Linux support which is wonderful.  The only technical hiccup I had was screen tearing during scenes of heavy movement.  My monitor does that worse than many and I normally use vsync because of it but this game had no option for it and it wasn't bad enough to force it in the drivers.
My first playthrough, getting all 17 achievements was 7.9 hours.  That may seem on the short side but that time was devoid of tedium or reptition, the game never overstayed its welcome and progressed very naturally.  The quality of this was so good I regret getting it so cheap as part of a Humble Bundle, its worth every bit of its current $9.99 US price tag.  If you like exploration games and/or the idea of manipulating an ecosystem for life to thrive you will enjoy this game!

The hierarchy is immediately made evident in CoZ--and more importantly the fact that you're somewhere near the bottom of it. The game does a good job of explaining the fantasy world it's sent in without bogging you down with irrelevant details and names, building atmosphere and immersing you in it. Yours is a dark and dismal world where violence us a constant and meals are not guaranteed, but somehow the battlefields still manage to be interesting to look at with little details and particle effects to add a layer of realism.
Combat in CoZ is a bit slow paced, though in response to complaints the developer, Cardboard Utopia, added a fast forward function. In typical turn-based fashion, you and the enemy have your own phases during which you'll move your units and use abilities. Abilities are tied to the card system: you select the skill you want to use, after which you're taken to the dice roll screen where you essentially affect the effectiveness of your attack. Dice dictate which end of the range--shown when you highlight an enemy to attack it--your damage will fall into and also what additional buffs/snuffs will be applied. There are a few different markings on your dice: crystals add power, stars activate the special effect listed denoted on the card, shields protect you from counter attack damage, if applicable, and hearts recuperate health. You can reroll up to two dice should you not agree with the outcome of your initial roll.
CoZ is combat-focused, meaning there's no over world to explore and you'll never have control of your characters outside of a combat situation. This means that you'll be fighting back to back battles and learning the story through dialogue exchanges before, during, and after combat. There are also quiet moments after you've cleared a battle node where you can view an oftentimes humorous discussion between your party members.
In lieu of equipment, your party management boils down to crafting and equipping dice sets and deck building. Each dice set has six dice and the ones that aren't marked with a lock icon can be upgraded or traded out for a different one if you so choose to.
Crafting is a matter of consolidation. Depending on what die you want to craft, you need to select sets to meet an icon threshold. Please note that the entire set of the dice used to craft will be destroyed, so this is a good way to get rid of low level or cursed dice sets. Sets with cursed red dice can be totally reborn by crafting to replace the negatively effected die.
I don't want to spoil the story, so I'll just comment on the quality of the writing. The story is a bit cliched in some parts, but the exchanges between characters are believable and oftentimes humorous. The narrative is delivered via character dialogue on and off the battlefield with a few still images--hand drawn, by the look of it--sprinkled in. The music is orchestral and suited to the atmosphere, bouncing between quieter, more melancholic tunes and lively, adventurous scores.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
Children of Zodiarcs is a solid strategy RPG with unique gameplay elements and an interesting story. It isn't perfect, but with continued support from the developer, it's getting better and better every patch. Personally, I would have liked for there to be more to do between battles, even if it meant going to a battle field and searching for points of interest using the same turn-bases formula, sans enemies, but the game is still fun in short sessions. I recommend this to fans of the genre, though those who aren't as enthusiastic about it may find themselves losing interest.

35mm tells a story of a post-apocalyptic world, but is is very different from what you can see in other games or movies. In this quiet and desolate world, reclaimed by nature after the global epidemic, ordinary people are just trying to live their lives, slowly returning to its old ways. It's not another game about chaos and a chosen one hero, it's a travel of an ordinary man through the remains of the old world, and a philosophical story about life and about people who don't need action and crazy fighting for survival, but are simply tired from these troubles and just want to live. The game is slow-paced and almost meditative, it won't point you what you supposed to do or how you should feel about all happening around you, it actually encourages you to think by yourself.
This game was developed not by a studio but almost entirely by one man, so there are some gameplay flaws and unpolished features, but its unique atmosphere makes it more interesting to play than many huge open-world and story-rich games. The game has a lot of memorable moments, events and locations and often surprises with unexpected turns. The exploration part is interesting and rewarding, sure if you like constant action you will be bored, but if you're enjoying the atmosphere, the story and want to understand the world better, you'll be excited! Technically the game is done great as well, it does not feature anything outstanding but you'll enjoy beautiful sceneries (that lighting in sunny locations!!!) and atmospheric music.
Personally I am very impressed about this game and would recommend it to any fan of exploration and story-oriented games, and generally to anyone who are tired of clichés and wants to experience something new and different.

It's an incredibly basic survival game with a dinosaur progression system that is nigh impossible to actually progress through. It takes over eight hours of solid, focused playing to get to the final tier of the carnivores tree, and that's without dying once. With that said, you'll die a lot. It's a cool system in theory, with it balancing the number of smaller and largers dinosaurs, but in reality it just takes an absurd amount of time. That is where the game is failing at the moment. It's not an awesome dinosaur survival game, it's a waiting simulator. Once you've waited and somehow not died for two straight hours, you can move onto the next tier. Then, rinse and repeat. It's a long, tedious yet incredibly boring process, and for almost no reward whatsoever. On top of all of this, the controls are confusing with no guide or tutorial at all, and the user interface is almost entirely nonexistent. The planned features for this game make it look like down the road it will be a great game, but for the time being, I'd highly recommend to stay away from this one until it's become something more polished and put-together.

Where to begin.  This game is as advertised.  It's a game similar to Secret of Mana (SNES), Crystalis (NES), Zelda-esque, Final Fantasy Adventure (Original GB)  and many other old RP games.
You can customize your character physically by gender, colour of your clothes, hair style and colour, and name.  Additonally, you get a vanity part for your hat, face, weapon, and shield.
The gameplay is very nice, you can be a full warrior, full mage, whatever you want to be; a combination if you want.  Although, being a healer is not an option.
This is a beta game, it's not complete, from my estimation it's a little near half done, if that.
You can play cooperatively, over the internet, using your steam friends list or direct IP!  This is awesome!
You grind in the game, if that wasn't obvious.  (What old school console RPG didn't have you grind?  It's part of the fun!)
The transition between keyboard and controller playing is seamless, you just start using your keyboard and it swaps to keyboard mode, you use your controller, it swaps to controller mode.  I found this particularly great!
The host of the game's save file is progressed in the story, however - if you're not the host - you keep everything you gained.  You simply have to play through the story (by hosting or single player) to go through it.  The rewards though, you do not acquire again, you already have them!  :D
This is an awesome game!  As far as I'm aware only three people are working on it and they're from Sweden.  They have me as a fan.  The sprite animation is awesome, the artwork for the avatars is great and expresses much emotion, and the game looks very polished for a beta that is not even half done!
I used to pay $50+ US dollars for games like these, and wait years for the next to come out.  I love the game very much, and I haven't even started exploring the Arcade Mode.
tl;dr - Buy this game if you loved Secret of Mana or any similar games on the console or PC.  Especially if you want to play it co-op with friends over the internet!

(Full review follows below)
is an action FPS with strong narrative elements and a stylish, graphic-noir atmosphere.  The gameplay feels both familiar and fresh simultaneously, while the characters and story keep the player engaged and interested.  Also, the addition of an XP system and skill-trees allow the player to continue to work towards new goals and to customize their character according to their preferred combat style.  All of these elements mesh together to create a very enjoyable game that I feel all but the most extremely discerning gamers should appreciate.
One of the most intriguing aspects of
is the story, and the characters that make it.  The twisted and confused thoughts of the main character set the tone of the game from the first level, and evolve as the story progresses, in a similar fashion to games like
and
.  The auxiliary characters are diverse and interesting, enticing the player to initiate optional conversations. The narrative is a perfect blend of mafia drama and psychological thriller that should enthrall anyone who enjoys being told a good story.
The actual gameplay experience is also exquisite.  The combination of familiar FPS aspects with some well-integrated novelty goes a long way to make the game downright
.  There are various guns and abilities to use to wreak havoc on your enemies during action-packed fight sequences.  Additionally, the XP and skill-point system will keep you goal-oriented and allow you to unlock new abilities as you play to keep things fresh.
For those itching for more after beating the main campaign, there is also an entirely separate Co-op Mode, which expands upon the universe of
and allows for multiplayer gameplay.  Fortunately, all the missions in the Co-op Mode can be completed in solo play if you don’t want to spend time trying to find others to play with.  While not quite as pristine as the main campaign, it adequately provides some supplementary gameplay to a game that would otherwise be only medium-length (in terms of total hours).
In summary, I posit that
is a superb all-around game with many positive elements contributing to its overall quality.  I would say it is a pretty safe bet for most gamers who have a broad taste for games, and a definite safe bet for those gamers who enjoy FPS games and interesting narratives.  Expect about 6-18 hours of gameplay, depending on how much of a “completionist” you are.  If you can get it for a price you are comfortable with, it is definitely worth the pick-up.

Hey I 100% this game in like 35 hours/3 days straight, and Cleod9 (One of the fine gentlemen who created this) asked nicely for a review, so here I am, even though I don't really type much :sandbag:
Let's see here, Yeah Jam Fury: UME is a super fun and really heckin' challenging Puzzle-Platformer (And sometimes just Puzzle or Platformer, and once or twice a Truck Driving Simulator) game staring three mango-lovin' Genies (Called "Grins,") on their quest to figure out how to get rid of their paradoxical crisis of the fact that none of them can exist at the same time, and they really wanna hang out.
You got Yeah, who places blocks n' jumps high but isn't really fast at all, he's great for traversing and is pretty heckin' cute but that's about all he's got, he's the basic fellow
Jam is the speedyman who packs the speed and can run up walls/use his mallet to Boost which can be used for more speed/height or Walljump, but his traction is pretty terrible meaning if you're on ice or just generally aren't careful you're gonna fall down, a lot
Fury is the big man who's taller than the other two (That's important) and can destroy blocks just by falling down/punching/existing for Yeah to place again, but his movement's a little funny (But don't tell him that, he's trying to become a dancer, believe in his goals) and he can't even Jump, so getting used to the big guy will take some time
Together they strive to collect the Mango (and sometimes also Orange, Potato and Fresh Milk, but not always) at the end of every level (There's just over 200 of 'em, that's a big ol' bowl of tropical fruits I'll tell ya what)
Basic jist; levels are divided into two halves, A-Side and B-Side
A-Side is probably what you came here for, it's good ol' puzzle platforming fun using all 3 dudes through a story that kinda-sorta-exists (The story gets told as you obtain Trochievals, not necessarily just going through the game, but it's a real cute story, you get to see Yeah, Jam and Fury have nice banter to eachother by writing in Yeah's Memory Book) but is mostly just "Mangoes are everywhere, I'm hungry." But I'm honestly fine with that since the original YJF didn't have any story at all aside from "Mangoes are everywhere, I'm hungry," so reading some cute conversations between the trio is neat.
B-Side, is where you wanna go if you want the really-challenging-Challenge Mode. You unlock it (All 100 levels of it) after beating A-Side's challenges, and B-Side is a "Remix/Challenge Mode" which can range from something as simple as just tweaking the layout a tiny bit/making you have less blocks to work with or something as infuriating as a puzzle you can't figure out for the life of you due to limited resources/Fury not being very helpful but the game urges you to use him and depending on how well you can think/act it can either be just mildly upsetting/stump you for a moment while you experience or you can just sortof ask why the Game Developers would ever do that to you since you thought that the devs were your friend. Expect Play Time to do a bit more than Double if you're planning on taking down the B-Side and getting the "True Ending" and all the Achievements.
Also, there's Steam Workshop support! Which is really neat. You can make all sorts of stuff (More stuff for the editor is unlocked as you progress through the game, some of which can be added to your levels for more challenge whilst others is just neat stuff like the ability to place Fresh Milk everywhere) and then either save it to just keep to yourself or Upload it to the Steam Workshop for all to see (There are some Trochievals tied to the Steam Workshop and also the Stage Editor, I'll tell you that, so be aware of them if you're going for 100%) so basically the game can last as long as the community wants it too (And whilst it isn't quite that vast, there's still a ton of options especially if you complete the game fully to unlock everything so I'm sure you'll come up with something great) which is always something nice to have in a game.
As for exploring levels, you're absolutely free to come back to any levels you've either already completed or skipped (You're completely allowed to skip levels you find too tough or just don't wanna do and come back to them later) VIA the Level Select, you can also watch Replays to remind yourself how you went about completing the challenge or try and score the fastest time to rank on the Leaderboards which is also fun, going fast is fun in YJF, ya gotta be good to go fast
Let's see what else
Ah yes, Difficulty. Let's have like 1-to-5 scale, 1 being like real easy and 5 making me want to slam my face into a pillow to calm down,
A-Side, I would say is a nice steady 3. Sometimes it throws a bit more precise stuff your direction (Mostly involving Fury) it's all good fun times that keeps the challenge at a nice little standard that you'll get used to as you go along.
B-Side..B-Side is around the 3-5 range whenever it feels like. I HIGHLY, super highly recommending practicing up before tackling B-Side (If you can help it, if you plan on 100%-ing the game, please play the original YeahJamFury first, you can find it on Newgrounds and/or McLeodGaming's website, playing it in the middle/after UME will take a bit to get used to because of how much UME improves on the little things, but it's always nice to practice up) and also watching the Quick Trick videos you can find on YeahJamFury's youtube to learn some super useful stuff that'll definitely help you get the Mangoes on B-Side. They can and will test both your puzzle-solving skills, platforming abilities, and also sometimes your sanity questioning with stuff like precise timing/placement, super limited resources or also just forcing you into a pit as the guy who can't jump. Sometimes it's just a nice little tougher-than-usual, but still relatively comfy experience that would fit in A-Side nicely (Which is the parts ranked 3 on my difficulty scale) but other times it's definitely a 5 and will test you, so take caution in that.
Fun scale? I'll say a 5 for all of A-Side and like half of B-Side, probably a 3-4 on the rest of B-Side since sometimes it makes me a little unhappy, but trust me, this game is SUPER fun. Once you get the grasp of what's going on (I guess I kindof already did going into this, I played the original YJF a ton and was waiting for this game since they teased the Remake that was gonna be on the Wii U/Steam but never came out years ago) going fast is really fun and just messing around is pretty enjoyable. Especially with the tunes, holy bananas some of the tunes in this game are AMAZING foot-tappers that'll just make you feel happy, believe you me. Especially the Overworld/Rainbow/Sky (Day Time)/whatever theme, I love that song. Can we get a soundtrack soon? I want a soundtrack.
Opinions/TL;DR
+Really fun and enjoyable
+Going fast is fun and the game rewards you for using stuff you learned in places not exactly intended, opening new routes to go fast
+Everyone is cute in their own ways and acts incredibly silly, the art style fits really nicely too
+Soundtrack is amazing
+Level editors are always something I enjoy
+Trochievals are fun/sometimes challenging (but a good challenging) to obtain and there's lots of 'em
+You can be a truck
+Honestly more fun than Shovel Knight imo
+Thank you TSON for getting me this game <3 <3
-Sometimes the game likes being really hard/precise and you just gotta put up with it, angry face
-They force you to go Fury at the end of one level in B-Side and if you don't plan ahead you'll get flung into a pit right beside the Mango and can't get it which forces you to restart the level (and it's pretty long), it was a bit mean and I didn't exactly like that, but it's the only time the game does that
-Can't turn into a truck and slam a snowman into the pavement
Overall rating? 5/5. Sometimes the game is a bit of a meanie but I'm more than willing to set that aside for this wonderful game. Is real good.

Waking Mars puts you into the shoes of Dr. Liang Qi, an astrobiologist sent to Mars to SCIENCE! 0CT0, an AI probe sent to investigate the planet's caverns, has gone missing in the vast network of tunnels that is Lethe Cavern. Assisting you are Amani Ronga, who chats with you from Base Camp, and ART, another AI who sounds like a Borderlands Claptrap.
I like Liang. He's a thinker. When he speaks, he sounds... not quite subdued, but distracted, by the scientific inquiries and dilemmas surrounding him at all times. So that he's only able to spare a small portion of his thought processes for the conversation at hand. Amani provides the heart, and ART provides the comic relief. Altogether, they have a fascinating dynamic that
OH look at me all wrapped up in people gazing. Where are my manners? Let me tell you about the gameplay.
Gameplay's weird, yo.
This is a game about two things: research, and... well, waking Mars. Science-minded fellow that he is, you'll be helping Liang investigate all of the weird fauna and flora (which is also technically fauna, actually) of Lethe Cavern. You do this by collecting and planting "seeds", throwing things at things to see how they react, coaxing things to eat other things, and generally being a bother to everything. Every creature provides a boost to the biomass of an area, and as you become more knowledgeable of your surroundings, you can use that information to help you increase Lethe Cavern's biomass to all new heights, and spread it to all new depths.
There is a story, here. Bits of mystery and intrigue to investigate. A couple different endings to shoot for. I won't spoil anything, but it's enough to give you goals as you go.
Waking Mars looks nice. I should use a better word there, but "nice" is what I feel in my heart, so judge away. Everything looks painted, but not in an artsy-fartsy way. There's a bit of a papery look to things, but you probably won't notice most of the time. It actually makes the game look really cool at times, though, when there are like four or five layers of background scenery moving by at different speeds.
Waking Mars is not for everyone. There's no shooting, and the closest thing you get to a puzzle is the basic physicsy calculational resource management gameplay. You may find yourself spending your time herding creatures or waiting for the local population to build itself up while watching handfuls of hard-earned biomass repeatedly wander straight to their stupid, stupid deaths. But it certainly hooked me, and I certainly enjoyed playing it. So if it sounds like your bag, then maybe take a crack it, why not?

This is my first review. I probably won't write another after this, but I think this game deserves one. I didn't want to dislike this game. I wanted to love it. I even did love it for the first 20 hours or so. I loved it enough to buy the season pass based on my initial experience with the game mechanics. It didn't take long after that to figure out that there were glaring problems with the game, but I figured that Ubisoft would surely fix the problems with for honor because there is no way that they would squander all of the opportunity that this game has. I have not played this game in a while because I grew tired of the issues it has, but I still had hope that Ubisoft would fix the issues with this game before it was too late. I continued to visit the for honor reddit page after I stoped playing to see how things were progressing, and just recently, I have given up on for honor. For honor is probably my most regretable gaming purchase ever. It isn't the worst game ever, and I did actually enjoy it at first. It is specifically because I know how good this game could have been that makes me regret buying it so much because now I feel sad for what could have been, but seemingly will never be.
________________________________________________________________________________
---ACTUAL POINT BASED REVIEW---
Gameplay: 10/10 when you're new. 5/10 when you understand the most effective way to play the game.
Graphics: 8/10 Not much to be said here. The game is pretty, but it isn't trying to blow you away.
Matchmaking: 4/10 If you are playing a game mode with gear enabled, you will find yourself matched against players with much more gear than yourself, and then there is the skill difference between players to consider. 1v1 has decent matchmaking since there are fewer players per game, and gear is not enabled. Other game modes suffer from poor matchmaking to some degree.
Netcode: 3/10 The netcode is downright awful. The only game mode that you can play without experiencing frequent disconnects or lag is in 1v1 because of the peer to peer system in this game. Even in 1v1 you will experience lag often enough to become obnoxious.
Microtransaction Model: 2/10 The expensive cosmetic microtransactions can be forgiven to a degree, but with the way that matchmaking works in this game, being able to buy loot boxes with stat based gear is not acceptable in a full priced game.
Balance: 5/10 Most things that are unbalanced only give slight advantages, but there are a few characters with gamebreaking balance issues that have been left untouched since release. This is more of a problem in 1v1 than anywhere else.
Dev Response to Community: 4/10 The devs exist, and they used to try to talk to people. That is the best I can say for them. Now they won't even allow people to speak. In the March 21st dev stream, comments were disabled. That is pretty much all I have to say about that. They are done listening. They are just going to milk this cash cow as long as they can, and then they will make For Honor 2 and do it all again.
Overall Score: 4.4/10

Before you scroll down and see all the other review stating this game is not Final Fantasy tactic well, no it is not final fantasy tactic it is Children of Zodiarc, if you wish to play Final fantasy tactic... go buy it. Now that it is out of the way I'll start my review.
- Gameplay -
Game mechanic
The game is a grid based strategy role playing game (SRPG) and thus the gameplay include two player face player and ennemy. Doing those face you can move your characters and do several other options and it is where the game get interesting.
Children of Zodiarc employ a deck building mechanic meaning that the character do not have any ability list per say, each character have a set based ability cards that they unlock by leveling up and you can, in between missions, personalize their decks.
Additionally, the game have a dice mechanic during ability usage. What it mean is that you are never sure how your ability will turn out. You can craft and change dices to help the odds in your favor, but at the end of the turn the dices are the one that will dictate if your turn go well and not.
Personally, I found those mechanic quite interesting as it raise the strategic uncertainties. You can not become too powerful in this game that you just wipe the floor with your ennemies with only one unit and it make it a challenging strategy game.
Characters and party
(Disclaimer: I am aproximatively at halfway point I do not know anything beyong the start of act 3 when I am writing this review)
From what I played so far the game is mostly about surviving with what you have. Most of the time your party will be about 2-4 characters big against ennemies that can easily reach over 10 units of the same level (if it is not higher). In that sense the game is quite hard as you need to make most of your character move count, or else your party will crumble.
Each character have their pre-determined role in the party with a few tweak here and there depending on their deck built. Some are better at doing physical damage and others magical. The challenge of the game is to mainly being able to manage your party to avoid unecessary fall and make sure your characetrs attack the ennemies they should.
There is no class change, equipements or actual money or shop in the game. everything is directly linked to your character levels and the dices you use. The better the dices, the better stats you will have in combat.
- Story and Lore -
The game story is a run out of the mill RPG game. In a world that seen lot of dark age a few abandon kids from the slum raise to oppose corrupted nobles and steal an ancient artefact from them.
I will not go too deep into this, but it is a case of "if it is not broken don't fix it". Simple story, but an interesting dystopian city in a fantasy like universe.
- Art Direction -
The sprite work on this game are pretty good. The characters are easily recognizable without being too overcharged and their personality shine in their facial expression and dialogues. You can easily tell lot of effort was put on them both for the main characters and the ennemies.
The soundtrack is pretty good as most of the song mesh pretty well with the game maps you can tell the feel of a scene instantly from the music and it help the immersion.
The 3d spirtes on another part are not really bad, but nothing out of the ordinary. You can easily tell what unit is what but there is not much diversity in them. The ragdoll physique when a unit die can at time be janky and all over the place, but I guess it is good for a laugh when an ennemy decide to slingshot off to the moon.
- Easy to read summary -
Pros:

- Fresh and intriguing Game mechanic
- Good looking game overall
- Good strategy gameplay focused on a small party
- Not too easy , but not too hard
- Intriguing World
- Battles that are never the sames
Cons:
- Personalization of the party is not possible
- Some 3D models look a bit odd and bland
- Camera angles that get stuck behind map objects on certain maps
Neutral:
- Linear story
- A bad roll dice can screw your whole game
- A good roll dice can save your game
- Is a story based single player experience
Overall, it is a good indie game I reccomend to everyone liking challenging SRPG.

To me, endings are extremely important. And, I am not going to spoil anything, but I did not care at all for this game's ending. It is the primary reason I am giving the game a thumbs down. I do not want to say anything else for fear of spoiling.
It plays like a table top board game and you build decks for your characters and you throw dice to power your cards. To say that I love this design is an understatement. It truly feels like a board game and throwing the dice is fun. (Though the fun does wear off, and you'll probably swap to auto-dice as I did. B,ut the luck of the draw and the anticipation and drama of dice is ever present and amazing).
I started in hard mode, and I experimented with a lot of different builds with the characters as I progressed until finally settling on one that I really enjoyed. There is a lot to think about with deck construction, and you will tool your decks to match the mission here and there as well. I feel like they really hit the nail on the head with the cards and dice. The look and feel of the game matches the cards and dice as well. It's very well made.
There is a feature of the gameplay revolving around exp that, in my opinion, is a feature more than a glitch, as it forces decisions that would otherwise be nonexistent. This is also a warning to you. Keep the EXP of your team even. The game gives exp based on taking actions. Healing, buffing, hitting an enemy close to your level, gives about 17 exp. Killing an enemy gives double that. Enemies much higher level give more, and lower ones, give less. Healing for 0 gives 1 exp (even if you activate a side effect buff of a heal spell). Counter attacking gives about 6. This is all fine except some characters can take extra turns, and they then gain more exp. Also, if you 'last hit' with one character too much, he might out level your team. Or if a character counter attacks more. It may seem trivial, but the game bases the level of the enemies on only the highest level character. Trust me that if you have a character even just 2 levels higher, that means that enemies are 4! levels higher than your lowest level teammate and that means they deal less damage, take more damage, and what happens is they have a really hard time catching up because your highest level character has to do the bulk of the work (and as a result gains more exp). I recognized this very early on... I want to say mission 4? And started the game over from scratch because it's very easy for Nahmi to get ahead.
I did enjoy the game, but again, the ending really ruined it for me.
What in the hell did I just play...

Micro-transactions are definitely there, but so far don't seem to be a hinderence and dont give a pay-to-win feel. However, this may change as the development continues, for better or worse.
All in all, a good game, better than some paid games i own, and it's free. Recommended.

One of the best flight simulators out there!
This sim has a lot of negative reviews on steam, basically all are because the sales model or difficult to get things to work, and not because the game itself, but actually this is only peoples fault.
This is not really a free game, the main package is free but it came with just a couple of planes. Actually you can have some fun with it, but i see many people got frustrated because they try to fly a mission that requires a plane that is not included in free package, then they get mad about it.
If you use free version you have to select missions who uses the planes that came with it. Although you really can have some fun with it, it´s very limited and you need to buy some dlc to enjoy plentiful what this sim offers.
I´m not a fan of this sales model, but i have to say it´s contents really worth even the full price. If you got a couple of dlc´s on sale then you have a really great deal and a lot of content to enjoy many and many hours of fun for a modest price.
About the sim itself, what i expect from a flight simulator is to be realistic, and this game just delivers. It´s totally focused on realism and to replicate the conditions you would face when flying at WW1. It has a lot of history embededd and very atmospheric WW1 environment so it´s a gem for WW1 and combat simulator enthusiasts. You really feel like you are in the middle of the Great War.
You can play career mode through the war, historical missions, quick mission, campaigns, multiplayer etc. so you never run out of game modes to play.
The planes are incredible well modeled and behave very similar to their real life versions.
It features full control customization, nice and tweakable graphics, and good optmization so it runs smooth and stable even on a mid range PC.
This is not an arcade game, it´s a simulator. It´s always trick to learn a new sim and this one specially is not easy. It´s early age of aviation and WW1 aircraft have a lot of particularities that can make those things very hard to dominate. I´m experient IL2 pilot but struggling a bit to get good on this. So you have to put some hours on it and do some research if you want to get good. Of course you can disable some realism to make things easier. (but i try not to go that way.)
This game was released 8 years ago, but i think it didn´t aged at all. I just don´t know why i took so long to discover and start playing it. I´m surely gonna have hundreds of hours on it soon.

You need a relatively modern computer to run it at decent framerates. Windows XP dual core without GPUs can run the game albeit slow.
The free aircraft given are an albatros, a SPAD (which is apparently lighter tha nthe albatros despite how huge it feels) and a french nieuport aircraft that supports upward firing rockets. The albatros can fit a modern style colimator sight that you get in WWII aircraft and the SPAD has a similar telescope-like device that has a black ring inside for an aiming circle without any magnification which seems to work best when viewed from the middle to the rear of the seat position and not leaning forward.
I haev issues with being able to turn around like I can in IL2: Battle of Stalingrad and this game also lacks input joystick filter which IL2 BoS has (it lags the input gently and can act as a modifier) so 3D pro logitech users will have to deal with the twitchy aim especially at high speeds beyond like 130 kph.

Here's a 2D Indie game that is most likely nothing like anything you've ever played. In a great way, I must add!
In Waking Mars you're an explorer of Mars' caves and its newfound life. As you interact with more and more life, the game registers your findings in a log, showing the amount of work that has been put into designing everything about this game. Every piece of life is highly detailed, and it's worth reading the information you gather as you play.
BUT this isn't a merely exploratory game, despite that being a big focus. After you learn about the life you encounter, you learn how to use it to your advantage, creating the most aproppriate habitat for a certain type of plant or animal to live. In doing so, they'll eventually interact with each other, prospering further and further, that being the main mechanic of this game. Each room has a certain Biomass level requirement for you to progress, a mechanic that makes sense in the context of this game , as the caves' natural defense is to block the exits until there's self-sustainable life in it.
The story was there merely to guide you through your adventure deeper and deeper into Mars, giving you a helping hand in this journey.
As you progress, you start grasping the game's mechanics, and you'll be able to create some pretty cool environments and interactions with everything at your disposal, which feels very satisfying.
So, I'd advise anyone to definitely try out this game. The sense of discovery is present at all times, keeping you emersed in the world from start to finish. There's a constant drive to keep you moving forward and exploring more and that's a really big plus! The game's world and mechanics fit perfecty, which is fairly rare, so yea, give them your money already and... enjoy!

Thomas Was Alone is a wonderful game. You might look at the graphics and think it looks dull, well I assure you that it is not! There is a really good chip-tune soundtrack that plays throughout the game, with variations and changes in theme.
There is also a really complelling storyline weaved into the platforming style levels. The puzzles are not that tricky, with a little lateral thinking, you will find them simple enough.
Where this game really shines is in the story that is told throughout the game, and in the character development! Yep, each one of those coloured blocks is an actual character. Thomas, Chris, John, Claire and all the others. Each one is different to the others, each have their own unique abilities. More than that, each one is their own person, they have different personalities and like the others to a greater or lesser extent. I found it so easy and natural to slip into calling each one by their names, rather than thinking "Red block here, orange one there" I found myself thinking more along the lines of "Chris can't reach here, so Thomas will have to boost him up". Strange how natural it felt, but that is the caliber and quality of the writing, naration and character development in this game.
I played the whole game through in one sitting, smiling all the way through and I got more than a little attatched to Thomas and his little group of friends.
This is a lovely game that I would strongly suggest to anyone with a heart ;-)

She Remembered Caterpillars is extremely impressive mechanically, boasting a ruleset that is simple yet compelling, and puzzles built on those rules that never fail to challenge. Its appearance is equally simple but the longer you spend with it, the more you begin to appreciate the care with which it has been crafted. One such detail is the distinctive designs to each of the puzzle elements that were conceived specifically to allow people with color blindness to enjoy a game about mixing and splitting colors. Where the game's appeal waned for me was with its story. The attempt to abstractly tackle something as profound as the death of a loved one unfortunately fell flat for me as it lacked the detail I would have needed to get invested. Overall, though, the game's mechanical competence far outweighed any drawbacks. I fully recommend the game and hope for even better creations from Jumpsuit Entertainment in the future.

Personally I didn’t realize I even owned this game. I picked it out to play through a randomizer because of the sheer volume of games I own. Despite that, no matter what reasons it fell into my hands to play, I’m glad it did. This is a game that length wise is short and refreshing while offering up some difficult puzzles. All of which is tied to a story that while vague is beautiful.
The puzzles are something I still don’t really know how to feel about. I’ve mulled over it for a while and I thinks while there’s a few negatives, the positives outweigh them. It’s a colour based puzzle, separated into acts with each act introducing a new mechanic. At first this seems like a good idea, the more mechanics they add, the more it seems to simplify the puzzle. Once you figure out the one hard little knot, the puzzle falls into place for you and you’re left feeling a little unsatisfied. Compared to other puzzles games, you don’t get a sense of accomplishment from completing the puzzles. The last puzzle I think is very charming and really finishes the game off well.
This game’s art is charming. It’s reminiscent of a children’s book which is only aided by the story. Each act brings a new environment that matches the pacing and the puzzles quite well. As you journey up through the puzzles you start to understand how each location reflects within the story itself. I feel that the game may have been better off as a phone game but having the art in full resolution and colour works far too fantastically. It’s whimsical yet doesn’t undercut the sad and emotional tone of the game.
I could honestly say that this music was one of the main reasons I cried. The story had already bore a hole in my heart and the music just further opened it up. It was well composed with nothing that would make it harder to think yet still conveyed a certain feeling. They’re shooting themselves in the foot by not making a soundtrack so great purchasable. Each song is perfectly tailored to the environment especially the act. The final act is what I would say a perfect culmination of a game. Everything peaks, the art, the sound, the music and the puzzle at the end is fun and charming.
This is where I want to address the story throughout the game. It was lovely and it did in fact make me shed tears. I fell the only thing that might of made the writing slightly better is if it was voiced as to address some of the confusion over who is talking and to also add another layer of emotions. I do think that everything about this game ties around the story like a neat little package. Overall this game gives a nice but succinct finish. All the ideas are addressed and it doesn’t really give a feeling of longing at the end. You can tell it was made with love and that they knew it had to finish when it did.

TL;DL - Excellent gameplay and graphics, recommended only for players who aren't looking for a deep story or likeable characters.
Children of Zodiarcs is a mechanically ambitious project. It attempts to combine tactical turn-based combat and art and sound design reminiscent of Final Fantasy Tactics, with a genuine deck-building strategy card game. And for the most part, this works. However, the game is a missed opportunity for a truly special experience that's been sorely lacking in the genre for quite some time due to a weak story and incredibly unlikeable characters.
Pros:
- The meat of the game, the deck building, is very well realized. For each of the three characters you play, several possible strategies (I can count at least three distinct deck strategies per player) quickly emerge, and they are fun to experiment with and watch evolve as the cards upgrade through leveling. And in my experience, especially at the upper levels, when the deck strategies start to come to fruition, the battles get exceedingly fun.
- The game is challenging, but not overwhelming. It does require grinding for levels, but there are a few options for this. In addition to the normal story missions, there's a side mission, battle arena, and skirmishes to keep you occupited. For an indie title, this offers plenty of gameplay.
- The art is good, the models are solid, and the music is good.
Cons:
- There is no choice regarding how players level up. The only choice in the hands of the player is how the decks are constructed and dice customization (which is limited). So if you're into character builds, this isn't the game for you.
- Dice. In a strategy game. Like Risk. Not a fan. There's enough randomness in card draw, they did not need to add dice to the mix as well. The game does offer dice customization options, and these are useful to enhance certain deck strategies, but the options are limited.
- Playing with a mouse and keyboard is annoying as compared to a controller. The mouse-picking is terrible due to the design of the levels, and the fact that many desired target spaces are occluded by other objects in the world with no way to reach them. There are a few other UI quirks that are obnoxious (you have to change "menu modes" before actually entering a character's menu, and you can't scroll through available dice without first selecting which equipped die you want to replace, etc.).
- Not being able to resurrect characters in battle makes certain situations overly unforgiving. Accidentally position a character 1 space too close to the enemies on the first turn? You're fighting this battle with 2 character instead of 3. This happens A LOT during the first half of the game, and it's incredibly frustrating.
- (Minor spoiler) The biggest negative in this game is clearly the story, as several other reviewers have pointed out. The characters are not only unlikeable, but I was actively rooting against them by the end. During the last 3 story misssions, the story ramps up to finally be interesting. However, this is at the expense of characters acting in character, and I actively started rooting against them. Not only are the characters terribly unlikeable, the plot is meh (basically the depth and theme of the movie The Warriors). The developers had a golden opportunity with really interesting combat and deck building engines to put together an enthralling game, and fell woefully short.
Overall, I liked the gameply enough to pump a lot of hours into it, and don't regret it. If you are looking for a successor to Final Fantasy Tactics, this isn't it. However, if you want a good battle system with an interesting deck building twist, this game is for you. It's joining a growing list of indie titles that try various strategies to reproduce the magic of tactical turn based classics like FF Tactics, but without being able to reproduce the engaging story (like Regalia or the Banner Saga Series).

, combines RPG elements and turn based strategy play ala Fire Emblem, FF Tactics and other grid based games with a card and dice system. Each character starts with 5 cards and can choose to attack, heal, defend, or draw cards on a turn. You then roll dice to add to what the card does. Depending on what get on the die you can trigger additional affects such as regeneration on your heroes, opponents to discard cards, draw more cards yourself and more. It is an interesting system although the number of card choices are not great. Thanks to this system you will never miss. When you attack with a damage based attack you will always do damage. There are no 95% chance hit misses ala Xcom and other games.
I do like that you get different options and I'm sure people will choose to play the characters differently. While overall I did enjoy the game it was not all that long nor was it very difficult on normal. I did have a few mission failures however so it was not a cakewalk by any means either. One thing I really liked about the Fire Emblem series was the permadeath aspect. Without spoiling anything the only thing I will a say is you will not lose any characters from having them perish on missions that you control them.

Although I'll keep playing this game and probably grind to the max level, I wholeheartedly cannot recommend the game in its current state. All the impatient folk who quickly get frustrated should not download this game. So ... here's what I think developer should fix ASAP - and I mean ASAP!
- Animation-cancelation MUST be implemented. Basically, if you're knocked down you're probably dead. And, since once you start the attack animation, you have to go through it, if some enemy accidentally flanks you (AI is pretty bad, so it won't be on purpose), and knocks you down it's ... gg. Even if you see it coming. So, roll should cancel all the animations and take the priority.
- Better animations in general. Yeah, they look cool and stuff but ... they're too rigid. Jump + attack animation barely looks animated actually. Even if there are a lot of combos, animations seem too clunky, even for MMO. I know it's possible to have fluid animations seeing as several games have already done it, especially in dungeon-crawler style of MMO games.
- Crashes / loading times. During my short gameplay of this game, the game crashed at least 3 times for no reason. As an Early Access game it's understandable, but developers should work on this as a priority. Even animations can wait. And then the loading times ... each time I go back to the main hub (and you have to, to turn in quests), I have to wait like a minute of a damn loading screen. Game's graphics and scale DO NOT justify such lengthy loading times. Also, game is filled with loading times. Each time you want to leave a certain area you'll be welcomed with a loading screen. Hell, there are loading screens in-between dungeon parts (by the way, if you're going to separate dungeons into parts, at least don't rehash the exact same locations. Thanks). So, yeah ... fix that.
- More zoom out. I know this seems like nit-picking but it's really bothering me. Camera is too close to the character. I just like if they gave players a bit more options, everyone could find their own style. And mine is to zoom out a bit.
- More character customazation. What we have right now is pretty much bare bone, and seeing as this is Early Access I know it will change, but I just wanted to point this out.
So, for all of you out there who get quickly frustrated by some bad design, glitches and stuff like that, I cannot recommend this game. It's still too rigid, animations don't flow the way you want them, game is extremely punishing to the point that if you get knocked down in the group of enemies you ain't getting up. Some combos look cool, they have a dude that wields scythe (which is always a HUGE plus to the game - I freaking love scythes) etc. but until they fix some key things, I cannot recommend this to a casual gamer who just wants to have a couple of hours of fun. Cheers.

I'll try and keep this fairly short (I will fail, though), since CopperBot's review has pretty much covered every aspect of the game.
35mm's premises were good, the world looks amazing and the screenshots and videos sure are eye-candy.
But... that's it. That's the whole game. Just pretty (and very confined) environments you have to (kind of) explore at an almost nerve-wrecking slow pace while listening to, I have to admit, a very nice soundtrack.
Let's start with
.
Plot-wise you can't expect much: post-apocalyptic genre has seen so many fiction at this point in time, that for a particular game to stick out of the mass is no easy task. But 35mm's plot fell below my expectations. There's not much of it, and the little there is, is both dull and messy, with (way too) much left to the imagination. Sure, there are some notes scattered around the (again) confined world, but they don't add enough "lore".
Game's mechanics are, well... clunky. In addition to the slow walking pace, the supply system is barely a side dish, since gathering batteries for the flashlight is useless (never ran out of them in the whole playthrough), gathering medkits and food is also kind of useless (devs chose to tell the player their character's health status by blurring his vision and dirtying his diary with blood, but food and medkits effect only lasts few minutes, so you'll either spend the whole game eating and patching up non-existent wounds, or give up and endure the blurred vision), weapons and ammo are almost useless too (you'll really have to shoot just in a couple of occasions), and that's it once again, you can't do much besides these things.
Characters are way too plain. None of the two main character's story is explained or elaborated at all until the ending, where you just get a tiny little piece of their story, and there's no interesting side character.
Animations and textures (especially of "important" things, such as food and meds) could've been more polished and differentiated.
The world looks big, but it isn't. Even leaving out the fact that you can't stray too far from the chosen path, apart from the first two environments there isn't much later in the game to explore.
There are some inconsistencies. With no spoilers: both the first (scripted) and the second shooting are simply unrealistic because of how many ammo you need to take down the enemies you're facing.
Lastly, english translation could really use a overhaul. Yeah, most of the dialogues and notes are understandable, but a better english would be, well... better.
Now to
.
The atmosphere. Wow. If one manages to overlook the immersion-breaking features stated above, it becomes pretty easy to get (metaphorically) lost in the game. Most of the environments (with a couple of exceptions) feel alive (or dead), without overdoing it and, while maybe a little too empty and, in some instances, too repetitive, they sure are well done. Which leads to the second good point.
The soundtrack. This is maybe the most polished aspect of the game. Music never feels off, or odd, or inappropriate to the situation. There's a lot of very well executed tracks too, and I often found myself staying still and listening to the music. Kudos to that!
The lighting, the colour palette and the chromatic aberration sure add to the feeling the game was meant to convey.
All in all it's not the absolute worst game out there, but I can't recommend it. Maybe getting it at a price cut (at least half of the current price), if you're curious about this particular game, could be okay.

This game just didn't seem that well made to me. The Voice acting seems rushed (In the intro you can hear the guy taking deep breaths, and also many skips within that intro can be heard), and the Tutorial also seems rushed. There are 2 "Types" of tutorials in this game, and only one is useful, but it is the one almost no one will see.
At the start of the game, you move around, kill things, look around, kill more things, grab their loot (On which the game doesn't even tell you want it is/does), and then go to the main City. And that is when the Non-usful tutorial ends.
The useful tutorial is only displayed as tips on the bottom of your screan that you have to click on in order to see what they say, and even then, about 90% of the time nobody reads them.
When you enter the main city, a window pops up saying to go talk to someone (I think, all I remember is that it says to press T to talk to people). The person you talk to gives you a very generic quest; go here and kill X amount of baddies, and I will give you X reward. In this case, you have to kill around 10 goblins. Now, the only way the game presented players to kill said goblins was to enter a dungeon. This wouldn't be such a bad Idea if the options to make a dungeon weren't available right away. I found myself kinda wanting to choose other options, only because they were all present there for me to choose from. (What I am saying here is that they should either make the others un-clickable intill a certain level, or at least tell you in a more Direct way what they all do.) Then at the end of a dungeon, you play a game of Rock-Paper-Scisiors, that even if you lose it, you still get extra money and items.
Then with the combat system, oh boy. The game seems to want to sell off "Look at this awesome combo!" for the combat. All I had to do to kill everything in my way, was left click 4 times  in a row. I did the same combo every time, because it was also the
combo i could do. I tried to hold the left button longer, press it faster and more times, everything! But all it allowed me to do was swipe three times, and jump above them for a smash.
Also with the combat is a grabbing system, that needs to be re-thought about. You can grab anything that isn't a boss from what I have seen. But grabbing is also confusing for the point that when you grab the, you don't want to press left click, for that drops them doing no damage. You want to press the spacebar to deal any damage with the grab.
Then with the character creation... none. You choose what class you want to be, and if you want to be a Femail prest, or a male Mage... then you are out of luck. The genders are locked for the classes, which leaves little room for customising. The hair options you can choose from are Pre-colored, so even when changing the hair color option, you will still have the tink of Purple/Pink/Whatever that certain hair style's color is.
When "customising" your clothes, you only change the main color of your shirt, pants, gloves, and shoes.
The story also seems kinda bland, just read this: You are part of a nation (which one I am still unsure of, but I think Vermont) that is trying to save a captured War-Hero from terrorists.
... What? You wanted more story? Well that is the jist of it from what the game is willing to say at the start. Now I will say that story's like this are common for games like this, starts with something very simple, then works it's way up. (See every Final Fantasy game) But really, a fallen country now has a Terrorist group that is planning on bringing the country back from the ashes by... kid-napping the person who helped kill it in the first place? I'm not to sure what is going on in their minds, but I will let it be, since i have not played for even an hour.
The countries are also wierdly names. There is Syria, Vermont, some other country that I couldn't be bothered to remember, and Growl (Or ground? The voice actor seems to say both in the intro).
All in all, I guess this is a F2P game, that could get some work done on it to make it better, but for now it doesn't seem that good to me, so I would give this game a 2/10. I know there are some people who really love this game, and good for them! They found a game that they can enjoy, and it isn't even fully released yet!
Thanks for reading!

The idea behind this game is something I can really get behind, I feel more games should engage the gaming community and teach them something about the world or in this case another culture. This being said, platforming games should be built from the ground up starting with their platforming mechanics. Without smooth platforming mechanics a platformer becomes at the very least frustrating, boring, or unrewarding and at the very worst unplayable. It is very clear that this game was made as a vehicle to teach people about a culture through adapted folklore and as a result the platforming mechanics have taken a backseat to storytelling. The platforming mechanics can get clunky and cumbersome at times and swimming portions can become down right irritating. However, overall I was won over by the concept behind, art direction and storytelling of this game.

The story keeps you hooked the entire time, constantly keeping your focus on moving towards the next point. And don't think the gameplay is TERRIBLE, they really put detail into working the little things, light switches, cupboards, drawers, etc., and you must move your mouse in the direction the drawer/door opens which is a neat little quirk I love :).

For a game as visually beautiful and full of atmosphere as this is, the game itself, well.. kinda sucks. The visuals, as mentioned before are stellar. I am not exaggerating when I say that this game is gorgeous. The sound, likewise, is amazing. This game really could be described as a work of art.
Now if the game wasn't so full of bugs and bad play mechanics, it might actually be a joy to play. Right about the point where you start to get into the meat of the game, it becomes an exercise in frustration. From bugs that prevent moving forward because of bad wall/ledge detection, to a stupendously BAD aiming/shooting mechanic for the bolo, this game sets you in places where it's almost impossible to progress. A shame because everything else about the game, from the wonderful cultural videos, to the amazing stylistic storytelling, to the aforementioned beautiful visuals, is PERFECT.
But the game is so fricking frustrating I simply cannot recommend it for purchase.

I'll try to make this brief. Overall the game is fun to play, and looks great. The main characters are enjoyable (at first anyways) and there's a lot of interest built on the culture and stories of the Inupiat people, and it's worked well into a game, for the most part. The game mechanics work well together (for the most part) though they're a bit overused in parts.
My major grievances with the game are really mostly minor. First, the camera can lag behind the characters at times (particularly when sliding or climbing) leading you to slide completely off the screen. Normally it wasn't a problem but I did die once or twice from this, as I slid off the screen and fell into a pit of water.
Second, let's talk about that pit of water... one issue that rather irks me is the overall inconsistency. You barely touch water in the first part of the game and you die. The next part of the game... you're swimming all over the place. After that? Water kills you again. I understand that they want to make certain parts of the game challenging, but mechanics like that just kind of kill immersion or enjoyment since it feels very forced. In this same vein there's some issues with what's being told in the story not showing up on screen. Not to give anything away, but let's just sayif you tell me my character is supposed to be carrying some big object, I expect to see that, not just her running around like normal.
If I'm "inside of an area" *cough*not spoiling it*cough*  that logically would not be full of ice caves, why does it look like ice caves?
The partner AI generally doesn't pose too much of a problem but there were some times I was getting rather irritated by it, and in fact a few times where it killed me.
Finally, my last issue with the game is that mi-late game (about 60-70% through) The "puzzles" start looking pretty much the same. They start to become more tedious than anything else, and they're setup in such a way it kind of breaks the flow of the game.
As I stated though, despite my explaining them out like this, the problems weren't really that major. I did enjoy the game a lot, and would recommend it, though the game's a bit short. My play time lasted a little over 2 hours.
If you're on the fence about it I'd suggest waiting until it's on sale, but it's still a pretty decent game overall.
For those of you who like ratings, I'd give it about a 73%.

DO NOT BUY THE RAINBOW SIX SIEGE: STARTER EDITION (Why later..)
Short explanation:What is Rainbow Six Siege?
Rainbow Six Siege is a team-based 5 vs 5 shooter with asymmetrical game-play. One team has the role of Attack and the other plays Defence. The choice of 'Operators' differs with these roles. Operators are the characters you play as which have different guns and gadgets, gearing them towards a specific role in the team. One example is the Medic Operator who has multiple weapons like MP5,SG-CQB-Shotgun or a P90, with a deployable shield or barbed wire and (as his gadget)a gun that can heal team-mates. He can attack just fine, but has more of a supportive role. He is only available to the Defending team.These equipments differ with each operator(ATK and DEF) and so it brings a lot of individuality.
Big + points:
Many parts of the maps are  destructible, which makes the game very dynamic.
The rounds are not long and have good tension.(15-20min)
The game gets regular updates which refreshes the gameplay and improves it.(adding new operators or new maps)
THE GRIND NEVER STOPS:
The only criticism I have is the purchasing system for 'DLC' operators or even standard ones.
If you dont have the Season Pass or own THE RAINBOW SIX SIEGE: STARTER EDITON
you have to invest a lot of time in the game to unlock new operators.(~20h for a DLC and ~10h for a standard operator)
I would highly recommend NOT TO buy THE RAINBOW SIX SIEGE: STARTER EDITON,
it makes the game much more frustrating just by this worse purchase system.
Short Conclusion:
Just buy the normal Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege and you have good game in your hands.

♥♥♥♥♥this review is a long time after the game came out, but I'm bored and my internet isn't fast enough for CSGO. The Darkness II is a fantastic arcade style first person shooter experience.
PROS
-Story is for the most part excellent thanks to great pacing, writing, voice acting, character development, and an interesting setup.
-There lore behind the game is great. You collect pieces of history related to the Darkness called relics, and it's awesome to hear the Darkness expert talk about each of them. His speeches are psychotic, informative, and funny.
-I'm a sucker for cell shader graphics, and this game delivers. Everything is colorful and bloody.
-The gameplay: If you have even the slightest of power fantasies then this game is perfect for you, because you are one of, it not the most, badass ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in all of gaming. Don't believe me? You are a streetborn Italian mob boss who has two demon arms from hell emerging from his back, and you ♥♥♥♥ up enemies by either ripping them in half with said demon arms, dual weilding hell infused weapons into their face holes, or eating their hearts (often times all three things happen at the same time).  There are few things as satisfying as impaling a guy through the skull with a parking meter and then eating his heart. It's the most metal ♥♥♥♥ing thing ever. The upgrade tree also makes the already badass Jackie even more badass. Obviously that's what upgrading does, but some other games give you passive upgrades. There are some of those in the Darkness II, but there are also other ones that give you cool, USEFUL (not too many games get this one right) abilities like channeling the Darkness through your guns or releasing locusts through your hands. Gameplay can be summaraized with one word: badass.
CONS
-The game is only about 4-5 hours long. It took me about 6, but I was stretching it out. When you beat the game you feel like there should've been more. There is a 4 player coop mode, but unless you have friends, nobody is online.
-Aside from new game + and getting all of the upgrades (which is small incentive), there is no replayability to the game. I'll definitely play it again, but it won't be for awhile.
Those two flaws are pretty damn big, which means it's not worth the $30 price tag (unless you were a big fan of the first game, and in such a case you already bought and enjoyed the Darkness II). Wait until it's about $20.
Overall, superb game. Hoping for a third installment.

TL:DR; Incredibly well written story set in a sci-fi setting will leave you astonished and overwhelmed by its presence. SOMA is ambitious but very well executed title that provides fullfilling narrative set in the Atlantic ocean.

Taking a role of Simon, bookseller from Toronto, you quickly embark on a magical destination in a world where you'll question your very existence. Creators of previously very successful title named Amnesia: The Dark Descent take on very ambitious but interesting story that holds nothing back. Voice acting is great and leaves a imminent impact on you connecting with most of the characters you encounter. Ending while revealing nothing, is something to leave you speechless but also disturbing in a certain kind of way.

While the game follows same tradition as Amnesia: The Dark Descent, SOMA offers interesting puzzles that are relatively fair to the player but can leave you in frustration while searching for the right answer hunted by annoying monsters. While it's definitely not a walking sim given that it combines puzzle elements and exploration very well, monsters that you encounter although will set that eerie and disturbing atmosphere, are nothing but nuisance that prevent you from progressing further into the depth of SOMA.

Visually SOMA doesn't offer anything revolutionary. But it definitely sets a fantastic tone combined with audio design that will be appeal to many. Optimisation although not perfect, is nothing to worry about.
Fan or not of this genre, story that this game presents is incredibly written and is a must-buy to anyone looking for a great tale presented in a rather interesting but disturbing way.

If you're looking for a chill puzzle game with some exploration, get this.

I purchased Hitman:GO because I adore board games and puzzles, so this review is coming from someone who isn’t familiar with the Hitman franchise. For the most part, Hitman:GO was an enjoyable turn-based puzzling experience. I loved the board piece visuals, the sleek and minimal interface, and how the game would gradually introduce trickier enemies to evade and obstacles/helpful items as I progressed.  I do, however, have 2 design flaws I want to stress to all potential buyers:
1) There are different level packs that you unlock by completing objectives. Some objectives, such as “don’t kill any enemies” or “don’t kill any dogs”, make sense. The “complete the level in X turns or less” objective, however, is thoroughly asinine without a turn counter. I don’t consider myself a spoiled gamer by any means, but I think it’s rather ludicrous that a person should have to count 20+ turns in their head (while also trying to solve the puzzle at hand) in order to complete an objective.
2) Positioning is key in a turn-based puzzler where you need to evade your enemies. However, in some levels, certain areas of the board (and your options to move) are obscured by walls. Sure, I can use the right mouse button to reposition the camera, but this is VERY clunky.
Hitman:GO is a good turn-based board game. Design flaws prevent it from being a great game in the puzzle genre. I recommend it to board game and puzzle lovers, but with reservations.

Alright, here's a bit of advice/things to know before you start. Wish I had known this stuff before starting, believe me.
1. Don't judge this game because of its low ratings. It's free, give it a shot. You might just like it.
2. This game isn't really P2W. Honestly, it really isn't. I will concede that buying gear can give you a
advantage, but with enough skill you can counter basically anyone, regardless of class or gear.
3. Learning this game is arguably the hardest part of starting. The game isn't so good at explaining things, but reading the ingame guide (the F1 key brings it up at any time) can definitely clear up confusion on certain game mechanics.
4.
Do not make the same mistake I made and create a Female Rockstar because she looked hot on the cover of this page. Learn your playstyle preference through the plethora of Beginner scrolls they give you; you're bound to get enough of a variety of classes to try a bit of everything. Then, do your research and pick a class you won't hate and make that your perm. You can get better characters later, don't worry.
5. Once you pick your perms, actually do their training segments. They're actually pretty good at helping you get familiar with your skills, and they even give you some good combos to work with. Honestly, the more you educate yourself in this game, the better.
6. You don't need the DLC packs available through Steam. They're kinda a waste of money imo.
7. Don't try to start super competitively. Play to have fun. Learn the mechanics by playing the fun modes. Prisoner is a fun and common mode that isn't
competitive, and if you hate playing against people you can do a private lobby of that one Forest attack mode where you kill NPCs. Take advice from the community; a majority of people I've met and complained about not being good to have been nice and offered some kind of helpful advice. It's a pretty good community, surprisingly. (except for that one guy who tried to scam me by asking for my phone number to give me free stuff >_>)
8. If you
heck up and you regret some kind of decision you can't undo, don't worry. You can uninstall the Steam version and make a new account, then play through their client instead. That's what I did, because I was dumb. Don't be me. I know the Rockstar is hot and reminds me of Orchid from Maplestory, but that's no excuse to make a Perm.
9. Don't expect to pay money. You can totally get Premiums and Rares you like without cashing out some dollars, but it is still an option if you don't mind it.
To summarize: give the game a fair shot. Try to have fun above all else. Find the character you like and create the ultimate waifu (or guyfu). Enjoy the game :)
