I paid 6 dollars for this on steam sale, and that is why I am not very critical of the game. To be fair, anyone who would have paid the full price would be crushingly dissapointed. In the original Force Unleashed, one had a clear two fold mission, Vader was to use Starkiller as both his inquisitor to hunt down the last remaining Jedi, and then together they would destroy the emperor. His origins on Kashyyyk made him an original character, conceived by the union of two Jedi Knights, a violation of their sacred vow. Galen Marek was a boy when Vader finds him, and he molds him to the Dark Side, but the plot thinkens in a riveting fashion and its conclusion is absolutely surprising, whether you choose light or dark side.
The sequel was underwhelming. Yes, we are reunited with General Rham Kota, but it feels empty, almost distracting. We never get to see Captain Juno Eclipse, except extremely briefly and mostly only at the end of the game in a devastatinly dissapointing way. The lack of clear pursuit, and choices makes the Force Unleashed II somewhat less fulfilling.
It is a worthy note to mention that the fact that we fight mostly unknowns and over the top monsters (The Gorog sequence felt like I was suddenly playing as a certain God against a certain titan from a certain popular game franchise) make it one of the more unoriginal games I've played and recycled many of the prequels ideas and concepts without really bringing anyhting new.
Overall, I would rate this game 6 out of 10 only because the genre was faithful to the universe but I often felt the urge to stop playing from boredom.

Imagine a game with Metroid-style exploration of a world, except instead of shooting everything that moves, you're a scientist on an expedition to explore Mars, you've discovered life in an underground cave system, and the only way to procede is to plant seeds and create little ecosystems in each chamber of the caverns to open up access to new areas. You have no special powers or abilities other than the seeds you collect and the jet pack on your space suit, and it's fairly interesting what that changes about the way a game like that plays and what things stay the same. There are lots of different ways to solve the rooms, depending on how they're laid out and what you're in the mood for doing with them, whether it's friendly and cooperative or antagonistic with everyone eating each other, micromanagement-heavy or something that sprouts from nothing and grows all on its own because of a couple careful decisions you made. The story and voice acting are pretty decent too, and it's worth spending the extra couple hours to get the "real" ending(s) if you're into the gameplay, both to find out more of what's going on and because figuring out how to make the most of what you've got in each room is usually what's the most fun.

A modern rpg that's a true homage to the old school jrpg's not because it is identical to them in terms of gameplay mechanics etc. but because it emulates games like Chrono Cross and Final Fantasy VII in that it's exploring it's very own brand new mechanics and bring fresh ideas and systems to a familiar table. Update 7/21/2017 - Today's patch added a speed up option which address the #1 complaint I and many other reviewers have had: length of each battle due to slow animations. In addition they have  made some balancing changes that should address some of the complaints concerng difficulty.
On a personal note after another four hours of playing this game I am now ashamed that I gave the graphics a meh rating. Partially this was because I was playing on a very small screen for the first six hours or so but no excuses I was wrong. There is a great deal of detail put into each battle ground and indivdual units. Top that off with excellent character portraits (excluding the first one that you'll see in game which leaves a bad impression imo) and ragdoll effects that have enemies falling into chasms and the like and I'm impressed. Easily a 7/10 in terms of presentation.
OG REVIEW
Marketing for this game seems to be at odds with what I found here (and from the looks of it alot of other people feel the same) so I'll do my best to help frame the gameplay experience I've ran into thus far (7 or so hours at this point).
This is a single-player mostly linear SRPG featuring tabletop board game DNA. The boardgame DNA is apparent in that you are going to find both card draw and abilitiy card alongside dice as core mechanics. While it's not a feature that provides alot of options there is a "lite" deck-building element. The deck builder along with a choice between various unlockable die allow you to customize each units playstyle a little bit and actually replace the inventory and perk/skill system usually found in this type of game.
Graphics/Sound/Writing....None of these are game ruining but none of them really shine either and I would rate all of them around 5/10.
I love the combat system and that's what makes this a winner for me.
Quality of Life Improvments are SORELY needed but if you can be patient and want to try something a little different I say give it a go.
If you are not patient and/or are expecting a more traditional RPG experience I would avoid.
Otherwise?....
8/10

Survarium is certainly a beautiful environment with fleshy gun play and great ideas. Unfortunately, when I read through the developers diary and look at the amount of time spent so far, it feels like the project is going down the path of Half-Life 3. Quite a few features of the game, such as factions, seem to have been hurridly thrown in to give some semblance of story line. I have freely switched between the different factions without any penalties so far, and would have liked to see some gameplay where the faction you just left punishes you according to their nature e.g the Black Market could hunt you down, or the Army could attempt to arrest you.
Survival does not feel like a part of the game just yet, as most items can be bought in the shop using in-game coins, or gold bought using real money. Artifacts, while most certainly useful during matches, hold no real appeal as they are removed from inventory after a match. It is a real shame, considering Survarium is a spiritual successor from S.T.A.L.K.E.R, which in turn was influenced by the novel Roadside Picnic. Artifacts should have a greater role in Survarium, as it did in the novel and games.
Survarium feels like it's feeding on the feel-good- vibes, left over from the days of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. I would highlight this game to those who have played either S.T.A.L.K.E.R or Metro, or both -  not as a recommendation but as a game to keep an eye on. Hopefully the long waiting time for other features e.g PvE will be worth the wait.

The Darkness 2 is more linear than the first game, but more fast-paced and action packed. The game is almost all shooting, with arcadey and precise shooting and a decent weapon variety (most weapons feel distinct). On top of the typical one heavy weapon and 2 smaller weapons that can be dual-wielded, there is a darkness arm for picking up and throwing things or consuming people (either for health or ammo). So you can rip a car's door off and use it as a shield while dual wielding, throw it to cut an enemy in half, then pick another enemy up, dismember them, and take their ammo. In addition there's a decent upgrade system that encourages the player to vary gameplay as much as possible for points and to plan out their purchases. At first it seems like a lot to keep track of, but it's not long before you get used to it and settle into a nice flow.
The visuals are very comic book like (like Borderlands but darker) and incredibly gory. The levels are mostly cool with the exception of the somewhat bland warehouse. All of the enemies look cool, are just varied enough to keep things interesting, and look great torn into pieces and strewn about the level.
Occasionally the game takes a short break at your home base, but never for kmore than a few minutes thankfully. These parts give a little bit of a breather and give time for the story progression.
The story is mostly great but sometimes the main character comes across as stupid and whiny in certain scenes involving his dead girlfriend from the first game.
. Be warned that one of the endings is a
cliffhanger (especially if you love the comics) and there's no sequel confirmed.
The Darkness 2 is also short (like 6-7 hours), which is both good and bad. On the one hand it's laser-focused and well-paced, but on the other it's possible to complete in one sitting. There is a co-op mode, but it's nothing special. It's pretty cheap as it is, but some might want to wait for it to go on sale.
Only negative is that having 'grind' in the game name makes it hard for me to convince friends to buy it!

Ahhh man..this game.... It's so difficult to rate it using Steam's system, cause I don't know if I can recommend this to anyone, even though it's a decent game.
First of all, this is a platformer. Any good platformer relies on two very important things: responsive controls and interesting gameplay. Does this game have any of those two things? No.  The characters sometimes don't jumb, they don't move where you want them to, they don't aim where you want them to and in general don't feel as responsive as they should. Is this gameplay interesting? Well, it's alright. Nothing new...just some good ol' jumping and running.
I've seen games that did what this game is trying to do, in a MUCH better and interesting way (e.g. Brothers).
How much game-time do you get from this game? 5 hours max. (Which is not much, given what this game costs)
Is the story interesting? Again, it's alright.. I've seen games with much more interesting storylines and characters.
So, what are the pros? It looks nice... and the music is calm and relaxing.. Shame that all of this is overshadowed from your frustration, since you'll find yourself dying over and over again even due to the bad controls or the incredibly stupid AI.
So, at the end of the day, this game is a platformer, but not a good one. It's trying to be a relaxing game, but it's incredibly frustrating. It a story-driven game, but the story is average. And it costs 15euros even though you can finish it in less than 5 hours.
Buy Brothers instead.

This game is staggeringly good and I believe its story and ending rank amongst the best science fiction/horror in any media.
The enviornments are amazingly detailed and often filled us with a sense of wonder and dread.  From the begginning, the player's character is well established as both real and human.  His confusion as he explores and comes to grip with his unusual situation is shared play for play by the player leading to some wonderful reveals.  The story unfolds slowely but with good pacing.  Some of the key story elements are mandatory but much of the story is revealed through optional audiologs, journals, and other information found by the player.  The best story elements take the form of discovery as the player comes across something unexpected or enlightening in the environment.  Sometimes this takes the form of a hostile entity the player must circumvent.  These experiences were never overly long and were quite veried.  Many evoked fear or terror and had us shrieking out loud as we were startled.  Others were sad or thought provoking.  There are just enough of these encounters that the game never stalls but yet you always fear what is around the next corner.
No leveling, no collecting, no dumb achievements, almost no item management.  Just explore, survive, let the story play out, and enjoy the amazing atmosphere of SOMA.

You are Atlus and you fight other famous people by rolling a giant boulder (of which you unlock different kinds as you go) trying to stay on the track and avoid / destroy defenses until you reach the enemy stronghold and try to knock the door down over several rounds.  Each round you place defenses to try and slow down or destroy the enemy boulder and they do the same.  You can chose which defenses to take with you and try and come up with a strategy that fits the map and your opponent.  Not everything is available at the beginning though, you have to find them on the campaign map as you go.  There is also an obstacle mode for each enemy / map which is just a race with no placement by you.  Each battle starts with a little cutscene showing off you opponent.  These can be quite funny and really help the game being worth the purchase price.  As humor is subjective, look at the trailers or other content to see if that is for you.  Other than that there are some boss battles, where different rules apply.  They aren't hard as I don't think you can lose most of them, just keep retrying until you hit the right thing. Never played the multiplayer, I could see that being pretty fun though if you have a good partner.  The non-campaign stuff seems to be mainly the same maps and enemies with the same modes other than the new skeet shoot.  I didn't find skeet shoot fun though, just hit some targets and then try and hit a ramp to get a good multiplier.
Really enjoyed the game but because it is short I would recommend waiting for a good sale.

Having played through Flower Shop: Summer in Fairbrook and having finally gotten all of the endings, I'm now ready to post my review of this game. As many others have already summarized what the game is about, I won't go through the trouble of repeating that. Instead, I'll get right to the point and give my opinion, pointing out certain features and such as necessary.
Although this is the first game by Winter Wolves that I've ever played, I have played a lot of VNs (visual novels), dating sims, etc., so I would consider myself a pretty avid gamer in regards to those genres. When I play these games, the most important aspect for me is the story. If the story doesn't catch my interest, I won't be motivated to play more.
Now I have to admit that it did take me some time to tolerate the main character Steve. He isn't likeable at the beginning but then I suppose that was the point when his character was designed. Initially, he comes off as a lazybones, unmotivated person who has no direction in his life. He has no idea what he wants to do with his future, etc. So he gets shipped off to his uncle's farm near Fairbrook in order to change for the better. Well, this is the basic idea. Although I didn't like Steve in the beginning, I ended up liking him in the end. He changes into a motivated, hard-working person although I suppose this does happen if he ends up pursuing a romance with one of four dateable female characters.
In regards to the other characters, I liked Steve's uncle. I found him to be quite entertaining and he can help change Steve for the better, doing it in a more effective way than Steve's father. As to the four dateable characters, I liked them although at times, I thought they had drastic mood swings. However, that may just be because the way they suddenly change their behavior wasn't written or portrayed as well as I would have liked. That's just my personal preference, though. If there was one character that I disliked, it would have to be Steve's father. His father comes off as angry in the beginning although I could understand that since Steve initially came off as being lazy and unmotivated. However, even near the end when the father makes an appearance again because of a certain event, his father still comes off as angry despite that Steve has changed for the better. Now I know that the father is a minor character but I would have liked for there to be some development between him and Steve. Perhaps some background as to why the father behaved the way he did would have helped. Also, I would have liked there to have been the option throughout the game for Steve to improve his relationship with his father. Yes, I know that this game is a dating sim but having this other aspect would have made the game more interesting.
As to the gameplay, I liked the farming aspect. I thought it was fun and it added more rather than simply having Steve meet one of the dateable characters and build relationships with them. As to that aspect now, I think this could have been improved on. Even though Steve can pursue one of the females, simply building up a favorable relationship with them isn't enough. Steve also needs to build up their favorable stat and the game doesn't really provide clues on which stat each female favors. Well, it is hinted with two of them but not with the other two so unless you have a walkthrough or even a general hints guide to indicate what stat you should go for with each female, then it's kind of a guessing game.
As to the flaws, I'd say that the proofreading aspect could have been improved. I noticed mistakes here and there but then I suppose I would tend to pay more attention to them because of my job. Other than that, the only other flaw I can think of is that the game can get repetitive after playing through it once or twice. However, I suppose that is the nature of most dating sims in general so I can't really place much fault there.
I do like how the gallery is set up. As I've played numerous VNs, I'm used to how galleries in general are set up. The one that's set up here is a little different. Rather than displaying CGs (core graphics), music, etc., Flower Shop replays certain endings or scenes that you earn upon reaching a particular path. It's different from what I'm used to but I do like this feature.
Overall, I'm recommending Flower Shop: Summer in Fairbrook for anyone who's a fan of dating sims. It does have some replayable value so you can go for different endings. (There are two different endings for each female and there is an alone ending, too.) It's fun and light-hearted (for the most part) and if that's what you're looking for, then give it a try. ^^

Let me just say; this game is great. I have almost finished the campaign, and I realised that I laughed at least every level. This game is incredibly original and has a very funny 2d artstyle (which looks like something pulled out of a painting), along with very good looking 3d graphics for the levels, boulders and defenses. I think this is an incredibly interesting and original take on the Tower Defense genre of games, and this is pretty much the only way to experience it. Each level is comprised of two identical downhill slopes which both lead to a castle. The aim of the game is to control a boulder down a slope and smash into the castle gate with the highest possible speed and lowest damage taken in order to deal the most damage. Both you and your enemy have the option of building defenses to slow down and damage the enemy's boulder as it makes its way towards your castle gate. There are defenses such as ballistas, cannons, lions strapped to balloons, explosives and even cowfields that you have the option of placing on your slope. There is also a lot of variation in the boulders. There's a boulder with another, smaller one orbiting around it, a fast boulder which is shaped like a tyre, another boulder with a fuse on it which eventually makes it explode etc. Another thing I loved about this game is the variation in level design. While yes, there were 3 or so levels which had a very similar structure, the colours and look were very different, as well as your opponent. Along with that there are some hilarious boss fights (that I would like to see more of) such as a bossfight where you have to break off the Sphinx's nose! And all this is just the campaign! There are many more modes to explore along with multiplayer (which I have not tried yet), which can suck up hours of your time. Not to mention that the campaign has lots of replayability with many different difficulty modes. There are some cons though, the most important of which being that the campaign level can get (just a little) repetitive, along with the campaign being short and only lasting between 6-7 hours.

Sniper Elite v2 is a third person stealth shooter from Rebellion software. It shares it's gameplay mechanics with Sniper Ghost Warrior series, but in a WW2 setting.
As a, surprise surprise, sniper you'll operate behind enemy lines to eliminate some prominent nazi generals, explode rockets and help allies win WW2. Sniper Elite v2 is a game for rather patient people, it's kinda like Hitman. You should move unseen and eliminate or avoid enemies quietly. You can try to run and gun, but the main character is not bulletproof and dies in a few shots. Kinda like Agent 47.
It's a good enough stealth game, even if it has some annoying issues. Mechanically the game is solid, the sneaking usually works, the shooting usually works, but sometimes it doesn't. Enemies might spot you through trees, from 300 meters, and shoot you through these trees to death. The sometimes odd camera will not show you the guy that is just around the corner and as soon as he sees you the whole map will know where you are. Some enemies will bug into a car or tree just to unbug at the perfect moment to break your cover and start shooting at you. So yeah, the game can be annoying. And the worst thing, one level where you're forced into close quarters. Ugh, that one is bad.
Still, it's like WW2 Hitman with the possibility to shoot people in the head over long distances with nice slowmos of their vital organs being shattered into tiny pieces. It's actually quite cool. The game is not too short and not too long and should take about 10hrs on normal difficulty. The story is there, it's not too bad, a good excuse for some long distance headshots.
I liked:
* shooting people over long distances
* cool slowmos of gruesome headshots
* when sneaking and sniping works it's really cool
* not too long not too short
* the gfx in general
I disliked:
* jerky animations
* AI that can see you from 300m and can be deadly accurate with a machine gun
Get this if:
* WW2 Hitman seems interesting enough for you
Don't get this if:
* you're more of a run and gun type fellow
* you can't stomach glitches and/or occasionally unfair AI

Truly I wanted to like this game, it has everything I love, turn based grid combat with a squad of unique characters, dice, cards.  But it all feels very shallow and disappointing.
Its a neat world, the lore you do get through the optional dialogues is interesting and I'd love to explore it more, but just in a different game.  Each story mission ramps up the difficulty to  point where you'll likely need to grind out dice or levels to stand a fighting chance because every map I've encountered is your 3 units vs between 10 to 15 enemies that can usually 2 hit your guys.
There are optional side quests, but you can't level those characters so your often thrust into a situation where pure luck determines your success or failure, because you can't edit those characters decks or dice loadout.
Speaking of, there is little to no variance in your deck, each character's level progression is linear and certain cards just seem far better than others, leading me to believe there is a right way to build your deck and a wrong way.  Each character has 12 cards to choose from to build their deck...
Combat becomes tedious rather quickly, the developer listened to the players and added a feature to speed up enemy animations, but each action the player takes causes the camera to zoom in and watch the static boring animation you've likely seen a hundred times already.
This game is an interesting beast that had quite a bit of potential, but despite how unique it is, it's just not very fun.

If you are looking for a Tactics game, Children of Zodiacs (CoZ) is a great one!
My main experience with Tactics games is Final Fantasy Tactics (FFT), which the dev team, Cardboard Utopia, has said was one of their inspirations for this game. I feel like the gameplay is very similar to, and much smoother than, FFT. However, there is one thing to be aware of:
This is NOT FFT. Do not come expecting a large party of 20 generic units with a job system.
Instead (at least as far as I have gotten) there are only 3 main characters, and they generally comprise your entire party. Instead of being able to change classes, each character has a deck of cards which you can customize, with more cards unlocking the farther you go. Additionally, as you level up, these cards improve and gain new abilities.
Another addition to the game is using dice to alter your attacks. These dice can either increase damage or healing, activate special abilities on your cards, let you draw additional cards, or even take an additional action. What is fascinating about this system is you are also able to craft dice to fit the gameplay you want.
For my last note: While this is a great tactics game which feels very unique, the customization is perhaps not as deep as you might expect based on other tactics games, but the gameplay is solid and the story (so far) has been engaging. I am a very happy Kickstarter backer!
EDIT: I just wanted to add that, within 3 days of release, Cardboard Utopia patched in a feature to fast forward enemy turns and fine tuned the difficulty of 2 levels based on feedback on the forums.   Just something to keep in mind.
EDIT 2: While I am still enjoying the game, I'm at about story mission #14 and I've done some sidequests and grinding and it's starting to feel a bit repetitive. I still have plenty of cards to unlock though, and I haven't changed my characters set-ups too drastically yet, so there are still ways for me to spice it up. I am worried about grinding for dice and expect I might just power through the story as much as I can and not worry about min-maxing so I can avoid the grinding.

At his uncle's farm, Steve has to help tend his uncle's farm by cultivating 8 different types of crops and making a certain profit. At Fairbrook, Steve will get to meet and interact with his uncle Sam, his ex-girlfriend Jill, the owner of the flower shop in Fairbrook Susana, the daughter of a neighbouring farm owner in Fairbrook Clara, the librarian in Fairbrook Marian as well as additional supporting characters Trent who is Susana's brother, Jacob who helps out at Clara's farm, Orpheus who is Sam's pet cat and Steve's father.
The game has plenty of save slots to enable quicker replays to reach a different romance ending, a tell-all relationship meter with any of the main characters that goes up or down depending on your dialogue or option choices and the option to skip and fast-forward already read sections.

I really enjoyed this game.
It's farmville meets dating sim, and I love it. You play as Steve, a lazy college kid shipped off to his uncle's farm in order to build some character.
Which he does, by growing crops and getting to know the locals. As is usual for these games, there are four potential, quirky love interests.
Unlike many such games, in order to get close to any individual love interest, you have to get to know everyone, and level up several stats.
Getting the specific ending you wanted can prove tricky, as the stat you level up by spending time with a woman, is not the one that is vital to her romance path.
This means you may be trying to romance one woman, only to wind up with a different one.
And they're all quirky, there's your bossy ex, the neurotic poet librarian, the relatively normal girl attempting to escape from country life, and Susanna.
Susanna appears in a LOT of WinterWOlves games (she's Myrth in 'Loren the Amazon Princess', and Sally in 'Roommates'), either because she's a neat archtype to write around, or someone on the team knows her in real life.
She's vegan, into nature and natural healing. You mention in passing you'll take an asprin for your headache, and get treated to a lecture on chemicals and how natural remedies are so much better.
But the game is gentle and fun, it is quite entertaining to see Steve learn, mature and grow up. The characters are not particularly deep, but they don't really need to be.
You manage stats and get to know people, what more is there to say?
Not worth the frustration.

This is a good story, masterfully told with bonus information thats educational but not intrusive to the game. An inexpensive joy of a game.

I've played way back when this game first came out on the OGP release. I'm going to say this, on this version's release of Lost Saga I'm very.....mixed.
The game seems more easy to grasp onto, but if you haven't played any kind of Beat-Em-Up or never even played a game, I'd....well I'd probably not touch this. People say this game is P2P (Pay 2 Win) and....well it always was. Remember when Hazama first came out on the NA release? Everyone either stole their mother's/father's credit card, wasted a LOT of time on surveys, begged to be gifted Hazama, or just whined about not having Hazama passive-aggressively, and sometimes very aggressive to the point of everyone kicking for Toxic-ness. Censorship is more of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ than before, so whenever I say class (because I'm stuck on the whole classes thing) it comes out as cl***** which is stupid. On that topic, the game has became more PG than PG-13. The only "cuss" I can say is dammit. Now I understand cussing is bad and all that, yada yada, but still. Anywho, disruption of the first ammendment is not the topic at hand. You care about the gameplay and the community. The gameplay is laggier than before, but I've rarely ran into that problem. I guess I must be lucky. Every hero is awesome~ Except for the guy with the purple axe that charges and slams into you and it drops you through the ground. That's not even a special move, it's just a charged attack. Broken hero. P2W (Pay 2 Win) confirmed. That's the only problem I have gameplay wise. Now the community tends to either be non-existant, or salty. Matches are harder to find now, many plazas have AFK people who fish or people who relic search. So it's really not the place to converse with others. The game is very competitive.....aggressively competitive. The game no longer rewards teamwork, and the raids and crusade aren't an excuse. All this is obnoxious....but unlike other's, I have a twisted way at looking at the game which keeps pulling me back, because don't get me wrong, I love the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game, even if it has A WHOLE LOT OF KINKS THAT NEED TO BE ADDRESSED + the whole "owners keep getting swapped". that's what really REALLY killed the community I'd say. So, quick summary:
Pros:
- Nostalgia geeks will love it, and be drawn into it as long as they aren't sensitive little brats. No offense.
- The game easily gives you two free permanent characters. Now we don't have to constantly farm to get ourselves a hero. Let's be honest, for the people who actually couldn't use a credit card, this was a MAJOR turn off. The rest are somewhat hard to obtain, and what I mean is that it's now reasonable in my opinion.
- You're going to be able to get practicly every hero that's ever been released ever. At least, in the NA version.
- Events are common, hard to go by without noticing that.
- Battling is the same. Game modes are diverse, and fun.
Cons:
- Laggy
- Salty/Non-existant community
- Purple axe guy who makes you fall through the floor and needs to be removed/nerfed HARD
- To Nostalgia Geeks of OGP? Awesome. To Veterans of Lost Saga in general? Not awesome.
6/10.......not bad........but needs a lot of work. Still pretty fun and playable. Do recommend to competitive peeps and nostalgia geeks. Not so much to hard asses....honest opinion.

Incredibly engrossing, with great voice work and an art style all its own, Waking Mars caught me completely by surprise. Although it borrows heavily from many other games, most noticeably Metroid/Castlevania, it nonetheless feels very unique and is a refreshing change from the usual shooter heavy gameplay of other contemporaries.
It's not however without any problems. The controls are far from ideal, with keyboard and mouse suffering being too imprecise, and controller support feeling tacked on do to a lack of full implementation. There are also times when the game just doesn't give you enough direction, instead forcing you to wander around until you stumble upon a path to the next area.
In the end though Waking Mars is an absolute triumph despite its flaws. The presentation is superb, and I couldn't help getting sucked into the game for hours at a time. It definitely isn't for everyone, but those that let it sink its roots into them will find an experience unlike anything else, and a world simply begging to be explored.

Okay, SIZE MATTERS. TFU 2 is too damn short - completed it in under 5 hours - one day of not-that-intensive playing. But if you have to choose during developement process between long, meh-game and short and awesome one - answer is obvious. Well, maybe not really, but LucasArts picked the right one. I will complain a lot, but still, it was awesome 5 hours.
The Force Unleashed 2 continues the story of Darth Vaders apPrentice - Starkiler. In the end of first game, he was believed to be killed. TFU2 starts from this point - reason for protagonist being alive is introduced pretty nicely - Starkiller we are playing as is one of clones of original Starkiller - with all his memories and skills. As Vader prepares himselft to kill the student after failed tests, Starkiller escapes cloning facilites in Vaders own TIE Advanced. Then follows the piece of information that Vader accidentally gave him and rescues General kota from Cato Nemondia. Later Starkiller tries to find Juno - their meeting is interrupted by Boba Fett and impearial boarding party, who kiddnap Juno and deliver her to Vader. Rebel Alliance attacks Kamino, while Starkiller confronts Vader and his army of clones. Vaders get captured, and thats whole plot.
Character levelling system was much simplified - we get points for kills, holocrons and sometimes from destruction - and using them we can increase level of our saber skills or force powers up to level 3. There is a new skill - mind trick, which makes weak enemies either fight for the player, or comitt suicide. As for me - nice.
Holocrons are to be found scattered across the maps, they come in 4 different colours - yellow will give more experience points, Red will contain saber crystalls or costumes, green will increase max HP pool, and blue will do the same with force meter.
Saber crystalls... yea, they are also much less complex if compared to TFU1 - you have only colour crystals, each colour has it own properties (to compare, in TFU1 you have 2 types of crystals - colour ones with purely cosmetic effects, and ones that gave you specified bonuses like lifesteal or so). While of course, simple, you may end up running with some ugly-colored blades :/ Okay, you can pick different one for each saber (you have two) - two ugly colours instead of one XD
QTE - as normally I have nothing against them, here they could have been done a bit better. Yeah, they still look awesome and all.  Sitll we have 4 keys that can be used in QTEs - by default space, LMB, E and Q - but now they appear at the opposite parts of the screen, which means - instead of admiring juicy finishers you look for the key you should press all over the damn screen. Good side is, QTEs are the same for every type of enemy requiring them - so all flamer robots will be finished the same way, all rocket walkers ect.
I will also mention some stupid ambiguities. I've been eagerly awaiting this game since I kickstarted it a while ago, and it's definitely got its ups and downs.
Fun game with a diverse cast and a female, person of color lead. A somewhat traditional Tactics RPG game with the card/dice twist in lieu of equipment that allows someone to really customize the characters; the dice crafting element also is very necessary.
The problem however are, as other reviews have pointed, is the inability to skip animations, making the battles so drawn out when there are a lot of enemies acting. It also lacks the ability to reload/pause the game when the enemy is acting, so if they get some good rolls or are about to rout your team, you have to wait for them to finish or kill off everyone before you can restart, making for some pretty frustrating battles. These are pretty standard for the genre, so it's baffling that they were left out in the final release. For a game that had a pretty extensive time in development (three years!) with multiple testing/alphas/betas, it's really crazy to think that these small changes were overlooked.
And to top it all off, the main gimmick of the game adds even more randomization to a genre that is already pretty RNG heavy. The game also suffers from some situations where some characters (mainly the main character) run away with levels and XP because of their kits (the main character has the ability to get extra actions, meaning that she'll soon widen the gap between her and the other party members you get) meaning that anyone who wants to keep your characters somewhat close to each other will have to spend time grinding. There also seems to be a 3 party member limited, and the game doesn't really tell you when a character will or will not be available for the next mission, meaning you can end up wasting time grinding and leveling people you won't be able to use.
There's also some weird missions where it puts you in command of stronger/higher level characters and then pulls you back in to your regular crew, which comes off as jarring rather than incentivizing.
Overall, it's a good idea poorly implemented, but for the price point and the content, it's a fairly good deal. With any changes it could definitely pass the threshold into a solid yes to recommending it, but for now it's only barely there.

The first Darkness was the first modern first-person-shooter I ever played, and I never expected it to ever get a sequel---I just didn't think there was that much of an audience for it. I'm happy there was though, because the Darkness II was a sequel that I didn't know I wanted until I played it.
Mechanically, the game is better than the first in many ways, including a much more interesting and expanded move tree, which was a pleasant surprise and features some pretty cool ways to kill. (Throwing black holes is pretty badass). The gunplay is also just as fantastic, with the ability to quad wield with your darkness tentacles....which is a Jason Stathem level of ridiculousness and badassness.
The story is a bit lackluster, although it also wasn't the best in the 1st, either. The cool parts from the first, in my opinion, was revisiting the past and seeing your ancestor in World War I. They somehow managed to shoe horn that in here too. And there are constant references to your dead girlfriend in the last game, Jennie. In fact, she is the entire center of the plot....even though she is already dead and has been dead for a couple years. Other than that, the characters actually are pretty interesting and you will come to appreciate your cockney darkling and his dark humor.
The only other complaint some may have is the length, which is around 10-15 hours depending on the difficulty chosen. (I played it on normal). On sale though, it's definitely worth looking into.

The game is much like old SRPG games with a card and dice system instead of skills and gear. If you're an old SRPG fan you most likely will enjoy this if you allow yourself to explore a different approach to the class system.
Children of Zodiarcs is a SRPG in the lines of Final Fantasy Tactics or Tactics Orge. In lieu of gear and skills, the game uses cards and dice. At first, I was disenfranchised by this choice, after about 5 hours of play I must say it is an interesting system. Currently, I prefer the classes and gear system, but I have a lot more experience with it.
Each character has a specific deck of cards that determine the skills they can use in a fight, much in kin to the class seen in related games. Each character has a different deck that can be customized, which adds an interesting layer of depth by "customize classes."
Attacking consists of you selecting a card and throwing your dice, much like in tabletop DnD. Each die augments the card used, for example, increasing damage or unlock latent powers. You are allowed to reroll two dice for each card use. The rolling system gives you a lot of control over the flow of the battle. For example, if you are low on health you can roll for a healing bonus - or if you are running out of cards, roll for card draw. The die themselves can be customized as you progress throughout the game. I found that having specialized die is more beneficial than trying to have a 'jack-of-all-trades' die - as it removes control of what you want each card to do.
The story does have me asking questions about the origins of the characters, the Zodiarcs, and the world itself. The graphics give you the false impression the world is cheerful and full of joy, but in reality, the world is very dark. It is an odd contrast that I never realized until I started reading the flavor dialogues the game offers between missions. It has peaked my interest, whether it fleshes out as it progresses remains to be seen.
In closing, I had no intention of playing the game this long. It hit the SRPG itch I have had for a few years. I will try to keep this updated as I progress throughout the game.

And that's on top of the beautiful boardgame/diorama esthetic that is perfect throughout. The levels do a great job of providing a steady but fair difficulty curve, with the later levels in each box, and even more so the final levels of the game, providing a very hearty challenge, with the goal of completing all the optional objectives being especially mind-bending at times. There are a few levels or objectives that can feel a bit like duds when compared to the vast majority of the levels in the game that are great, and the camera/controls can be a bit of a pain in some levels (even with the alternate camera angles). It is also worth noting that I played entirely with a controller, and the game controls very well with one.
All in all, Hitman GO is a puzzle game that has very simple mechanics at its core, with many layers of complexity steadily piled on throughout to keep those core mechanics feeling fun, with all that wrapped up in an awesome aesthetic. And that's exactly what I want from a great puzzle game. I'm looking forward to one day being able to buy Lara Croft GO again on Steam, as well as Deus Ex GO.

The battle mechanic and graphics are great. It's a fresh kind of multiplayer game.
But it being player to player instead of having dedicated servers severly cripples the experience. You keep getting kicked out of games over and over, and since you never finish your matches you don't get any rewards or experience. This also means it takes forever completing your orders, daily missions, for the in-game currency steel.
The orders is also very bland and boring and usually is "play this class in this mode", forcing you too play characters you don't even like, in modes you don't like.
And then there are the steel problem. If you don't want to spend more money on this buggy mess of a game for sometimes necessary equipment just so you don't have a disadvantage in some game modes, don't get this game. If you don't have a lot of free time, I'm talking hundreds of hours, you are willing to spend, don't get this game. Because if you want to be able to play all the characters in this game, and not just one or two, you will need to spend a lot of steel on them. Also the ornaments, cosmetic skins, are way too expensive for being a triple A game. Too give some insight on this, you get around 30-40 steel per match, none if you get disconnected anytime during the match. The daily missions can give you 600-1200 steel, but that's only if you have time to put down four to five hours a day playing this game. Now, an ornament can cost 1000-7000 steel, depending on how flashy/new it is. So if you wanna customize only ONE character you have to put down heaps of time.
But that doesn't affect the gameplay. What DOES affect the gameplay is gear stats. If you have enough steel to buy crates and then also upgrade your equipment you get a clear advantage in different game modes. It makes it extremely difficult to test out new characters when you get matched with others with maxed out gear stats because you have an other character with higher gear stats.
The bottom line.
Ubisoft is treating this game like if it was a free to play game, the way they are urging their playerbase to buy steel packs to play several characters efficiently, and also for customizing. Ubisoft is also not taking the criticism from it's customers well, going out and saying that they never intended you to play more than one to three characters of all the twelve that exists in the game. Not having dedicated servers makes it really hard and frustrating to even play the game sometimes. The gameplay is the most redeeming thing about this game, it feels great and viable to play as diffrent classes, it just needs som tweaking in some areas. I just wish it was another publisher than Ubisoft that made this.

This game, like most of the girls in it, gives a bad first impression, but you'll soon warm up to it.
It's a fun little story with nice artwork, but with only a few hours of play time and very little replay value (5 endings which barely branch), I'd recommend waiting until it's at least 50% off. There's just not enough to content to justify 15$.
The stand out element of this game is the gardening mini game, and combined with the dating sim parts, makes it kinda like a very striped down Harvest Moon game. The farming works well, but the money you get from it only serves as a cap for the special endings, since only thing you can buy is more seeds (32 blackberries is all you'll ever need).
The format and interface of this game is instantly familiar to any one who has played any visual novel from Winter Wolves before. Rather bare bones, with no voice over, sound effects, or special artwork other than the 4 endings, and there's not much options other than save and load, but works just as needed.
The other interesting change from other Winter Wolves games is that you actually play as a guy, Steven, and get to know a hand full of female characters. He starts off as lazy and apathetic with a wandering eye for other girls, much to his current girlfriend's frustration, but this low start is mostly just to serve the growth in his story arc.
Like Steven, the four main female characters in the game mostly start off with rather abrasive introductions. Jill, the studious student, dumps Steven in the first act for being a lazy jerk. Susana, the vehement vegan, rants at you how 'chemicals are bad'. Clara, the hyper hick, complains about how everything not 'big ciy' sucks. At least Marian, the librarian, greets you warmly and politely. Unlike Steven though, they all stay the same throughout the game and have no growth other than obtaining their goals mentioned when you first meet them.
The third interesting dynamic of this game, which would most likely net you a 'bad end' first play through,  is that to woo any of the girls, you have to spend most of your time with another girl. Each girl is interested in a certain character stat, and you raise that stat by spending time with the girl that represents the stat. This helps motivates talking to all the characters more, even the ones you might not care for, but is not really made clear in game and comes off as counter intuitive.
Lastly, for a game called “Flower Shop”, you spend very little time in the flower shop. You only ever go there to buy seeds (if you need them) or if you want to talk to Susana.

As an experience, this game is absolutely amazing.  Great, dark stroytelling, in a gorgeous post-apocalyptic environment.  I knew nothing about this game when I bought it, except that Rock Paper Shotgun had recommended it.  I was pleasantly surprised with the rich story and overall experience.  I keep saying "experience" because that is what you are getting from this "game".  The writing is great; it felt like I was guiding a well-paced foreign film that happened to last (and remain exciting) for 3-4 hours.  It was absolutely beautiful in every sense of the word; graphics, atmosphere, writing, emotion.
As a game though it was very frustrating.   It was VERY deliberate; do not expect to solve things/find things your own way as it is completely prescribed.  Minute details occasionally preclude you from moving forward which, for someone that loves puzzles and mutliple ways to approach problems, is beyond frustrating.   I'll avoid any spoilers but an event near the end of the story needed to be completed in a very specific sequence (for really no discerible reason), and when it wasn't I ended up frustratingly exploring for over an hour, finding NOTHING, before searching online.  Unfortuntately, this had a negative impact on my enjoyment of such a beautiful story.
Either way, I'm very glad I experienced 35mm and at it's price it's SO incredibly worth it.  When you have the ability to be fully immersed in a beautiful 4 hour long story for $4 CAD, it makes me wonder why I pay $20 plus to go to the movies (and I love movies!).
Great value, great story, great immersive experience.

If we try to cut long story short it will be "moderately paced puzzle platformer". However, does it tells anything about the story or presentation? To be honest puzzle-platformer part is not the strongest part of the game since objectives of some puzzles are not always easy to figure out and some puzzles feels a bit unfair in comparison with the rest which leads to quite a lot of deaths. There is no limit to how many times you can continue, though.
But I want to say it's a truly unique game and here are my reasons:
* It's a traditional Inuit legend presented in a form of a game which is something really new. I can't recall even one another game based on Inuit legends and I really do hope that there will be more. Inuits living in an extreme environment which heavily affects their way of life and folklore.
* The quality of music, art and animation both in the game and in the story intermissions really stand out. You will literally feel how developers loved the game which they made.
* There are a lot of developer comments with stories about Inuits way of life and culture directly connected to the events in the actual game. They are implemented as collectibles, so you will really want to find them all. There are not so many and most of them are easy to find, though. Chapter select screen even tells how many you collected per chapter.
The only real issue with this game is the length. Unfortunately, it's really short and when you collect and watch all the cultural insights there are almost no replay value unless you have someone to play it in a local co-op.
Is it worth to buy? I think yes, It's a masterpiece which provides the unique experience and that easily outweighs short story and a bit unfair puzzles.

Rise of Flight is easily one of, if not the best flight sim I have ever played.  It even shows in the negative comments, you don't see many negative comments about the gameplay, you see negative comments lamenting the fact that you have to pay to get more planes.  This is not misadvertizement on the publisher's end, as the game says it is free to play, not free to own every plane in it, and the description of the game lays out the three free planes you get.  Now that I've denfended the game in that respect, let's talk about the many great features RoF has to offer.  It has an incredibly extensive library of planes, and, with any kind of simulator--farm, flight, or train, youo will be paying for the extra content.  But it is more than worth it.  The DLC regularly goes on sale for 66% off which means that you can get a pack of nine planes and a whole new map for $9-10, in reference to the Channel Battles DLC, which I would reccommend getting first as it gives a huge variety of planes, many of which are featured on  multiplayer maps, such as the stellar Fokker Dr. VII and Felixstowe F2.a which is flyable on the Inspiration Island multiplayer map.  It is a flying boat with the capacity to carry two 230-ish pond bombs and is, by far, one of the most fun planes to fly in the game.  Let it be noted, however, that the feld and weapons modifications must be purchased in the "Ace Pack," which is one small gripe I have.
The graphics, sound, and physics are all absolutely wonderful--even on low settings the planes and landscape look quite good, you wouldn't expect this game to be as old as it is.  Physics can be adjusted, as can ease of piloting, which can be expected wiht any simulator.  The menu is laid out well and makes sense, and there are extensive biographies and specs for all the planes that are pretty spot-on for accuracy (and yes, I have cross referenced many of them).  You can do campaigns, careers, multiplayer, and quick battles.  Quick battles are especially fun because you can put 30 planes in the air and stage an end-all dogfight.  Before we move on, though, let's talk about multiplayer.  This is one of the most fun games to play with friends.  You have very realistic physics and even better damage models.  Crashes are, for the lack of a better word, sublime, and you will have hours of fun messing with your friends and playing back mission  logs on the built-in movie recorder.  So this game gives you a lot more opportunity than you would think for free.
I have invested in a lot of DLC and my friend has invested in none.  We still have a blast playing it together though, even if he only has the three planes.  It's a great game to play with friends and mess around with that quickly turns into a very real and exciting experience that you want to invest in.  Having all the DLC planes just gives you something else to fly, it doens't change the game that much at all.
The bottom line is this: you can tell that a lot of care and hard work went into this game by a relatively small team.  They have made the game free to play as a demo that offers you every single feature of the game except for the Channel Map and all the other planes.  You can get hours of enjoyment just flying the Albatros D V.a around in a quick game shooting at other planes (you can fly against any plane in the game in a quick match, you just can't pilot them yourself).  I know I sound like a fanboy, but I have a real passion for aviation and flight simulators, and this one is incredible.  So to see it getting bad ratings just because players can't have the 60 or so planes that the game offers for free agitates me slightly.  This game has a lot to offer, whether you want to invest in it or not.  So I encourage you to give it a try--it truly is as close to perfect I've seen a WWI flight sim get.  Happy flying :)

By far one of the best fighting games I ever played. The customization is also amazing. Being able to use image software to recolor and redesign your own gear is perfect for individualists like myself. The only problem is it is addicting. I played since 2011. Spent around $600 USD on the game and the company shut down. I'm about $400 USD maybe more in now over the past 2 years. It is good if you do not spend a dime on it. Over time there will be free events to get heroes, legendary gears, and more. If you do spend money, just buy rare heroes. They dont come by that often. People say this game is pay to win, but it is really experienced based. Experience + powerful gear + high stats most-likely will net you a win. Take away the experience and a skilled player using a new account will probably win. Objective is mainly to learn what all the heroes do and how to counter them. Also to set up a strategy when going into battle. I really like this game obviously, but I wish I never heard of Lost Saga to be honest. I have a life outside of Lost Saga and this game sometimes interferes with it. It is everything I would want in a game, but it is so addicting that I feel trapped playing for hours, despite the new alert that goes across the screen every hour of playtime. I feel like this game needs a stamina system or something to prevent prolonged play. I deleted and quit the game on several occasions, but I always find myself sucked back in. There is something mind-controlling or supernatural about it. At 19, I was bored and searching for a fighting game to kill time. I am 24 and if I would have known that I would feel trapped playing Lost Saga, I would have never downloaded it. Honestly a good game, but not worth it in the long run. Do I recommend it? No Will I play it? Yes IGN: LilHazy

Quick summary: 35MM is deeply flawed on numerous levels but I can't bring myself to hate it. Only buy this game if you are fully prepared to look past numerous clunky game mechanics/very vague guidence and enjoy the atmosphere of the game.
-
When I bought this game, I had just finished Firewatch. A slow narative driven journey through an empty countryside where you rarely interact with others (It's a fantastic game by the way). With the journey I had just been on in mind, 35MM looked like a perfect way to continue that first person 'walking-simulator' experience and for the first half an hour it was.
The bleak atmosphere for the game and scant story falls in line with other russian simulators such as S.T.A.L.K.E.R (Did you know that is based off a book, by the way?) We join our russian prontagionist on a journey to somewhere for reasons vaguely explained. Which works just fine for me - so I settled in to enjoy the game.
Unfortunately from then on in the problems started to become apparent. Subtitles in badly broken english that keep changing position and are unreadble on light backgrounds, reams of untranslated dialogue some of which is cartoonishly reminisent of 80's kung fu flicks where they would talk for ages only for the subtitles to say a few short words.
The animations are stiff presets and if you trigged events out of order actors will fly through you to their new position.
None of the games controls were explained leaving you to try keys until things happened, if you died when there was text on the screen it stayed there forever until you restarted the game and even that wasn't enough as sometimes it would launch with the language set to russian for no reason. Don't even get me started on how bad the guns are, lack of hit animation or incredibly non-specific instructions that leave you googling russian guide to figure out just where the ♥♥♥♥ a password is.
I could go on but at this point it would just be whinging. The game is still under constructions and marked as such for a very good reason. I probably t shouldn't even be on steam at this point given how unfinished it is. But the steam approval process is a mysterious one and I like gambing on cheap games so here we are
In the end, despite all the negative things I have to say about the game I can't entirely dislike it, I can't reccomend it either though. The heavy forboding atmosphere and very russian take on the story is nice. It's quite different and even refreshing to have a game where you have to read subtitles for the dialogue and although simple visually it's passable.
Is that enough to outweigh all the negatives? For me, no. I would suggets waiting until it has been heavily patched and trying then. Or trying one of the stalker series which fills the same gap.
I look forward to seeing how this game is updated in the future and wish the dev and his team all the best.
PS I can give you a list of the bugs I found if you'd like.

First "Sniper Elite" titled game from Rebellion was disgustingly bad. It was pretentious, sure, and it created some vile fan community... But it was awful all over. Yet, it was upgraded, and it evolved into something better! "Sniper Elite" V2 isn't horrendous game, like V1. Now it's just silly. Sure, there is some "unique" charm, made by combination of intrusive usage of sniper rifles, with kinda tricky "almost realistic" ballistic part, and slow-mo "x-ray bullet cam" effect. Which is literally provokes people to make shot after shot, again and again, and see another dummy's brain or testicles splattered.
But, again, all over it's just another silly game about World War II made by people who know nothing about it and don't give a shoot about it. And made for people alike, with carefully cultivated by the gaming industry bad taste for lame on-rail scripted shooters.
What were the worst points in the Sniper V1? By gameplay terms, in the first place, the shooting was bad. All the weaponry in hands of player besides the main rifle, was nerfed up to no use. V2 saved that feature, as one of its own personality markings, but still, other guns now are slightly more useful. To the point when I'm able to do some room cleaning without long and clumsy scoped boomstick. Not good enough, yeah, but way better than it was.
Next, the AI. Now, the player and his enemies are learned to take covers, and even walk around corners from different sides! Sure, they're still dummies, blindly running forward on your position, even on the hardest difficulty setting. Eagle-eyed snipers, who can peek you from great distance in one place, but will neglect your presence in close-combat range, are also there. The "stealth" part is also spoiled from the start to the end of the game - you'll never need that, anyway. Except for two optional achievements, in the DLCs "St.Pierre" and "Neudorf Outpost". But, but, all in all, AI is surely much more complicated than in the V1, and has some fairplay tricks to make you feel oppressed, at least in some moments. Respawning-stormtroopers-on-your-back cliche is still widely in use, sure. But now you can make some traps on your way, which seems kinda useful in some dire situations where you're supposed to hold the point for some time against hordes of enemies. That part was even kinda hilarious. But not all that useful, alas!
The other bad part of Sniper V1 were level maps. There was about 5 of them for 28 "missions"... And they were poorly made, for the most part. Except maybe, occasionally, there was a place to perform a shot for more than 300 meters range. In the Sniper V2, there are 10 maps for 11 game missions (+some dlc's, each is 1 new map for 1 new mission, usually). Each map in the V2 is usually covered in an half of an hour... Yeah, the maps are That Short. They're looking not bad overall, but it's all the same - narrow corridor, with the ability to walk around some house from one side or another - at most. So, the marketing passages about "Sniper's choice" and "using the Environment"  are about the "hide behind chest-high wall and squeeze the trigger as you please". Since the maps are quite short, I doubt that many players will ever achieve range above 350-400 meters (except the very last shot of the game, which is not skill-based, by all means).
Finally, the story and player's motivation. In the first game, the player was an American agent in '45 Berlin, dressed as german paramilitary, and killing soviet soldiers before they dig up some really dirty nazi secrets. In the second game, the scenario is slightly more evasive. Now, the Russians are not the targets just because they are Russians and Commies, and whatever. No, there they're planning to shoot the V2 rocket armed with some nerve gas from Berlin straight to London (3 times of its actual range) and pretend it was Nazies! And actual Nazies who made the rockets and the gas - are helping the Soviets with the attack! To make Germany's reparations even higher, supposedly. Yeah, I guess people who've bought CoD Black Ops will buy any kind of crud, coming as a "history-based scenario". Why not the Soviets bombing their Allies? Because that's what evil tyrants like Stalin always do, right? Or not? Oh, who cares! Just pop more heads and see their brains exploded, that's what this game about!
Finally, before I set my mark, I'll say a few words about multiplayer there. It is always a room full of campers, isn't that great? Well, I know some good shooters where some maps are made for this kind of self-entertainment... But to make all the multiplayer around campers is surely extreme way of thinking. Even the fact that ballistic there, with bullet derivation and all that, in reality looks quite arcade and dumbed down... Well, like I said from the beginning, the game is silly and stupid. And better than the first one. And aimed to some blood-thirsty 13-years-old maniacs who're not caring about whom to shoot, or why.
Mark is 6/10. And downvote, for it's all still not fun enough.

Best flight simulator available, imho. Period.
This is not simply a game but a complex, detailed, researched and well developed simulator which recreates not only the shape, sound, speed and behavior of some of the most wild machines to ever fly on the skies of Europe, but even their feeling. If you haven't the required hardware (joystick, a good video card and a decent PC) and the required mindset (will and patience to try, fail, retry, read, learn, hardly shoot and easily get shot), this is not the game for you. Some people complain the fact that you have to buy planes and extras, something I find utterly ridiculous considering than even smartphone games nowadays give you "buy to play" contents, and here we are talking about well researched, designed and developed planes fo a century ago, each one reproduced with a lot of care and detail.
Surely it's not a game of simple "click and shoot", but when you are on an open cockpit with wind and engine sound in your ears, surrounded by a beautiful landscape, clouds and light effects, looking from above a group of unaware foes below you, ready to dive on them to empty your machine guns on their wood and canvas machine, you get one of the most sincere reproduction of a dogfight a computer game has ever given to a player.

I’m a fan of action RPGs. I’ve poured hundreds upon hundreds of hours into the likes of the Diabo, Torchlight and Titan Quest franchises to name just three. I like too many games across too many genres to be able to claim that I’m a master of any one genre, I’m closer to a jack of all trades, but if there’s one that I could almost make that claim for it would be action RPGs. Therefore you can imagine my curiosity and my interest when I got the opportunity to cover Soulcraft for Steamified. Of course, it had registered as a game that I put on my wishlist when it came out back in June of last year but with so many big budget even bigger time investment titles released around that time (e.g. The Witcher 3) I simply hadn’t gotten to it until now.
If truth is completely told then I would have to tell you that SoulCraft is not a great game. It may not even be a very good game. But, and this a pretty big but, I legitimately enjoyed my time with it. This is really one of those guilty pleasure games for me. I had no right to enjoy this game as much as I actually did. I very rarely feel this way about games. There are a litany of issues that  plague this game but at the end of the time that I allocated towards it I was still having fun with it. Sometimes that’s all you can possibly ask for from a game.
There were a few things that I kept playing for. The first was that although rather simplistic I found the actual fighting in the levels to be enjoyable. Battles – entire levels rather than just individual fights –  are rather short and quick affairs that provide sharp, short bursts of gameplay. You could easily play this game in 10-15 minute spans if you so chose to. Given that the game is a mobile port that is most likely the way that it is supposed to be played. It’s not until you sit down for lengthier sessions that all of the faults in the game become so apparent (although they’re there and sometimes undeniably so). The second thing that I really enjoyed was the fact that there are so many unlockables. You rarely go between fights without the ability of upgrading a piece of armor, a weapon, a spell/skill or what have you. It can make the game downright addictive and classic ‘one more turn, let’s see what I got this time’ type gameplay.
The biggest problem with the game is that it is a mobile port. The PC game still carries with it the mobile strategy of it being a free to play game with microtransactions driving the game’s income. Once again not enough is done to eliminate this system before the developer slapped a buy to play price on it and called it a day. For once I’d really appreciate seeing a gaming developer call a spade a spade and if they were going to put their mobile freemium game onto Steam to do the same. Put it up for free and enable microtransactions to those who want to advance further or faster into the game. I’m not ashamed to buy some in game credit if two conditions are met. First, that the money I’m spending does aide those that developed the title. I know your game costs money to make and even if you put it up for free you need to have some way of making a profit from it so if I am going to be putting money into your pocket to either maintain the game or so that you can develop new titles then that’s fantastic. Secondly, I’d like to know that what I’m buying in game is actually going to be worth it. It will help me and give me the sense that I’ve helped myself as much as I’ve helped you.  If you need an example of games that do this well on Steam look no further than a couple of the clicker games but to narrow it down to one Adventure Capitalist. Some players wouldn’t have been able to complete the Christmas special had they not purchased in game tokens. They got the reward that they wanted and the developer, Hyper Hippo Games, profited from a well thought out campaign. A smart move for the developer and their addicted paying customer.
The next problem is that the unlockables are rather pointless. There are so many of them and they come so quickly that you’re often swapping them in and out more quickly than the game can keep up. I didn’t find myself using in game gold (which I’m sure of the two currencies is the one that is the most expensive in regards to microtransactions on the mobile platform) but rather the ‘skulls’ currency which too comes quick and fast especially when you purchase an in game animal who collects the in game drops before they vanish. This both decreased the difficulty of the game to the point of making it trivial at some points but also makes me not worry about micro transactions. Having not played the mobile version I wonder if this is a similar case and if it is then I worry that the game isn’t making the developer enough.
Combat too can feel a little unfair at times. Instant stuns, unavoidable damage and at higher levels instant-death plague the game without you ever having anything to do about it. This might be a consequence of the game being a mobile port – encouraging people to spend money – or it could just be bad code. Either way it’s more than a little frustrating and equally disappointing. You need to give your players a chance. That is what makes games such as Dark Souls so popular. As difficult as they are the player knows that if they learn how to play each encounter the right way that they should eventually win it.
SoulCraft is an absolute guilty pleasure in that it’s not a great game but I love returning to it. It’s also a game that is flawed but could serve as an example to freemium mobile developers to learn from. Either keep your game free to play with microtransactions which other Steam games do or develop the PC version in such a way that the mobile pay wall doesn’t impact negatively against your PC players. Players will support you if you do it the right way.

Ever since FFTA2, possibly the best tactical game ever to be created, I have sought out every tactical game that looked worthwhile. Fire Emblem is great, as is XCOM. Both represent masterpieces of the genre.
This game is a solid addition to that genre. From a pure aesthetic standpoint, the art, colors, sound, environments, and overlay is great. I absolutely love the feeling. The art seemed inspired by Transistor to a degree, possibly one of my all time favorite games as well, but was overall enjoyably original. Story is great too.
But for the point everyone would look at reviews for: is this game enjoyable from a tactical standpoint, not just art and styling?
Yeah. 7.1/10. I'm pretty picky. But this was worth the $16-$17 I paid. From a tactical game standpoint:
Pros:
-The custom dice builds allow you to attempt to focus a character in a specific way, such as attempt to take many moves in sequence or always nail your abilities with stars, or just glass cannon it with shards.
-Positioning is important, though no height bonuses are given
-Unique decks for each character are the modification of traditional "jobs" so to speak...while I love jobs, this is cool too
-Customization of said decks allows for further character specification
-Character progression exists, though in smaller degree than I would like.
-The AI seems reasonable
-Damage fluctuates, though there is never chance to miss. While different, I don't mind. It provides slightly more tactical element to gameplay already involving dice.
Cons:
-I won't lie, I'm only a couple hours in but I worry about unique character progression. I love building characters to fit team roles (something that XCOM, FFTA2, & Fire Emblem excel at), but my characters just all seem to be damage, damage, and more damage...and they have surprising few drawbacks. All can self heal, area/multi attack, or use range.
-I completely ignore the curse cards initially because...well actions are expensive, and why waste a turn reducing someone's damage from 12 to 9 when you have 20 hp when you could just use an attack and kill them?
-Played a bit, but am not struck with the thought of "this is the next FE" or anything. It's good, but I'm not going to stay up all night to play through. Hopefully I will get more invested in the game.
-Are there only 4 characters?
What I would love to see in the future:
-Gear, even 1 or 2 trinket/weapon/armor equip slots. Anything to statboost to help specialize
-Maybe custom card crafting? Have blank abilities that can be created with resources and applied to anyone?
-Maybe create a card tree for each kid where they can fuse two cards of a type from their deck to create a higher power, new card with better abilities?
-maybe make a rare dice set that applies various effects, like pierce, vampiric, or hold, but the other three side are big detriments? it would make some dice more risk and reward.
Overall though, as I write this late at night, I like it. I'll play it through. It's an enjoyable, new system that utilizes deckbuilding and dice.

TL:DR VERSION FIRST THEN LONG VERSION AFTERWARDS
GOOD:
-GRAPHICS BEAUTIFUL
-GAMEPLAY FUN
-CONTROLS PRETTY DARN GOOD ON MOUSE AND KEYBOARD (obvious advantage using mouse/keyboard over controller more on that in the bad section)
-The How to Play Section with videos and tips on how to learn each hero is very very good and informative highly recommend you check this out before deciding which character you want to play in multiplayer learn the combo's learn the moves and practice against a lvl 2 bot most players in multiplayer are slightly better than a lvl 2 bot worse than a lvl 3 bot.
-Ai is impressive if you put it on the hardest difficulty (AKA lvl 3 bot)
-Single player mode teach's the player A LOT Play it for at least 30 minutes then move onto to multiplayer if you cannot stomach the bad story. (tho its still fun)
BAD:
-Controller controls are fun at first then you realize you are severly limiting yourself because its very uncomfortable to use the X button or the B button (xbox 360 controller) while using the right analog stick infact u will almost definitely lose more games if u do not buy a controller with additional buttons to reprogram similar to an xbox elite controller. For this reason mouse keyboard works shockingly well in this game and gives u a great advantage by being able to remap ur keys to better accomodate your hands.
-Connections problems  (PERSONALLY i have very little connections problems now that I have followed the guide to forwarding my ports) Keep in mind I play 90% duel / brawl mode which is 1v1 or 2v2
-Single Player mode is fun and a great introduction to how the game is played if you play it on normal difficulty you will learn quite enough to play it on multiplayer if u play it on hard it will help u a lot l8r for multiplayer. The story is kinda dumb but its a fighting game at its core you're not here for the single player its a multiplayer game with a brief story that helps introduce you the player to the combat system and the various ui things. (this could be bad or good so good job helping players learn bad story so-so voice acting.)
I love the combat. The game is geared towards a player that seeks a skill based game more than an RNG based game. It's fairly addictive to me I love the rush you get when you out play your opponent. Overall I play the game for Duel 1v1 / 2v2 mode I dont really venture into the bigger game modes due to the fact that I find the game more entertaining in the smaller fights plus I dont particularly like the gear stats and how they effect the bigger game modes. So if you are looking for something with solid combat solid controls and a great game experience I would give this a solid 7/10 Stars. Not worth $60 Wait until its about $39-49 then its worth it imo. Though I don't regret paying $60 to be honest since I do enjoy it so much but I love this niche type game.
-I deducted 1 star for the obvious need for additional game modes. (game modes without gear scores)
-I deducted 1 star for the grind to get gear is pretty rough i have about 120 hours at the time of this review and I'm almost finished gearing my 1st main character i need to max 1 more piece so im at like lvl 103 out of a possible lvl 108 for gear score. It feels as though they made this grind gnarly on purpose so you would pay for the microtransactions to buy more gear for other characters i get it that's the idea behind games with microtransactions but i definitely feel like this games grind to unlock pieces is harder than most games that allow you to grind the game to unlock the content for free ill give you a perfect example I play a lot of hearthstone and that game has quite a grind to it as well and i feel like this game's grind is either on par or harder.
-the last star deducted is simply no game I have played has ever been perfect so no one gets a 10/10 so right off the bat u minus 1 star! .
