Nether, in all of it's rights, is an excellent game. It keeps you on your toes, and whilst doing that, blesses you with decent graphics and gameplay. The first thing that hits you upon entering the world of Nether is its setting. Though it is not the first time such a mood was set by other games that focus on such a possible time period, Nether gets it right. Many games like to go post-apocalypse, providing an interesting backdrop for the players...But not quite like this. Usually you can say to yourself, its not the creatures that pose the biggest threat, it is other players....not the case here. It’s a moody, tension-filled setting, providing players much in the way of strong atmosphere, if done right and is allowed to serve its purpose. Unfortunately, not that many games have actually done the setting justice. Game’s like STALKER and Metro most come to mind when thinking of just what titles did just that. As does Nether, thankfully, and this game does a lot to remind players of those aforementioned titles, STALKER in particular.
That being said, it has its issues, mainly hardline connection problems, and worst of all, trying to get a password reset. All in all, I think with improvement, it could be bigger than it is right now. I highly recommend it.

Mu Cartographer is a landscape exploration game where you scroll across the screen to find unique places and color skins.It took me about 3 hours to learn how to play but the process was actually very simple. Saying that this game may feel very relaxing or very frustrating. This is one of those games where learning the game is the game, so you should play it blindly to get the full experience.
It is pretty clear to me that it lacks a proper tutorial do to the subtext of the game(you are lost). Well technically it teaches you basic controls with blue images but they are not very helpfull. I made a guide for playing the game which you should only you as the last option. It was fun for me to figure out how to play but I can certainly understand that some people hate feeling confused with goals and controls.
This is not just a pretty sandbox although I still spend like 10 hours just playing with shapes. The game has a story that is told through text and visuals which should take around 4-5 hours to complete. Yes, there is an actual goal in the game and it is not just pressing buttons. Apparently, it is based on real explorer and I think some of the locations are inspired by it. The ending was a little disappointing for me and I think the developer could have done a lot more with it. My Cartographer is more of artwork than a video game but if you like abstract and atmosphere it is worth trying.
This game really looks a lot more complicated than it actually is. I thought that when you in the right area you need to adjust all Knobs until you get the exact combination to find structures (which would be cool). Well it would be near impossible to do that manually because of how precise it is. Instead, all the game ask of you is to follow steps that more or less do it for you.
So this whole Elevation thing has little to do with the actual gameplay. You following blue images but not really using landscape in a meaningful way .
I like the ambient feel of the game . It does feel unique  I will give it that. Playing with the environment can create some pretty combinations of colors so there is some aesthetic value . There are few enjoyable soundtracks but I really wish you could find more music choices around the map .

Mu Cartographer is a different kind of experience that will appeal to people who enjoy ambiance, abstract and feeling of discovery. I enjoyed it but I can see people getting frustrated because the game does not provide a tutorial on purpose.Unfortunately, this game is about following few steps that don't really require you to look at environment yourself. My biggest problem with the game is just the fact that developer could have done a lot more with it and there should have been a way to get a more satisfying conclusion.

went through the first 3 or 4 missions. (V2 Rocket production place was the last one I completed). It’s from 2012 so it’s a little dated but still really looks great. Actually, to some degree, I’d say it looks better than my next random roll, Shadow Warrior that came out a year and a half later (I played a little of that last night). There are some issues that I don’t particularly care for about getting through spaces and climbing things. Like there was one mission where there was a pretty large gap between a wall and a big rock that wouldn’t let me through even though it looked like I should be able to. Forced me to take a more direct approach through an enemy area when I’d prefer sneaking in somewhere else. Sigh. I couldn’t climb the rock either.
Sometimes I think the guards see me easier than they should, and other times where they don’t see me and they probably should. Standing vs. sneaking (where I crouch down ever so slightly) makes a really dramatic difference, even standing still. Kind of silly. So the stealth mechanics aren’t the best. The shooting mechanics, at least sniping, is obviously pretty good. The hip shot guns (pistol and submachine gun) are not very good. You can aim them, but they are horribly inaccurate and you can’t aim down sight to improve it. I’m hoping later I can get a scoped silent pistol or something, because you have to be within like 6 ft to get a headshot with that thing otherwise.
Enemy AI is decent. They search for you a lot longer than most shooter games. I think you are supposed to be able to sneak through areas better than it really works though. If you shoot without a covering sound, you’re SOL. But sometimes those covering sounds are very localized. I was walking through this tunnel and you could map the location precisely where some machinery would move and make noise to cover your shot. Move back one step and it would no longer move. Irritating, especially for such long range gunplay. You can also move bodies but there is never really a great place to stash them, so I never bother.
Level design is hit and miss. There are lots of cubby holes for you to hide in, but at the expense of making it difficult to always tell which way to go. One time I was searching through this broken down building because I thought I had to go through it to get to the other side for the level. Nope, never needed to enter it at all.
So on that note, you are supposed to move around a lot to find new sniping nests, and it shows where enemy last saw you with this ghost (Freaked me out the first time I saw it because it never actually explains it in game, I just deduced it). But it doesn’t work as well as I think it should. It’s almost worthless to move sometimes because it seems like they find you WAY easier than they ought to. I’m playing on normal difficulty too, so it’s not like they should have enhanced abilities.
Pretty cool thing you can do is incapacitate an enemy to draw out another guy. I haven’t figured out how to do it consistently yet though. I tried shooting out a guy’s leg once and he was hurt but just kept on moving. Maybe it has to be a really precise shot to the knee, idk.
Overall, great game. More challenging than I expected and it’s fun. The x-ray and kill cams are pretty neat, but I might end up reducing the frequency that it shows, as it’s pretty often.

This is a great sniping game, but it does not come without flaws. The gameplay can become repetetive and the third person mode breaks the game. You can be behind a corner and use the crosshair to shoot an enemy sniper on top of a distant building. Mind you that you are completely behind a wall and your gun is sticking through the wall. Another pet-peeve of mine is that 90% of the sniping is under 200 meters. You have to pull out your submachine gun or pistol several times a firefight because you will go around a corner in a street and there will be 10 enemies staring right at you with their submachine guns. However, the biggest mistake the game developers made was a mission where it is in close-quarters for the entire mission except for the very beginning and end. Lastly, I would love if the Nazis or Russians could point me to a training session where every single soldier in their militaries go to learn how to pin-point where a person is after they fire a single shot. It would be very usefull against enemy snipers. However, even with all the parts that are bad about this game, I still loved every second of it when I did not think that I had cleared out a block and six enemy snipers decided to screw me over. (Play this game in the hardest difficulty if you want an actuall sniping game because if you hold your breath when you do not have it on the hardest difficulty, it shows exactly where the bullet will drop. What is the point of a realistic sniping game if you somehow obtain divine knowledge on the exact ballistics of your each and every shot.)

TLDR: A pretty game with a neat concept, ruined by a combination of camera, control, and second-character-AI issues. I suspect most issues go away if you're playing co-op rather than single player.
---
Just a heads up: I've noticed some co-op players mentioning unresponsive controls. If you're attempting co-op play on a keyboard, please look up keyboard ghosting. Many keyboards can't support enough simultaneous key-presses for keyboard-only multiplayer to be viable.]
----
The biggest problem is that both characters need to be in roughly the same spot for certain things to happen, and that the second character AI's "leash" is too long to make that reliable. I've had many instances where I brought the girl to the next part of the level only to get stuck wondering what I'm supposed to do. Then in messing aronud, I find out the fox needed to take 3 steps forward for the next platform to appear.
It gets more complicated when the characters have to take separate paths, since the other one will just sit still until you move them yourself. For example, at one point the girl has to swing across two ghostly ropes over a spike pit, while the fox takes a tunnel above. The problem here is that the second rope for the girl only appears when the fox is at the half-way point in his path, and in singleplayer the fox will just sit at the start of his path. Since this is the first rope-swing in the game, I wound up making several suicidal jumps into the spike pit, since nothing hinted at the second rope even existing.
The camera tends to add to this type of problem, since it's one of those that will lag behind your character when running. Most of the time, you can only see a quarter-screen ahead of you, so it's hard to know whether you're going to jump into a pit or a ledge.
As for controls, it's really just a matter of animations sticking too much. Like if you want to stop running to use the bolo, you have to wait until the two "slowing down" steps finish after letting go of your direction keys, before it'll let you attack. Or how you have to actually turn around first, as a separate action, before jumping or attacking in the opposite direction.

I'm afraid I'm going to have to not recommend this game, which is such as shame after the first one was such a blast.  Whilst fun in parts, everything about this screams "making a sequel for the sake of cashing in on the success of the first".  The first Force Unleashed game is highly recommended in my eyes.  It had a good story, fitting within the cannon.  But this, whilst starting promising, with the whole storyline around cloning which fits well in the Star Wars universe, then fails to go anywhere, and they somehow manage to make the entirety of the game about Starkiller (if you are indeed the original one, and not a clone, though this is never cleared up) hunting down his love Juno, the pilot from the first game.  Oh, and of course foiling Vader in the process.  No real story arc or character development, with the only real other character in the game being general Kota from the first game.  Juno is the stereotypical damsel in distress, and there are a few of the iconic characters from the universe that are crowbarred in for the most unnecessary cameos (including one of the bad guys which seems to imply we were going to face-off against them at some point, but they were promptly dropped and never mentioned again.  Possibly this is potential for another sequel?  Though maybe the developers got a bit of sense as they went along as when the game ends it doesn't really seem to point that way).
Okay, so the story is rubbish, how is the gameplay?  Again, this starts by showing promise.  Combat seems fluid, intuitive, varied, challenging and fun, at first glance.  Then you realise you're up against the same array of enemies constantly, with the "tougher" ones being felled by tiresome quick-time events that you have to do nearly every single time and is indeed the quickest way to bring them down.  This gets tiring, especially later only, when you face increasing numbers of them.  I say "tougher" in quotes because as long as you know where the dash key is (there's no stamina, you can dash to your hearts content all day long) you can zip round the battlefield and tear the larger enemies apart with ease.  You're as likely to be felled by them as if you're blindsided by a paltry few troopers.  Speaking of which, if you're quick on the lighting key and pointing vaguely in their general direction you can fell entire legions of the troopers within mere seconds.  And once you've figured out the other enemies weaknesses they go down just as quick.  Unfortunately, you level up to the point you're an absolute killing machine very quickly, so much so that it makes being a badass seem boring.  And as far as I could tell they only introduced 1 new move which was used in the tutorial and then I barely used it again ever.  Basically force lightning and the occasional force repulse is all you need.  Playing on hard was not a challenge and you can breeze through this game in merely half a dozen hours.  This is shockingly brief, even with the ridiculously overlong and padded end boss sequence which wasn't difficult in the slightest, and I wouldn't be an expert, reflexes-wired-to-the-max kinda player by any stretch of the imagination.  To top off the slog, near the end of the battle, a new element is added to the fray without warning which can kill you if you aren't quick and then you have to go back to very near the start of their health bar again!  Such lazy game design by adding a few zeros to a bosses health.  Basically every other boss during the game was more fun than this, even the annoying mechanical spider.  I chose the "good" ending at the end and honestly I've never regretted it so much in my life as it was so hideously saccharine and unexplainable.
So, in a nutshell, cheap cashin, which ticks just enough boxes for it to be deemed sellable.  Avoid.

This game is the proof that there can come good things from the Mobile Game scene... see... i never thought i would write that sentence, but here i have to.
Originally released on the app store and for androids, then converted to a well done PC version that has no technical flaws as far as i can see. Brought to Steam Greenlight and voted by the community to be sold on steam. And the community was very right in this one.

You also can mess it up. This game has the possibility of making and breaking the biosystems that you manage and build. Too many games have the possibility of failing completly eradicated, and thats not a good thing.
The graphical style... alot of pepole seem to dislike it. For me, it simply works. And its unique and gives the game its own charme. Also, because of this it will be remembered, even in some years from now. I prefer that than cutting edge graphics with zero gameplay.
Now go and buy this gem of a game and play it, its worth your time and money!

OK, let me start by saying that the game itself is good. The online interaction is usually bad. I'll give you a simply overview (based obviously on my opinion) below.
Pros:  Excellent combat mechanics. It really is the selling point of the game.

The maps are beautiful and even creative at times.

Each faction has its own take on 4 different classes, each being very unique.

The 3 gamemodes it offers are good fun, but are the only 3 things to do.

The customization for your characters is pretty detailed, including the different parts of each weapon.
It is quite fun to play with friends and coordinate attacks.
Cons: The online play is painfully unstable. Almost constantly refreshing and I've been disconnected fairly often.
The "story" is a complete throwaway. After playing it I feel no more informed as to whats going on as I did when I watched the trailer. I only finished it for the unlocks.
While the progression has a rewarding feel at first, it quickly feels like a grind to unlock the "cool stuff" for each character. Yes, all twelve characters have their own individual level.

Not enough maps or gamemodes. It feels repetitive very quickly, at least it did for me. I usually only play dominion(capture 3 points and kill the bad guys until you win) because it has the most going on and doesn't bore me after 2 or 3 games. I know it's a game about war, but I would enjoy this so much more if there were more objective based gamemodes.
In summary, I like the game. I still play it fairly often with my wife, but I would never suggest you pay full price for this. Wait for a sale, and enjoy this good, but not totally finished game.

This is a fantastic game.  I found it very addictive.  This game consists of short little puzzles challenging you to get Agent 47 through levels filled with guards, briefcases to collect, and targets to "kill".  The game plays out like a board game with chess-like pieces.  New pieces (both enemy and support for Agent 47) and new mechanics are slowly introduced over the game's missions.
This is probably the first mobile game I've really played.  I do have a smart phone and a tablet, but I have virtually never use those for gaming.  I was reluctant to try this game out because of it's mobile roots, but watching a Twitch stream changed my mind.  It seemed like a lot of fun.  I was not disappointed.  I'm glad it came to PC.
The game is played with the mouse only, swiping Agent 47 to the direction you want him to go.  I would definitely have appreciated a single click option.  There's no keyboard support but I don't think that's a big deal for a game like this.
I do think it's unfortunate that a level editor of some sort wasn't created for this release (as suggested by other reviewers).  It would have been pretty awesome if the community could have built more levels.  The game is a bit short.  It took me about 6 hrs to complete (totally worth the $6 and some change I paid).  I was good enough that I want more.

I vividly remember playing Hitman: Absolution a few years ago and feeling like the guy from this Youtube clip:
(you'll have to copy and paste the url without the $ at the start because embedded Youtube videos tend to freeze the Steam client). Ok, it wasn't that bad. But while both Hitman: Absolution and Hitman GO are not true Hitman games... the latter's better for it. Unlike Hitman: Absolution, Hitman GO is a solid title that confidently knows what it wants to be and because of this it can stand strong on its own two feet.
Hitman GO is very much a puzzle game at its core. Each map resembles a typical game board filled with pieces. The player controls the Agent 47 piece and the ultimate objective is to reach the marked destination point (or assassination target on some rare levels) using whatever's placed on the map to your advantage (distraction objects, disguises and so on). The player always starts first and has to make their move. Afterwards, every other piece on the board gets to make their move and then it's back to the player to make their move again. It might sound simple but this turn-based game does get challenging once the player passes the early levels and new enemies start getting introduced.
Speaking of levels, there's 15 in each chapter (or game box) and 4 main chapters. A further 2 bonus chapters are supposedly inspired by levels "Curtains Down" and "St. Petersburg Stakeout" which come from games Hitman: Blood Money and Hitman 2: Silent Assassin respectively, and there's yet another bonus chapter called "Airport". So that all adds up to 91 levels (since the Hitman-inspired chapters only have 8 levels each). Truth be told I've only played a little past the first chapter but I'm really enjoying what I have played so far. Each level has a set of 3 objectives, and 2 of them are always different, so it's likely the player will be revisiting each level more than once. On top of that, most players will want to see if they can beat each level again in less moves so the replayability's there.
The game doesn't look fancy graphically but that's completely fine because it does its job. It looks just fine on my PC and I'm especially fond of the 3d sets. There's no story but I didn't expect there to be one. The game has a lovely theme that plays on the main menu and level selection screen - it's calm, soft and appropriate for a thinking game such as this one. There's not much music for the levels themselves (mostly ambient or background noise) but Ave Maria did play on one of the levels and I couldn't help but stop and listen. For those of you who are not familiar with the song, it was the main theme for Hitman: Blood Money. Fantastic choice.
As for the port itself: it's nothing extraordinary but performance and everything the player would expect out of a game like this is perfectly satisfactory. I could do with a little more options though (since the Options menu is currently very limited and I know some might not like that). Apart from that, the Steam achievements seem to be bugged at the moment (seeing as though I and several people on the game's Community Hub haven't got any achievements whatsoever) and other than the minor facelift this game's received as well as the removal of in-app purchases, there's not much difference between the mobile version and this "Definitive Edition".
Overall this is one of those rare mobile games that I can recommend and thus I strongly suggest you consider purchasing. By supporting a good spin-off game like Hitman GO, you'll be sending a message to Square Enix that games like this are what we expect of them and not anything else. I only hope the newest Hitman game will end up being this good. For all of this, I'm giving Hitman GO a 8/10.

FOR HONOR REVIEW
By Matthew Cooper (total play time before review 38hrs)
First Impressions
Well it’s unfortunate to say that my experience within the first ten minutes was not up to par, this has nothing to do with the game, but to do with U-play, when purchasing the game, Ubisoft (or whoever sends out the activation codes or self-activated the game for me) did not activate the game for me, so I had to spend around £5.31 ($6.50) on the phone to Ubisoft UK hotlines, to my prevail they didn’t answer, so I had to go back on to the Ubisoft website to get the support email and send them an email about what was happening, I thought my day was ruined, I had spent 36 hours of non-stop downloading (my broadband is really bad – 4.13 mbs down) but luckily, someone on the steam support page on the “For Honor page” had a similar problem and gave me a solution for it,
Okay so now for gameplay, from the get go this game is absolutely beautiful to look at and play, the incredible details on the characters and the buildings also the environment, just wow, kind of breath-taking, once loaded into the game you are greeted by a 4 to 5 minute cut scene of a war with a beautifully read paragraph in a females voice, really gives you the feel of war and the impending hell and doom you are about to go through, playing through the tutorial took a total of nine minutes and thirty three seconds and surprisingly it taught me all I needed to know about the game, how to attack, how to predict attacks how to dodge and how to use your mouse and keys properly so all in all you knew what you were doing from the get-go
(first impressions 8/10)
Initial Gameplay
Although the game is beautiful, For Honor kind of loses its touch, half way through the Viking missions I became bored of doing the same things, running around, cutting people in half, defeat a boss and repeat, yes the story does interest me I feel like it could have been done a little better and a tad more interesting, it doesn’t mean I didn’t enjoy the game, but it made it hard to play through, now, I know what you may be thinking, “Devv I really liked the story”, well so did I but after playing the campaign for 23 hours over the space of a week I feel like the story drones on, it’s not well acted, and there’s even a time where the voice and sound go out of sync with the game. (Initial gameplay 6/10)
Technical Difficulties
After mission four in the first chapter I started noticing subtle voice glitches where the voice would go out of sync with the game, I have quite a beastly pc and the game was running on 140-190 frames per seconds at all times so I couldn’t put it down to that, so I assume it’s a glitch with-in the game, it’s nothing big and it only happened quite a few times, but at the time when I was recording it, it ruined the video and I had to re shoot, luckily I was only about three mins into the video, after that I had another set of difficulties such as my player totally disappearing through the ground and then re appearing a couple of seconds later with about eighty health missing and when you are playing on realistic/hard difficulty that is a massive flaw, oh and let’s not forget about the massive loading times whether it be online or even getting into the campaign I averaged a time of one minute and thirty-four seconds just to get into the campaign, I don’t think GTA V has a loading time of that long, recently the servers just haven’t even been working, I tried to play the game again yesterday and it just wouldn’t load into the main menu, it was just stuck on the loading screen, I do put this down to Ubisoft servers and not the game itself, that is all for
Technical Difficulties (2/10)
Playing Online
Well now this is a whole different story, when I first started playing the game online there was many players, many games I wouldn’t have to wait more than a minute and that was great, but once you get into the game, it was just a cluster f**k off connection interruptions and three v ones sometimes four v ones, honestly Ubisoft, surely you have enough money to buy or rent some permeant servers for “For Honor” and I’m not saying peer to peer connection doesn’t work, it does if everyone has like Twitch Streamer internet  of one hundred megabytes down you’ll have no problem but when its regular people with internet like mine with four megabytes up and down it doesn’t work, nowwwww there has been a staggering  %50 player loss there is rarely a chance to play online, it takes me a long time to get into a game and when I do its just a  cesspool of cancer and d*ckheads, so the online experience isn’t really there anymore
(7/10)
Overall 8.3/10
Sorry about this being a short review guys, I do all in all really enjoy this game and I will continue to play it, this is just my honest review and that’s what my job is, so sorry if you don’t agree with this, if you have any opinions of your own let me know on twitter @CSDevv

In short: The narrative is better than the gameplay, and the gameplay is better than the horror, but all three of those things are expertly crafted and incredibly well done.
Here's the deal: SOMA tells a story, first an foremost. There is horror, yes. There is exploration and survival, yes. But those exist only to serve the story that SOMA tells. This game won't terrify you, it won't keep you hiding under the covers, so if you're looking for something that's strictly about fear, this isn't for you.
If, however, you're looking for something that balances exciting areas to explore, intriguing mystery, expert storytelling, and a touch of horror, this is something worth buying, at full price or not. Each of these aspects takes dominance at one point or another, some sections are strictly about fear, others reveal large amounts of lore, others will just have you wandering around following your gut and hoping you get where you need to. The trick is that each of these sections is expertly done by the people at Frictional Games, I personally loved it, but if games built on exploration, story, and fear rather than action, heroism, or addrenaline aren't your thing, take one last look at SOMA, smile, and move on to another purchase.

Okay, this game is pretty cool.  I really had no idea what to expect.  In a way it reminds me of Mirrormoon, but with a slightly lower frustration threshold.  You are doing things, learning the interface and progressing a story.  The story itself is okay, but a little vague.  The generated environments are pretty nice looking and the different functions are fun.  It takes quite a while to understand exactly what you are doing and when you think you have a handle on it, it changes.
The music is great, the graphics are nice for what they are, the gameplay is pretty good with one issue (which I'll get to soon).  This game is a good purchase and will give you a nice evening of play.
The problems with it are as follows:  Gameplay gets repetitive after the second half, it doesn't change the gameplay up anymore and you kind of know what to expect, the ending (if I actually hit the end) is really vague, it isn't clear if you have finished the game or not, so at this point I'm not even positive I finished.  Since I got three story pieces from three characters I assume I am done.  In a way I would also say a lot of people would think the lack of any kind of explanation on how the game works is a negative, but I understand it now that I've played it through.  It's necessary and adds a nice challenge.
Fun game, grab it if you like challenging your mind and exploring.

Rock of Ages 2:
~~~~~~~~~~~~
Why did you decide to go to war against Zeus? Wasn’t obvious that you would be defeated?! Look at you now, Mr Atlas - the leader of the Titans. You are Zeus’ little pet! How does it feel to carry the world on your shoulders while the almighty God enjoys his newest passion, painting? Oh no, by the name of Zeus, you dropped the world. . . what are you waiting for? Get it back . . . Dear oh dear, that’s not the world, it’s a boulder . . . not a clever fellow, are you Atlas? Just when you think it can’t be worse, you fall down to earth with your boulder! Welcome to Rock of Ages 2.
Rock of Ages 2 is a combination of a parkour/racing and tower defence game where you have to defeat legendary characters (as well as some quirky monsters) throughout ages, by squashing them with a boulder.
Before you manage to squash your opponents, you must smash the gates of his/her castle to pieces. The trick is, Mr Atlas, they going to try to flatten you ahead of being pressed like a leaf themselves. It will take both of you several stones before destroying the doors of each castle. Make sure your boulder reaches its full speed and is not damaged in order to maximise the power when it slams into the doors. You will be given a set of coins at the start of each of your runs to spend on your defences. These defences will inflict damage on your opponent’s rocks and if you are really clever, Mr Atlas (it might happen), you could even destroy his/her boulder before it reaches the castle gate. Make sure to choose carefully which units to use before entering the battle. Bear in mind, some are inexpensive but don’t inflict too much damage to your opponent’s boulders.  While other units seem to be over-priced, they will deliver greater damage to their boulders. However, you’ll only be able to place a certain number of each unit on the parkour. For example, you can only place ten catapults within the map. If any have been destroyed by your opponent’s runs, you will be able to put them back into the parkour (if you have enough coins) but you won’t be able to place them in their previous positions. There are plenty of fun units; some, like the cow field unit, are designed to slow down your rival boulder, and others (like the big canon) will cause massive damage, but will reload slowly. The catapult or ballista units will reload quickly, but they don’t cause much damage to the rock. The other ways to cause or be damaged is by sticking to the parkour or falling off the map.

I nearly forgot one more thing about the boulders . . . at the start of the campaign, you only have one at your disposal, but as soon as you beat an enemy, you’ll unlock his/her boulder. Not all rocks are the same; some will have better acceleration, be stronger and/or bigger, or cause more damage than others.  Some will also have special abilities, which can help you in different ways.  Make sure to explore the map and don’t neglect to pick up new units on your way to your next enemy castle. I really like the hilarious cut-scenes before you play against the new enemy. I was in stiches more than once - MARVELOUS!
The other good thing is that you can play two versus two online, which is a lot of fun.
Graphically the game is great and runs like a charm; I personally did not experience any crashes. However, the game does seem to take a while to launch. The controls are working fine whether you play with a gamepad or the keyboard.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Hilarious cut-scenes
-	Campaign and online mode
-	Boulder customization
-	Fun, fast and addictive
-	Achievements and Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	I would like to see more adversaries in the campaign mode.it will give this game better replay-ability.
Hilarious cut-scenes, extremely fun and fast gameplay. Rock of Ages 2. . . Just Rock!

This will be a genuine review, not some angst-fuelled♥♥♥♥♥♥post about "devs being abusive". Those need to stop. Anyway...
For those who don't know, The Isle is a survival game where you play as a dinosaur, finding food, water and hunting other players in order to survive and progress to the next tier. On joining a server, players start off as the lowest tier dinosaur for their chosen faction (carnivores or herbivores); a Velociraptor for carnivores or an Orodromeus or Psittacosaurus for herbivores. Successfully progressing through all the tiers could lead to being a mighty T. rex or a fiesty Triceratops. Players also have the ability to build nests as raise other players as their young.
With that little introduction out of the way, lets get on with the reviewing. The environments in which you prowl and graze are beautifully designed with plenty of foliage for hiding or stalking, a variation of edible plants for herbivores and numerous lakes, rivers and marshland. You may even find yourself somewhat lost in a forest in which gigantic Sauropods browse on the treetops.
The dinosaurs are also well modelled (unless you have an unhealthy obsession with feathers, then you may not think so) with a superb variety of skins to choose from, whether you're looking for the best camouflage or something that'll stand out amoung the rest of your kind. The animations, for the most part, are also well done. However, at the moment one or two of them are looking a bit off and could do with a little tinkering, but it's nothing to kick up a fuss about.
Game mechanics such as bleeding and broken bones, aimed interrupt your survival if you get in a fight or make a silly mistake by misjudging the length of a drop, work well; it can feel very uncertain when your bleeding level is high, your health is gradually being wittled down and you're unsure whether you'll make it or not. Broken legs also add a sense of trepidation as when you move you'll have a visible limping animation, signaling to predators that you're vulnerable and a potential meal. Nesting, which is a lovely, cute idea in theory, is one of those things that could also use a bit of tweaking; don't get me wrong, baby dinosaurs are adorable but the rate in which eggs are produced and babies hatched quickly leads to an overpopulation of higher tier dinosaurs, both herbivores and carnivores. At present, the Tyrannosaurus is the only species to have a juvenile model (which is so cute btw), I believe the others are still a work in progress which I look forward to seeing. A recently added
mechanic, scent, has much potential and could be a game changer. At the moment, using scent allows you to follow recent scent trails left behind by other dinosaurs, making tracking your prey that little bit easier.
There are many servers to play on, each with different style of gameplay to suit different people, such as realism or with rules limiting what a player is allowed to do, such as a common rule against "Killing on sight" or "killing for sport". Other servers are rule-free where players are free to play as they wish. And as they say, each to their own. Whatever floats or boat, etc.
The development team are quite interactive with their audience, particularly through The Isle's discord server, which you should consider joining to keep up to date with discussions and announcements. Occassionally you'll find a developer streaming some of their work which is nice and intruiging to see. Don't be too afraid to ask questions (like I was), baring in mind you keep the level of 'stupid' to a minimum. Use common sense. They also actively encourage users to help test recent changes/updates in dev branch in order to get the best results possible before releasing it to public.
It holds great things for us. I enjoy seeing the game grow into the marvelous thing it has the potential to be, and look forward to what the future has in store.
But in the meantime, The Isle is already an enjoyable game to play. If you're into dinosaurs, survival and nature, I'd highly recommend this to you.

TL;DR: Bottom line, it wasn't as good as the first one and felt a little rushed.
So let me just start by saying that I am writing this review as a huge Star Wars fan and even as someone who loves this universe and it's lore, this game was not impressive.
Pros:
1. It has more graphics settings options than the first game, which basically only had one option: high detail or not.
2. You use two lightsabers instead of one. I was a marauder in SWTOR so this really appealed to me.
3. Improved lightsaber violence. I've played a few games as a Jedi/Sith but this is the first where you actually dismember and decapitate your enemies when you hit them with your lightsaber. Nice detail there.
Cons:
1. Short. I beat the game in only about 6 hours and I played the first game for almost three times as long. I have not yet nor do I really plan to try the challenges.
2. It was choppy. I certainly meet the recommended requirements but I still had issues with screen tearing and just low levels of detail. I don't think it looked as good as the screen shots.
3. The story wasn't all that interesting. He's a clone, wants to be with Juno and fights Vader. The end. I'm glad I never read the novelization for this. Based on the final cut scene there might have been a TFU3, but that'll never happen.
4. The attacks weren't as detailed as the first game. I didn't get to buy various attacks like the first game.
5. Dagobah was a huge ripoff. What was the point of it?
6. WAY too much action. Seriously the game was non-stop storm trooper slaughter; you never got a break from it. Always moving forward and killing. It was like a bad action movie. No puzzles or side quests or explorable worlds.
At the end of the day, I don't recommend you buy it and play it. If you got it as part of the Star Wars bundle like I did, feel free to give it a shot but don't expect a quality game.

I want to like this game- but I just can't. There are so many small-to-medium flaws in this game that completely overshadow the obvious hard work the developers put in. I'll start off with the pros:
Pros:
- The artwork is beautiful: music, animations, visuals are all amazing.
- The concept of the game is great: I really like the idea of following a Native storyline, and the plot is fun/cute enough that it's not boring.
Cons:
- The controls are clunky, slow, and sometimes unresponsive. It makes even basic movements in the game (jumping, aming the Bola) really hard, and you tend to die a lot.
- There are bugs a-plenty. I'm pretty sure the fox isn't supposed to be able to travel through some walls. Grabbing onto platforms, walking around, everything is just a little less precise, and it's hard to control your character.
- The AI is not great: in single player mode, your partner character (controlled by AI) will sometimes die for no reason, sending you to your previous checkpoint at no fault of your own.
- Gameplay logic isn't consistent: in the first zone, if you fall into the water, you die. Next zone- you need to swim. Hmmm...
Visually this game is very pleasing, and it looks like the developers put a lot of work into it. I just don't think it's worth the price (even with the 40% discount). Otherwise, if the developers could iron out some of the bugs, it would absolutely be worth it.

Visually a great game, but besides the initial fun of setting up the shot and seeing the bullet cam the fun kind of drops off. It gets repetitive and in some cases makes the game hard to play as a sniper. You get in to close quarter fights that you can only really survive by pulling out the pistol or machine gun to complete. And it amazes me that every single enemy in the area instantly knows exactly where you are once you fire a shot. In an urban setting with buildings, streets and walls, the sounds of gunfire would echo and be pretty difficult to pinpoint.
Straight up: this is not a tactical game about sniping, and definitely not realistic. If you want a very arcade-like shooter then maybe go for it based on its one big draw: slow-mo bullet cam. I have played the game for hours just for this feature, but once it wears off you are left with flawed and rough game mechanics and plot. Plot is bad, but not critically so, I've seen worse. The gameplay features firefights mainly at under 200m with very unrealistic features (such as shooting through corners due to bullet tracing form the crosshair rather than the gun, and using 3rd person to peek and scout the area). The actual situations it places you in as a sniper are also poorly chosen, as most snipers excel in situations of patience, strategy and long-range targets. Forget all of that; it is very linear and confined, and you have will be just as good firing quick snapshots between sprints as you would if you crawled to a good spot, steadied your heartbeat, controlled your breathing and took a good shot. Additionally you just shrug off bullets call of duty style.

The Isle... Wow. I'll start with this; The Isle is the greatest Dinosaur-Releated game that I have ever had the pleasure of participating in. I simply cannot express my love for this game with words.
-There is a large selection of amazing Dinosaurs, from the smallest, such as Velociraptor, to the largest, like the famed Tyrannosaurus Rex, the swift Giganotosaurus, or the bizzare but unique Spinosaurus. Triceratops, Stegosaurus, Utahraptor, and even the massive Puertasaurus are just a few of the many great animals that you can play as. There are many more to come, as well. Alongside the dinosaurs we already know and love, the Developers have created their own Dinosaurs. Mutated beasts that would surely send chills down your spine.
The Hyperendocrin family: Monsterous in size, as well as appetite, these beasts are the first that we have had the pleasure of viewing. With their heavily armour scales, and their violent attitude, they are some of the most dangerous and terrifying creatures in the game.
Tissoplastic: Stealth is their game. Not much is know yet of these silent assassins, as the Developers have not revealed much. However, we do know this; These creatures will rarely be seen by our eyes, and when they are... it will already be too late.
Neurotonic: These guys are the real brains of the bunch. With the ability to communicate with all races, they could unite us... or destroy us.
-The game is an open world survival, so the world is yours to freely explore and live in. The enviroments are gorgeous, and there is much to admire, from the expansive plains to the great redwoods. There is alot more to be seen in the future, as well.
-There are many who say that the Developers aren't the nicest, and they could be right. However, even if the Developers seem rude, is it really right to disrespect them? They work on this game tirelessly, doing their very best to turn the game into what they hope it can be. They work day and night to ensure that the next update doesn't bring any problems or bugs, and if it does, they fix it. As I said before, the game's creators may be somewhat irritable toward us, but personally, I respect them for how hard they've worked on this game. and I must thank them for allowing us to help it grow.
At the end of this review, I must say this; With Dinosaurs, Monsters, Man, and an amazing open world, The Isle is going to change the way we all look at Dinosaur Games... forever.

The Darkness II is a surprisingly good first-person shooter albeit a bit too basic for my tastes. It's a very linear game with the same old experience points and upgrade system which seems to be how most first-person shooters are doing it nowadays, but at least there are a couple of interesting ideas to save it from monotony.
The Darkness is based on the comics of the same name. I've unfortunately never read them so I'm not informed enough to make comparisons between it and the video game adaption. I also can't point out any improvements it has made over its predecessor as I don't have any experience with the first game. I'll be treating The Darkness II as its own entity.
So it's lucky that beginners are offered an optional recap of the first game. No need to play catch-up, to play the game. The Darkness II stars an Italian-American don of the Franchetti crime family, Jackie Estacado. Good ole' Jackie has had some problems ever since his girlfriend, Jenny Romano, died in the last game. On top of that, he wields the Darkness, an entity with a mind of its own that has given him supernatural powers. So everything seems to be going well as he has finally gotten the Darkness under control, but then a secret society randomly shows up to try and take this power away from him. As luck would have it, it turns out Jenny is alive somehow and you'll need The Darkness to save her. AND If that wasn't enough, the main character also suffers from hallucinations which may or may not be real meaning that Jackie was a mental patient this whole time and that all of the first game and some sequences in the second game never even happened to begin with.
So it's basically your average comic book plot. It's only a bit disjointed as there are certain elements in the story that really don't go anywhere. Like the fact that you're the head of a crime family, but don't do any mafia-related activities and the gang doesn't really seem to be very helpful except for telling you where to go next. Or the fact that you keep having these visions when time is of the utmost importance and really shouldn't be wasted staring at a wall like say during a chase. There are lot of little things like that, but to its credit the game does wrap up very neatly with every loose end connected.... Well mostly...
I only have two major gripes with the story. One is that the villain is weak. A secret society doesn't sound very interesting to begin with, but their leader fails to impress. You'd think looking like Quasimodo's deformed even uglier cousin would at least make for an intriguing backstory or a good motive, but very little comes of it. Even though he's portrayed as the main villain, he also comes off more as an inconvenience than anything else because his timing really couldn't be worse when it comes to deciding when to steal the Darkness. Secondly, It ends on a cliffhanger and we still haven't seen or heard anything of The Darkness III. The Darkness II came out in 2012 so you can imagine how infuriating it was to see the very last cutscene in the game knowing that they still haven't followed up on it. Sure, there are still the comics, but I don't have easy access to these because I'm a European. Game developers, can you please not end your games like this unless a sequel is guaranteed. Signed, me.
I probably wouldn't have cared a lot about the story if it weren't for the characters. Some of them are very played out with its stereotypical mob characters with the same Italian accents you swear you've heard in ten other games, but it's surprisingly well-acted. Jackie sounds great and you really get the feeling that he really cares about Jennie. In fact, a lot of the characters just sound very human, very convincing if you will. There's a lot of quiet time where characters can develop and reflect on certain events making even the basic grunts a lot more three-dimensional characters than what you would see in most games.
So like I said the before the game is very basic. You get a very limited amount of guns that you could count on one hand and you've got the standard upgrade system in which you spend your experience points. You can sadly only hold three guns at the time. Two one handed guns you can dual-wield and one two-handed gun like a shotgun or a machine gun. What distinguishes The Darkness II from other first-person shooter is obviously the Darkness itself. For one thing, you control an (adorable?), little, British imp called the Darkling. He's practically invincible, able to revive himself an infinite amount of time and will aid you in battle by distracting mooks by hitting them in their stupid faces and then proceeding to urinate on their burning corpses. With later upgrades, you can even throw him at your enemies and causing him to self-destruct after launch. You also have access to two giant tentactles with mouths that come out of your back. These have a lot of useful abilities making the game a bit more interesting. You can swipe them at your enemies, you can grab certain objects and throw them or use them as your shield or you can perform unique execution animations to gain ammo, health, a shield and meter for a special moves (like fusing your gun with Darkness). These animations can sometimes be annoying because they can be very long and occur in quick successions as you'll need all the health and ammo you can get especially in harder difficulties. This can potentially drag out the game.
There's also an interesting dynamic going on related to the light. You see, the Darkness is weak against it. If you find yourself subjected to something that can even be vaguely construed as a light source (like say a street light, a cars headlight, Agent 47's bald head or anything that J.J. Abrahams can somehow turn into a lens flare) then you'll be weakened by it. The tentacles and Darkling will disappear, you can't regenerate health and you can even be blinded by it. In the first part of the game, it comes down to mostly being affected by lightbulbs, but later on enemies will actually use the light against you by either carrying gigantic flash lights or just using traps involving the light. I'm also not sure if this was intentional, but sometimes enemies holding light sources will hide behind enemies with shields making them very hard to fight against as you'll need the Darkness to remove said shield. It's a very interesting mechanic to see and I hope it gets fleshed out in further... oh....
My only real complaint with the game is that it's too easy. I recommend going after the hard difficulty as normal makes the game a bit too boring. I also recommend eventually transitioning to the hardest difficulty "Don". I managed to beat Don in my first playthrough, but it's probably not the best setting for your first time.
There's also a seperate cooperative campaign called Vendetta which explains a couple of things the main campaign left out. It allows you to play as four different hitmen with unique, but very limited capabilities especially compared to Jackie. It's a bit more boring as the enemies are limited to "guys who shoot at you" and the light is also underused. I suppose it's not too bad when you play it with a buddy, but if not it's a waste of time. The characters on the other hand are very consistent with the main story in the sense that they are once again really good. One of my personal favourites being the Scottish, Football-loving, English-hating Jimmy Wilson voiced by David Shaughnessy. It also has a very diverse cast of characters if you're into that sort of thing.
So that's all I've got for the Darkness II. It's a surprisingly good game and would have had a lot of potential for future installments if it didn't disappear from everyones radar. If you like simple roller-coaster first-person shooters then I recommend you check this one out. It's a very fun with a really good story and interesting mechanics.

This game is meant to be played for the storyline and cultural knowledge. It gives you a glance into a culture you are most likely not familiar with (I wasn't either), namely an Alaskan Native people, called the Iñupiat.
As you play through this game, you find yourself listening to a storyteller speaking in their native language, telling you a story about a terrible blizzard. You set out to explore its origin, accompanied by an arctic fox, as the protagonist of this intruiging story, as it is being told.
On the way you will be confronted with a series of challenges, in a world that is stunningly portrayed and supported by beautiful music.
And one more thing in particular that makes this game so fantastic to play (if you have interest in such things), are the videoclips you unlock as you progress. It's like watching a Discovery Channel documentary, where the commercial breaks are replaced by well-crafted platformer puzzles you have to solve!
For me the only downside was how short this game was, because it takes ~3 hours to 100% this game, and it doesn't have a high replayability after that. But it's definitely worth the experience if the above interests you!

This is not a bad game at all and I'd recommend it at where it currently stands.
That being said, there are a few easy fixes that can be put in place, that would make the game a far better experience.
-Suggestions-
#1 - Some people don't want to be the counselors/Jason. Far too often I'm stuck being the counselors, when I really just want to play Jason. Sometimes it is the opposite. Selecting Jason as your spawn preference doesn't really have much of an effect on who you get. Most people put Jason as their preference as default anyways, so it's mostly a roll of the dice. Don't force people to play a certain way. Let them choose.
#2 Mid-game quitters. They need to be punished. If someone leaves a match mid-game, give them an abandonment penalty. Each time they leave within a certain timeframe, the penalty increases. It's frustrating when you are a counselor, and half your team leaves 5 minutes into the game. You know at that point you are screwed.
#3 Find a better balance for Jason. I love playing Jason, but he is OP as hell. Granted, he IS a supernatural killer, and he is really powerful in the movies. I don't mean to completely nerf him, just make some small adjustments. Maybe reduce the amount of traps he has, or the distance he can shift by a little. Playing against 8 counselors should feel competitive, and currently it isnt. If I am playing Jason and I camp/trap the 3 locations (cars/boat/phone), I'll never lose. It shouldn't be that way.
I am looking forward to the future DLCs, and I hope it improves the experience a little bit. I think the 7/10 rating it has here on Steam is an accurate one. It's worth playing, but it's just barely above average. Making some of the changes I listed would improve that score a bit more.

By Matthew Cooper (total play time before review 38hrs)
First Impressions
Well it’s unfortunate to say that my experience within the first ten minutes was not up to par, this has nothing to do with the game, but to do with U-play, when purchasing the game, Ubisoft (or whoever sends out the activation codes or self-activated the game for me) did not activate the game for me, so I had to spend around £5.31 ($6.50) on the phone to Ubisoft UK hotlines, to my prevail they didn’t answer, so I had to go back on to the Ubisoft website to get the support email and send them an email about what was happening, I thought my day was ruined, I had spent 36 hours of non-stop downloading (my broadband is really bad – 4.13 mbs down) but luckily, someone on the steam support page on the “For Honor page” had a similar problem and gave me a solution for it,
Okay so now for gameplay, from the get go this game is absolutely beautiful to look at and play, the incredible details on the characters and the buildings also the environment, just wow, kind of breath-taking, once loaded into the game you are greeted by a 4 to 5 minute cut scene of a war with a beautifully read paragraph in a females voice, really gives you the feel of war and the impending hell and doom you are about to go through, playing through the tutorial took a total of nine minutes and thirty three seconds and surprisingly it taught me all I needed to know about the game, how to attack, how to predict attacks how to dodge and how to use your mouse and keys properly so all in all you knew what you were doing from the get-go
(first impressions 8/10)
Initial Gameplay
Although the game is beautiful, For Honor kind of loses its touch, half way through the Viking missions I became bored of doing the same things, running around, cutting people in half, defeat a boss and repeat, yes the story does interest me I feel like it could have been done a little better and a tad more interesting, it doesn’t mean I didn’t enjoy the game, but it made it hard to play through, now, I know what you may be thinking, “Devv I really liked the story”, well so did I but after playing the campaign for 23 hours over the space of a week I feel like the story drones on, it’s not well acted, and there’s even a time where the voice and sound go out of sync with the game. (Initial gameplay 6/10)
Technical Difficulties
After mission four in the first chapter I started noticing subtle voice glitches where the voice would go out of sync with the game, I have quite a beastly pc and the game was running on 140-190 frames per seconds at all times so I couldn’t put it down to that, so I assume it’s a glitch with-in the game, it’s nothing big and it only happened quite a few times, but at the time when I was recording it, it ruined the video and I had to re shoot, luckily I was only about three mins into the video, after that I had another set of difficulties such as my player totally disappearing through the ground and then re appearing a couple of seconds later with about eighty health missing and when you are playing on realistic/hard difficulty that is a massive flaw, oh and let’s not forget about the massive loading times whether it be online or even getting into the campaign I averaged a time of one minute and thirty-four seconds just to get into the campaign, I don’t think GTA V has a loading time of that long, recently the servers just haven’t even been working, I tried to play the game again yesterday and it just wouldn’t load into the main menu, it was just stuck on the loading screen, I do put this down to Ubisoft servers and not the game itself, that is all for
Technical Difficulties (2/10)
Playing Online
Well now this is a whole different story, when I first started playing the game online there was many players, many games I wouldn’t have to wait more than a minute and that was great, but once you get into the game, it was just a cluster f**k off connection interruptions and three v ones sometimes four v ones, honestly Ubisoft, surely you have enough money to buy or rent some permeant servers for “For Honor” and I’m not saying peer to peer connection doesn’t work, it does if everyone has like Twitch Streamer internet  of one hundred megabytes down you’ll have no problem but when its regular people with internet like mine with four megabytes up and down it doesn’t work, nowwwww there has been a staggering  %50 player loss there is rarely a chance to play online, it takes me a long time to get into a game and when I do its just a  cesspool of cancer and d*ckheads, so the online experience isn’t really there anymore
(7/10)
Overall 8.3/10
Sorry about this being a short review guys, I do all in all really enjoy this game and I will continue to play it, this is just my honest review and that’s what my job is, so sorry if you don’t agree with this, if you have any opinions of your own let me know on twitter @CSDevv

Hitman GO beautifully encapsulates the Hitman experience all whilst switching the genre to a turn-based strategy game. Previously on mobile, with fantastic art style, ambient music and absolutely lovely environments inspired by physical board games and dioramas that look even better in higher resolutions, GO is still a game I adore.
It uses all classic Hitman gameplay mechanics, such as disguises, timing your movement, learning enemy pathings, hiding in plain sight (here with help of a plant), sniper rifles and of course, 47's trusted Silverballers and mixes them up to create an enthralling little title that's both easy to get the hang of and difficult to master. Hey, it's just like the regular Hitman games!
GO starts easy and slowly introduces more gameplay mechanics to the mix, ramping up the difficulty. The game is never too easy or too hard and even though I finished it multiple times on my Android device, I still have trouble with some challenges.
Unfortunatelly, the only problem I had with this game is still present in this version - the challenges are uninspired, usually consisting of picking up the briefcase or finishing the board in a set amount of turns. In most cases, those challenges also cancel each other out (in most cases, you cannot waste turns on the briefcase when you're trying to finish the level fast) therefore, for hitting that 100%, you will have to finish the levels multiple times.
The boards are never as long for it to become a hassle though and coming up with different strategies for different challenges starts feeling desirable as the game piles up its mechanics.
I never found it frustrating or cheap, the difficulty curve is perfect and I would totally recommend this game for everybody. Not just Hitman fans, but also puzzle game enthusiasts.

Review Score: -7.75/10- As of Nov. 21, 2014. 'Fun n' quick to play, Replayability is up there, Challenging Modes and More'
Summary: This game is a diamond in the rough. To rebuttle all the negative reviews on the game - This is not a Zombie game, where the enemies are super slow and predictable in movement. This game is absolutely not easy to pick up and play when it comes to combat. Imagine if you were in real life, and some how the world got infected, and zombies can teleport.. Would you go guns blazing against these teleporting enemies who are based completely on sound? No.
Once you understand the Paragraph above, you'll basically know how to play this game properly.
I'd like to include an additional semi-paragraph; I watch people who play this game, go guns blazing, or decide to punch a Nether in the face (Teleporting zombie) At level 1, and die a needless and helpless death while I watch from afar and walk over and take all their stuff. What I'm saying is this, most of these players are expecting a really stealthy game; Where the bar has been set by - Infestation (The game), DayZ, or something else of the sort. This is not the same game. And when players like this tend to die, they rage and complain all over world chat; Without further ado let's get to the scoreboard.
Pros:
- Crafting system is extremely rewarding IMO.
- True to the idea "Bosses are impossible"
- Game is amazingly addicting - Easy to forget time.
- Backpacks are more realistic than many other games.
- Game is extremely challenging; From players to NPCs.
- Territory take-overs provide bonuses- tribe/clan control.
- Safezones are not safe, they can be invaded.
- Forced to stock supplies for new lifes after death.
- Dying does not remove your global stash.
- Guns are realistic enough where if you held your gun down, prepare to miss everything and everyone. Guns are all unique and powerful in their own aspects. However...
Cons:
- If you die, you lose EVERYTHING (Except account level).
- There is a low variety of guns unfortunately.
- The crafting system doesn't have any true "Entry level"
- Crafting system lacks variety as well.
- Crafting system should have split categories (more UI friendly)
- Voice chat/conversations are extremely laggy.
- Game sometimes lag spikes to doom, but luckily nethers are mostly sound based, so if you start lagging, just lay down/prone. However, in heavily populated servers, you can die for this aspect.
- Has an Arena mode, which is absolutely fun, it's like a Deathmatch of Survival. Regardless of all the Reviews on the Arena being junk, I think it's cool - And it provides items to your Real account if you do well/top 3 categories, or final survivor).
Ending Conclusion; The game is amazingly unique, and good to play. Not a favorite, but my most fave'd game for category in True Survivor games, with First Person(Shooter or melee). While, I have to say, it's not impossible to melee Nethers of all kinds... It's just a lot more difficult and requires some experience before doing - Especially before doing at level 1 with only a kitchen knife.
To add - This game has decent amount of replayability, from getting ATVs off a territory, to scavanging for high gears, such as a completely silent and long range semi-automatic sniper rifle. To finding the best backpacks, to attaining more gear for future life(Living after a death). To trying to attain territory, etc. However, I can see because of the current content, that you can end up feeling like a grind - And replayability is not Virtually Unlimited.
The game has a low variety of gears, and the game has a low variety of End-Game content; But because of death, you might repeat it all over again, thus recycling, but can feel as a bore. If the game reduced the amount of death penalty, included new gaming content; Perhaps dungeons/raids, or the production of houses/creation of Guild/Tribe Castles, or something of the sort, the game would become a lot more wanted.
-V.

This is like a simultaneous step up and step down from its predecessor.
Hexen II retains its predecessor's base aesthetic, you have four weapons, a basic manaless weapon, one that uses blue mana, one that uses green mana, and one that uses both. Alongside this you have an inventory system that retains some of its predecessor's items such as the Icon of the Defender and the Mystic Urn. The game also continues with having a hub world that you can go through, revisit, and unlock more of.  This is pretty much where the similarity ends.
While not a bad game in its own right, its method of progression is less intuitive than Hexen: Beyond Heretic. Where H:BH had levers and puzzle pieces you needed to find, there was always a cohesive identifiable pattern. If you were lost, it was likely you were in the wrong section. In Hexen II, it's less obvious where you need to go. In the first hub level, Blackmarsh, the way you progress is to find a list of unrelated items, such as the Bones of Loric, the Amulet of Hunger, as well as several frustratingly difficult to find keys, all so you can find some sand, melt it into glass, and them grind it into a lens so you can somehow kill an otherwise unkillable golem, and that's only if you manage to find your way through the confusing and poorly designed levels. There is no unified 'theme' to the items, no specific puzzle you need to overcome, just a literal laundry list of actions and items to stumble upon while bumping against walls hoping to find a slightly stuck out switch or invisible wall.
The enemies you encounter get progressively stronger, but even though there is a leveling system, your character does not get stronger. The weakest enemy still takes the same amount of hits throughout the game, while the tougher non-boss enemies become bullet-sponges.
The game also can have the occasional game-breaking bug that prevents you from progressing. For me, the worst was at the very end, where I fought Eidolon, killed him, and destroyed the Chaos Orb, only to have the message 'Frame 79 Not Valid' appear and the end-game text not appear.
It is not necessarily a bad game by itself, but as a sequel to H:BH, it is a definite step down, and proof that better graphics (for its time) and better engine (for its time) do not equate to a better game overall.

I remember playing this as a kid and not knowing what in the hell to do.  I got to the first foretress, maybe got inside the castle a couple times, and that was about it...Now that I'm older, I realize why that is.
The games worlds consist of a (literally) laundry list of chores to do in order to complete the objective.  Every single thing you accomplish is meant to chain together with some other cryptic item you need to grab, key you need to find, or enemy you have to kill in order to move on to the next world where it all starts again.  This is a problem.  While the core of the gameplay is enjoyable, each class having unique weapons with fun enemies scattered throughout, you wonder why those chose THIS as their modus operandi of creating purpose in the worlds.
In the original Hexen, you had to essentially find switches and levers to open new sections of the hub so you could find and unlock the boss.  Was it annoying?  Sure.  But one thing that's different is that it didn't feel arbitrary, and when you found that key or switch, it felt like you'd made progress, unlocking more of the world to explore.  In Hexen 2, there's twice as much back-tracking, the worlds are less interesting and visually inspiring.  You had murky, fog-ridden swamps, craggy ice fortresses, and castles made of steel and iron.  In Hexen 2, you have generic mountain valley, stereotypical aztec ruins, egyptian ruins, and Rome...Or Greece...It seems to mix the two together.
They could've done so much more with Hexen 2, but ended up squandering it under bizarre design choices that alienated players with the mystifying level lay outs, and obscure puzzles.

When I started playing the game, I loved it, and I actually disagreed with the negative reviews here.Pretty much till about half way playing through the game it went like a blast. The graphics was not how I would expect of, especially when I saw animals and some of the npcs being animated, but I was giving this game a chance, since this was one of the first ever story/post apocalyptic game I have played (most of the time I play things like terraria or don't starve) and that the graphics does not matter if the actual story itself was gripping enough. Talking about that, the story itself felt rather gripping at the time, but had no real plot, and overall I was worrying more about the scenes that would scare me to death because of the unknown. But when I come back to think of it, it did not have anything to interest me, its not the sort of story that would give you so much emotion and give you something to remember about. It gives you puzzles that are hard to solve, and most of the time you are walking. Most of this may not seem like a bad thing, but a proper game should be trying to grip the player. After about half way through the story, the game seemed to tip itself upside down. I spent this half of the game listening to creepy sounds as I would crazily run around, trying to find out the puzzle. Yes, its atmospheric, but it got to the point that it was uncomfortable. It took ages for you to actually get back to the real story and there was no proper guideline as to what to do. I'm fine with a game with really hard puzzles but when it gives you no pointers and then you have to put up with a story which is not interesting, a game that mostly makes you hear creepy sounds rather than solve the puzzle, its just not how it should work. I am currently so close to the end yet I cannot find any solution at all. At some points of the game I had to use walkthroughs to actually solve the puzzles because I was too focused on the fact of how scary it was. Although to some that is fun a) it spoiled the game and b) this game, along with all its other traits, made most of it seem like the game was just trying to creep you out rather than a proper story as to why you should experience this in the first place. It reminds me (remotely) of fnaf, where its just having scary things to 'compensate' for the weak story. The story is like the backbone to a game yet its not there!
The conclusion:
The way it scared you was brilliant, but it had no proper story and like I said before, it would just compensate this by adding creepy scense. I'd love to finish the game, but it's overall not convincing enough to go through these poorly made scenes. If it had improvement to the story and such, maybe I would change my mind, but It would probably be better if the price was lower, for it just doesnt have the traits you would want to pay for in this sort of game.

Sniper Elite V2 is a third person shooter released in 2012. There used to be a lot of low budget third person shooters, but it became somewhat of a a niche genre since then. Sniper Elite V2 does a decent job at filling the void.
This game has a kill cam that shows your bullet in slow-motion. If its bothering you, you can turn it down a bit, but you can't turn it off. Also, you earn points for killing soldiers. Sadly, I couldn't disable them although I don't want them on my screen the whole time.
++ there is a coop mode
+ gunplay works
+ it looks great
+ loud noises cover up your shoots
+ you can customize your difficulty settings
-- There are advertisements in the menu. Some of them you can't turn off.
- close combat is hit or miss on third person view
- not possible to save manually
- the enemies are speaking, but they are constantly repeating the same lines all over again.
- you can't turn off the kill cam nor the point system
- MPs are too weak and practically useless
- everytime you use your scope you hear your heartbeat, which is loud and annoying. you can't turn it off either.
I encountered a crash in the church. I'm not sure if this fixed my problem, but it didn't occur afterwards anymore.
Honestly, I'm not really into third person shooters, but if you want to get one, you might like Sniper Elite V2, 3 or the Nazi Zombie Trilogy.

I'm not usually one to write reviews, but this is a charming little game that needs more attention. The story is endearing, though some may find it short for the price. Friday the 13th excels at creating and maintaining the atmosphere of an '80s slasher film. Jason feels omnipresent and appropriately unstoppable, and playing a counselor feels like playing a gazelle running from a lion. The best you can hope for is to avoid notice, or hold him off long enough for you to escape or for him to lose interest for the time being.
The game is an absolute blast with friends, or in the extremely unlikely event that you're matched with a group of random players that happens to mesh and coordinate well (and have a reasonable grasp of the same language). At its best, the game is as much fun as any multiplayer game released in the past ten years.
The bad? Where to start.
The game is buggy. Numerous exploits still exist as of the writing of this review. Counselors can clip through the walls, or get on top of roofs, or find spots of water where Jason can't get to them. Vital objective items will fall through the ground and be irretrievable upon a player dying, rendering some objectives impossible to complete.
The game crashes constantly. My average is around four games before a crash that either goes to desktop or necessitates ending the game in task manager. Get a full lobby of 8 friends together, and you're virtually guaranteed that someone is going to crash and be left out for that game. If you're the host, this kills the game for everyone.
Hosting is another problem. There's no host migration, so if the player hosting decides to quit for whatever reason (didn't get picked to be Jason, died early, is just generally a jerk, etc.) the game ends with no input from anyone else.
There are long periods of inactivity. You die, you get to wait through the entire match if you want the experience points that you earned. Doesn't matter if there's 15 minutes left or 15 seconds. You sit there and you wait. If you leave, you get nothing.
The game, when it goes badly, slows to a crawl. Someone grabs an important objective item, runs out into the wilderness to deliver it, and dies in the woods. No one knows where their corpse, and therefore the item, is. There are only enough items to complete every objective once. It's entirely possible (and a not infrequent occurence) in a pick up game to lose enough of them that every single item based objective is impossible to complete, rendering the game effectively unwinnable unless you're able to hide for 20 minutes. A lot of players are going to die, which means a lot of players are going to be sitting in spectator mode watching a high stealth character do absolutely nothing but hide under a bed for a quarter of an hour. This is profoundly unfun for absolutely everyone involved.
Finally, and in my opinion, most maddeningly, is the RNG factor. The game is totally reliant on RNG. RNG determines who plays as Jason. It determines where you start (Bad RNG and start next to an important objective? You're likely to be killed unless you're lucky enough to find something useful in the first house, which is reliant on...) RNG to determine what items are in the cabins, and in the drawers found inside the cabins. RNG to determine who gets to come back as the max stat summoned character, Tommy Jarvis. RNG to determine if the perk you buy is any good, or a waste of time (mitigated somewhat by being able to 'sell' perks back, but the worse the perk the worse the refund) and it's entirely possible if not likely that you'll burn through several thousand points and get absolutely nothing worthwhile.
Overall, I WOULD recommend Friday the 13th, but ONLY if you intend to play it with friends. This is not a game that's fun to play alone. It's not a game that's worth 40 dollars unless you have a group of people to play it with. The gameplay in pick up groups is often slow and painfully repetitive, which would be acceptable if it were a predominantly skill based game where you made incremental improvements, but the game's over reliance on RNG means that there's a computer imposed ceiling on how well you CAN do in any given match.
Friday the 13th's mechanics are absolutely wonderful for creating a fun, authentic slasher film experience that's wonderfully entertaining to explore with friends. They're not very good at creating a GAME that's fun to play as a competitive activity for any length of time.
